  - stored documents changed under their digests, and every check a pull makes,
    refused when the image is found again too.

### Credentials, certificates and `shards pull image` (D23)

`docker login` state and Docker's certificates work unchanged
([registry-pull](../research/registry-pull.md) §3.3, §6.3, R5). The code is
`crates/registry/src/credentials.rs`, `certs.rs`, and `crates/shards/src/pull.rs`.

- **Credentials** are found as the Docker CLI v29.8.1 finds them:
  - `config.json` from `$DOCKER_CONFIG` or `~/.docker`;
  - Docker Hub's key `https://index.docker.io/v1/`, or else the host;
  - `DOCKER_AUTH_CONFIG` first; then the host's `credHelpers` entry, `credsStore`, or
    `auths`;
  - the platform's default helper when the config holds no credentials at all;
  - helpers spoken to over their protocol, with `<token>` marking an identity token: a
    pull's helper started as its registry is made, its answer read only where the
    registry's own host challenges, a wait for it said, and a cancel ending it (D184).
  - dockerd's precedence: a registry token, then an identity token, then a password.
  - Written by `shards login registry` alone (D171), where docker writes them.
- **`certs.d`** is read as dockerd reads it:
  - `*.crt` files hold CAs, beside the platform's roots;
  - a `*.cert` with its `*.key` is a client certificate. dockerd offers all of them;
    rustls takes one, so we use the first by name.
  - The directories are Docker Desktop's `~/.docker/certs.d`, the rootless engine's
    `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/docker/certs.d`, and the native engine's `/etc/docker/certs.d` or
    `%PROGRAMDATA%\docker\certs.d` (docker/docs `engine/security/certificates.md`).
  - One TLS configuration serves every host of a pull (registry, token realm, CDN): the
    trust its user set for a registry is for the hosts its pulls go to.
  - Or the one directory `SHARDS_CERTS_D` names, alone, in their place, as
    `SHARDS_DAEMON_JSON` names one daemon.json (D194), and as there one named must be
    there (2026-11-13, CI cluster 14). A client sends it to the daemon with the rest of
    `REGISTRY_ENV`. The tests name their own, empty (tests/common `as_tests_run`): a
    stand-in host certs.d under `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` holding, for the tests' own registry, a
    client key with no certificate failed a build from it (red at 60216c106), and reaches no
    test now (`images`' `a_hosts_certs_d_reaches_no_test`; `certs`'
    `the_certs_d_named_is_read_alone`).
- **The store** lives in `$SHARDS_HOME/images`, else in the platform's data directory:
  - `~/Library/Application Support` on macOS, per Apple's guidance;
  - `$XDG_DATA_HOME` or `~/.local/share` elsewhere on Unix;
  - `%LOCALAPPDATA%` on Windows.
  - It is created 0700: it is its user's alone.
- **`shards pull image`** prints `docker pull`'s lines: the default tag, `Already exists` or
  `Download complete` per layer, `Digest:` and `Status:`.
- **Checked against real registries** (2026-09-28, from the M5 Max):
  - Docker Hub (`alpine`, and by digest), GHCR (`ghcr.io/containerd/busybox:1.36`) and
    Quay (`quay.io/prometheus/busybox`).
  - `alpine` took 1.5 s the first time and 0.33 s once stored.
  - Its EROFS image booted in a shards microVM and ran `/bin/sh` in Alpine 3.24.2.
- **Tests:**
  - fake credential helpers that answer, mark an identity token, have nothing, or fail;
  - `DOCKER_AUTH_CONFIG` and its fallback;
  - `certs.d` CAs, and a mutual-TLS handshake with and without its client certificate.

### `shards run vm IMAGE` (D24)

`shards run vm [OPTIONS] IMAGE [COMMAND] [ARG...]` runs a command in a new microVM booted
into an image, as `docker run` runs one in a new container. The code is
`crates/shards/src/run.rs`. The VM and the workload are D16's.

- **The image** comes from the store, or is pulled first (D22, D23), as `docker run`
  pulls it: "Unable to find image … locally", then `docker pull`'s lines, on stderr.
  `--pull missing|always|never` as for `docker run`.
- **The workload** merges the command line over the image's config, as dockerd merges
  them (moby docker-v29.8.1 `daemon/commit.go`, `merge`):
  - the user and working directory are the image's unless given;
  - the environment is the given variables, then each of the image's whose name was
    not given, and D16 lays that over Docker's `PATH` and `HOSTNAME`;
  - the image's command applies only when neither an entrypoint nor a command is given;
  - its entrypoint applies unless one is given, and `--entrypoint ""` clears it.
- **Not yet:** ports and volumes. A kernel and shards-init that ship with shards came
  later (D28), as did terminals and detached runs (D16, D27).
- **Checked against Docker Hub** (2026-09-28): `alpine`, `busybox:1.36` pulled on
  demand then run (1.0 s in all), and `hello-world` from its own `Cmd`.
- **Tests:**
  - unit tests for each rule of the merge;
  - E2E, a loopback registry and a real VM: the image's user, directory and
    environment apply. A second run uses the stored image, fetches nothing, and the
    command line wins.

### Templates for `shards run vm` (D25)

Repeated runs of an image restore a template of it instead of booting (D2, D14). The code
is `crates/shards/src/run.rs` and `crates/shards/src/guest.rs`.

- **The guest, by content.** `shards guest use --kernel FILE --init FILE` copies both
  files into `$SHARDS_HOME/guest`, named by their SHA-256, and records them as the guest.
  A run then knows what it boots by digest, without reading either file.
- **Templates, by content.** A template's name is the SHA-256 of what goes into it:
  - the snapshot format;
  - the kernel's and init's digests;
  - the image's root filesystem, whose EROFS file is named by ChainID (D18);
  - the CPU count, memory and kernel command line.

  A change to any of these names another template. Nothing is compared by time.
- **The first run saves it.** The first run of an image on the guest in use boots. Once
  the image is mounted it saves the template, then resumes and runs the command
  (`AfterSnapshot::Resume`, D16).
  - It saves into a directory of its own, renamed into place only when complete.
  - If another run's template got there first, the other copy is removed.
- **Later runs restore it.** A template that does not restore is removed; the run boots
  instead and says so on stderr, and the next run saves the template again.
- **Its files held open.** The daemon holds each template's files open from its first
  restore until the template is removed or replaced (`snapshot::hold`): its memory, its
  writable layer's and DAX windows' heads, and the files its guest only reads, its root
  filesystem among them. A file no process holds open gives up its vnode once its host's
  vnode table is full, and the pages cached of it with it (XNU `vclean`). On a Mac whose
  263,168 vnodes recycled 2,800 a second, a cold run after a build's worth of files had
  been looked at read its template's whole working set back from the disk a page at a time,
  and its guest its programs from its root filesystem: 7.9 to 11.0 s where a warm one took
  0.2 to 0.6. Held, 0.46 to 0.96 s [PM M315]. On Windows a view of its memory is held
  mapped too (`platform::keep_cached`): Windows drops a sparse file's pages from its cache
  once no process maps them, held open or not, where a dense file's stay, and a memory file
  is sparse; 1,000 pages of a sparse file's data took 200 to 573 ms each time, read from
  the disk again, and 1.6 to 2.1 with a view of it held [PM M421].
- **A run records the working set**: each guest page it touches until its command
  answers, or a while after the command starts, saved with the template as
  `working-set`. REAP found that restored copies of a serverless function's snapshot
  touch nearly the same pages (Ustiugov et al., ASPLOS 2021).
  - **HVF: the first run**, from the snapshot on, for up to 50 ms past its command's
    start [PM M30]. Its guest memory is taken away at stage 2 (`hv_vm_protect`), and
    each page goes back on its first fault, read-only if read, so a later write is seen
    too. Recording slows that run's command about sixfold, on a run that is a boot
    anyway. The boot's set covered 99.7–100% of what warm VMs touched while serving a
    run. A page any vCPU has written goes back writable to every vCPU after, and each
    page goes back under the recording's lock, in the order decided: a read's page given
    back read-only after another vCPU's write had it writable took the write away, and the
    writer, faulting on a page it had just had back whole, ended the VM (4 of 60 templates
    of 18 vCPUs; none of 180 since, PM M183).
  - **KVM: the first warm restore without one** (`vm::RESTORES_RECORD`), from its restore
    on, for up to 1 s past its command's start [PM M33]. A restore's memory is mapped
    from files, copy-on-write, afresh, so the pages its host maps when the recording ends
    are the ones touched, and a private copy is one written (`/proc/self/pagemap`: the
    present and file-page bits, which need no privilege). Recording costs it nothing.
    The saving run's pages are not a restore's: only 5–16% of a restore's request pages
    were among them, while one restore's were 99.7–100% of the next's [PM M33].
    `shards restore DIR` records one the same way on a generation's first restore, its
    spawner keeping it (D30), and later restores map it ahead. A page its host maps is
    not always one its guest touched: a read fault on a file maps the pages around it its
    page cache holds too (fault-around), and the comparison's working sets held 4.6 to
    5.2 times the pages their guests faulted, every one mapped ahead, 2.5 to 3 MiB more
    of the memory file than a restore without one held [PM M312]. A restored machine
    holds the host's fault-around off over its guest's memory and pmem for its life
    (`platform::FaultAroundOff`: a userfaultfd registered for asynchronous
    write-protection, Linux 6.7, that write-protects nothing and handles no fault), so
    that a working set records, and a restore maps ahead, what its guest touched: 739 to
    778 pages where 2,753 to 2,902, its memory file 3.7 to 3.9 MiB resident where 11.6 to
    12.3 and Firecracker's 11.6 to 14.1. Held only while a working set was mapped ahead,
    letting it go reset its pages' tables, and KVM's stage 2 with them, and the guest
    faulted them all in again [PM M312]. Before 6.7, or where a container's filter
    refuses userfaultfd, it goes on as before. With both, 20 runs of the Firecracker
    comparison in a row, on every CPU CI's runners land on, held its envelope on every
    metric, a restore reaching its guest's first beat 5.0 to 8.2 ms before Firecracker's
    and holding 7.7 to 8.2 MiB less of its memory file [PM M316].
  - The whole way from the request to the command's start is recorded, however long a
    host takes over it; the cap only ends a long command's recording.
  - It is written through the directory held open since the snapshot (or the restore),
    since the daemon renames a new template into place meanwhile. A damaged one is
    ignored, and on KVM recorded again.
  - A generation keeps the first it is given (snapshot `accept_working_set`), and
    replaces only one a restore could not read. On KVM each restore made before a set
    lands records one, a pool's first VMs together, and each sends its own as its run
    ends: written over the one before, the last one won, and once that was one recorded
    as its guest gave memory back, 9,529 pages where the first held 41,834; a budget the
    FUSE budget E2E set from what the next restore held was then 24 MiB short of what
    its run needed, and its read did not end in 600 s (PM M320).
  - A recording keeps what its host held of the RAM its guest gives back while it
    records (D151's free page reports; `GuestMemory::keep_given_back`): the pages its
    host maps when it ends no longer show one given back, and the set would leave it
    out. It sends none where it could not see a range given back.
  - *What its written pages, copied ahead, hold at a first beat* (measured, open; PM M616).
    A restore copies ahead every page its working set says the guest wrote
    (`mapped::copy_written`), so in the Firecracker comparison each restore of one snapshot
    held the same private copies of its guest's memory by its guest's first beat: 218 to
    231 pages over four snapshots on an AMD EPYC 9V74 and 222 to 231 over four on an Intel
    Xeon 6975P-C, where Firecracker's guest, copying only as it writes, held 124 to 145, and
    shards-vm's own anonymous pages were 35 to 37 to Firecracker's process's 114 to 132.
    The comparison's guest runs no command, so its working set is recorded over a
    restore's first second, where a run's ends as its command answers. How many of those
    pages its guest writes before its first beat, with nothing copied ahead, is
    unmeasured: a restore of the comparison's snapshot without its `working-set`, its
    `written_pages`. Copying ahead only those would hold the rest uncopied until its guest
    writes them, each then copied on its first write, as Firecracker's are; the cost to
    `to_beat` and a command's first second is unmeasured too. Not taken for 0.8.0 (ROOT,
    2026-11-17). Decided (ROOT's ruling, R08/R14, 2026-11-17): the copy-ahead stays, the
    trade it is (CI 44189693085, an Azure Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C: copies 223 to 231 pages
    to Firecracker's 125 to 145, shards-vm's own 37 to 112 to 129, the first beat 8.2 ms to
    11.7), and the comparison reads both VMMs' memory after the same guest time, the end of
    this recording's window (`RECORD_FOR`, now `shards_vmm::vm`'s, which the VM process and
    the bench share): D36.
  - *A restore whose guest runs no command ends its recording at its spawner's word*
    (amended 2026-11-18, ROOT's ruling, kiln goal #39).
    - The failure: CI 44227612442's comparison (7ca9f46, Intel Xeon 6975P-C) read
      `fleet_pte` worse, +0.0068 MiB [+0.0039, +0.0117], a page table's page more a VM.
      It is not a change: shards read 160 to 164 KiB on 6975P-C runners at every revision
      since b18952a.
    - The cause is this recording. A restore whose guest runs no command recorded for
      `RECORD_FOR` from its start, a second, where the comparison's guest beats at about
      10 ms. About 100 of the 218 to 231 pages its sets said written were its idle guest's
      after its beat (Firecracker's guest writes 127 to 157 by its beat, restore-anon), at
      places that differ by recording. Every restore maps and copies them ahead, and each
      recorded 2 MiB span its own guest does not touch costs a page table's page. pages.tsv's
      restores show it: on the 6975P-C (7ca9f46) shards alone touched the spans at 68 and
      70 MiB, about 10 copies each (fleet median +4 KiB); on an AMD EPYC 9V45 (0f83166)
      shards alone 56 MiB (+3 KiB); on a Xeon 8573C (0782de3) Firecracker alone 68 MiB
      (0 KiB). The same pages were `fleet_private`'s and `rss_anon`'s gap.
    - The reason: a run's recording ends as its command answers; the comparison's
      recorded a second only because its guest runs no command. Ending it at the guest's
      first beat makes the comparison measure what a run does, not a bench tuned to win.
    - The change: such a restore takes `--record-until FD` (Windows: NAME) beside
      `--working-set`. A byte or the end on it ends the recording, handed at once while
      its guest goes on; without it, `RECORD_FOR` as before. Runs, warm VMs and restores
      with a command keep their answer-ended recordings, and the flag refuses them. The
      comparison's recording restore says it at its guest's first beat, `to_beat`'s own
      point, so its set is what its guest touches to its beat, which the restore before
      it holds whole (PM M310: share 1.000 at the median).
    - Copying ahead only a run's pre-answer writes in production (PM M616's open item)
      stays declined for 0.8.0.
    - Tests: vm_run.rs `a_spawners_word_ends_a_bare_restores_recording` and
      `record_until_is_a_bare_restores_with_its_working_set`; snapshot.rs
      `a_bare_restore_told_to_end_its_recording_hands_what_it_had_recorded_by_then` (told
      at once, fewer pages than one recorded until its VM ends). Red:
      lanes/redgreen/own-38d-record-until.patch. Whether it clears `fleet_pte`,
      `fleet_private` and `rss_anon`: the next CI comparison, owed.
- **Where it applies.** Builds that can snapshot (HVF on arm64, KVM on x86_64,
  `vm::SNAPSHOTS`, and so `vm::WORKING_SETS`); elsewhere every run boots. `--kernel`
  and `--init`, or `SHARDS_KERNEL` and `SHARDS_INIT`, name files by path, so those runs
  always boot.
- **Saved quiescent.** The kernel is still running its crypto self-tests after init
  mounts the image, for about 20 ms. The template waits for them (D16), or every restored
  run would replay the rest: most stalled for a tick (PM M21).
- **Measured** (docs/benchmarks.md, "Image"), over 10 templates on a busy host: 7.5 ms at
  p50 against 34.2 ms for a boot. It was 16.5 ms before templates waited for the
  self-tests.
- **Not yet:** removing templates and guests nothing uses. A working set is recorded
  once, from its template's first command; later commands' own pages still fault.
- **Tests** (E2E, a real VM):
  - the first run boots and saves one template, and then (HVF) its working set, or (KVM)
    the second run, the first restore, records it;
  - a later restore prefetches it, and a damaged one only costs the prefetch;
  - the second restores it, with no `INIT_STARTED` marker, the image's settings and the
    host's clock;
  - a corrupted template is removed and that run boots;
  - the next run saves the template again, under the same name.

### Warm pool (D26, in progress)

A per-user daemon hands each `shards run vm` to a **warm VM**: a VMM process that has already
restored the image's template, resumed the guest and let it connect, and now waits only
for a command (D2). The client asks the daemon for a run, passes it its stdio, and waits
for the exit status.

- **Built: warm VMs** (`crates/shards/src/warm.rs`; messages in `crates/ipc`).
  - `shards restore DIR --warm FD` is one, where FD is its socket to the daemon.
    `shards run vm … --rootfs R [--snapshot-dir D] --warm FD` boots one instead, saving a
    template on the way if asked.
  - It says `READY` once the guest waits for its command.
  - The daemon answers with `RUN`: the command, plus four descriptors passed by
    `SCM_RIGHTS`: the client's connection, then its stdin, stdout and stderr. They become
    the warm VM's own stdio, so the workload writes straight to the client's. The VM
    answers `TAKEN`.
  - Signals come from the client on its connection, as Linux numbers, from the moment its
    request is on its way; one that would end the client (SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP or
    SIGQUIT, not ignored as it started) as `INTERRUPT`. Until the run is prepared (its
    image pulled), the daemon's watch of the client reads them: an `INTERRUPT` is the
    client's end, which the daemon answers (`INTERRUPTED`), cancelling the prepare and
    making no microVM, and the client ends with 128 and the signal's number, nothing said,
    the status a script reads of a command its signal ended; the rest are for a command
    yet to run, and go. After, they wait for the run's VM, which takes an `INTERRUPT` as a
    signal for the command. Only the daemon knows which side of the run's making a signal
    came: the command's output reaches the client on a stream of its own, before the
    client may have heard `CREATED`, which the daemon's slot relay passes on from a thread
    of its own (PM M332). Once the VM has taken a run, they queue until the command runs.
  - The exit status goes back the moment the command ends, before the VM is torn down.
    Any error reaches the client's stderr first. The VM lets go of the client's stdio
    before the status, so a pipeline reading it ends with the client, and again when the
    client hangs up, so a command outliving its client writes nowhere. A container's
    output likewise stops reaching a `docker run` that has gone.
  - Before `READY` it makes room in its descriptor table for what a run brings and opens
    (warm.rs `reserve_descriptors`): Linux grows a table its threads share only after an
    RCU grace period, which held a run's hand-over 8 to 15 ms on a 32-CPU host whose warm
    VMs' 64 descriptors filled their first table (PM M470).
  - Each message to the daemon goes whole, under one lock (warm.rs `to_daemon`), as the
    daemon's to a VM do (`RunSocket`): the VM's threads send on its connection and on
    clones of it (the run's end and its working set, its processes' records, its log's
    asks, a save's answer), and Linux queues a stream message larger than one buffer in
    pieces, between which another's could land. A working set of 341 KB was read with
    another's bytes in it, refused, and the stream broken, the daemon taking the VM for
    ended: 1 of 511 sets taken on CI's runners (PM M319).
  - The warm VM serves one request, then exits.
- **Built: the daemon** (`crates/shards/src/daemon.rs`), with `shards run vm` as its client
  (`client.rs`).
  - One serves each SHARDS_HOME, holding its `daemon.lock`. `shards run vm` starts it when
    none offers its request slots, in the home's `requests/` (D185; a socket,
    `daemon.sock`, before), through `shards daemon --detached`, which starts it in a session of its own and exits: init adopts the
    daemon and reaps it when it exits (APUE §13.3). Left the child of the client that
    started it, it stayed a zombie for as long as that client lived.
  - Every process that uses the slots first makes the home its working directory, and
    names them relative to it, as it named the socket, whose name had to fit a socket
    address whatever the home's path. The per-user directories macOS offers for sockets
    cost each new process 0.4–1.3 ms to look up [PM M26].
  - **A renamed home remains its daemon's directory** (runs-02, 2026-11-13).
    On Unix every stored home-relative pathname starts at `.` after the daemon's one
    chdir, including its lock, registry, requests, stopping markers and final cleanup.
    Renaming A to B and recreating A therefore never makes the old daemon write into A.
    An unlinked lock still ends the daemon; final removal uses the current directory's
    actual name, not `.` as a directory-entry removal. Windows keeps its absolute path:
    its current directory cannot be renamed or removed while held (D185).
    The subprocess unit reproduces the overwritten replacement marker before the fix
    and verifies retained offers/PID and removal of the old remainder after it. See
    [runs-fixes](../research/measurements/runs-fixes/README.md); live daemon/VM checks
    remain ROOT's. This adds no timeout, polling, cache or platform manager.
  - *Handed whole across a launch* (ROOT, 2026-11-14). A VM process does not start in the
    daemon's directory: macOS App Sandbox starts it in its container's `Data` directory, so
    a `./…` path handed it named another file there, and every HVF run of an image with
    agents ended 125 (`<chain>.over-<hex>.erofs: No such file or directory`; bisected to
    this entry's d3b11258a, member_exec at 8fdd66512). `launch.rs` `absolute` makes each word
    before a VM's `--` that is `.` or `./…` absolute from the launching process's working
    directory as it launches, which names the home where it is then, renamed or not; the
    guest's words past `--` stay as given. Red: HVF member_exec at 8fdd66512; unit
    `launch::tests::a_vms_paths_from_here_are_handed_it_whole_and_its_guests_words_as_given`.
  - It admits only clients of its own user: its slots are FIFOs of mode 0600 in a
    directory of 0700, and a connection's peer is checked besides (`getpeereid`,
    `SO_PEERCRED`): a home in a shared directory must not let another user run commands as
    this one [PM M25].
  - **Its clients are bounded (audit A07).**
    - A client has 10 s to send its whole request. The deadline bounds the message, not
      each read, so a client trickling it out a byte at a time gains nothing
      (`shards_ipc::recv_by`).
    - It holds as many clients at once as the threads it may have hold (review 7.9),
      each a thread, the watcher of a VM started for its run, and up to six
      descriptors; past that, connections wait in the listener's backlog. The threads
      are the system's to say: `kern.num_taskthreads` on macOS (16,384 here, so 8,187
      clients past the daemon's own eight threads and the dispatch worker a framework
      it calls keeps [PM M98]), and on Linux the least of
      `RLIMIT_NPROC`, `threads-max` and the `pids.max` of its control groups, up to the
      root its namespace sees, where a container's limit is (Linux
      Documentation/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.rst). Windows keeps no count of them: there
      they are the fewest its address space, its commit limit (its job's, where that
      holds it to less) and a process's handles hold of a thread, each cost read off a
      thread started as std starts every thread of shards' (D181, PM M529). Where none
      is said, POSIX's `_POSIX_THREAD_THREADS_MAX` (64), which Windows took before.
      `SHARDS_MAX_CLIENTS` sets fewer. The 256 before was chosen, not derived.
    - A client that waits long, on a microVM's end (`wait`) or its output
      (`logs -f`), counts among those in hand no more, so that waiters shut out no
      client however many there are. A thread that cannot be spawned still drops its
      client.
    - Out of descriptors, it waits for room rather than spin on a listener that stays
      readable, and accepts again only once a descriptor is free: an accept that fails
      for want of one leaves the client queued on Linux (net/socket.c,
      `__sys_accept4_file`) but drops it on macOS ("Don't put this back on the socket
      like we used to, that just causes the client to spin. Drop the socket.",
      xnu-11417.101.15 bsd/kern/uipc_syscalls.c). On macOS it looks for a free
      descriptor before every accept, a `dup` and a `close`, 250 ns [PM M99], and drops
      no client; looking only once starved, it dropped two, the one whose accept found
      none and, once room came, the one after the first it took, which had taken the
      last.
    - It raises its soft limit on descriptors to its hard one, capped at
      `kern.maxfilesperproc` on macOS, as Go's runtime raises its own (go1.25.0
      src/syscall/rlimit.go, after go.dev/issue/46279): macOS starts a process with 256.
  - It keeps up to SHARDS_POOL warm VMs (default 2) of each template it has served, as
    many as its runs need (below). A pool refills once its VM has taken its run, since
    starting the next VM on the request's path cost 200–600 µs [PM M26]: on the refiller's
    thread, which takes every pool asked for meanwhile, each once. A run with no template
    boots a VM that saves one on the way, and a run with its own kernel and init boots
    every time. A template is removed and saved again once a VM of it fails for its
    template's sake, and for nothing else (below).
  - **What breaks a template: its own fault alone** (ROOT's ruling of 2026-11-17, D26 against
    D261; goal 1453357d). It was three warm VMs failing in a row (`MAX_FAILURES`, a count no
    record derived: R03). EC2's Intel runners (Xeon 6975P-C, nested KVM) refuse entries in
    bursts (D261), and three refills refused in a row broke a good template: its next claim
    deleted it and booted, every run still waiting on its pool was told at once that "none is
    starting for it" (no refill can be planned without a template), and the runs after it
    booted cold. Read from the code (daemon.rs `claim`, `watch`; refill.rs `plan_refill`); the
    shape of CI's Intel Arrival runs, 362 and 108 of 386 requests failed at 40 a second
    (`docs/research/measurements/arrival-drain/`), the next Intel run's kept daemon log to
    confirm (R09). Now a VM that took no run tells its daemon by its status whether it ended
    for its template's sake (`shards_ipc::TEMPLATE_FAILED_STATUS`, vm_run.rs `serve_workload`),
    and only these classes are its template's, each from the code:
    - its template's files did not read: `shards_vmm::snapshot::read` refused its pointer, its
      generation's state or its memory, or what its machine keeps beside its memory, its
      writable layer's head or file system (D190) or its DAX windows' heads (D189), each opened
      as the generation is read (`snapshot::Pinned`; vm_run.rs `restore_reported`,
      `read_snapshot`);
    - its guest reset before it took a run, as its kernel's panic does under `panic=-1`
      (`ExitReason::Reset`);
    - its guest powered off before it took a run, its init having ended
      (`ExitReason::PowerOff`).
    One such end breaks its template (`Pool::broken`), for its next claim to remove and boot
    instead: what a template's files or its guest do, every restore of it does again, so one
    is the whole of the evidence, and no count stands in for a cause. A pool whose root
    filesystem was replaced since its template was keyed is broken as before.
    Not its template's, counted against nothing: its host's hypervisor refusing to enter a
    vCPU (`ExitReason::Refused`, D261), whether or not D261's gate takes the refusal for its
    host's, as the gate tells its host's refusal from its VMM's and neither is its template's;
    its VMM's error (`ExitReason::Error`); its stop (`ExitReason::Stopped`); a start that failed
    short of its template's files (its hypervisor, memory, vCPUs, confinement); a launch its
    host had not let run (macOS's grants, PM M166); its start's judge giving up on it (`ready`,
    D215). Init's refusal of another build's contract (`workload::OtherInit`) comes after READY,
    as a run is taken: it fails that run, 125 as `docker run` fails a command that never ran,
    and touches no pool; the guest's configuration is its cause, which a cold boot repeats.
    A template's files fail as it is read, not later (ROOT's word, goal 1453357d): its layer's
    head and file system and its windows' heads were opened inside the VMM's restore, past
    `snapshot::read`, where a missing one was not told from its host's failures and counted
    against nothing; the read opens them now, beside its memory, by what its machine keeps
    (`snapshot::Pinned`), and the restore and its daemon's hold (`snapshot::hold`, PM M315)
    take them from it, opening none again. Red under `own-38b-beside-unread.patch` (the read
    opening its state and memory alone): snapshot's
    `a_generation_reads_only_with_what_its_machine_keeps_beside_its_memory`. What a restore
    does with them after counts against nothing still, as each step there mixes its
    template's file with its host's: its layer's copy into the restore's own file
    (`platform::copy_used`, reading its template's, writing to its host's disk) and its head's
    mapping (`pmem::Layer::restore`).
  - **A run waiting on a pool fails only where a judge refuses it** (the same ruling). A refill
    that fails for no fault of its template's leaves the runs that wait waiting: each wakes and
    plans the next refill for the runs with none starting (`plan_refill`'s `for_runs`), and
    "none is starting for it" is said only where no refill can be planned (its template gone or
    broken, its root filesystem unrecorded or replaced) and none is starting. A refill that its
    start's judge gives up on (D215, `ready`: it ran nothing past the slowest start seen) fails a
    run left waiting with no refill starting for it, in the judge's words (`Pool::refused`,
    typed `NotReady::Refused`); one for each such refill, no more than the runs that wait. A run
    waits on a judge of its own (ROOT's ruling of 2026-11-17, D215 by the record of starts,
    `Answers::ready`, the kind it waits on): at each look due, its pool progressed where a
    refill came ready since the look before (`Pool::readied`); it is live (`Found::Held`)
    where a refill still starts, its own start's judge following it, and none has ended
    unready since; it is still where its refills keep ending unready for no fault of its
    template's (`Pool::ended_unready`: its host refusing every entry, a VMM's error on every
    start) or none starts. Still for a whole W* of starts, its wait is refused, the run told
    that none of its pool's refills came ready, its template whole. A kind not yet taught
    judges nothing, its wait following its refills alone, as D215's cold waits do.
  - Held by daemon.rs `refills_no_fault_of_their_templates_keep_it_and_the_next_serves_the_run_waiting`
    (three refills ended NOT_RUN leave the template whole, and the run waiting is served by the
    next), `a_refill_failed_for_its_template_breaks_it` (one ended TEMPLATE_FAILED_STATUS breaks
    it, its claim then Broken) and `a_refill_its_judge_gave_up_on_fails_the_run_left_waiting`
    (a refill silent past W* fails the run waiting, "ran nothing for", the template whole), and
    `a_run_waiting_on_a_pool_that_keeps_refusing_refills_is_refused_by_its_own_judge` (refills
    ending NOT_RUN one after another, a W* of 100 ms taught: the run refused, "none of its
    refills came ready", the template whole): stand-in processes and links, no VM. Their reds
    are mutations of `watch`'s `Fault` (every end the template's; none; the judge's as any
    other) and of `claim`'s own judge (its refusal ignored), kept in the lane's record
    (lanes/redgreen/own-38b-*.patch). Owed (ROOT): those tests and the pool tests, clippy on
    every target, and the next EC2 CI run's Arrival, its kept daemon log saying each refill's
    end and fault.
  - **VMs start outside the pools' lock** (review 7.8). What a pool needs is planned under
    it and counted as starting at once, so that no other claim or refill starts it again,
    then started without it: a start spawns the VM and its network process. A claim that
    finds no VM ready starts its own on its own thread. Started under the lock, they held
    every other claim, refill and the listener's look at the pools for up to 1.3 ms (p99
    0.7 to 0.9 ms); now under 0.2 ms. A burst's runs took as long either way, its restores
    outweighing its spawns [PM M91].
  - **Warm VMs are speculation, and bounded; runs are served regardless** (audit A13,
    A14).
    - A run that finds no VM ready has one started for it, unless one is already
      starting for a run before it: a pool of 0 (`SHARDS_POOL=0`) keeps nothing warm and
      restores each run's VM on demand, and a burst larger than the pool waits for no
      refill. Before, a pool of 0 never filled, and every repeat run waited 60 s and
      failed.
    - All pools together keep at most `SHARDS_WARM_MAX` (16) VMs ahead of runs: a warm
      VM's own memory is 3.4 MiB, so about 55 MiB; RSS, about 20 MB a VM, counts the
      template's pages it shares in full (PM M49).
      A pool that would pass it first ends the ready VMs of the pools least recently
      claimed from. Only a ready VM can be ended, so once a pool's VM becomes ready, the
      pools claimed from since that are short refill again, and it gives way to them.
    - Settings are counts, checked before the daemon serves: a malformed one, a pool
      larger than all pools may keep, or more than 256 warm VMs (the clients' bound, for
      the same threads and descriptors) stop it, and `shards daemon --detached` says
      why to the client that started it, at once.
    - **A pool keeps what its runs need while they come** (`daemon/demand.rs`, since D253
      shards-api's `demand.rs`, which an orchestrator's pools keep theirs by too).
      - Its size is the largest burst of runs seen within its keep-alive, at least one
        and at most SHARDS_POOL. A burst is the runs that arrive within one refill of
        each other, the refill's time, from a warm VM's start to its `READY`, estimated
        as TCP estimates a round trip's, and its window that estimate's retransmission
        timeout, SRTT + 4·RTTVAR (RFC 6298 §2; its 1 s initial RTO until the first
        refill is timed): runs closer together than that may wait for a refill.
      - Its daemon says each refill it times, and the window it then keeps ("pool of DIR: a
        refill ready in N us; runs within W us of each other are one burst", 2026-11-17,
        goal fb3528f9), as only the daemon measures them. daemon.rs'
        `pools_keep_what_their_runs_need_while_they_come` spaces its runs past the window
        said, and starts its daemon again with a keep-alive as long as that window (R03). Its
        fixed keep-alive of 15 s was under a loaded host's window: CI 43968984258's x86_64
        musl job found runs 16 s apart still one burst.
      - A pool idle for SHARDS_POOL_KEEP seconds (600), none of its runs going and none
        claimed or ended within them, ends its ready VMs and keeps none until its next
        run, which is served all the same: a fixed keep-alive, as AWS and Azure keep a
        function's resources 10 and 20 minutes "after a function execution" (Shahrad et
        al., "Serverless in the Wild", USENIX ATC 2020, §1, §2), a keep-alive that "only
        starts at the end of function executions" (§4). Counted from its claims alone, a
        pool whose runs outlasted it kept nothing for the next: a loaded host's runs took
        28 to 31 s, past a test's keep-alive of 15 s (PM M346). Their hybrid histogram
        policy, which sets each application's keep-alive and pre-warming from its
        inter-arrival times, is not taken: the thresholds that say when its histogram is
        representative are not published, and no traces of agents' runs exist here to set
        them.
    - **What nothing needs is collected** (`Store::collect`, daemon.rs
      `collect_garbage`), at the daemon's start and once a pull, by a run or by `shards
      pull`, has moved a reference (it leaves `images/collect-due`, whose coming the
      daemon's watch of `images` sees).
      - The roots are the references: each one's manifest, config and layers, and the
        root filesystem of its layers' ChainID, and so each platform of its index that is
        here, which a run of that platform unpacked (D179). Every other blob and root
        filesystem goes, with older versions' records and root filesystems and what
        `ingest/` holds.
      - Content in flight is under the store's lease, a shared `flock` of
        `images/.lease` (flock(2)): a pull holds it until it has recorded its
        reference, `local` while it may build a root filesystem, and a run's
        preparation until its VM has its root filesystem. A collection takes it
        exclusively or not at all, and stays due; it holds the store until it has
        collected the templates too, so no run begins meanwhile. Each of the store's
        locks is unlocked before its file closes: a lock is its open file's, which a
        program another thread is starting shares until its exec, so that closed alone
        it stays held that long (PM M244: 5 to 14 times in 20,000 on macOS, 3 to 8 on
        Linux, with a program starting beside them; never once unlocked first).
      - A template records its origin, its root filesystem and guest (`origin.json`).
        One whose root filesystem has gone, that another guest saved, that records no
        origin, or that a daemon before this one left half saved is removed, and its
        pool's VMs ended; one this daemon is saving stays.
      - A running VM keeps what it has open or mapped: removing a file removes its
        name, not the file (unlink(2)).
      - It runs on a thread of its own, the collector's (review 7.14): on the thread that
        accepts clients, every client waited in the backlog for as long as it took, 4.5 s
        for 20,000 files left in `ingest/`, against 3.9 ms at most now [PM M94]. It waits
        for the store's lease, the kernel waking it once the last is let go (flock(2)).
        None starts while the listener is out of descriptors, which its files would take
        from clients macOS then drops, nor once the daemon is stopping.
    - Measured with 1, 10 and 100 templates [PM M49]: 100 keep 16 warm VMs, 54.5 MiB of
      their own; a template without one restores on demand, p50 16 ms against 5 ms
      warm; bursts of 8 find two ready and restore the rest, p50 about 16 ms; every
      run succeeded, and `daemon stop` left no VM. Not measured: 1,000 templates, whose
      35 GiB of templates this machine cannot spare, and low host memory.
  - **It keeps its copies of the client's descriptors until the VM says `TAKEN`.**
    XNU's collector of in-flight descriptors flushes a socket in flight that no process
    holds: the client's connection then read end of stream, and 1 run in 13 to 53 never
    got its signals [PM M24]. A VM that ends before `TAKEN` is replaced.
  - A client of another build, told apart by its binary's file identity, gets
    `RESTART`. The daemon removes its socket, ends its runs as `shards daemon stop`
    does, and exits; the client starts its own, which takes the home once the old one
    has gone. The client asks again after a RESTART where it came from another daemon
    than the last it asked again after, each the one `daemon.pid` named as its request was
    asked (its ID and start): a takeover is the old daemon's RESTART, then its successor's
    answer. The same daemon answering so again as itself, nothing about it changed, would
    answer so for ever, and the client fails naming it; a count bounded it before
    (`RESTARTS`, 4; D185, *A request asked again*). A daemon ending its runs names itself
    in `daemon.stopping` first, as it closes for any reason, and the new daemon and the
    client wait while that process lives, however long its runs' stop timeouts make it;
    otherwise a daemon waits 20 s for another's lock, and a client 30 s for its daemon to
    listen. `daemon stop` waits on the lock it holds beside it until it has let go of the
    home (D185, *A stop's wait*).
  - It follows each run to its end. The warm VM tells the daemon of its command's start
    (`STARTED`) before its client has any of the command's output, and of its end
    (`DONE`) before its client has the status; a Unix socket's send puts a message in
    the daemon's queue before it returns. Every command on runs first takes what
    each run has sent (`settle`), under a lock per run that the followers' loop (below)
    reads under too, so it answers with all any client has seen: `ps` lists a run whose
    output has appeared, and not a `--rm` one whose `run` has returned, as dockerd
    records a container's state before `docker run` learns it (docker/cli run.go
    `waitExitOrRemoved`). Waiting for the daemon to acknowledge each instead cost a run
    241 µs at the median (95% [206, 293], `build-ab/ab.py`, n = 400); this costs none
    measurable (+16 µs, 95% [−30, +73]). The daemon can signal a command meanwhile, on
    the same socket.
  - **It waits on events, not a clock** (review 7.16, 7.22). Each run had a thread
    following it and another for its health checks, check or none, each waking every
    250 ms, as the listener and every `wait` and `logs -f` did: an idle running
    microVM cost the daemon two threads, 0.18 MiB and about 40 µs of CPU a second, and
    threads, 16,384 a process on macOS, would stop runs near 8,000, where their VMs take
    60 GB of a 128 GB host [PM M89].
    - One thread follows every run: a readiness poller over all their VMs' sockets
      (`platform::Poller`: kqueue(2) on macOS, epoll(7) on Linux, level-triggered) takes
      each run's messages as they come in whole. A socket the poller cannot take has its
      run followed on a thread of its own. It waits on no write: a run's end is kept in
      memory, in its reservation if its record is not yet written, its record written by
      the recorder and a `--rm` run's removal set aside by the completer. Waiting
      there for the record, or for the removal's rename, held up every other run's
      messages by 81 ms at a loaded host's p90 [PM M96]. Nor does it make the files a
      run's VM asks for: a working set is gathered there, in memory, within the bound
      read where the VM was started, and the set written, and each log segment made, on
      the files' thread (`daemon/files.rs`). On the loop, a segment held them 10.9 ms at
      a loaded host's p90 [PM M98].
    - The same thread follows every VM process to its end, and its network process to its
      own (`Poller::add_exit`: kqueue's `EVFILT_PROC` on macOS, a pidfd on Linux 5.3 and
      later), reaping each as it ends: a network process still running its grace after
      its VM, a second, is ended, and the VM's ports are freed once both have gone. A VM's
      watcher thread lives until its VM is ready, where it waited out the VM's life, the
      one thread an idle run still cost [PM M90]: now the daemon's threads stay 6 at 10
      running microVMs and at 100, and an idle run costs it about 10 KiB [PM M92];
      8 since the collector's and the files' threads [PM M98]. macOS watches only ends
      to come, and
      refuses a child that has ended already (`ESRCH`, measured), which is then reaped at
      once; a process whose end cannot be watched is waited for on a thread of its own.
    - One thread schedules the health checks of the microVMs that have one, from a
      heap of their due times, and runs each probe on a thread while it runs; dockerd
      keeps a goroutine per container and one per probe (moby 0fed273 daemon/health.go
      `monitor`).
    - One thread makes `--rm` runs' removals durable: one sync of their directory
      serves every removal pending, so runs that end together share it. A run named as
      one still being removed waits for the name.
    - One thread makes the files runs' VMs ask for, in the order asked: log segments, and
      working sets, each synced into its template.
    - The listener sleeps until a client arrives or leaves, a run ends, a warm VM comes
      ready, a name comes or goes in the home or in `images` (kqueue's `EVFILT_VNODE`,
      inotify(7)), or its next duty is due: the idle exit once nothing runs, or a pool's
      keep-alive. It looks every 250 ms only out of descriptors, or where a watch cannot
      be made.
    - A `wait` sleeps on a socket its run's end writes to and on its client's
      connection together, as a `logs -f` sleeps on that and on its log.
  - It exits after SHARDS_DAEMON_IDLE seconds (900) with no run in progress and none
    asked for. `shards daemon stop` first ends the runs in progress as dockerd ends its
    containers when it shuts down (moby daemon/daemon.go `shutdownContainer`,
    daemon/stop.go): each command gets its run's stop signal (SIGTERM if it has
    none), then SIGKILL once its stop timeout is up (10 s if it has none, never if it
    is negative), and its VM ends once its guest has had what tearing the command down
    costs it and has since run nothing of it for a slice (D217). The settings are those
    the run was made with, read before its record is written if need be. A
    daemon that another build replaces does the same: two daemons never keep one home's
    records.
    Keeping runs through a restart (live-restore) is a later milestone. A daemon killed
    outright takes its runs with it too: each VM is told its run's stop as the run is
    tracked (`STOP_ORDER`: its stop signal and grace, as above), and once its daemon's
    connection closes with the run going on, stops it so, its signal then SIGKILL. Before,
    a killed daemon's waiting VMs ended and its running ones ran on, reached by nothing: a
    failed test's restored microVM ran for a day and a half
    (`a_killed_daemons_runs_end_with_it`, a run and a restored run; mutation-checked: the
    order not sent, not taken). Its machine goes with them (ci-leaks, 2026-11-17): the order
    ends a run's command alone, and a guest goes on past that command where joiners run in it
    (D119) or it waits on its host, which nothing reaches once its daemon has gone. So each VM
    keeps its course (warm.rs `Course`): its run going, its end told, its end had (told, its
    layer kept or sent as asked), and its daemon there or gone; once its end is had and its
    daemon gone, it stops its machine, whatever its guest still serves. A link closing shows
    the daemon gone only while the run on it goes on, since a daemon that goes on lets go of a
    run's link once done with it, its end taken, its layer settled and its joiners ended: the
    VM's own link closing before its run's end is told, or a joiner's before that joiner's.
    Told no order (a visit's VM, D37, whose standby holds until it is killed, or a run whose
    daemon died before sending one), the command is SIGKILLed at once, as the daemon sends
    SIGKILL for a signal it cannot send; a grace waited out ends early at the run's end, its
    SIGKILL then unsent. Before, a joiner running as its daemon died held its microVM up for
    ever. (CI 43968984258's two microVMs, 20 minutes past their daemons, were held instead by
    a layer's ask their guests never answered, fixed where it was asked: D119, `SAVE` where a
    joiner ever joined.) Tests: daemon.rs
    `a_killed_daemons_joined_microvms_end_with_it` (a microVM whose command the daemon's going
    stops, and one whose command had ended, each with its joiner running), warm.rs
    `a_vms_machine_ends_once_its_run_is_over_and_its_daemon_gone` (every order of the
    course's moves). Not covered: a guest that never ends its command once SIGKILLed, nor
    answers its layer's ask, holds its VM still, as a cold home's daemon waits on one (D217);
    and a microVM held at a live move's last save (D176 part 7) stays held.
    **Amended (goal #36, CI 44077430171):** the layer's ask is covered. A daemon that ends
    settles no layer still to come: `tell_end` takes a run out of `runs` at its end, and the
    stop thread (`stop_each`) and the exit (`quiet`) look at `runs` alone, so a daemon whose
    home went stepped aside and exited while a microVM it still followed for its layer had its
    end told and its layer's ask out (x86_64 musl, containers.rs
    `run_limits_a_microvms_resources`: daemon 143243 gone as the test ended at 14:45:48, its
    microVM 208470 and network process 208466 still there at 14:50:37, reparented to the
    container's init, the VM's `workload` thread reading its run's connection, no relay of its
    daemon's or its client's, its signal connection ended at its command's end). Its own link
    closing past its end told showed nothing, as a daemon that goes on lets go of it then. Now
    it shows the daemon gone while the VM still owes it its layer's word (warm.rs
    `LAYER_OWED`, `Course::shows_gone`): from the run's taking, where it asks for the layer,
    to the word that it is sent; a layer kept in its file is said once its machine is down, and
    owed until then. And its machine ends once its end is told and its daemon gone, its layer's
    word unwaited for (`Course::ends`): it is its daemon's alone, and an ask its guest never
    answers held it for ever. Tests: warm.rs
    `a_vms_machine_ends_once_its_runs_end_is_told_and_its_daemon_gone` and
    `a_daemons_link_closing_shows_it_gone_while_it_follows_the_run`. Still open, the daemon's
    own close: it neither waits for nor ends a microVM settling its layer (`settling` is
    awaited only by requests on that microVM: its start, commit, inspect and visits), so a
    `stop daemon` right after a run's end leaves that layer unsettled. `stop` returns
    once the daemon has let go of its home: the daemon unlocks it and closes the stop
    connections itself, last, since the kernel closes an exiting process's descriptors
    in no order to rely on (XNU `fdt_invalidate` closes the highest first).
  - **A stop waits for nothing it can end (audit A07).** It shuts down the connections of
    clients still sending their requests and of commands on runs, so their reads and
    writes fail and their threads return, and cancels what runs being prepared are
    downloading, images or the guest kernel (`shards_registry::http::Cancel`, which shuts
    down the connections in use, as cancelling Go's request context ends them). A run
    waiting for a warm VM gives up; the run is refused, "the daemon is shutting down".
    Runs already handed over end as above.
  - A `wait` ends when its client hangs up, and forgets its registration: it waits for
    no one; so does a `logs -f`, output or none. `stop`, `kill` and `rm -f` go on regardless: "Cancelling the request should
    not cancel the stop" (moby docker-v29.8.1 daemon/stop.go).
- **The command's stdin** is /dev/null, or with `-i` a pipe the client fills from its
  own. Under `-t` it feeds the guest's pty, which never closes (D16).
  - It ends when the client does, as `docker run -i`'s does when its client goes
    (StdinOnce).
  - Only the client reads its terminal. The client then leaves SIGTTIN unforwarded, so a
    background run stops for terminal input as any reader does; a blocked SIGTTIN would
    make the read fail with EIO instead [POSIX XBD §11.1.4].
- **Children get only what they are given.** A descriptor received on macOS is not
  close-on-exec until the `fcntl` that follows (there is no `MSG_CMSG_CLOEXEC`), so a
  child spawned by another thread in between could inherit another client's stdout.
  shards starts children with `posix_spawn` and, on macOS, `POSIX_SPAWN_CLOEXEC_DEFAULT`:
  a child gets only the descriptors named for it (`shards_ipc::spawn`). On Linux every
  descriptor is close-on-exec from the start.
- **Receives take every descriptor.** Each read is a `recvmsg` with room for the most a
  kernel passes at once (254 on macOS), parsed within `msg_controllen`: macOS installs
  descriptors that do not fit and never closes them.
- **Signals reach only children.** The daemon's kills go through the handle its waiter
  holds, and a pid stays the child's until the waiter marks it reaped (`waitid` with
  `WNOWAIT` first), so a kill never reaches a process that reused the pid.
- **Measured** (PM M23):
  - Handing a request and its stdio to a warm process costs 31 µs at p50 and 75 µs at
    p99; §4 budgeted 10–50 µs.
  - A waiting warm VM costs 12.3 MiB of RSS and no CPU.
  - A thin client's process costs 1.4 ms at p50. `shards` costs 3.5 ms before doing
    anything, because its frameworks load at every launch. Only a thin client leaves room
    for the 5 ms target at p99.
- **Built: the thin client.** `shards` links the standard library and `shards_ipc`
  alone. It serves `run` and `daemon stop` itself, and runs `shards-vm` for `vm` and
  `shardsd` for every other command, found beside it, in its own place.
  - Its launch no longer loads Hypervisor, Security and CoreFoundation, nor runs
    AWS-LC's constructor [PM M23].
  - A pooled run fell from 5.15 to 3.4 ms at p50 and from 5.6 to 3.9 ms at p99. The
    client's peak RSS fell from 6.3 to 1.6 MiB [PM M26].
  - Raising the request path's service threads to user-interactive QoS changed nothing,
    on a busy host or a saturated one [PM M22, M26].
- **Built: working-set prefetch.** A warm VM, and a held restore, maps its template's
  working set (D25) before the guest runs, so stage 2 is filled before the request
  instead of on it.
  - **HVF** maps guest memory only as the guest touches it, and a touch from the host
    does not count [PM M5]. vCPU 0 touches it, before its state is restored: a loop the
    VMM maps below RAM for the purpose (`layout::PREFETCH`), with its MMU on over an
    identity map of write-back 1 GiB blocks. It reads each page and adds zero atomically
    to each page the guest wrote, a write that copies the page now and changes no byte.
    It ends with `tlbi vmalle1is`, and the restore then sets every register it used.
  - The alternatives cost more. Reads alone left the writes' faults on the path. Copies
    by the host counted twice their size in the VM's footprint, once the guest mapped
    them [PM M30]. With the MMU off, the loop's accesses would be uncached, and whether
    HVF keeps those coherent with the host's cached copy is undocumented (ground-truth
    doc §5 row 25): a write-back could store a stale byte.
  - Measured: the guest's part of a pooled `alpine true` fell from 1422 to 517 µs at
    p50, and the whole run by 857 µs (95% [834, 891]) [PM M30]. A waiting warm VM holds
    the pages its run will write, 2.9 MiB for that run, at no cost to the run's peak.
  - A template's first two pooled VMs are restored before its working set exists, and
    do not prefetch; on KVM, neither does the third, restored as the recording run took
    its VM.
  - **KVM**: the restore copies the pages the guest wrote while recorded, as its writes
    would (`MADV_POPULATE_WRITE`, Linux 5.14), then vCPU 0, its state restored, maps
    every page into the stage-2 tables (`KVM_PRE_FAULT_MEMORY`, Linux 6.10, with
    two-dimensional paging): writable where copied, since KVM maps a read fault
    writable when the host page is (kvm_main.c `hva_to_pfn_fast`). A write to a page
    mapped read-only would have faulted, copied, flushed and faulted again. Where KVM
    cannot map ahead, the copies alone are made.
  - Measured on nested KVM (GitHub's AMD runners, paired, n = 100 each on 5 runners):
    a pooled `alpine true` took 26–39 ms less than without the working set, of
    191–226 ms, and 9–14 ms less than with the copies alone [PM M33]. On one Intel
    runner mapping ahead cost 1.4 ms against the copies alone, of 13 ms.
  - The pool still refills at the handover. Its restore and prefetch now overlap the
    run's tail, which costs the run about 45 µs. Refilling at the run's end instead
    saved 49 µs at the median, but lands on the start of a run that follows at once
    [PM M30].
- **Tests:**
  - the IPC crate: descriptors that work on arrival, are close-on-exec, and respect the
    limits; descriptors past the limit, or on any part of a message, are closed; children
    that inherit nothing else (a mutation removing the flag fails it), and a reaped child
    is never signalled;
  - the daemon's handoff: a connection handed over while collections run still carries
    the client's bytes (without the wait for `TAKEN` it fails every time), and a VM that
    ends first fails the handoff;
  - E2E, a real warm VM driven by the test as daemon and client:
    - the client's stdio carries the command's;
    - exit statuses are `docker run`'s: an exit code, a signal, 127 with a reason;
    - interactive stdin works, and signals arrive as the command's;
    - the VM lets go of the client's stdio before the status and on hang-up (a VM
      frozen at the status still holds none);
    - the warm VM tells the daemon the command's status, then exits; `--warm` refuses
      stdio and non-sockets;
  - E2E through the daemon: parallel runs keep their own stdio; signals, errors and
    timing reach the client; `-i` stdin ends with the client; a background run on a
    pseudo-terminal stops by SIGTTIN; `stop` ends a run by SIGTERM; a killed daemon, a
    rebuilt binary and idleness each end what they should.

### Containers (D27)

A run is a microVM, its record the one Docker's tools read as a container's. The daemon
names it, follows it to its end, and keeps its record after it, until `shards remove vm`
removes it; `--rm` removes it once it ends.

- **Command lines** (`crates/cmdline`). `run` and the commands on runs (`ps`, `wait`,
  `logs`, `rm`, `stop`, `kill`, each also under `container`) are read as docker/cli
  v29.8.1 reads them. The thin client answers `--help` and usage mistakes itself, with
  no daemon, as `docker` answers them without dockerd; the daemon reads the same words
  by the same code.
  - pflag's parsing: shorthands run together, `=` values, booleans given values, Go's
    number syntax (`0x10`, `1_000`), `--`, and flags after arguments except in `run`.
  - cobra's order and the CLI's words: a flag mistake exits 125 with the usage; then
    `--help`; then a wrong count of arguments, exit 1; then flags shards does not serve,
    exit 1. Deprecated flags print pflag's notice on stdout, where cobra prints it.
  - A command of Docker's answers `--help` with the CLI's template, its options wrapped to
    the width of the terminal on stdin, or 80, as pflag wraps them; a form of shards'
    grammar with its own page (D123).
  - Every flag `docker` takes parses. Those shards does not serve yet are left out of
    `--help`, as the CLI leaves out what its daemon cannot do, and refuse any value but
    their default: `"--publish" is not supported by shards yet`.
  - `-e NAME` takes the client's value, as the CLI's `ValidateEnv` does. `--init` is
    served as given: shards-init is every command's PID 1, forwarding signals and
    reaping, the work docker-init does beside a Docker container's command.
  - **Evidence:** a differential test. The real docker/cli command tree answers 110
    command lines (scripts/docker-cli/oracle_test.go), and shards gives the same stdout,
    stderr and status byte for byte (crates/cmdline/tests/command_lines.rs), except where it
    refuses a flag it does not serve, which the test checks the CLI ran.
  - Escapes and widths come from the CLI's own code, dumped by scripts/docker-cli/generate:
    Go 1.26.1's `strconv.IsPrint`, go-runewidth v0.0.29 for the tables it aligns, and
    golang.org/x/text/width (Unicode 15.0.0) for the commands it cuts short. The locale's
    East Asian widths travel from client to daemon.
  - **Cost:** about 20 µs of a pooled run, outside the guest, most of it the larger
    client's launch [PM M29]. `docker` flags shards does not serve are one string rather
    than a table, whose page of pointers every parse would fault in.
  - **Known gap:** go-runewidth counts a grapheme cluster as at most two columns; shards
    counts its runes, which differs only for clusters of several visible runes (emoji
    sequences, flags, Hangul jamo) in `ps`'s COMMAND column.
- **Records** (`crates/shards/src/containers.rs`). Each has a 64-hex-digit ID from 32
  random bytes, a name, the image and command, and its life: created, running once the
  guest reports its command started, exited with its status once it ends.
  - An ID is drawn again while its first 12 digits are all decimal: they name the
    command's host (`hostname`, and `HOSTNAME` in its environment) unless `--hostname`
    does (moby daemon/internal/stringid, daemon/container.go).
  - The daemon writes each to `containers/ID/config.json` in the home when it starts and
    when it ends, so exited runs' records outlive the daemon. A daemon starting finds them
    as dockerd restores its own (moby daemon/daemon.go): one left running is exited
    with 255, the status nobody saw, and a `--rm` one goes.
  - Names are unique. A name must match `[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+`, and a taken one
    is refused with dockerd's message (moby daemon/names.go, daemon/errors.go).
  - A run without `--name` gets one as dockerd makes them by default: an adjective and a
    surname; from the second try a digit follows; after six collisions, the short ID
    (moby internal/namesgenerator/legacy, daemon/names.go). The word lists are shards'
    own.
  - A run's request path writes nothing: it takes a spare record, an ID with its
    directory and open log, made after the last handover.
- **Output.** Every run writes its output to the run's log, as records of stream,
  time and bytes, in the order they arrived (`workload.rs`); `--rm` takes the log with
  its record. The VM reaches no run's directory: the request brings its log's
  first segment open, and the daemon makes each next one as the VM asks
  (`kind::LOG_SEGMENT`, `segments.rs`). Before, every warm VM could write the whole
  `containers` directory, every run's log and record, since a pooled VM cannot know
  its run ahead; and on macOS its grant cost each warm VM's start about 4.5 ms
  [PM M73].
- **The guest says when the command started** (`STARTED`), before any output, so a
  microVM is running only once its command is.
- **Detached runs** (`-d`). The ID goes to stdout once the run's record exists, before its
  command starts, as `docker run -d` prints it; the client exits 0 once the command has
  started. The run's output goes only to its log, and it reads nothing.
- **Commands that cannot start.** shards-init says why in the words of runc's Go
  (`exec.LookPath`, `os.PathError`, Go's errno texts): `exec: "/x": stat /x: no such
  file or directory`. The client prints `shards: Error response from daemon: …` and the
  hint, exiting 125, 126 or 127 by the CLI's `toStatusError`; the run stays created
  with the exit code dockerd gives it, 126, 127 or 128, from the message dockerd amends
  (moby daemon/errors.go, setExitCodeFromError). Nothing goes to its log, as nothing
  reaches `docker logs`. A detached client gets the same, after the ID.
- **A run's start has one owner** (`daemon.rs`, `RunState`; audit A06). The record
  and its pending run appear together, under the records' lock, and the run then moves
  through three states the commands and the daemon's shutdown consult:
  - *Pending*: no warm VM committed to yet. `rm` removes the record and cancels the
    run, so that a run removed never starts; the run's warm VM goes back to its pool
    unused, and its client hears `No such container: ID`, exit 125, what scripts hear from
    `docker run` of a container removed before its start.
  - *Handing*: committed to a warm VM, which has the request or is getting it. `rm`,
    `stop`, `kill` and `wait` wait to learn whether it started, then act on what
    happened, as dockerd's removal waits for a start under way (moby daemon/start.go
    holds the container's lock throughout).
  - *Tracked*: taken, and followed until it ends, registered before the client stops
    counting as busy, so shutdown always sees one or the other.
  - `stop` and `kill` of a microVM still starting act once it runs: `shards run vm -d`
    prints the ID before the start, where `docker run -d` prints it after, so a script
    that stops what `run -d` printed stops a running command in both.
  - `stop`, `kill` and `rm -f` end every microVM they name at once, from one loop over
    the runs' end sockets, each escalating on its own clock (signal, SIGKILL at
    its grace, its VM 10 s on). docker/cli sends 50 requests at a time
    (cli/command/container/utils.go, parallelOperation), so stopping 60 containers that
    ignore SIGTERM takes two graces; here one, with no thread a microVM
    (`stop_ends_every_container_at_once`). Answers come as the CLI's do: in the order
    asked, each once it and those before it are done.
  - A daemon told to stop commits no pending run: `ending` is set under the runs' lock,
    so a run either committed before and is signalled once it runs, or sees it and is
    refused.
  - A warm VM says TAKEN before it touches the client's stdio or starts anything, and if
    the daemon cannot hear it, it runs nothing. So one that ends without a word surely
    never started the run, which goes to another VM; one that answers otherwise, or not
    in time, may have, and is ended and followed like any run, never retried: no run
    starts twice.
  - **Which VMs a run tries** (runs-11, R03). A run once tried three warm VMs and failed
    after them whatever stood ready (`HANDOFF_TRIES`, a number picked). Now a VM that
    surely did not take it gives way to the next only where it had been waiting in its
    pool before the run asked (`Ready::pooled`, the instant it joined its pool's waiting
    VMs, before the run's): those are as many as the pools held then, each tried once,
    however many ended unseen, so the tries are bounded by VMs that exist, not by a count.
    One started after the run asked (for it, or a refill since) that surely did not take
    it ends the start, said as `the VM started for the run did not take it: WHY`: a VM
    made for the run failing so is no sign the next one would not, and starting VMs on
    against a failure every VM may share has no end of its own. Cold start: an empty
    pool's first VM is started for the run and is tried once. Unit test
    `untaken_pooled_vms_give_way_to_each_other_and_a_fresh_one_ends_the_start` (four
    pooled VMs ended unseen, the fifth serves; one started for the run, ended unseen, ends
    the start after one ask); with the count of three put back, it fails (the run is
    refused with a healthy fifth VM ready).
  - A record changed after it went is an error, not nothing to do.
  - **Evidence:** deterministic unit tests that play the warm VMs over socket pairs and
    hold each step (acquisition, TAKEN, STARTED, DONE) while `rm`, `rm -f`, `wait`,
    `stop`, `kill` and daemon stop act, fourteen mutations of the fix each caught; and
    the audit's real-VM reproduction, a `shards-vm` held at a gate, which the old
    daemon fails (the command ran, exit 7, after its record was removed or the
    daemon stopped) and this one passes (`containers::rm_cancels_a_run_whose_vm_is_not_ready`,
    `a_stopping_daemon_starts_no_pending_run`).
  - *The gate, 2026-11-16 (ci-fixes, kiln goal fb3528f9).* On x86_64 gnu CI (job
    133659472581) `rm_cancels_a_run_whose_vm_is_not_ready` ran over 13 minutes, to its
    step's limit, with no dump. Two causes left it blind:
    - The gate polled for its open every 10 ms. Each judged wait's party (its client, the
      daemon and what descends from it) so always ran, and no stuck client was ever refused.
    - CI's hang watcher (`scripts/ci/hang-watch.sh`) took only the e2e copy's commands, never
      the gate's own copy in its test directory.
    Now the gate's VM process waits in its open of a FIFO (`Gated`), running nothing, until the
    test opens the gate or ends. A stuck client's wait is then refused, and its failure says
    its home's daemon log and processes, read with no client of its own: one of another build
    than its daemon's would replace it (`Identity::of_build`). The watcher takes the gated
    copies too, and asks their guests nothing, for the same reason. No cause of the hang was
    found from the code: `wait` registers its waiter, and `rm` wakes it, both under the
    registry's lock, and a pending run learns of its cancel as a VM comes for it (`commit`).
    Owed (ROOT): the three gated tests on Linux and macOS, and the next red's dump.
  - *The stop, 2026-11-17 (ci-read-5, kiln goal b2124227).* On x86_64 gnu CI at f6ad71083
    (run 43990298220, job 133729067961) `a_stopping_daemon_starts_no_pending_run` ran from
    about 01:27:36 to its step's limit at 01:50:18, undumped; the other 164 of containers.rs
    ended, and it passed in the same run on arm64 gnu and musl. Its run's client had ended (the
    watcher takes such a client at 40 s), so the wait that never ended was `daemon stop`'s.
    That wait was cold (no record of its kind on a fresh runner; CI keeps records only from a
    passing job, D261), so it followed its party's liveness alone (D209), and the watcher
    passed over every command line holding `shards daemon`, the stop client's too. The watcher
    now passes over a daemon's own command lines alone (`shards daemon`, `--detached`,
    `--ready`), and finds a home's daemon among them, not the stop client that works in the
    home too. No cause of the stop's hang was found from the code: a stopping daemon refuses a
    claim waiting for a VM (`claim`), and SIGTERMs its starting VMs as it finishes. Owed
    (ROOT): the next red's dump, or `--test containers -- --exact
    a_stopping_daemon_starts_no_pending_run` in a loop on x86_64 KVM with the watcher beside it.
- **Commands** (`crates/shards/src/daemon/commands.rs`), answering with dockerd's and the
  CLI's words:
  - A microVM is named by its ID, its name, or the start of its ID and of no other's
    (moby daemon/container.go).
  - `ps`: the CLI's table, byte for byte: tabwriter widths, go-units durations,
    commands cut to 20 columns and quoted as Go quotes them, images by their familiar
    name without digest; `-a`, `-q`, `--no-trunc`, `-n`, `-l` as the CLI and dockerd
    combine them.
  - `wait`: one microVM at a time, its exit code once it stops: 0 for one that never
    started, dockerd's code for one that could not.
  - `logs`: stdout to stdout and stderr to stderr, in the order they arrived; a line
    of any length arrives whole, in messages of at most 1 MiB, and output that does not
    all reach the client fails the command (audit A08); `-f`
    while the microVM runs; `-t` with RFC 3339 times; `--tail` (not a number: all);
    `--details` adds the space before the attributes shards' lines do not have.
    `--since` and `--until` are read as the Docker client reads them, on the client's
    clock and in its zone: Go durations, Go's time layouts with their error texts, Unix
    timestamps (`shards_cmdline::gotime`, matched against the client's own code); the
    daemon then reads the timestamps, and takes the tail, by the meaning `docker logs`
    gives `--since`, `--until` and `--tail` (dockerd's log forwarder's).
  - **Logs are read in bounded memory, and followed without a timer** (audit A12;
    `daemon/logs.rs`, spec.rs `LOG_STDOUT`, workload.rs `Logger`).
    - Each record's start goes into an index beside the log once the record is whole,
      with its stream and whether it ends a line. Readers find records by the index, so
      a record cut short, or bytes a guest wrote to look like one, are never taken for
      records. A log from an earlier shards is indexed as it is first read.
    - A record is read in 64 KiB pieces, and a line held until it ends or reaches 16
      KiB, moby's copier's buffer; then it goes out in pieces, its prefix before the
      first, so the client's bytes are the whole line's.
    - Reading on, it takes the index 8,192 entries at a time and the log 64 KiB at a
      time, each record whose head and output lie in what is read taken from it, and
      sends a stream's lines in messages of up to 64 KiB, sent as one fills, as the
      stream changes, and once what is there is read: each record read alone and each
      line sent alone cost a log of a million short lines 1.7 s of the daemon's CPU,
      against 0.2 s, and its `logs` 1.70 s, against 0.29 s (review 7.10, PM M95).
    - `--tail` reads the index back from the end, and only the records of the lines it
      shows: on a 2 GiB log, 3 ms and 8 MiB of daemon, against 1.6 s and 8.2 GiB (PM
      M48).
    - `-f` waits on the log (kqueue on macOS, inotify on Linux), the run's end and
      the client, not a timer: a hundred idle followers cost the daemon nothing, where
      each looked 50 times a second. On Linux every watch of a process is one inotify
      instance's, which one thread reads, each watch woken through an eventfd of its
      own: a user may have 128 instances, and a KDE Plasma desktop with a few apps
      open held 101 of them (PM M257); with an instance each, the followers past the
      rest failed. On Windows a watch hears names through ReadDirectoryChangesW, and its
      log's appends through a read oplock held on a handle of its own, which each append
      through the VM's handle breaks. ReadDirectoryChangesW said none of 20 appends by a
      writer holding its file open within 5 s each; each such append broke the oplock 8.7 µs
      on at p50, 21.8 at p99 (PM M344). One completion port and one thread serve every watch
      of a process. Where no watch can be made, a follower reads again every 250 ms.
    - **A log keeps only its newest output**: at most its user's history (`shards
      configure disk --log-history`, 1 GiB by default, D186), in equal segments of at
      most 20 MiB, two at least, the oldest removed as the next begins; the daemon's
      environment (`SHARDS_LOG_MAX_SIZE`, `SHARDS_LOG_MAX_FILE`) gives the segments' size
      and count instead, where it is set. The daemon reads them as each run starts and
      sends them with it; the run's VM writes the segments in the run's directory,
      which it is given open. Until D186, Docker's `local` driver's 5 segments of 20 MiB.
      - Segments are numbered, `log`, `log.1`, …, and never renamed, so a reader never
        pairs one segment's log with another's index. A segment is there once its index
        is: made after its log, removed before it. A later segment there says one is
        whole, and a reader asks that before it counts the records.
      - A reader reads on in a segment removed under it, and past those removed before
        it reached them; lines in segments gone are gone, as rotated lines are from
        Docker's. `--tail` reads back through only the segments its lines are in. `-f`
        watches the directory for segments coming, and the segment it reads for
        appends.
    - A record the log cannot keep, on a full disk or a log removed, costs the log, not
      the run: it is taken back from both files and counted; the run's VM tells the
      daemon, its record keeps the count, and `logs` says so and exits 1 rather than
      show the log as all the output. A log that is gone is said, not shown as nothing.
  - `stop`, `kill` and `rm` act on up to 50 microVMs at once. Each success prints its
    argument once it and those before it are done, and the errors follow (docker/cli
    parallelOperation).
  - `stop`: the signal (SIGTERM), then after `-t` seconds (10; negative: never)
    SIGKILL, 10 s more, the VM itself, and 2 s more (moby daemon/stop.go, kill.go). A
    stopped microVM stops again without complaint, and a signal is checked only for a
    running one.
  - `kill`: SIGKILL, waiting for the end as `stop` does after its signal; any other
    signal is only sent. Signals are named by the names `docker kill -s` takes
    (moby/sys/signal's), real-time ones included, and every error names its microVM.
  - `rm` trims `/` from its arguments, refuses a running microVM unless `-f`, which
    kills it, says nothing of a missing one with `-f`, and removes one microVM at a
    time; one still starting as above.
  - Whoever waits for a microVM is told its exit code as its record changes, under
    the records' lock, so that `wait` never reads a record before its end is written.
- **`run -t` and `-it`**: a terminal for the command, and the client's own raw while it is
  attached (docs/research/tty-and-interactive-runs.md §2.1):
  - `-it` with a stdin that is not a terminal is refused before anything is created:
    `cannot attach stdin to a TTY-enabled container because stdin is not a terminal`,
    exit 1. `--detach-keys` is checked next: its syntax is the one `docker run
    --detach-keys` takes (moby/term's), and so are its refusals' words, which scripts read.
  - Under `-it` the client's terminal goes raw with moby/term's flags, which Apple's
    `cfmakeraw` does not set, unless `NORAW` is set. It goes back as the client ends
    with the command's status, a start that failed, a detach, or a signal it forwards
    and would end by; as with Docker, not after SIGKILL.
  - The detach keys (ctrl-p ctrl-q, or `--detach-keys`) end the client with status 0
    and nothing said; the microVM runs on. As moby/term's proxy does, a byte that may
    start them waits for the next.
  - The pty is as big as the client's stdout, 0×0 if that is no terminal. Each SIGWINCH
    resizes it, then goes to the command too, as both reach a Docker container. XNU
