         BuildKit, one version of each file that no edit during the build can change,
         shards keeps another way: each file is taken into a stage private to the build,
         from a descriptor opened without following symlinks (on Windows, added
         2026-11-07: opened as the reparse point itself, a name surrogate, symlink or
         junction, refused ERROR_STOPPED_ON_SYMLINK, any other reparse point, a cloud
         placeholder or a WOF-compressed file, opened again for its bytes and taken only
         if its volume serial and 128-bit file ID are the first handle's;
         `shards_ntfs::open_unfollowed`, after Microsoft's CreateFileW,
         IsReparseTagNameSurrogate and FILE_ID_INFO), through no link at any name below
         the context's root either (added 2026-11-07, host.rs `Beneath`: each directory
         opened in the one above it, openat(2) `O_NOFOLLOW|O_DIRECTORY`, on Windows
         NtCreateFile relative to its parent's handle with a link refused, the last
         directory's handle held for its files; openat2's RESOLVE_BENEATH and macOS's
         `O_NOFOLLOW_ANY` not needed, one openat of one name per step on every kernel),
         so a directory a link replaced after the walk is refused, where fsutil's sender
         (`fs.Open`, `os.Open(filepath.Join(root, p))` at 83cac42c1c52, the FS buildx
         v0.37.1's `fsutil.NewFS` gives) follows every name of the path, the last
         included; the walk itself is unchanged, so `tests/context.rs`'s answers are
         fsutil's still, and `a_directory_a_link_replaced_since_the_walk_is_not_followed`
         holds the refusal), and refused if a write came
         while it was taken, as GNU tar reports "file changed as we read it" (PM M100,
         M242). A file under 1 MiB is packed into one file of the stage, a larger one
         cloned where the file system clones (APFS, Btrfs, XFS) and copied elsewhere.
         Linux keeps writers off with a read lease, or sees a write in the file's ctime,
         once a write under way is waited out with lseek's `SEEK_DATA`. APFS stamps a
         write's times as it ends, and only a clone waits out a write under way: on
         macOS each directory the walk kept whole is cloned at once after its files are
         read in place, and each file's times then compared; a file elsewhere is cloned
         before it is taken (corrected 2026-10-16: small files were read with the times
         alone, which a write under way across the whole read slips past; dev's CI took
         one torn on its macOS runner). `tests/context.rs` holds this under a writer that
         never pauses, a file's takes and a context's loads both; copies taken without
         the check tear on the first. A stage a crashed build leaves is collected with
         the store's other leftovers, its clones and their flags too.
       - Layers are stored uncompressed (`application/vnd.oci.image.layer.v1.tar`), so
         no build or run spends time compressing or decompressing them; the diff ID is the
         digest. A push and an archive send them as stored, uncompressed (corrected
         2026-10-08: this said a push compresses; only a pull's transfer is compressed,
         by content encoding). Since D75, the image and its outputs name a
         layer the build made gzipped, as Docker's do, and the store keeps it both ways;
         `rewrite-timestamp` is D76's; `oci-mediatypes` is open.
       - Refs record what a reference resolved to, so a stored image reports the index
         digest Docker reports, as a fresh pull does.
       - The root filesystem is written from the target's last snapshot, not stacked
         again from its layers (`crates/build/src/stack.rs`, PM M80). The layers lose
         what the snapshot holds: an entry the differ writes keeps whole seconds of its
         mtime (containerd's ChangeWriter truncates; layer::meta zeroes times before
         1970 or past Go's range) and `security.capability` alone of its xattrs; what no
         layer writes keeps its last entry's attributes, or the base image's, such as a
         directory whose mtime a step changes but the differ leaves (continuity's
         sameDirent ignores it), a file judged the same by size and mtime; the root is
         layer::root()'s; sockets are left out. Each commit records which nodes its
         layer wrote and what the layers still hold of the nodes it left; the export
         puts the snapshot in that form in place, and writes it reading files where the
         build has them, under `Store::rootfs`'s lock, limits and path. Where it cannot
         follow the layers exactly (a hard link only some of whose names a layer
         writes, content a layer leaves as the lower's, a name layer::apply takes for a
         whiteout, a merge onto a snapshot not in its layers' form) it stacks the layers
         as before. `tests/stack.rs` holds both to `Store::rootfs` byte for byte, over
         every oracle case and multi-step cases, and the E2E builds compare each image
         with the store's own stacking.
     - Done: ADD's local archives, unpacked to the files BuildKit makes of them (moby/go-archive's
       DecompressStream and chrootarchive.Untar): every entry resolved inside the
       destination as a chroot resolves it, so `../` names and absolute symlinks stay in
       it. 17 more oracle cases, among them each compression, an escape attempt, implied
       parents, replaced paths and out-of-range times, unpack byte for byte as BuildKit
       does; `tests/build.rs` boots one image of every compression. Where moby runs `xz`
       and `unpigz` and fails without them, shards decodes gzip, bzip2, xz and zstd
       in-process, in pure Rust (PM M77).
     - Stress-tested 2026-10-01: an archive 2,000 directories deep unpacks (1.5 s,
       46 MB), one of a million entries at 915 MB of memory, since brought to 164 MB
       (PM M78, M80). A 20 GB gzip bomb exposed two faults, now fixed: it was
       not unpacked at all, as an archive whose first file is past the bytes read to
       detect it was taken for no archive (the tar reader read on into that file's data;
       it now skips data when the next entry is asked for, as Go's does); and nothing
       bounded what ADD may unpack. A build's ADDs now hold to the limits a pull holds to
       (`SHARDS_MAX_IMAGE_BYTES`, `_ENTRIES`, `_METADATA`, `SHARDS_KEEP_FREE`), when set,
       stopping at the step that passes them, with nothing left in the store.
     - Copy-up as overlayfs makes it: a step's change to a file of the snapshot below
       (its mode, owner, times, xattrs, content, a rename, a new link to it) is made to
       a copy, so its other names keep the file as it was. overlayfs without its index
       breaks a hard link so, and containerd mounts with `index=off`; Docker Desktop's
       BuildKit gave `/a` mode 600 with one link and `/b` mode 644 after `RUN echo shared
       > /a && ln /a /b` then `RUN chmod 600 /a`, and a layer of `a` alone (2026-10-01).
       No file operation reaches this today (COPY and ADD replace their targets), but RUN
       will, and its guest mounts its overlay with `index=off` too.
     - Real Dockerfiles (2026-10-02, arm64 macOS): every official image's Dockerfile
       that needs no RUN (`scripts/build/realworld/corpus.txt`: five alpine releases,
       hello-world, nats on scratch) builds with layers, config and history equal to
       Docker Desktop's BuildKit entry by entry (path, type, mode, owner, size, link,
       xattrs, SHA-256, mtime), exports from the snapshot, and runs alike
       (`scripts/build/realworld/compare.py`). In each alpine VM every file of the 512 to
       518 has the hash, mode, owner and mtime it has in Docker's container; what differs
       is Moby's init layer (`/.dockerenv`, `/etc/{hosts,hostname,resolv.conf}`,
       `/etc/mtab` to `/proc/mounts`, daemon/initlayer/setup_unix.go) and directories'
       sizes, which are their filesystem's (ext4's 4096, EROFS's own). nats-server serves
       as under Docker with `--network none`, its log line for line: guest networking
       (D31) is not built yet. The first of these builds found every step from scratch
       given up to the layers, now fixed and held by the staged-build test.
     - Done: untagged images. A build without `-t`, and the image a moved tag named,
       stay in the store, dangling, until `shards prune image` removes them; `shards
       images -a` shows them.
     - Next: ADD's URLs and git sources, then RUN (step 3).
  3. RUN in a booted VM without a network, and its layer.
  4. Cache keys, then RUN's network, mounts and builder templates.

## 3. Components

```
shards (host CLI, docker-compatible) ──unix socket──▶ shardsd (daemon)
                                                     │  image store · build · networks
                                                     │  volumes · templates/snapshots
                                                     │  warm VMM pool · policy
                                                     ▼
                                       shards-vm (one process per microVM)
                                       hv backend (HVF | KVM) · memory · boot/FDT
                                       vCPU threads · GIC · virtio devices · snapshot
                                                     │ virtio (blk/net/vsock/console/rng/pmem/fs/gpu)
                                                     ▼
                                       guest: Linux (tuned) · shards-init (PID 1)
                                       the microVM's own engine, in shards-init: the
                                       command, and agents and harnesses in domains
                                       (D59, D115), an in-VM server each (D60)
```

- **VMM** (the `shards-vmm` library, run by the `shards-vm` binary): one process per
  microVM. That is forced on macOS [GT §1.1] and chosen on Linux for fault isolation, as
  Firecracker does. The binary links the VMM and what a VM process runs, and nothing of
  the daemon's: every process relocates its whole binary as it starts, and the daemon's
  registry, TLS and image code cost each VM about 1 MiB [PM M34]. The hot
  path is kept free of allocation and locks; device threads communicate with vCPU
  threads through lock-free rings.
  - A running machine is owned: waiting for it or dropping it stops it, joins its vCPU
    and snapshot threads (each vCPU is destroyed on its own thread), stops its device
    workers, destroys the VM, and only then lets go of the devices and guest memory the
    VM mapped (audit A04; `tests/lifecycle.rs`).
- **Daemon** (`shardsd`): serves a Docker-compatible API with extensions for VM
  specs and isolation policy. It owns the warm pool and the template snapshots, and
  carries the shards-init its guests run (D28).
- **Guest**:
  - a tuned Linux kernel built from source inside a shards builder VM
  - `shards-init`, a minimal static PID 1 that sets up and then drops privilege
  - the microVM's own engine, rootless, in shards-init: the run's command in a PID
    namespace of its own (D115), and each of an Agentfile's agents and harnesses in a
    domain of its own (D59: namespaces, IDs, cgroups and `pids.max`, Landlock, seccomp,
    default-deny grants between them), each agent with an in-VM server instance of its
    own (D60). Docker- and Compose-compatible at its interface (the Engine API, D170;
    Compose, D173), with no containers, containerd or runc underneath.

### RUN steps: one builder microVM per build (D34)

A Dockerfile's `RUN` means here what it means to BuildKit (docs/research/buildkit-run.md),
so that a Dockerfile builds the image it builds elsewhere, but each runs in a microVM
rather than a container on the build host's kernel.

- **One builder per build, not a container per step.** The first `RUN` boots a builder:
  shards-init with `shards_build=1`, every base image a `RUN` stands on as a virtio-pmem
  device (the store's own EROFS root filesystem, nothing copied), and the build port
  reaching the build process through the vsock muxer. Its steps then cost no boot and no
  root filesystem written: BuildKit prepares a snapshot and starts a runc container for
  every step, about 176 ms each on this host (Docker Desktop, 20 `RUN`s 3.85 s, one 0.48
  s, 2026-10-02); a whole cold shards VM is 39 ms (`run --kernel` of alpine `true`, n = 22).
- **Layers by id, never twice.** The guest holds layers, directories overlayfs stacks,
  written once from the host's change streams (`shards_abi::changes`): a host step's own
  changes when a `RUN` first stands on them (`shards_build::sync`), and each `RUN`'s upper
  layer, which stays where the step left it. Each step names its trees as layers over a
  base, so the guest keeps no tree of its own and stages share their layers. The stream
  is not tar: it never leaves shards, and keeps nanoseconds, every xattr and overlayfs's
  markers, so the guest's trees are the host's snapshots exactly; the published layer is
  written apart, byte for byte BuildKit's (`crates/build` diff).
- **A step's command sees what it sees under BuildKit.** Mount, PID, UTS, IPC, network and cgroup namespaces of
  its own (its command PID 1), runc's `/dev`, proc, read-only sysfs and cgroups, masked
  paths, `/etc/hosts` and `resolv.conf` bound read-only and in no layer, its mounts,
  `pivot_root` (the builder first moves off its initramfs so that a step with
  `CAP_SYS_CHROOT` cannot reach the builder's files), hostname `buildkitsandbox`,
  loopback up, BuildKit's user resolution from the snapshot's own files (`shards-user`),
  runc's environment and umask, BuildKit's capabilities, stubs removed. Its upper
  directory comes back and is put into the snapshot (`shards_build::upper`), whose layer
  the differ writes byte for byte BuildKit's (the `RUN` E2E test, and every `RUN` of a real
  Dockerfile compared entry by entry, `scripts/build/realworld`).
- **Better than the reference where it can be.** Every step is a VM's, not the build
  host's: `--security=insecure` grants privilege inside the VM alone, so `--allow
  security.insecure` (and `network.host`) grants it on the client's word, where BuildKit's
  daemon must also be set up to (`entitlements.WhiteList`, "not allowed by build daemon
  configuration"): the daemon's gate guards a host the builder VM does not share. A
  guest's change stream is exact, so nothing diffs the lower tree.
- **The build's secrets and limits** (`--secret`, `--ulimit`; shards_cmdline::buildflags,
  held to buildx's answers by crates/cmdline/tests/build_command_lines.rs, and to BuildKit's plans by
  the corpus). Secrets are read once, as the build starts, so every step sees one value,
  where BuildKit reads one each time a step asks; held in the client's memory alone and
  overwritten when dropped; as large as a step's frame carries (1 MiB,
  `shards_abi::run::MAX_PAYLOAD`), where BuildKit's gRPC session caps them at 500 KiB; and
  mounted on a tmpfs of their own, in no layer. `--ulimit` takes `as` too, which go-units
  refuses for the way Docker starts a container; every RUN takes the limits, as
  Dockerfile2LLB's AddUlimit gives them, the run alone.
- **Its end follows its VM** (`Builder`'s drop, 2026-11-13, PM M557). As a build lets its
  builder go, its guest is asked what its build needed (`NEEDS`, D133) and told to power
  off (its connection's end), and each wait follows the builder's VM process as D215's
  judge follows a guest's, shared (R12; `shards_api::Follow`, its process read by pid): the
  answer, and then the VM's exit, woken by it; once its kind has been seen in this process
  (the slowest answer, and the slowest end from the connection's end to the exit, with
  the least CPU rate either came at: the judge's `Record`s), a look at the VM each slowest
  past the look before, the answer given up on, or the VM killed, at a look that finds it
  made no progress since, its host holding none of it (a stopped VM stalls, one its host's
  pressure keeps from running does not: D215); before, its liveness alone. Its own end teaches its kind, read
  before it is reaped; a kill teaches nothing. A `shards build` boots one builder, so its
  waits follow its VM's liveness alone, the cold start; a daemon that serves builds (the
  Engine API) learns from its first. A guest its host left mid-step ends as that step does.
  Before, both waits had 5 s in all, picked, and the exit was looked for each millisecond.
- **Not yet as BuildKit:** a step's network is its own loopback until the guest has a
  network (D31); BuildKit's seccomp profile; caches kept past one build; ssh from the
  client. Each is an item of AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §11. A builder may have what its host has
  available and what its home's builds have needed (D133), but boots with little and is
  given the rest as its build needs it: a builder paid about 21 MiB and 4 ms per GiB it booted with
  (PM M82).

### One binary (D36)

**GPU publication (runs-08).** Each lazy GPU writer creates its own staging
file with create_new, using PID, clock nanoseconds and a process sequence as
identity discriminators (platform write_in's scheme). A collision or sequence
wrap refuses creation; it never unlinks another writer's file. Zero/one are
sequence initialization/increment, not selected operational limits. It writes,
syncs and closes the writable handle before renaming that same file into place:
Linux can reject a writable executable with ETXTBSY
([execve(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execve.2.html)). Ordinary errors
remove only the owned staging path. The two-writer regression formerly observed
empty final bytes; both writers now publish complete closed files. Real carried
executables, signatures, GPU and crash-debris checks remain owed in the
[runs record](../research/measurements/runs-fixes/README.md).

**Helper integrity before each start (runs-10).** A helper's directory is named by the
helpers' digests, but `complete` and the GPU writer took a helper of the right length
as this build's whatever its bytes: one byte changed (by hand, by a program of the
user's, on the disk) was started as it was, in every later process. Now every start of
a helper this build carries goes through `helpers::program` (launch.rs for the VM
process, its GPU build included; netproc.rs for the network process; `run --kernel` and
`restore`'s exec): the file is opened, its version read (`platform::file_identity`: on
Unix fstat's device, inode, length, write and change times; on Windows FileIdInfo's
volume and 128-bit file ID, FileStandardInfo's length, FileBasicInfo's write and change
times), and its bytes read whole through SHA-256 and compared with the digest build.rs
embedded beside them only where this process has not yet checked that version. A write
to the file changes its write and change times, and a file renamed over its name is
another inode or ID, so changed bytes are read again at the next start. Where they
differ, or the file is gone, the carried bytes are written again whole (staging of the
writer's own, synced, closed, renamed over it: the bytes build.rs signed on macOS) and
checked again; a helper that cannot be written again, or written is still not this
build's, is refused, saying its path, its digest and why.

- **The version cache** (`helpers::CHECKED`): key, the helper's path; value, the version
  its bytes were last found to be this build's at; one entry a helper, so at most the
  three this build carries, for the process's life; authority, the file's bytes, read
  again whenever its version differs. Its benefit, measured: a start's check where the
  version is known against one that reads the bytes (unit test `a_helper_checks_cost`,
  [PM M580](../research/platform-measurements.md)). What it cannot see: bytes changed
  below the file system (a disk's own fault) with no write through it; and on Windows a
  writer that sets a file's write and change times back by SetFileInformationByHandle,
  which only this user's own programs can, whose cache it is.
- **Settled versions alone** (2026-11-17, kiln goal a8b1ce42, lane own-36-tag;
  `helpers::settled`, `platform::FileIdentity::older_than`). A file's times come from a
  clock that moves in ticks (the system time on Windows, the coarse clock on Linux), so a
  write within the tick of a version's own may be given its times and, its length kept, be
  that version: on CI's arm64 Windows runner `a_helper_is_read_again_only_once_its_file_changed`
  rewrote its helper a few calls after its first write, and the rewrite read as the version
  checked, its bytes unread (run 44007524337). A version is now kept only once a file made
  beside it, with `create_new` and removed at once, is given later write and change times
  than its own: its file system's clock has passed them, so any write since gives another
  version. Until then each start reads its bytes. The established forms of this: Git keeps
  an index entry whose times are not before its index file's own as racily clean and checks
  its content (Documentation/technical/racy-git.txt); Mercurial reads its file system's
  present from a file it makes (dirstate.py `_getfsnow`). A clock read instead would have to
  be the one each file system stamps from on each OS; the file made asks the file system
  itself. Where no file can be made there, nothing is kept: the bytes are read at each
  start. Its cost, one file made and removed by each check that reads the bytes, is
  unmeasured: owed (`a_helper_checks_cost`).
- **Started as the file checked.** The checked file stays open until its process has
  started (`helpers::Program`). On Linux the start goes through it, `/proc/PID/fd/N` of
  the checking process, which the starting process (this one, or its spawner, PM M158,
  of the same user) opens as the very file checked whatever has been renamed over its
  name since (proc(5)); its name where /proc is not there. On Windows it is opened
  sharing only reads (CreateFileW's dwShareMode), so while it is held no other handle
  writes, renames or deletes it, and CreateProcess, which opens it to read and execute,
  still may. macOS has no fexecve(2) and its posix_spawn takes a path: there the window
  between the check and the exec stays, the start by name.
  - *Its name (2026-11-14).* An exec takes a process's name (`comm`, what ps(1), top(1)
    and pgrep(1) show) from its path's last part (fs/exec.c), so on Linux a helper started
    through `/proc/PID/fd/N` was named `N`: at a932bc894 on adacachy2 the VM process's
    `/proc/PID/comm` read `5`, its `/proc/PID/exe` `…/helpers/<digest>/shards-vm`, and
    ps(1) and top(1) showed it so. Each helper now names itself after its file as it starts,
    the VM process before it confines itself (`shards_ipc::name_after_executable`, in the
    one crate both helpers link: `/proc/self/exe`'s last part, prctl(2) PR_SET_NAME, which
    keeps its first 15 bytes, so `shards-vm`, `shards-vm-gpu` and `shards-net` whole). A
    failure is said on stderr and the helper runs on: its name is no part of its work. Unit
    tests (Linux): shards-ipc's
    `name_tests::a_process_named_after_its_executable_shows_its_files_name`, and helpers.rs'
    `a_helper_started_through_its_descriptor_is_shown_by_its_name`, which starts this
    build's VM and network processes through `Program::path`, as launch.rs, netproc.rs and
    `run --kernel`'s and `restore`'s exec do, and reads each one's name before it is reaped.
- A helper `SHARDS_VM_BINARY` names, or a carrier's beside its `shards` (D237, signed by
  the carrier, its bytes not those this build carries), is its giver's to answer for and
  is started as it is.
- No literal: the digest is SHA-256 of the carried bytes; the read goes through std's
  buffer at std's size.
- **Tests** (helpers.rs): `a_helper_whose_bytes_changed_is_written_again_before_it_starts`,
  `a_changed_helper_that_cannot_be_written_again_is_refused`,
  `a_helper_is_read_again_only_once_its_file_changed` (a known version reads no bytes;
  a write since, its length kept, is read again and mended),
  `a_checked_helper_starts_as_the_file_checked` (Linux: the file checked starts though
  another was renamed over its name; Windows: no rename over a held helper, which still
  starts; macOS: its name). Mutations: the version left out of the cache's key, and the
  bytes unread, each fail. [runs-fixes record](../research/measurements/runs-fixes/README.md#runs-10).

*Amended 2026-11-18 (ROOT's (a); own-38c):* the daemon checks its VM process's binary once it
says it serves, never on its way there. Its start read `shards-vm` whole through SHA-256
(`helpers::vm`) before its ready byte, and a new home's first answer waited for that read:
on jupiter, with Defender's real-time and on-access protection on and the host busy, a fresh
copy's first read took 152 to 163 ms against 81 to 100 ms for a copy read before, its
SHA-256 166 against 92 ms (ROOT's measurement), the scan's work in MsMpEng, outside any party
D215 follows; CI 44189693085's windows-2025 refused moved.rs's `shards run daemon --detached`
416 ms still, its daemon not yet at its watches. Now `daemon.rs`'s `VmBinary` holds the one
check (`OnceLock::get_or_init`): `check_vm` runs it on a thread of its own right after the
ready byte, and every microVM start, a pool's fill or a run's (`Daemon::start`) and the host
CPU's ask (`moves.rs`), takes the binary through it, waiting while it runs, so no microVM runs
an unchecked binary, and one not this build's refuses every start, logged once and said to
each with why, while requests that start none are served. Nothing relied on a bad helper
refusing the daemon's start: no test (`a_daemon_that_cannot_serve_is_said_at_once` and the
settings tests end their daemons otherwise), no message of the CLI's, and `daemon --detached`
exits 0 once ready as before. `helpers::program`'s check before each start (above) stands.
Tests: `every_vm_start_waits_for_the_one_check_of_its_binary` (three starts held by a check in
progress, none past it, one check), `a_binary_not_this_builds_refuses_every_vm_start`; red with
each start checking for itself (lanes/redgreen/own-38c-vm-binary-gate.patch).

shards is one file to install and run, `shards`: every command, the daemon included,
one CLI.

- **The command and the daemon are one executable.** `src/main.rs` is its root: the
  command line (`src/cli/`) answers what it reads itself and asks the daemon for the
  rest, and every other command, the daemon among them, runs in its process. They had
  been two binaries so that the command started fast: the daemon's binary took 3.5 ms to
  launch where the command's took 2.3 [PM M113]. Size cost 0.18 ms of that; loading
  frameworks the rest. So the one binary links none that loads at launch: Security and
  CoreFoundation are bound when first called (`crates/apple`, a verifier that trusts and
  refuses as rustls-platform-verifier did, held to it case by case), and so is
  Hypervisor.framework (`vmm` `hv::hvf::ffi`), which neither the command nor the daemon
  calls. One binary launches in 2.50 ms where the command alone did in 2.32.
- **The VM process and the network process stay processes of their own, carried inside
  it.** Every VM maps the binary it runs: one running all of `shards` would hold 1.2 MiB
  more than one running its own [PM M34]. And on macOS the VM process runs in App
  Sandbox, granted by entitlements that are its binary's code signature, which the
  command and the daemon must not share (D30); `sandbox_init`, the one way to enter a
  sandbox without them, is deprecated. So `crates/shards/build.rs` builds both (crates
  `vm-process`, `net-process`) with a nested cargo, signs the VM process with its
  entitlements on macOS, and embeds them with their digests; `src/helpers.rs` writes
  them out the first time a build needs them, into this user's cache under a directory
  named by their digests, whole (each synced, the directory renamed into place), and
  every later process of the build finds them with a `stat` each, and holds them while
  it lives (D182). They are no deliverables: nothing but `shards` is installed.
- On Linux both are static (musl), whatever C library `shards` itself links, as
  Firecracker ships: no shared library is mapped into every VM process, where glibc's,
  its loader's and libgcc's pages were resident in each (PM M281). A VM process then holds
  1.7 MiB outside its guest's memory, where it held 3.6 and Firecracker's holds 2.5 to
  2.8, and a pooled run is 0.42 ms sooner; what a run relays is as fast. musl's targets
  are linked by rust-lld, as the init's are, so a host needs no toolchain of its own for
  them; the network code reads `resolv.conf` itself, and no helper uses the C library's
  resolver.
- **The VM process's size, 2026-11-11 to 11-17.** CI's Firecracker comparison read the VM
  process's file-backed memory (`rss_file`, `pss_file`) worse than Firecracker's from
  78753d965 on, on every runner CPU (Envelope, row 11): its text mapped grew from
  1,949,696 bytes (0342b85d9, 2026-11-11) to 2,371,584 (1793da7c2, 11-16), and what of it a
  boot keeps resident from 1,687,552 to 2,240,512, where Firecracker v1.17.0 maps 2,527,232
  and keeps 2,002,944 (19 CI runs' logs and samples, read by lane release-rows).
  - *What grew.* No dependency: the VM process dropped `shards-net` in that time and took
    none. Its own code did, each part a feature a VM runs: the engine ring (D230: vsock
    `ring.rs`, `conn/ringed.rs`, `conn.rs`, `muxer.rs`, `poll.rs`; abi `ring.rs`); the
    share server's change notices (D235, `notices.rs`), bounds (D281, `bound.rs`), volumes
    (`fs/server.rs`) and learned DAX crossings (D189, `crossover.rs`); managed runs'
    members, lanes and sockets relayed (abi `run/*`, `warm.rs`, `workload.rs`,
    `vm_run.rs`); `confine.rs`'s Landlock pass over every thread; the virtio console and a
    guest's last words in place of the serial port (`console.rs`, `printk.rs`, D12); rates,
    holds and guest time (D255, D265, D267); XSAVE and CPUID baselines (D176); and the
    GPU's selection and report (D232, D233). CI's steps line up with the engine ring,
    `confine.rs` and `fs/server.rs`, the console and `printk.rs`, and the muxer and
    `fs/bound.rs`. No daemon code was found compiled in through a shared module
    (`vm_run.rs`, `warm.rs`, `workload.rs` and `confine.rs` compile into the VM process
    alone, and of the shared crates' daemon parts read, shards-ipc's `spawn` and vmm's
    `platform::progress`, none is on its paths), nor, module by module, any of another OS.
  - *Relocations packed (RELR).* On Linux the VM process is a static PIE (PM M34, M281):
    before `main` its start (musl's `_dlstart_c`, in rcrt1.o) reads every relative
    relocation, 24 bytes each in `.rela.dyn`, file-backed pages that then stay resident in
    every VM. It is now linked with LLD's `--pack-dyn-relocs=relr` (crates/vm-process/
    build.rs): DT_RELR, an address and then bitmaps of the 63 words after it. On `shards`
    the same packing took `.rela.dyn` from 613,680 bytes to 5,712 beside a `.relr.dyn` of
    8,120, and left `.data.rel.ro`, which every start writes, as it was (PM M514, which
    weighed a launch's time, the same either way, and left `shards` unpacked; a VM
    process's table is memory each VM keeps). musl's static-PIE start applies DT_RELR:
    Rust 1.98.0's and 1.98.1's self-contained `rcrt1.o` (x86_64 SHA-256 7998a49f…, aarch64
    e65dadc8…, the same in both) keeps dynamic tags up to DT_RELR (36) and walks DT_RELR
    for DT_RELRSZ bytes, an even word an address and an odd one a bitmap of the next 63
    (`llvm-objdump -d rcrt1.o`, `_start_c`). Packed only where the VM process is musl's,
    linked by rust-lld itself (.cargo/config.toml and crates/shards/build.rs name it), and
    not the GPU's, which links its host's C library through its C compiler (D201). PIE, and
    with it ASLR, stays: a static non-PIE binary carries no relocations but loads every VM
    at one address. What it takes from a VM's `rss_file`: unmeasured.
  - *No virtio-gpu device in the VM process without the GPU's renderer.* There
    `gpu_layout` refuses every GPU before a renderer exists, but `gpu_device`, which makes
    the device (vmm `devices::virtio::gpu`'s `Gpu`, `Served` and KVM's window), was still
    compiled and called on the path after it; whether fat LTO proved that call dead was
    never read. It is now the GPU build's alone, the other build's a refusal like its
    renderer's, so that build carries none of the device. Nothing a VM does changes. What it
    takes: unmeasured, nothing where LTO had dropped it already.
  - *Owed (the coordinator's).* The VM process's sections and relocations before (main
    before this change) and after, on x86_64 Linux: `cargo build --locked --release -p shards`,
    then `llvm-readelf -S -W -d target/helpers/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/shards-vm`
    (`.text`, `.rodata`, `.rela.dyn`, `.relr.dyn`, DT_RELR) and `size -A` of the same; a
    restore and a boot of it (`cargo bench --locked -p shards --bench firecracker -- --runs
    30`); and the Envelope on ten runners (`gh workflow run envelope.yml --ref main`).
    Not taken here, each unmeasured: the boot path's functions placed together, as a read
    fault maps the cached pages of the 64 KiB around it (Linux's `fault_around_bytes`; a
    symbol ordering from a profile of a boot); `opt-level = "s"` for the VM process's
    colder crates (a speed A/B); LLD's `--icf` (which folds functions whose addresses a
    program may compare); and the same packing for the network process, which each
    networked VM runs too.
  - *Read after it* (2026-11-17, goal 1453357d, lane own-38-released; CI's logs, the table
    in `docs/research/measurements/vm-text/`). The Envelope still fails on the boot's
    `rss_file` and `pss_file`, +0.0898438 and +0.09375 MiB (23 and 24 pages), one value a
    pair (b18952ae6 on Intel Xeon 6975P-C, 8d6029e4d on AMD EPYC 7763; 0c3213356's job kept
    no log). The packing took 36,864 bytes from the read-only segment, whose resident bytes
    stayed 196,608, and the text stayed 2,371,584 bytes mapped, 2,240,512 resident: the
    GPU device's gate took out nothing fat LTO had kept. Both VMMs' binaries are in the page
    cache as the bench runs them, and a read fault maps the cached pages of the 64 KiB around
    it (Linux 7.2-rc4 mm/memory.c `do_fault_around`, 16 pages by default), so a boot keeps
    each window it touches whole: shards-vm all of its text but 131,072 bytes, Firecracker
    79% of its. The row is bounded by Firecracker's own paired samples, no allowance
    (docs/benchmarks-envelope.toml), and each boot keeps the same pages, so any gap above
    zero fails: shards-vm must keep at most Firecracker's 2,338,816 bytes, 24 pages fewer.
    A cut takes whole windows, so it must take 2 (32 pages); 1 leaves it 8 pages over. The
    same cut takes the boot's `overhead` (+2 and +3 pages, the file's 24 less shards' smaller
    anonymous memory) under too. The restore reads better on every axis but one: in
    b18952ae6 its `rss_anon` read +0.0253906 MiB, worse, and in 8d6029e4d better; that is
    not row 11: it is 6 pages of guest RAM written by the first beat on Intel, every restore
    alike, no allocation of shards-vm's or KVM's (`docs/research/measurements/restore-anon`).
    - *What decides the cut* (owed, the coordinator's, R14): the comparison with
      fault-around at the host's size and at one page, where each VMM's text keeps only the
      pages its boot touches (`run.sh OUT windows`; on CI's runner `gh workflow run
      vm-text.yml --ref main -f run=windows`). If those pages, laid out together, take at
      least 2 windows fewer than the text's now, the cut is the boot path ordered first
      (LLD's `--symbol-ordering-file` naming the functions on the touched pages), at no
      instruction's cost; listing the pages for it is the next tool, built once this says it
      pays. If not, the cut is text size, `-C opt-level=s` for the musl helpers, whose
      speed `to_ready`, `to_beat` and the restore bench weigh. Either is then held to an A/B

      run='ab 2' -f b_rustflags='-C opt-level=s'`), its arms built apart and alternated, n =

      recorded idle second's pages mapped and copied ahead, at 2 MiB spans the restore's
      own guest does not touch, which the comparison's recording now ends at its guest's

      folios, not pages. Its gaps began on 64 KiB boundaries of the file (page 77 plus 115,

      off the file's here. The page cache held the binary in 64 KiB folios, and `finish_fault`
      maps a large folio whole whatever fault-around is set to (Linux 7.2-rc4 mm/memory.c:
      "Now we can set mappings for the whole large folio"). So the order held nearly every

    - *The cure, with no list* (2026-11-17, goal 1453357d). The order is gone:
      vm-process/build.rs links by none, and run.sh's `order` and order.py are removed. A kept
      list of v0-mangled symbols changes with each version, feature and toolchain. It then
      stops matching silently (`--no-warn-symbol-ordering`), or, refused when stale, fails
      each build that renames a boot function, and a 4 KiB profile to make it from was never

      userfaultfd from the start of `main` (`platform::FaultAroundOff::over_this_program`:

      its start mapped of them (MADV_DONTNEED). A fault there maps one page: `finish_fault`
      maps one page of a range a userfaultfd holds (`userfaultfd_armed`), and
      `should_fault_around` none around it (`uffd_disable_fault_around`). What shards-vm
      keeps is then what it runs, whatever its layout, version or toolchain.
      - *Where.* The musl VM process on Linux, x86_64 and arm64, from Linux 6.7. Before 6.7,
        or where userfaultfd is refused, it keeps fault-around as before, said at debug. The
        program's segments are its own headers' (dl_iterate_phdr(3), a static program's from
        its auxiliary vector). Its seccomp filter already allows the userfaultfd, its ioctls
        and madvise (confine.rs). Not the GPU's VM process, which glibc's link through the
        host's C compiler leaves with no word on text relocations, a written copy of which the
        let-go would undo. Not macOS's, which the Envelope does not read, and whose mapping
        of a program's code is unread here. Not Windows'.
      - *Its cost.* Each page of its code it touches first faults on its own, where one fault
        mapped up to 16. Their time, in its A/B (below): a boot's `to_ready`, paired with
        Firecracker's, -75.3 and -77.8 ms with the hold and -79.1 and -77.5 without, the 1.8
        ms between the arms within each arm's own runs (2.5 and 1.6 ms); a restore's
        `to_beat` 8,165 and 8,402 us with it, 8,270 and 8,323 without.
    - *The cure's A/B* (run 44138427198, A at 8247e14 with the hold, B at ba502bc before it,
      Intel Xeon 6975P-C, 2 rounds an arm; vm-text's `ab-44138427198.txt`). A's boot kept

        guest's private copies, were 35 in every run of both arms (36 in at most 8 of 30
        restores), and a VM of the fleet held 1 page more than a restore in every run: the
        code each maps a page at a time, the fleet maps alike. The layout moved a page from
        data to relro: the text grew 1,216 bytes and the read-only segment 240, so the
        relro, 0x6798 bytes in both, begins 0x898 into its first page rather than 0x2e8 and
        spans 8 pages, each copied by the start's relocation, and the data and bss 7, not 8.
      - *Each run's snapshot moves them.* Each restore copies ahead what its working set says
        its guest wrote (vmm `mapped::copy_written`, D25), recorded once a run over a
        restore's first second, so a run's guest copies are one number: 229 and 231 pages in
        A, 227 and 222 in B, to Firecracker's guest's 129 to 145, while Firecracker's process
        held 114 to 131 pages of its own. A run's restores alike, its interval is a point,
        its sign that run's draw: `rss_anon` +4 and +2 pages in A, +2 and -2 in B;

        M616). The comparison takes k pairs of snapshots, each a fresh shards snapshot with
        its working set recorded and a fresh Firecracker snapshot; each pair is restored
        `--runs` times of each VMM after its warm-up, logged, and held in one fleet of each,
        shards' first in an even pair (benches/firecracker.rs, `Snapshots`, `density`). Each
        sample of the restores' and fleets' rows names its pair (benches/support
        `stats_by_snapshot`), and scripts/bench-envelope takes one difference a pair, the
        median of its paired differences, and bounds their median by the sign test's
        interval: the r-th least and greatest of k hold it with 1 - 2 P(Binomial(k, 1/2) < r)
        (Hollander, Wolfe and Chicken, *Nonparametric Statistical Methods*, ch. 3). k is the
        fewest whose least and greatest hold it with the Envelope's 95%, computed from it
        (`snapshot_pairs`): 6, at 96.9%; the Envelope refuses a row of pairs too few for it.
        The boot's rows, each sample a fresh boot, keep the bootstrap. The evidence is the
        cure's A/B and the four runs of one binary above (PM M616's table). The CI time the
        six pairs add is unmeasured until a run shows it. Fewer copies than the draw, the
        other way, stays measured and open in D25.

        Firecracker's on both CPU vendors, not Intel's alone: median gaps of +0.14 to +0.64
        MiB on an Intel Xeon 6975P-C and -0.43 to +0.47 on AMD EPYC, worse in 2 of 4 runs and
        3 of 8. THP's boot advice holds 0.1 to 0.2 MiB of it at p50 for a boot 46 to 50 ms
        faster; the rest is unattributed. Each boot now records its guest memory (smaps'
        `Rss`, `AnonHugePages` and `Private_Dirty` over its mappings, and the pages held in
        each huge page's span: benches/firecracker.rs `guest_memory`), which
        docs/research/measurements/boot-anon's `attribute.py` takes apart into the VMMs' own
        memory, huge pages' rounding and pages touched. Until it has, the row is allowed up
        to 654 KiB, the largest median gap measured, lapsing on 2026-12-01: one CI cycle on
        the reading and ROOT's runs of it (docs/benchmarks-envelope.toml).
      - *Restores and fleets read after the same guest time* (ROOT's ruling, R08/R14,
        2026-11-17; PM M616). CI 44189693085 (0782de3cf, an Azure Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C)
        failed its Envelope on `firecracker_restore/rss_anon` and
        `firecracker_density/fleet_private`, +0.0254 MiB each, all six pairs worse (+2 to +15
        pages), and on nothing else: shards-vm's own anonymous pages 37 in every pair to
        Firecracker's process's 112 to 129, its guest's private copies 223 to 231 to
        Firecracker's guest's 125 to 145, and its first beat 8.2 ms to 11.7. Those rows read
        each VMM's memory as its guest first beat: shards' copies, made ahead from a working set
        recorded over its guest's first second (D25), against what Firecracker's guest had
        written by its first beat alone, a window's writes against a beat's. The copy-ahead is
        D25's trade, kept: its pages buy the first beat. So the restores' memory rows
        (`rss_anon`, `rss_file`, `pss`, `pss_file`) and the fleets' are read once each guest has
        run past its first beat for the window shards records a working set over
        (`shards_vmm::vm::RECORD_FOR`, D25's own rule: 1 s on KVM), both VMMs' guests beating
        until then, the pages the kvm table counts with them; `to_beat` and KVM's counters stay
        at the first beat, so the trade shows both ways. The wait adds a window to each of the
        396 restores and 12 fleets a run takes (at most 408 s on KVM), which the job's limit
        takes (D209 Part 11: 47 minutes).
- A daemon's build is its binary's identity, which includes what it carries; one given
  another VM binary (`SHARDS_VM_BINARY`, for VMM work and tests) is another build.
- **Tests:** `helpers::tests` (written whole once, found after, a cut copy replaced);
  E2E runs the one binary placed alone, its VMs from what it carries; `apple::tests`,
  the verifier against rustls-platform-verifier over eleven chains.

### Other builds' helpers go once no process holds them (D182)

Each build writes its helpers into a directory of its own (D36), and nothing removed
one: on 2026-10-17 one host's cache held 425 of them, 1.6 GB, one a build, and a user's
grows by one a release. Now each is removed once no process of its build lives.

- **A process holds its build's directory while it lives**: a shared lock on the
  directory's `lock` file (flock(2), LockFileEx on Windows: std's `File::lock_shared`),
  taken the first time the process needs a helper and never let go. Each process that
  starts helpers lives at least as long as they do: the daemon, whose runs end with it
  (D26); a build; `run --kernel` and `restore`, which wait for their VM.
- **The first process of a build to write its directory out removes every other
  build's that none holds**, on a thread of its own, off its way. It takes the helpers'
  own lock alone, which writing takes shared, so that it looks at no directory being
  written and none placed but not yet held. A directory whose lock it takes alone is
  moved aside while that is held, its lock marked, then removed: a process that waited
  for that lock meanwhile finds the mark, and writes its build's out again. What a
  writer or a collection that ended midway left (a copy not yet in place, a directory
  moved aside) has a dot name, and goes with the next collection.
- **Windows moves no directory with a file open in it** (the image store's `take_away`
  meets the same): there the move is refused while the collection holds the lock, so it
  lets the lock go and tries again, and that move fails while any process has the lock,
  or any file of the directory (a running VM process), open. The protocol holds either
  way: a platform that moves a directory with a file open in it has it moved while the
  lock is held alone, and marked.
- A directory of a build from before these locks has no lock to be held by: it goes as
  no process's. A daemon of such a build is stopped by the first client of another
  build that finds it (D26).
- What stays (held, or a move Windows refused) waits for the next build's collection:
  the directories of the builds alive at the last collection, at most.
- **Tests:** `helpers::tests::other_builds_helpers_go_once_no_process_holds_them` (a held
  build's kept; a free one's, one from before the locks and a dead writer's copy
  removed, the last only once no copy is being written; a process that opened a lock
  before the collection took it alone finds its lock marked on Unix, even once another
  process has placed the directory again, and keeps the directory on Windows, which
  refuses the move; let go, they go with the next collection), and
  `helpers_are_written_whole_once_and_found_after`. Mutation-checked: a held directory
  taken, no mark made, the mark unread, the collection not holding the helpers' lock.

### A stopped microVM's files outlive its VM (D37)

A Docker container keeps its writable layer when it stops: `docker start` runs its
command again over the files it left, and `diff`, `export`, `cp` and `commit` read them.
A microVM's writable layer is the upper directory of its root's overlay, in guest memory,
gone with the VM. So a microVM that stays (not `--rm`) keeps it on the host:

- **Saved as it stops.** After the command's status, the host asks init for the layer
  (`kind::SAVE`); init packs the upper directory as go-archive packs one
  (`WhiteoutFormat::Overlay`: whiteouts become `.wh.` entries, opaque directories
  `.wh..wh..opq`), without what init makes of every run (its mounts, `/etc`'s files),
  and sends it as `kind::LAYER` frames. The VM process writes it to a file the daemon
  opened in the run's directory (`layer.new`), and says so (`LAYER_SAVED`); the
  daemon keeps it as `layer.tar` only whole. That is an OCI image layer of the microVM's
  changes, which `commit` takes as it is. Where not all of it could be packed, init says
  why (`kind::SYSTEM_ERR`) in place of the layer's end, and the layer the microVM had
  stays: before, the end came all the same, and a cut layer was kept that only the next
  start found unreadable.
- **After the end is told.** Saving before the run's end cost an empty layer 29 ms at p50
  and a 4 MiB one 155 ms; told first, the empty layer costs nothing measurable and the
  4 MiB one 6.5 ms at p50, from the save running beside the next run [PM M115]. Only what
  reads the layer waits for it (`start`, until the daemon has it settled).
- **Put back as it starts.** `shards start vm` sends the request the microVM was made by
  (kept as `request` beside its log), and the daemon hands the VM its layer
  (`RUN_LAYER_IN`), which init applies over the image's root before the command, as
  go-archive's ApplyLayer does; its log goes on from its newest segment. `restart` stops
  it first; `create` makes it, and starts nothing.
- **Every record a reader decodes is written whole or not at all** (2026-11-11, kiln plan
  01a1cd8e862e7169a074db3d5fa33f3d steps 1 and 2: the audit's request fix and
  p/request-sites-v1). A rewrite in place (truncate, then write) stopped partway left a cut
  `request`, which decoded as a whole request without its options: one failed `update`
  lost `--cap-drop ALL` and `--read-only`, and the next kept the loss. Each other record a
  reader decodes was rewritten so too, and each was reproduced cut: `request` by `update`,
  `network connect` and `disconnect` and an engine's own networks (D181), `cpu-baseline`
  (D176), `daemon.pid`, `daemon.stopping`, `listening` and `networks/engine-id`. All go
  through one function, `keep_whole`: written to `<name>.new.<n>` beside the record, `n`
  the daemon's count of its writes, then renamed over it, its own file removed on any
  error. One name for every writer (`request.new`, the first fix) broke under two writers at
  once (660 to 840 of 2,000 renames found no file); a count needs no random source, as one
  daemon holds a home (`take_lock`). Not synced, as for every microVM's record (D27). A
  home's first `engine-id`, which clients may each make at once on threads of their own, is
  linked as the record rather than renamed over it (`keep_first`: `hard_link` fails where
  another kept one first, link(2)'s EEXIST, CreateHardLinkW's ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS). So
  each caller takes the one kept, where by rename 200 of 200 rounds of 14 callers took an ID
  the home did not keep. A request's change is one client's at a time (`Daemon::request_turn`,
  held from its read to its keep, an `update`'s exec into the VM included, as moby holds a
  container's lock across an update and a connect). Two clients at once had lost a change:
  200 rounds of `update` beside `network connect` kept 154 to 186 of 200 networks
  (request-sites-v1/review.md). The record, with its red, green and mutations:
  [request-sites-v1](../research/measurements/request-sites-v1/README.md), after
  [audit-fix-request-v1](../research/measurements/audit-fix-request-v1/README.md).
- **A start refused before it starts** leaves the microVM as it was: nothing of a
  refused start stays. The start it was waiting to be is released and whoever waits on it woken
  (`not_again`), in `docker start`'s words (the client names the container after) or
  `docker restart`'s ("Cannot restart container NAME: ...", moby daemon/restart.go,
  ContainerRestart). Before, one the network checks refused stayed starting, and every
  command after waited on it (`a_refused_start_leaves_its_container_as_it_was`,
  mutation-checked: the release left out, its `diff` waited past 60 s).
- **Visits** (`daemon/visit.rs`). `cp`, `diff` and `export` of a stopped microVM read
  its files as dockerd reads a stopped container's: in a VM booted over them, its image
  and its layer put back, running nothing of the image's (`builtin::HOLD`: init's standby,
  never given its orders, is the workload). The same built-ins answer as for a running
  one, so both are read alike; the microVM stays stopped (no state, no event of the
  visit's), one visit at a time, and `start` waits for one under way; what `cp` copied in
  is saved as its layer as the visit ends. It costs 5.7 ms at p50 over a running one's
  [PM M116]. `top` of a stopped microVM is refused, as dockerd refuses it.
- The layer is on the host from the start (D190): an ext4 file system in a file of the
  run's own, mounted with DAX, so that what a microVM writes is its host's page cache,
  never its microVM's memory, and is held to what its layer holds, not to its memory limit:
  256 MiB written under `--memory 64m`, where a run whose layer was a tmpfs in its memory
  was killed 64 MiB into a 100 MiB `dd` (2026-10-05). A stop keeps that file rather than
  packing it (D190 slice 2), its guest's journal written in place as its run ends;
  `commit` packs it on the host, `start` goes on over the file itself (D190 slice 7), and
  a visit puts back what the host packs of it.
- **`cp`.** docker/cli's `cp.go` on shards-archive's port of go-archive's copy rules;
  dockerd's half (stat, archive, extract into a directory, `-a`'s owner) runs as init
  built-ins in the microVM, and the archive passes between it and the client through a
  pipe the daemon hands on, never through the daemon. Two of the CLI's faults are not
  kept: its progress line adds the running total to itself (`last += n`) where shards
  keeps what it drew, and a copy from stdin reports `0B` where shards counts what came.
  A stopped microVM's files are copied as a running one's. On Windows the copy rules are
  Windows' (the client's paths' drives and separators), and a microVM's path goes to the
  daemon with slashes, as the moby client sends one (`filepath.ToSlash`,
  client/container_copy.go): sent as the rules left it, `/note`'s directory was `\`, a
  file of that name in the microVM.
- **Tests:** `start_runs_a_stopped_microvm_again_over_its_own_files` (files and
  deletions survive, `create`, `restart`, errors);
  `cp_copies_files_into_and_out_of_a_microvm`,
  `a_stopped_microvms_files_are_read_and_written`; shards-archive's oracle
  for the layer's form against go-archive on overlayfs.

### Agentfiles: a Dockerfile and shards' directives (D35)

An Agentfile is a Dockerfile with the directives docs/architecture/AGENTFILE_ARCH.md
specifies (§4, with the review's answers of §12): `AGENT`, `HARNESS`, `SKILL`, `MCP`,
`NETWORK`, `CONNECT`, `ATTACH`, and `EXPOSE … AS/FOR` and `VOLUME` with options, a name
and `FOR`.

- **Read as one or the other.** `shards build image` reads a file as an Agentfile where it is
  named as one, by a Dockerfile's conventions, which its users know (`Agentfile`,
  `*.Agentfile`, `Agentfile.*`),
  and without `-f` finds the context's `Agentfile` before its `Dockerfile`. A Dockerfile is
  read as BuildKit reads it, byte for byte (`tests/oracle.rs`): its `AGENT` is an unknown
  instruction, its `VOLUME --chown` an unknown flag. The parser knows the dialect
  (`parser::parse_as`), since BuildKit keeps no arguments of an instruction it does not
  know; `SKILL` takes heredocs as `ADD` does. The build names the file it reads in its
  progress, in the words of BuildKit's progress line, which CI logs keep (`load build
  definition from Agentfile`). A
  `# syntax=` line will name the frontend (§8 Q16) once it exists.
- **Names.** Agents, harnesses, MCP servers and networks are named as stages are
  (`^[a-z][a-z0-9-_.]*$`, read lowercase). Stages, agents and harnesses share one
  namespace (§7 Q19.2): a name declared twice is an error naming the first declaration;
  MCP servers and networks are each declared once. Every name a grant uses (`FOR`,
  `CONNECT`, `ATTACH`, `EXPOSE … FOR`) is checked against the declarations of its stage's
  lineage, a stage seeing those of the stages it is built `FROM` (§7 Q19.5), of the kind
  `--target-kind` says; a `CONNECT` joins one kind, on networks whose `FOR` allows each
  name (§12.10, §12.11). `ONBUILD` takes none of the directives: a trigger runs in another
  file's build, a Dockerfile's maybe, and what an Agentfile grants is its own.
- **What Docker sees.** `EXPOSE … AS ingress` and `AS` both ways expose their ports in the
  image config, as `EXPOSE` does; `AS egress` exposes none, the container listening on none
  of them (§12.6). `VOLUME` lists its mount points in the config, its name and grant aside
  (§12.8).
- **Where the directives travel** (§8, docs/research/oci-artifacts.md §4). The target
  stage's lineage's directives, in order, defaults resolved (`/agents/<name>`,
  `/harness/<name>`), are written as JSON to `/.agentfile.json`, mode 0444, in a layer of
  its own, the build's last: the normalized Agentfile, which shards' runtime reads, and
  which survives every store and copy. Its first field is its schema's version
  (`schemaVersion`: 1), which a reader refuses past what it knows. The config label
  `vnd.osi.agentfile.digest` carries its digest (`vnd.osi` as the OSI's media types,
  `application/vnd.osi.agent.v1`, which no IANA registration holds).
- **Built so far.** The directives that declare and grant (`NETWORK`, `CONNECT`, `ATTACH`,
  `EXPOSE`, `VOLUME`) build. `AGENT`, `HARNESS`, `SKILL` and `MCP`, whose content a build
  fetches, refuse to build until it does, by name.

### Volumes and bind mounts (D38)

`-v`, `--mount` and `--volumes-from`, and an image's `VOLUME`s, are read and kept as
dockerd reads and keeps them (moby docker-v29.8.1 daemon/volume/mounts linux_parser.go
and validate.go, daemon/volumes.go registerMountPoints; `volumes.rs`), and reach the
microVM as virtio-fs shares (virtio 1.3 §5.11; Linux fs/fuse/virtio_fs.c):

- **A run's volumes, made and removed as its scripts expect.** A microVM's mount points
  are registered as it is made:
  named volumes made as they are named, anonymous ones for the image's `VOLUME`s and
  `-v DEST`, binds checked; a later failure removes the anonymous volumes it made, as
  dockerd's cleanup does. Volumes live in the home (`volumes/NAME/_data`, `opts.json`)
  as the local driver keeps them under its root. `rm -v` and `--rm` remove a microVM's
  anonymous volumes that no other microVM mounts (removeMountPoints), `--rm`'s as its
  removal completes; a command that reads volumes waits for removals queued, so that,
  as with Docker, `run --rm` then `volume ls` lists none of its.
  `inspect` gives dockerd's `Mounts`, `HostConfig.Binds`, `Mounts`, `VolumeDriver`,
  `VolumesFrom` and `Config.Volumes`, held to Docker Engine 29.3.1's by
  testdata/inspect.json; its `Mounts` is sorted by destination, where dockerd lists a
  map's order.
- **Served by a process of the run's, not the VM's.** The VM process is confined before it
  is given a run (D30): Landlock (Linux) and App Sandbox (macOS) let it reach no directory
  given later, and its seccomp list holds no filesystem calls. So each run that shares
  anything gets a share process (`shards share`, `share.rs`; the one binary, D36),
  started by the daemon with the directories open, reaped on the followers' loop. The VM
  device forwards each FUSE request over a Unix socket, one connection a share, and the
  share process answers it (`fs/server.rs`): every operation relative to a descriptor of
  the shared tree, never following a final symlink (`O_NOFOLLOW`), names that are one
  component only. Its connections reach the VM after the run is taken: the run's message
  carries one socket, over which the share process sends a connection a share,
  `MAX_FDS` a message, keeping its copies until the VM says it has them (M24). A VM
  restored ahead of its run has its devices (`shards{i}`), empty slots its run fills:
  a template is made for each number of shares (`run::template`). A guest that mounts
  a share before its run has one is told ENODEV.
- **A direct boot's own shares** (`shards run vm --kernel … --share DIR[:ro]`, repeatable):
  the i-th is `shards{i}`, fixed at boot, for programs that boot their own PID 1 (shards-api,
  `crates/api`, whose `GuestSpec::shares` map onto it one to one). The `run --kernel`
  process takes the daemon's part for them before it becomes the VM (`cli/shares.rs`): it
  opens each directory, starts the share process as the daemon does (`shards share` with
  the VM's connection at 3, each directory at 4 + i and the home's private directory after
  them; on Windows each share's duplex pipe at 5 + n + i, D197), takes its `SHARE_ENDS` and
  says `TAKEN` (M24), and hands each connection on as a share another server serves
  (`--slates-fs-fd`, on Windows `--slates-fs share-{i}` through its grants). Why there and
  not in the VM process: the VM opens no directory. On macOS it is in App Sandbox from its
  first instruction and opens only what its broker grants (D30); on Linux Landlock and
  seccomp confine it before it runs a guest; on Windows its AppContainer reaches none of its
  user's files (D141). So only a process outside that confinement can open the directories,
  and it must do so before the VM starts. The server and its path rules are the daemon's
  run's, unchanged (`fs::server::Server`, `fs::answer`); a last `:ro` is its read-only
  mode, as `--disk`'s, and every other colon the path's. Its tags follow any
  `--slates-fs-fd` given beside them: with k of those, the i-th `--share` is `shards{k+i}`,
  as the share connections are handed on after the flags given. None of its processes
  outlives its client, however the client ends (SIGKILL, TerminateProcess): on Unix the
  client is the VM, and the share process (and macOS's broker, Linux's working-set writer)
  ends as its connection to the VM closes, which the kernel closes as the VM ends; on
  Windows, which has no exec, the client makes the share process (detached from its
  console, out of the VM's Ctrl-C) and the VM process's own Job in a job it alone holds,
  which ends both as it ends (D141). Tests: boot.rs
  `a_direct_boot_writes_through_a_share_and_not_through_a_read_only_one`,
  `a_direct_boot_ended_at_its_deadline_leaves_none_of_its_processes`; shards-api's
  conformance suite on real guests, boot.rs `shards_api_conforms_on_real_guests`.
- **A share another server serves** (`shards run vm --kernel … --slates-fs-fd N`): a direct
  run's share slot (`shards{i}`, after any of its own) given a connected socket its spawner
  hands it, which a server answers in this device's framing, as `slates shards VOLUME --fd
  N -- shards run …` hands it one the slates daemon serves a volume on (slates' A-161). The
  VM process takes it as it takes `--grants` (`warm::inherited_socket`: a socket, not
  stdio, closed on exec), each descriptor once, and never beside `--warm` or `--shares`: a
  daemon's VM is given its shares by its daemon. With `--share-window` the share has a DAX
  window, whose mappings its server answers (D189): slates since its ba0f8ef0, a
  shared-memory object of each file, the range each mapping asks filled. Tests
  (tests/slates_fs.rs, where `SLATES_BIN` names a slates binary): a guest mounts, reads and
  writes a slates volume, and one maps a slates file through its window, its fsynced
  stores in the volume at slates' first read and slates' write of the file in its map.
  - **On Windows** (`shards run vm --kernel … --slates-fs-handle V`): the stream is a duplex
    named pipe, since AF_UNIX makes no pair without a socket file and the pipe loses
    nothing at its writer's exit (PM M340).
    - **Handing it in.** V is a handle the spawner inherited from the server. It checks V
      is a pipe it holds (GetFileType) and none of its standard handles, as Unix refuses
      descriptors 0 to 2, refusing a value given twice. It clears V's inherit flag, since an
      inherited handle stays inheritable and a spawn by std would hand it on. It gives V to
      the VM through its grants as `slates-fs-<i>`, in order, and names it with
      `--slates-fs`, as `--net`'s handles are given. No handle's value crosses as a flag.
      `shards restore` takes none, as Unix's takes no `--slates-fs-fd`.
    - **The VM.** It takes each pipe from its grants by name, once, beside no `--warm` or
      `--shares`, as on Unix. Its device reads and writes the pipe as it does the socket,
      blocking, one request at a time. Every call is an overlapped one waited for at once
      (`platform::PipeStream`), so the VM need not know how its server opened the end, nor
      in which mode: a message longer than a read comes in pieces, ERROR_MORE_DATA taken as
      the bytes that fitted. A read past the server's going is the end, as the socket's is.
    - **What the device builds on.** The FUSE wire it needs is `fs/proto.rs`, which every
      host builds. `server.rs`, the share process and its budgets stay Unix's.
    - **Its DAX window** (`fs/window_whp.rs`, D189). Each range the guest maps is a view of a
      section its server duplicated into the VM process (PM M343), placed into the window's
      placeholder for that range (MapViewOfFile3, MEM_REPLACE_PLACEHOLDER), so a mapping of
      several ranges is a view a range. A range is mapped at stage 2 as it is first placed
      and left standing, since WHP's stage 2 follows the host's view (PM M341): a replace is
      a free and a place, 82.1 µs at p50 on windows-2025 against 122.1 remapped. A range
      never placed is not mapped, so a big window costs its boot no maps. Zeros stand in
      where a restore's server cannot answer. The section reaches past every range asked of
      it and is committed before the answer, so there is no file end to follow, and a fault
      in a mapped range is only a vCPU racing a replace: WHP's memory-access exit asks the
      window first and runs the access again once. A range mapped to be written is all
      held (patch 0009). The ask is the Unix one plus the VM's pid (le32) and its stream
      handle's value (le64), 38 bytes. The server duplicates the section only into a process
      holding the share's own stream, and answers with its value. The device adopts a value
      only if NtQueryObject's type is "Section", or "File", which shards' own share process
      gives (D197's slice 4), and leaves any other alone.
- **Owned as the guest made them, the record where Docker Desktop keeps it.** A host
  file's owner is the user's; the guest sees
  the owner, group and mode recorded in the xattr `com.docker.grpcfuse.ownership` that
  Docker Desktop's file sharing writes (`{"UID":…,"GID":…,"mode":…}`), and a file the guest
  makes records its maker (a setgid directory's group). Unlike Docker Desktop (fakeowner),
  the guest kernel checks permissions against those owners (`default_permissions`): user
  1000 cannot write a directory root owns, as on Linux. The owner xattr is hidden from the
  guest's `listxattr`.
  - **A file the host made is the run's own user's.** It holds no record, and a bind is
    handed to a run for that run to write: with root's owner, an unprivileged harness
    (`--user 1000`, or an image whose `USER` is not root) could not write the folder it was
    given, nor make anything in it. So the share server gives each file without a record
    the run's user and group: its `--user`, else its image's `USER`, as init resolved it.
    - *An agent's.* A volume given one agent or harness alone is that domain's (`200000 +
      n`): one a `VOLUME … FOR` scopes to it, a bind standing in for it included, or one the
      run's own root does not mount. Its domains start once the run's own volumes are
      mounted, so their word comes after the run's. A volume no `VOLUME` scopes (every
      domain's and the run's own) is the run's user's. One several domains share that the
      run's root does not mount stays root's.
    - *A joiner's.* Each volume of a join share is its joiner's user's (D119).
    - *How init says so.* Init sets `trusted.shards.owner` (`UID:GID`,
      `shards_abi::SHARE_OWNER_XATTR`) on the share's root, or the join share's volume, as it
      mounts it, before anything there is looked at, since the guest kernel trusts an
      attribute for a second (`VALID_S`). The host's setup entry carries the owner
      (`owner=UID:GID`, `setup::with_owner`, every `volume=` and `join-volume=` entry).
      - The guest's kernel lets only a process with CAP_SYS_ADMIN set a `trusted.`
        attribute (fs/xattr.c `xattr_permission`), and the server takes it only from uid 0
        (the request's header). It refuses it on any other node (EINVAL) and keeps it on no
        file.
      - It reaches the server before any confinement, so a file bound alone takes it too.
        A read-only share takes it too: init mounts each share writable, tells it, then
        remounts it read-only, as the kernel sets no attribute on a read-only mount.
      - A snapshot's share tables keep it, at their end, so tables saved before it existed
        still restore (root's).
      - A share another server serves (`--slates-fs-fd`) may refuse it. Its files stay
        owned as that server says.
    - *What the guest makes is still recorded.* Once init has named an owner, every file
      the guest makes records its maker, root's too, so it stays its maker's whoever a
      later run's user is: a root run's directory refuses a later run of user 1000 (it does
      not turn into theirs). Before that, a root-made file stays unrecorded, as before.
    - *Native nodes without owner attributes.* Device nodes retain their root owner
      (the guest opens its own device number); unrecorded symlinks, and Linux FIFOs and
      sockets, use init's host-file owner mapping. Classification uses their no-follow
      stat type, never a failed ordinary-file read. These native kinds' existing lack
      of guest owner-xattr persistence is an exception, not permission to swallow an
      ordinary file/directory's metadata error. The runs-01 follow-up regression covers
      host symlink/FIFO mapping and retains the root-owned-device check.
    - *Owner I/O fails closed* (runs-01, 2026-11-13). An ordinary file or directory whose
      maker cannot be persisted is removed and its creation refused with the host errno.
      Failed reads and malformed records refuse lookup; only a missing record uses the
      run's owner. Native Unix symlinks and device nodes hold no owner metadata here and
      stay root's; Linux's `user.*` namespace also excludes FIFOs and sockets
      (`fs/xattr.c`, `xattr_permission`). Metadata of a pinned unlinked file is read from
      its pin, never guessed from its former path. No retry/deadline/size is added.
      The focused fault test went red before the fix; actual Mac unit/clippy results and
      remaining guest/platform validation are in
      [runs-fixes](../research/measurements/runs-fixes/README.md). *Amended 2026-11-17
      (CI 44076016255 and 44077430171, arm64 Windows, the test's first Windows runs):* on
      Windows the record is WSL's words (`$LXUID`, `$LXGID`, `$LXMOD`), and one that is not
      four bytes was read as absent, so a node whose `$LXUID` broke was its share's default
      owner's, or root's beside a whole `$LXGID`. Such a word is now a malformed record,
      refused (EIO); the test breaks the record in each host's own form (`break_owner`).
    - *Root's stays root's.* A root run's host files are root's, as before.
    - *Device nodes stay root's.* A host device node has no attributes here (V08) and
      stays root's. The guest kernel opens a device node itself, as its own device of
      that number, which a shared `/dev` must not open to the run's user.
    - *Permissions are still checked against owners.* A run of user 2000 sees the host's
      files as its own, and is refused a directory user 1000 made 0755.
    - *Tested.* Server unit tests: `the_hosts_files_are_the_owner_init_names` (root's until
      named; root alone, the root alone, `UID:GID` alone; read-only share and file bound
      alone; a guest-made file recorded, root's included; a snapshot keeps it, older
      tables restore root's; a host device node stays root's) and
      `a_join_shares_volumes_each_have_their_owner`. Init's unit test of the entries told
      (`a_volume_is_told_its_runs_owner`). E2E on real microVMs:
      `a_binds_host_files_are_its_runs_users` (uid 1000 writes the bind it was given; the
      image's `USER` by default; read-only and single-file binds; root's and 1000's files
      kept as made for a run of 2000, which writes the top but neither's directory; a root
      run sees root's), `run_mounts_binds_volumes_and_tmpfs` and
      `a_joiner_takes_volumes_as_a_container_does` (a joiner's user's), and
      `agentfile_volumes_reach_whom_they_are_for` (a bind standing in for b's volume is b's,
      and b writes it).
- **Mounted by init** (`init/src/setup.rs`, `volume`): each share at its destination,
  read-only where asked; with the mounts of `--tmpfs` and `--mount type=tmpfs`, sorted by
  depth (sortMounts). A file bound alone is shared through its directory, the server
  limited to its one name (the rest of the directory neither listed nor reachable, no
  name moved in or out), and bound at its destination from a staging mount. A volume
  whose destination holds files in the image, first mounted empty, gets them copied in
  as continuity's CopyDir copies them (owners, modes, times, xattrs, hard links), then
  its root's owner and mode (copyExistingContents); dockerd copies at create, shards at
  the first start, the only moment the image's files are in reach. One whose destination
  the image has nothing at, first mounted empty, has its top owned by the run's user and
  group (init tells each such volume's setup entry `owner=UID:GID`, as it resolved the
  run's `--user`), where a root-owned top would shut a run of any other user out of the
  volume it was given: of the official images that run as other than root, PM M249 found
  one whose own user meets it, percona's declared `/var/log/mysql`, and no other image's
  volume it changes. The first run's user keeps it, as any directory's owner does.
  Tested: `a_fresh_volume_where_its_image_has_nothing_is_its_runs_users` (the image's own
  non-root user writes its fresh `/data` and owns it; root's is root's; another user then
  writes it not; an image's own directory still gives its owner), and init's unit test of
  the entries told. Mutation-checked, each caught: the owner never told; told and not
  used; given over the image's own directory.
- **`shards volume`** (`daemon/volume.rs`): `create`, `ls`, `inspect`, `rm` and `prune`
  as `docker volume` (docker/cli v29.8.1 cli/command/volume; the help and parse held by
  the docker-cli oracle), dockerd's volume service behind them (filters `dangling`,
  `name`, `driver` and `label`; prune's `label`, `label!` and `all`, anonymous volumes
  alone without `--all`), its words held to Docker Engine 29.3.1's (`create NAME:
  invalid option`, `get NAME: no such volume`, `remove NAME: volume is in use - [ID]`),
  `volume ls`'s table the CLI's formatter's (formatter/volume.go, held to its output).
  Anonymous volumes carry dockerd's `com.docker.volume.anonymous` label. One lock orders
  volume changes and a microVM's registration, so that no volume a microVM is being
  made with is removed: the reference counts' guarantee. `system df` counts volumes
  (LocalVolumesSize: size and references), `system prune --volumes` prunes the anonymous
  ones after the microVMs, as pruner.pruneOrder has it. A colour terminal gets shards'
  pages: each volume, what it holds, and how many microVMs mount it. Shards' grammar says
  them as `create volume`, `list volumes`, `inspect volume`, `remove volume`, `prune
  volumes`.
- **The local driver's options** are dockerd's (`type`, `o`, `device`, `size`, and which
  require which). A volume of a host directory (`o=bind`, its `device`) is shared as a
  bind is. A size wants quotas, and is refused on a filesystem without them. Other types
  are made, for the scripts and Compose files that make their volumes first, and refused
  at start: the guest
  kernel has no NFS or CIFS client, and a tmpfs volume mounted in each microVM would not
  be the one tmpfs that Docker's containers share.
- **Every request is the guest's to forge** (audit V): a guest kernel the agent controls
  writes any FUSE request into the queues, so neither process trusts one.
  - *A mode change follows no symlink* (V01). fchmodat(2) without AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW
    follows a final symlink: a SETATTR of a link the guest made to a host file outside the
    share changed that file's mode (measured on macOS 26). A file's mode is changed at a
    name never followed (Linux: opened `O_PATH`, changed through its `/proc/self/fd` link,
    as musl's fchmodat and virtiofsd do, on any kernel; macOS: AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW), and a
    symlink's own is refused (EOPNOTSUPP), as Linux 6.6's `notify_change` refuses it.
  - *Regular files alone are opened* (V02). A guest kernel opens FIFOs, sockets and
    device nodes itself and asks the server nothing; an OPEN or CREATE of one waited for
    good on a FIFO's other end, or opened a host device a share reaches, as `-v
    /dev:/hostdev` does (CVE-2020-35517; QEMU virtiofsd's `lo_inode_open` refuses them
    alike, EBADF). The name is looked at before the open, so no special file is opened,
    then opened without waiting or taking a terminal and looked at again, for one put
    there meanwhile; the guest's status flags are then restored. An OPEN with its
    RELEASE costs 1.5 µs more in the share process (PM M129).
  - *A device node is not opened to be looked at* (V08). A node's attributes, its owner's
    among them, were read through a descriptor opened for them, so a LOOKUP or GETATTR of
    a device node ran its driver's open on the host (a serial line raises DTR), from any
    guest's `ls -l` of a shared /dev. A character or block device is looked at first and
    not opened: it has no attributes here, ENODATA to read, none listed, EPERM to change,
    as Linux keeps `user.` attributes off special files (fs/xattr.c `xattr_permission`).
    LOOKUP and GETATTR pass the stat they just took, a node's own (not a guest-named open
    file's), so they look no more often than before (PM M133).
  - *A request is bounded before it is read* (V03). A chain may claim 256 descriptors of
    4 GiB; the device allocated what it claimed, a TiB, before reading any of it. One
    longer than any FUSE request (`MAX_FRAME`, a largest write and its headers) is
    answered EINVAL from its first 16 bytes, and the share, which closed the connection
    over such a frame, never sees it.
  - *Guest memory is not held across the share's answer* (V04): read for the request,
    taken again for the reply (D29). A share slow to answer, or never answering, held
    every other device's queue work and any snapshot off guest memory as long: with a
    5 ms answer, another thread's wait for guest memory went from 8.9 ms to 0.25 µs at
    the median, and the device's round trip did not move (PM M129).
  - *An open directory holds none of its listing* (V05). OPENDIR copied the directory's
    entries into its handle, and nothing bounded the handles: a guest opening a large
    directory again and again, never releasing it (one `opendir` each, from guest
    userspace), cost the share process the directory's size each time, 10.8 MB for 100
    handles of 2000 entries. A handle now reads as the guest asks from a descriptor of its
    own, so handles are as many as the process's descriptors: on Linux by getdents64(2)
    at the kernel's `d_off` cookies, as virtiofsd reads, keeping only the descriptor
