    (glibc's stream would keep 32 KiB a handle); on macOS a stream of 2.2 KiB counted in
    entries, holding the entry a reply had no room for, read again from its start for any
    other offset; on Windows the directory's own handle, whose enumeration NTFS keeps
    between calls (GetFileInformationByHandleEx's FileIdExtdDirectoryInfo, its Restart
    class for the start), counted in entries as macOS's, holding what of a 4 KiB batch a
    reply had no room for, enumerated again from its start for any other offset (until
    2026-11-06 Windows' handle still read the whole listing at OPENDIR: 10.77 MB for the
    100 handles on CI's windows-2025, `tests/fs_dir_handles.rs`). 100 handles hold 8 KB of
    the heap; a whole listing of 10,000 entries
    went from 17.7 ms to 4.4 ms at the median, as READDIR no longer copied the rest of the
    listing for each page (PM M130).
  - *A listing comes a largest read at a time* (V06). READDIR's reply grew to the
    guest's `size`, any u32: a directory listed in one request past a frame was refused
    by the device unread, whose next requests then took its leftover bytes for their
    replies. `size` is held to `MAX_WRITE`, the largest read INIT tells the guest.
  - *A guest's POSIX ACL is its data, never its host file's ACL.* A guest-to-host isolation
    fix (2026-11-18, kiln goal #39, ROOT's word), found while reading the server for
    FUSE_POSIX_ACL.
    - The hole: on a Linux host the server kept a guest's `system.` attributes under their
      own names, so a guest's `setfacl` on a shared file (`system.posix_acl_access`)
      became the host file's real ACL. The host's kernel (v6.18 fs/posix_acl.c
      `set_posix_acl`, `posix_acl_update_mode`) set the file's mode from it, which could
      take away the owner access `host_perm` keeps for the share process. And it granted
      the host's users and groups by the guest's ids: a guest could grant a host user
      access to its files.
    - The fix: the whole `system.` namespace is kept as `trusted.` and `security.` are,
      under `user.shards.` (`kept_by_kernel`), as data the guest reads back. The whole
      namespace, because the host kernel acts on each of its names: NFS's
      `system.nfs4_acl`, SMB's `system.cifs_acl` and ntfs3's `system.ntfs_security` set
      those file systems' ACLs and security descriptors. The host's own attributes there
      (an ACL the host set) are none of the guest's, as the host's own SELinux labels are
      not.
    - Other hosts: macOS keeps no namespaces and no ACL in an attribute, so a guest's
      `system.posix_acl_access` was already data there, under its own name. Windows keeps
      each guest attribute as an EA of its own (`SH.` and its name's bytes,
      `ntfs::xattr_ea`), never the file's DACL.
    - Found beside it, the same kind of hole on macOS. A guest's process may send an
      attribute name of no Linux namespace, as virtio-fs takes every name (v6.18
      fs/fuse/xattr.c, its one handler of prefix ""). On macOS such a name reached the
      host's own attributes: a guest could read them, and take `com.apple.quarantine` off a
      host file in a shared folder so that Gatekeeper would not look at it. Windows kept
      such a name as any other. Now every host refuses it (EOPNOTSUPP) as Linux's does
      (`namespaced`). Test: `a_guest_reaches_no_host_attribute_outside_linuxs_namespaces`.
      Red: lanes/redgreen/own-38d-namespaced.patch (macOS and Windows; Linux refused it
      already).
    - Enforcing the guest's ACLs in the guest (FUSE_POSIX_ACL) is a later piece.
    - Test: `a_guests_acl_is_its_own_data_never_its_host_files_acl` (the guest reads,
      lists and removes what it set; the host file's mode is unchanged, and on Linux its
      ACL; a host file's own ACL is none of the guest's). Red with `system.` left out:
      lanes/redgreen/own-38d-guest-acl.patch, on Linux.
  - Tests: `fs::server::tests` (`a_mode_change_follows_no_symlink`,
    `special_files_are_never_opened`, `a_listing_comes_a_read_at_a_time`,
    `a_directory_is_read_whole_a_page_at_a_time`,
    `a_device_is_never_opened_to_be_looked_at`), `tests/fs_dir_handles.rs` and
    `fs::tests` (`a_request_longer_than_any_is_refused_unread`,
    `guest_memory_is_free_while_the_share_answers`), each mutation-checked. The looks
    after an open guard only a name replaced between two looks, which no test can time,
    nor can one put a regular file and a device in one share without root, which a
    GETATTR naming one's open file for the other's node would need.
- **The kernel** has `CONFIG_VIRTIO_FS` and `CONFIG_FUSE_DAX` (kernel-6.18.48-98788948976a).
- **A share holds the descriptors the host can spare, not what the guest names** (audit
  V09). A directory held its descriptor until the guest forgot it: a walk past the share
  process's limit failed EMFILE, and at the limit the daemon gives it (245,760 here) one
  guest pinned half of the host's file table and two all of it (PM M132).
  - *By path and identity.* A node keeps its parent, its name, kept current through the
    guest's renames and lookups, and its (dev, ino). A lookup opens nothing; a directory
    is opened when used, along its path from the nearest directory held, each component
    never followed (openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH and RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS on Linux 5.6+,
    O_NOFOLLOW a component at a time before it and on macOS), then checked to be the
    directory the node was: one renamed or replaced on the host since, or reached through
    a symlink even to itself, is stale (ESTALE), which has Linux's VFS look it up again
    (`retry_estale`).
  - *Walked through where it may only be searched* (memory-19, 2026-11-14). A kernel's walk
    asks only search permission of each directory on the way (path_resolution(7)), so a bind
    mount reaches `a/b/c/file` through `b` of mode 0111. The share process, the host files'
    owner, cannot read such a `b` (open(2) O_RDONLY: EACCES), which refused its LOOKUP and
    everything beneath it. A directory its host refuses the server to read is held to be
    searched alone (server.rs `Held::Search`, `search_beneath`): Linux's O_PATH, which asks
    no permission of the directory itself, and macOS's O_SEARCH, its search permission
    (open(2) of each); names are looked up through it, and the host's own permissions still
    decide each (a 0000 directory's names are refused EACCES by the host's walk). Nothing
    more of it is had: its listing reopens it to read (`DirStream::open`, EACCES); its
    record, which xattr(7) gives only to who may read the file, is unread, and the guest is
    told the owner of the host's unrecorded files, as the guest's own modes always leave the
    server its directories (`host_perm`), so only its host makes one so; its attributes are
    neither read nor set (EACCES), nor its mode, times or owner changed (SETATTR, EACCES: on
    macOS a chmod through the O_SEARCH descriptor was made, the guard's mutant). A hold is a
    search alone only while its host refuses the reading: `dir_fd` reopens it to read each
    time it serves, and keeps that once it can. On Linux it is walked through unwatched, as
    inotify(7) refuses a watch to who may not read it (D235). Windows: NTFS modes refuse the
    server nothing (`MODES_REFUSE_OPENS`), so `search_beneath` refuses, as before. macOS's
    0000 directory stays refused at its LOOKUP (O_SEARCH asks search permission); Linux's is
    looked up, as its stat is. Held by `an_exec_only_directory_is_walked_through_and_never_listed`
    (red before on macOS arm64; mutants of the fallback, the attribute and SETATTR refusals,
    the unrecorded owner and Linux's unwatched walk each red).
  - *A cache, never a limit the guest meets.* Directories' and the guest's open files'
    descriptors sit in an LRU, let go between requests and never during one, and opened
    again along their paths as they are next used: a handle keeps its node, its open flags
    (O_CREAT, O_EXCL and O_TRUNC acting once) and the identity it opened, so a file the host
    replaced, removed or took its mode away from since is stale (ESTALE). A held descriptor
    serves first, as a kernel's open file outlives its unlink. The guest's handles are as
    many as its own kernel lets its processes have.
  - *Pins, the budget's alone.* Descriptors no path could open again are pinned: taken
    before the guest unlinks or renames over a node it has open (let go where the removal
    fails), before its chmod refuses the access its open handles have, and for a file made
    with a mode refusing its own handle. Past the budget none is taken: a node the removal
    leaves another name of is reached by that name, and a last name's handles are stale
    once their own descriptors go, those opened after reaching what the path then leads to.
  - *Its size, derived* (`fs::server::Limits`): the process's limit raised as Go's runtime
    raises its own (`platform::raise_descriptor_limit`, the daemon's too), less what it holds
    and `REQUEST_FDS` (3) a server; and no more than its part of the system's table with as
    many share processes as runs the user may start. This host: 90 a share process (PM
    M136). A walk costs 2.1 µs a directory more (6%); a reopen 8 to 10 µs a component
    walked on macOS. What a guest's workload pays past the cache, a reopen for each file
    read again (a tree read round and round, a package manager's), is unmeasured end to end.
  - Tests: `tests/fs_dir_budget.rs` (a walk of 584 directories within 24 descriptors,
    `REQUEST_FDS` exactly enough), `handles_past_the_budget_each_serve_their_file` (1,000
    handles past a budget of 4, read round and round), the pins' (an unlink, a rename over,
    a chmod, a read-only file filled, hard links, a reused inode number, a removal that
    fails), `a_directory_let_go_is_found_by_its_path_or_is_stale` (renames, a host's rename
    and replacement, symlinks to itself and out of the share),
    `a_budget_is_reckoned_from_the_hosts_limits`, and on a real microVM
    `a_shared_directorys_files_stay_open_past_the_shares_descriptors` (300 files of a `-v`
    directory open at once, past this host's 90); mutation-checked (handles capped at the
    budget fails both). Linux's openat2 path runs in CI's Linux jobs only.
- Open, unmeasured: the forwarding hop's cost per request against an in-process server,
  and throughput against Docker Desktop's virtiofs; DAX windows, which would let file
  data skip the hop; the local driver's other types (NFS and CIFS clients in the guest
  kernel; a tmpfs volume held where every microVM that mounts it shares it).

### Restart policies (D39)

`--restart` takes what `docker run --restart` takes, and refuses what it refuses
(docker/cli opts.ParseRestartPolicy, `--rm` with it; dockerd's ValidateRestartPolicy), and
is kept with the microVM's record. Each policy means what Docker's clients rely on it to mean
(moby docker-v29.8.1 daemon/internal/restartmanager, monitor.go handleContainerExit;
`daemon/restart.rs`):

- **Whether.** `always`; `unless-stopped` unless stopped by hand (any stop or kill, but
  the daemon's own); `on-failure` on a non-zero status, under its count where it has one.
  A command that never started is not restarted. A stop or kill by the microVM's stop
  signal or SIGKILL cancels the next restart (ExitOnNext); a SIGHUP does not.
- **When.** After a wait that doubles each time, as dockerd's does, from and to what this
  host's restarts cost, learned as it runs (D219), where dockerd's are figures (100 ms, a
  minute, from scratch after a run of 10 s). The wait is a deadline on the followers' loop
  (no thread waits it out); the start then goes through the daemon's own door, a detached
  `start` from a client of its own making, so a restart is handled, followed and recorded
  as any start is.
- **Meanwhile.** The microVM is restarting: running to `ps` (listed without `-a`,
  `Restarting (CODE) X ago`), to inspect (`Status` restarting, `Running` and `Restarting`
  true) and to `wait`, which waits on; `RestartCount` counts, and `shards start vm` starts it
  over. `stop` and `kill` stop it there; `rm` refuses it without `-f`, as it refuses one
  running.
- **As the daemon starts**, the microVMs its stop ended start again where their policy
  says: a policy outlives the daemon that ran it. shards' daemon starts with the first
  command, so they start with it.

### Updates (D40)

`shards update` is `docker update` (docker/cli container/update.go; moby docker-v29.8.1
daemon/update.go and container UpdateContainer, `daemon/update.rs`): what is asked
checked as at create (verifyContainerSettings with its `update` flag: swap alone
passes), merged into what the microVM has with dockerd's refusals (Nano CPUs against a
set CFS period or quota and the reverse; a memory limit over the swap kept, which for a
microVM made without one is none, since memory and swap together cannot be less than
memory; a restart policy beside
`--rm`), kept with its request, and written to a running workload's cgroup at once by an
init built-in (`builtin::CGROUP`, the writes runc's fs2 makes as it starts). A limit the
guest refuses changes nothing. Its words and its order of output are dockerd's and the
CLI's, held to Docker Engine 29.3.1's.

- `--blkio-weight` (run, create, update) is BFQ's weight where the guest kernel has BFQ,
  else `io.weight` on io.cost's scale, converted so that a weight means what it means
  under Docker (runc's ConvertBlkIOToIOWeightValue).
  The guest kernel has both; Docker Desktop's VM has neither and refuses the update.
- **A running microVM's memory moves with its limit, both ways** (the user's plan, item
  3): every run plugs its memory as it needs it, up to its limit (D148), so `update -m`
  tells the run's VM its new most to plug (`kind::PLUG`, before the exec that writes its
  cgroup, on the same link), then init writes `memory.max`, reports what its guest may now
  plug (D149) and holds the run at what is plugged again, which its grower lifts once all
  of an old most was plugged and is woken by no more. Raised, a workload past the old limit
  holds what the new one allows, and the guest reports it; lowered, `memory.max` ends one
  past it, its memory staying plugged until it is given back (D148's unplug, the plan's
  item 4). A joiner's limit is its cgroup's alone, its microVM's most its provider's.
  Before, a microVM's memory was sized as it started (PM M117), and a limit raised past it
  bound at the VM's size until its next start. Held by `update_moves_a_microvms_memory_both_ways`
  (tests/containers.rs: 512 MiB killed at `-m 256m`, held at `1g`, MemTotal a gigabyte,
  killed again at `256m`; mutation-checked: without `PLUG`, and without the hold again,
  each killed at `1g`).
- **A running microVM's CPUs move with its limit, both ways** (the user's plan, item 3;
  D191): its microVM has every CPU of the host's, so `update --cpus`, the quota,
  `--cpu-count` or `--cpuset-cpus` writes the workload's cpuset with its quota, a raise
  giving it CPUs it had not (PM M288: 4.01 CPUs used after `--cpus 4` of a `--cpus 1`
  run, where its one vCPU held it to 1.00). Held by `update_changes_limits_of_running_microvms`.
- `--cpu-rt-period` and `--cpu-rt-runtime` parse, and are not served: cgroup v2 has no
  real-time CPU controller to write them to.
- inspect's raw-JSON fallback (a template Docker's typed struct cannot answer) decodes
  numbers as encoding/json's Number, which prints its digits and encodes as a number.
- **Sizes** (`ps --size`, `inspect --size`; list.go asks for them too where a format
  shows `.Size`): SizeRw is the disk the writable layer uses, counted as containerd's
  snapshots count it for Docker 29 (continuity DiskUsage: each inode's blocks once,
  directories too): by an init built-in while the microVM runs (`builtin::SIZE`), and as
  its last run left it after, which init counts as it saves the layer (`kind::USAGE`).
  SizeRootFs adds the image's root filesystem as it is on the host (its EROFS disk). The
  numbers are the guest filesystem's blocks, not Docker Desktop's ext4's: the same writes
  measured 16 kB in a microVM and 8 kB under Docker 29.3.1.

### Import (D41)

`shards import` is `docker import` (docker/cli image/import.go; moby docker-v29.8.1
image_routes.go postImagesCreate and daemon/containerd/image_import.go, ImportImage;
`daemon/import.rs`): a tarball from a file or stdin, which the client sends, or a URL the
daemon fetches (BuildKit's HTTP source, `build/http.rs`), made an image of one layer, its
config BuildFromConfig of `--change` over an empty one, its platform `--platform`
normalized or the host's default spec (`v8` on arm64, the variant images name it by,
containerd's DefaultSpec), its
history one step with the comment (`-m`, else `Imported from -` or the URL), its ID the
manifest's digest. Its output, refusals and ordering are the CLI's and dockerd's, held to
Docker Engine 29.3.1's.

- The layer is kept as it came where it is a layer already: gzip and zstd as they are,
  bzip2 and xz decompressed (neither is a layer's media type), and a plain tar as it is,
  where dockerd spends a gzip on it: no compression on the import's path, the same diff ID.
- What an import or a commit writes is under the store's lease until it is named: a
  collection, which a daemon starting runs, took an import's blob from `ingest/` before.
- What it makes is a microVM, as a pull makes one (D25): an import of a container's files
  builds the image's EROFS disk at once and publishes it to the local engine as
  `shards.local/NAME`, so that its first run builds nothing. The
  tarball is kept once as it came and then read by what it is: an OCI image layout or a
  `docker save` archive is taken as `load` takes one (each image made a microVM, the one
  image it holds also named by the reference given), where dockerd would make a
  meaningless one-layer image of the archive's files; and a shards microVM (below) is one
  already, imported whole, its disk its root filesystem with nothing to unpack.
- A shards microVM is an OCI artifact (`application/vnd.shards.microvm.v1`): its own
  config the empty one, and two layers, its EROFS disk (`application/vnd.shards.erofs.v1`)
  and the image config it was made from (`application/vnd.shards.microvm.config.v1+json`),
  which `inspect` shows and a run runs by (`Manifest::image_config`). Docker 29.3.1 loads,
  lists and saves it and will not run it; `docker save shards.local/NAME | shards import -`
  brings one back.
- Publishing to the local engine never holds up what asked for it, and is robust to the
  engine (`local_store.rs`, PM M118). A pull, import or `rmi` only queues its request;
  each name's requests go in order on a thread of the name's, the ones queued behind a
  request in flight collapsed to the last, and names do not wait on each other. No upload
  is cut off part way, by a deadline or otherwise: Docker keeps the content of an upload
  cut off locked, and later loads of it fail with 502 after 60 s or never end, while other
  content still loads; an engine stuck on one image's content so holds up that image
  alone. A microVM the engine holds already, by its manifest's digest (the ID it gives
  it), is not sent again: one GET of 5.4 ms p50 in place of an upload of the whole disk,
  which took 10 to 50 s on the same loaded host.
- The engine is the client's: `DOCKER_HOST`, `DOCKER_CONTEXT` and `SHARDS_LOCAL_STORE`
  are sent with each request, so that the engine is the one the client's environment
  names, the daemon's where the client sets none. The E2E tests set `SHARDS_LOCAL_STORE=none` (`common::command`) and
  publish only to an engine of their own; before, every test daemon published to the
  host's Docker, and any upload a test's end cut off would lock its content there.

### Security options and seccomp (D42)

`--security-opt` on `run` and `create` is Docker's (docker/cli opts.go parseSecurityOpts
and parseSystemPaths; moby docker-v29.8.1 daemon/daemon_unix.go parseSecurityOpt,
daemon/seccomp_linux.go WithSeccomp, oci_linux.go; runc v1.3.4's init), held to Docker
Engine 29.3.1's words and to what its containers see (`security_opt_confines_the_workload`):

- The CLI reads a profile's file and sends its JSON compacted (Go's json.Compact, its
  words on what is no JSON), takes `systempaths=unconfined` out for no masked or
  read-only paths, and refuses an option without a value but `no-new-privileges`.
  dockerd refuses the rest as the container is made ("invalid --security-opt 1/2"), keeps
  them in HostConfig.SecurityOpt (`label=disable` after for a privileged container), and
  takes labels and AppArmor profiles as a host without SELinux or AppArmor does, which
  the guest kernel has neither of; `writable-cgroups=true` leaves the cgroup hierarchy
  writable.
- The workload runs under Docker's default seccomp profile (moby/profiles seccomp
  v0.2.3), the one a run names, or none (`unconfined`, or privileged and naming
  none), resolved for its capabilities, the guest's architecture and the guest kernel's
  version (`minKernel`), compiled at start, cached per profile, capabilities and kernel,
  and loaded by shards-init where runc loads it: before the capabilities go, or with
  `no-new-privileges` just before the command; an exec takes the microVM's. A profile
  that cannot be loaded fails the start, not the making, the microVM kept created with
  exit code 128 and the reason in State.Error, which shards now keeps for every start that
  fails (it was always empty); `docker run` exits 125.
- The filter is shards' own (crates/seccomp). Its rules are kept as libseccomp 2.5.4
  keeps them (db.c ported), so that a profile's overlapping rules mean what they mean to
  Docker, and Docker mode in its tests decides as runc's program does on every input of a
  grid and refuses in its words, for 33 cases on both guest architectures recorded on
  native Linux (scripts/seccomp/generate). Where Docker's toolchain gets a profile wrong,
  shards does better, each difference pinned by its tests:
  - Names are read by the guest kernel's own tables (Linux 6.18.48,
    scripts/seccomp/kernel-tables). Docker's runc reads them by its libseccomp's: Docker
    Desktop 29.3.1's refuses listmount, statmount and mseal, which its own default
    profile allows and its kernel has, with ENOSYS (PM M119).
  - runc's -ENOSYS stub for syscalls past the profile's last is kept; a number below it
    that is no syscall is ENOSYS too, as the kernel's own answer.
  - On x86, libseccomp writes socketcall(2)'s call number over a socket rule's first
  comparison, so that `socket` allowed but for some families is socketcall allowed for
  every family; here the multiplexer takes such a rule's action only where it is the
  more restrictive. ipc(2)'s call is compared in its low 16 bits, which are all the
  kernel reads of it.
  - libseccomp's slip merging 64-bit LT/LE rules (it sets the true action) is fixed.
  - `--privileged --security-opt seccomp=builtin` is the default profile; dockerd reads
  `builtin` as JSON and fails.
  - The program: ranges of one decision by binary search, identical decisions shared, a
  third of runc's length and 43% fewer instructions per syscall at the median (PM M120).
  - Compiling it takes 1.3 ms at the median on either architecture (PM M167): where the
  kernel's syscalls begin and end is read off its tables. Until 2026-10-10 each number up
  to the stub's line was tested, which on arm64 lies past 32-bit Arm's private syscalls at
  0x0f0000, each test a scan of the tables: 1.7 s a compile, paid by each daemon's first
  run (by an Agentfile's three times, its domains' two filters with it) and by each build
  that ran a step, as its builder started. Every program is unchanged, byte for byte, for
  the 33 cases on both architectures under five kernels in both modes; a test holds a
  compile's lookups to its tables' size (mutation-checked).
- Not served: SCMP_ACT_NOTIFY, which needs a seccomp agent (listenerPath) shards does not
  run; it is refused as the microVM starts.
- What the filter costs a syscall: the guest kernel ran it interpreted until D227, which
  builds the kernel with its BPF JIT and no interpreter; seccomp's action cache skips it
  for a syscall allowed whatever its arguments. Each call's cost and each load's, loaded
  with and without `no-new-privileges`, interpreted against compiled: PM M489.

### stats (D43)

`shards watch vms` reads each running microVM's guest as dockerd's collector reads a
container's cgroup (moby daemon/stats/collector_unix.go): shards-init's STATS built-in
says the workload cgroup's CPU time, memory in use and its inactive file pages, its
limit (memory.max, else the VM's memory), its processes and its block devices' bytes,
the VM's CPU time from /proc/stat and its online CPUs, and the bytes its interfaces but
loopback's moved. docker/cli's helpers make the figures of two samples a second apart
(calculateCPUPercentUnix; memory less inactive_file on cgroup v2), and its formatter
(container/formatter_stats.go, `format::stats`) lays them out, `--format` with it; a
stopped microVM under `-a` shows zeros, as Docker's does. Every microVM is sampled at
once, each on its own thread. The CPU's denominator is the host's clock between the
samples, where docker/cli's is the system's CPU time from /proc/stat: inside a VM on a
loaded host that does not keep time (one spinning vCPU read 329% and 2503%). A paused
microVM's guest cannot answer; it shows the sample taken as it was paused, its CPU 0%,
where dockerd reads a frozen cgroup's files from outside it. Before, `stats` showed the VM process's own CPU and
resident memory and `--` for the rest. Memory is the guest's truth: the files a
microVM writes are memory while its writable layer is in guest memory (D37's open
item).

**Each vCPU's guest time** (2026-11-11, kiln plan 01a1cd8e862e7169a074db3d5fa33f3d step 2's
p/guest-cpu-time-v1, for Hex's charge by measured use, step 14). A runtime that charges a
microVM by what it uses needs the VMM's own CPU apart from its guest's: the VM process's CPU
time less what its vCPUs ran of their guest. XNU does not split a thread's time between
guest and host from outside, so each backend reads what its host keeps of it:
- HVF: `hv_vcpu_get_exec_time`, which the framework answers on the vCPU's owning thread
  alone (macOS 26.4 SDK `hv_vcpu.h`, its check seen in the framework's disassembly), read at
  every exit and published; a reader makes a vCPU that is in its guest exit once
  (`hv_vcpus_exit`) and waits for that exit alone, never blocking a running vCPU;
- KVM: the vCPU thread's `gtime`, field 43 of `/proc/self/task/TID/stat`, in clock ticks
  (Linux `fs/proc/array.c`; KVM's binary stats count exits, not guest time), which costs the
  vCPU nothing;
- WHP: `WHvGetVirtualProcessorCounters`' runtime set, `TotalRuntime100ns` less
  `HypervisorRuntime100ns` (Windows SDK 10.0.26100 `WinHvPlatformDefs.h`; the TLFS's
  virtual processor run time register).

Each vCPU's time is kept by its index, and a departed vCPU's is added to a total that never
falls; a read that fails gives the last value and why. The daemon asks its run's VM
(`GUEST_TIME`, kind 88, answered `GUEST_TIMED`, 89), and the Engine API's stats carry it in
their `microvm` object (`guest_ns`, `departed_guest_ns`, each vCPU's). Not carried: `read
metrics`, `shards stats`' table (Docker's, byte for byte), and shards-api's image runs
(D231), whose `Stats` has no field for it yet, which Hex awaits (Hex's
`docs/design/shards-image-class.md` §8, `GuestCpuTimePerVcpu`). Sources, the R03
derivations and what ROOT owes (the real-VM test on each backend, HVF's read cost):
[guest-cpu-time-v1](../research/measurements/guest-cpu-time-v1/README.md).

### D12's sizes and waits, and the boot console's: each from what it bounds

**Found.** The vsock device's muxer (crates/vmm `devices/virtio/vsock/muxer.rs`) and the
NS16550A console (`devices/serial.rs`) each held figures picked, not derived: 2 s for a
host client's handshake line, 256 RSTs owed, a 32-byte handshake line (Firecracker's
buffer, `src/vmm/src/devices/virtio/vsock/unix/muxer.rs` `read_local_stream_port`,
edb60617) and a 4096-byte receive buffer whose overflow lost what a host pasted.

**Decided** (the device's connection limit and what a snapshot keeps of its streams are
D12's too, derived apart):
- **A host client's handshake waits on no clock.** A pending handshake costs a slot and
  nothing else; a client that is gone is seen at once, as its socket's end. One that is
  alive keeps its slot while no other wants it, and gives it up only when every slot is
  taken and a newcomer (a host client or a guest's dial) wants one, the handshake silent
  longest first: its last progress is its accept, then its line's latest bytes
  (`Muxer::make_room`). The line is a local process's to write as it runs, so a host so
  loaded that the process runs late fails nothing, where 2 s cut it; and a cut cannot be
  asked again on the client's behalf, which D222's cut lookups rest on.
- **RSTs owed for packets that matched no connection follow the guest's rings**
  (`stray_rsts_bound`, read at activation from the sizes the guest negotiated): one RST
  answers one guest packet, and a round takes a TX ring of those at most (`step`); it
  goes out in one RX buffer, and the RX ring holds at most its size, which Linux keeps
  full. A guest taking its RSTs as they come has no more owed than the larger of the two;
  past that it is not taking them, and more are dropped (a TX flood cannot block RX's
  turn, audit A09, so they are not held back instead).
- **A handshake line is as long as the protocol's words make it**, at compile time:
  `CONNECT`, a space, a port of at most `u32::MAX`'s digits, and `\r\n` (a client's
  terminal may end it so; `\n` is Firecracker's). Case and spacing are taken as
  Firecracker takes them, within that length; a longer line is refused before its end.
- **Superseded 2026-11-14 (hvc0): the NS16550A is gone.** The console is virtio-console
  (`devices/virtio/console.rs`), and host input goes into the buffers the guest posts. Its rings
  hold one buffer each: Linux's driver posts page-sized receive buffers until the ring is full
  (drivers/char/virtio_console.c `fill_queue`, l. 1290-1311), and sends one transmit buffer at a
  time, spinning until it is used (`put_chars`/`__send_to_port`, l. 596-640, 1118-1123). What the
  guest has not taken waits in the host, so nothing is lost. The rows below for `serial.rs` record
  what was replaced. Its successors are `RECEIVE_SIZE`/`TRANSMIT_SIZE` = 1 and `INPUT_AT_ONCE` = 4 KiB,
  one guest page (x86-64's only size; arm64's `CONFIG_ARM64_4K_PAGES=y`).
- **The console's receiver is the NS16550A's**: its 16-byte FIFO, or in 16450 mode its
  one register, as the guest's driver sizes it. Host input waits for room instead of
  overrunning it, as Firecracker reads stdin only as far as its FIFO has room, so nothing
  typed or pasted is lost: what the guest has not drained waits in the host's own pipe or
  terminal. A loopback write past the room overruns, as the datasheet's does. A change
  of mode clears the receiver, FIFO to 16450 and back, and FCR1 clears it only with FCR0
  set (PC16550D datasheet, National Semiconductor, June 1995, 8.5 FIFO Control
  Register: "When changing from the FIFO Mode to the 16450 Mode and vice versa, data is
  automatically cleared from the FIFOs. This bit must be a 1 when other FCR bits are
  written to or they will not be programmed"; QEMU's hw/char/serial.c flushes on a
  change of FCR's enable bit too). Before legacy4 (2026-11-14) a reset of FCR0 kept
  what the FIFO held, so a 16450-mode receiver could hold 16 bytes, which is why legacy3
  bounded a restore by the FIFO in either mode. A snapshot's receiver now restores whole
  up to what its mode holds (`rx_capacity`: 16 bytes in FIFO mode, 1 in 16450 mode, the
  mode read first); one that holds more is refused as a malformed state (`DecodeError`,
  "the console's receiver"), never restored (legacy3, legacy4). Red/green: serial.rs
  `a_change_of_mode_clears_the_receiver` (16 bytes kept past FCR0's reset before) and
  `a_receiver_past_its_modes_depth_is_refused`'s 16450 rows (2 to 16 bytes restored
  before). Only builds before
  66652aafb (2026-11-09) kept up to 4096 (`RX_CAPACITY`): v0.6.0's and v0.7.0's snapshots
  (formats 24 and 28) among them; every format-29 writer (83b09843a, 2026-11-11, after
  66652aafb) bounded it. Refused, not migrated: a template is a cache the daemon makes
  again, keyed by the snapshot format (D25), so this build never looks up an older
  format's, and one that does not restore is removed and booted and saved again (D25,
  *Later runs restore it*); its receiver is filled only by `run --kernel`'s console
  (`forward_stdin`), typed input the guest had not read as it was saved, which no
  rewrite could give back to a 16-byte receiver without dropping it. The reader of the
  older 4096 bytes is gone. Red/green: serial.rs
  `a_receiver_past_its_modes_depth_is_refused` (16 restore; 17 and 4096 refused), which
  restored the 4096 before.

| Literal | Was | Now | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` (muxer.rs) | 2 s | none: `Duration::ZERO`, a slot given up only to a newcomer | the slot it holds (`make_room`); a client's end seen at once (poll.rs) |
| `MAX_STRAY_RSTS` (muxer.rs) | 256 | `stray_rsts_bound(rx, tx)` = the larger negotiated ring, `QUEUE_SIZE`'s before activation | virtio 1.3 §2.7 (queue size); Linux net/vmw_vsock/virtio_transport.c `virtio_vsock_rx_fill` (`while (vq->num_free)`, l. 336) and `virtio_transport_more_replies` (replies owed < the vring's size, l. 374-383), Linux 1590cf03 |
| `MIN_HANDSHAKE` (muxer.rs) | 10 | `handshake_len(decimal_digits(0), "\n")` = 10 | firecracker docs/vsock.md l. 55-57 (`CONNECT PORT\n`, decimal), edb60617 |
| `MAX_HANDSHAKE` (muxer.rs) | 32 | `handshake_len(decimal_digits(u32::MAX), "\r\n")` = 20 | the same, and the port's type, a u32 (virtio 1.3 §5.10.6, `le32 src_port, dst_port`) |
| `RX_CAPACITY` (serial.rs) | 4096 | `RX_FIFO` = 16 in FIFO mode, 1 in 16450 mode, host input flow-controlled | PC16550D datasheet ("16 byte FIFOs"); Linux drivers/tty/serial/8250/8250_port.c `uart_config[PORT_16550A]` (`.fifo_size = 16`, l. 66-68); Firecracker src/vmm/src/devices/legacy/serial.rs `recv_bytes` (l. 220-236) |

Held by unit tests (`handshake_lines_are_bounded_by_the_protocols_words`,
`a_silent_handshake_keeps_its_slot_until_a_newcomer_wants_it`,
`stray_resets_owed_follow_the_guests_rings`, `host_input_waits_for_room_and_loses_nothing`,
`an_older_snapshots_longer_receive_buffer_restores`). Owed: E2E runs on KVM,
Hypervisor.framework and WHP, and the 8-target lint.

### D12's rings and the console's reader: each from what it holds

**Found** beside D12's figures above: the vsock device's rings, 256 descriptors each
(Firecracker's), and the console's reader of host input, 256 bytes at a time, both picked.

**Decided:**
- **The vsock rings hold one guest socket's whole credit** in its guest's receive buffers, so
  a host stream to it waits on its credit, never on the ring first. A socket gives its peer
  at most its buffer's maximum, 256 KiB unless its program raises it; each receive buffer
  holds less than a page, so more than 64 hold it, and a split ring is a power of two: 128.
  Linux's driver makes its rings as large as the device offers and fills RX whole, so this
  is also the guest memory RX holds: half of what 256 held.
- **The console's reader reads as much as the receiver takes at once**, its FIFO: what the
  guest has not drained waits in stdin, not in the reader, as `Serial::input` waits for
  room.

| Literal | Was | Now | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| `QUEUE_SIZE` (vsock/mod.rs) | 256 | `(256 KiB / 4 KiB + 1).next_power_of_two()` = 128 | Linux net/vmw_vsock/af_vsock.c l. 200-201 (`VSOCK_DEFAULT_BUFFER_MAX_SIZE`); include/linux/virtio_vsock.h l. 138 (`VIRTIO_VSOCK_DEFAULT_RX_BUF_SIZE`, `SKB_WITH_OVERHEAD(1024 * 4)`); virtio 1.3 §2.7 (power of two); drivers/virtio/virtio_mmio.c l. 374-381 (the ring as long as QueueNumMax); Linux 1590cf03 |
| `forward_stdin`'s buffer (crates/shards vm_run.rs) | 256 B | `serial::INPUT_AT_ONCE` = the receive FIFO, 16 | the NS16550A's FIFO, as `RX_FIFO` above |

Held by `vsock::tests::the_rings_hold_a_guest_sockets_credit`. Owed: a vsock throughput run
of several host streams at once on each hypervisor (the rings halved), E2E, the 8-target
lint.

### D12's credit and window: a guest credited before it runs out, a window lent where it is used

**Found** while measuring the engine path (2026-11-11, kiln plan
01a1cd8e862e7169a074db3d5fa33f3d step 1,
[vsock-credit-v1](../research/measurements/vsock-credit-v1/README.md)). Linux caps a vsock
socket's credit at the lesser of its peer's buffer and its own (`virtio_transport_tx_buf_size`,
upstream 8ee784fdf006, in the pinned 6.18.48), so a guest socket sends no more than its own
`SO_VM_SOCKETS_BUFFER_SIZE` (256 KiB by default) unacknowledged. The device sent a credit
update only once the guest's view of its free space fell below 4 KiB (Firecracker's
`CONN_CREDIT_UPDATE_THRESHOLD`): a guest socket with less buffer than the window never heard
one and waited for ever (a 1 MiB stream through a 16 KiB guest buffer stalled with 1,032,192
bytes left), and a window past 256 KiB stalled every default guest socket at 262,144 bytes. A
guest's `CREDIT_REQUEST` went unanswered, where virtio 1.3 §5.10.6.3 answers it (latent:
Linux 6.18 sends none).

**Decided:**
- **Credit by half the guest's window.** The guest's window is the lesser of the device's and
  the guest's own `buf_alloc`, read from its every header. It is credited once what was
  forwarded unannounced reaches half of that, a receiver's update at half its buffer (RFC 1122
  §4.2.3.3), so it has the other half to send while the update travels. The 4 KiB threshold
  is gone, and a `CREDIT_REQUEST` is always answered.
- **A window lent where it is used**
  ([vsock-window-v1](../research/measurements/vsock-window-v1/README.md)). Every connection
  keeps `WINDOW_LEAST`, 64 KiB, one packet of the largest a driver sends (the bound each had
  before). A connection whose guest has used half its window grows toward `WINDOW_MOST`,
  `shards_abi::VSOCK_WINDOW`, 4 MiB: the knee of guest-to-host throughput over windows, 256
  MiB in 194.8, 87.5, 55.5, 52.6 and 57.7 ms through 64 KiB, 256 KiB, 1 MiB, 4 MiB and 16 MiB
  on KVM (r429), 37.7, 20.7 and 14.3 ms through 256 KiB, 1 MiB and 4 MiB on HVF (r433). It
  grows never past the guest's own buffer, out of `WINDOW_LENT` (MOST less LEAST), which the
  device lends across all its connections: one stream's window at the knee, as one worker
  moves every connection's packets. Its right edge never moves left (RFC 1122 §4.2.2.16). A
  connection's buffer grows to what its guest may still send and, after a flush, gives back
  what lies past twice that, so that each move costs fewer bytes than were forwarded since
  its room was made; the device holds at most N·LEAST + LENT buffered. Init's engine relay
  asks its socket for `VSOCK_WINDOW` as it dials.
- **Host socket buffers** (`SOCKET_BUFFER`, 256 KiB each way): with a 4 MiB window, 256 KiB
  moved as fast as 4 MiB (14.3 ms guest to host either way, r433), where macOS gave 8 KiB.
  Not set on Linux, whose confined VM process's seccomp filter allows no `setsockopt`
  (`confine.rs`), and whose `wmem_default` (212,992) is about the size: whether to allow it
  there is open, ROOT's.

The credit fix: red on the base in unit tests and in a real VM on KVM, green in 31 of 31
vsock unit tests and 5 of 5 real-VM tests, each guard's mutant red again (r416, r423). The
window's light tests, bounds (`Conn::check`, `Muxer::check` in every test step) and the
shrunk-buffer stall it found are vsock-window-v1's. **Owed** (ROOT): the vsock real-VM
tests on HVF and WHP, the window's clippy and unit tests there, the shrunk-buffer stall
in a real VM, and the 7-target lint.

### The other virtio devices' rings: each from its driver's traffic (D12, D31, D38, D133, D144, D151, D154)

**Found** beside the vsock rings: every other virtio device's rings were picked too:
virtio-net's, virtio-blk's and virtio-fs's 256 (Firecracker's), the GPU's 256 and 16 (QEMU's
and libkrun's), and 64 for the balloon's three, virtio-mem's, virtio-pmem's and
virtio-iommu's two. And a restore held a saved ring to what the device offers now, so the
vsock rings' halving refused every template saved before it.

**Decided:**
- **Where its driver bounds what it puts in flight, a ring holds that**, every entry a
  descriptor where the device offers no indirect ones: the balloon's inflate and deflate
  one array of page numbers at a time (1 each), its reporting at most
  PAGE_REPORTING_CAPACITY ranges, which Linux takes no smaller ring than (32); virtio-mem
  one request and its response from the one buffer it keeps (2); virtio-pmem one flush
  (2), as the device answers one at a time, each a flush of its file whole, and a flush
  finding the ring full waits in the driver's list as it would in the ring; virtio-iommu's
  events none, the device reporting no faults (1, so its driver allocates one event
  buffer); the GPU's cursor none, with no scanout (1).
- **virtio-net's rings hold the frame ring's bytes** in the guest's receive buffers, which
  Linux makes a page at most: 1 MiB / 4 KiB = 256, the figure it was, now derived, so a
  frame waiting in the frame ring waits on its guest, never on RX first; TX holds as many of
  the guest's frames, one entry each with indirect descriptors, the frame ring the other way
  holding their bytes.
- **A restored ring keeps the size its driver made**, held to the specification's maximum
  rather than to what the device offers now: its driver sized it once, against what the
  build that saved it offered, and does not size it again. A new driver is held to the
  device's offer.
- **Not derived, owed a measurement:** virtio-blk's ring (256), virtio-fs's (256), the
  GPU's control ring (256) and virtio-iommu's requests (64). Their drivers bound nothing
  they put in flight but by the ring (blk-mq's tags are the ring's entries, virtio_blk.c
  l. 1477-1488; FUSE's synchronous requests one per task; virtio-gpu's submissions by its
  programs; virtio-iommu's unmaps batched until a sync, x86-64's DMA being lazy), and each
  device's worker serves one request at a time, so a longer ring only moves what waits from
  the guest's queues into the ring. The size that keeps a worker from waiting on its
  guest's refill is Little's law over the worker's service time and the guest's refill
  time, both to be measured on each hypervisor under load (block and share I/O, Venus
  submissions, a passed-through device's DMA); these keep their figures until then.

| `QUEUE_SIZE` (mem.rs) | 64 | 2 | drivers/virtio/virtio_mem.c l. 1389-1417 (`virtio_mem_send_request`: `vm->req`, `virtqueue_add_sgs(vq, sgs, 1, 1, …)`, waits) |
| `QUEUE_SIZE` (pmem.rs) | 64 | 2 | drivers/nvdimm/nd_virtio.c l. 72-102 (`virtio_pmem_flush`: one out, one in; -ENOSPC waits for an answer) |
| `EVENT_QUEUE_SIZE` (iommu.rs) | 64 | 1 | drivers/iommu/virtio-iommu.c l. 1131-1138 (`viommu_fill_evtq`: a buffer for each free entry); the device sends no fault |
| GPU `QUEUE_SIZES[1]` (gpu/mod.rs) | 16 | 1 | no scanout; drivers/gpu/drm/virtio/virtgpu_kms.c l. 221-227 (both queues found) |

and a compile-time assertion of the net rings. Owed: E2E of each device on each hypervisor
(the balloon's reporting, a grow and a shrink by virtio-mem, a pmem flush, a GPU guest, a
passed-through device behind the IOMMU), a template saved by the build before restored by
this one, a network throughput run, the measurements above, and the 8-target lint.

### D12's console kept to quote: learned for each kernel

**Found** beside D12's figures above: a VM whose console no one reads kept its last 4096
bytes (`SAID`, serial.rs, "a page") to quote as its guest resets, and shards-api copied the
figure (`CONSOLE_SAID`) to size the tail it keeps of shards' output (`TAIL`). Picked, not
derived: one panic (6.18 on arm64, 1,129 bytes to a `quiet` console) stood behind it, and
every other VM, whose console nothing quotes, kept the same.

**Decided:**
- **What a VM keeps is learned, for each kernel, from how its kernel's reports came out.**
  The spawner of a VM that quotes its console reads `<home>/said/<pin>` and gives the VM
  `--console-said N`, N = `shards_abi::bounds::console_said`: the longest whole report
  recorded, and twice the most kept of one that ran out (it needed more), at least a
  panic's frame, the report it is kept for (a run-out at nothing kept says nothing of its
  length); with no records of its own kernel's, the same over every kernel's; with none at
  all, a panic's frame.
- **A panic's frame** is the two lines that carry the kernel's panic message,
  `Kernel panic - not syncing: %s` and `---[ end Kernel panic - not syncing: %s ]---`, each
  as long as the buffer the message is formatted into, `vpanic`'s `static char buf[1024]`:
  2 x 1024 = 2048 bytes. The 1,129 bytes above fit it.
- **A kernel's pin is its identity, the SHA-256 of its bytes.** The guest store names its
  files by it (`<home>/guest/sha256-<hex>`, shards' pinned kernels among them, whose
  `Pinned::sha256` is the same digest), so a stored kernel is never hashed; one given by
  path is hashed once for each file as it is (its path, length, time of change, and on Unix
  device, inode and ctime), the digest kept in `<home>/said/kernels`. A restore's spawner
  does not know its kernel: its records are `unpinned`'s, which count among every kernel's.
  (The plan named a pinned kernel by `Pinned::name`; its SHA-256 is the same identity and
  lets a path to the pinned kernel's bytes share its records.)
- **A record is one whole line**, `report N` (a report whole, the console's N bytes all
  kept) or `cut N` (its first bytes lost past the N kept), appended in one write (`O_APPEND`
  on Unix, `FILE_APPEND_DATA` without `FILE_WRITE_DATA` on Windows, std's `append`), so
  writers beside each other never interleave; a reader passes over an unfinished last line
  and any line that is no record.
- **The console says whether its ring lost bytes**, and the reset's report says so: `its
  console's last lines, those before them lost past the N bytes kept:`. A report cut before
  its first line is a run-out.
- **The VM writes no record.** It tells its spawner `report N` or `cut N` on a pipe the
  spawner gives it (`--said-to`); the spawner holds it to the size it gave (a whole report
  no longer, a cut recorded at that size) and appends. The VM process, in App Sandbox on
  macOS, opens only what its spawner grants it (D30).
- **The spawners:** a build's builder (build/builder.rs, which records on a thread of its
  own); the command line's direct boot, `shards run vm --kernel … --no-console` and `shards
  restore vm … --no-console` (cli/mod.rs: on Unix, which becomes the VM, a recorder it
  starts first, `shards console-said`, reads the pipe to the VM's exit; on Windows the
  command line itself, which waits for its VM); and shards-api's client, which reads the
  records and passes `--console-said N`, the command line it starts recording, and keeps
  the tail its report fits in (`tail(N)`).
- **A VM whose console nothing quotes keeps none of it**: one whose console is shown, one
  that serves a command (`--rootfs … -- CMD`), and the daemon's warm VMs. Where a spawner
  says nothing, a VM that quotes keeps a panic's frame. The tests that run a machine in
  their own process and read its console as it goes keep all of it (`cfg.said =
  usize::MAX`).

| Literal | Was | Now | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SAID` (serial.rs) | 4096 | `Config::said`, its spawner's `--console-said N` = `console_said(kernel's records, every kernel's)`; 0 where nothing quotes it | this kernel's own reports (`<home>/said/<pin>`) |
| no records (bounds.rs `PANIC_FRAME`) | none | 2 x `PANIC_MESSAGE` = 2 x 1024 = 2048 | Linux 6.18.48 kernel/panic.c l. 431 (`static char buf[1024]`), l. 483 and 596 (the two lines that print it) |
| `CONSOLE_SAID` (shards-api client.rs) | 4096 | the `--console-said N` it passes, read from the same records | as `SAID` |
| `TAIL` (shards-api client.rs) | prefix + 4096 x 6 + 1 | `tail(N)`: the longest prefix (a cut's, N's most digits) + N x `ESCAPED` + 1 | vm_run.rs `last_said` |

Held by unit tests (`a_consoles_kept_bytes_are_what_its_records_need`,
`console_records_are_whole_lines`, `the_last_bytes_said_are_kept_in_whole_lines`,
`a_kernels_records_teach_what_its_vms_keep`, `a_path_kernels_digest_is_kept_until_it_changes`,
`records_appended_at_once_never_interleave`, `only_a_vm_that_quotes_its_console_learns`,
`a_guests_last_words_move_no_terminal`, shards-api's
`the_longest_report_shards_writes_is_quoted_whole`). Owed: E2E on KVM, Hypervisor.framework
and WHP (`a_reset_with_no_console_says_its_guests_panic`, a builder's reset), what a direct
boot's recorder process costs (its start beside the VM's, its memory while it waits) and a
path kernel's first hash, both unmeasured; the 8-target lint and CI.

### D13's boot and hypervisor limits: each the protocol's, the architecture's or the hypervisor's

**Decided:**
- **What the hypervisor counts, it is asked.** KVM's MSR index list and a vCPU's register list
  are read as KVM's interface offers: asked with room for none, KVM answers E2BIG and the
  count, and the list is read with room for that many, where a cap of 1,024 MSRs or 4,096
  registers was guessed. A GPU's devices are as many as Vulkan counts, where 64 were.
- **A machine has a vCPU for each APIC id its MADT can give one** on x86-64: every 8-bit id
  but 0xFF, the broadcast, which Linux ignores in a Local APIC entry and which is past its
  xAPIC driver's highest, 0xFE: 255. 254 had come from Firecracker's MP table, whose IOAPIC
  takes an APIC id; shards' MADT gives its IOAPIC id 0, another namespace. KVM's and WHP's
  limits and WHP's snapshot decoder take the one constant (`acpi::MAX_VCPUS`), and so, since
  2026-11-14, does the machine's own reader of its vCPU states (vm/x86_64.rs
  `decode_vcpus`), which had kept 254: every 255-vCPU machine's snapshot, and so its move,
  was refused as it restored ("sequence of 255 (limit 254)", snapshot.rs' storm on KVM);
  unit test `a_snapshot_holds_a_state_for_each_vcpu_a_machine_may_have`. On arm64, a
  machine has as many as its memory map has GICv3 redistributors for (`layout::MAX_VCPUS`,
  123), which a snapshot's decoder takes too.
- **A kernel's program headers are as many as its ELF header says**, below the gABI's escape
  (PN_XNUM), and their table must lie in the file, which is checked before anything is
  allocated for it: 64 had been picked.

### D176's decoders: what a snapshot holds is what its machine and its hypervisor make

**Found.** The decoders of a snapshot's state, which a restore reads as untrusted, held picked
bounds: 1,024 vCPUs, 512 system registers, 32 of the CPU interface's, 64 ID registers and
16 MiB of GIC state on arm64; 4,096 registers on arm64 KVM and 65,536 GIC writes; blobs of
64 KiB and 4,096 MSRs on x86-64 KVM; blobs of 64 KiB, 256 registers, 64 leaves and 254 vCPUs on
WHP; runs of plugged memory and of RAM's data for 1 TiB; paths of 4,096 bytes and generation
names of 64; and a live move's records of 1 MiB.

**Decided:** each bound is what the machine the state describes, its architecture or its
hypervisor can make, so a state past it is no machine's and is refused as it is read; and
what only the hypervisor knows the size of, the input bounds and that hypervisor judges:
- **Counts by the key space they are drawn from.** System registers and the CPU interface's
  are keyed by their 16-bit encodings, so a list of more than 2^16 names one twice; ID
  registers are of the Feature ID space, 192. KVM's register IDs on arm64 are of five
  classes, each told apart by 16 bits (5 × 2^16).
- **Counts by the machine.** vCPUs by the vCPU limits above (D13); runs of data by the RAM's
  blocks (one a block at most, as runs that meet are one); runs of plugged memory by every
  other block of the plug region (`hotplug_mib` rounded up to Linux's memory block); both
  read from the same state before them. Generation names are as long as `fresh_name` makes
  them (60); paths as long as the host's own (PATH_MAX on Unix, an extended-length path on
  Windows).
- **Counts by what a save makes.** KVM's GIC writes: as many as `gic::save` makes of the
  restoring VM's vCPUs, with or without LPIs (2, 81 for each 32 SPIs, and per vCPU 17
  private, 5 for LPIs, up to 15 of its CPU interface); the ITS's registers: the 13 it saves.
  WHP's registers: every name a save keeps, each once (its 69, its optional ones and 16
  variable MTRR pairs); its CPUID: the leaves of `IDENTITY`.
- **Sizes by the structure.** KVM's x86-64 structures are each exactly their ioctl's size;
  its XSAVE area at least `struct kvm_xsave`'s and at most what its own CPUID says (leaf
  0DH's ECX, which KVM's KVM_CAP_XSAVE2 says the same of); WHP's APIC state its register page.
  An XSAVE area of another size than the restoring host's (another host's, D176 part 6) is
  laid into one of this host's KVM_CAP_XSAVE2 size (amended 2026-11-14, review finding
  migrate-07): KVM_SET_XSAVE reads that many bytes, and "the offsets of the state save areas
  in struct kvm_xsave follow the contents of CPUID leaf 0xD on the host" (api.rst §4.43), so
  `arch::x86_64::xsave::lay_into` keeps the legacy region and header as saved and puts each
  component the guest enabled (XCR0, from its saved XCRs) or holds (XSTATE_BV) where both
  hosts' leaf 0xD lay it out alike: the saved vCPU's CPUID, as its own host's KVM offered it,
  and this host's; the rest is zeros, the initial state XRSTOR gives a component its
  XSTATE_BV leaves clear (Intel SDM Vol. 1 §13.8.1). A component laid out otherwise or
  nowhere, a compacted area, one shorter than its header or past either area is refused
  typed (`XsaveRefused`, `hv::kvm::Error::Xsave`), after the CPU coverage check and before
  anything of the vCPU is set. Before, an area shorter than this host's was refused: a
  non-AMX host's 4096 bytes on an AMX host's 11008, under a baseline without AMX. No literal
  is chosen: the offsets and sizes are the two hosts' CPUID, the header's the SDM's (512 and
  64 bytes, §13.4.1-13.4.2). Held by `a_smaller_hosts_xsave_area_is_laid_into_a_larger_ones`,
  `an_xsave_area_laid_out_otherwise_is_refused` and `xcr0_is_read_from_a_vcpus_xcrs`. Owed to
  ROOT: a move between a non-AMX and an AMX host of one vendor under their common baseline
  (`SHARDS_MOVE_INVITE=<destination-invitation-file> cargo test -p shards --test moved
  a_microvm_moved_to_another_host_keeps_its_cpu_image_files_and_connections`), its guest's
  vector registers checked after.
- **The hypervisor judges what only it sizes.** A GIC's state on arm64 is its backend's own
  serialization: KVM's and WHP's restores bound theirs (the writes above; WinHvPlatformDefs.h's
  layouts), and Hypervisor.framework refuses a state not its own. WHP's XSAVE area is as long
  as its partition's, which takes it or refuses it. KVM's MSRs are fewer than its MAX_IO_MSRS,
  which a save and a restore each pass in one call.
- **A live move's records are a memory file's blocks** (`DATA_BLOCK`, 2 MiB), the unit the file
  says data in; both ends are one build's.

| arch name (snapshot/mod.rs) | 32 bytes | the input's: it is only compared with this build's | `decode_head` |
| `MAX_TABLES` (fs/proto.rs), `MAX_CONTROL` (fs/mod.rs) | `MAX_STATE`, 64 MiB | `CONTROL - 1` = 2^31 - 1: what one control frame's length word says below its mark | fs/mod.rs `CONTROL`, `read_any_into` |

**A state is bounded by its machine.** A state is read whole into the process that restores
its machine, beside the RAM that process maps for the guest: one of no more than that RAM
costs a restore no more of the host than the machine it describes may use as it runs, so a
hostile state gains nothing past the machine it claims to be, and is refused past it before
more than its head is read; its parts are bounded as they are decoded by what that machine
makes (above). Its disks, pmem files and shared directories are among its machine's virtio
devices, each on a transport of its own, as many as the architecture's interrupt lines for
them. The bytes of the files a guest holds open on a share that no path reaches are the
one part nothing of the machine bounds: a save of a state past its RAM is refused, as one
past 64 MiB was, and the share's tables travel to and from their server in one control
frame, as long as its length word says.

**And by the host that reads it (amended 2026-11-14, review finding migrate-04).** The
head's RAM is the file's own claim: a head forged to u64::MAX MiB saturated `most_state`,
and a sparse state as long as its sender liked (a move lays a FILE's length with
`set_len`, daemon/moves.rs) had all of it allocated and zero-filled before its decoder
refused it. A state is now refused, typed (`snapshot::StateRefused`), from its head and its
length alone, before its whole is allocated: a RAM of more bytes than a u64 counts
(`PastAnyMachine`), a length past its machine's RAM (`PastItsMachine`), and a length past
what the reading host can hold now (`PastHost`): `platform::holdable_known`, what its kernel
says it has available (Linux's MemAvailable, proc_meminfo(5); macOS's
kern.memorystatus_level of its memory; Windows' ullAvailPhys), else all its memory
(sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES), GlobalMemoryStatusEx), the shards daemon's existing `holdable`
moved to vmm's platform for both processes. That is the bound the file does not say. It is
read where it runs, at each read, so it has no cold start; a host that says neither is
refused (`HostMemoryUnknown`), never read past. The confined Linux VM process reads the
host's memory by sysinfo(2), which glibc's and musl's sysconf ask and its seccomp filter
now allows (`confine.rs`); /proc/meminfo is past its Landlock rules. Every way in reads by
it: a move's `relocate` of what it placed, a restore's `read`, `backing_named`, `layout`.
Held by `a_forged_states_head_has_no_more_allocated_than_the_host_holds` (with each bound
removed, red) and `a_state_past_its_machines_memory_is_refused`. Owed to ROOT: reads at once
are each bounded alone (two within the host's available memory may be past it together:
an admission held across a home's concurrent restores is the design); the probe's cost on
the restore path (R14: a read of /proc/meminfo in Linux's daemon, a Landlock-refused open
and a sysinfo(2) in the confined VM process, two sysctls on macOS, one call on Windows); a
template restored on Linux KVM (its VM process confined), Hypervisor.framework and WHP; and
the bounded-RSS run of a forged sparse state through a move's import (`tests/moved.rs`).

Held by unit tests (`a_state_is_bounded_by_its_machine`,
`a_state_past_its_machines_memory_is_refused`, `a_state_past_what_a_machine_has_is_refused`,
`a_decoders_bounds_are_what_kvm_gives`, `a_restore_takes_the_writes_a_save_of_its_vcpus_makes`,
`a_decoders_bounds_are_what_a_save_makes`, `runs_are_bounded_by_the_machines_memory`). Owed:
a template saved and restored on Hypervisor.framework, KVM of each architecture and WHP of
each (E2E), a live move, and the 8-target lint.

**A reader looks again as long as its generation was replaced** (migrate-10, 2026-11-14). A
reader that found the generation its pointer named gone looked again 8 times
(`READ_ATTEMPTS`, picked), then refused "its generations kept being replaced", however many
generations a newer writer had yet to publish and however soon one would stay. Now it looks
again as long as the pointer names another generation than the one it found gone
(`pointed_open`): each look again follows one writer's whole publication (a generation
written, synced, pointed at and the one before removed), each under a name no generation had
(`fresh_name`: the time, the process and its count), so it reads the first that stays put for
one look's length, and the loop is bounded by the writers' publications, not by a count. A
pointer that still names the generation found gone is no replacement and is refused as that
("its pointer names generation …, which is gone"); a pointer gone is "no snapshot here", as
before. Red at `READ_ATTEMPTS` (ten replacements in a row refused), green without it:
`snapshot::tests::on_disk::a_reader_follows_every_replacement_and_refuses_a_pointer_to_a_gone_generation`.
Owed to ROOT: a reader beside writers that publish without pause (a template saved again and
again while restores read it) on each backend, its reads' p50/p99/max of looks and time.

### D191's hold: CFS's period, and reads when the share could be spent

**Found:** the governor read its vCPUs' time at least every 10 ms while they were busy, a
picked cap.

**Decided:** a machine's governor reads their time when the share could first be spent were
every vCPU to run, and no later: none can spend it sooner, vCPUs using at most their number's
CPU time. A group's governor reads as soon as the group's room could be spent, its own
vCPUs alone or, sooner, at the rate the group was last seen eating into it (`room_lasts`),
which its other machines spend too; a group no further ahead than at its last read leaves
the first.

**Decided, the least wait and when to read so closely:**
- **`SOONEST` is CFS's own precision, 1 ms.** CFS bandwidth control takes no quota or period
  below 1 ms and leaves each CPU up to 1 ms of runtime past a cgroup's quota: the hold, which
  holds vCPUs as CFS holds a cgroup's threads, reads no closer, its vCPUs each running at
  most that past their share, which comes off the next period's.
- **A machine reads closely when its own use foretells its share spent**, not at half of it:
  where its last period's use, grown again by as much as it grew from the period before,
  reaches the share (`busy_next`), or it was held, or a new limit begins. A machine's first
  period, after none, is foretold twice its use, the half mark it had; one holding steady
  below its share reads once a period, and one growing toward it reads closely before it
  gets there. A group reads closely when the rate it was seen eating into its room
  (`room_lasts`, its last two reads) would spend the room within a period, where it had read
  so at half its room.

| Literal | Was | Now | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PERIOD` (`HOLD_PERIOD`, vm/mod.rs) | 100 ms | none: each limit's period derived as it is set, vcpus × g over its share (`granule::period`; "Its period, in force", below) | the machine's vCPUs; g learned where it runs (`platform::granule`) |
| `SOONEST` (vm/hold.rs) is `granule::LEAST_WAIT` | 1 ms | 1 ms, cited, g cold | as `SOONEST` |
| the group's look with no quota (vm/hold.rs `govern_group`) | `PERIOD`, 100 ms | the group's own `cpu.max` period, which `max` keeps (`group::Budget::period`) | the group's `cpu.max` (kernel/sched/core.c `cpu_period_quota_parse`: `max 100000` where unset) |
| `BUSY` (vm/hold.rs) | 10 ms | none: `(allowed - used) / vcpus`; a group's, the lesser of that and `room_lasts` | the vCPUs' own count; the group's charged rate (`GroupCpu::charge`) |
| `SOONEST` (vm/hold.rs) | 1 ms | 1 ms, cited | kernel/sched/core.c l. 10054 (`min_bw_quota_period_us`); kernel/sched/fair.c l. 7179 (`min_cfs_rq_runtime`); Documentation/scheduler/sched-bwc.rst l. 94-95, 179-186 |
| the machine's busy mark (vm/hold.rs `govern`) | `used * 2 >= share` | `busy_next(before, used, share)`: `used + (used - before) >= share` | the machine's own last two periods |
| the group's busy mark (vm/hold.rs `govern_group`) | `ahead * 2 >= room` | `room_lasts(before, now, room) < whole` | the group's own last two reads |

All in Linux 1590cf03. Held by `hold::tests` (`a_machine_is_busy_as_its_last_two_periods_foretell`,
`a_groups_room_lasts_at_the_rate_it_was_seen_spent` and the governors' spinning tests, which
need a host whose CPUs the test threads get: run through
`docs/research/measurements/macos-sched/launchd-run.sh` or on a quiet host). Owed: the hold's
E2E on each hypervisor, a group of machines held on a loaded host, and how far past their
share machines that go from steady to busy run under each mark (the old and the derived),
measured.

**Its period** (2026-11-13, R03: decided by ROOT, built once measured). `PERIOD` is CFS's
default period (kernel/sched/sched.h l. 444-447, `default_bw_period_us`), an upstream
default, which R03 holds insufficient alone.
- sched-bwc.rst gives the period as a tradeoff its operator makes (l. 210-234: a longer
  period for burst capacity, a shorter for a consistent latency). On Windows, where
  GetThreadTimes charges whole 15.625 ms ticks (PM M294), a hold whose share of a 100 ms
  period is under its vCPUs' count of ticks is never resolved within a period: 4 vCPUs held
  under 625 milli-CPU are held on average alone.
- *Decided.* A hold's period is the shortest one in which the governor resolves its share:
  P = vcpus × g / share. The share is in CPUs (the rate over `MILLI_PER_CPU`). g is the
  greater of the governor's measured soonest wake and the measured resolution of the vCPU
  threads' clock (`platform::ThreadClock`). Cold start: g is the soonest wake until each is
  measured.
  - No clamp: CFS's 1 ms and 1 s bounds (core.c l. 10053-10054) are its operator's range,
    not this governor's limits. P ≥ g already holds wherever the share is at most the vCPUs.
  - An orchestrator derives its window from whatever the run reports (D247's
    `rate_period`), so it follows the change when it comes.
- *Owed to ROOT before it is built* (R14): the cost of a kick on each backend (HVF, KVM
  x86-64 and arm64, WHP x86-64 and arm64). A period kicks every vCPU once at most, so shorter
  periods kick more: 4 vCPUs at 2000 milli-CPU would hold over about 2g, where today they
  hold over 100 ms.
  - Measure on each backend a machine of 1, 4 and the host's vCPUs, every vCPU spinning in
    its guest. Hold it at rates whose derived periods run from g to 100 ms, and at today's
    100 ms beside each, interleaved.
  - Read, n times a point: the kicks a second; the VM process's CPU time past its vCPUs'
    guest time (the governor's and the kicks' own cost); each vCPU's exits; the guest's
    progress (its spin count); and the guest time past the rate over a window. Report
    p50/p90/p99/max, with host, OS and revision.
  - Until then the period stays 100 ms, and no code of the derivation is written.
- *Its learner, built* (2026-11-14, migrate-09; ROOT's takeover brief: the learner and its
  cold start built ahead of the measurement). `platform::granule` learns g where it runs:
  - *Wake* (`Late`): the least a governor's timed wait ended past what it asked, over every
    such wait of the process's; a wait woken early (a new limit, the end) is not counted. The
    least, as the soonest a wait ends is what the host resolves; a wait late on a loaded host
    only adds above it.
  - *Clock* (`clock_step`, `measure_clock`): the step the governor thread's CPU clock counts
    in, read while it spins until the clock has moved twice, the second move a whole step;
    once a process, as a hold's first limit begins, so it spins two of its steps at most
    (31.25 ms on Windows, PM M294; nanoseconds' reads elsewhere). A clock that cannot be read
    is typed `Unclocked`, and g is its wake's.
  - *Cold*: neither known, g is `SOONEST`, the governor's least wait.
  - `hold::derived_period(vcpus, milli, g)` is vcpus × g × 1000 / milli, none where it
    outgrows a u64 of ns (typed, never saturated into a period). The governor feeds its waits
    to `Late` and says each limit's derived period in the debug log beside the one in force.
  - Still in force: `PERIOD`, 100 ms. Two things stand before the switch: the kick-cost
    measurement above, and the image API's `RATED`, which carries no period, so the period an
    image run's host says as the run starts (`Started::rate_period`) would no longer be the one
    a rate is held over (wire VERSION 28; Hex reads it): `RATED` must carry each rate's period,
    as the direct path's `RATE` answer (`Answer::Held { period_ns }`) already does.
  - Held by `platform::granule::tests` (g cold, by its wake, by its clock; early ends not
    counted; a clock's step its second move, and this host's measured) and
    `vm::hold::tests::a_holds_derived_period_resolves_its_share`.
  - *Owed to ROOT, exactly*: on each backend, `SHARDS_LOG=debug` runs of
    `cargo test -p shards --test boot a_managed_guest_is_held_to_the_rate_its_client_asks_on_its_socket` (or the
    run D191's measurement drives) at the rates above, reading each limit's "derived … from g"
    line beside the kicks a second and guest progress; then the switch, with `RATED`'s period.
- *Its period, in force* (2026-11-14, migrate-09: ROOT's brief, "finish wiring the hold's
  period to the learned value, so no fixed period is left in production"; the kick-cost
  measurement stays owed, below). `HOLD_PERIOD` and `vm::hold_period` are gone.
  - *The derivation, shared* (`platform::granule::period`): vcpus × g × `MILLI_PER_CPU` over
    the rate, in u128, refused typed (`granule::Outgrown`) where it outgrows a u64 of ns,
    never saturated. Windows' priority governor holds one thread's half a CPU by the same
    function (platform-11).
  - *When*: as each limit is set (`Hold::set`), from g as the process knows it then
    (`granule::g`, `step().g(LEAST_WAIT)`); the governor holds that limit's periods over it
    (`State::period`) until the next limit. g learned later (a wait's lateness) moves the next
    limit's period, never one already answered, so a period said is the one held.
  - *Cold start*: the first limit measures, on the setting thread, before any period is
    derived (`granule::measure`, ROOT's review 2026-11-14): the host's wake, one timed wait of
    the least a wait can ask (a nanosecond), its lateness counted in `LATE` as the host's own
    wake granularity (a timer tick where the host waits in ticks, µs on high-resolution
    timers); and the thread clock's step (two of its steps at most: µs where clocks count ns,
    31.25 ms on Windows, PM M294). The first g is so `LEAST_WAIT` plus the measured wake, or
    the clock's step where coarser: never `LEAST_WAIT` alone. A clock that cannot be read is
    typed `Unclocked` and g its wake's (the debug line says so).
  - *`LEAST_WAIT` (1 ms), its source*: CFS bandwidth control's own precision, cited above for
    `SOONEST` (core.c `min_bw_quota_period_us`, fair.c `min_cfs_rq_runtime`): the least the
    governor waits between reads, as D191 holds vCPUs as CFS holds a cgroup and no closer. It
    is not any host's timer resolution, and no longer stands as one: g adds the host's
    measured wake above it. Held by `granule::tests::a_cold_wake_is_measured_before_any_wait`.
    A g learned low only shortens the period: the share is then held on average across
    periods, as the debt carries, never over more than it gives.
  - *Let be* (no rate, or every vCPU's whole CPU): the period is g, the formula at a share of
    every vCPU, the finest the governor resolves, which `RATED`'s period must still say (it is
    never none, `shards_abi::rate`).
  - *Refused*: a period past a u64 of ns refuses the limit, the hold as it was
    (`Running::hold_rate`'s error, `REFUSED` on the wire).
  - *Told*: the direct path's `RATED <milli> <period>` carries each limit's period (D255);
    the image channel moves the period from `Started` to each `RATED` answer (version 31,
    `wire::Rated`), the VM telling the daemon its answer as the managed machine's line
    (`shards_abi::rate::answer`, read back by api_run's `rated_of`). `ImageGuest::rate_period()`
    is the last answer's, none before one (Hex's learner reads it there; its re-vendor owed).
  - *The group's look*: a group with no quota looks again each period of its own `cpu.max`,
    which `max` keeps and the daemon now writes with it (`group::Budget`, `groups::CpuMax`);
    a budget never written refuses `hold_group`, typed, never a picked look.
  - Held (red/green): vmm `hold::tests::a_limit_is_held_over_the_period_derived_from_g` and
    `the_governor_holds_over_the_limits_period` (red with the period in force at 100 ms: the
    hold returned no period, and a thread at half a CPU held 50 ms past its 10 ms period's
    share), `granule::tests::a_derived_period_resolves_its_share`, `group::tests`'s
    `a_budget_written_is_read_through_another_mapping`, api `wire::tests::a_rates_period_reads_back_as_its_vm_said_it`,
    `session::tests::a_rates_answer_is_kept_for_its_awaited_ask_alone`, shards
    `api_run::tests::a_rates_answer_reads_as_it_was_asked`, `vm_run::tests::a_rates_answer_is_its_hold_and_its_period`,
    `daemon::groups::tests::cpu_budgets_read_as_the_kernel_reads_them` and
    `a_cpu_budget_of_every_cpu_holds_nothing`.
  - *Owed to ROOT*: the kick-cost runs above, now of the period in force:
    `SHARDS_LOG=debug cargo test -p shards --profile test-release --test boot a_managed_guest_is_held_to_the_rate_its_client_asks_on_its_socket -- --nocapture`
    and `cargo test -p shards --profile test-release --test api_image the_orchestrators_rate_holds_its_run_to_it`
    on HVF, KVM x86-64 and arm64 (L1), WHP x86-64 and arm64, reading each "held … over …
    from g" line beside the kicks a second and guest progress (`docs/research/measurements/macos-sched/launchd-run.sh`
    on macOS); the hold's E2E (`--cpus`) on each; Hex's re-vendor to channel version 31.

### D38's and D197's virtio-fs frames: FUSE's own structures

**Decided:** a frame holds the longest request a guest sends, a WRITE of the most INIT lets
it write with its header and arguments, which is longer than any other request (a SETXATTR's
at its longest) and any reply (a READ's of as much), as two compile-time assertions hold;
4,096 bytes of room had been picked. `MAX_WRITE`'s 4,096 is the guest's page, which FUSE
counts `max_pages` in.

| Literal | Was | Now | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MAX_FRAME` (fs/mod.rs) | `MAX_WRITE + 4096` | `IN_HEADER_BYTES + WRITE_IN_BYTES + MAX_WRITE` (40 + 40 + 1 MiB) | include/uapi/linux/fuse.h l. 839-847 (`fuse_write_in`), l. 868-873 (`fuse_setxattr_in`); include/uapi/linux/limits.h l. 15-16 |
| `MAX_WRITE`'s page (fs/proto.rs) | 4096 | `GUEST_PAGE` = 4096, cited | fs/fuse/inode.c l. 1342-1344; Intel SDM Vol. 3A §4.5; resources/kernel/firecracker-aarch64-6.18.config l. 437 |

Owed: the share's E2E on each host (a guest's largest write and SETXATTR), the 8-target lint.

### Devices and block I/O (D44)

A microVM's workload reaches the devices Docker gives a container and those it is given, and no other of
its VM's: before, it could make a node of the VM's image disk (259:0) and read it. Its
cgroup has runc's eBPF device filter (opencontainers/cgroups v0.0.4, which runc v1.3.4
pins: the rules emulator of devices_emulator.go, the program of devicefilter.go), over
moby's default rules (daemon/pkg/oci/defaults.go) and runc's own (specconv
AllowedDevices, less those whose path a device given takes), in `crates/devcgroup`, a
crate of no dependencies that shards-init builds. Its program is runc's, byte for byte:
`tests` hold it to what `scripts/devcgroup/generate` records of runc's own deviceFilter,
run in a pinned Go on Linux, for 27 rule sets (Docker's own, `--device`s, every kind of
`--device-cgroup-rule`, privileged, the emulator's refusals). Execs are in its cgroup and
under it, as a container's execs are.

`--device` takes the VM's devices as a run on Docker names its host's (D44; WithDevices,
DevicesFromPath): one by its path, a directory's each, at the path in the microVM
asked, with its permissions, refused as dockerd refuses one it cannot find; the VM's
devices are the nodes of its devtmpfs, which shards-init keeps (D152), with the modes
systemd-udev's default rules give a host's (fuse, net/tun, vsock and vfio 0666, rfkill
0664; v257 50-udev-default.rules.in) where devtmpfs's are 0600, so that the image's user
opens `/dev/fuse` as on a Docker host; `--privileged` makes its nodes from all of it. A
CDI device's name is a device request, as the CLI makes it, which no VM has a spec for:
refused in the words scripts read from Docker. `--device-cgroup-rule` takes what the
CLI's pattern takes, meaning what it means to dockerd; `--device-read-bps`,
`--device-write-bps`, `--device-read-iops`, `--device-write-iops` and
`--blkio-weight-device` take what docker/cli's validators take, their paths looked up
(dockerd's getBlkioThrottleDevices), and are written to the guest's cgroup as cgroup v2
takes them: io.max, and BFQ's per-device weights where its weight file takes them, which
the kernel refuses for a bio-based disk, the image's, as on any host whose disk BFQ does
not schedule (runc's setIo writes them so). Init does it all, outside the workload's
cgroup, in the order a start meets them, so that a failing start names the first failure
a Docker start would: the lookups (the I/O limits' paths, the devices, the rules, the CDI
devices), the nodes, then the cgroup's settings (pids, memory, the weight, the devices'
I/O, CPU, the filter, cpusets), each failure in the words scripts read, with runc's
procHooks prefix; dockerd's own fail the start with 128, untranslated. `inspect` says each
where Docker's clients read it.

Improvements over Docker, each measured or tested:

- **No cost to a run with Docker's rules.** Init attaches the default filter as the VM
  boots, before the template's snapshot: every VM restored from it has it. A run with
  other rules swaps its own in (BPF_F_REPLACE: never without a filter between the two), a
  privileged one takes it away. Loading the filter at each start cost a run 1026 µs of
  its time in the guest; at boot, nothing (PM M121). The filter runs on each device a
  run opens or makes: interpreted until D227, compiled by the guest's BPF JIT since; its
  cost to an open of /dev/null either way, against a cgroup with no filter, is PM M489's.
- **An `a` rule allows what it says.** runc's emulator reads any `a` rule as every
  device, every access: `--device-cgroup-rule 'a 1:2 m'` or `'a *:* r'` lets a Docker
  container read, write and make every device. shards reads one that is not `a *:* rwm`
  as a block and a char rule of its numbers and access (tested: `a *:* r` reads a loop
  device and cannot write it).
- `shards start vm` of a microVM that cannot start says why as `docker start` does, without
  run's help (it said run's before, for every start that failed).

A build's (`shards build image`'s) `RUN` steps reach the devices BuildKit gives a step's container, and no other of
their builder's: before, a step could make a node of the builder's image device (259:0) and
read it, as a run could before this entry. BuildKit v0.28.1's runc executor
(executor/oci/spec.go GenerateSpec) starts from containerd v2.2.1's default spec, which
denies every device (pkg/oci/spec.go populateDefaultUnixSpec), where dockerd's run starts
from moby's few; `--security=insecure` allows every char and block device in its place
(util/entitlements/security WithInsecureSpec); each CDI device node (D96) adds its rule, of
the access its spec's `permissions` gives, `rwm` where none
(container-device-interface v1.1.0 ContainerEdits.Apply); then runc's own, less those whose
path a device given takes (`shards_devcgroup::build_step`). Each step starts in a cgroup of
its own, under the builder's `steps`, which the first step confines to the default rules
once (a step of those rules, the most, costs no program of its own), or under `devices`,
