which nothing confines, where its own program is attached alone (a cgroup's programs and
its parents' must all allow an access). Unlike BuildKit, by design: CDI gives a node of
type `u` (an unbuffered char device) no rule, so that the step it is given cannot open it;
shards gives it its rule, as a `c` node's. Tested: devcgroup's
`a_build_step_reaches_runcs_devices_and_its_cdi_devices_alone` (the rules, run through
the kernel's evaluation of the program, the compiler held to runc's by the oracle above);
build.rs `run_steps_reach_the_devices_buildkit_gives_them_alone` (a step opens runc's
devices and makes a node of the builder's 259:0, and is refused it, "Operation not
permitted"; an insecure step reads it and /dev/kmsg) and `run_steps_take_cdi_devices` (a
CDI node of the builder's disk given `r` read and not written).

`shards attach` (D45) and the network commands (D46) touch no device rule: a joined or
attached process is the run's own, under the run's filter, and a network is no device.
Shards' own grammar names devices where a run takes them (`--device`, worded as the VM's,
never the host's, `cmdline::grammar`) and where a running microVM is given a host's PCI
function (`plug`, D214).

### attach (D45)

`shards attach` joins a running microVM's command as `docker attach` joins a container's (docker/cli
container/attach.go; moby daemon/attach.go, daemon/internal/stream CopyStreams): the CLI
inspects the microVM first, for its terminal and its stdin, and refuses a stopped,
paused or restarting one, a missing one, and a terminal's stdin that is not one, in
docker/cli's words; the client goes to the microVM's VM process as an exec's does (`ATTACH_RUN`,
held until the VM has it, M24), which writes it the command's output from then on,
passes its stdin on where the microVM's command reads one (`-i`), its signals without a terminal
(`--sig-proxy`), and its terminal's size, one row and column larger first so that the
command redraws (resizeTTY), and tells it the command's status, its own. The detach keys
leave with "read escape sequence" and 1, the microVM running. A client's stdin ending
closes the command's where moby's does (StdinOnce, no terminal), so a detach never closes
a shell's: before, `run -it`'s detach did.

Beyond Docker: where its stdin's end does not close the command's, an attached client's
output goes on to the command's end, where dockerd ends the attach with its stdin and
what the command says after is lost (measured: `echo hello | docker attach` of a
`run -di` container that answers printed nothing; shards' of a `run -di` microVM prints the answer; tested).
A slow client holds the command's output back: what a command writes is never kept
without bound.

### Networks of microVMs (D46)

**Relay progress correction (network-08, 2026-11-13).** A persistent TCP client's
lifetime no longer owns 127.0.0.11's UDP/accept loop. Each TCP worker owns its
client and upstream sockets; observed descriptor capacity admits it, counting
three possible sockets through every return/spawn failure. Both guest resolvers
share one in-flight DNS-ID owner, bounded by the complete 16-bit ID space and
current per-asker share. Responses/expiry release ownership; allocation/clock/full
refusals admit no untracked query. Waits use readiness or the earliest deadline,
including agentdns's former periodic expiry probe. The inherited five-second
timing and worker memory-envelope validation remain owed under network-12/R14.
Four functional unit tests and init clippy pass on Linux arm64 GNU; real guest,
fault and resource coverage remain ROOT's. [Evidence and exact remaining runs](../research/measurements/network-fixes-v1/README.md#network-08-independent-dns-relay-clients).

**The network controls' derivations (network-12, 2026-11-13).** Six of the review's
fixed controls now rest on a cited or derived basis: IPv6 extension headers are walked to
the packet's end (RFC 8200 §4.1, hop-by-hop first alone), not to a chosen eight; the
gateway's TTL and hop limit are the Assigned Numbers default (RFC 1700, RFC 1122
§3.2.1.7, RFC 4861 §6.3.2), named; a queue's page size is the OS's or a typed error; a
ring's shared memory on macOS takes the next free name however many are taken; the
window scale offered is the least that says the whole queue (RFC 7323 §2.3); a peer's
read holds one whole message. The rest keep their values until their learned designs
land, each with its cold start, typed failure and the measurement ROOT owes, in
[the row-by-row record](../research/measurements/network-fixes-v1/README.md#network-12-the-network-controls-derivations-row-by-row):
the TCP queues and retransmission (RFC 6298, RFC 1122 R2), window updates (RFC 9293),
the per-turn budget (deficit round robin), the backlog, the poller's batch, the
ring's size, the resolvers' wait and the daemon's bind tries. UDP lifetimes (2026-11-14):
a UDP flow of the network process lives RFC 4787 §4.3 REQ-5's two minutes past its last
datagram, either way, answered or not (`shards_abi::bounds::UDP_MAPPING_IDLE`), where it
lived conntrack's 30 s until answered and streaming, which broke REQ-5 for every port past
1023 (red `a_udp_mapping_outlives_two_minutes_of_quiet_but_none_past`). Each datagram going
out refreshes it (REQ-6, which MUST) and each coming in (REQ-6a, which MAY: its host socket
is connected to its one granted peer). REQ-5a's shorter timers for well-known ports and
REQ-5c's RECOMMENDED five minutes are not taken, with why and the measurement ROOT owes in
the row-by-row record.

`shards network` makes networks of microVMs as `docker network` makes them of
containers, with Docker's inputs and words: create, ls, inspect, rm, prune, connect and
disconnect, as docker/cli parses them (held byte for byte to docker/cli by
`scripts/docker-cli/generate`) and as dockerd 29.3.1 (f78c987a) answers them, measured
on an isolated Docker Engine 29.3.1 (a docker-in-docker container, so that no probe
touches the user's Docker). Networks are kept in the home, one file each; dockerd's
predefined `bridge`, `host` and `none` are listed beside them, the bridge on the subnet
the daemon elected (D31).

- **Addresses, as libnetwork's IPAM gives them.** A network's IPv4 pool is the subnet
  asked for, or the lowest of dockerd's default pools that overlaps no other network's
  nor the host's (InferReservedNetworks); its gateway is the first free address of its
  range, or of its subnet; each microVM's is the lowest free one (not the next: a freed
  address is the next given), or its `--ip`. Status' counts are dockerd's (IPsInUse
  marks the network and broadcast addresses, the gateway, auxiliary addresses and
  members). IPv6 pools are kept and shown where Docker's clients read them, the ULA one
  derived from the home's engine ID: a stable 40-bit Global ID for each home (RFC 4193
  §3.2; the formula is dockerd's); each microVM takes an address of one as of
  D99.
- **One template for every network.** A microVM on a network boots on the default
  bridge's template, as every run does, and shards-init moves eth0 to its own address
  and gateway as the run starts (one netlink address swap and route replace, only where
  the address differs), before it writes /etc/hosts, which names it. Its network process
  takes the address over its control socket (`NET_ADDRESS`).
- **MicroVM to microVM.** The daemon pairs the network processes of every two members
  with a stream socket (`NET_PEER`); a process sends a frame whose destination is a
  peer's address to that peer whole, its virtio header's segmentation cleared (a
  65520-byte MTU's TCP sends no aggregate) and its partial checksum kept, which the
  peer's device takes (GUEST_CSUM). A peer's frame is taken only from its own address to
  this guest's, and given the gateway's MAC as a routed frame; every peer is reached
  through the gateway's MAC, which the process answers ARP with. A frame a full socket
  cannot take whole waits only for the frame before it; others are dropped, as a full
  switch port drops them, and TCP sends them again. Each end holds a ring's worth each way
  (1 MiB, `shards_netring::RING`): macOS gave a socket pair 8 KiB, five full-size frames,
  and of a fast sender's bursts of 200 datagrams the link lost 35 to 54% (PM M182).
  Members reach each other past the
  default deny; nothing else is opened (D31): a network is what Docker's `--internal`
  one is, and a name off it is refused (below).
- **Names, at 127.0.0.11.** A microVM on a network asks 127.0.0.11 (resolv.conf
  `nameserver 127.0.0.11`, `options ndots:0` after its own, no comments naming an engine),
  the address programs written for Docker ask by address (nginx's `resolver`), which so
  work unchanged; a process of shards-init, outside the workload's cgroup, relays each
  query there, by UDP and TCP, to the network process at the gateway. It answers the names
  the network gives each member: its name, its aliases (Compose's service names), its
  short ID and its host name (clustered software, Elasticsearch, RabbitMQ and Kafka
  among it, gives its peers its host name to reach it by), whatever the case, and each as
  `name.network`; as A records, and AAAA where the network has IPv6 (D99); and an address
  back to `name.network.`, which resolves forward to it. Each answer's TTL is 0 (RFC 1035
  §3.2.1: used for the transaction in progress, not cached): the table changes as
  members come and go, a name is given again to the next run under it and an address to
  the next member, so an answer kept past its member could name another microVM. A
  resolver that caches asks again each time, a round trip to the network process of
  184 µs at p50 and 407 µs at p99 on a quiet host (83 and 668 µs loaded, PM M247). A name
  the network does not hold, where no grant reaches past it, is
  refused at once (REFUSED, a refusal by policy, RFC 1035 §4.1.1): SERVFAIL, a server's
  failure, which it answered until 2026-10-17 as Docker's embedded resolver does, is
  taken for a passing one and asked again (musl reads it as `EAI_AGAIN`). The daemon
  sends each member its own table as members come and go (`NET_NAMES`): its own names and
  those of the members it reaches, and no other's. Networks are default deny: a name is a
  grant's, never membership's alone, so a member no link reaches has no name either (one of
  an `enable_icc` false network, below), where Docker's embedded resolver answers every
  container of the network, reached or not (libnetwork's resolver answers from the
  network's service records, which `enable_icc` does not touch). Unit-tested
  (`a_member_is_answered_the_names_it_reaches_alone`) and on real microVMs
  (`a_networks_options_are_what_its_microvms_do`: a peer's name refused at once, its own
  answered).
- **Members.** A microVM is a member while its run lasts: from its start, under the
  network's lock (no two take one address), to its end; one whose start fails is no
  member, however it failed. An address a run asked for is free once its end is told,
  as dockerd's is once `run --rm` returns: a run asking for it takes the holder's end
  first, if it has come, as a name's is (PM M182). `network rm` refuses a network with members in dockerd's
  words; inspect lists them, and a microVM's NetworkSettings carry its endpoint as
  dockerd's, its network's ID and DNS names kept while it is stopped.
- **Measured and tested** (containers.rs `microvms_on_a_network_reach_one_another_by_name`):
  reach by every name and by address, the server seeing each client's own address, no
  reach from a microVM off the network, its resolv.conf, a member's name answered with a
  TTL of 0 and as `name.network`, a name past the network refused at once, inspect's
  endpoint, and dockerd's refusals; the network's names (`shards-dns`) in unit tests of
  their own; the IPAM (networks.rs) and the CLI's consolidation (daemon/networks.rs) held
  to Docker's answers in unit tests. Mutation-checked, each caught: answers kept for
  600 s; `name.network` not answered; the network's table answering what it does not
  hold; a name no grant reaches left unanswered (the asker waited 3 s). A lookup's cost,
  PM M247.

A network's options are what its microVMs do (moby docker-v29.3.1's bridge driver,
drivers/bridge/bridge_linux.go, port_mapping_linux.go; netlabel). Before, they were
checked (two of them) and ignored, and two of those asked for less reach: a network made
with `enable_icc` false or `host_binding_ipv4` 127.0.0.1 got neither, and was not told.
- **`enable_icc` false keeps its members from one another:** no link between their
  network processes (`NET_PEER`), the only way one reaches another, and none of their
  names: each is answered its own alone (default deny; until 2026-11-08 their names were
  answered, a name with no flow behind it).
- **`host_binding_ipv4` is where a port published with no address is bound**, alone, as
  the option means to Docker's clients: an IPv4 address or an IPv6 one, whatever its name says; 0.0.0.0 or
  unset, every address, IPv4's and IPv6's (`configurePortBindingIPv4`, `IPv6`).
- **An MTU is kept as given, and its members keep their devices', 65520.** The option is
  there so that a container's packets fit the host's wire, which they cross as they were
  made. A microVM's flows end in its network process and leave through the host's own
  sockets, which fit what they send to each path's MTU, so the wire's limit is met at the
  device's full size. A smaller MTU would only cut throughput, and have the guest
  fragment datagrams its network process takes whole (net/src/wire.rs, no reassembly).
  `network create` says so on a terminal; a script reads the ID alone.
- **A routed network publishes no port.** `gateway_mode` routed reaches a member at its
  own address, no host port bound for what it publishes; a microVM is reached through its
  network process alone, so its ports could only be bound on the host's, which the mode
  keeps closed: a run publishing ports on one is refused, its reason said.
- **Each option takes what `docker network create -o` takes**, refused in the words
  scripts read (`failed to parse LABEL value: V
  (why)`: Go's strconv errors, `unknown gateway mode`, `nil ip`; `invalid MTU number`;
  `isolated` only on an internal network), where only the MTU's and `enable_icc`'s were
  read, and the MTU's range errors were called syntax errors.
- **The default network says what it does:** `enable_icc` false (every member has the
  same address, so that one template serves them all, and none reaches another), MTU
  65520, masquerading and every host address true of it as before; no `docker0` bridge
  name. A home whose record says what an older shards said is told the truth as it is
  read.
Tested (`a_networks_options_are_what_its_microvms_do`: the default network's options,
an old record's made true; each refusal in dockerd's words; a member of an `enable_icc`
false network neither resolved by another's name (REFUSED) nor reached; its port bound at 127.0.0.1 alone and
reached there; the MTU kept in inspect, 65520 in the guest; a routed network's port
refused; publish.rs `a_port_at_no_address_takes_its_networks`), mutation-checked: members
linked whatever icc says, the host binding ignored, the default network saying icc, an
old record kept, a routed network publishing, isolated outside an internal network,
gateway modes unread, a negative MTU taken, Atoi's errors ParseInt's, a binding address
unread.

An endpoint's sysctls (`--network NAME,driver-opt=com.docker.network.endpoint.sysctls=…`),
as dockerd sets them (PM M171): written on eth0 by init, its name in place of `IFNAME`
(or `ifname`, as the CLI lowercases it), after the run's own sysctls, as libnetwork
writes them on the interface it configures after runc's; libnetwork's checks and words (a
key with no file "… is not a sysctl file", a value the kernel refuses "unable to write
to …", the start failing "failed to set up container networking: failed to add interface
eth0 to sandbox: …", where dockerd names its veth); a value already set is not written;
none on `none`, which has no interface. An interface's sysctl given as the run's own
(`--sysctl net.X.Y.ethN.Z`) is refused, as clients of API 1.48 and on are told (moby's
create route's handleSysctlBC), before anything else is checked, for any
network of the run's own. Beside an Agentfile's agents whose flows cross the
command's namespace, refused as any net.* sysctl is (D115). Tested
(`an_endpoints_sysctls_are_its_interfaces`, mutation-checked: written before the
run's own, eth0 kept all's; `interface_sysctls_are_endpoints`).

A run's own MAC, as dockerd gives it (PM M173): the one given (`--mac-address`, or its
endpoint's `mac-address`), in any form Go's ParseMAC reads (colons, dashes, dots or bare
hex; 6, 8 or 20 octets), else one made for each start, random, locally administered and
unicast (containers.rs `a_runs_mac_is_its_own`), so that no two runs of a template share the
template's. init gives eth0 it before its addresses, as libnetwork sets it before
configuring the interface (rtnetlink RTM_NEWLINK with IFLA_ADDRESS; virtio-net takes a new
address on a running device, IFF_LIVE_ADDR_CHANGE), the kernel taking the first six
octets of a longer one as it takes them of dockerd's; one it refuses (multicast, all zeros)
fails the start in libnetwork's words, eth0 where dockerd names its veth. The daemon tells
the VM's network process before the VM has the run (`NET_MAC`), and from then on it frames
to that MAC and hears from it alone. Given on `none` or another's network it is taken, and
nothing has it, as with dockerd. inspect shows it while the run lasts and, given, before its
first start, and none once it has run, until it runs again; `network inspect` shows each
member's. Refused by the CLI in the words scripts read from docker/cli: a malformed one,
and both ways at once.

Unlike dockerd, by design: inspect shows the MAC the interface has or will have, the first
six octets of an EUI-64 given (dockerd echoes all eight, which no interface has) and none
on `none` (dockerd echoes the one given). Two runs given one MAC on a network reach each
other, each network process framing to its own guest alone and every peer reached
through the gateway's MAC; on dockerd's bridge neither reaches the other (PM M173). Tested
(`a_runs_mac_is_its_own`, mutation-checked: the network process not
told, init not setting it, inspect not showing a created run's; the network process's
`a_runs_mac_is_the_one_frames_go_to`; the CLI's parser held to Go 1.26.1's ParseMAC and
`HardwareAddr.String`, `macs_parse_as_net_parses_them`).

A run's link-local addresses (`--link-local-ip`, its endpoint's `link-local-ip`), as dockerd
gives them (PM M175):

- **On eth0** once it has its addresses, as libnetwork adds them (setInterfaceLinkLocalIPs):
  IPv4's as /16 with its broadcast, IPv6's as /64 without duplicate address detection, an
  IPv4-mapped one as IPv4 and a zone dropped.
- **dockerd's checks, in its words.** An unspecified one is refused as the run is
  made (validateEndpointSettings). One that is not link-local fails the start after the
  network is found, on `none` too (libnetwork's createEndpoint). IPv6 where its network has
  none fails with "permission denied", 126, the status docker/cli gives it, and one given
  twice with "file exists". On `none` and another's network one is taken, and nothing has
  it. inspect's `IPAMConfig.LinkLocalIPs` holds them as given, where clients read the
  request's.
- **Reach, by each address's own scope.** The daemon tells each network process its guest's
  (`NET_LINK_LOCAL`), and each peer's beside its addresses (`NET_PEER`). A packet goes to a
  peer at any address of the peer's that the sender's link reaches: a link-local IPv6 one
  always, as fe80::/64 is every interface's; a link-local IPv4 one only from a guest with
  one of its own, whose route makes 169.254.0.0/16 its link's. A packet from a link-local
  address goes nowhere past the link (RFC 3927 §2.7, RFC 4291 §2.5.6). On a network with
  IPv6, a member's link-local addresses include the one its kernel makes of its MAC (RFC
  4291's modified EUI-64), the run's own (PM M173).
- **Beside an image's agents**, whose flows past the microVM cross init's link
  169.254.77.0/30 (D59), a link-local address in that link is refused, in shards' words, by
  the daemon as the run is made and by init as it starts.
- **Tested** (`a_runs_link_local_addresses_are_its_own`; the network
  process's `link_local_addresses_reach_their_peers_alone`; the CLI's
  `top_level_flags_land_on_endpoints_as_run_puts_them`, held to docker/cli's own
  applyContainerOptions).

Unlike Docker, by the microVM: a microVM has one network device, so it is on one network.
One left on the default bridge and connected to one user network is on that network
alone, which under default deny gives it all the bridge would. A microVM on two user
networks is refused ("a microVM on more than one network is not supported by shards
yet"), and so is connecting or disconnecting a running one.

Open:
- A microVM on several networks, and connecting a running one: a network device per
  network, added to a running VM.
- The TTY pages of `network ls` and `inspect`, in shards' own design (they print Docker's
  table on a terminal too).
- Egress grants for a network (AGENTFILE_ARCH §4.6 `NETWORK --egress`), with the
  Agentfile.

**Amended (lane xnet-s6, 2026-11-16, ROOT's decision): NXDOMAIN, not REFUSED.** A question no
table of the network process holds and no grant lets past the microVM (a name the network does
not hold, a peer no link reaches, an `enable_icc` false network's among them, a name past the
network; D59's ungranted names; a shared network's, D285) is answered at once NXDOMAIN
(`shards_dns::denied`), by UDP and by TCP (D79's relay), where it was REFUSED, as the agents'
resolver answers one since D278's amendment of the same day. musl's stub drops REFUSED: "Only
accept positive or negative responses; retry immediately on server failure, and ignore all other
codes such as refusal" (src/network/res_msend.c, its `switch` on the RCODE: 0 and 3 kept, 2 sent
again, the rest `continue`), so a member's lookup of a name its network refused waited out
musl's timeout (`RES_TIMEOUT`, 5 s) and ended EAI_AGAIN (lookup_name.c `name_from_dns`), where
NXDOMAIN ends it at once, EAI_NONAME; glibc ends either at once (resolv/res_send.c `send_dg`).
The answer carries no SOA, so that no resolver caches it past a grant that names the name later
(RFC 2308 §5). REFUSED stays for what is no query of one question.
- *Literals* (R03): NXDOMAIN, 3, and REFUSED, 5: RFC 1035 §4.1.1's RCODEs.
- *Tests* (written, not run, by the person's word of 2026-11-16): shards-dns
  `a_responses_addresses_are_read` (a question no grant names: NXDOMAIN, its ID and question
  kept; one of two questions: REFUSED), `tcp_questions_go_on_whole_and_only_as_granted` and
  `tcp_refusals_wait_for_an_answer_to_end_and_answers_are_learned` (by TCP); containers.rs
  `a_networks_options_are_what_its_microvms_do` (a peer no link reaches: `dnsttl rcode 3`) and
  `microvms_on_a_network_reach_one_another_by_name` (`example.com`: rcode 3). Owed (ROOT):
  `cargo test -p shards-dns --profile test-release`; on real VMs (HVF, KVM, WHP), `cargo test -p
  shards --profile test-release --test containers -- a_networks_options_are_what_its_microvms_do
  microvms_on_a_network_reach_one_another_by_name`.

### Every action makes an image a microVM first (D47)

`shards run vm IMAGE` has made a microVM of a container image as it pulls it since D25:
any OCI image a registry or Docker holds is one shards runs. Shards' grammar does the same
for every other action on an image or a microVM that names an image: `inspect vm IMAGE`,
`inspect image`, `history image`, `tag image`, `push image` and `save image` pull an image
that is not here yet and convert it, as `run` does (one path, `run::find_image`, saying
the pull as `docker run` says it), and then act on the microVM it makes. `inspect vm IMAGE`
of a name that is no microVM describes the image's microVM. Removal converts nothing: it
fetches nothing to delete it. Docker's own order (`image inspect`, `history`, `tag`) answers
in Docker's words, "No such image" included (tests/images.rs), so that scripts written for Docker see the
answers they parse; the conversion is shards' grammar's (`--convert`, shown under shards'
options in each command's help). Tested in `images.rs`
(`actions_on_an_image_not_here_convert_it_first`, on real microVMs, and that neither
Docker's order nor removal fetches anything) and in the grammar's unit tests.

### D216. Commands on microVMs: the user's list, closed (built)

The user's list of 2026-10-04 asked that every command work on microVMs, in shards' own
grammar, `shards ACTION THING [NAME]` (`crates/cmdline/src/grammar.rs`), with Docker's own
spellings still read as Docker's scripts write them. Each item's state:

1. **shards' own words say microVM.** Docker's byte-exact texts (help from the oracle
   tables, docker/cli's and dockerd's refusals) keep `container` where scripts parse them,
   and `look::ours` rewords them on a terminal; every form's page says microVM
   (`every_form_of_shards_grammar_answers_help_with_its_own_page`). The refusals shards
   wrote itself in container's words now say microVM: a paused microVM's files, changes and
   commit, a copy or a read of changes that failed, a commit whose image is gone, a
   snapshot of one not running, a join (`--pid`, `--network`, `--ipc` of `container:NAME`)
   of one whose request is lost or too far removed, a microVM that stopped before its
   command started, a health check its microVM ended.
2. **`shards vm ls`.** `list vm` was the form; `vm ls`, `vm rm`, `vm exec` and every other
   action said after `vm` (or `microvm`) are now read turned round, as Docker's
   management form `image ls` is (`vm ls` is `list vm`), keeping shards' own options
   (`vm inspect IMAGE` converts the image, which `container inspect`, Docker's, does not).
   Pulled and converted images are listed by `list image` (D25).
3. **`remove image` frees the image.** It takes the image's stopped microVMs, unpublishes
   it from the local store, and its blobs go with the daemon's next collection
   (`rmi_removes_images`).
4. **`remove vm` removes the microVM**, its writable layer, log and snapshots
   (`names_are_unique_and_rm_leaves_nothing`).
5. **`shards vm rm`**: item 2's turned-round form; `remove vm` is the documented one.
6. **The container image a microVM is made of** is kept but not shown: listings show the
   microVM, `push` and `save` stay byte for byte the image's, and `remove image` frees both
   (the user's call, 2026-10-04).
7. **`exec vm NAME COMMAND`** runs in a running microVM, by its name or, as item 10, an
   image's.
8. **A form for each command a microVM needs.** Added now: `attach vm NAME` (D45),
   `update vm NAME` (D40), `import vm|image FILE|URL|- [NAME]` (D41: a shards microVM
   brought in whole, or one made of a tarball's files or an image archive), and `wait vm
   NAME` in the help (it was read but not listed). The others were there: `copy vm`,
   `create vm`, `read changes`, `watch system`, `export vm`, `read history`, `inspect`,
   `kill vm`, `load image`, `read logs`, `pause vm`, `read ports`, `list vm`, `rename vm`,
   `restart vm`, `remove image`, `save image`, `tag image`, `read processes`, `unpause vm`,
   `inspect system`, `prune system`, `inspect disk`.
9. **The microVMs shards makes appear in the machine's local image store**, as
   `shards.local/NAME` (D41's publisher): a pull already, and an import; now also the image a
   run, `create` or an action's `--convert` pulls, a tag's new name, a named commit, each
   named image a load or an imported archive holds, and a build's `-t` names. A build ends
   before an upload would, and a publish cut off part way leaves Docker's content locked
   (D41), so a build asks its daemon to publish (`shards_ipc::PUBLISH_STEP`), whose
   publisher outlives it; it asks only where a local store is there to publish to, so no
   daemon starts for it otherwise. A name already of `shards.local/` (an archive of one
   brought back) is not published again under `shards.local/shards.local/`. The emulator a
   run of another CPU's image pulls is shards' own part and is not published.
10. **An image's name reaches the microVMs made from it**: `stop`, `kill`, `pause`,
    `unpause` and `remove` already; now `wait` and `restart` too, which reach the running
    ones (`restart` asks its daemon which, `shards_ipc::NAMES_STEP`, as it restarts each
    by its own request). A name of a microVM is that microVM first.
11. **`shards vm run` folded into `run vm`**: a kernel booted with `run vm --kernel`, a
    snapshot resumed with `restore vm DIR` (since 2026-10-04).
12. **Verb, then noun**: `stop vm NAME`, `stop container NAME`, `remove vm|container|image
    NAME`, with Docker's `rm`, `rmi` and `stop NAME` still read.
13. **`run container X` where X is a shards microVM** is refused, and says why: `X is a
    shards microVM, not a container image: it has no container's layers to make one of.
    shards run vm X runs it as the microVM it is` (`create container` the same, `shards
    create vm X` making it). A container
    image is converted as it runs, as `run vm` converts it. The grammar says it with the
    hidden option `--container-image`, which Docker's order (`container run`) goes
    without: a Docker script's `container run` of a microVM runs it.

**A microVM's record of processes** (the user's call, 2026-11-08: keep it, and show it in
shards' grammar): D123's record is it, kept as files of the microVM's own in the home
(`containers/ID/processes.N`, segments as its log's), read with `read processes NAME` and
followed with `watch processes NAME`; it outlives the run and the daemon, and goes with
the microVM's removal. No flag or subcommand of Docker's shape carries it.

Tested: the grammar's unit tests (`actions_on_things_are_said_as_shards_runs_them`, every
form above), and on real microVMs (`tests/containers.rs`
`microvms_are_reached_in_shards_grammar_by_their_names_and_their_images`: `vm ls`, `vm
exec`, `wait vm` and `restart vm` by an image's name, `update vm`, `read processes` the same before and after the daemon stops, `vm rm` taking the record;
`import_makes_images_of_tarballs`: `run container` of an imported microVM refused, `run vm`
of it run; `created_microvms_are_published_to_the_local_store`: a tag's, a commit's and a
run's pull's microVMs sent to an engine the test serves).

### ADD of Git repositories: shards' own client (D48)

`ADD <git URL> DEST` builds as BuildKit's git source builds it (moby/buildkit v0.28.1
source/git/source.go, the backend of Docker Engine 29.3.1, measured there against a real
smart HTTP server: every form, file header and error), but without a `git` beside `shards`
(D36): `crates/git` is a client of its own, written from git's documents
(gitprotocol-common, gitprotocol-v2, gitprotocol-http, gitprotocol-pack, gitformat-pack,
gitformat-index) and its code where they leave a format to it (tree-walk.c, commit.c,
tag.c, submodule-config.c).

- **Fetching.** Protocol v2 over smart HTTP(S) (the registry's client, its proxies and
  TLS) and over `git://` (git's daemon); a server that speaks only v0 is refused, as is an
  SSH remote until `--ssh` is served. One commit is fetched one deep (`deepen 1`), a full
  commit name too, where BuildKit fetches all of its history (`--unshallow`). Packs are
  read with both delta kinds; every object is named from its data with collision-detecting
  SHA-1, as git's sha1dc names them, so a pack holds only what it claims; the pack and each
  object are bounded by what a build may unpack.
- **Refs** resolve to the commits BuildKit resolves them to, so that a Git context builds
  what it builds elsewhere: the default branch from HEAD's target;
  `refs/NAME`, then `refs/heads/NAME` before `refs/tags/NAME`; an annotated tag peeled; a
  40- or 64-digit lowercase name as a commit, a shorter one as a ref. `--checksum` and
  `?checksum=` take a hex prefix of the commit's or the tag's name. Errors are BuildKit's
  (`repository does not contain ref NAME, output: ""`, `invalid subdir ...`, `expected
  checksum to match ...`, under `failed to load cache key:` where BuildKit says it).
- **The checkout** is git's under BuildKit's umask: files 0644 or 0755 by the owner's
  execute bit (canon_mode), symlinks, directories 0755, all root's; `#REF:SUBDIR` takes a
  directory every part of which is one (validateDirsOnly); submodules, unless
  `?submodules=false`, fetched one deep from `.gitmodules`' URLs, relative ones resolved
  against the superproject's, recursively.

Unlike BuildKit, by design:
- **Every entry's time is the commit's** (its committer's), where BuildKit's is the clock's
  at checkout: the same commit makes the same layer on every builder and every build
  (tested: built again with `--no-cache`, the layers are the same bytes), as frontend
  1.27.1's `mtime=commit` asks of a build context. Measured: BuildKit's two fresh
  checkouts of one tree made two layers differing only by mtimes.
- **No submodule `.git` file naming the builder** (`gitdir: ../../../../52/fs/modules/...`,
  BuildKit's, a path into its snapshot store that dangles in every image).
- **A ref's checkout is that ref's alone.** BuildKit checks out through a repository shared
  by every build of a URL, whose index and config outlive them: measured, a commit with no
  submodule checked out after one with a submodule got that submodule's files.
- **A checksum that matches neither an annotated tag nor its commit names both**
  (BuildKit's message loses the tag's: `got  or <commit>`).
- **`--keep-git-dir` keeps a `.git` that is the commit's alone:** HEAD detached at it,
  `shallow`, `origin` the URL without credentials, the ref asked for (a branch under
  `refs/heads`, a tag under `refs/tags`, none for a commit's name), the fetched pack with
  its index, and an index of the work tree at the commit's time; each submodule's
  repository under `.git/modules`, its work tree's `.git` naming it. BuildKit's holds the
  builder's inode numbers and times, its hostname in a reflog, and refs that depend on
  what earlier builds fetched. git reads shards' as its own (`verify-pack`, `fsck`, a
  clean `status`; crates/git/tests/real_git.rs). With a subdir no `.git` is kept, as
  BuildKit keeps none.

Tested: crates/git against git itself (its packs object for object, a shallow fetch from
its upload-pack checked out as `ls-tree` and `show` list it, refs as BuildKit resolves
them, `git daemon`, a kept `.git`); `build.rs` `add_fetches_git_repositories` on real
microVMs, from a git daemon and from smart HTTP served by git's own upload-pack.

- **Credentials from the build's secrets**, as BuildKit's git source takes them (v0.28.1
  source.go authSecretNames, getAuthToken, tokenScope): the first of
  `GIT_AUTH_HEADER.<host>`, `GIT_AUTH_TOKEN.<host>`, `GIT_AUTH_HEADER`, `GIT_AUTH_TOKEN`
  (`--secret id=...`); a token sent as `basic` credentials of `x-access-token`, a header as
  it is; to the remote, or to all of github.com for a github.com remote, scoped as git
  scopes `http.<url>.extraheader` (urlmatch.c), so a submodule elsewhere is not sent them
  (tested: `add_fetches_git_with_the_builds_secrets`, refused without them).

- **SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH from a Git stage**, as dockerfile/1.27.1 takes it (epoch.go,
  `sourceDateEpochFromMetadata`): the stage's ADD made the source `llb.Git` makes
  (`plan::git_identifier`, which planning shares), its ref resolved and checked as a fetch
  resolves it, the commit fetched with the build's secrets and SSH agent, and its
  committer's time, not its author's (tested: `source_date_epoch_is_taken_from_a_source_stage`,
  mutation-checked; a ref the repository lacks fails the build). In the committer's zone,
  and from named and remote contexts too: D127.

- **A commit a server will not send alone** ("not our ref": a commit asked for by its
  name, or a submodule's pinned commit, that is no ref's tip, from a server that keeps
  `uploadpack.allowReachableSHA1InWant` off): every ref's history fetched whole, the one
  way to reach a commit such a server will not send by name (`git fetch --tags origin`),
  and a kept repository not shallow, its
  history whole; a commit in no ref's history refused in the server's words (tested:
  `add_fetches_a_commit_a_server_will_not_send_alone`, against a server that refuses as
  such hosts do; mutation-checked). git's own upload-pack, speaking protocol v2, sends
  such a commit (measured, git 2.50.1), so the fallback is for hosts that do not.

- **Its formats' literals are git's** (audit of picked constants, 2026-11-09). A checkout
  refused trees past 4096 levels, a figure its comment gave as git's own: git v2.51.0's
  core.maxTreeDepth is 2048 where BuildKit runs git, on Linux (512 and 1280 in Windows
  builds only), and its walk recursed once a level, so a thread's stack, not git, bounded
  a hostile repository's nesting; a pack's delta chains recursed the same way, to git's
  4095. The walk keeps the trees open on a stack of its own, a chain is followed in a loop,
  and the walk refuses what git refuses (`trees_nest_as_deep_as_git_checks_out_and_no_deeper`:
  2048 levels walked on a 256 KiB thread and 2049 refused, as git's read-tree takes and
  refuses the same trees). The host's git is asked at 2048 only where its own
  core.maxTreeDepth reaches it: Git for Windows' MSVC and arm64 clang builds stop at 512
  and 1280, as their stacks hold no deeper (git v2.56.0 git-compat-util.h:594-616,
  `DEFAULT_MAX_ALLOWED_TREE_DEPTH`), and held to 2048, CI's arm64 git (2.56.0.windows.4)
  died of STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW (0xC00000FD) instead of answering; there the walk alone is
  checked, and the test says so.

  | Literal | Was | Now | Source |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `checkout::MAX_DEPTH` | 4096, recursion a level | 2048, iterative | git v2.51.0 environment.c:105-106 (`max_allowed_tree_depth`), tree-walk.c:445 (`traverse_trees_cur_depth > max_allowed_tree_depth`) |
  | `pack::MAX_DEPTH` | 4095, recursion a delta | 4095, a loop: deltas kept on the way to the base, applied from it up | git v2.51.0 pack-objects.h:15 (`OE_DEPTH_BITS` 12), builtin/pack-objects.c:5033-5036 (pack.depth forced below `1 << OE_DEPTH_BITS`) |
  | `pktline::MAX` | 65520 | kept | git v2.51.0 pkt-line.h:233 (`LARGE_PACKET_MAX`), gitprotocol-common.adoc:87-89 |
  | `pktline::FLUSH`, `DELIMITER` | `0000`, `0001` | kept | gitprotocol-v2.adoc:45-46 |

SSH remotes: D69.

### RUN steps under Docker's default seccomp profile (D49)

BuildKit runs every step under moby's default seccomp profile (its executor's
oci/spec.go WithDefaultSeccomp; `Seccomp: 2` in a step's `/proc/self/status`, measured), an
insecure step unconfined. shards' builder does the same: the profile `docker run` applies
(D42, `crates/seccomp`, compiled as libseccomp and runc compile it) is compiled once per
build for a step's capabilities (the defaults a run has, `shards_abi::run::CAPS`), the
builder's architecture and its kernel's version, and carried in each step
(`shards_abi::build::Step::seccomp`); the builder guest loads it while the step is still
root with every capability, before it changes user, no_new_privs unset (BuildKit sets
none, and a step's setuid programs work as they do there), so that the change of user,
the capabilities and the exec that follow run under it. Tested in
`run_steps_take_the_builds_secrets_ulimits_and_entitlements` (mutation-checked: a step's
`Seccomp:` is 2, an insecure step's 0).

### The build cache (D50)

A step `shards build image` has run before, from the same definition and inputs, is not run
again: its result is the layers it made then, and its progress says so in BuildKit's
words (`#N CACHED`, tests/build.rs), which CI logs and tools read.

- **Keys.** A step's key is the SHA-256 of shards' version, its definition, and each input's
  key in its inputs' order, not where they sit in the plan. An input a chain of layers
  makes, a base image or an earlier step, is keyed by what made it; one none makes, the
  build context, a download or a Git checkout, by its content: each path's kind, mode,
  owner, extended attributes, link target and bytes, without times, so that touching a
  file runs nothing again (BuildKit's content checksums take them so too); a cached
  step's layers keep the times they were made with. A source is keyed by what it is and what it holds, not its session
  attributes (`local.unique` differs on every build).
- **Records** are the store's (`buildcache/v1`), one per key: each of the step's outputs
  as its layers, with their history, the size of the step's own layer, when it was made and
  last used, and how often it has been. Their blobs are roots of the store's collector
  while a record is there, as a reference's are.
- **What uses them.** `--no-cache` takes none, and still records what it makes, as
  BuildKit's does. `system df` counts them on its Build Cache row and lists them under
  `-v` (each step's own layer, shared where an image holds it, reclaimable where not);
  `system prune` removes them all, as `docker system prune` removes all build cache no
  build is using, its blobs collected where no image holds them.

Tested on real microVMs (`builds_reuse_the_steps_they_have_run`): built again, every step
is cached and the image's layers are the same; a changed context file runs again what
reads it and what follows, not what came before; `--no-cache` runs all; `system df` and
`system prune` count and remove the records.

What this left open is done since: `--no-cache-filter`, `--cache-from` and `--cache-to`
(D62); `docker builder prune` and its filters (D65); a step keyed by what it reads, a bound
on what the cache keeps (dockerd's default GC policy) and `RUN --mount=type=cache` kept
across builds (D114).

### RUN steps reach the client's SSH agent (D51)

`RUN --mount=type=ssh` reaches the agent `--ssh` names: `--ssh` takes what buildx takes
(each `ID[=PATH,...]` kept, not normalized,
commands/build.go), its agents as BuildKit's sshprovider takes them (an id `default` where
none is given, `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`'s socket where no path is, one socket an agent, BuildKit's
errors word for word: held to buildx v0.37.1 and BuildKit by `scripts/buildx/generate`);
the mount at `/run/buildkit/ssh_agent.N` with `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` set, an empty id read as
`default`, a mount not `required` left out without an agent, a required one refused in
the words BuildKit's users read.

- **Through the microVM.** The builder guest listens on a socket of the step's own, of the
  mount's mode and owner, bound at its target, and relays each connection to the host
  over vsock (`shards_abi::build::SSH_PORT`), opened with a token the host made for that
  mount of that step (16 bytes of getrandom) and the agent's id; the host takes relayed
  connections only while a step runs, and only of a grant of that step's, closing any
  other at once, so that a step given no agent, or another step's, reaches none by
  dialling the port itself (tested: an insecure step, which can make vsock sockets, is
  closed on unanswered). Both ends' relays stop as the step ends.
- **Read-only: a step uses the agent's keys, and never changes them.** BuildKit serves a step a read-only wrapper of the
  agent (readOnlyAgent): keys and signatures, no adding, removing, locking or extensions.
  The host relays an agent request only if it is one of those (identities, sign, unlock)
  and answers any other SSH_AGENT_FAILURE, each message bounded by OpenSSH's 256 KiB.
- **On Windows, an agent's pipe is waited on while it frees instances** (PM M493). OpenSSH
  for Windows' agent keeps one instance of its pipe listening, and makes the next only
  once it has started a worker process for the last connection; a client that dials
  meanwhile is told the pipe is busy. A build dials once for each connection a step
  makes. go-winio, which BuildKit dials with, waits 2 s in all: with 128 clients at once
  on jupiter, 6 of 6,146 busy dials waited longer (2.80 s at most), while the agent freed
  an instance every 1.35 ms at the median and 8.6 ms at most; a dial's whole wait grows
  with the clients ahead of it, an instance's does not. So a dial follows the agent, with
  no time of shards': it dials again each time an instance is freed (WaitNamedPipe),
  another client may take it first, each wait the one the agent's pipe says
  (NMPWAIT_USE_DEFAULT_WAIT, its CreateNamedPipe timeout) before the pipe is looked for
  again; it ends as the agent serves it, or as the agent goes, its pipe gone. An agent that
  holds its instances and serves none is waited on as a read of it would be, until the
  build is stopped. The first dial is as any other. The measurement shows the method's
  need, not a number shards keeps. `a_dial_waits_while_its_agent_serves_the_clients_ahead`
  holds a dial waiting past 2 s through an agent-like server that frees each instance
  150 ms after the last; `a_dial_ends_as_its_agent_does` a dial still waiting while the
  agent holds its instance, and ended as the agent goes.
- **Tested** on real microVMs against a real ssh-agent holding a key ssh-keygen made
  (`run_steps_reach_the_clients_ssh_agent`): the step lists the key and has the agent sign,
  its request to forget the keys is refused and the agent keeps them, a rogue dial is
  refused; both the filter and the token check are mutation-checked.

Open: key files given to `--ssh` (BuildKit loads them into an agent of its own, which signs
with them: an in-process agent with AWS-LC's signatures); Git remotes over SSH (`ADD
git@...`), which need an SSH client; a `default` agent added where the build context is an
SSH Git URL, which needs one to clone (buildx adds one too).

### Builds write their outputs as BuildKit's exporters do (D52)

`--output` and `--push` are read and checked as buildx v0.37.1 reads them (ParseExports,
CreateExports, the `--push`/`--load` folding and `mode=delete`'s check; held to buildx by
`scripts/buildx/generate`), and each output is written as BuildKit v0.28.1's exporter
writes it through buildx, measured inside dockerd 29.3.1 (Docker's containerd store) and
read in its source (fsutil a2aa163d723f, containerd v2.2.1, buildkit client/ociindex):

- **`local`** (`-o DIR`): the whole root filesystem, received as fsutil's DiskWriter
  receives it (`shards_archive::receive`): the directory made 0700 if new and merged into
  if not (emptied of the rest with `mode=delete`), a directory over a directory taking
  only its attributes, anything else replaced; modes with set-id and sticky bits, hard
  links, symlinks, empty directories, nanosecond times (directories' set last), every
  entry owned by the one who builds: an output is its builder's files (buildx's receive
  filter sets them so too).
  - **Better than fsutil:** every name is walked from the destination as Go's os.Root
    walks it, so neither the tree's symlinks nor ones the destination already held take a
    write outside it; fsutil joins paths and follows what the destination held.
- **`tar`** (`-o -`, `type=tar`): fsutil.WriteTar through Go's archive/tar
  (`shards_archive::tar`, held to Go): walk order, no root entry, owners kept with no
  names, times rounded to the second, `PaxHeaders.0` records only where USTAR cannot hold
  a field, two zero blocks; stdout's and a file's are one archive (tested).
- **`oci`/`docker`**: the image as an OCI layout of the store's own blobs, in a tar as
  containerd's exporter writes one (names in order, times 0, blobs 0444, documents
  0644), with `org.opencontainers.image.created` (export time, or SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH) and an
  index entry per name (`io.containerd.image.name`, `org.opencontainers.image.ref.name`);
  `docker` adds `manifest.json` and names its manifest and layers in Docker's media types
  (`toDockerLayerType`). With `tar=false`, `oci` writes a content store as buildkit's
  client does: blobs it lacks, `ingest/`, `oci-layout` 0644, `index.json` read and
  merged under a lock (`latest` its name without one).
- **Images and pushes**: an image is kept and named only where an output loads it (none
  given, `--load`, `image`, `docker` without a file); one to files alone leaves none, as
  BuildKit's leave none. `--push` and `type=registry` push each name.
- **Refused before the build** where BuildKit refuses when its solve begins, in its words
  (an exporter it has none of, `tar` no bool, `source-date-epoch` no number, `docker`
  into a directory, two OCI directory layouts): BuildKit says so before any step runs
  too, so nothing is built in vain.
- **Times.** The filesystem outputs are written from the build's last snapshot, whose
  times are the kernel's to the nanosecond, before it is put in its layers' form.

Deviation, recorded: a layer shards made is uncompressed (D15's layers), where BuildKit's
are Go's gzip, which no other compressor reproduces byte for byte; an `oci`/`docker`
archive holds the same documents over different layer blobs. A non-directory reached by
two names is a hard link in every kind (fsutil writes a hard-linked symlink as a symlink
to its first name).

Tested on real microVMs (`builds_write_each_output`: six outputs
of one build, the refusals, a merged layout, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH; the hard-link rule
mutation-checked) and in `shards_archive::receive`'s unit test (merge, mirror, a symlink
refused its escape).

Open: the attestations `image` outputs carry (provenance), `--platform` lists.

### Builds take named contexts (D53)

`--build-context NAME=VALUE` is read as buildx v0.37.1 reads it (ParseContextNames: each
name a reference's familiar form, `:latest` dropped; held to buildx by
`scripts/buildx/generate`; build.rs `named_contexts_stand_in_for_what_they_name`) and handed to the planner as buildx hands it (loadInputs) to
the frontend: a remote URL or `docker-image://` as it is; a directory as a local of the
context's name (`_context`, `_dockerfile` for those two), keyed by its base name, its own
`.dockerignore` read. The planner applies them as Dockerfile2LLB does (dockerui
NamedContext, dockerfile/1.27.1):

- a stage whose name is a context's is that context, its own steps never run; a base or
  `COPY --from` name a context names (looked up as `NAME::os/arch`, then `NAME`) is that
  context: an image (`[context NAME] REF`, its config's environment, working directory and
  platform, its ONBUILD triggers run), scratch, a Git repository, an HTTP file
  (`context`), or a directory read with only the paths the stage copies from it;
- BuildKit's own quirks kept: `--from=context` reaches a context named `context`, its
  name being normalized before the check that spares `context`; BuildKit's errors word
  for word (`invalid context specifier`, `unsupported context source`).

Held to BuildKit by 14 plan cases its own converter planned through a gateway client that
`scripts/agentfile/oracle` fakes (images.json's images, contexts with no
`.dockerignore`); one recorded deviation: an SSH Git context carries no host keys scanned
over the network while planning (BuildKit's sshutil.SSHKeyScan), the fetch verifies them.
Also held to buildx: a `local` or `tar` output refused beside `--iidfile`. Tested on a
real microVM (`named_contexts_stand_in_for_what_they_name`); the platform-keyed lookup
mutation-checked.

`oci-layout://PATH[:TAG][@DIGEST]` contexts take what buildx takes (ocilayout.Parse reads
them, the digest found as its resolveDigest finds it (the index entry named the tag, by
image name then reference name, else the only entry; build.rs `oci_layout_contexts_are_the_images_they_hold`), and planned as BuildKit plans them
(`oci-layout://` over a stand-in of the context's name and that digest, `oci.store` the
layout's store; 4 more plan cases). Where buildx serves the layout to BuildKit as a session
content store, shards takes the image's blobs into its own store, each checked against its
digest as it is stored, the platform's manifest chosen from an index, so a layout's image
is built on as any base is (`oci_layout_contexts_are_the_images_they_hold`). buildx locks
the index to read it, leaving a lock file in the layout; shards only reads.

### Supplied agent and harness startup (D54, continued)

A supplied directory or archive may hold its command in the root `agent.json` or
`harness.json`, with the user-approved fields `entrypoint` (a command string) and
`options` (an optional array of literal arguments). The same applies after a Git or
HTTP source is fetched. A nonempty entrypoint is split into quoted/escaped words, with
no implicit shell or variable, glob or command substitution; options follow as separate
arguments, including whitespace and empty strings exactly as given. An explicit `nohup`
is left as an ordinary program. No `ENTRYPOINT` or `CMD` scoping syntax is added to an
Agentfile, and startup does not install a program through `RUN` or `VOLUME`.

`startup::config` normalizes the simple descriptor to the existing OSI config, using the
Agentfile's declared name; `shards build agent` and `shards build harness` use the
explicit `-t` repository's basename instead, never a filesystem name. With no explicit
name a simple descriptor is refused, while legacy OSI input keeps its own name. The
full OSI descriptor remains readable with its schema,
path and platform checks. `DomainConfig` is a graph operation over the unpacked source,
so native builds and the BuildKit frontend run the same regular-file check and parser
before copying `osi.json` beside the domain. Symlinks and non-regular descriptors are
refused. A missing descriptor retains passive layout compatibility. The existing domain
content checks still refuse escaping links, special files and set-ID bits.

At runtime the domain's own root and `bin` precede the system directories on `PATH`,
which is inherited by children too. This makes a supplied bare `codex` or `claude` work,
and makes `nohup codex ...` find the same artifact's executable. This changes neither
its cgroup nor its filesystem, process or network grants. Output routing is a separate
contract; this startup decision makes no output grants.

| Literal or field | Source |
|---|---|
| `agent.json`, `harness.json` | The supplied startup contract; the existing OSI artifact descriptor filenames |
| OSI `schemaVersion` | Existing `osi::SCHEMA_VERSION`; simple manifests do not supply it |
| DomainConfig protobuf field | The next shards-owned operation field after the existing Skills field, `SKILLS + 1` |
| Generated directory/file modes | `0755`/`0644`, COPY's generated directory and regular-file modes |
| File-action indices and `-1` | BuildKit `pb.FileAction`: one source input, actions chained after it, `-1` for scratch/no output |

Tests: `startup::tests` covers Codex and Claude commands, quoted and escaped words,
literal options, empty arguments, rejected malformed descriptors and retained OSI
metadata. `supplied_domains_read_their_local_startup_config` covers planner copies,
`a_supplied_harness_startup_is_normalized_through_the_gateway` the frontend's check,
and `supplied_agents_and_harness_archives_start_their_declared_entrypoints` observes
both a supplied directory agent and tar harness started in real confined domains.

### Fetched sources: S3, pins, secret headers and grants (D54, continued)

`AGENT` and `HARNESS` take a source from Git (https, ssh, `git://`, scp-like), an http(s)
URL, and now an S3-compatible store: `s3://BUCKET/KEY` (AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Mantle's
object store). Every fetched source is pinned, and every one is held to the grant its
directive makes.

**Forms.** `AGENT|HARNESS [--checksum=sha256:<hex>] [--redirect=HOST[:PORT]]…
[--endpoint=URL] [--region=R] [--path-style] [--version-id=V] [--credentials=aws-default]
<name> FROM <source>`.
- An http(s) source needs `--checksum`: the content behind a URL changes without notice.
  Bytes that hash to another are refused, `digest mismatch GOT: WANT`
  (`a_directives_source_serving_other_bytes_than_its_pin_is_refused`).
- An `s3://` source needs `--checksum`, `--version-id`, or both. A version is immutable in
  S3; the bytes are hashed either way.
- `--endpoint`, `--region`, `--path-style`, `--version-id` and `--credentials` go only with
  `s3://`; `--credentials` takes `aws-default` alone.
  `--checksum` goes only with http(s) and s3, as a Git source is pinned by the commit its
  `#REF` resolves to (recorded as before). `--redirect` goes only with http(s) and Git.
- `SKILL` and `MCP` take `--redirect=HOST[:PORT]`, repeated, exactly as `AGENT` and
  `HARNESS` do, where their source is fetched from http(s) or Git. It is refused for a
  context path, a skill `--from` another stage or agent (copied, not fetched), and a
  remote MCP server's URL, which its agents reach at run under the network's grants
  rather than the build fetching it (`skills_and_mcp_servers_grant_their_redirects`).
- Each refusal names what to write instead (`fetched_sources_are_pinned_and_say_where_they_are`).
- `MCP` takes no `s3://` source: it has no flags to pin one.
- Dockerfile `ADD` keeps BuildKit's grammar and meaning. BuildKit's ADD reads `s3://…` as
  a context path, so a Dockerfile's ADD of one means what it means to BuildKit. Nothing
  deviates, and `testdata/deviations.json` needs no entry.

**Plan.** The planner lowers an http(s) source with `http.checksum`. An s3 one becomes a
source op `s3://BUCKET/KEY` with `s3.filename` (the key's last part), `s3.checksum`,
`s3.versionid`, `s3.endpoint`, `s3.region` and `s3.pathstyle`, unpacked as an http(s)
download is. Every http(s), Git and s3 source an `AGENT`, `HARNESS`, `SKILL` or `MCP`
makes carries `shards.grant`: the `--redirect` origins, `,` apart (empty for none). The
source a `COPY --from=<agent>` reads again carries the same pins and grant
(`fetched_sources_carry_their_pins_and_grants_into_the_plan`).

**S3: one client (D88).** `build::s3::Object` fetches through the cache's `Bucket`: its
SigV4 signing, endpoint rules (virtual-hosted, or path-style with `--path-style` or a
bucket that cannot be a host label), and the SDK's endpoint and region settings where the
directive names none. Its errors say `s3 source` where the cache's say `s3 cache`.
- One `GetObject`, with `versionId` where pinned. The body streams to disk, hashed, within
  the limits an HTTP source's download holds to (audit A10).
- A `--checksum` mismatch is refused (`digest mismatch GOT: WANT`).
- Credentials are taken only by explicit reference, never implicitly (`build::s3::Signer`):
  - the build's secrets `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`
    (AWS's own variable names), each `NAME.<bucket>` before `NAME`, as Git's
    `GIT_AUTH_TOKEN.<host>` comes before `GIT_AUTH_TOKEN`. A key ID without its secret, or
    the reverse, is refused (`the build's secrets name half a key`), not completed from
    elsewhere;
  - or `--credentials=aws-default`, which opts into the host's AWS default chain
    (crate::aws::credentials: the environment, profiles, SSO, sign-in, web identity, a
    container's endpoint, EC2's instance metadata, a credential process). The opt-in is
    the grant to the chain's own endpoints, as its configuration names them; the chain
    records each origin it reached (`Chain::reached`, and `credential_process` where it ran
    one) and the build names them on the source's step: `s3://B/K: signed through the
    host's AWS default credential chain (--credentials=aws-default), which reached
    http://169.254.169.254:80` (or `no endpoint` for the environment's keys). The build's
    secrets are not read for such a source;
  - with neither, the GET goes unsigned, as the SDK's anonymous credentials send it: a
    public object's. The step says `sent unsigned: …`, and a store that requires
    signing refuses it with its status, the refusal ending with why it went unsigned.
  Before, a source with no secrets fell back to the host's chain, which reached IMDS,
  SSO or STS without the Agentfile naming any of them. The S3 cache keeps BuildKit's
  rule (its attributes' keys, else the chain): `Unkeyed::Chain` for it,
  `Unkeyed::Unsigned` for a source. A policy sees the opt-in as `input.s3.credentials`.
  The copies the client is made from are zeroized once it holds its own.
  Tests: `an_s3_source_is_signed_only_by_what_the_build_names` (unit, against a stand-in
  that refuses unsigned requests with 403 and a container endpoint as the chain; and on
  real VMs).
- The build records the object as `s3://BUCKET/KEY?versionId=V` (or `?etag=E` where S3
  keeps no versions) with its SHA-256, among the provenance's materials.
- An s3 source is fetched and keyed by its content, as an HTTP source is
  (`cache::source_key`): a changed object changes the build's key.

**Secret headers for http(s) (BuildKit parity).** BuildKit v0.28.1's http source sends an
Authorization from the build's secrets (source/http/source.go newHTTPRequest; solver/pb
attr.go `http.authheadersecret`): the secret `http.authheadersecret` names, which must be
there; else `HTTP_AUTH_HEADER_<host>` (the whole header) and `HTTP_AUTH_TOKEN_<host>`
(`Bearer` + it, which wins where both are), `<host>` the URL's hostname as written. shards
sent only URL userinfo; now every http source (an `ADD`'s and an Agentfile's, its policy
metadata and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH fetches, and a remote context) sends what BuildKit sends.
- The header replaces the userinfo's Basic credentials (net/http Client.send).
- An Agentfile directive's fetch is refused with the server's status
  (`invalid response status 401`) even when a checksum pins it. BuildKit fetches a pinned
  source whatever the status, so a refusal would only show as a digest mismatch; `ADD`
  keeps that.
- On a redirect it goes only to the first host or a subdomain of it, by host alone
  (client.go shouldCopyHeaderOnRedirect, isDomainOrSubdomain). Once dropped it stays
  dropped (Go 1.23.5, CVE-2024-45336).
- A secret is never written to a layer, the build record or a log. The provenance keeps the
  URL with its userinfo redacted, as before.
- Tests: `a_hosts_secrets_authorize_its_fetch_as_buildkits_do`,
  `a_secrets_header_stays_within_its_hosts_domain`.

**Default deny for directive fetches (ROOT's decision, 2026-11-14).** A microVM's network
is default deny, but these fetches run on the host, in the build process. Their rule: an
Agentfile directive's source is its own grant.
- A fetch connects only to the origin (scheme, host, port) its source names: the URL's;
  for s3 the host the client derives from the endpoint or AWS's region; for Git the remote.
  It also reaches each origin a `--redirect=HOST[:PORT]` names, in the source's scheme, at
  the port named or the scheme's own (RFC 9110 §4.2). No wildcards, no scheme change.
- Each connection is checked before it is made (`build::grant::Hops`, through the HTTP
  client's per-hop `authorize`), every redirect hop and both smart-HTTP requests of a Git
  fetch included.
- A redirect elsewhere is refused before anything is sent there: `redirected from FROM to
  TO, which the source does not grant: name it with --redirect=HOST[:PORT]`
  (`Refused::RedirectNotGranted`).
- A Git submodule at another origin is refused too (`Refused::NotGranted`). git:// and SSH
  remotes connect only to the host their URL names, and S3 requests follow no redirect.
- An environment proxy stays the host's egress path; the grant is what it connects to.
- `ADD` and remote contexts keep BuildKit v0.28.1's fetch (redirects anywhere, 10 hops
  through Go's client). Docker's inputs stay BuildKit's byte for byte; a build policy
  (D101) is how a build refuses an `ADD`'s hosts.
- Tests: `a_fetch_reaches_its_own_origin_and_what_it_grants_alone`,
  `a_git_source_opens_only_the_remotes_it_grants`,
  `a_git_sources_redirect_elsewhere_is_refused_until_granted` (a smart-HTTP advertisement
  redirected to another origin: refused naming both, nothing sent there; followed once granted),
  `a_granted_fetch_is_refused_a_redirect_it_does_not_name`,
  `a_skill_from_a_redirecting_source_is_fetched_once_granted`; real VMs:
  `a_skill_from_a_redirecting_source_builds_once_granted`.

Rejected:
- **Fetching inside the builder microVM under its network policy.** SSH keys and agents
  never enter a VM (D51, D69), and a fetch there would need the credentials inside it and
  a fetcher in the guest.
- **A shipped default Rego policy.** It denies only by opt-out, and a policy sees a source,
  not its redirect hops.

**Literals.**

| Literal | Source |
|---|---|
| `sha256:` and 64 hex digits | the pin is a SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4), as `http.checksum` is |
| `HTTP_AUTH_HEADER_`, `HTTP_AUTH_TOKEN_`, `Bearer ` | BuildKit v0.28.1 source/http/source.go |
| `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN` | AWS's own variable names (SDK configuration) |
| `aws-default` | shards' name for the SDK's default credential chain (aws-sdk-go-v2 config.LoadDefaultConfig), the one value `--credentials` takes |
| ports 80 and 443 | RFC 9110 §4.2 |
| labels of 1-63 characters, names of at most 253 | RFC 1035 §2.3.4 |

**Policies over s3 sources.** A build policy (D101) is asked of an s3 source as
`input.s3`: its URL, bucket, key, endpoint, region, path style, version and checksum, as
the directive gives them. buildx's input has no S3 form; this one is a recorded deviation
(`policy-input` in `crates/agentfile/testdata/deviations.json`). Before, any build with an
s3 source and a policy was refused (`unsupported source scheme: s3`).

**Not yet.**
- Real-VM builds of each kind are owed to the coordinator (`crates/shards/tests/build.rs`).

### Skills checked as the Agent Skills reference checks them (D54)

`SKILL` takes skills in the Agent Skills format (AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §8 Q12): a directory
whose `SKILL.md` opens with YAML frontmatter, `name` and `description` required. Each is
checked as the format's reference validator checks it (agentskills/skills-ref
`validate`, 69ef37e; `shards_build::skill`), held to it by `crates/build/tests/skills.rs`
over 131 skills, every error and every parsed frontmatter alike, as
`scripts/skills/generate` records skills-ref (on Python 3.14.3, from its own lockfile)
making of them:

- the 14 Apache-2.0 skills of anthropics/skills (683bc88), committed with their licence;
  skills-ref refuses one of them (`claude-api`, a 1068-character description), and so
  does shards;
- 117 crafted ones, for each rule: names (NFKC-normalized and stripped, Python's
  `str.isalnum` taken from the same Python, lowercase, hyphens, length in code points,
  the directory's name), descriptions, compatibility, unknown fields, and the YAML.

The frontmatter is read as strictyaml reads it, by a parser of its subset written for
this: block style only, every scalar a string, a document that is no collection its raw
text; flow style, anchors, aliases, tags, merge keys, repeated keys, tabs outside quoted
and block values, and `-`, `?` or `:` before a space where a value starts all refused.
Two of its found quirks kept: a value of the key's indentation on the next line is an
error, and NEL, LINE and PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR fold within a value without ending its line.
Deviation, recorded in the test: where the YAML is refused, shards says what is wrong and
on which frontmatter line after skills-ref's own prefix; strictyaml's texts (ruamel's,
naming `<unicode string>`) are not reproduced. Mutation-checked: a description limit
moved, and a value's `: ` let through, each fail the corpus.

**What the directives lay out.** `AGENT`, `HARNESS`, `MCP` and `SKILL` build (no longer
refused by name), each a layer of its own (`--link`, §7 Q19), so a domain's files are its
directive's alone:

- **Sources** (§12.2) are told apart as written: a Git URL (by the rules BuildKit's git contexts
  read one) is cloned; an http(s) URL is downloaded and unpacked (an agent served over
  HTTP is an archive); a path (`.`, `./`, `../`, `/`) is taken from the build context as
  `ADD` takes one, a local archive unpacked; anything else is an OCI reference, an OSI
  artifact, which shards does not fetch yet (refused with what to name instead). A path
  ending in a `:tag` is refused: a version is an OCI reference's.
- **Where each goes** (§12.1): an agent at `/agents/<name>`, a harness at
  `/harness/<name>` (or `TO`'s path); an MCP server over stdio at `/mcp/<name>`, or with
  `FOR` at each grantee's `/agents/<name>.d/mcp/<server>` (`/harness/<name>.d/…` for a
  harness, by `--target-kind` or what declares the name); a remote one (an http(s) URL)
  fetched not at all, the normalized Agentfile carrying it.
- **Skills**: the source taken as `ADD` takes one (`--from`, `--checksum`,
  `--keep-git-dir`, `--exclude`), then a step of shards' own: each skill it holds checked
  as the reference validator checks it (above), and laid out in a directory of its name.
  A tree is one skill when its root holds `SKILL.md`, its name to match the directory it
  came as (a path's, a Git repository's or subdirectory's; none for a URL or heredoc);
  one Markdown file is a skill's `SKILL.md`; otherwise each entry at its root must be a
  skill. Anything else fails the build, each skill and what is wrong with it named. The
  skills then go to `/skills/` for every agent (shards' choice: one copy beside `/mcp/`,
  which §4.3 leaves open), to each grantee's `.d/skills/` with `FOR`, or to a destination
  given without `FOR`; a destination with `FOR` is refused, for a grant writes into its
  grantee's domain alone.
- `SKILL --from=<agent>` (§12.12) is refused until OSI agent configs, which list an
  agent's skills, are fetched.

Tested on a real microVM (`agentfile_directives_lay_out_what_they_bring`): an agent's
directory, a harness's archive unpacked, an MCP server granted to one agent and a remote
one not fetched, a skill granted to one agent and a directory of shared skills; and a
skill the reference refuses failing the build in its words.

**OSI artifacts.** Agents, harnesses and MCP servers are OCI 1.1 artifacts of their own
types (§8 Q1), and their content and config are as §12.17 proposes
(`shards_image::osi`): `artifactType` `application/vnd.osi.{agent,harness,mcp}.v1`, a
config `application/vnd.osi.*.config.v1+json` (schema version 1; a reader refuses another
version, unknown fields, a name no Agentfile could give, and a path that is absolute or
climbs out), and content layers `application/vnd.osi.*.content.v1.tar` (`+gzip` and
`+zstd` read).

- **Made** by `shards build agent DIR -t NAME` (and `harness`, `mcp`, in shards' own
  grammar, `shards agent build …` the group it is said as) of a directory and its
  `agent.json` (`harness.json`, `mcp.json`), which is the config and not content: one
  uncompressed tar, names in order, owned by root, times kept, refused if it holds what
  §9.2 keeps out of any domain (device nodes, FIFOs, sockets, set-ID bits, symlinks whose
  targets leave the directory).
- **Kept, pushed, pulled, listed, inspected, removed** as images are, in the same store
  (`shards push|pull|ls|inspect|rm agent`), pushed by the registry client every image push
  uses.
- **Taken** by `AGENT`, `HARNESS` and `MCP` `FROM` an OCI reference: resolved from the
  store, or pulled (with `--pull`, pulled again), its `artifactType`, config and layer types
  checked against what the directive takes, and its content read through and refused for
  whiteouts, devices, FIFOs, set-ID bits, absolute or climbing names, and links leaving
  the directory, each time a build takes it, however it came to be stored. Its content is
  laid as a layer of its own at the domain's directory and its config at
  `<directory>.d/osi.json`, where the runtime reads how it runs; the source names the
  artifact by digest.

Tested on a real microVM (`agents_are_osi_artifacts_made_pushed_and_taken`): an agent made
and pushed to a registry (its manifest, config and layer types as specified), listed,
removed here, then pulled by an Agentfile's `AGENT` and laid out with its config; a
harness `FROM` an agent refused; a symlink out of the directory refused when made.

### Domains checked at build time (D55)

An image with agents or harnesses is checked before anything of it leaves the build
(AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §9.2), every path placed in its domain: an agent's or harness's
directory and the `.d` grants beside it, or the system. The planner records each domain
where its directive lays it (`TO`'s path, which must now be absolute, as grants and checks
find a domain by it whatever order the file declares things in; grants follow it to
`<dir>.d`), and the build fails, naming each path and why, where:

- a symlink in a domain resolves, inside the image and through any symlinks on the way
  (40 at most, as Linux follows), outside it: absolute or relative, into the system or
  another domain;
- a hard link's names lie in two domains;
- a domain holds a device node, FIFO or socket, or a file with set-ID bits or file
  capabilities (`security.capability`);
- **a step other than a domain's own directives writes in it** (§7 Q19.3): every file
  operation and command of the target's lineage is marked, and each domain's own steps
  with the destination they write; each marked step's new layers are read entry by entry,
  a removal (a whiteout) counted as a write, and a path in a domain not the step's own
  fails it, naming the file. A step the cache answers is checked as one that ran.

Found while testing: a directive's path source (`AGENT … FROM ./agent`, `SKILL ./x`) did
not count among the context's paths, so a build that also `COPY`ed from the context sent
the context without them; it counts now.

Tested: the rules over trees made in memory (`build::domains` tests: symlinks out by
absolute and relative targets and through another symlink, in by both, a hard link across,
devices, FIFOs, set-ID bits, a grant's symlink), and on real microVMs
(`domains_are_checked_before_an_image_leaves_the_build`,
`only_a_domains_own_directives_write_in_it`: `RUN` writing in an agent's directory after
its `AGENT` and before it, `COPY` into its grants, all refused; `RUN` elsewhere built);
the write rule mutation-checked.

Owners, the last of §9.2's rules, came once the runtime decided its uids (D59): the n-th
domain, agents in the order declared and then harnesses, runs as uid and gid 200000 + n
(`shards_abi::DOMAIN_FIRST_ID`, init and the build reading one constant). A path whose
uid or gid is a domain's user, outside that domain or in another's, fails the build,
naming it (`--chown=200000` on /etc). Tested in memory (system and other domain, by uid
and by gid, an ID past the domains' none's), mutation-checked, and on a real build
(`a_domains_user_owns_nothing_past_its_domain`). Open: §9.8's triggers.

### The extensions expand their words; `COPY --from=<agent>` (D56)

The Agentfile's directives expand `ARG` and `ENV` where `ADD` does (BuildKit's
`dispatch` expands a command's words with the stage's environment before it runs it):
`AGENT`'s, `HARNESS`'s and `MCP`'s sources and `TO`, `SKILL`'s source, destination,
`--chown`, `--chmod` and `--checksum`, and `VOLUME`'s paths and options. Names stay as
written, as a stage's name does (`FROM … AS $x` is not expanded either), so a grant's names
are checked before any build argument is known.

`COPY --from=<agent or harness>` copies the domain's content, its files at the root, into
any stage, without the domain (§7 Q19.1). A domain's name is no stage (one namespace,
Q19.2), so the copy's source is the content state the directive itself copies from: the
context's, git's, http's, or the OSI artifact's. The stage that declares it is made a
dependency of the stage that copies, as `COPY --from=<stage>` makes it, so it is
dispatched first and its source expanded in its own scope (found by the test: expanding
with the global `ARG`s alone gave a declaring stage's `ARG SRC` the empty string). A domain
a later stage declares is refused, as a stage named before it is defined is.

Tested: `agents_expand_their_words_and_are_copied_from` (an `ARG`-named source,
`COPY --from=main` into a stage without the agent, the image holding the file and no
`/agents`), the dependency mutation-checked; BuildKit's oracle unchanged.

Checked once expanded (2026-11-15). P4.1 to P4.3 (a9f17f701) checked `AGENT`'s and
`HARNESS`'s sources as parsed, as `MCP`'s and `SKILL`'s already were (D54's pins, refusals
and grants), so an `ARG`-named source (`AGENT a FROM $SRC`) was refused before its stage
expanded it, and `agents_expand_their_words_and_are_copied_from` failed on every backend
from then (PM M608). A source that names no variable is checked as parsed; one that does
(a `$` anywhere in it, an escaped one included) is checked by the plan once its stage has
expanded it, by the same functions (`fetch_checked`, `mcp_checked`, `skill_checked`). Each
source is checked once, on what will be fetched, and a literal one still fails at parse.
Tested: `a_sources_variables_expand_before_it_is_checked` (`$SRC` and `${MCP_SRC}` parse as
written; an `ARG` that expands to an unpinned https or s3 `AGENT`/`HARNESS` source, an s3
`MCP` source, or a `SKILL --redirect` on a path is refused once expanded, with the words a
written-out source gets), mutation-checked (no check once expanded: the unpinned source
plans).

### An Agentfile's manifest says what it holds (D57)

The manifest of an Agentfile's image carries annotations (OCI image-spec `manifest.md`,
"annotations": arbitrary metadata, `vnd.`-prefixed keys for vendors) so that a registry's
listing, or the referrers API, finds it without fetching its config:
`vnd.osi.agentfile.digest` (the normalized Agentfile's digest, as the label), and
`vnd.osi.agentfile.agents` and `vnd.osi.agentfile.harnesses`, each the names
comma-separated in name order, left out when empty. `json.MarshalIndent` order is kept
(ocispec.Manifest writes `annotations` after `layers`), and a Dockerfile's manifest is byte
for byte what it was.

Tested: `an_agentfiles_manifest_says_what_it_holds` (the stored manifest's annotations for
an Agentfile with two agents and a harness; none on a Dockerfile's).

### Reach is transitive (D58)

The build computes, over the target's directives, what each agent and harness reaches
(AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §9.5). Edges: a network both join (`CONNECT … ON`), a named volume
granted to both (`VOLUME name … FOR`), `ATTACH`. A domain reaches the world when it joins a
network that is not internal and lets some port cross both its own boundary
(`NETWORK --expose/--ingress/--egress`) and the microVM's (`EXPOSE … FOR` it), either way
(an ingress-only port answers what reaches it, so replies carry data out; §12 answer 6:
a flow crossing both needs both, corrected with D59 part four, which first read either
alone as enough), or an external network (the host's, whose reach the build cannot see), or when a
remote MCP server is granted to it or to every agent. A local MCP server is no edge: each
caller has an instance of its own (§9.6). An internal-only domain (§9.5: one that joins
an internal network, and does not reach the world itself) with a path to one that does
fails the build with the shortest path, read outward:
`agent b -> network back -> agent a -> network world`. A domain on no internal network
holds nothing declared internal, so a harness driving an agent that reaches the world is
no error; one attached to an internal-only agent and to a world-reaching one is (§9.8).
No exception allows such a path: relays and declassifiers were dropped (§12 answer 14,
2026-10-07), the grants being what decides reach. Found by the suite: a first rule that took every domain not reaching the world
as internal-only refused the plain harness-drives-agent Agentfile of D54's test.
