record of one part of the guest's capture: `run::MAX_PAYLOAD`, the run protocol's part, plus
`control::exec::LOG_OUTPUT_HEAD`. The control lanes already held every frame to its exact length or
its lane's credit before taking it (`control::lane`, `exec::steer`, `exec::told`, `unix::read_answer`,
`managed::input`, `input::said`, the driver's output records), and do. Tests:
`frame::tests::a_lane_takes_its_own_kinds_to_its_own_bounds`, and loopback's
`a_clients_stdin_past_a_read_is_refused_from_its_header` (a chunk of `READ_MOST + 1` refused from its
header; with `Stdin` admitted up to the host's memory, as under the old bound, the daemon waits for
its bytes and the test is refused by its judged wait).

#### A client's authority, judged of what runs and of whom its key is now (remote-01 to 03, 2026-11-13)

The adversarial review of D180 (docs/bugs/2026-11-13/remote.md) found three ways a client
reached more than its enrollment grants. Each was reproduced red at 9efde7252 before its fix
(the tests named below, run on macOS arm64, and the Windows one on the Windows 11 guest).

- **An owner's command is judged as it runs, not as its first word reads (remote-01).** The
  daemon judged `Request.args`' first word; the child shards took a context's choice off the
  front (`--context NAME`, `-c NAME`, `--context=NAME`) and ran the rest, so
  `--context default client grant alice --dir /` granted a client this machine's root
  (`red_remote01_an_owners_command_behind_a_prefix`: chosen `Here`, child's first word
  `client`, the daemon's `owners` none). Now `daemon/remote.rs` `judge` refuses any context's
  choice outright (`Refused::Context`: a client's command runs on this machine and reaches no
  other context of its owner's), and judges the words `cli::command_words` gives, which are
  `dispatch`'s own: `help CMD…` as `CMD… --help`, and shards' grammar said as its command, to
  a fixpoint, a turn back to words already given ending it (no count of turns is chosen). The
  file-reaching words (`client_grants::refuse_words`) are judged of the same words. A build
  step's command (`\0sync build KEY WORDS…`), which no `owners` judged, must be a build's
  (`commands::build`, or an agent's, harness's or MCP server's `build`), else
  `Refused::NotABuild`, before any of its files come. And independently of the daemon, the
  child refuses a `context`, `client` or `invitation` command wherever it runs for a client
  (`cli::owners_alone`, of `SHARDS_CLIENT`, which the listener sets last): what reaches the
  administration handlers is judged there too. The refusals are typed (`Refused`), the wire
  carrying their text as `Tag::Refused` as before.
- **A build file's name is one file's as the machine's paths read it (remote-02).** The name's
  check refused `/`, `\`, NUL, `.` and `..`, but on Windows `C:context` is a path of drive C's
  current directory, which `PathBuf::join` takes in place of the copy's directory: the
  daemon's home's `context` or `identity` was overwritten
  (`red_remote02_a_drive_relative_name_escapes_the_copy`, the Windows guest: the file written
  in the test's current directory). `synced::name_alone` now refuses, on Windows, a colon (a
  drive's prefix, or an alternate data stream), the characters no Win32 name holds
  (`< > " | ? *` and controls 1-31, which also cover `\\?\` and `\\.\`), a trailing dot or
  space, and a device's name with any extension (`CON PRN AUX NUL COM0-9 LPT0-9`, superscript
  1-3 too, and CreateFileW's `CONIN$ CONOUT$`): Microsoft's "Naming Files, Paths, and
  Namespaces" and CreateFileW's documentation, the only sources of the set; no number is
  chosen. Linux and macOS take each such name as the name it is there. Refusals are typed
  (`NotAName`), before any file is opened. The build's other words that name paths (`--file`,
  `--output dest=`, `--iidfile`, a tree's) are held to the copies by remote-09, below.
- **A client is its key as its connection proved it, judged for each operation (remote-03).**
  The listener judged a connection's key once and kept the client's name: a removed client's
  held connection, or the old key of a name enrolled again under another key, ran new
  commands, and an Engine API connection kept open served calls after the removal
  (`red_remote03_an_old_keys_connection_runs_a_new_command`: `echo again` ran). Now each
  command's start judges again, apart from the driver, whether the machine enrolls the key
  its connection proved under the name it was judged (`server::start_apart`); one it does not
  is refused (`REVOKED_WORDS`) and its connection closed with code `REVOKED` (3, an
  application error code of RFC 9000 §20.2's space beside `UNENROLLED`'s 2: an identifier,
  not a tunable), its commands hung up as a lost connection's are, and its client says why.
  The daemon watches the home's `clients` directory (`platform::FileWatch`, one instance
  for the daemon's life) and tells the listener each change (`Stopper::revalidate`), and once
  as the watch begins, for a removal before it: every connection whose key the machine no
  longer enrolls so is closed at once. An Engine API connection a client opened through its
  context carries the key it proved (`context::Proved`), and each call on it is judged by
  whether the home's record still holds that key, refused 403 (RFC 9110 §15.5.4) and the
  connection ended where it does not. A command or a call under way as its client is removed
  is hung up as the connection closes; none is judged anew mid-flight. The record is read for
  each judgment, no cache kept: it is the one account of whom the home enrolls. Where the
  watch cannot be made (a host's inotify instances spent, PM M257), the daemon says so in its
  log, and a removed client's held connection is refused at its next command instead.
  Tested: `tests/loopback.rs` `a_removed_clients_held_connection_runs_nothing_more` (refused,
  closed `REVOKED`, its `cat` hung up, the name's new key served) and
  `a_removed_clients_connection_closes_as_the_daemon_is_told` (closed at once, a client still
  enrolled served on), `context::tests::a_proved_client_is_enrolled_while_its_record_holds_its_key`.
- **A build step names no path but its client's copies (remote-09).** remote-01 held a build
  step's words to a build's, but not their paths: `placed` passed every value that is no
  marker through, so `--output=type=local,dest=/any/dir` wrote this machine's files
  (`red_remote09_a_build_steps_output_names_this_machines_path`). `synced::named_paths` now
  enumerates every path buildx v0.37.1's build grammar takes (crates/cmdline BUILD's
  path-typed values: the context's argument, `--file`, `--iidfile`, `--metadata-file`,
  `--output`'s `dest`, `--cache-from` and `--cache-to`'s `src` and `dest`, `--build-context`'s
  path and `oci-layout://` directory, `--secret`'s `src`, `--ssh`'s paths and `--policy`'s
  `filename`; its other flags name none). An agent's, harness's or MCP server's build names its
  directory alone. Each is judged twice:
  - **Before any file comes** (`held_to_copies`, `Refused::NotHeld`). Each path must be its
    copy's marker form: the context is `\0context`; the build file is a `\0dockerfile/NAME`;
    anything written is an `\0out/NAME`; anything read beside the context is a `\0tree/KEY`
    of 64 hex digits; a secret is one of the `\0secret/N` the step sends (N below their
    count); an agent is an `\0agent/ID`; and a policy's file is a name within the context.
    Each NAME and each part is one file's name by `name_alone`, so Windows' forms count.
    `--secret type=env`, a secret of no `src`, and `--ssh` of no path read the machine's own
    environment or agent, and are refused as `NotHeld::Machines`.
  - **Where the build runs for a client** (`refused_for_client`, of `SHARDS_CLIENT`, in
    `build::build` and the artifacts' `build`). Each placed path must lie beneath the client's
    copies (`HOME/synced/CLIENT`), lexically and part by part, with no part `..`, a root or a
    prefix. A secret's or an agent's path must be a descriptor the build was given
    (`/dev/fd/N`).

  The client's own shards sends nothing else (`context::tests::what_a_client_sends_of_a_build_is_held_to_its_copies`).
  A path the client sent as it was given because no directory of that name was there (a
  `--cache-from` or `--build-context` it lacks, a policy outside its context) is now refused
  on the machine rather than by the build. No number is chosen: the markers and buildx's
  grammar are the bounds. Tested: `synced::tests::a_clients_build_names_no_path_but_its_copies`,
  `a_placed_build_names_nothing_outside_its_copies`, `a_build_run_for_a_client_refuses_this_machines_paths`
  and `daemon::remote::tests::a_build_step_naming_this_machines_path_is_refused_before_its_files`.
- **Owed (ROOT's).** The real-daemon E2E of each: tests/context.rs's removal with an Engine API
  keep-alive connection held across it and a native connection held across a removal and a
  re-enrollment of its name; a client's raw `--context` and `\0sync build` requests; a Windows
  listener receiving `C:context`; a client's crafted `\0sync build` naming
  `--output dest=`, `--iidfile`, `--file` and `--secret src=` paths of the machine's, refused
  with nothing written, and a context build of every path-typed flag still served. The per-call
  record read's cost (R14).

### D181. `--use-api-socket`: a run's command reaches its own microVM's engine (slices 1 to 3 built)

The [current guest stream pump closing record](../research/measurements/managed-engine-relay-root/README.md)
compares the original and shared implementations over actual carried KVM VSOCK:
both close orders preserve exact response/end/late-write behavior, then the
ordinary managed-output/code-mode and seven-target gates pass at4fa823919.
The guest engine now uses one shared readiness/retained-tail pump; its existing
connection worker remains, while the extra scoped upload thread is removed.
Engine peer EOF closes the client's two halves before EOF publication. The
historical first-candidate late-write regression, guard removal/restoration,
current pressure-witness miss and initial test-helper lint failure remain retained.
No new networking authority or production interception route is installed.

New engine buffer literals are derived: two buffers are the actual directions;
one `sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE)` private mapping per direction is the minimum mapping
unit, with no growth/cache; HELLO is `HEADER + TOKEN`. Native poll uses its signed
millisecond ABI range and -1 event-wait sentinel. These bounds do not establish
parent/kernel admission, optimal throughput or a measured performance win;
those management obligations stay open.

The need: a CI job, a test suite with testcontainers, or an agent's tool runs `docker run`
from inside its workload, as on a host with Docker. The user's call (2026-10-16): what it
reaches is the microVM's own engine. Docker's flag (docker/cli v29.8.1
cli/command/container/create.go, marked experimental) does two things, both what shards
does not: it binds the host engine's own socket into the container, so the workload
controls the host's Docker, every container and image of it, as root does; and it writes
every registry credential the CLI holds into the container's files
(`/run/secrets/docker/config.json`, `DOCKER_CONFIG`), which its own comment says stay
there where the container is not removed.

- **What the command gets.** An Engine API endpoint of its own microVM's: a socket in its
  own files, `/run/shards/engine.sock`, and `DOCKER_HOST=unix:///run/shards/engine.sock`
  where its run's options name none (over its image's own, which names an engine the
  flag replaces), so that the docker CLI, Docker's SDKs and testcontainers find it
  unchanged. No socket of the host's, and nothing at Docker's own path. The socket is the
  standby's to make, in the command's own view of its files, after the run's mounts (a
  tmpfs over `/run` holds it) and before its root is made read-only (`--read-only` keeps
  it), mode 0666: whoever the command runs as or becomes reaches it, and no process but
  the run's own sees the path.
- **On Windows**, where a VM's process gives its daemon no handle (D195: a child's end
  takes handles only from its spawner), the VM asks for each connection whose token
  holds (`ENGINE_CONN`, no handle), and the daemon makes a pair of pipes written in
  messages (`Stream::plain_pair`): it serves one end as the connection, scoped to the
  microVM as Unix's, and gives the VM the other, onto which the VM relays its guest's
  connection each way on a thread of its own (warm.rs `relay_engine`), each side's end of
  writes passed on: the pipe's message of no bytes one way, the socket's half-close the
  other. A run with no engine of its own is answered with no pipe, and its connection
  closed. Tested on jupiter: tests/engine.rs's own-engine tests and the docker CLI's
  `--use-api-socket`.
- **What it makes: joiners of its own microVM.** A container it creates there is a joiner
  of its microVM (D119): its own image, its own mount, PID, IPC and UTS namespaces and
  cgroup, its record, log and end; its network a namespace of its own on the microVM's
  switch, granted what it declares and nothing else (slice 3), `host` the command's own
  namespace where its client asks for it, `container:X` one of its own joiners'. The
  microVM's boundary holds the host from all of them. It is named in the scope as the command named it, and on the
  host after its microVM's name (`PROV.NAME`), so that two microVMs' engines making the
  same name (two CI jobs of one project) never collide, where a shared dockerd's do. Its
  record keeps which microVM's engine made it (`engine_made`). It ends as its microVM's
  command does, as a nested engine's containers end with it: init kills each joiner its
  engine made as the command ends (`engine-made`), where a joiner made otherwise outlives
  it (D119); and it goes with its microVM, removed as that is.
- **Scoped, whatever is asked.** Through it, a command sees and acts on what its own
  engine made alone, by the names it gave: list, inspect, start, stop, kill, wait, logs,
  attach (`docker run`'s, before the start), resize, exec, remove; `_ping`, `version`, and
  an `info` of its own (its containers, its images, its microVM's CPUs and memory where
  its run limits them, its hostname; none of its host's name, directories, proxies or
  descriptors). Another microVM, its own included, and an exec of another's, are not there
  for it (404, as one that is not). What would reach past the microVM is refused with
  what asked for it (403): a named volume, another network, the host's GPUs, CDI and VFIO
  devices, a log driver that sends logs from the host past the microVM's grants, another
  runtime, an engine of its own for a joiner. A call it does not serve is answered 501
  before its body is read, naming what it serves; a registry login, 403.
- **A bind is of its microVM's own files**, as a bind on any engine is of that engine's
  host's, and the microVM is its host: `-v /work:/src` in the CI job binds the job's
  `/work`, where Docker's flag binds the host's path, which the job's files are not. The
  joiner's init copies the source from the workload's mount namespace while that is in
  reach (setns(2), open_tree(2) `OPEN_TREE_CLONE | AT_RECURSIVE`: a bind brings its
  submounts, which `-v`'s users rely on, Docker's binds being
  recursive), resolved from that namespace's root, the command's files, past none of them
  (`..` and links, absolute or not, stop there): its volumes and tmpfs mounts are in it,
  and a link to one resolves as the command's processes see it. Read-only binds are so
  with their submounts (mount_setattr(2) `AT_RECURSIVE`, Linux 5.12). `-v` makes a missing
  source, which scripts written for Docker rely on; `--mount` does not, and skips the host's check for
  it, the source being none of the host's. A propagation that would share mounts with the
  command's (`shared`, `slave`) is refused: a copy shares none.
- **Its images are its own.** A create runs its microVM's image, and those its engine
  pulled (`engine_images` in the microVM's record); another image the host's store holds
  is not there for it (404), so the docker CLI pulls, as on an engine without it, and a
  scope never reads an image it was not given. `images` and `image inspect` list its own
  alone; `info` counts them.
- **No credential enters the microVM.** A pull through it is the daemon's, with the
  registries' environment the run's client sent with the run (its `DOCKER_CONFIG` and the
  rest, `registry_env`), kept in the daemon's memory for the run's life alone, as a log
  driver's credentials are (D168), never written into the microVM, nor into the run's
  kept request; credentials a client in the microVM gives (`X-Registry-Auth`) go over
  them. A registry login asked from inside is refused.
- **The docker CLI's own flag, asked of shards' engine** (`docker run --use-api-socket`
  over `engine.sock`): its bind of its engine's socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`, bind
  options none set) is the microVM's own engine instead, and its `DOCKER_CONFIG` goes with
  it; the copy of its credentials it makes after the create (an archive whose first entry
  is `/run/secrets/docker/config.json`) is refused, which the CLI warns of: they never
  reach the microVM.
- **How a request travels, by no socket of the host's.** The command's connection is
  taken by a process of init's (outside the command's cgroup, as the DNS relay is, started
  before the command so that what keeps it from starting keeps the command from starting;
  inside the run's from its first engine ring slot, a leaf `run/engine` beside the
  workload's, so that its slots are the run's memory, D230),
  which dials the host over vsock (`ENGINE_PORT`) for each, says a hello with its run's
  token first, and relays the bytes each way; the host's end ends the client's both ways,
  so that no relay outlives a connection the engine closed. The VM process registers the
  port only for a warm VM's run, and serves it only where its run has a token: its hello
  reader (exec's, review 8.8) checks each in constant time and hands the daemon those that
  say it, over the run's own link (`ENGINE_CONN`), holding its copy until the daemon says
  it has it (M24); any other is closed, and a run with no engine has no port (refused). A
  process of the microVM's that dials the port itself, past its seccomp filter, says no
  token its init was given. The daemon serves the connections of a run that has an engine
  alone, on the listener's threads, scoped to that run's microVM. A save keeps the token,
  which its restored guest's relay goes on saying (D176). No path on the host names the
  endpoint.
- **No microVM's engine takes the host's daemon.** Each of its connections holds a thread
  of the daemon's, and is counted as a client in hand (`busy`), of the clients the
  daemon's threads hold (`most_clients`: the process's thread limit past the daemon's own
  threads, at a client's two each; macOS gives 16,384 threads a process, and Windows'
  is derived, below). A microVM's
  engine holds an equal share of them alone, among the host's own clients and each
  microVM whose engine holds any: one alone holds half, two a third each. Past its share,
  or where the daemon holds as many clients as its threads do, a connection is answered
  503 with why and closed; one of its own going makes room. Without it, a workload's
  1,023 idle connections (the vsock muxer's bound, Firecracker's) held as many of the
  daemon's threads, and sixteen microVMs held them all.
- **On Windows the thread limit is derived (PM M529).** Windows keeps no count of a
  process's threads ("The number of threads a process can create is limited by the
  available virtual memory", CreateThread), so `platform::thread_limit` said none there and
  `most_clients` took POSIX's least, 64: 27 clients, of which a microVM's engine alone held
  13, and the 32 streams at once of engine_ring's pins test at 32 vCPUs were answered 503 on
  WHP (ring-pins-v1 r16). It is now the fewest threads any of three limits holds of one:
  - the process's address space (MEMORYSTATUSEX's `ullTotalVirtual`, "the size of the
    user-mode portion of the virtual address space") of a thread's stack's reservation,
    which "is limited to the virtual address range" (Thread Stack Size);
  - its commit limit of the commit a thread is charged: its stack's "initially committed
    pages ... remove pages from the system total commit limit, which is the size of the
    page file plus the size of the physical memory" (Thread Stack Size). The limit is
    `ullTotalPageFile`, "the current committed memory limit for the system or the current
    process, whichever is smaller", or the process's job's where less, which that leaves
    out (in a job holding it to 64 MiB it said the host's 141 GB): the job's
    `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_PROCESS_MEMORY` or `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_JOB_MEMORY`
    (JOBOBJECT_BASIC_LIMIT_INFORMATION), read by QueryInformationJobObject of "the
    immediate job of the calling process". A job above that one holding it to less ("the
    most restrictive memory limit in the job chain") is not for the process to read;
  - a process's 2^24 handles ("Kernel Objects"), of which a thread whose handle is kept
    (std's `JoinHandle`) holds one; the daemon drops its clients' as it starts them.

  Each cost is read on the daemon's own host, off a thread started as std starts every
  thread of shards' (`thread::Builder`, std's default stack: `RUST_MIN_STACK`, else
  2 MiB): the reservation GetCurrentThreadStackLimits gives; what Windows commits of every
  thread's stack however far its code goes, its initial commit ("the initially committed
  size is the default size specified in the executable header", Thread Stack Size: the
  image's `SizeOfStackCommit`, the linker's 4 KB) and its guard pages, VirtualQuery's
  PAGE_GUARD regions (std's `SetThreadStackGuarantee(0x5000)` and a page); and winternl.h's
  TEB in whole pages, the least a TEB is ("Do not assume a maximum size for this
  structure"). Not the pages its code has touched, which differ from thread to thread: a
  process's first thread runs its one-time initialization on its own stack, a page more,
  and under a test's output capture so does each. On jupiter (Windows 11, 10.0.26200;
  123.6 GiB, a commit limit of 141.1 GB) a thread reserves 2 MiB and is counted 4 KiB of
  initial commit, 24 KiB of guard pages and 8 KiB of TEB: its commit holds 3,827,251
  threads, its address space 67,108,863 and its handles 16,777,216, so 1,913,620 clients,
  956,810 of them a microVM's engine's alone.

  Windows charges a thread more than any call reports of it, which is not counted, so that
  the threads said are never fewer than Windows starts: the pages its code touches and its
  share of the heap (in jobs of 16, 64 and 256 MiB each std thread was charged 47.9 KB,
  36.9 KB of it counted; the limits said 455, 1,820 and 7,281 threads, and Windows started
  333, 1,380 and 5,563, then refused the next, ERROR_COMMITMENT_LIMIT, with less than a
  counted thread's commit left), and the kernel's own commit for its kernel stack, which
  "can vary among different hardware platforms and different versions of the operating
  system" (Using the Kernel Stack): about 35 KB of the system's commit more a thread on
  jupiter, from bursts of 20,000 threads that other work's commit moved by up to 3 GB. As
  Linux's `threads-max` counts a thread's kernel stack and not its user stack, this is a
  limit, not what is free on a loaded host: a client whose thread cannot be started is
  dropped, logged, as on every host. Tested natively on jupiter (windows_process.rs:
  `the_threads_held_are_the_fewest_each_limit_holds`;
  `a_thread_limit_is_what_the_host_holds_of_a_thread`, red while `thread_limit` said none,
  and a thread that has touched 256 KiB of its stack counted as a fresh one;
  `a_jobs_commit_limit_holds_the_threads_it_says`, a child in a job of its own whose limit
  is the job's over a thread's count, and whose 64 threads Windows charged at least what
  was counted of them). Owed: the pins test's 32 streams at once past the old bound on WHP
  (ROOT's).

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_command_reaches_its_own_microvms_engine`: made, started,
waited for, logged, listed, inspected and removed through it, the host's other microVM and
itself unseen, a named volume and a login refused, a call not served answered 501, one left running
ended with its command and removed with its microVM;
`the_docker_clis_use_api_socket_is_the_microvms_own_engine`; isolation's
`a_microvms_engine_port_answers_its_inits_token_alone`, a tmpfs over `/run` and a read-only
root among its cases, and the engine port among those a workload reaches none of), and in
the daemon (`an_engine_connection_is_served_for_a_run_with_its_own_engine_alone`) and the
scope (`a_scope_sees_its_own_containers_by_their_names_there`,
`a_create_stays_in_its_microvm`).

Slice 2 tested on real microVMs (`a_microvms_own_engine_runs_binds_execs_and_pulls`:
`docker run`'s calls, a create, an attach before the start and the start and wait on one
kept connection, its output from its first byte; binds of the command's file and of its
volume, read-only and written through, a link to its volume resolved as the command sees
it; an exec in its joiner, another microVM's exec unseen; a pull from a registry that
asks for credentials, which the run's client alone has, the image not its own before, its
own after; its images listed, none of the host's it never pulled), and in the scope
(`a_create_stays_in_its_microvm`).

Slices: (1) and (2) built, as above; (3), the joiners its engine makes on networks of
their own and Compose through them, designed as follows and built in five parts. A first cut of
(3) (part 3a, b6083246) put each joiner on a bridge of its own in the command's
namespace, with every port open between them and their flows translated to the command's:
no part of the microVM's own network design (D59, D61), it is replaced.

- **The need.** A test suite, a CI job or an agent's tools in a microVM start services
  through its engine (Testcontainers' `docker run -p 0:PORT`, Compose's project of
  services), each listening on its own ports, two on one port among them, each reaching
  the others it needs by name; and they run under the microVM's own rule, default deny,
  beside its agents.
- **Each is a member of the microVM's switch.** A joiner its engine makes gets a
  network namespace of its own, linked to init's switch through a gate of its own (D59
  part three, D61), as each of the image's agents is: known by its link, never by an
  address it could claim; what it opens tracked in its gate's table alone; no state of it
  kept by the switch. Init makes the namespace, its gate and its link before the
  joiner starts, and its processes enter it (setns(2)); the switch and the gate are
  outside every namespace they have.
- **Its engine's networks are the switch's.** A network its engine makes (Compose's
  project networks, a test's own) is a network of the switch: a /24 of the switch's block
  (10.244.0.0/16) clear of eth0's subnet and of every network of the microVM's, the
  agents' among them, or the subnet its client gives where that is clear of them too; its
  gateway its first address, or the one given. Init holds them, and gives each member the
  lowest free address as it joins: a /32 routed through the gateway on its link, as an
  agent's is. The engine's default network, which its clients call `bridge`, is one; a
  joiner named onto no other is on it.
- **Joining grants nothing; what a joiner declares does.** Each flow is named
  (AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §4.7): a joiner accepts, from each member of a network it shares,
  on the ports it declares, and on no other: its image's `EXPOSE`, its create's
  (`--expose`, Compose's `expose:`), and the joiner's side of each port it publishes.
  That is the receiver naming what it accepts, as `CONNECT --port` names it for an agent:
  the network says who may ask, the receiver on what. The default network names no peers:
  a joiner on it is alone, as an agent with no `CONNECT` is. Nothing else crosses: no
  port a receiver did not declare, no member of a network the two do not share, no agent
  of the image, not the command.
- **Names, of granted peers alone.** A joiner resolves its own names and those of each
  peer it is granted a flow to, and no other (§4.7). Its names on a network are its name
  in its engine's scope and the aliases its client gives it there (Compose's service
  names, `--network-alias`); nothing else names it. Its `/etc/hosts`, a file of its own
  mounted read-only as an agent's is, names it alone: an agent's lists its granted peers
  too (D59 part seven), which its build fixes, but a member's peers come and go as it
  runs. The agents' resolver answers its peers' names, by the link the question comes up
  (`IP_PKTINFO`, D59 part seven), from a table init keeps for each member as peers join
  and leave; each answer's TTL is 0, which no cache keeps past the answer (RFC 1035
  §3.2.1), so a name goes with its grant. A granted peer's name is answered in the
  microVM, never asked past it.
- **Published ports, to the command alone.** A port it publishes (`-p HOST:PORT`, `-P`)
  reaches it from the command, its engine's host, at `localhost:HOST` in the command's
  namespace: init's proxy there passes each connection and datagram on to the joiner's
  port, and the switch and its gate let that port alone in, up the switch's link from
  init's namespace. Nothing past the microVM reaches it but through a port the run itself
  publishes. The command reaches no joiner on any port it did not publish.
- **Past the microVM, no more than the command.** A joiner acts for the command that
  asked its engine for it: what it reaches past the microVM is what the command reaches
  (the run's own grants, the network process holding the microVM to them; beside agents
  whose grants reach past it, eth0's own subnet alone, as `confine_eth0` keeps the
  command), its flows given eth0's address as the agents' egress is (D59 part four); on an
  internal network, nothing. Names past the microVM likewise: it asks the agents'
  resolver, which forwards what the command may resolve.
- **What it tells where a flow is refused.** A peer's connection to a port its receiver
  never declared ends at the receiver's gate, as any flow no grant names does.
  `shards read ports` of a joiner lists each port it listens on that no grant lets its
  peers reach, with what would declare it (`EXPOSE`, `expose:`, `--expose`), so the gap
  is seen at once rather than as a connection that hangs.
- **Its own values.** A joiner's link takes the hardware address its kernel gives it,
  as an agent's does. The proxy keeps a UDP client's mapping a UDP mapping's two
  minutes past its last datagram, either way (RFC 4787 REQ-5 and REQ-6,
  `shards_abi::bounds::UDP_MAPPING_IDLE`), as the network process keeps one (D46). It
  kept the guest's conntrack timeouts (30 s until answered, then 120 s), which break
  REQ-5 past port 1023 (network-12, 2026-11-14).
- **`--network host` is the command's own namespace**, as the client asks: the engine's
  host's network, the command's reach and no more. `none` is a namespace of its own with
  its loopback alone; `container:X` the namespace of X, one of its own joiners.
- **The networks API** (create, list, inspect, remove, prune, connect, disconnect) takes
  what Compose and the SDKs send, and answers in the shapes they read, with the switch's
  values: its subnets, its members' addresses. A driver no microVM's switch can be
  (`overlay`, `macvlan`, `ipvlan`) and a setting it cannot hold are refused with why.
- **Named volumes it makes** are its own: the host's volume store's, named after its
  microVM's as its joiners are (`PROV.NAME`), mounted through the join share (D119),
  removed with its microVM.

Each difference from Docker is deliberate: membership carries no flow, where Docker's
network carries every port both ways; the default network names no peers, where Docker's
carries every port between its containers; a joiner resolves its granted peers alone,
where Docker resolves every member by name, alias, short ID and hostname; the command
reaches a joiner through what it publishes alone, where Docker's host reaches every
container's address; and a joiner reaches past the microVM no more than the command.

Built in parts: (3a) members on the switch, the default network, published ports, `host`
and `none`, built; (3b) the networks its engine makes, their grants and names, and the
networks API, built; (3c) its
named volumes, one joiner in another's namespace (`container:X`, Compose's
`service:`), and Compose end to end, built; (3d) the undeclared listeners `shards read
ports` lists, built; (3e) connect and disconnect of a running member, built.

- **How 3a is built.** The daemon asks for a membership by network and name (`member=`,
  with `own-publish=` for each port it publishes), and nothing of addresses. Init holds
  the engine's networks (`members.rs`), each a /24 of the switch's block clear of eth0's
  subnet and of every subnet the switch carries (the agents', which the switch now keeps
  from its making); it gives each member the lowest free address, the lowest free link
  index past the domains', a namespace of its own with its loopback, and links it through
  a gate of its own (`Switch::attach_ns`, as `attach` links a domain by its process). The
  switch keeps what it carries (the domains' grants, its uplink once there is one, its
  subnets, each member's), and programs its rules and init's again from that, each chain
  emptied first in the same transaction, as members come and go (`admit`, `release`): the
  domains' rules come out as before, a member's are its own. A member's way up the
  switch's link is every TCP and UDP port, as far as the command goes (init's `forward`,
  marked and given eth0's address as the agents' egress is; to eth0's subnet alone beside
  agents with egress); the command reaches it on its published ports alone (init's `own`
  chain, before its drop, and the switch's and gate's rules for that port from the
  uplink). It asks the agents' resolver, which now takes askers as members join and leave
  over a control link of init's. The joiner's child enters the namespace (setns(2)) by
  init's descriptor, which it inherits as init's fork, and its `/etc/hosts` names it, its
  `/etc/resolv.conf` the switch's resolver. Init says the membership to the host before
  the joiner starts (`MEMBER`: its network, address and prefix, gateway and the kernel's
  hardware address), which the daemon keeps for inspect while it runs; its end lets the
  membership go. The proxy relays what is published, its UDP mappings kept RFC 4787 REQ-5's
  two minutes past their last datagram (above; before 2026-11-14 the guest's conntrack
  timeouts, read in a run of the pinned kernel, arm64, 2026-10-17: 30 s, and 120 s once
  answered), and says a
  port it cannot bind in shards' words. `--add-host NAME:host-gateway` is refused: a
  member reaches nothing of the command's.
- **Found and closed: TCP DNS sessions held their accept's names (network-09,
  2026-11-13).** The agents' resolver cloned a TCP asker's table of names and grants at
  accept, so an open DNS-over-TCP connection answered a departed member's name, and never
  a joined one's, for as long as it stayed open. Each question is now judged under the
  relay's live askers, found by the connection's link and source address, with a typed
  verdict (`Here`, `Upstream`, `Refused`); an asker let go of, or whose link no longer
  has that address, has its connection closed. A question already sent upstream finishes
  on its connection. Red/green and a mutation (`None => continue`) of
  `an_existing_tcp_session_uses_the_members_current_names` on Linux x86_64;
  [evidence](../research/measurements/network-fixes-v1/README.md#network-09-a-tcp-dns-session-judged-by-its-asker-as-it-stands).
  The real-guest witness is ROOT's: an engine's three members, A's TCP session held
  across B's end and D's start, A's old TCP and a fresh UDP question agreeing.
- **Tested on real microVMs.** `a_microvms_own_engine_makes_each_container_a_member_of_its_switch`:
  two members serving one port, each at the port it was given on the command's loopback
  and at its own address on that port, from init's end of the switch's link; a port one
  declares but does not publish, dropped for the command; on the default network, a
  member reaching neither another's published port nor its declared one, and the other
  serving its next connection to the command; `--network none`'s loopback alone; its host
  name, and its name in its hosts file at its address; `host-gateway` refused; and its
  flows to a microVM on the host's network the command is on, from the command's address
  there. `an_engines_member_reaches_no_farther_than_the_command_beside_agents`: beside an
  agent granted a host's port, neither the command nor a member reaches it; with no
  agents, a member reaches what its command reaches. Every agent network test of D59 and
  D61 holds as before. Mutation-checked, each caught: a member beside agents reaching as
  far as the command of a run without them; the command's published ports not let
  through init's `own` chain; the default network carrying every port between members;
  members reaching nothing past the microVM.
- **How 3b is built.** Init makes and removes its engine's networks (`members::network`),
  asked by the daemon through a builtin (`NETWORK make NAME SUBNET GATEWAY RANGE FLAGS`,
  `remove NAME`, `default`) that init does itself before the builtin's fork, so that what
  it holds stays its own; the daemon keeps what its clients read of each (its ID, name,
  creation time, labels and options as given). A network's subnet is the lowest /24 of
  the switch's block clear of eth0's subnet and of every subnet the switch carries, or the
  one its client gives (a /8 to a /30, clear of the same), its gateway and range in it. A
  member on several networks has an address on each, routed on its one link
  (`Switch::routes`), and says each (`MEMBER`). Its grants are built again from every
  member whenever one joins or leaves (`members::grants`): for each two members of a
  network whose members are peers, the ports the receiver declares, held at two points
  that each hold them alone: the switch passes those only between the two links, and the
  receiver's gate accepts those only, from the opener's addresses. The opener's gate is a
  third that holds them alone: it opens those only to its peers, and what it opens past
  the microVM (every port, for a member that reaches past it) to none of the microVM's
  own subnets, its agents' networks' and its engine's, each gate made again as its engine
  makes or removes a network, as an agent's egress (D61). Each gate is programmed again
  in one transaction, the switch in one. A member's gate holds its declared ports from its start, before it has any peer,
  so that its own connections' ports are chosen clear of them (`local_ports`, D61). Its
  peers' names init gives the agents' resolver with its asker, over init's control link;
  the resolver answers a question that comes up the member's link from them first, and
  any other as that member's (forwarded where it reaches past the microVM, refused where
  it does not). The answerer is `shards-dns` (once `shards_net::dns`), a crate init and
  the network process share. Of the options its clients send, `enable_icc` false makes a
  network of no peers, `gateway_mode_ipv4` isolated an internal one, and
  `host_binding_ipv4` the address its members' published ports are bound at in the
  command's namespace where a binding names none. Refused, each with why: drivers other
  than bridge, IPv6, a network without IPv4, IPAM drivers, a second subnet, auxiliary
  addresses, ingress, configuration-only and configuration-from networks, a scope but
  `local`, gateway modes but `nat` and `isolated`, `enable_ip_masquerade`,
  `inhibit_ipv4`, a bridge's name, an MTU, an interface prefix; an endpoint's hardware
  address, link-local addresses and driver options; an alias on the default network,
  which names no peers. Connect and disconnect change a joiner's
  networks for its next start (the request it was made with), and refuse one that runs,
  with why, until 3e. Inspect's `NetworkSettings.Networks` has an entry for each of its
  networks (its address, prefix, gateway and hardware address as init said them, its
  aliases, and `DNSNames`, the names its peers resolve it by, none on the default
  network), and a network's inspect lists its running members.
- **Tested on real microVMs.** `a_microvms_own_engine_makes_networks_whose_members_reach_what_each_declares`:
  two networks made, a third by a name taken refused, a `macvlan` one refused; listed
  with the engine's own, and by label; db, first on its network, declaring 7000 and
  40000, takes its own connections' ports clear of both; it is reached by its alias and by
  its name on 7000 from members of its network, its alias answered with a TTL of 0;
  stray, declaring 7000 and listening on 7001, is not reached on 7001; neither a member
  of the other network, by db's address or its name, nor the command reaches db, whose
  second connection is web2's; a network with a running member stays; a joiner that
  does not run joins one for its next start and resolves db there once started, and one
  that runs is refused; stray resolves db's alias while db runs and not once it has ended;
  a network naming 127.0.0.1 for its members' published ports binds one there, reached at
  the command's loopback and not at eth0's address; and the networks go once their
  members have, by name and by a prune. `a_microvms_own_engine_makes_each_container_a_member_of_its_switch`
  now has a member of an internal network alone reach nothing past the microVM, which a
  member of the default network then reaches. Mutation-checked: with the switch alone,
  the receiver's gate alone, or the opener's gate alone left holding a pair's ports, an
  undeclared port stays shut, and with every point opened (the opener's egress let onto
  the microVM's own subnets as well) the test catches it. Caught, each: grants
  past the networks two members share; peers' gates not built again as a member joins;
  the switch carrying no member's pairs; the resolver answering one member's question
  from another's table; grants not built again as a member goes; peers' names answered
  with the TTL the network process gives; a network's address for its members'
  published ports ignored; a member's own ports chosen before it has a peer; and, in the
  other test, the default network making peers of its members, and an internal
  network's member reaching past the microVM.
- **Found on the way.** A member first on its network had no peer as it was linked, so
  its gate then held none of the ports it declares, and its own connections took ports
  from the kernel's whole default range; once a peer joined, the gate left a declared
  port in that range untracked, and dropped the answers of the member's own connections
  that took it. The three-point check led to it: a receiver's gate made to accept every
  port left its member's own connections untracked too, which is what a declared port in
  the range its own connections take does. A gate now holds its member's declared ports
  from the start.
- **How its volumes are built (3c).** A volume a microVM's engine makes, through its API
  or as a joiner it makes names one (`-v NAME:DEST`, `--mount source=NAME`), is in the
  host's store, on disk rather than in the microVM's memory, where its writable layer
  is. The store's record says whose it is (`Of`, the microVM's ID) and what its engine
  calls it (`There`); on the host it is named after the microVM, as its joiners are
  (`PROV.NAME`, or `PROV.NAME.N` where the host has a volume of that name: a host name is
  only how it is shown). Its engine finds its own by that record alone, so a renamed
  microVM keeps them, and no name of its reaches another microVM's or the host's own. A
  joiner it makes mounts them through the microVM's join share (D119), a fresh one
  taking the image's files at its mount point and their owner as it is first mounted,
  and its anonymous ones are the microVM's too. Its engine lists, inspects, makes,
  removes and prunes them by its own names, with no path of the host's in what it says
  (`Mountpoint`, a mount's `Source`); a volume takes no driver and no driver options, the
  local driver's binding a directory of the host's (`o=bind,device=...`). One a joiner
  mounts stays; the rest go with their microVM, each as the last joiner that mounts it
  goes.
- **Tested on real microVMs.** `a_microvms_own_engine_makes_volumes_of_its_own`: a volume
  made through the API by its name, at no host path, and none with driver options; a
  joiner writes to it by `-v`, another reads it through `--mount`, a third's named
  volume made as it is named; its engine lists its own alone, by their names, and a
  joiner's mount by that name at no path; the host lists them after the microVM's
  name; the host's own `prov.secret` neither taken nor seen by the microVM's `secret`,
  which is named `prov.secret.2`; renamed, the microVM keeps them and reads what it
  wrote; another microVM's engine finds none of them, its own `data` its own; one a
  joiner mounts stays, and goes once none does; and the rest go with the microVM,
  the host's and the other microVM's staying. Mutation-checked, each caught: its engine
  listing every volume; one found by its host name alone, which a rename lost; no free
  name taken, the host's `prov.secret` refusing its `secret`; no free name and another's
  volume taken, which read the host's file; its volumes left as it went; a host path in
  a volume's document, and in a joiner's mount; driver options taken. With a free
  name taken, the store's refusal of another's volume is a second guard the test does
  not reach.
- **One in another's namespace (3c).** `--network container:X` of a joiner its
  microVM's engine made, and Compose's `network_mode: service:X`, shares X's network
  namespace as it is: a member's (its link, address, gate, grants and names), one on
  `none` (its loopback alone), or the command's where X is on `host`. The daemon names the
  namespace to init by X's exec in its provider's guest (`net=joiner=ID`, as `pid=joiner=`
  names a PID namespace), following X to the one it shares where it shares another's; init
  enters it, and X's UTS namespace, before anything of the new joiner's runs. Its
  `hostname`, `hosts` and `resolv.conf` are X's, the same files read-only, copied from X's
  mount namespace (open_tree(2)), so that a link X put there resolves in X's files alone.
  It publishes and declares no ports of its own, refused as any joiner's are at create
  (D119), for it has no link to have them on. Found on the way: before, any such joiner
  but a member's was given its provider's namespace, the command's, so one beside a
  joiner on `none`, loopback alone, reached as far as the command; and one beside a
  member was refused.
- **Tested on real microVMs.**
  `a_container_in_anothers_namespace_shares_that_ones_as_it_is`: beside one on `none`, its
  loopback alone; beside a member, that member's server on their loopback, its host name
  and its hosts file at its address; ports of its own refused. Mutation-checked, each
  caught: init entering its provider's namespace (it saw the command's eth0 beside one on
  `none`); the daemon naming no namespace of the one it joins; X's files not shared; its
  provider's UTS namespace.
- **Compose end to end (3c).** `a_compose_project_runs_in_its_microvms_own_engine`: docker
  compose's own client for Linux (v5.6.0, pinned by its release's SHA-256), unchanged,
  run by a microVM's command against that microVM's own engine: `up -d` makes the
  project's network, volume and services; `ps` lists them running; `exec` in one reaches
  the other by its service's name on the port it declares (`expose:`); a file written to
  the project's named volume is read back, the volume on the host as `PROV.shp_data`;
  and `down -v` takes the project's joiners, network and volume. What it relies on is
  mutation-checked in the tests above.
- **How 3d is built.** `shards read ports` of a joiner its microVM's engine made, a
  member of the switch, says each port it declares or listens on, where it is
  published, and who reaches it there (REACHED BY): the command where it publishes it;
  its peers on each of its networks that make peers of their members where it declares
  it; no one where its networks make no peers; and no one where it listens without
  declaring it, with what would (`EXPOSE`, `expose:`, `--expose`), so that a connection
  that would hang is seen at once instead. What it listens on init reads by a builtin
  (`LISTENS`) through its own `/proc` by the joiner's process (`/proc/PID/net/tcp`,
  `tcp6`, `udp`, `udp6`: TCP in LISTEN, UDP bound and unconnected), past the loopback,
  which nothing but itself reaches. Tested in the 3b test (stray's declared 7000 reached
  by its peers on app, its 7001 undeclared by no one, with what would declare it) and the
  3a test (one's published 7000 by the command, quiet's declared 7002 by no one, the
  default network making no peers); the socket tables' reading, IPv4 and IPv6, loopback
  and states, in init's unit tests. Mutation-checked, each caught: what it listens on
  ignored; what it declares ignored; a network of no peers taken for one; what it
  publishes ignored.
- **How 3e is built.** A joiner that runs is connected and disconnected at once, by
  init (`NETWORK connect ID NETWORK ADDR NAME...` and `disconnect ID NETWORK`, ID its exec's
  in the guest). Connect gives the member an address on the network, the one asked or the
  lowest free, routed on its one link as a member's addresses are: the switch's route to
  it through its gate, the gate's gateway on in0 and its route down to it, the member's
  address and its subnet's route through that gateway; then its reach as its networks now
  say, and every grant built again, its peers' names with them. Disconnect takes them
  back the other way round, and makes its way out of its namespace again through its next
  network where the one let go was its first (the kernel flushes an address's routes with
  it). Its last network stays, refused with why: it would be left a link with no address.
  The daemon records the address init gives, which inspect shows, and keeps the change for
  its next start. Its own hosts file stays as it started; its peers resolve its new names
  through the agents' resolver. A joiner that runs on `none`, or in another's
  namespace, gains no link as it runs, and is refused with why.
- **Tested on real microVMs.** `a_running_member_is_connected_and_disconnected_at_once`:
  a member of a, connected to b as it runs, has its address there at once in its
  namespace, is resolved by its alias and reached on its declared port by a member of b;
  disconnected, it has none, is resolved and reached by none, and is still reached on a;
  its last network is refused; off its first network, it resolves its peers through its
  next. Mutation-checked, each caught: connected with no address of its own; connected,
  or disconnected, with no grants built again; disconnected keeping its address; its last
  network taken; no way out through its next network.

### D230. A microVM's engine bytes through a ring in its guest's memory (decided; building)

The full record, its evidence and the measurements it owes:
[engine-ring-channel-decision-v1](../research/engine-ring-channel-decision-v1.md) (section
16: pins bounded by use and by the run's room, protocol version 2; its implementer's record,
kiln plan 01a1cd8e862e7169a074db3d5fa33f3d step 2's p/ring-pins-v1:
[ring-pins-v1](../research/measurements/ring-pins-v1/README.md), r1 to r16). D181's
relay moves a run's engine connection over vsock, which bounds it: 256 MiB took 244 ms
guest to host and 124 ms host to guest relayed on KVM, and vsock's best (the credit fix
with a 4 MiB window) still 84 and 86 ms, where a ring both sides share moved it in 3.8
and 25.1 ms (vsock-path-v1, r378, r429, r430). The target is 10x the relayed path's
throughput both ways, small requests no slower, on every host.

- **The ring is guest RAM.** Init's relay makes each slot from a memory file of its own,
  has the guest's kernel pin its pages long-term (an io_uring registered buffer:
  `FOLL_LONGTERM`, so compaction, offlining and khugepaged leave them), reads their
  guest-physical addresses from `/proc/self/pagemap`, and offers them in its hello. The
  host reaches them as it reaches virtqueues, through `GuestMemory`, on KVM, HVF and WHP
  alike: no window, no device, no snapshot format. Init makes the io_uring instance
  before it forks the relay and holds it for the VM's life, so a relay that dies leaves
  its slots pinned, and the device never writes a page its guest has reused.
- **Pins only for streams, freed on the device's word.** A slot is made as a stream (an
  engine connection) starts and freed as it ends or as the room asks for it while it is
  idle, never pooled: an idle microVM pins nothing. The relay frees a slot only after the
  device's `DETACH`, which it says once it has dropped its pins and will write the slot no
  more: asked (the relay's `DETACH` or `SWAP`), as the host's socket ends, and before every
  RST it sends itself. A slot with no such word (a device's reset, a restore) stays pinned
  and counted.
- **Supply is the run's room (D188); cost is the run's.** The relay joins the run's cgroup
  (`run/engine`) with its first slot, so that its slots are the run's memory, which the
  budget's hold, its give-back and its metrics read, and are counted pinned to init
  (`VmPin`). A slot is made only where the budget's hold leaves it past what the run holds
  and the room the run needs to go on (`working_room`), or with no budget where the
  guest's `MemAvailable` does; a stream it cannot fit goes over plain vsock. A told room
  short of the run's working room has idle slots let go; a give-back (`RECLAIM`) lets every
  idle slot go, counted by the next answer. A live stream is never broken: it keeps its
  ring, grown no further, until it goes idle or ends. No user knob.
- **A stream's rings are its own, learned.** A ring its producer fills whole within one
  wake of its consumer held it back: it is swapped (`SWAP`) for one twice as large, within
  the room; the next stream starts at the ring the last one needed.
- **The host end is the VM process's vsock device.** Once the engine's hello reader has
  checked the run's token, the device attaches an offered ring to the connection and moves
  its bytes between the ring's pages and the host socket the daemon already serves
  (Windows: the VM's relay onto the daemon's pipe, as before), by `readv` and `writev` as
  it moves packets now. Not the daemon: it would map memory the guest writes, where shards
  keeps guest-driven parsing in the confined VM process (D30, D31). Not a pump thread
  between the device and the daemon: one more wakeup and Unix socket hop each way, which
  the relay's own hop shows costs about 10 µs a round trip (r378, r421) and macOS's
  stream sockets 22 µs (PM M83).
- **Wakeups are vsock bytes to a side that said it waits** (a flag beside the ring, set
  with a full fence before it sleeps, swapped clear by the side that publishes: netring's
  protocol, PM M83); the device says it waits from the moment it attaches (a device that
  did not hung every first request, ring-pins-v1 r1 and ROOT's r521). A message costs the
  wakeups it costs today; a bulk transfer rings only where a side ran dry or full. No
  spinning in this decision.
- **Control bytes, then plain.** On an attached connection each side's bytes are control
  bytes (`DOORBELL`, the client's `END`, `DETACH`, `SWAP` and its offer) until that side's
  `DETACH`; after it, plain vsock. What the slot still holds each way when the device lets
  go, the relay passes on: to its client, and to the host as plain bytes.
- **vsock stays** for setup, the token, the control bytes, and the whole path wherever no
  ring is made: a host or guest of another protocol version, a guest kernel without
  io_uring's sparse buffer table (Linux 5.19) or pagemap's frame numbers, a stream the
  room cannot fit, an offer the device refuses.
- **Security.** Nothing of an offer is used before the token is checked (it names guest
  memory the host writes); a swap's offer comes only on a connection already checked.
  Every extent must be guest RAM on 4 KiB boundaries, the slot whole; positions are read
  once a turn and believed only within the ring; offsets are positions modulo the ring;
  bytes are moved by system calls on pinned pages and never parsed by the host; ring
  memory is the guest's, so no host memory grows with a guest's asks. Only the relay maps
  its slots.
- **Snapshots.** Templates hold no ring. A microVM saved whole keeps its slots and init's
  instance; its restore resets every stream (D12), whose slots stay pinned for want of a
  word, and the next streams make slots of their own.

| Literal / bound | Source or derivation |
| --- | --- |
| Ring per direction, learned per stream from `MIN_RING` to `MAX_RING` | A ring its producer fills whole within one wake of its consumer (bytes found in it as the consumer wakes from waiting on it empty, or put in it between ringing a sleeping consumer and its first take) is the stream's rate times the wake, censored at the ring: doubled, the search for an unknown bound by doubling (Bentley and Yao, 1976), a power of two for mask arithmetic. The next stream starts at the last one's need; a relay's first at `MIN_RING`. |
| `MIN_RING` 4 KiB | The least an offer names: a page of every supported guest. |
| `MAX_RING` 2 MiB | The largest power of two each turn of which one `readv`/`writev` reaches whole, its pages each apart: a turn of S bytes from any offset spans S/4096 + 1 pages, within 1,024 iovecs (Linux `UIO_MAXIOV`, macOS `IOV_MAX`): 513 for 2 MiB, 1,025 for 4 MiB. |
| Control page, 4 KiB; fields 128 bytes apart | The smallest page of every supported guest; Apple silicon's 128-byte line (hw.cachelinesize), x86's paired-line prefetch. |
| Slots in use | No count: one a stream (two while it swaps), within the room. |
| Room for pins | With a budget: init's hold (`plug::cap`) less what the run holds (`memory.current`, the slots among it) and its working room (`plug::working_room`, D188, PM M309/M321, of the CPUs online as read); with none: `MemAvailable` (free pages less the zones' high watermarks and reserves, with reclaimable cache) less the working room. Read as each slot is reserved, under the same hold of the relay's pool lock as its reservation: read and reserved apart, a slot another stream made between the two was counted by neither, and streams that started at once pinned past the room (review F3). |
| Idle slots owed a told room | The working room less the room told, where positive. |
| Fixed-buffer table | Twice the relay's `RLIMIT_NOFILE` over 3 (a stream's client, vsock and wake descriptors; two slots while it swaps), within io_uring's 16,384 (`IORING_MAX_REG_BUFFERS`). |
| Doorbell 0x01, end 0x02, detach 0x03, swap 0x04; offer header 16 bytes, extents 16 bytes, reply 8 bytes; version 2; the owner's cue to its own device after an offer, `CUE` 0x00 (host-side) | Protocol constants. |
| Offer extents at most (4 KiB + 2 S) / 4 KiB | A slot's pages, none merged. |

The pins E2E of section 16 (idle microVMs pin nothing, pins go as streams end, a give-back
and a shrinking room let idle slots go, a stream past the room goes plain; at 1, 2 and many
vCPUs with as many streams as vCPUs and twice that) and the bulk test ran green on KVM x86_64
and arm64 (L1) and HVF; on WHP x86_64 the give-back and the shrinking room, the bulk test once
in two (its microVM stopped, as one with no engine did), and the pins test was refused past
13 connections at once by the daemon's bound on Windows (D181's share of `clients_for` 64
threads, as Windows states no thread limit), not the ring's (ring-pins-v1 r13, r16). Every
supported target lints clean (r15, r16). Owed to ROOT: correctness and hostile-offer E2E; the
pins E2E on WHP arm64, and on WHP x86_64 past that bound; and throughput, small-request
latency (paced and back to back), connection setup with its slot's making, a ring's ramp, CPU
and pinned memory, on KVM x86_64 and arm64, HVF, WHP x86_64 and arm64.

**Review (plan step 2):** [ring-pins-v1/review.md](../research/measurements/ring-pins-v1/review.md) (F1 fixed, b81d707a9; F2 fixed by ROOT, a6edfb8e9; F3 cured, 6557c8597, and F4, a2c887eeb: its "Cures, F3 and F4", with the real-VM runs F4 owes; F5, a failed slot's room given back without moving `room_gen`, cured: its "Cures, F5").

**The pins E2E's waits** (goal 71's CI cluster 9, 2026-11-13; review.md "Cures, goal 71"). They
follow the person's ruling of 2026-11-13: "No record seeds. The cold start, and every wait after
a run-out, follows the party's liveness and progress. After that the bound is the slowest answer
seen. No ×2."
- *The settle*, the wait for a guest's pinned pages to come back to what it pinned idle once the
  device has let go of every ring, is D215's judge, shared, its progress a slot freed (the pins
  at a new low).
  - Its kind is a work (the setup's connections, one at a time, or the streams', V at once and
    then 2V) at a microVM's vCPU count, each kind's record its own, in the test's memory. The
    release is as large as the slots the work leaves the relay and as quick as the vCPUs that
    run the relay's streams free them, and the work and the size set both.
  - A kind not yet seen follows its microVM's liveness alone: each look an exec it answers, one
    unanswered failing the test. A kind seen is looked at once each W* and refused where no slot
    was freed since the look before. In one run each kind settles once, so each settle is a cold
    start.
  - Its looks are paced by D215's `sqrt(2 c w)` (`shards_api::pause`, shared), `c` a look's own
    time. Its progress is told on stderr as it comes, and each settle's time is reported per
    size.
  - It was refused before once a window as long as its own work had passed with no slot freed
    (a2c887eeb), a seed of no answer of its own. At dc7f45bc6 on HVF that refused 18 vCPUs, 21
    pages pinned 207 ms into their settle where their streams had taken 177 ms, after 1 and 2
    vCPUs had passed. Nothing on the ring's path changed between HVF's green batch at 9483b5a84
    and that run (init's ring.rs and engine.rs, the vsock device, the ABI's ring.rs, the test
    guest's engine_bulk.rs, engine_ring.rs and tests/common/mod.rs), and the test's binary ran
    its tests at once, as libtest does.
- *Its gap.* A slot never freed while its microVM lives is not refused on its kind's first
  settle: its looks go on, ever further apart, its last progress told, until its caller ends it.
  A learned settle's looks read the guest's pins alone, not its host's hold on its VM process,
  which shards-api's followers read privately. So a host that held the relay's vCPUs for a whole
  W* would refuse it.
- *The held connection* of the give-back and shrinking-room tests is awaited by the device's word
  that its ring attached, which the log keeps, not by its ring attached still, which a give-back
  ends. At f5c0c8b04 (CI run 43435318858, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) the daemon's give-back for
  its runner's own memory pressure let it go 31 ms after it attached, between two looks, and the
  test waited 600 s. Each test now checks that its ring was not let go before it asks for the
  slot. The shrinking-room test hears its host's pressure only through a pipe of its own, never
  said, as the give-back test does; `common::Told` is named per instance on Windows, so both live
  at once.
- Owed to ROOT, on real VMs: the four E2E tests on HVF arm64 (the pins test at 1, 2 and every CPU
  of the host), KVM x86_64 (glibc and musl jobs), KVM arm64 through L1 and WHP x86_64.

### D183. `--cgroup-parent`: a microVM's processes under a slice of the user's service manager (slices 1, 2 and 3 built)

**2026-11-13, platform-12:** a delegated leaf's cleanup now arms the existing shared
`platform::FileWatch` on `cgroup.events` before reading its state. Linux v6.18's
[`kernfs_notify_workfn`](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.18/fs/kernfs/file.c#L912)
emits FS_MODIFY for kernel-originated changes, which the watch receives as IN_MODIFY.
The watch is cleared before each read: a change before the read is in that read, one
after it remains pending. Removal is also watched on the directory. The only timed
wait is D215's next learned judge deadline; a cold record has no timer. Watch/open/wait
errors remain `io::Error` refusals. This removes the chosen 10 ms read loop without
adding a per-leaf thread or inotify instance. Direct POLLPRI was considered; the existing
FileWatch handles ordinary-file fixtures and kernel notification through one owned
interface. [Evidence and remaining real-cgroup validation](../research/measurements/platform-fixes/platform12.md).

Decided by the user on 2026-10-14 ("so long as they apply appropriately to microvms").

- **The microVM need.** A host running many microVMs needs to cap and account groups of
  them with its own resource manager: a project's agents under one memory and CPU
  budget, a CI job's microVMs under its job's slice. A microVM's guest memory, vCPU
  threads and I/O are its VM process's, and its network process's, so `--cgroup-parent`
  (`run`, `create`, the Engine API's `HostConfig.CgroupParent`) names the group those
  processes go in. Inside the microVM, its cgroups stay its own.
- **On Linux, a slice of the user's own systemd manager.** `NAME.slice` (a `-` nesting
  it, `a-b.slice` under `a.slice`, systemd.slice(5)) is a slice of the user's manager,
  asked on the user's bus (`shards-bus`: the D-Bus Specification 0.43's EXTERNAL
  authentication as the user, `StartTransientUnit`, waited for to its `JobRemoved`, which
  systemd sends the client that started the job: src/core/dbus-job.c). Rootless, with
  nothing to configure: the manager is delegated the user's cgroups (on the GPU desktop
  `user@1000.service`, `Delegate=yes`, cpu cpuset io memory pids), and where the daemon
  was started from an ssh login, in a session scope the manager may not move a process
  out of, the manager has the system's manager move it (systemd's src/core/cgroup.c,
  `unit_attach_pids_to_cgroup`), which moves only a process of the uid that asks
  (src/core/dbus-unit.c). M248 placed 300 of 300 so, from a login and from inside the
  manager's tree.
- **Born there, charged there from its first page, never moved.** A process moved
  between cgroups keeps its memory charged where it was (cgroup-v2.rst, "Memory
  Ownership"; M248: a child that touched 64 MiB first left its scope 0 KiB), and each
  move waits out an RCU grace period (kernel/cgroup/cgroup.c, `cgroup_attach_lock`; M248:
  the manager's start of a scope 6.7 ms at p50 and 18.6 at p99 past its reply, a move by
  hand 8.4 and 16.7), past the whole start budget (§4, 5 ms). So no microVM is moved: the
  daemon keeps a spawner (D158's) for each parent, placed once by the user's manager as
  the one process of a scope of its own in that slice, and every process of a microVM
  under that parent, its VM process and its network process, is made by that spawner:
  in the scope from its first instruction (a child is born in its parent's cgroup, which
  takes no grace period), charged there from its first page. The first run under a
  parent pays the one placement (M248: 10 ms at p50 from a login); every one after, none.
- **Warm under its parent too.** A warm pool (D26) is kept per template and parent, its
  microVMs made by that parent's spawner: a warm microVM taken for a run has been its
  parent's from its first page, and none of another parent's is taken.
- **Refused before anything starts, each with why**: on Linux, a value that is no slice
  name nor a path, no user manager on the user's bus for a slice, a slice the manager
  refuses (its own words), a path naming no cgroup or one not delegated to the user
  (slice 2); on macOS and Windows, a name no group shards keeps may have (slice 3).
- **Shown as given**: inspect's `HostConfig.CgroupParent`.
- **Past a container's cgroup parent.** Rootless with nothing to set up, from an ssh login
  as from a desktop session; the microVM's whole host footprint, guest memory, vCPUs and
  its network process, under the parent and charged there from its first page, warm
  starts included; a run under a parent costs nothing past the first; and every refusal
  before anything starts.
- **How slice 1 is built.** The daemon's own spawner (D158) makes a spawner for each
  parent as its first run asks (`shards_ipc::start_group`), holding nothing the daemon
  lets go of, which the user's manager places before it makes anything
  (`shards_bus::place`: a match rule for `JobRemoved`, then `StartTransientUnit` of a scope
  `shards-PID-N.scope` in the slice with it as its one process, gone once its processes
  have, `CollectMode=inactive-or-failed`, its memory counted, `MemoryAccounting=yes`, which
  systemd turns on for its slices too, waited for to its job's end); one parent's
  placement keeps no run under another waiting (`daemon/parents.rs`). Every process of a
  microVM under that parent is made by it (`spawn_in_group`), in its scope from its first
  instruction: the VM process, its network process, its share process, a stopped
  microVM's visit's, and the join share of a microVM others join, under that microVM's
  own parent. Warm pools are kept per template and parent (`PoolKey`), and a template
  collected ends its pools under every parent. A spawner found ended as a run asks for it
  (its first connection, which it never writes, readable: one `poll(2)` that waits for
  nothing) is ended and another placed: one stopped with its slice is replaced by the next
  run. Each is the daemon's for its life, and goes with it, its scope once its processes
  have. Refused before anything is made, each saying why: any parent off Linux; a value
  that is no slice's name, as systemd's own check has it (src/basic/unit-name.c); a joiner
  (D119) naming a parent other than its provider's; and from a microVM's own engine (D181),
  403, with slice 4's reason (below). Inspect's `HostConfig.CgroupParent` says it, and the Engine API takes
  `HostConfig.CgroupParent` as the command line takes the flag (D170's create bodies, a
  case of it among them).
- **Tested.** On real microVMs on Linux, where CI's x86_64 runner has its user's manager
  (lingering, `SHARDS_REQUIRE_USER_MANAGER`): `a_microvm_is_made_under_the_slice_its_cgroup_parent_names`,
  a run under a slice made in a scope of it whose processes are its VM process, its
  network process and the spawner alone; all the VM process's own memory charged to the
  slice (its `RssAnon` within the slice's `anon`); a second run under it made in the same
  scope; a run without one, its template's pool warm, outside the slice; `inspect` saying
  it; a joiner naming another slice refused, its provider's taken; and the scope gone once
  the daemon has stopped. On macOS, the same test's refusals. Unit tests: slice names as
  systemd's check has them, the check before anything starts, the Engine API's create
  bodies, a microVM engine's refusal, a group's spawner making its children apart (their
  parent its process, watched, signalled and reaped through it; ended, signalled no more)
  and a killed one found ended; shards-bus against a bus of a test's own.
  Mutation-checked on macOS, each caught: a parent served off Linux; a path taken for a
  slice; the Engine API's `CgroupParent` dropped; a microVM engine's joiner given a
  parent; a group's children made by the process's own spawner; a killed group's spawner
  never found ended.
- **Where no user's manager is.** A slice there is refused before anything is made,
  naming the bus it looked for (its `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`'s, or `/run/user/UID`'s): a start
  would fail with it otherwise. A path is slice 2's, below, and asks no manager.
- **Slice 2, built: a cgroup delegated to the user, where no user's manager is.** The
  kernel lets a process of the user place one in a cgroup only within a sub-hierarchy
  delegated to it, both of them in it (cgroup-v2.rst, "Model of Delegation", "Delegation
  Containment"): a cgroup namespace's root where the hierarchy is mounted `nsdelegate`
  (a container's own, the hosts of OpenRC, runit and s6 having no per-user delegation),
  or a directory an administrator gave the user, its `cgroup.procs`, `cgroup.threads` and
  `cgroup.subtree_control` theirs. There `--cgroup-parent PATH` names a cgroup of that
  sub-hierarchy, the daemon's own cgroup in it, and the parent's spawner is moved into a
  leaf of its own there once (a move, PM M248's cost, once per parent), its
  children born there as slice 1's are.
  - **How it is built.** A value starting `/` names a cgroup by its path from the
    hierarchy's root, as `/proc/PID/cgroup` says one (a cgroup namespace's root where the
    daemon has one), on the cgroup v2 hierarchy at `/sys/fs/cgroup`, where D188's budgets
    read it; asked of no manager, so it serves a host with one too, wherever the kernel lets
    the user. Refused before anything starts (`parents.rs`, `delegated::check`), each
    saying why: a `.` or `..` in it; no cgroup v2 hierarchy; no cgroup there (its
    `cgroup.procs`); a directory the daemon may make no cgroup in (access(2) `W_OK|X_OK`,
    mkdir(2)'s); and a cgroup the daemon may move none of its processes into, the
    `cgroup.procs` of the nearest cgroup both are within not the user's to write
    (cgroup-v2.rst, "Delegation Containment"). The parent's spawner (slice 1's,
    `shards_ipc::start_group`) is moved, before it makes anything, into a leaf the daemon
    makes in the cgroup, `shards-PID-N`, by a write of its PID to the leaf's
    `cgroup.procs`; a refusal there ends it, removes the leaf and says what the kernel
    said. A leaf, which no manager collects, is removed by its daemon as it exits, its
    spawners ended and reaped, once its `cgroup.events` says `populated 0`, waiting
    at most 10 s for the warm VMs it told to end; one left (a daemon killed, or processes
    that ran on) is removed by the next daemon placing a spawner in the same cgroup, which
    removes each `shards-PID-N` whose daemon PID no process has (kill(2) `ESRCH`; rmdir(2)
    refuses one still holding processes). Warm pools, joiners, budgets (D188 watches the
    leaf as it watches a slice's scope) and `inspect` are slice 1's.
  - **Tested** on real microVMs on Fedora 44 (kernel 6.19, x86_64), with no bus of a
    manager's: `a_microvm_is_made_in_the_delegated_cgroup_its_cgroup_parent_names`. The
    delegation an administrator would give stands in as a scope of the user's manager's
    with `Delegate=yes`, laid out as a delegated tree is, the daemon in a leaf of its own and
    the parent beside it with the memory controller (cgroup-v2.rst, "No Internal Process
    Constraint"), the daemon started there with `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` a directory with no bus
    in it; a holder process keeps the scope, so that the daemon, not the manager, removes
    the leaf. The test makes the scope's leaves itself, and no process but its shell is ever
    in the scope's own cgroup: a child waited for holds its cgroup populated until its last
    context switch (Linux 6.19, d245698d727a), and a populated cgroup takes no controller
    (EBUSY: CI's ubuntu-24.04, kernel 7.0, run 41959673660).
    A run under the parent made in a leaf whose processes are its VM process, its network
    process and the spawner alone; the VM process's own memory charged to the parent from
    its first page; a second run in the same leaf; a run without one in the daemon's own
    cgroup; `inspect` saying it; a path with no cgroup, and `/`, not delegated, refused;
    and the leaf gone once the daemon has stopped, the parent kept. Unit tests: the
    refusals, the nearest common cgroup, and the sweep of leaves of daemons gone.
    Mutation-checked on that host, each caught: the spawner never moved into its leaf
    (the VM process made in the daemon's own cgroup); the leaves never removed as the
    daemon exits (the leaf outlived it).
- **Slice 3, built on macOS and Windows: groups shards keeps, where its host has none a
  user's tools cap.**
  macOS has no group of processes a user may make and cap (its jetsam bands and
  coalitions are the system's own), and Windows' job objects are made by programs, none
  named by a tool of its user's. There `--cgroup-parent NAME` names a group shards keeps,
  a directory of the home, `groups/NAME`, made with the first run under it: its name a
  file's of letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_` alone (daemon/groups.rs); its budgets
  files in cgroup v2's own formats, as a Linux user writes a cgroup's (cgroup-v2.rst):
  `memory.high` and `memory.max`, bytes with the kernel's binary suffixes or `max`
  (mm/page_counter.c `page_counter_memparse`), and `cpu.max`, a quota and its period in
  microseconds, the period 100000 where left out, each at least 1 ms, the period at most
  1 s (kernel/sched/core.c `cpu_period_quota_parse`, `tg_set_cfs_bandwidth`). Each starts
  `max`. The daemon watches the files and holds the group's microVMs to them as they
  change:
  - **macOS** (built): what the group holds is its microVMs' VM processes' footprints
    (proc_pid_rusage's `ri_phys_footprint`), summed every pressure window while it has
    microVMs, its files read again then, so that a budget written is heard within one.
    Each microVM is told the room under the least of its budgets as D188 tells a slice's
    (init's `ROOM`), and where the group is short each gives back what it holds cold,
    then unplugs. Past `memory.max` with a pass that gave nothing back, the microVM of
    the group that holds the most is stopped, its record marked OOM-killed, as a
    cgroup's OOM killer takes its largest. Tested on real microVMs
    (`a_microvm_under_a_group_is_held_to_its_budget`, M355): 1,254 MiB held under a
    `memory.high` of 998 MiB, given back to 281; past a `memory.max` of 793 MiB, the
    microVM that held 679 MiB of 960 stopped, 137 and OOM-killed, the other running on.
    Mutation-checked: no give-back; no stop. A microVM that may swap (D159: as much again
    as its memory by default) is held within its room by its guest, whose kernel swaps
    what passes its run's `memory.high` to its swap window, a file of the host's, whose
    pages are no part of a footprint (XNU's `phys_footprint` counts anonymous memory and
    what the compressor holds of it at full size, osfmk/kern/task.c and arm64's pmap.c,
    xnu f6217f891ac0): its group stays within `memory.max`, and it runs on, as a cgroup's
    process swaps rather than meet its OOM killer. M355's second microVM had swap, and was
    stopped only as it held 679 MiB where its group left it at most 512: init holds a run
    at what it uses as its room is told and that room (`hold_within`), so its first room
    came after it had grown. At dc7f45bc6 (HVF, 2026-11-13) the same microVM, `-m 1g` and
    so 1 GiB of swap, held its 768 MiB and slept, the daemon never said its group past its
