    budget again, and no stop came. The test's second microVM has no swap
    (`--memory-swap` its memory): its guest's `memory.high` slows it and refuses it nothing
    (cgroup-v2.rst), so it passes `memory.max` whether its room comes before its growth or
    after, as nothing it holds can go to swap.
  - **Each microVM's words its own** (built, macOS and Windows). The groups' thread told
    each member its room and asked each to give back one after another, each waited for
    while its VM process lived (`Wait::WhileRuns`): a member whose guest never answered a
    room told before any room was answered, which a wait follows while its VM process
    lives, held every other member's words and every group's stop for as long as its VM
    process lived: `a_member_that_never_answers_holds_up_no_other_member_or_group`, red at
    1e391c093 (adas-mac-studio.local, macOS 26.2 arm64: group two's member never stopped
    in 20 s), plays it.
    Now each member's word, its room told and then, for a round, what it holds cold asked
    back, goes on a thread of its own, one word at a time, judged as D215's judge judges a
    wait, its give-back waiting out one of its host's pressure under way as a budget's does
    (reclaim.rs `give_after`); an ask made meanwhile waits behind it, its newest room and
    any give-back kept. The groups' thread asks at its passes, hears each answer as it
    comes (its condvar), and waits on none. A group found short with no round under way
    begins one, each member asked once; it is judged once each has answered, ended, or
    its own exec judge has refused its word. A word publishes that typed refusal before
    it waits for its exec's kill acknowledgement (`Wait::GroupWord`, `WordState::Refused`),
    so a stalled guest that never acknowledges cannot hold the verdict. The group consumes
    that outcome, never elapsed wall time: `Record::stalled(word.since, now)` was a second
    timer that OOM-killed a progressing or host-held member, or one still waiting behind
    host-pressure reclaim (review waits-01). Before the kind's first answer, liveness
    alone still governs; another member teaching the record does not bound a wait begun
    cold. The parallel-group fixture therefore starts its stuck word learned. A refusal
    stands while the exec its judge refused does: each exec of a word (its room told, then
    its give-back) begins `Waiting`, so a refused room is no verdict on the give-back that
    follows it, which its own judge judges, nor on a round opened while that give-back runs
    (red `daemon::tests::a_refused_room_is_not_the_next_rounds_verdict`: round 2 counted a
    member whose give-back was under way as one that gave nothing and OOM-killed it). A
    refusal of an exec of a round's word is that round's answer too, nothing given, queued
    with every answer (`Answered`, `refuse_word`): as a state alone, reset as the word's
    next exec began, a round whose groups' thread looked only after its give-back began
    lost it and waited on that give-back. A round its answers finished is judged before the
    pass that follows, so that pass opens the next where its group is still short. A round
    asks the members it began with: one joining while it runs is told its room at each
    pass, and asked to give back by the round after. The test had its second member's join
    open round 2, true while passes waited out a 2 s pressure window; on D215's pace
    (2275e3829) the pass after round 1's verdict comes first and opens round 2 with the
    first member alone, so the second was told its room twice, `16 != 15` (`ROOM` where
    `RECLAIM` was due; CI run 43876891053 at 1b8d1cddd, macOS and three Windows jobs, and
    adas-mac-studio.local-2 at 4999d113a, after the queued refusal, 3 of 3). A thread now
    plays the second's guest whichever round asks it, and the first's give-back brings its
    group within its max, so the round after, ended by the first's unanswered room, stops
    nothing. An answer or refusal wakes the existing groups condvar. No new bound, reader
    or cache.
    A round is judged with the members its group had as its last answer came (flake-harden,
    2026-11-16). The groups' thread kept joins, ends and answers in three lists, and took a
    wake's joins in before its answers, so a round whose last answer came before a member
    joined was judged with that member whenever the thread looked late, as a loaded host
    holds it: in `a_refused_room_is_not_the_next_rounds_verdict`, round 1 (the first member
    alone, its room refused) judged with the second's 500 MiB, past the max of 1000, and the
    first OOM-killed. That test failed 1 of 24 at 6f5755ae1 under load (lane shards-green),
    0 of 48 after, its output not kept: the cause read from the code, its reproduction
    owed (R09). Now what the thread hears is one list in the order it came (`Heard`), and a
    round an end or an answer finishes is judged as that is taken, before any join after it.
    Guard: `a_round_is_judged_with_the_members_its_group_had_as_its_last_answer_came` holds
    the thread in a pass (`Groups::hold_passes`) while the first's room is refused and the
    second joins (red with joins taken first, where the held pass began before the refusal,
    as it does unless the host delays it 20 ms). Both tests print, as they fail, what the
    thread and its members' words heard and did, in order (`Groups::trace`, tests alone),
    on the test process's stderr. Not changed: a refusal stands while its exec does, so a
    round opened before a refused exec's kill is answered is judged by it (`judge_round`);
    no test has shown that wrong.
    Past `memory.max` with nothing given back its largest is stopped. A group whose
    budget goes tells each member it told a room that it has none, its hold let go of.
    [Red/green and owed real-VM validation](../research/measurements/waits-fixes-v1/README.md).
  - **A member's room as of the footprint it was read with** (built, macOS and Windows).
    The groups' thread read what each member's VM process held, then told each its room,
    and init held its run at what it used as the word came plus that room: a member that
    grew between the read and the word had that growth counted twice, its group past
    `memory.max` or not as the two came in one order or the other
    (`a_members_room_holds_as_of_the_footprint_it_was_read_with`, red at 1dc8eeff8: a member
    of 400 MiB beside 300 under 1000, grown to 600 before its word came, held to 900). Now
    its room goes with the footprint its VM process held as it was read (`ROOM`'s second
    word), and init holds it as of what that process holds now, read from its VMM
    (`control::FOOTPRINT`: the VM process's own footprint as the daemon reads one,
    proc_pid_rusage's on macOS, its private working set on Windows) just before its hold
    reads what the run uses: `run::room_now`, the room less what it came to hold since, all
    of it read values. So it grows into its room once, whichever comes first. Where its VMM
    cannot say its footprint, init holds the room as told and says so (`ROOM_UNREAD`),
    which the daemon logs. A one-word `ROOM`, a budget's (D188), holds as it did.
  - **Each VM process once** (built, macOS and Windows). A joiner runs in its provider's VM
    process (D119), and the group summed its footprint by run: a joiner in its provider's
    group counted that process twice in `memory.current` and listed it twice in
    `cgroup.procs` (`a_joiner_and_its_provider_in_one_group_count_their_vm_process_once`,
    red at 9d7e74bc0: 1300 MiB where 700 were held). A member now keeps its VM process's
    identity, its pid and when it started (`shards_ipc::started`, read as its run joins),
    and the group reads each identity once: its `memory.current`, its `cgroup.procs` on
    macOS, each member's room as of its process's footprint, and its verdict's largest. A
    member whose pid now names a process that started at another time holds nothing of it.
  - **Windows** (built): every process of a microVM under NAME is made in a job object of
    NAME's, nested above the VM process's own (PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST, the
    group's first; Job Objects, "Nested Jobs", Windows 8 on), its warm VMs too: a VM
    process in a job of its own may join a group's job only while that holds nothing (the
    second was refused, M359), so a group's warm VMs are made in its job from their start,
    its pool its own. `memory.max` is the job's memory limit (JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_JOB_MEMORY,
    which refuses its processes' commits past it: 512 MiB alone, and 160 MiB beside
    another's 160, under 256, M359), set again as the file changes; `memory.high` the room
    its microVMs are told, as on macOS, whose give-backs on Windows are the platform parity
    plan's step 7. `memory.high` alone (`Budget::room_of`): told a room under `memory.max`
    too, a run past it was held at that room by its guest's own `memory.high`, which slows
    and ends nothing, and the daemon's stop past `memory.max` never came, its VM processes'
    private working sets within what the job lets them commit; the test's run of 2 GiB
    under 1 GiB ended 69 s after its workload began (CI 42046987905, windows-2022). Tested on real microVMs on CI's windows-2022 and windows-2025
    (`a_groups_job_holds_its_microvms_to_its_memory_max`, budget-e2e run 40624202863):
    under a `memory.max` of 1 GiB, a run that allocates 2 GiB never holds it, where one
    that allocates 2 GiB under no group, and one that allocates 128 MiB under it, run to
    their ends. `cpu.max` is not the job's CPU rate (below). The microVM's network process
    is made in the group's job too, its own AppContainer's job nested under it
    (`netproc::start`), so that the group holds the microVM's whole host footprint, as a
    slice's scope does on Linux (slice 1): before, its VM process alone was. The group's
    `cgroup.procs` lists the job's processes, a line each, as a cgroup's lists its own,
    written by the daemon from the job (JobObjectBasicProcessIdList, `GroupJob::processes`)
    each pressure window while the group has a microVM; on macOS, which has no group of
    processes, it lists the group's microVMs' VM processes, whose footprints it holds.
    Tested on Windows by `a_groups_microvm_is_made_in_its_job_its_network_process_too`: a
    run under a group, its `cgroup.procs` its VM process and its network process alone
    (`shards-vm.exe`, `shards-net.exe`, as tasklist names them), and a run under no group's
    VM process not in it.
  - **CPU, on both** (built): a group's microVMs hold themselves to its `cpu.max`
    together, as CFS bandwidth control holds a cgroup's threads
    (Documentation/scheduler/sched-bwc.rst), where macOS has no mechanism to cap a group
    of processes and Windows' job CPU rate holds no second: under a hard cap of one CPU,
    a 30 s spin's mean was 1.04 CPUs, and single seconds ran up to 1.88 (windows-2025)
    and 2.19 (windows-2022) (M361). The group's count is a file of its directory,
    `.cpu-budget`, the daemon's, mapped shared by the daemon, which writes the budget as
    the file says it (within a pressure window of a change), and by each of the group's
    VM processes, handed it with its run (`RunHead::group`, after its swap); a joiner's
    CPU is its microVM's. What it counts is the group's theoretical arrival time, the
    generic cell rate algorithm's (ITU-T I.371): each VM process's second governor
    (`vm::hold`, beside D191's own) reads its vCPU threads' CPU time as D191's does and
    charges it, at the budget's rate, to that one word by compare-and-swap, on the host's
    monotonic clock, one in every process (POSIX CLOCK_MONOTONIC; QueryPerformanceCounter,
    "consistent ... even when measured on different threads or processes", Microsoft
    Learn); while the group runs more than a period ahead of its rate, every microVM of
    it holds its vCPUs out of its guest, by D191's kick, until it is within it. Over any
    stretch the group uses at most its rate and a period's quota more, as a cgroup's
    periodic quota allows, and over a long one its rate: nothing of a period wraps, and no
    process waits on another. A budget of every CPU of the host's, or past what the word
    holds (a host of more than 4,295 CPUs), holds nothing. Tested: `vm::group`'s own
    (charges add up across mappings and threads, idle time no credit past a period),
    `vm::hold`'s `machines_of_a_group_are_held_to_its_budget_together` (two machines of
    two threads each under one CPU: 1.13 to 1.15 s of CPU in 1.14 to 1.15 s, three runs;
    with the hold off, 4.52 s in 1.13) and `a_group_whose_budget_goes_holds_nothing`; the
    groups' `cpu_budgets_read_as_the_kernel_reads_them`; and on real microVMs
    `a_groups_microvms_are_held_to_its_cpu_max_together` (two microVMs of a group of one
    CPU, four threads burning in each: on macOS 3.21 s of CPU in 3.02 s, with `max`
    23.9 s; on jupiter's WHP 3.08 s in 3.08 s, with `max` 23.97 s in 3.04; mutation-checked,
    the VM ignoring its group's budget, 23.85 s in 3.02 s, which fails it). Each second's
    hold, M370: under one CPU, p99 1.07 CPUs a second on macOS and 1.12 on Windows.
  - Shown as given (inspect's `HostConfig.CgroupParent`); the group's `memory.current`
    file the daemon writes as it sums it, as a cgroup's says what it holds.
- **Slices.** 1: Linux, a slice of the user's manager (built). 2: a delegated cgroup
  where no user's manager is (built, above). 3: macOS and Windows, groups shards keeps
  (built, above). 4: the microVM's own engine's members (D181), a cgroup within the
  microVM: refused (403), each part of the need already met, and what is left of it no
  one in the microVM could use (checked 2026-11-07):
  - What a parent is for is a budget its members share, set by whoever owns the
    parent: on a host, its administrator writes the slice's or cgroup's files, and the
    run names it alone (`HostConfig.CgroupParent` is a path, with no budget of its own).
  - Every member of a microVM's engine is a joiner of that microVM (D119), so its
    members already share one budget, the microVM's own, under the host parent it was
    run under (slices 1 to 3), and each member takes its own limits as any joiner does.
  - A parent within the microVM, for a group of its members apart from the others, would
    be a cgroup no process in the microVM may budget. The workload, the engine's only
    client, is in a cgroup namespace rooted at its own cgroup, mounted `nsdelegate`, and
    may write no cgroup outside it (cgroup-v2.rst, "Delegation Containment"); and a
    parent under the workload's own cgroup could enable no controller for its members
    while the workload's processes are there ("No Internal Process Constraint"). Init
    alone could write its files, and no input names what to write.
  - A group of agents with a budget of their own is a microVM of their own, under a
    host parent of their own. So slice 4 stays refused, with that reason, unless an
    input that carries a member group's budget is found.

### D184. A credential helper is asked at once and waited for only where its registry asks (built)

**Found.** `shards pull image alpine:3.22` with a user's own Docker config (2026-10-17) waited
12 minutes and more on `docker-credential-desktop get`, Docker Desktop's backend not
answering: sampled, the daemon's thread read the helper's output (credentials.rs
`run_helper`). The client's Ctrl-C ended the client alone: the lookup took no cancel, so
the daemon's thread and the helper stayed. The lookup ran before the registry was asked
anything, so the pull waited on the helper whether or not the registry wanted
credentials, and said nothing of it. A docker client asks its helper before it sends a
pull too: the Engine API takes a pull's credentials in its request (`X-Registry-Auth`).

**The microVM need.** A pull is how a microVM gets its root, and a run that pulls is a
start: what an external holds of it must be only what it has to hold, isolated, said,
and ended with the pull.

**Decided.**
- A helper is started as the pull's registry is made (`credentials::find`): its key
  written and its input closed at once (a registry's key is far under a pipe's buffer, so
  the write never waits), and never waited for there. It runs while the registry's first
  round trip does: a pull that needs its answer waits for the longer of the two, not for
  both in turn.
- Its answer is read the first time the registry's own host challenges (`auth.rs`
  `Authorizer::credentials`, Basic or Bearer), never for another host's challenge, and
  never where the registry asks nothing: a registry that takes anonymous pulls is not
  held by a helper that never answers. It is read before the authorizer's lock of its
  hosts, so that no request to another host waits behind it; requests challenged
  meanwhile wait for the same answer (one read).
- Where the pull waits on it, it says so, once, as the wait begins: on a terminal a line
  of the pull's own, piped a line on stderr (`Waiting for docker-credential-desktop to
  answer for https://index.docker.io/v1/ (credsStore in ~/.docker/config.json)`), the
  helper, the key it was asked and where it was named, so that the user can answer it,
  mend it, or end the pull.
- No anonymous fallback and no deadline: a late answer is not a stuck one. osxkeychain
  asks the user to allow it, pass's gpg-agent asks for a passphrase, secretservice for a
  keyring's unlock, ecr-login goes to AWS. An anonymous pull in its place would race a
  user typing a password, and spend Docker Hub's anonymous allowance where the user is
  logged in: Docker Hub counts an unauthenticated pull against its IPv4 address or IPv6
  /64, 100 in 6 hours, and an authenticated one against the account, 200 for a personal
  one and no limit for a paid one (docs.docker.com/docker-hub/usage/pulls, read
  2026-10-18). The
  credentials the user configured are the ones used, whenever the registry asks.
- A cancel of the pull (its client gone or interrupted, the daemon stopping) ends the
  helper at once: started for a pull, it leads a process group of its own (a script's
  children with it, which hold its output open), which the cancel kills (`http::Cancel`,
  `watch_helper`); the read of its answer then ends, and the pull ends cancelled. A helper
  whose answer is never read is ended and reaped as its pull ends. None is left, process
  or thread.
- A registry token in the file wins over a helper's answer (dockerd's precedence), so
  with one the helper is not asked at all. A helper that cannot be started (not on
  `PATH`) fails only the pulls that need its answer.
- A build's base pulls, resolutions and cache imports say the wait among the build's
  plain lines, on stderr as they come (build/mod.rs `saying_waits`); the live display keeps
  its own frame, the step shown waiting.
- The eager callers (`shards login`'s check, a context's client sending credentials,
  `shards search`) read the answer at once, as before (`lookup` = `find` and `answer`),
  their helper in their terminal's process group, where a Ctrl-C reaches it.

**Tested.** `crates/registry`: a helper asked is ended and reaped as it drops unread; a
cancel ends a wait for one, its script's own child too; one that answers is read as its
registry challenges, a password and an identity token; another host's challenge waits on
none; a registry token asks none. `tests/login.rs`
`a_credential_helper_that_never_answers_holds_only_what_needs_its_answer`: with a helper
that never answers configured, a pull from a registry that asks for nothing completes
and leaves no helper; from one that asks for Basic credentials, the client says what it
waits on, and killing the client ends the helper. Mutation-checked, each caught: the
answer read as the helper is found; a helper dropped unread left running; a cancel that
ends no helper; one that ends the helper alone and not its group (its script's child
holds its output open); the answer waited for under the hosts' lock; a wait never said.

### D185. The client and its daemon meet through files in the home (built)

**Control-08 follow-up (2026-11-13), owed to ROOT.** The inherited `UNWATCHED`
250 ms fallback in log lanes remains picked and violates R03; it is not validated by
its reuse. Proposed design: notify the authoritative writer's append, rotation and
terminal transitions over a shared per-run notification source, subscribing before
checking the current segment to avoid a lost wakeup. Member append already crosses
the host keeper; command append in the VM needs a compatible host notification. Cold
start must establish that source or return typed watch-unavailable, rather than choose
a first polling period. Cancellation and source end must wake the same wait. No new
protocol or timing behavior is implemented here; [required fault scenario and proof](../research/measurements/control-fixes-v1/README.md).

**Control-08, built (2026-11-14).** Log lanes no longer read on a clock (D238, "The daemon's
log host"): a followed lane's watch is made before it says `Started`, as its wake latch is,
and a lane no watch can be had for is refused `Unstarted::Failed`, its cause in the daemon's
log and its run's end waiter forgotten. Alternatives weighed: (a) a learned interval, for
which nothing in the lane gives a cost to trade latency against (its records' times give the
writer's cadence, not what a reader's late look costs); (b) the producer notification above,
which needs a host notification from the VM process for a command's log, a wire change not
needed while the watch itself is the notification; (c) the refusal, taken: a watch needs what
the latch needs (a descriptor; two on macOS, kqueue(2) and its directory's) and on Linux a
watch of the process's one inotify instance (`max_user_watches`, inotify(7)), or an instance
where the process could not make that one (`max_user_instances`), so a lane refused it is one
the host is out of resources for, which its controller may ask again. The other `UNWATCHED`
users (the listener, `logs -f`, a process's events, a log driver's copier) refuse as well
since runs-11 (below).

**Why.** shards is filesystem based (the user, repeatedly; 2026-10-18: `daemon.sock` was an
error). Its own interfaces are files in the home; a socket stays only where an outside
client's protocol demands one: the Engine API's `engine.sock` (D170), a context's
`e/ID.sock` (D180). The CLI's channel to its daemon, `daemon.sock`, is shards' own, and
goes.

**What crosses today.** A request (a run, an exec, an attach, a command of the catalog's:
`ps`, `inspect`, `rm`...), the client's stdin, stdout and stderr as descriptors
(`SCM_RIGHTS`), the streams of `save`, `export`, `import`, `load` and `cp`, answers (`OUT`,
`ERR`, `END`, progress), and, for a run, the client's connection itself, which the daemon
hands to the run's VM, which then sends `EXIT` and reads `RESIZE` and `SIGNAL`; a microVM
given a host's devices sends its process's pidfd with `EXIT` (D154). Files carry no
descriptors.

**Measured.**
- How each end of a FIFO learns the other has gone (PM M253): a blocking read(2) sees its
  writer's end at once on macOS and Linux, in every one of 5,000 trials each; on macOS
  poll(2) and kqueue(2) never do, and a writer learns of its reader's end only as it next
  writes (`EPIPE`). But on macOS a read that has just taken its writer's last data can
  sleep through the end that follows at once: 6 in 224,000, where select(2) saw all of
  192,000. So each side holds the read end of a FIFO the other writes, and waits on it in
  select(2) on macOS, in a read on Linux, never in poll or kqueue: but for the many clients
  of one list (M262, below).
- What a request costs (PM M254), against the socket's 23 to 30 µs at p50: a directory
  made for each request, 413 to 562 µs on macOS (APFS's metadata operations, with tails to
  21 ms under load) and 55 µs on Linux; a slot the daemon made ahead, which the client takes
  and opens, 83 to 112 µs on macOS (each open by path 10 to 28 µs) and 34 µs on Linux. A
  FIFO's round trip itself costs no more than the socket's. macOS refuses flock(2) on a
  FIFO.

**Decided.**
- **Slots, made ahead.** The daemon keeps requests' slots in `$SHARDS_HOME/requests/`,
  0700: each FIFOs named by its number, `N.say` and `N.answer`, and for a command with
  streams `N.in`, `N.out` and `N.err` too, made before any client asks, the daemon holding
  its own ends of each: `say`'s reader and a writer of its own until a client has written,
  `answer`'s writer. A slot is used once, then removed, and its number never again: no
  client can meet another's leavings in a FIFO.
- **Handed out by a FIFO.** The daemon writes each free slot's number to `requests/free`,
  or to `requests/free-streams` for a slot with streams, a record of fixed length, far
  under `PIPE_BUF`, so written whole; a client takes a slot by reading one record, which
  no other client can then read. No lock file, and no search: the client opens the list it
  needs, reads, opens its slot's `answer` to read and `say` to write, and writes its
  request. Where every slot is taken, the client's read waits until the daemon has made
  more. A slot a client took and never wrote to is removed
  after a minute, its wait ended through a pipe of its own, never a byte on its `say`,
  where a client may be writing; a client that finds its slot gone reads another.
- **Liveness, each way.** The daemon reads `say` (waiting in select(2) on macOS, then
  reading); once a client has
  written, the daemon drops its own writer, so the client's end, its exit or its kill, ends
  the read. The client reads `answer`; the daemon's end, or that of the VM it handed it to,
  ends the client's read. No timer, no process ID.
- **No daemon.** `free` with no writer reads its end at once: the client starts the daemon,
  as it does today where nothing listens, and waits for its first slot. One daemon a home:
  it takes `daemon.lock` with flock(2), exclusively, as it starts.
- **Streams.** A run's, an exec's and an attach's stdio, and `save`'s, `export`'s,
  `import`'s, `load`'s and `cp`'s streams go through the slot's `in`, `out` and `err`: the
  daemon gives the VM its ends, as it gave the client's descriptors, and the client copies
  between them and its own stdio. A microVM with a host's devices sends its process's ID
  with `EXIT`, and the client waits for that process's end itself (pidfd_open(2), as the
  same user).
- **Messages** are today's frames without descriptors, each FIFO of one writer at a time:
  the daemon's, until it hands `answer` to a run's VM.

**Built.**
- `shards_ipc::slots`: the slots, made, handed out, taken, read and written, each end seen.
  A slot is taken at its client's first byte, which says which streams it opened; the rest
  of its request says what each descriptor it stands for is (`slots::fds`), then the
  request itself.
- The daemon serves its clients through slots alone (`daemon/slots.rs`), each session
  bridged to its handling of a client: a connection of its own, taken as a socket's client
  was, the request's descriptors the slot's streams. The client's messages go on to the daemon, or
  to the run's VM it hands the connection to, and theirs come back, each side's end the
  other's. A device run's EXIT waits for its VM process's pidfd. So what serves a socket's
  client serves a slot's unchanged, the VM included.
- Two slots of each kind are kept offered, without streams and with (M255: making and
  removing a slot is 125 µs of the daemon's CPU on a loaded Mac, 317 with its streams, so
  none is made ahead that no client asked for; a hundred clients at once, each adding one,
  left the daemon making a hundred spares in a quiet 3 s). A client counts among those in
  hand from its first byte: past the daemon's most (`max_clients`), its slot is replaced
  at once but its request waits its turn, and no slot is offered, so that further clients
  wait on their list and cost the daemon nothing. A closing daemon unlinks its lists at
  once, so that a client looking for a slot asks the next daemon, and answers RESTART to a
  client that took a slot meanwhile; a client asks again after each RESTART that is another
  daemon's than the one whose RESTART it last asked again after (*A request asked again*,
  below).
- The client asks through a slot for every command: the catalog's, its streams (`save`,
  `export`, `import`, `load`, `cp`) copied by the client to and from the slot's (`cli::Stream`:
  what the daemon writes, what it reads); a run's, an exec's and an attach's, its stdin
  filled into `in`, and `out` and `err` shown as they come, unbuffered, all of them before
  it ends; a detached run's none. Its signals and resizes go on its slot's `say` beside its
  request (`slots::Sender`, each message written whole). A daemon of a build from before
  slots (v0.5.0's), which offers none, is never asked: see *No `daemon.sock`*.
- On macOS every read of a FIFO waits first in select(2) (M253 part 3): the slots', the
  client's copies, and `shards_ipc::read` of a FIFO, a run's stdin in its VM among them;
  all but a client's wait on its list for a slot (M262, below).

- **No `daemon.sock`** (slice 4). The daemon makes its lists as soon as it holds the
  home's lock, so that a client that finds them waits on them for its slot rather than
  start a second daemon. A home is served while
  its list `free` has a reader, the daemon's own (`slots::served`): a starting daemon
  waiting for the lock (`take_lock`) and a context's look at its machine ask that.
  *No path to a pre-slots daemon* (legacy-audit, 2026-11-14; runs-11 found it): the client
  asked a daemon of a build from before slots (v0.5.0, the last release with
  `daemon.sock`) on that socket, its run's, command's and stop's requests sent there, so
  that it stepped aside, and `take_lock` took its socket's answer for a served home. All of
  it is gone (`Asked::Socket`, `Says::Socket`, `stop_socket`, `shards_ipc::SOCKET`, the
  run client's socket-peer reading of an end): a client and its daemon are one build
  (D36), and a daemon of another build is stopped through its slots by the rule above,
  which a pre-slots one cannot hear. Where one still serves a home (its socket takes a
  connection, closed unasked), the client's ask and stop and a starting daemon's
  `take_lock` refuse, typed (`shards_ipc::PreSlotsDaemon`, `no_pre_slots_daemon`),
  saying to end that daemon's process, rather than wait on a holder that offers no slot. Unix
  only: no daemon ran on Windows before slots. The Engine API's `engine.sock` (D170),
  Docker's clients' socket, is not this and stays. Tests: the client's
  `a_runs_signals_go_on_its_connection_from_its_request` now on a real slot's sender;
  E2E stand-ins for a daemon that never answers (`an_interrupted_save_leaves_nothing_behind`,
  `a_client_waiting_for_its_daemon_ends_on_sigterm`) hold the home's lock on every OS, as
  Windows' did, where Unix's listened at `daemon.sock` (owed to ROOT: both E2E).
  `daemon stop` asks through a slot and waits for
  the daemon to let go of its home (*A stop's wait*, below); the
  requests a daemon puts to itself for a context's steps go through slots of its own home
  (`cli::ask_here`), which start no daemon. The default context's endpoint is the Engine
  API's socket, which Docker's clients take.
- **Lists made again.** Lists someone removes as the daemon serves are made again, the
  slots' numbers going on from the last, and what was offered on the old ones let go of:
  the waits of those no client took, read back from their lists, end through their own
  pipes. The maker looks as it is told to, never on a timer: by the listener, as a name of
  the home comes or goes (a removal of the home takes `requests/`), and, for lists removed
  by hand inside it, by the daemon the next client starts, which, finding the home's lock
  held and nothing offered, makes and removes a name in the home (`daemon.waiting`) once.
  Under `socket_at`, which `close` holds as it unoffers them, so that a daemon told to stop
  never offers again (PM M188, of the socket it replaces).
- **An idle daemon wakes for nothing.** The maker offers what its lists hold no client's
  of (their records counted where they wait, FIONREAD), so that a client dead after it
  took a slot holds no place; and sweeps only while a slot is taken with no request
  read: a minute after it is first seen so, and again a minute after, when a slot still
  unwritten goes. With none, it sleeps until it hears something (PM M260).
- **A request in time.** The rest of a request is waited for while its client goes on with
  it: one that sends nothing past its first byte for as long as the slowest rest the daemon
  has seen whole that waited on its client is cut, and one whose rest has begun is read until it is whole or its
  client ends ("Admission", below); no longer, either way, once the daemon ends its clients
  (`requests_end`, a pipe written once). A client cut hears RESTART, as one whose request
  no thread had read does, and asks again. (Was 10 s, `REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, after which the
  slot ended unanswered; then D222's restart cutoff, doubled for each cut in a row.)
- **Out of descriptors**, the maker offers nothing, says so once, and offers again as it is
  told descriptors were let go of (`Event::Room`, from `wake_listener`); no collection
  starts meanwhile, and clients wait on their lists. A slot taken whose serving finds no
  descriptor (its bridge's socket pair) tells its client RESTART on the slot's own FIFO.
  (Was a look every 250 ms, `RETRY`; "Admission", below.) A slot is about 7 descriptors,
  13 with streams, its FIFOs' ends and its stop pipe: four offered hold 40. At its most
  clients in hand it says so too, once a minute at most.
- **A request of any size.** The bridge starts the daemon's handling of its connection
  before it writes the request there: written first, a request past the socket pair's
  buffer (a run's labels; 8 KiB on macOS, 208 KiB on Linux) waited for ever for a reader
  that came only after (x86_64 CI's journald test, a request of 540 KB). Found on Linux CI,
  with the cap test's race: its silent clients now wait to be counted, which the daemon's
  log says, before the next asks.
- **Stdin after a restart.** A run's, an exec's and an attach's client fills its command's
  stdin only once its daemon has said the request is its own (`HEARD`, after the build's
  check): what went to the slot of a daemon that then asked for a restart went with it, and
  a piped stdin was lost, the next daemon's command waiting for ever. A client of an older
  build ignores the message.
- **What it said last** (PM M261). A daemon exits only once no slot holds it
  (`Daemon::live`, `slots_hold`): each slot is counted from its offer until its client has
  all the daemon will say to it, there in its FIFO whether or not the daemon is (pipe(7)),
  or until its serving ends. So what a closing daemon said last reaches each client still
  reading: a stepping-aside daemon's RESTART, and the RESTART a slot taken as the lists
  went is answered with by its own thread. Before, it exited once no client was in hand,
  and its exit cut off what its slots had yet to pass on: the client heard its slot end
  unanswered, "the command's microVM stopped before the command ended" (three tests on
  x86_64 CI, run 39191414199; 23 of 40 runs of them at 79caf2d7 on a loaded Fedora host,
  1 of 40 counting only the slots that pass a daemon's messages on). While it serves, a
  slot its client opened holds it; once it has closed, every slot does, but a client that
  takes nothing, stopped, or held by a pager that waits, holds it no longer than the wait
  a client that takes nothing has (`Seen::answer_wait`: twice the longest a client took a
  piece in, RFC 1122's R2 at least; was a request's time, `REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, 10 s) from the
  start of the piece of its answer it leaves untaken, or, its request not yet gone on, from
  its last step or the close, the later: the daemon says so, and exits, and the next daemon
  starts. A slot whose request went on, with nothing of its answer yet to take, holds it
  until the daemon has answered, its answer's last word (`EXIT`, `END`, `RESTART`) passed
  on (was: and a request's time at most after; the word is its client's in its FIFO
  whether or not the daemon is, "Admission", below): an attached run its stop ended after a 35 s timeout said nothing meanwhile, and
  timed from the close, its slot let go of the daemon, which exited as the run's VM said
  DONE, before its slot passed on the EXIT the VM wrote next. The run's client said its
  microVM stopped before its command ended (125 where its SIGKILL's 137 was due), once in
  608 runs of the daemon suite on CI (PM M331). Held by
  `a_closed_daemon_waits_for_what_a_slot_it_passed_on_has_yet_to_hear`, mutation-checked. A FIFO takes 8 KiB on macOS and 64 KiB on Linux
  (M261), so an answer past that is what such a client leaves untaken. A slot writes an
  answer 64 KiB at a time, what a Linux FIFO holds, each piece a step on as its client
  takes it: a client taking a long answer slowly goes on (timed from the whole answer's
  write, one reading 16 KiB at a time, 60 ms apart, was let go of a request's time in, 3 s
  in the test, still reading). A stop's slot is not counted: the daemon holds that session
  until its exit, which is how `daemon stop` learns of it.
- **A stop's wait** (2026-11-13). A daemon holds a stop it took until it has let go of its
  home (`finish` ends `stoppers` after the home's unlock), but `stop` took any end of its
  slot for that: a RESTART from a daemon closed already (another stop's word, an idle
  exit) or no slot offered returned at once while that daemon still ended its runs and held
  `daemon.lock`, and a RESTART from one serving on (its request cut, no descriptor left) for
  a stop though nothing stopped. managed_output's HVF run at 4a426c367 showed a stop
  returned with its daemon still stepping aside, which its single taken stop does not
  explain and ea6f4b53b did not show again. Now a daemon names itself stopping as it
  closes, for any reason (`name_stopping`): `daemon.stopping` as before, and
  `daemon.stopping.lock` (`shards_ipc::STOPPING_LOCK`), a file made beside its name, locked
  (flock(2), LockFileEx) and renamed there, held until the home's lock is let go of and
  only then let go of, its name removed last. `stop`, its slot ended, answered RESTART or
  given none, takes a shared lock of that file where there is one, and so returns once the
  daemon that stops has let go of its home, whatever its slot said; where there is none
  and the daemon it asked still holds the home (`daemon.pid`, `shards_ipc::Named`), it asks
  again after that answer, where that daemon is another than the one it last asked again,
  by its ID and start (`Named`): the same one answering again as itself, nothing changed, is
  no progress, and the stop fails naming it (`NotStopped::Untaken`), where a count of asks
  bounded it first (`RESTARTS`, `slots::OFFERED` + 2, derived for one takeover's RESTARTs and
  no basis for asking one daemon again; ROOT's R03 ruling, 2026-11-13). Each ask follows an
  answer, never a clock. No serving daemon holds that file (a starting
  one removes a dead one's), so a stop never waits on a next daemon's lock of the home, as
  one blocked on `daemon.lock` could once a successor polling `take_lock` took it first;
  nor on a process's ID, whose exit Linux watches only from 5.3 (pidfd_open(2)). It is
  apart from `daemon.stopping`, whose readers (`exiting`) Windows' mandatory byte-range
  locks would refuse. Held by `a_stop_returns_once_its_daemon_has_let_go_of_its_home`
  (cli/client.rs: a stand-in daemon, this process, holding the home's lock and, closed,
  `STOPPING_LOCK`, serving real slots: a session ended early, a RESTART from a closed
  daemon, no slot, a RESTART from one serving on), red before;
  `a_stop_its_daemon_answers_again_as_itself_without_taking_it_fails_naming_it` (a stand-in
  that answers every stop RESTART as itself: asked twice, then named; red before, asked four
  times); and on real VMs by
  `a_stop_while_another_stops_its_daemon_waits_for_its_home_let_go_of` (tests/daemon.rs).
- **A request asked again** (2026-11-13, R03). A run's, an exec's and an attach's client
  (`serve`) and a command's (`container`, `ask`, `ask_here`) asked again after a RESTART
  (or, until legacy-audit, a socket a pre-slots build shut unread), within `RESTARTS` (`slots::OFFERED` + 2 = 4): a
  count derived in its comment alone, for one takeover's RESTARTs (the step-aside
  request's, each slot the closing daemon had offered of the kind asked, an older build's
  socket), and in no D-entry. No count bounds it now. The client reads `daemon.pid`
  (`shards_ipc::Named`: ID and start) as it takes its slot or connects, before it asks, and
  after a RESTART asks again only where the daemon so named is another than the one whose
  RESTART it last asked again after (`cli::client::Again`): the same one answering so again
  as itself, nothing about it changed, would answer so for ever, and the client fails
  naming it (`Untaken`: "the daemon (process N) answered again without taking the request;
  see <daemon.log>"), as `stop` does through the same `Again` (*A stop's wait*). The name
  read is the slot's daemon's: a daemon names itself before it offers any slot, and holds
  its home until each slot it offered has its last word (*What it said last*), so no
  successor names itself between a client's take and its ask. Cold start: nothing has
  answered yet, so the first RESTART is asked again whoever said it, and a takeover is two
  answers, the stepping-aside daemon's RESTART and its successor's. A `daemon.pid` naming
  none is `None`, so two such RESTARTs in a row fail the client. Nothing is counted, timed
  or learned, so nothing overflows; a writer of `daemon.pid`, a process its home lets in
  (0700 on Unix), keeps a client asking only by naming another daemon each time, as a real
  succession does.
  Held by `a_request_its_daemon_answers_again_as_itself_without_taking_it_fails_naming_it`
  (each client in a process of its own, its daemon a stand-in, this process, serving real
  slots and answering every request RESTART as `4242 1`: asked twice, then named; red
  before, asked four times, "the daemon kept asking for a restart"; red with the identity
  check removed, asked to the stand-in's limit) and
  `a_request_its_daemon_stepped_aside_from_goes_to_the_daemon_after_it` (RESTART as
  `4242 1`, then `4343 2` answers: asked twice, status 0). On real VMs, owed: a takeover's
  `a_rebuilt_binary_replaces_the_daemon` (tests/daemon.rs).
- **Whose end a run's client heard** (PM M530). A run's, an exec's and an attach's slot
  passes on what its VM says, so the slot ends both where the VM's connection closes with no
  last word and where the daemon itself ends: a killed daemon closes every slot it served.
  The client said the same of both, "the command's microVM stopped before the command
  ended", and blamed the microVM for kiln's between-turns sweep, which ended the WHP E2E's
  daemons with `taskkill /F` (jupiter's kiln.log, 2026-11-12): a hunt through WHP, the VMM
  and the guest. M188's and M331's daemons that exited under their clients were taken so too.
  Now the slot says `UNANSWERED`, last, where the run's side ended without its last word
  (`EXIT`, `END`, `RESTART`), and the client says so as the microVM's stop; a slot that ends
  with no last word at all is its daemon's end, and the client says "the daemon ended before
  the command did". A command's client (`END`) reads any early end as its daemon's already;
  no other peer is read (a pre-slots daemon's socket, whose peer was the run's VM, is gone,
  legacy-audit). Held by
  `a_side_that_ends_without_its_last_word_says_so` and
  `a_runs_client_tells_its_daemons_end_from_its_microvms`, each red with its guard removed,
  on Linux, macOS and Windows; live on WHP, a daemon ended mid-run said so and a VM ended
  said the microVM's words.
- **Many clients on one list** (PM M262). On macOS a client waiting in select(2) for its
  slot could stop waking at all while the others took theirs: 12 of 16 clients slept
  through 20 s of records others took, and one of an E2E test's 16 waited 60 s while its
  daemon served the rest. A waiting read(2), poll(2) and kqueue(2) saw every record, but
  only select(2) and a read see a FIFO's writer go there (M253). So a client waits on its
  list in kqueue(2), for its records, its name's removal (a closing daemon unoffers it; a
  new one makes its own), and its daemon's exit (the process `daemon.pid` names, by its ID
  and start, "Admission", below; a killed daemon leaves its list's name), and reads after
  each, not waiting; where `daemon.pid` names no live process, it looks again every
  250 ms. On Linux a read waits, which sees
  both. Held by `clients_waiting_on_one_list_wake_for_its_records`, which failed in each
  of 6 runs with select(2) put back, 8 to 12 of its 16 clients asleep.
- **Measured** against slice 3 (build-ab, PM M259): what slots alone change costs a run
  nothing, within ±31 µs of none at every quiet round's p50 of 2.3 to 2.6 ms, and within
  the noise loaded; a request's own cost through a slot is M254's and M255's. Slice 4's
  first cut woke an idle daemon once a second, its maker looking at its lists on a timer
  (30 context switches in 30 s, where the daemon before had none, M259), which the looks
  above replaced.

**What a request names (audit of picked constants, 2026-11-09).** A request named at most 8
descriptors, "a run's three and room to spare": picked. Each it names stands for one of its
slot's streams or for none in that stream's place, so it names at most as many as a slot has
streams (`slots::fds::MAX`, the count of `streams::IN | OUT | ERR`, 3), as a run's do.

| Literal | Was | Now | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fds::MAX` (ipc slots.rs) | 8 | a slot's streams, 3 | `slots::streams`; cli/client.rs, a run's `ways` |

**Admission (audit of picked constants, 2026-11-09).** Three figures of how the daemon admits
and lets go of its clients were picked: how long a request's rest was waited for, how often a
daemon out of descriptors looked for one, and how a client knew its daemon. Each is now what
it follows: the request's own times, the descriptors' being let go of, the daemon's own
process.

- **A request's rest is waited for while its client goes on with it, and a client cut asks
  again** (`slots::Seen`, PM M545; the person's ruling of 2026-11-13: a wait follows the
  party's liveness and progress, then the slowest answer seen, never a doubling). A request
  cut is begun nowhere, so asking again is a restart: its slot answers RESTART, as a
  closing daemon's does, and a client still writing finds its `say` gone and asks again
  through the next slot (`ask_slot`'s BrokenPipe).
  - *Its first byte alone.* A client writes its request in one write (`Client::ask`), so
    its rest comes with its first byte. A client that sends nothing past it is waited for as
    long as the slowest rest this daemon has read whole, from its first byte, of those its
    client was waited on for, and then cut.
  - *What teaches.* A rest there as the daemon reads it waited on no client, and teaches
    nothing, as an answer's write the FIFO takes at once does not (below). Only a rest whose
    reader found nothing there and waited for its client to write it does
    (`shards_ipc::slots::Asked::waited`: a poll(2) or select(2) that does not wait finds
    nothing, or PeekNamedPipe says no bytes): a request larger than a FIFO holds, coming in
    parts, or a client paused past its first byte.
  - *Its cold start.* Before any such rest has come whole the daemon has seen none, and
    bounds none: the wait follows the client alone, its end (the FIFO's, or the pipe's) or
    the daemon ending its clients (R03's cold start). It was every rest read whole: the
    request that starts a daemon came whole, its rest read microseconds after its first
    byte, and from then on each client that paused past its first byte was cut that far
    into its pause. So `clients_past_the_cap_wait_their_turn`'s sixteen silent clients were
    never in hand at once, on every job of CI's run at f5c0c8b04 that ran it: "request slot
    N: nothing past its request's first byte in 8µs; its client asks again" on aarch64
    macOS, 5.384 µs on aarch64 glibc, 6.408 µs on aarch64 musl, 5.68 µs on x86_64 glibc,
    6.261 µs on x86_64 musl, 24.1 µs on aarch64 Windows; and 2.334 µs on a KVM x86_64 host at
    e72239dd3. A first slowest of microseconds, or none, is no bound for a client still
    writing (ROOT, 2026-11-13).
  - *Its rest begun.* A request whose rest has begun is read until it is whole or its
    client ends. One larger than a FIFO holds (a run's spec, up to `MAX_PAYLOAD`, 6 MiB)
    comes in parts, each as the daemon reads and its client is next run: a gap no rest of a
    request written whole measures, so a window learned from those would cut such a request
    each time it was asked, for ever.
  - *What it costs.* A client stopped mid-request (`SIGSTOP`) holds its slot's descriptors
    until it goes on or ends, and keeps an idle daemon from exiting meanwhile; a closed
    daemon ends its read at once (`requests_end`, set as it closes, as at a stop), and the
    client, told RESTART or finding its `say` gone, asks the next daemon. The slowest rest is this
    daemon's alone, in memory: a client of the home's own user can make it longer by
    writing its request slowly, which only waits longer on a silent one.
  - It was D222's restart cutoff (Luby, Sinclair and Zuckerman 1993, over the daemon's
    requests' times, Kaplan and Meier 1958 over its cuts), a second at least and before any
    (RFC 6298 §2.1, §2.4), doubled for each cut in a row (§5.5), drawn from [t, 2t). The
    registry's own waits follow the same rule since (D222, PM M555). The daemon's own handling of a connection waits on no
  clock at all: every connection it takes is a socket pair one of its threads writes the
  request on whole (a slot's bridge, a request it puts to itself), and a bridge that cannot
  send ends its writing.
- **A client taking its answer holds a closed daemon while it takes, and one that takes
  nothing for longer than the slowest take seen holds it no more** (`slots::Seen`, PM M549;
  the person's ruling of 2026-11-13: the slowest answer seen bounds a stall, a gap with no
  progress, never an answer's whole length). Its command done, it cannot be told to ask
  again.
  - *Its progress* is room it makes: its answer is written as its FIFO takes it, a write
    that does not wait (`slots::write_all_waiting`), and only where the FIFO takes none of
    what is left is its client waited on, until it reads some: for its FIFO's room
    (`await_fifo_room`: select(2) on macOS, where poll(2) slept through a reader's end,
    poll(2) elsewhere), or, where no more than PIPE_BUF is left, in the write itself, which
    goes whole (POSIX write(2)), as macOS's FIFOs say POLLOUT with less than that free (PM
    M549). Each such
    wait that ends is a take; what the FIFO takes at once waits on no client and teaches
    nothing. A wait for room ends only with a write after it that moved bytes: its
    reader's end wakes `await_fifo_room` too (POLLERR/POLLHUP; select(2)'s writability),
    and the write after it fails EPIPE, so that wait is told no end and teaches no take
    (review waits-04, PM M576; red `slots::fifo::tests::a_readers_end_is_no_take`), as
    the Windows twin's write finished as its reader went is none (PM M553).
  - *Its bound*: a closed daemon lets go of a client whose writer has waited on it longer
    than the slowest take seen. One that reads, however slowly, ends each wait as it reads.
    The listener sleeps until the first slot holding the daemon lets go, and a slot whose
    answer is still to come holds it with no such time: a wait that begins once the daemon
    has closed wakes it (`slots::Living::answer`), as that wait's time is set only then.
    Before, nothing did, and a write that began to wait after the listener's last look held
    the daemon until its client ended (`daemon::tests::a_closed_daemon_waits_for_what_a_slot_it_passed_on_has_yet_to_hear`;
    found reading the stop that held CI 44138098584's aarch64 musl job, 2026-11-17).
  - *Its cold start*: before any take, a client holds a closed daemon until it ends (its
    FIFO's end), and the daemon says so of each such slot once, "held until that client
    reads or ends" (`say_held_slots`), so that a stop held by a stopped client or a pager
    that waits names what holds it. A take is a write that waited: clients that read each
    message as fast as the daemon writes it teach none, the FIFO taking each write's rest as
    its client reads. `a_stopping_daemon_waits_for_no_client_that_reads_nothing` took one
    for seen before its stop, and read its clients only after it, which held it until the
    step's limit on that job; it reads the cut client once the daemon says it holds it.
  - *Windows*: a named pipe says nothing of its room before a write, and
    `NtQueryInformationFile`'s `FilePipeLocalInformation` is no room either: its
    `WriteQuotaAvailable` is the outbound quota less what is charged to it (ReactOS npfs,
    `drivers/filesystems/npfs/fileinfo.c` `NpQueryPipeLocalInfo`), which a read the client
    has pending is charged too (`read.c` `NpCommonRead` queues it `Buffered`, of its whole
    length, and `datasup.c` `NpAddDataQueueEntry` charges a buffered entry what the quota has
    free), and which a stalled write takes as the client frees it (`datasup.c`
    `NpCompleteStalledWrites`): a client waiting in a read of a quota or more, as a frame's
    payload is read, shows none, though a write would go at once into its read; and while a
    write of the daemon's waits, it stays none however the client reads. Cygwin met the
    first: "WriteQuotaAvailable is unreliable ... if a pipe read is currently pending,
    WriteQuotaAvailable on the write side is decremented by the number of bytes the read
    side is requesting" (`winsup/cygwin/select.cc` `pipe_data_available`, which works round
    it by setting the pipe nonblocking for a moment); and Wine reports its whole quota,
    unreduced ("FIXME: Needs to be reduced by ReadDataAvailable at the other end",
    `server/named_pipe.c` `pipe_end_get_file_info`). What says room is the write's own pend:
    an overlapped WriteFile that its pipe holds whole, or hands to a pending read, finishes at
    once, and one it cannot pends until the client has taken enough (npfs above; Wine's
    `reselect_write_queue` completes a pending write once the reader's unread bytes fit its
    buffer). So an answer is written in parts no larger than its line's outbound quota
    (GetNamedPipeInfo's out buffer size, the system's, `Window::System`, platform-11), each waiting on the client for no
    more than a quota's worth of its reading: a part that finishes at once teaches nothing,
    and one that pends is a take, from its pend (`ERROR_IO_PENDING`, `pipe::write_telling`)
    to its completion (ROOT, 2026-11-13), where the pipe is connected still as it finishes
    (`NamedPipeState`, `pipe::connected_now`): Windows 11 finishes a write that pended on a
    client that then went, `Ok`, its data dropped, and fails the next with ERROR_NO_DATA,
    where ReactOS's npfs completes it `STATUS_PIPE_BROKEN` (`statesup.c`
    `NpSetClosingPipeState`); so one that finished as its client went is no take, told no end,
    and the write fails `BrokenPipe` (PM M553: the line holds its quota exactly, 65,536 bytes,
    before a part pends). WriteQuotaAvailable is no measure of a client's room; it was a
    closed daemon following its clients' ends alone there, no take seen.
  - It was twice the longest a piece of 64 KiB took, at least TCP's R2 (100 s, RFC 1122
    §4.2.3.5).
  A slot whose answer's last word is its client's holds it no more: the word is in its FIFO
  whether or not the daemon is, and nothing its client reads comes after it.
  - *A request not yet gone on* holds a closed daemon until its serving ends: its wait is
    the request's own (above), and none once the daemon has closed, whose reader ends at
    once (`requests_end`), its client told RESTART; never the answers' record. A slot no
    client has opened has no client: it holds nothing, and the daemon says it leaves only
    the clients whose answer's writer waits on them. It was the slowest take after the
    slot's last step or the close, which judged a request by its answers' record and said
    it left slots that had no client to leave: a closed daemon whose slowest take was
    3.1 ms said "request slot 2: its client went no further in 3.096667ms; exiting without
    it" and slot 3 alike, beside the one client it did leave (an HVF host at dc7f45bc6,
    `a_stopping_daemon_waits_for_no_client_that_reads_nothing`).
- **Out of descriptors, the daemon refuses the client it cannot take and is woken as
  descriptors are let go of: nothing looks on a clock.** What it accepts on, and how:
  - *The Engine API's socket and the contexts' (Unix)*: a listener whose accept finds no
    descriptor (EMFILE, ENFILE) keeps its client in the backlog and stays readable. The
    listener holds one spare descriptor (the null device's, as libuv's `loop->emfile_fd`),
    lets it go, accepts with it, closes the connection at once (its client reads its end,
    as a refusal), and opens the spare again (libev's "the special problem of accept()ing
    when you can't", ev.3; libuv's `uv__emfile_trick`; the vsock muxer's `refuse_one`,
    3447c5a7). Where another thread took the freed descriptor first, the listener polls
    those sockets no more until it is woken (`wake_listener`: as a client, a run or a
    connection ends) and holds its spare again (`refuse_api`, `spare_held`).
  - *Their named pipes (Windows)*: a pipe's client comes on an instance that waits for it;
    accept makes the next instance, and out of handles cannot. The client is refused by its
    own instance, disconnected (DisconnectNamedPipe) and made to wait for the next client
    again, which makes no handle (`shards_ipc::Listener::refuse`): no spare is needed.
  - *The request slots (D185)*: a slot holds its descriptors from its offer, so a client
    waiting on a list waits in a backlog that keeps nothing of the daemon's ready; out of
    descriptors, the maker offers again as it hears `Event::Room`, which `wake_listener`
    sends. A client that took a slot whose serving then finds no descriptor (its bridge's
    socket pair and the null device) is told RESTART on the slot's own FIFO and asks again.
    A slot that could not be offered for another reason (its FIFOs, its thread) is tried
    again after a random share of how long the trouble has lasted (D222's `Trouble`).
  - *The collector*: short of descriptors, it marks the daemon starving and waits for the
    wake that says some were let go of (`have_room`), where it waited 250 ms.
- **A daemon is known by its process ID and start** (`shards_ipc::Named`): `daemon.pid` and
  `daemon.stopping` hold `PID START`, START the process's start as its OS counts it (Linux
  `/proc/<pid>/stat` starttime, proc(5); macOS `proc_pid_rusage`'s `ri_proc_start_abstime`,
  as crates/api's taken.rs reads it; Windows `GetProcessTimes`' creation time), and a
  daemon lives only where the process of that ID started then. A client's wait for a slot
  (`daemon_lives`, `exiting`) and the macOS list watcher's wait for its daemon's exit could
  wait for ever on an unrelated process given a dead daemon's ID. `PID START` alone is
  read: a record by its ID alone is refused typed (`shards_ipc::NotNamed::IdAlone`; other
  forms `Malformed`) and is stale, as a dead process's record is, never a live daemon
  (legacy3, 2026-11-14). Every release to v0.7.0 wrote `PID` alone (v0.7.0's daemon.rs
  `format!("{}\n", std::process::id())`; the start came in fb1f28d42, 2026-11-09, in no
  release: `git tag --contains fb1f28d42` names no `v*`), so such a record is a daemon of
  another build's (D36), which this build never waits on by its ID: the home's lock is
  what its successor waits on (`take_lock`; `judge_holder` follows a holder the home
  names no living process for by its lock alone), and a slot it offers is asked and steps
  aside as any other build's. The `Option` start, which read such a record by its ID
  alone and so could wait on whatever process held that ID since, is gone. Red/green:
  `a_record_by_its_id_alone_is_stale` (crates/ipc), and `a_daemon_is_exiting_while_its_process_lives`'s
  ID-alone row now `false`. crates/api's reader is its crate's own
  (`pub(crate)`, Unix only, and shards_ipc does not depend on it), so shards_ipc reads
  starts itself, the same way, and Windows' besides. A process that has exited lives no
  more though its parent has not reaped it (review waits-08, PM M576): a zombie answers
  kill(2) and keeps its start, so a client's wait for a slot from a daemon that a
  supervisor left unreaped waited for ever. Unix's `alive` also reads its exit: Linux's
  `/proc/<pid>/stat` state `Z` or `X` (proc(5)), with no thread of it left (amended below),
  macOS's `proc_pid_rusage` `ri_proc_exit_abstime`, set as its exit begins (XNU's
  `proc_prepareexit`; as crates/api's judge reads a process ending); one whose state cannot
  be read is not known to have exited. Windows' twin already asks its handle
  (`WaitForSingleObject`, no wait). Red `tests::an_unreaped_daemon_does_not_live` (its child
  left a zombie by waitid's `WNOWAIT`).
- **A process has exited only once its whole thread group has** (amended 2026-11-17, ROOT's
  ruling, goal fb3528f9). A thread-group leader that exits before its other threads stays a
  zombie while they run, hold its files and do its work, until the last of them has gone
  (kernel/exit.c: "we don't reap group leaders with subthreads", `delay_group_leader`;
  fs/file.c `put_files_struct`, which closes its files with its last thread's reference), and
  `/proc/<pid>/stat` shows the leader's own state (fs/proc/array.c `do_task_stat`).
  - *Why.* A SIGKILLed daemon whose leader went first read as no daemon while its other
    threads still held its clients' slots open. CI 44077430171 (x86_64 musl, a223a63bc8)
    refused `a_container_outlives_a_daemon_that_dies`' wait for its run's client 20 ms in, its
    party the client alone ("no daemon yet"), asleep in its slot's three reads.
  - *Linux.* `unix::ended_in` (`alive`) and crates/api's `taken::exited_field`, which its
    judge's `Watch` reads (D215), take a process as exited where its state is `Z` or `X` and
    its thread count, field 20 (`num_threads`, `get_nr_threads`), is at most 1: the count
    holds a delayed leader until it is reaped (kernel/exit.c `__exit_signal`). So a dying
    daemon stays its party's member, its threads' exit its CPU (D215's look), and a client's
    wait on it while it lives waits for its last thread, whose end lets go of its lock and
    slots.
  - *macOS, not changed.* `ri_proc_exit_abstime` is set in `proc_prepareexit` as an exit
    begins (xnu-12377.101.15 bsd/kern/kern_exit.c `exit_with_reason`: `P_LEXIT`, then
    `proc_prepareexit`, then `task_terminate_internal`), which a thread ending alone never
    calls: a process whose main thread has ended (`pthread_exit`) reads as living while its
    other threads run, so the ruled shape reads right. Its window is a killed process's: the
    stamp comes before its other threads have terminated, and its files close only in
    `proc_exit`, which its last thread calls (osfmk/kern/thread.c `thread_terminate_self`,
    `active_thread_count` at 0; kern_exit.c `fdt_invalidate`), before `SZOMB`. Unreproduced
    (R09). The reader that would hold it is `proc_pidinfo`'s short BSD info, `pbsi_status`
    `SZOMB` (zombies found where its `arg` is nonzero, bsd/kern/proc_info.c); owed a live case
    first.
  - *Windows, not changed.* A process ends once its last thread does, or `ExitProcess` or
    `TerminateProcess` ends it, and its object is signaled once its threads have terminated
    (Microsoft Learn, "Terminating a Process"; `ExitThread`: a process's last thread's exit
    ends it). Its main thread's `ExitThread` leaves it running, and its handle says so.
  - Red/green: crates/ipc `tests::a_process_whose_leader_ended_lives_while_its_threads_run`
    (Linux: a child of its binary whose main thread ends alone, by exit(2) from a signal's
    handler, while another waits on its stdin, lives; then, its stdin ended and the child left
    unreaped by waitid's `WNOWAIT`, lives no more), `unix::tests::a_zombie_leader_with_threads_left_has_not_exited`,
    and crates/api `taken::linux::tests::a_zombie_leader_with_threads_left_has_not_exited`.
    The tests' party says such a daemon's state and threads where its pid file still names it
    (6f81eeaae1).

|---|---|---|---|

| `REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, a handled connection's first message | 10 s | none: the daemon's own pairs | its senders write whole or end their writing |
| `REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, a closed daemon's client taking nothing | 10 s | `Seen::answer_wait`: the slowest take seen (none before any: its end); was 2 × longest piece, ≥ 100 s (2026-11-09 to 11-13) | its own takes: waits on it for FIFO room (`slots::write_all_waiting`), PIPE_BUF (POSIX write(2)) |
| `REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, after an answer's last word | 10 s | none | pipe(7): a FIFO keeps what was written as its writer goes |
| `RETRY` (daemon.rs), the API's and contexts' accept | 250 ms | none: refused with a spare, woken as descriptors go | libev ev.3; libuv `uv__emfile_trick`; muxer 3447c5a7 |
| `RETRY` (relay.rs, Windows), a context's pipe | 250 ms | none: `Listener::refuse` | DisconnectNamedPipe, ConnectNamedPipe (Win32 named pipes) |
