  the same side of a read's need as what it had left of the look before. A look that
  finds a verdict wrong (a budget set or lowered, room taken or freed by another process,
  its guest among them) restarts `w`, so looks come close together while the room moves
  across what reads need and spread out while it stays clear: a 10 µs look right for 10 s
  is next due 14.1 ms on, right for an hour 0.27 s on. It was a look's hundredfold time
  (`LOOKS_APART`), a chosen share of the share's time. Cold start: no look yet, it looks
  at once; a file that cannot be read is no bound, as before. Owed to ROOT (R14): the
  share's look count and CPU over PM M318's held reads, against the hundredfold rule's,
  `cargo test -p shards --test budget a_microvm_held_to_a_budget_reads_through_fuse_at_the_pace_of_reads_held_to_none`
  on a Linux host with cgroup v2 delegation. Within that room it keeps its copy, for the
  run's next reader. Held so short, a
  lone microVM's reads took 0.81 times their time with none at p50 with the copy dropped,
  1.9 with the tree's, and 1.01 with it kept until its budgets had no room left, its slice
  then within half a mebibyte of its budget; under a budget with room, a run's later reads
  of a written gigabyte took 1.74 to 2.45 s at p50 as with the tree's, where dropped under
  every budget they took 2.91 to 3.94, read from its host's disk again.
- **The share's own memory held still** (PM M314). A share's process, and its VM process's
  queue workers, read each request into and build each reply in buffers each keeps from
  one request to the next (`Server::handle_into`, fs/mod.rs `Buffers`), a frame's size at
  most. A MiB read through the share had made 5 MiB of fresh memory, freed as its reply
  went, in processes whose memory a run's budget holds, their threads waiting in mmap and
  munmap: held short of its budget throughout, a gigabyte's read took 2.2 to 3.1 times its
  unbudgeted time at every least room from 1 to 16 times this one (a Xeon's three reads at
  8 times, 1.07), and with the buffers kept 1.19 to 1.31 times on the EPYCs and 1.86 on a
  Xeon 8573C, its unbudgeted reads 0.50 to 0.62 times as long.
- **A template's zero gaps stay anonymous on restore.** Unix maps only the snapshot's
  recorded runs of data from its RAM file, as Windows does; the gaps keep their reserved
  anonymous zero memory. Mapping the sparse file whole made a read of a hole allocate a
  page in a tmpfs file (`mm/shmem.c`, `shmem_fault`), which stayed charged as shmem even
  after that restore ended. Repeated restores could fill the template's holes and leave
  a short budget with nothing its host could reclaim, throttling the share's reads at
  `memory.high`. The file-backed runs keep their private, copy-on-write mappings. A
  snapshot from before the runs were recorded still maps the file whole. The memory test
  `a_restores_zero_gaps_do_not_fill_its_templates_sparse_file` checks that reads and private
  writes leave those holes unallocated and another restore's bytes unchanged; on Fedora's
  tmpfs it fails before the fix and passes after it.
- **File pages alone.** A clean page of the page cache the guest drops is one the host
  could only have swapped out, written and read back; dropping it reads none of its data.
  Anonymous memory and the tmpfs layer, the host's own reclaim takes as well as the guest
  would, and taking them would read memory the host may have compressed, which Apple's
  header warns against under pressure (dispatch/source.h, `DISPATCH_MEMORYPRESSURE_WARN`).
- **Then what it holds plugged past what it uses goes back too** (D148's unplug): init
  asks its device for twice what the run uses, past what the microVM booted with, in whole
  memory blocks, as the grower asks for twice what the run reaches, and holds the run at
  what it will have first, so that the grower hears it grow again however much the driver
  unplugs; the grower asks for no less than the device is asked for now. The driver
  unplugs what it can: a block the kernel holds part of stays (plugged memory comes online
  as the kernel's own, D133). Reporting gives back a block's free pages either way;
  unplugging gives back its page structures too, a 64th of it, which a session that once
  grew holds for as long as it lives otherwise.
- **Never from a run as it grows** (M275): a pass keeps no less than the run used at its
  peak since the pass before (its `memory.peak`, counted afresh through a descriptor PID 1
  holds, Linux 6.12), and gives back nothing while memory the grower asked for is still to
  come (the device's request a block or more past what is plugged). Passes seconds apart
  under a host's pressure had each cut back to twice the run's use at that moment the
  request the grower had just raised, the one register both write; a hold slows an
  allocation past it but cannot refuse one with no swap, and a run that grew faster than
  its memory came back took the kernel's own and met its OOM killer: 3 of 30 runs of the
  benchmark with DAX windows, whose guests hold no page cache of the files they map and so
  keep less; none of 60 since, the host as short of memory and as much given back. Nor
  from one that grew within the window its host's pressure is measured over (2 s,
  `shards_abi::PRESSURE_WINDOW_US`; PM M466): the grower marks each ask and each block
  that comes in a page init, its grower and its builtins share, and a give-back that finds
  a mark within the window keeps all it has. Its keep counts from what the run uses
  (twice its `memory.current`), the grower's ask from what the guest has (twice its
  MemTotal), and a run raised to more (`update -m`) that had just had 128 MiB plugged for
  an allocation not yet touched was cut back to its keep, held there, grew, and was cut
  back again pass after pass of a host that stayed short, until its guest ran out of
  memory and killed what grew: 15 of 74 raised allocations in `update_under_pressure_stress`
  (the host's word every 50 ms), the slowest 42 minutes; none of 2,000 since.
- **No hold counts what goes** (PM M324): every hold init sets counts out the memory
  still plugged past its device's request, which goes as its driver unplugs it, free or
  not, as the give-back's own hold does; and what is plugged, for a run held at its cap or
  a grower lifting its hold once all its most is plugged, is what stays. The daemon tells
  a microVM its room again as it gives back, which came 10 to 15 ms after: worked out
  while the driver still unplugged, its hold counted the 128 MiB going as free, 261 to 274
  MB where its microVM would have 233 MiB, and its page cache filled its zones to their
  min watermarks, its guest's kernel throttling its own reclaim and its grower, woken
  only at the hold, plugging none: 5 of 384 past128 reads in the DAX budget job, and none
  of 288 since.
- **Said in the daemon's log** with what was given back since, at no fixed while
  (`pressure::Saying`): as a pressure begins, then each time it has gone on as long again
  as it had when last said, one pressure window at the least, so that a pressure that goes
  on for a time t is said about log2(t / window) times, its lines farther apart the longer
  it goes on, as a doubling search past what is known has them (Baeza-Yates, Culberson and
  Rawlins, "Searching in the plane", Inf. Comput. 106(2), 1993). A pressure that goes on is
  heard once a window, so a word after a whole window with none begins another, said at
  once. Before 0bc518367 it was once a minute, a while no measurement set.
- **Idle, it costs nothing**: with no microVM running it waits for one, hearing no
  pressure meanwhile, whose trigger fires each window while the host stays short (on a CI
  runner short of memory it woke an idle daemon's thread every 2 s: job 118535098642);
  then a thread blocked in poll(2) on Linux 6.4 and later and on macOS; on an older Linux,
  a read of the host's average every ten seconds.
- **A build's builders give back as runs do** (D133's builders; PM M442). A build's
  builders are its own process's, not the daemon's (`shards build image`), so the build watches
  its host's memory pressure as the daemon does, the same words on every host (PSI on its
  own cgroup on Linux, libdispatch's source on macOS, the low memory notification on
  Windows, `SHARDS_BUILD_PRESSURE` a test's), and a write to a budget over it (inotify on
  each `memory.high` and `memory.max` up its chain), and at each asks every builder on its
  give-back port (`build::GIVE_PORT`, build/give.rs) to give back what it holds cold of its
  files and what it holds plugged past twice what its build uses (init's `RECLAIM` and
  unplug, as a run's: what it keeps is counted as a run's, `shrink_run`, so a builder whose
  grower asked for memory or had memory come within the pressure window keeps all it has,
  PM M466), then tells each its share of the room the budget leaves (`ROOM`),
  counted as a run's is, which its guest holds the build within. A builder is told that
  room as it starts, before its first step; every builder is asked at once, one ask out
  to each at a time, its answer waited for until the next word can come, a pressure window
  (`give::PATIENCE`, the window its host's pressure is measured over and a pressure that
  goes on is heard again after, `platform::PRESSURE_WINDOW`), so that a pass never holds
  up the next word's; one not come by then is counted unanswered, looked for once a window
  after (`give::late`) and counted as it comes, and its builder asked again only once it
  has answered (a builder its host throttled answered in 9 s and more, PM M350). What they
  gave back is said on the build's plain output as the daemon's log says its microVMs'
  (`pressure::Saying`, above). While a budget holds the
  build, its builders are told its room again each pressure window where it changed, and
  given a word of pressure where it is short: a guest holds its build within what it was
  last told past what the build used then, and what its host gets back of it outside the
  build (blocks it unplugs, free pages reported after its answer) the build's own growth
  never shows; told 44 MiB as its builder's unplug of 128 MiB was under way, an apt build
  on Fedora was held within it for 200 s while its budget had 140 MiB to spare, 219 s
  against 31.5 s with none. Under a user scope's `MemoryHigh` the least that holds the
  build where its builder gives back all it holds cold, interleaved with the same builds
  unbudgeted (builder-pressure/measure.py; PM M442): at 2f82adb6, on eight of CI's
  runners (EPYC 7763, 9V45 and 9V74, Xeon 6973P-C and Platinum 8573C), every held build
  but one was asked to give back, its builder answering 5 to 33 ms after the word at p50
  (710 ms at most), giving back up to 202 MiB of its files a build and unplugging 128 to
  256 MiB at an answer, and held builds took no longer than unbudgeted beyond their rounds'
  spread in 23 of the 24 runner and build pairs: apt on the Xeon 6973P-C was 0.1 s slower,
  its build reading again 58 MiB at p50 of the cache layers it merges, whose page cache its
  budget had taken back, not slowed by its builder. Since d9c42120 a held build's caches
  are read and written for its guest by its writer, outside the budget (below), and on
  eight of CI's runners (EPYC 7763 and 9V74, Xeon Platinum 8573C and 6973P-C) and Fedora
  held builds took no longer than unbudgeted beyond their rounds' spread in all 27 host
  and build pairs, apt on the Xeon 6973P-C among them (held's fastest 28.0 s, free's
  slowest 28.2), no held build reading its caches again. On Fedora (i9-14900HX, NVMe, Btrfs) at
  b8c98e7f and 2f82adb6, the same builder, every build held answered (0 to 5 ms at p50,
  318 ms at most), an apt builder giving back 55 and 80 MiB of its files a build at p50,
  none slower beyond the spread. On an M3 Ultra at 9f2520c2, its builds told every 2 s that their host was short
  and the host loaded by other work (load 11 to 21), every word answered, 64 to 84 ms
  after it at p50, an apt builder giving back 142 MiB of its files a build at p50 and
  unplugging up to 1,152 MiB, none slower beyond the spread. The budget is the most the
  same build held under a budget that presses nothing: a build under a budget hands its
  own writes to its writer (below), so a free build's peak, which counts them, left a
  held build room it never filled (c3ce85e).
  A builder's room counts the file pages its processes map only where they are charged to
  the budget (`daemon::budget::charged_room`), where a run's counts them wherever charged
  (above). A builder boots cold, its guest's RAM its VM process's own memory, charged to
  the budget; what it maps charged elsewhere is its bases' images on its pmem devices and
  its VM process's program, page cache an earlier build or run read, which no reclaim of
  the budget takes (mm/vmscan.c `shrink_node_memcgs` scans the budget's own memcgs) and
  which, taken back by another's and read again, comes back charged to it and counted
  then; a run's guest maps its own RAM from its template (PM M309). Counted wherever
  charged, they made a held build's count exceed its scope's `memory.current` by exactly
  them at every held peak on CI's runners (13 to 14 MiB for npm, 55 to 64 for apt, 99 to
  100 for rust over rust:1-slim; d9c42120, PM M442), and a budget short of the build's
  charge by what its builder held cold told its guest it was short by them besides, which
  holds its build at what it uses (init's `ROOM`): builds of 10 s took 246 to 622 s
  (573e4bf8). The harness now holds each build to its held arms' own peak in that count
  less what its builder held cold, so that every held build is pressed. That, the room as
  charged, the window's keep (PM M466) and the saying above are not yet measured: owed at
  the commit that has them (PM M442, its last item).
  Before the writer (2d168658), held builds on CI's runners were 0.4 to 16 s slower in the
  steps that write to the host's disk, which the memory controller holds to the budget's
  share of dirty pages (`balance_dirty_pages`): the builder, held within room it never
  filled, was not what held them. On Windows
  too since 2026-10-28, free page reporting (D151) theirs there as a run's: on jupiter's
  WHP a builder holding a step's 256 MiB file gave back 253 MiB of it, its VM process from
  350,516 KiB to 96,168, and again at d1deefd9, from 352,088 KiB to 96,220
  (`a_builder_gives_back_what_it_holds_cold_at_its_builds_word`).
- **A budgeted build's own writes, outside its budget** (Linux; PM M442; built and
  measured). A write dirties page cache charged to its writer's
  cgroup, and `balance_dirty_pages` (mm/page-writeback.c, Linux 7.0) throttles the writer
  against its own cgroup's domain beside the host's (`mdtc`, the domain of the writer's
  own wb, `wb_get_create_current` in `balance_dirty_pages_ratelimited_flags`): what that
  domain may dirty is `dirty_ratio`'s share (`domain_dirty_limits`) of its file pages and
  no more of its headroom than the budget leaves (`mdtc_calc_avail`, `filepages +
  min(headroom, other_clean)`; mm/memcontrol.c `mem_cgroup_wb_stats`, the headroom
  `min(memory.max, memory.high)` less what it uses, the least of it and each cgroup above
  it). A build that fills its budget has none, so its `RUN` steps' changes, its layers and
  its image's root filesystem went at its writeback's pace, and its pages past the budget
  waited out `memory.high`'s throttle besides. So where its cgroup or one above it has a
  `memory.high` or `memory.max`, the build starts a writer of its own (`shards
  build-writer`), which its user's manager makes a scope in its application slice
  (systemd.special(7), `app.slice`) as the daemon places a spawner (D183); where that scope
  is not under the budget, every file the build writes through the store (`Partial`: its
  layers, its image's root filesystem; a cache's merged layers, `merge_run`, and its first
  content, `seed_image`) and its steps' changes (`upper::Applier`'s staging file) are
  written by it, each write to the build's own open file, passed with it
  (SCM_RIGHTS), at that file's offset (`shards_image::through`, build/outside.rs): their
  pages are charged to it, paced by the host's dirty limit alone. BuildKit makes its own
  writes so, in buildkitd, never in the cgroup its `RUN` steps are given (`docker build
  --cgroup-parent`: "the parent cgroup for the RUN instructions"). The builder's VM
  process, whose memory the budget is for, stays under it, its writes to a cache's range
  of the join disk (D134) with it, as a `RUN` step's writes to a cache mount are its
  container's in Docker; each of those is made durable before its record names it in
  either case (`mounts::finish`). Where nothing places the writer outside (no user
  manager, or a budget over the user's whole tree), the build writes its files itself.
  At 94838b88 the writer never ran: the command line refused `build-writer` as unknown
  (it was `shardsd()`'s word but not in the command line's own list), every held build on
  CI's runners wrote under its budget, and the steps that write were slower held, apt's
  `RUN`'s end 4.3 to 10.9 s against 2.6 to 4.4 free while apt itself was not (PM M442).
  The word is the command line's now, and a step's changes go to their staging file a
  chunk at a time (`through::CHUNK`, the most one message to the writer carries), not a
  write, and a round trip to the writer, for each file. At 0849ecb3 the writer ran in every
  held build. apt's `RUN` was still 0.7 to 1.9 s slower held on two runners, all of it
  after the guest's own end, which came no later held. That is where the build keeps and
  merges its caches. A merge's writes were the build's own writes still made under the
  budget, and they go through the writer now. The harness now splits that gap phase by
  phase and process by process (PM M442). At eb9f70a4 the rule held for 11 of CI's 12
  runner and build pairs; on every runner rust's export, its 926 MiB root filesystem, was
  0.21 to 0.29 s slower held, all of it in the writes: each MiB went through the socket,
  copied in, copied out into memory zeroed for it, and the build waited for each. The bytes
  now go in two slots of memory the two share, allocated by the writer so that their pages
  are charged to it (mm/shmem.c `shmem_fallocate`; cgroup-v2.rst, "Memory Ownership"),
  only which slot and whose in the message, and a buffered writer of a build's file goes on
  once a write is handed, its writes settled before the file is flushed, sought in, taken
  back or dropped (`through::Through`): the writer makes one while the build makes the
  next. So at b8c98e7f and after, the writer outside in every held build (150 on Fedora
  and eight of CI's runners), held builds took no longer than unbudgeted beyond their
  rounds' spread but apt's on one runner by 0.1 s, which read again what its budget took
  of its cache layers' page cache (above). Those were the scope's: its VM process read and
  wrote the caches' ranges of the join disk, and a page cache folio is charged to the task
  that adds it (mm/filemap.c `filemap_add_folio`, `mem_cgroup_charge`); over
  `memory.high` the kernel reclaims from the scope's own memcgs alone (mm/memcontrol.c
  `reclaim_high`; mm/vmscan.c `shrink_node_memcgs`) and, with no swap, from its file pages
  alone (`get_scan_count`, `SCAN_FILE`), the unmapped first. So where the writer is outside
  the budget, each of a builder's cache ranges is read and written for its guest by the
  writer, over a connection of its own, a request a round trip (`block::Through`,
  build/outside.rs `serve_range`), and the guest writes a cache's changes past its own page
  cache (O_DIRECT, init `caches.rs`): their page cache is the writer's, which no reclaim of
  the budget scans. With a round trip for each 4 KiB of a request (e0e430d5), apt's step
  end on CI took 0.31 to 1.00 s held against 0.10 to 0.54 free; in one (d9c42120), 0.09 to
  0.61 against 0.09 to 0.63, and no pair is slower held beyond the spread (PM M442).
- **An image's root filesystem over its base's** (PM M442; built and measured). An
  export wrote its image's whole root filesystem, rust:1-slim's 850 MiB again for a build
  that added 7 MiB; over its base's on Fedora's Btrfs, that export takes 0.1 s at p50
  against 0.9 (b8c98e7f against 2d168658). Where the store's file system clones a file
  (APFS's clonefile, Btrfs's and XFS's FICLONE: `shards_build::host::clone_file`), the image now
  starts as a clone of the root filesystem kept for its base's layers, sharing its blocks,
  and only what the build added is written past them: the image's metadata, whole, and the
  data of each file the base had not as it is (`shards_erofs::write_over`), each file the
  base had, its data unchanged (the same place in the build's sources as in the base's
  snapshot, and a file of that size at its path in the base's root filesystem read back),
  pointed at in the base's blocks. Its superblock replaces the base's first block; the
  kernel finds the metadata where `meta_blkaddr` says (erofs_fs.h, `erofs_iloc`) and a
  flat file's data at its `raw_blkaddr` wherever that is in the device (data.c,
  `erofs_map_blocks`), so the guest mounts it as any image, and it is a file of its own
  whatever becomes of its base's. Where nothing clones (ext4, CI's runners), it is
  written whole, as before. Its images are told apart by their producer (`snapshot 1,
  over its base's root filesystem 1`).

  Such an image holds its layers' tree, the same entries, kinds, modes, owners, times,
  xattrs, link targets, device numbers, hard links and file bytes, but not their stacked
  bytes: its metadata lies past its base's blocks, and its files' data where the base or
  the build put it. Nothing reads a root filesystem's bytes as its layers' (an image's ID
  and digests are its config's and blobs', `save` and `push` send the blobs, a guest reads
  the tree; store.rs: blobs keep the registry's bytes for them), but much takes a root filesystem's *name* to keep its bytes: a template is
  keyed by the path (run.rs `template`), saved with its guest's page cache, EROFS inodes
  and DAX mappings of it by block, and restored and its pool refilled by opening that path
  again later (run.rs `Origin`, daemon/refill.rs), and
  `Partial::commit` keeps a file already at a name as "the same bytes". A stacked image's
  name kept that, as stacking always lays the same layers out alike, and the snapshot's
  whole export alike (tests/build.rs `assert_rootfs_is_its_layers`, byte for byte); an
  image over a base, put at the same name, did not: once it went while a template of it
  stayed (a collection removes root filesystems, then the templates whose root filesystem
  has gone, and one that stops between, as `collect_garbage` does on an error, leaves
  those), a run would stack it again under that name and restore the template against
  other bytes. So an image over a base is named apart, by the SHA-256 of its base's name
  and of what is written over the clone (`<ChainID>.over-<hex>.erofs`), which make its
  bytes, and a record beside the stacked one's place names it (`<ChainID>.over`;
  `Store::kept_at`): a name is never given other bytes, whichever image goes and comes
  again. The tests hold an export over a base to its layers' tree, entry by entry and
  byte for byte of each file (`assert_same_tree`), and one written whole to their stacked
  bytes (CI 41989398811: APFS's export over its base's, failing the byte comparison).

  `pull --no-cache` is the one way a name comes to hold other bytes: it builds the image
  again where a file at its name may not hold what its layers stack to (a producer's whose
  rules proved wrong, a file changed on disk). Before, `Partial::commit` kept that file as
  "the same bytes", throwing the build away, and its producer's mark was removed first, so
  a kept snapshot-written image lost it. Now one that holds the same bytes, compared whole,
  is kept with its mark, and whatever was made of it holds; one that holds others is
  replaced by rename (`Partial::commit_again`), whoever holds it open keeping their own,
  given a later modification time than it (two seconds past it where the clock is not,
  past FAT's coarsest file times), and unmarked once in place, so that a crash between
  leaves a producer named of a file it never wrote, which its disowning only builds again.
  Templates are keyed by the root filesystem's length and modification time as their run
  found them (`shards_image::store::rootfs_stamp`, run.rs `template`), which the daemon's
  record keeps (`Origin`): a replaced file's runs key templates of their own, the old
  file's are live no more and go at the next collection, and a pool keyed before refills
  against the new file no more (refill.rs), its claims booting instead.

**Measured against DAMON (PM M293).** DAMON_RECLAIM, built into the pinned kernel, does
nothing in a run's guest as the kernel has it (its watermarks, which run it only while a
guest's free memory is between a fifth and a half of it, kept it off in five rounds of
six); held active it gives back 53 MiB of a gigabyte
read in 180 s, or 568 MiB in 90 s with min_age 5 s, monitoring one range of the guest's
memory, at 1.5% of a CPU idle against 0.2. D188 gives back 875 MiB within 10 s, and nothing
until the host is short. DAMON stays off.

**Measured (PM M267, M268).** On the Mac, the guest's 944 MiB of a read file reclaimed in
33 ms (p50); with the flush, 946 MiB back to the host within 0.5 s (p50, the builtin 81
ms), where reporting at its own pace gave back 374 MiB by 2 s, 630 by 4 s and 952 by 8 s.
51 MiB of the read's stays: the page structures of the memory it plugged, and the
kernel's. On Linux (KVM) the same: 835 MiB back within 0.5 s (p50, 70 ms with the flush),
paced 357 by 1 s, 615 by 4 s, 866 by 8 s, 50 to 59 MiB staying. Unplugged after the
working set shrinks, all but 12 to 20 MiB of a gigabyte the guest plugged, used and freed,
on both.

**Measured (PM M309).** On CI's x86_64 runners (AMD EPYC 7763, 9V45 and 9V74, Intel Xeon
8370C, 8573C and 6973P, each a virtual machine its KVM is nested in), a gigabyte read
through FUSE under a slice held to 384 MiB with no swap took 355 to 604 s where it took 3
to 5 s with no budget; held within its budget's room and never closer than the least room
a run goes on in to what it uses, 4.79 s at the median sparse and 4.99 written, 8.38 and
9.14 at the most, where it took 4.65 and 4.95 with none (n 24 each, f0a68074): every read
within twice the median of none, where runs held at what they used had crawled for 190 to
672 s. On 12 more runners, each of those six CPUs among them, every read under the budget
took within 1.59 times its CPU's median under none (n 36 each). Its guest's own RAM, its template's pages, stayed: a read refaulted 1,634 file
pages at the median sparse and 3,016 written, where one read had refaulted 16.5 million;
counting only the files charged to the budget, 20,586 written at the median and 273,132 at
the most. On bare metal (an Intel Core i9-14900HX, Linux 6.19), 1.10 s sparse and 1.32
written at the median, 2.13 and 2.59 at the most, where it took 1.25 and 1.42 with none
(n 12 each), and no read refaulted a page.

**Tested.** Unit (platform): the host's memory pressure can be watched where the daemon
runs. Unit (daemon): a budget's room, the least any cgroup over a microVM leaves, its
unmapped page cache counted as room and its shared memory not, none with no budget and
none at the root (`a_budgets_room_is_the_least_any_cgroup_over_a_microvm_leaves`); the
files a budget's processes map held, past what its cgroup counts mapped, and the kernel's
inactive buffer beside them; a give-back saying what it gave or why it gave nothing, one
with no answer in time said so; and a microVM that does not answer its give-back keeping
no other's from the host, nor asked again until it has ended
(`a_microvm_that_does_not_give_back_keeps_no_other_waiting`, which passes asking one after
another hang on). Unit (init): a run held within its room, never closer to what it uses
than the least room a run goes on in, which a room short of it raises no hold past
(`a_run_is_held_within_its_budgets_room`), that room covering what a reader of 1 MiB
blocks needed on 4 and 18 CPUs (`a_run_held_short_keeps_the_room_its_reads_need`); a
microVM held to a budget plugging no more than its cap needs. E2E on Linux, real microVMs
under a slice of the user's manager, no swap (tests/containers.rs
`a_microvm_held_to_a_budget_gives_back_what_it_holds_cold`): a microVM that read 512 MiB
through FUSE into its guest's page cache (a file of a window's range or more is its host's
page cache, mapped into it: D189) gives back what it holds cold once a `MemoryHigh` of 384
MiB short of it is set, idle as it is, the daemon's log saying what it gave back and that
it holds it within its budget, in which it reads a gigabyte, in files of a MiB, to the
end; each budget set anew said, whatever room it leaves (its host's give-back between a
budget's word and the next left its microVM within the next, which nothing said: CI
41344493548); a give-back whose answer is lost to the daemon's 10 s, its guest giving back as it
was ended, followed by the budget's word all the same (12 runs of 12 on Fedora, where 3 of
19 had the daemon say nothing of the budget, PM M391). tests/budget.rs
`a_microvm_held_to_a_budget_reads_through_fuse_at_the_pace_of_reads_held_to_none`: runs
restored from their template, its warm microVMs in the slice, read a gigabyte through FUSE
under a `MemoryHigh` its idle microVMs leave 128 MiB of, each read followed by the marks
its guest prints as it reads (testguest `read-marked`: as it opens the file and at each MiB
it crosses) and judged by the reads held to none before it (goal 71's cluster 8; D215's
shape and the person's ruling of 2026-11-13, "No ×2"): past the slowest of them, from its
first mark to its last, a read goes on while each window as long reads what their slowest
MiB keeps over it, and is refused, typed, at the first that does not (`Stalled::Slow`: how
far it had read, what it read over the window and what it had to, and the record); before
its first mark, past the slowest start seen, it goes on while its daemon or a microVM
shows progress, never refused before each of its VM processes has been judged over a whole
slice (`common::Patience`, D209), or while its slice's tasks stalled on memory within a
minute, as PSI's `some` total says (`memory.pressure`, Linux's
Documentation/accounting/psi.rst: a host's hold counts as held, R03), and is refused
otherwise (`Stalled::Unstarted`); the first read, with nothing seen before it, follows its
microVM's liveness alone, to its end. Until #77 a start slower than three of the slowest
start's looks was refused before any VM process had been looked at twice: under the budget
on adacachy2 (Linux 7.3.3 x86_64) at 8bfa6150e and 9d2da923d, 97.49 ms after its command
began against a slowest start of 32.44 ms, its slice at its `memory.high` with 4345 `high`
events. `a_slow_start_is_refused_only_past_a_whole_slice_without_progress_or_hold` plays
starts of 500 ms against a slowest of 30 ms, one with a running stand-in VM process not yet
judged and one in a slice its host holds all along, each followed to its end, and a start
that never comes, refused past a whole slice. The held slice's PSI total is read at each
look as its kernel sums one, a stall still on counted to the read's own clock (Linux 7.2
kernel/sched/psi.c `psi_show`, `get_recent_times`): the time since the stall began. Until
2026-11-17 a thread of the test's wrote it each 5 ms, and CI runs 43876891053 (x86_64 musl)
and 43926955660 (arm64 gnu) refused that start 60 and 361 ms in, a look finding the total as
the look before had where the thread had not run between them. The record is the reads held to none
alone, never seeded, so that a budget's reads never raise the bound they are judged by.
Until 237f3ebe7 the medians of 3 were held within twice those under none, a multiple, and
each read was waited on 600 s and past that while its microVM ran: on adacachy2 (32 CPUs)
a read held within the least room, its microVM thrashing at its slice's `memory.high`, ran
28 minutes reading all along, until it was ended by hand. The judge's own test plays reads
to it (`a_read_is_judged_by_the_pace_of_the_reads_held_to_none`: a crawl refused at its
second look, a read keeping 16 times the least pace past the bound let through, a cold read
with a second's stop followed to its end, a start that never comes refused): 1 of 1 on
adacachy2 (Linux 7.3.3-1-cachyos x86_64, rustc 1.98.1) at 9472ec737, with clippy
`--all-targets -D warnings` of shards and shards-vmm, and of shards-testguest for
x86_64-unknown-linux-musl, clean. The E2E itself, on a KVM host with a user's systemd
manager, is ROOT's. It runs alone in its test binary
so other daemon tests do not compete between its phases (CI 41365265628: 2.06 times beside
them; alone, 4 runs of 4 passed on Fedora 44, kernel 6.19.10, i9-14900HX, at 49ee67a5
with the host at load 24 to 45, the slowest phase's median 0.46 to 1.34 times its run's
median under none). A run begun under no budget, held to one set as it goes, is judged
so too, and so is a run alone in the slice, its daemon keeping no warm microVM there,
held under a budget short of what the slice holds, its kernel's inactive buffer and its
host's own reads' room, by a mebibyte, within the least room a run goes on in (where held
at what they used they read a gigabyte at 0.16 to 0.57 MiB/s, PM M309; with warm microVMs beside
it, the budget ended them for room, and room came back to every run, PM M314): dispatched
alone on CI, 32 of 32 copies passed on four runner CPUs (PM M318). On macOS and Windows,
which have no group of processes a user's tools cap, a group shards keeps (D183's slice 3):
`a_microvm_under_a_group_is_held_to_its_budget`, a share's files given back, on Windows
through D197's FUSE server over NTFS (its microVMs from 764 to 768 MiB to 272 on jupiter,
within a budget 451 to 492 MiB short); and
`what_a_joiner_reads_of_its_image_is_given_back_at_its_groups_budget`, 512 MiB of a
joiner's image read through its guest's page cache (D119), its group's `memory.high` written a
quarter GiB short of its VM process: told its room and asked to give back, the microVM
gives back what its joiner read, its VM process from 642 to 651 MiB to 261 to 266 on
jupiter's WHP and from 1,028 to 1,038 to 265 to 275 on the M5 Max, idle 253 to 256 (PM
M391). At its host's word, on every host
(`what_a_microvm_holds_cold_is_given_back_at_its_hosts_word`, its daemon told through
`SHARDS_PRESSURE`): what a joiner read, 128 to 382 MiB of it, given back, its VM process
back to within 6 MiB of what it held idle 1.1 to 1.2 s after the word on jupiter and 1.6
to 1.7 s on Fedora, and within 15 MiB 1.9 to 2.0 s after it on the M5 Max (PM M391). Unit (platform), Windows: each low memory
signal a word, one that lasts said again every 2 s and none while memory is not low (an
event standing in for the system's notification), and the system's own unsignalled while
a gigabyte is available; each of 8 mutants caught on jupiter. `an_idle_daemon_wakes_for_nothing` (tests/daemon.rs) holds the
idle daemon's threads still.

**Measured (PM M268, macOS).** Of a gigabyte a guest plugged, filled with its own pages
and the kernel's among them, and freed, the driver gave back 98% within 0.1 s, 18 MiB
staying (p50) in 3 of its 8 blocks; online as auto-movable, 14 MiB in one; all movable,
none. Plugged memory stays the kernel's own (D133).

**Not yet.** A budget below what a cold-booted microVM holds cannot be met: its guest's RAM
is all anonymous memory, which its host cannot take back without swap, and a read under
such a budget is throttled for as long as it runs (761 to 1,729 s a gigabyte, PM M318),
where one restored from its template holds that template's clean pages beside as much
anonymous memory, which its host may take back. A builder gives back its files and what
it holds plugged past its use at its build's word (above; PM M442, of its files a build at
p50 on each host: apt's 0 to 142 MiB, npm's 1 to 26, rust's 0 to 31), but most of what
its steps write it keeps in tmpfs layers, 148 MiB of Shmem after an npm install of 73 MiB
of packages against 1.4 MiB of file pages (PM M295), which no give-back of file pages
takes: that comes back as its layers leave memory, to its swap window or a layer on the
host's disk as a run's (D190). M268 at larger sizes.

### D189. Volumes' file data once, in the host's page cache: virtio-fs DAX windows (built: every share's window as long as its host's memory, but on a virtual machine on an AMD CPU)

**Review memory-09 (2026-11-14): which files a window maps, learned where it runs.**
`DAX_SMALLEST`, 1 MiB, PM M338's crossover on the Mac and Fedora, held on every host, is
gone. The server says which files *may* be mapped (a regular file it may read, and write
where the window needs it: `Server::dax_of`, whatever its size); each share's device
decides which *are* (`fs::crossover`), and only takes the window away (it clears
`fuse_attr.flags`' FUSE_ATTR_DAX in a reply), never gives it, so no cost moves a
permission. The device sees both ways: a READ, its server's answer timed from ask to
reply, and a SETUPMAPPING, its own, timed from its descriptor's ask to its window's
mapping, each a cost a byte of the file it served, kept by the file's size class (the
power of two at or below its size, known from the attributes the replies told) as the
cheapest and dearest seen, the spread its uncertainty. A class whose window's dearest
costs no more a byte than FUSE's cheapest is mapped; one where they overlap, or FUSE's
reach below, is read. The least class at and past which every known class is mapped is the
crossover, and a class past it not yet known is mapped too. *Cold start:* a class with
fewer than two costs of either way (two, the fewest that show a spread) is calibrating:
its files are told each way in turn as the guest learns of them (the first mapped), each
file keeping its way while it calibrates. *Failure:* a class in which a mapping failed is
read, its errno kept (`Verdict::Failed`). A file the guest maps already keeps its mapping
until its kernel lets the inode go (`fuse_dax_dontcache`). The learner is the device's,
in the VM process's memory, as a restored VM's starts cold. *What it cannot see:* the
guest's faults on a mapped page and its copies into its own page cache of what it read,
which are its vCPUs', and a reread's cost. *Owed to ROOT:* D189's file-size/working-tree
harness (PM M338's) on HVF, KVM x86_64 and WHP, and KVM arm64 through the L1 path: per
size class, cold read, warm reread and overwrite, and resident memory, n ≥ 20 per class
with p50/p90/p99/max, against the learner's chosen crossover; and `cargo test -p shards
--test containers a_volumes_files_are_mapped_as_its_share_learns`, `a_volumes_large_files_go_through_its_dax_window`
and the other DAX tests (dma, budget, saved, slates_fs), whose files are now mapped as a
cold share calibrates: the first file of each size class mapped, the next read.

**Found.** The user's plan, item 5. A volume's file the guest reads is in the host's page
cache and again in the guest's (944 MiB of a 1 GiB file, PM M267), and every read and write
goes through the share process: two copies a request, on one queue (the benchmark's
trial, n 1: 1.1 GB/s of 1 MiB reads, where Cloud Hypervisor's virtiofsd gave 4.4). Linux's
virtiofs maps a file's ranges into a window of device memory that the host fills from the
file itself (DAX, fs/fuse/dax.c), with the pinned kernel's CONFIG_FUSE_DAX: the data then
lives once, in the host's page cache, and reads and writes are the guest's own loads and
stores.

**Built so far.**
- Each shared directory's device, the join share's too, may offer a DAX window
  (`MachineConfig::share_window_mib`, snapshot format 22): virtio-fs's cache, shared memory
  region 0 (VIRTIO_FS_SHMCAP_ID_CACHE), at a GiB boundary past the swap window, whole 2 MiB
  ranges as the guest maps files in them, within the addresses the guest's CPU has. The
  daemon gives every microVM's shares one, as long as its host's memory unless
  `SHARDS_SHARE_WINDOW_MIB` says another length (below), and keys its templates by it.
- The VM process answers FUSE_SETUPMAPPING and FUSE_REMOVEMAPPING itself
  (devices/virtio/fs/window.rs). Linux names a mapping's file by its node alone, its
  handle -1 (fs/fuse/dax.c, `fuse_setup_one_mapping`), so the VM process asks its share
  process for a descriptor of the node's file (a control frame; the descriptor by
  SCM_RIGHTS), which the server opens along the node's path, checked to be the node, as
  virtiofsd does (`setupmapping`): to read, and to write where the mapping is to be
  written, never in a volume the guest may not write. The ask says the range the mapping
  maps too, its offset and length (`descriptor_ask`), for a server that keeps a file's
  bytes in an object of its own (slates' shares answer each with a shared-memory object
  of the file, agreed 2026-10-24); shards' own reads the node and the flag alone. The
  range is mapped into the window shared: on KVM one memslot covers the window and its
  MMU notifiers follow each range placed in it; on HVF each range is mapped at stage 2
  as it is placed, readable and executable (a guest runs programs from its volumes), and
  writable where the guest may write it.
- HVF maps a shared range only from a descriptor opened to write too (M17), and a private
  one goes on showing the guest the bytes it first read after the host writes the file
  (M270): there every range's descriptor is opened to read and write, and the guest is
  told to map only files its server may write, in volumes it may write
  (`window::SHARED_NEEDS_WRITE`); a read-only volume's files go through FUSE.
- Which files: init mounts each volume `dax=inode` (a kernel without FUSE's DAX refuses the
  option, and the volume is mounted without it), and its server says which files to map
  (FUSE_HAS_INODE_DAX, FUSE_ATTR_DAX): regular files of 1 MiB or more that it may read
  (`DAX_SMALLEST`, PM M338). Measured from 4 KiB to 2 MiB through a window and through
  FUSE on the Mac and on Fedora's performance and efficient cores (first reads cold and
  warm, re-reads, overwrites, memory, a working tree's 66,357 files and 70,000 of 4 KiB),
  1 MiB is the smallest size from which the window is no worse on every host: from
  256 KiB on the Mac and Fedora's efficient cores, from 1 MiB on its performance cores,
  where a 256 KiB file's cold overwrite took 251 to 258 µs through a window (the host
  reads the page a guest's store lands in) and 202 to 209 through FUSE. A smaller file
  goes through FUSE: below 64 KiB a mapping's round trip to the share process and host
  mmap cost a first read more than it saves, and a 4 KiB file's mapping held 23 to 28 KiB
  more of its VM's memory than FUSE's page. Linux on arm64 is unmeasured: no host here
  runs KVM on it. FUSE_INIT says the host's page size (map_alignment). The guest's kernel
  decides a file's DAX as it makes the file's inode (fs/fuse/dax.c `fuse_dax_inode_init`)
  and, told another later, lets the inode go once unused (`fuse_dax_dontcache`): a file the
  host makes while its guest runs, looked up by its notice (D235) before it is 1 MiB long,
  goes through FUSE until its inode is made again (PM M550).
- On Linux each of a VM's windows (its shares' and its join share's) is no longer than
  lets every range of them be mapped at once within the host's `vm.max_map_count`
  (`share_window_bound_mib`): a range of a file shorter than it takes two of its VM
  process's mappings (the file's and the zeros past it), a whole range one, a VM 385 of
  its own on 32 CPUs and a stack and its guard for each further vCPU (PM M338), and the
  guest maps every range when it must, the host refusing a mapping past the limit and the
  guest's access failing. Linux's default, 65,530, holds a VM of one volume to 31.8 GiB a
  window; Fedora's 1,048,576 to more than its host's memory.
- A range never holds a page of its file wholly past the file's end, which the host cannot
  give: HVF ends the vCPU's run at an access there (M271), and x86 KVM retries it without
  end, its vCPU spinning in KVM_RUN (M273). A range is the file's pages to the one that
  holds its end, and the window's anonymous zeros past it, from its mapping on; and before
  the device passes a reply that may tell the guest a file's size (its request's node's,
  and the entries a LOOKUP, CREATE, MKNOD, MKDIR, SYMLINK, LINK or READDIRPLUS gives), the
  window follows the file: its pages where it has grown, zeros where it was cut short.
- Another process cutting a file short under a mapping, which the guest reads past before
  it learns the size, never ends the microVM nor holds a vCPU. On Linux the VM names each
  file its windows begin to map to the daemon (`kind::WATCH`, the descriptor with it), and
  the daemon watches them with its one inotify instance, as an instance a microVM would run
  a user out of them (M257), and tells the VM of one cut short (`kind::CUT`): its window
  gives zeros there, and a vCPU that spun there runs on. HVF's abort and arm64 KVM's
  EFAULT have the window follow the file at once. Until the guest asks the file's size
  again it reads zeros there, as through FUSE it may read stale bytes from its page cache.
  A cut beneath a directory its share watches is a notice (D235): the guest's init touches
  the file, and the SETATTR's reply tells its kernel the size, so that a reader there reads
  zeros only until the notice lands, and then the file's end; a file moved out of the share
  and then cut is told as its name goes, its cut never, and its guest reads zeros there
  until it asks (PM M550).
- An OPEN of a file the window maps, and a CREATE that opens one there already, is told
  to keep what the guest has of it (FOPEN_KEEP_CACHE): Linux drops a file's cached pages at
  each open, and for a mapped file those are DAX entries its processes may still map, which
  it lets go of first and unmaps after, its 2 MiB pages' counts going wrong, and every build
  of the benchmark's cargo workload ended in SIGBUS (M274). A mapped file has no page cache
  of the guest's to go stale. A size change another process makes, seen in the file's
  attributes or in the reply to a SETATTR that sets no size (each notice's touch, D235),
  takes the same path in the guest kernel, which shards' kernel's patch 0007 closes
  (resources/kernel/patches): a DAX file's entries left to its layouts' own breaking. The
  SETATTR's is closed from the kernel inputs 54fba99afaee on, released as
  kernel-6.18.48-54fba99afaee (kernel.yml run 43459558423) and pinned in `src/kernel.rs` and
  the tests' `common::kvm_kernel`, each artifact by the release's own name, size and SHA-256:
  before it a notice of a size change to a file a guest process maps in 2 MiB pages let go of
  entries the process still maps, `fs/dax.c:415 dax_folio_put` in its guest's log (PM M550).
- A mapping is charged its file's bytes in its range against the microVM's I/O limits
  (D178) as it is made, once its file's size says them: a 5,000-byte file's range 5,000
  bytes, not the range's 2 MiB, which every file's last range was charged before, and a
  range past its file's end nothing (`a_dax_mapping_maps_the_file_of_its_node`). The
  guest's loads and stores through it are memory, which the host's page cache serves and
  writes back.
- A save (D176) keeps each mapping (snapshot format 23), and its restore maps each range
  again from its new share process, as the run gives the share its server, once that
  server has the tables the guest's node IDs are in, and before the guest runs; a range
  whose file that server no longer reaches is zeros, as past a file's end.
- **Each file's size looked at once a request** (PM M299). Each reply of the server's has
  the window follow the files it tells of first (`Window::reconcile`), the request's own
  among them; it looked at a file's size once for each range it mapped of it, so a request
  about a file mapped in 1,024 ranges took 1,024 fstat(2)s, and every write through such a
  file's window paid for the guest's requests about it: on Fedora a 4 KiB write took 288
  µs where a FUSE_WRITE took 86. Each file is now looked at once a pass (`window::Sizes`),
  and a write through the window costs less than a FUSE_WRITE at p50 in every case
  measured: 4 KiB at random over 2 GiB 30.6 µs against 44.6, close together 23.4 against
  44.4, 1 MiB close together 74 against 855. Held by
  `a_file_mapped_in_many_ranges_is_looked_at_once` (mutation-checked: 8 looks for 8
  ranges).
- **A file its window cannot follow is a reply refused** (memory-01, PM M573; D197's slice
  4 on Windows). Where `reconcile` cannot make a file's ranges what it is (its size unread,
  its grown pages not mapped), it refuses, typed (`fs::Unfollowed`), and the reply that
  would tell the guest the file's size is refused it (EIO): its guest never hears a size
  whose bytes its window does not hold, and the file is followed again at its next request.
- **Each window's page structures in its head, not its guest's memory** (PM M300). Linux
  describes a window's pages as it probes the device, with page structures (64 bytes for
  each 4 KiB page) it took from guest RAM: a 64th of the window (M269), from a guest that,
  given its memory as it needs it (virtio-mem, D133), boots with little. Each window's
  device now gives a head right before the window, shared memory region 0xfe (`fs::HEAD`):
  memory of the VM's own, sized so that head and window are whole sections, each
  section's page structures a 2 MiB block of the head (`head::window_head_len`: one 128
  MiB section for a window of 1 or 4 GiB), since a part section's would come from guest
  RAM on x86_64 (vmemmap_populate). The guest's kernel maps head and window as one range
  whose page structures are the head's, a vmem_altmap, as libnvdimm keeps a pmem
  namespace's (shards' kernel patch 0008); a kernel without the patch maps the window as
  before. A snapshot keeps the heads as it keeps a writable layer's (D190): each alike 2
  MiB block once, beside its memory (`window-heads`, format 25), mapped back after a
  template's save and privately by each restore. A microVM saved in format 24, as shards
  0.6.0 saves, is refused as it is resumed, its init another build's (D176, *A saved
  microVM resumes only in a shards whose init its guest speaks*). A window took a 64th of its length of its
  guest's free memory, 64.1 MiB for 4 GiB on Fedora, and 72.0 on the Mac with its linear
  map's page tables; with its head, none on Fedora (-0.2 to 0.1 MiB at every length, n 12)
  and those page tables alone on the Mac (8.3 MiB). Fedora's 4 GiB boot reached PID 1 20 ms
  sooner: its page structures go on the host's huge pages, not on a boot's base pages
  (D29). arm64 Linux maps memory it adds in base pages under rodata=full (arch_add_memory,
  force_pte_mapping), so that a page's permissions can change alone, which a DAX device's
  linear alias never does: shards' kernel patch 0010 maps a file system DAX device's memory
  in blocks, but where debug_pagealloc or a realm needs base pages, and an arm64 window
  takes none of its guest's memory either (0.0 to 0.1 MiB at every length to 4 GiB, n 12,
  M300). The pinned kernel carries both (since kernel-6.18.48-8df0015cca35); held by
  `a_dax_windows_page_structures_take_none_of_its_guests_memory`, its bound the spread of
  boots alone.
- **Whole pages a host does not hold written as FUSE_WRITEs** (PM M301). A store into a
  page its host does not hold waits for the host to read it, where a FUSE_WRITE's pwrite(2)
  of the whole page reads nothing (M283). Each window's device now keeps a record of which
  of the window's pages its host holds, one bit a 4 KiB page, in memory of its own right
  after the window, shared memory region 0xfd (`fs::HELD`, `head::window_held_len`): taken
  with `mincore(2)` as each range is mapped, cleared as it is unmapped, and taken again
  once a mapping after its first FUSE_WRITE, as the host reads around faults since
  (`Window::rerecord`). The guest's kernel (shards' patch 0009) maps, or upgrades from
  read alone, each range a write of whole pages meets, as a store would, then writes the
  host's whole pages its host does not hold as FUSE_WRITEs and the rest through the
  window, and records the pages it writes and reads. The host's page is FUSE_INIT's
  map_alignment, 16 KiB on Apple silicon: a FUSE_WRITE of part of one makes the host read
  the rest first, as a store does, so parts of host pages go through the window (on the
  Mac, 4 KiB FUSE_WRITEs into cold 16 KiB pages lost to the stores they replaced, M301). The record is advice: a page the host let go
  of since is read in as a store meets it, as before. Nothing keeps it: a restore takes it
  again as it maps each range (snapshot format 26, for the layout). The VM process's
  seccomp allowlist has `mincore`. On Fedora a cold file's scattered 4 KiB writes through
  the window took 315 to 319 µs at p99 where they took 1,604 to 1,905 (FUSE's 153 to 180),
  at twice the rate; 1 MiB into ranges not yet mapped a fifth to a third less at p50;
  nothing warm lost. Its first build sent a range's first write after a read as a FUSE_WRITE
  by a record taken before the read's fault read the range around, and the next store paid
  the upgrade after it (64 KiB writes 131.5 µs at p50 against 94.9): a read's mapping is
  upgraded as the write comes. A reply about a file the window maps in 1,024 ranges looks at
  that file's ranges alone, and its ranges follow it only where its size changed (`Table`,
  0.29 µs at p50 where walking every range took 8.54). Held by
  `a_ranges_held_pages_are_recorded_as_it_is_mapped`,
  `a_files_ranges_follow_it_only_where_it_changed`, and
  `a_volumes_large_files_go_through_its_dax_window` (whole pages written where the host
  holds none, read by host and guest). The pinned kernel carries the patch (since
  kernel-6.18.48-4970e0190ebe). On the Mac, evicted with msync(2) MS_INVALIDATE (M301: rewriting the
  file had timed the SSD's flush), cold 64 KiB writes into ranges mapped first took 306 µs
  at p50 where they took 2,459 (FUSE's 204 to 220), and 1 MiB into ranges not yet mapped
  1,310 where 2,811 (FUSE's 1,243 to 1,434); cold 4 KiB writes, parts of 16 KiB host
  pages, cost what they did.
- **One descriptor a file** (PM M302). The slowest write where ranges are mapped as
  writes come took 7.8 to 32.6 ms on every kernel (M301): the window kept each mapped
  range's descriptor, so its VM process's descriptor table grew as the run's mappings
  passed 128, 256, 512 and 1,024 descriptors, and Linux, growing a table other threads
  share, waits a grace period of RCU first (fs/file.c, expand_fdtable): 9 to 24 ms, once a
  growth. The window now keeps one descriptor a file (`Node::file`), which follows its size
  and maps more of it as it grows; each range's own, from its server, closes once the range
  is mapped, as virtiofsd's does: the slowest mapping took 0.25 to 0.5 ms. Mapping a
  file's ranges from one descriptor, which spares the server's open (6 to 19 µs), was
  measured and not taken: one open file's readahead stops reading around its faults after
  a hundred misses (mm/filemap.c, MMAP_LOTSAMISS), where each range's open begins anew
  (1,285 µs against 682 at p50 for kernel A's writes after a page of each range was
  written). A range mapped to be read alone keeps no record, which no guest reads: its
  mincore(2) took 51 to 53 µs of a warm mapping's 75 to 77. Held by
  `a_window_keeps_one_descriptor_of_a_file` (mutation-checked: 401 descriptors more for
  400 ranges where each range's was kept).

- **A device reaches the pages of the files its guest maps** (PM M304). A guest names its
  devices the pages a mapping of a file holds as any of its pages: an O_DIRECT read or
  write, and on a share a write that grows a file the window maps (fs/fuse/dax.c,
  `fuse_dax_direct_write`), whose user pages FUSE gives its device (fs/fuse/file.c,
  `fuse_get_user_pages`). A DAX file's are device memory, a pmem device's (the image's
  root, the writable layer) or a window's, which no device reached: in a microVM with a 64
  MiB window, an append to a file the window maps, from a mapping of another, was answered
  as done with 0 bytes written, and an O_DIRECT read into a mapping of one as done with its
  bytes missing; an O_DIRECT write from such a mapping was whole only because Linux's FUSE
  wrote it again, buffered, once the direct write wrote nothing (`direct_write_fallback`).
  Each device that gives its guest such memory now says so (`VirtioDevice::device_memory`:
  a pmem device's file, a layer's file system, a share's window), and its guest memory
  gives it to every device as RAM (`GuestMemory::give_devices`): system calls given its
  pages (`io_ptr`: a disk's transfers, vsock's), whose kernel answers EFAULT where one is
  gone, and an access's copies by `platform::copy_checked` (virtio-fs's requests and
  replies, a network frame), a copy whose fault its signal handler resumes as failed, as
  Linux resumes its own copies from user memory (its exception tables), never the end of
  the VM's process: a file cut short under its mapping by another process, which the window
  follows only as it learns (above), takes the request at it alone. It costs what the VMM's
  copy of RAM does on Fedora, and 1.2 times it for 1 MiB on the Mac, where a copy through a
  pipe cost 3.4 to 9 times memcpy (M304). A request whose bytes, or whose answer's, a
  device cannot reach is answered EIO (virtio-fs) or an I/O error (a disk), and a frame
  dropped (virtio-net), never served short. A GPU's renderer and a passed-through function
  are given RAM alone, as before. Held by
  `a_microvms_devices_reach_the_pages_of_the_files_it_maps` (mutation-checked: without
  device memory the append fails), and vmm's
  `device_memory_is_reached_as_ram_is_and_its_lost_pages_fail`,
  `a_requests_device_memory_goes_whole_and_its_lost_pages_fail_it`,
  `a_transfer_reaches_device_memory_and_its_lost_pages_fail_it`,
  `a_frame_from_device_memory_is_sent_and_one_whose_page_is_gone_dropped`,
  `a_checked_copy_fails_where_its_pages_are_gone` and
  `a_fault_outside_a_checked_copy_still_ends_its_process`.
- **What a window's guest makes of it, made as its guest uses it** (PM M306). A window's
  length cost its microVM what its guest's kernel made of the window at once, whatever it
  went on to map: its page structures, a 64th of it, written into its head as the guest
  probed the device (for 64 GiB, 1,044 MiB of its VM process's memory on the Mac and on
  Fedora, and 1.4 s of Fedora's boot), every one of which a template's save then read;
  the structures of its head's own pages, a 4,096th of it, each its own (each lists
  itself), so that every template kept them (18 MiB for 64 GiB); and FUSE DAX's mapping of
  each 2 MiB range, 128 bytes, made at every mount and freed at every unmount (a 64 GiB
  window's run in its microVM set up 3.0 ms slower and ran 4.2 ms longer at p50 on Fedora
  than with 0012 and 0013, n 40). shards' kernel makes each as its guest uses it: patch
  0011 a range's page structures as FUSE first sets the range up (`PGMAP_LAZY_MEMMAP`),
  0012 none of the head's own pages', its metadata, which no pfn of it hands out, and 0013
  a range's mapping as the range is first wanted. A head's save reads none of the blocks of its own memory its guest never touched
  (`Head::untouched`, by `platform::untouched`), where reading them gave each of their pages
  memory on macOS, and a block mapped from a snapshot's copy is read whole, its untouched
  pages the copy's; one its guest wrote zeros over is mapped back as fresh memory, where a
  discard (MADV_DONTNEED) brought the copy's bytes back on Linux. A 64 GiB window costs a
  boot 2.1 MiB of its VM process's memory on the Mac and 2.8 on Fedora, a template what one
  of 4 GiB costs, and a run with a volume nothing measured (Fedora, n 40: setup 2.69 ms at
  p50 against 2.84 with no window, 5.66 before 0013). The pinned kernel carries the three
  (since kernel-6.18.48-e39058b2b627). Held by
  `a_long_dax_window_costs_its_boot_next_to_nothing` (a 4,096th of the window, what the
  structures of the head's own pages take: 0011 alone took 20,544 KiB, the kernel before it
  1,069,184, an x86_64 CI runner 8,392 with all three while each boot wrote its whole held
  record, M307),
  `a_volumes_long_dax_window_takes_its_guest_no_mapping_for_each_range` (768 kmalloc-128
  objects in use with no window, 33,440 with a 64 GiB one before 0013), and vmm's
  `a_heads_save_reads_no_block_its_guest_never_touched` and
  `a_heads_blocks_from_its_copy_are_saved_whole_and_zeroed_ones_mapped_back_fresh`
  (mutation-checked on Linux and the Mac; the two above on the Mac).
- **Every share's window as long as its host's memory, by default** (PM M307). A window
  maps what its guest reads and writes of a volume's files from the host's page cache,
  which holds no more of them at once than the host has memory, and one shorter than what
  its guest maps churns its mappings (M276: 1 GiB under a 2 GiB file read slower than 4
  GiB). Its length now costs what its guest maps of it (above), so the daemon gives every
  share, the join share's too, a window as long as its host's memory, as it gives a run a
  swap window that long (D159); `SHARDS_SHARE_WINDOW_MIB` another length, 0 none. Where its
  guest's addresses cannot hold so many that long past its RAM, the memory it may plug and
  its swap window (each the host's memory too), its VM gives each the most whole ranges
  that fit and says so, as its swap window takes what the addresses leave
  (`share_windows`), and records the length its machine has: a restore, its heads kept for
  that length, has it or is refused. Eight volumes and the join share took 83,538 MiB each
  on the Mac (40-bit addresses, 128 GiB) and 41,202 on Fedora (39-bit, 62.5 GiB). APFS
  fills the holes a small file's writes leave as the file is synced, so a head's copy
  punches them (`platform::punch_hole`, F_PUNCHHOLE; ext4 keeps them): a window's heads
  file takes 12 KiB where 4 MiB, and a writable layer's head 6.5 MiB where 12. A device's
  reset, which every boot's driver makes, unmaps its whole window, and cleared the whole of
  its held record with it, writing every page of it (2 MiB for 64 GiB); it clears the
  record of the ranges it unmaps alone, the only ones whose bits are set. On the Mac, with
  a window of its host's 128 GiB, a template's boot takes 0.2 MiB more of its VM process's
  memory (4.2 before), its template is the size of one without (70 MB), its restored VMs'
  footprint is the same (19.2 MiB against 19.5), and a run with a volume sets up as fast
  (1.44 ms at p50 against 1.75, n 40); on Fedora a 64 GiB window's boot takes 0.3 MiB. A
  booted window's head is on the host's base pages, as a restored one is: where THP is
  always (x86_64 CI runners) its one page structure written at boot took a 2 MiB huge page
  (afa9b355), and with base pages the window's boot is within a huge page of guest RAM of
  none's (-1.9 to +2.1 MiB). Its held record is on base pages too: there the first range's
  words took a huge page, all 512 pages of a 64 GiB window's record (e1df33d4). A
  template's map-back gives a head's run of zero blocks back in one call (5.4 ms for nine
  83 GiB windows on the Mac, where 6.5; 187 µs on Fedora), and its save keeps the index it
  wrote and the blocks it found untouched for it: the map-back reads nothing back from the
  copy, whose index read back from APFS took 2.8 ms at the median and up to 22, leaves
  untouched blocks as they are, and takes from its guest, and gives back, only the blocks
  it changes (`Head::changing`), one a head where it took nine heads whole: 0.21 ms at the
  median and 0.35 at the most on the Mac, where 2.3 and 25 (n 30 each, PM M311). Held by
  `placed_window_heads_give_up_only_the_blocks_their_map_back_changes` (mutation-checked)
  and
  `a_volumes_large_files_go_through_a_dax_window_by_default` (a 4 MiB file mapped by
  default, through FUSE with 0), vmm's `share_windows_go_one_after_another` (fitted, none,
  a kept length refused), `a_kept_blocks_pages_of_zeros_are_holes_in_its_copy` (synced as
  a commit syncs it), `a_head_mapped_back_gives_back_its_blocks_of_zeros` and
  `a_cleared_window_leaves_the_record_of_ranges_it_never_mapped_untouched`, each
  mutation-checked on the Mac.
- **None by default on a virtual machine on an AMD CPU** (PM M308). There a guest's first
  touch of each 4 KiB page a window gives it is mapped twice, by the host's KVM and by the
  hypervisor beneath, which shadows the host's nested paging: on CI's x86_64 runners,
  Azure virtual machines, a 1 GiB read through a window took 41.2 to 138.4 s at p50 on AMD
  EPYC 7763 and 9V74 runners (139.9 to 178.9 s written out) where FUSE took 3.0 to 6.4,
  its pages landing in guest RAM already mapped on the host's 2 MiB pages; and under a 384
  MiB budget 23.2 to 134.0 s. The host's KVM took 1.4 exits a page, its vCPU threads busy
  half the run in guest mode, which is the hypervisor beneath's own time; Hyper-V's
  enlightened NPT TLB flush was in use, so no flush was the cost. Each range advised onto
  huge pages (`huge.patch`: 2 MiB folios, mapped whole, 58 times fewer faults and KVM's
  own 2 MiB entries) read no faster, and three times slower on the 9V74s (123.3 and 129.1
  s against 41.2 and 42.4): the hypervisor beneath shadows 4 KiB at a time whatever the
  host maps. So the daemon gives a share no window there unless `SHARDS_SHARE_WINDOW_MIB`
  asks for one, and says so as it starts (`share_window_default`, from `/proc/cpuinfo`'s
  vendor and `hypervisor` flag); an Intel runner there read 1 GiB through a window in 2.0
  s (3.5 written) against FUSE's 2.6 (2.9), 14 µs a fault, and under the budget in 2.6 s
  against 6.1, and Fedora's bare metal in 1.37 against 1.23, both with windows as before;
  there 2 MiB folios read five times faster sparse (0.39 s), and are not taken (below).
  Held by daemon's `a_shares_window_by_default_follows_its_host`,
  containers' `a_volumes_large_files_go_through_a_dax_window_by_default` (the host's
  default, none with 0, one given on any host) and
  `a_microvm_held_to_a_budget_reads_a_large_file_through_its_window_to_its_end` (512 MiB
  past a 384 MiB `MemoryHigh` through a window given, the budget met, to its end).
- **A range is mapped as its host's kernel faults it, not advised onto 2 MiB folios** (PM
  M339). Advised onto huge pages (`MADV_HUGEPAGE`, with `MADV_RANDOM` or without), a
  range's first touch reads a 2 MiB folio, two without `MADV_RANDOM` (mm/filemap.c
  `do_sync_mmap_readahead`), where its host's file system makes large folios (ext4 since
  6.16), and KVM maps it with one stage-2 entry. On three Intel CI runners (Xeon 8573C)
  that read 1 GiB sparse in 0.36 to 0.42 s against 1.91 to 2.15 and a range's second page
  in 2.2 to 2.4 µs against 313 to 337. But a range's first touch took 1.4 to 10.2 ms at p50
  against 0.52 to 0.55, and 10 to 38 ms at p99 against 1.0 to 1.1. A store into the folio
  dirtied all of it, 2 MiB written back where 6 KiB (ext4's `block_page_mkwrite`,
  `iomap_dirty_folio`). And 1,000 touches left 2.0 to 2.8 GiB of the file in the page cache
  where 240 MiB. On eight AMD runners (EPYC 9V45, 7763, 9V74) first touches took 1.6 to
  6.1 ms where 1.05 to 1.29; sparse reads were faster beyond the rounds' spread on two
  7763s and slower beyond it on the 9V74. On Fedora's Btrfs, which makes no large folios but
  in an experimental build, the advice made none, and its faults read 4 MiB around them
  already (fs/btrfs/disk-io.c).
  By the rule fixed before any number (docs/research/measurements/dax-huge/measure.py),
  neither arm passed on any host, so no class of host takes one. Linux on arm64 is
  unmeasured: no host here runs KVM on it. macOS's madvise(2) has no such advice.

**Measured (PM M269).** What a window costs a guest as it boots: its page structures, which
Linux makes of it as it probes the device (virtio_fs_setup_dax, devm_memremap_pages of
MEMORY_DEVICE_FS_DAX): 18.1 MiB of free memory for a 1 GiB window, 73.7 for 4 GiB, a 64th of
it and 15% and some 2 MiB more; a boot reached PID 1 no later for one up to 2 GiB. A
template pays it once; what its restores pay is to be measured with mappings.

**Next.**
- A window's ranges on 2 MiB folios: not taken, decided by measurement (above, PM M339).
- What a fault reads around it on Btrfs, 4 MiB (its read-ahead): on Fedora a range's
  first touch that read 2 MiB (`MADV_HUGEPAGE` with `MADV_RANDOM`) took 802 µs at p50
  against 1,076 and 1,698 at p99 against 2,284, but read 1 GiB written in 0.95 s against
  0.62 (PM M339). Whether a range's read-ahead should follow how its file is read is
  unmeasured.
- From what size a file is mapped: 1 MiB, decided by measurement (Which files, above, PM
  M338), as how long a window is (above, PM M306). Measured against FUSE (PM
  M276, the sustained-I/O benchmark, n = 10 a side): a window that holds what the guest
  reads through it (4 GiB under fio's 2 GiB file) reads 17 to 62 times as fast and writes
  whole MiBs 2 to 2.8 times as fast, the guest holding 28 MiB of memory where 2.1 GiB
  without, the host 43% less; one shorter (1 GiB) reads slower, its mappings churning.
  Random 4 KiB writes are 21 to 33% of FUSE's rate through either: a guest's store into a
  page its host's page cache does not hold waits for the host to read the page in, where a
  FUSE_WRITE's pwrite(2) of the whole page reads nothing (71 to 127 µs against 2 to 3 on
  Btrfs, PM M283), and M276's host, short of memory, held few of its file's pages.
  Reading each range ahead as it is mapped doubles the rate of a writer that writes a
  range about 20 times and halves that of one that writes it once, so it is not done.
  In the guest (PM M298, M299), what M276 and M298 took for a range's mapping was the
  device's own following of each file it maps, a look at its size for each range of it, as
  each request about it was answered: looked at once a request, a write through the window
  costs less than a FUSE_WRITE at p50 in every case measured (above). What stays is the
  page its host does not hold: a store there waits for the host to read it, which a
  FUSE_WRITE of the whole page does not, so a cold file's scattered writes have the worse
  tail (4 KiB, p99 1,483 µs against 206) and 1 MiB writes into ranges not yet mapped the
  worse middle (1,589 against 898 at p50). A guest's FUSE weighing each range's writes
  against its mapping (`dax-window-writes/fuse-writes-until-mapped.patch`, M299) was
  measured and not taken: its rationale was that cost. A whole page a host does not hold
  is written as a FUSE_WRITE now (above; M301), on Fedora and the Mac, and what a write into
  a range not yet mapped pays before it writes was measured part by part (M302): a cold
  file's 1 MiB writes into ranges not yet mapped cost 6% more than FUSE's, on Fedora's
  performance cores and on its efficient cores alike, their rounds' spread the cores the
  scheduler put a run on (M302). A window takes none of its guest's memory on either
  architecture (above: its page structures its head's, and arm64's linear map of it in
  blocks).

### D214. Devices plugged into a running microVM, and its disks grown (built: disks and shared directories through the CLI on Hypervisor.framework, KVM and WHP, WHP's run on CI's Windows runners; host functions in the VMM on KVM, and through the CLI for a run's workload on Linux, both passing nested on arm64 KVM; refused on WHP with Microsoft's documented limit, a function assigned as a VM starts alone)

Review devices-06 (2026-11-14): VFIO hot-unplug disables INTx/MSI/MSI-X and removes their host routes before closing eventfds and removing BAR windows. Slot route owners outlive a function, so descriptor close alone cannot reclaim their GSI records. A Linux unit fixture verifies each removal sees an open eventfd and repeated cleanup removes nothing twice. Hardware/error-path completion remains ROOT's validation; evidence is `docs/research/measurements/device-fixes/README.md`.


Review devices-05 (2026-11-14): a file disk publishes capacity and generation under one mutex, held from metadata acquisition through the monotonicity check and both updates. Each capacity/config-generation read takes that same mutex. A guest's split read therefore observes a coherent size or a changed generation; it needs no convention about odd generation values. The focused red/green is retained in `docs/research/measurements/device-fixes/README.md`.


**Why.** The long-session roadmap's item 6 (2026-10-18): a microVM that runs for hours is
given what it needs as it goes, not only what it booted with. Every shards device was a
virtio-mmio one, placed in the devicetree or the kernel's command line as the machine was
made, which no guest can be told of later (D119 worked around it with a join disk and a join
share made ahead), and a disk's capacity was fixed when its file was opened.

**Decided** (`devices/pci/hotplug.rs`, `devices/virtio/pci.rs`, `vm::Handle::plug_*`):

- **Slots kept at boot.** A machine made with `pci_slots` N (`run --kernel … --pci-slots N`)
  has a PCI bus (D153) with N places on bus 0 after its other functions, each a device's
  function 0 with the MSIs of its requester ID made ahead (a GICv2m frame's on
  Hypervisor.framework, the ITS on arm64 KVM, the local APICs on x86_64). A device plugged
  takes the first free one; a machine with none refuses. Its interrupts are MSI-X alone: a
  slot has no INTx line its firmware tables route.
- **Found by a rescan, let go by a remove; no hot-plug controller.** The guest's init writes
  `/sys/bus/pci/rescan`, which scans the bus, assigns the new function's BARs in its host
  bridge's window and binds its driver (drivers/pci/probe.c, pci_rescan_bus), and lets a
  device go by writing its `remove` (pci_stop_and_remove_bus_device: its driver's remove, a
  virtio device's reset). PCIe's native hot-plug was the alternative: a root port with a
  slot for each device, whose controller Linux's pciehp drives, and which waits 20 ms and
  then 100 ms for the link of each function it adds (drivers/pci/pci.c,
  pcie_wait_for_link_delay; PCIe 6.0 §6.7.3.3), 5 s after an attention button
  (pciehp_ctrl.c, pciehp_handle_button_press), and 1 s after powering a slot off; ACPI's
  hot-plug is x86_64's alone, and arm64's guests here are told of their machine by a
  devicetree. A rescan costs what the probe does: a disk's rescan 6.6 ms and its first read
  7.6 ms at p50 on KVM, 2.4 and 3.1 ms on Hypervisor.framework (PM M430). Every shards guest's PID 1 is
  shards' own, which is told; a guest of another init rescans as its owner does.
- **BARs where the guest places them.** Linux assigns a function found by a rescan BAR
  addresses of its own in the bridge's window, whatever its BARs held, as no firmware
  placed it (setup-bus.c, pci_assign_unassigned_bus_resources; Linux 6.18 and 7.2 alike,
  `linux,pci-probe-only` or not), so a plugged function's header is movable
  (`pci::Header::movable`): a BAR written takes the address written, aligned to its size.
  The bus's 32-bit window is one device of the machine's (`hotplug::Window`), which holds the
  BARs placed at boot and reaches each plugged function's BARs where its header says, while
  its memory decoding is on; an access nothing claims reads all ones (PCIe 6.0 §2.3.2).
  Plugged functions' BARs share the 32-bit window (752 MiB on arm64, 496 MiB on x86_64).
- **virtio over PCI** (virtio 1.3 §4.1): a modern, non-transitional function (1af4:1040+ID,
  revision 1), one 32-bit BAR of 16 KiB holding the common configuration, the ISR status,
  the device's configuration, the notifications (each queue's at four times its index) and
  the MSI-X table and pending bits, found by virtio's vendor capabilities after MSI-X's.
  Its registers are its device's MMIO transport's, read and written for it
  (`MmioTransport::with_interrupt`): one state machine, feature negotiation, activation and
  reset for every virtio device of shards'. Two MSI-X vectors, one for configuration
  changes and one its queues share, as Linux then takes them (virtio_pci_common.c,
  vp_find_vqs_msix: one a queue where the table has room, else one shared), held pending
  while masked and sent as unmasked (§6.8.2). No VIRTIO_PCI_CAP_PCI_CFG, which Linux's
  driver never reads.
- **Disks** (`Handle::plug_disk`: an open file, as a confined VM process is handed one) and
  **shared directories** (`Handle::plug_share`: a share's slot, its server put in by its
  owner, mounted by its tag), each charged to the microVM's I/O limits (D178) as its others
  are. A plugged share has no DAX window (D189): a window's guest addresses are laid out as
  the machine is made.
- **Taken off once its guest let it go.** `Handle::unplug` refuses, changing nothing, while
  the guest's driver still drives the device (its virtio status not 0; a passed-through
  function's bus mastering on, which pci_disable_device turns off), and then takes it off
  the bus, its BARs out of the window, its workers stopped by a reset.
- **A disk grown online** (`DiskSize::grow`, for a disk the machine was made with and a
  plugged one): its host grows its file, then the device takes the file's length as its
  capacity and sends a configuration change (virtio 1.3 §5.2.4), its configuration
  generation counting growths, so a driver reading the 64-bit capacity in two accesses sees
  a growth between them (§4.1.4.3.1). Linux's virtio_blk reads it and says so
  (virtblk_config_changed_work, set_capacity_and_notify: a uevent with `RESIZE=1`). A file
  that shrank is refused: it would take sectors from under the guest's file system.
- **A host's function plugged in** (`Handle::plug_vfio`, Linux): opened as D154 opens one,
  through its group or its device node, all of guest RAM mapped for its DMA, pinned, outside
  the guest's IOMMU; refused where the machine has memory to plug or a balloon (D154). Where
  the machine's slots sit behind its IOMMU, behind it instead (below, a run's workload's). Its BAR windows, the memory slots the guest reaches it through
  without exits, follow its BARs as the guest places and moves them, and leave as it is
  unplugged; KVM forgets its file then (KVM_DEV_VFIO_FILE_DEL, virt/kvm/vfio.c), which it
  would otherwise hold as long as the VM. KVM's VFIO device and memory slots are reached
  apart from the VM (`hv::VfioHost`), which the running machine owns. Off Linux
  `Handle::plug_vfio` refuses, changing nothing (`vm::plug_refused`): macOS's
  Hypervisor.framework assigns no device at all, and Windows gives a microVM a host's
  function as it starts alone (`PassthroughRefusal::NoPlug`): WHP allows a partition device
  assignment before its setup alone (M401), Microsoft documents Discrete Device Assignment for a VM
  given its device before it starts and giving it back once stopped, and WHP's pages say
  nothing of a virtual PCI device made in a partition that runs (D154's "No Windows host
  plugs a function"). Untested where a hypervisor assigns devices, as none here does.
- **Slots only where asked for.** A bus of four empty slots costs an x86_64 boot on KVM
  4 ms at p50, 60.3 ms against 56.1 (PM M430), where an arm64 boot on Hypervisor.framework
  pays nothing measured (18.90 against 18.88 ms): x86_64's guest finds its bus through
  ACPI, arm64's through its devicetree. So a machine has one only where its maker asks.
