- **Let go of with its machine.** The slots' MSIs reach its VM (WHP's partition, KVM's VM
  descriptor), so the machine's teardown drops its hot-plug once its devices are quiet: a
  handle that outlived its machine held them, and on WHP the next VM of the process could
  not be made (ERROR_VID_PARTITION_ALREADY_EXISTS).
- **A user's commands, in the grammar's ACTION THING** (`shards_cmdline::grammar`):
  `shards plug disk MICROVM FILE:PATH[:ro] [--size SIZE]`, `shards plug volume MICROVM
  SOURCE:PATH[:ro]`, `shards unplug disk|volume MICROVM PATH` and `shards grow disk
  MICROVM PATH SIZE`. A device is named by the path the run has it at, as `-v`'s
  destination names a mount; its source as `-v` gives one (a host file or directory by its
  absolute path, a Windows drive's included, or a named volume), its mode `ro` or `rw`. A
  disk is a file holding a file system; `--size` makes one empty, ext4 of that size (shards'
  own mke2fs, D190's), where FILE is not there. `plug` and `unplug` are actions of their
  own rather than `attach`, which Docker's `attach` holds, or `update`, whose flags are
  Docker's.
- **The daemon asks the run's VM, then its guest's init.** `DEVICE` (shards-ipc) carries the
  step and, as descriptors, the disk's file or the connection to the share's server (a
  share process of its own, share.rs, as each run's shares have: on Unix the connection
  the share process sends and waits to be taken; on Windows the share's stream itself, a
  duplex pipe the daemon makes, its server end given the share process as it starts and
  its other duplicated into the VM process, as a run's shares are given it, D197, D207,
  and taken there as a `PipeStream`); the VM plugs it into a
  slot and answers its place (`DEVICED`, by number, as a pause is answered). Init's DEVICE
  built-in (init hotplug.rs) rescans the bus through a sysfs of its own, kept from boot
  now in every microVM, as the run's root's is read-only (D154's `shards_vfio` reason),
  mounts the disk's file system (ext4, XFS, Btrfs, FAT or EROFS, tried in turn) or the
  virtio-fs share by the new mount API, attached nowhere, and attaches it at PATH in the
  workload's mount namespace (move_mount), so nothing of it is init's; a fresh disk's top
  is given its run's user, as a fresh volume's is (D38). `unplug` unmounts it in the
  workload first, refused while anything there uses it (EBUSY), writes the function's
  `remove`, then has the VM take it off the bus. `grow` sets the file longer, has the VM
  grow its disk, and init grows its ext4 online once the kernel reads the new size
  (EXT4_IOC_RESIZE_FS, as resize2fs grows a mounted one). What a run has plugged in is the
  daemon's to know while it runs, and goes with its microVM.
- **A microVM's device steps one at a time, so a disk only ever grows** (devices-01,
  docs/bugs/2026-11-13/devices.md). Each client's command is served on a thread of its
  own, and `grow` read its file's length, refused less, then set it, apart: two growths
  of one 64 MiB disk, to 128 and 256 MiB, could both read 64 MiB, the larger set 256 MiB
  and have its guest's ext4 grown and written past 128 MiB, and the smaller then set
  128 MiB, cutting those sectors from under the mounted file system; the VM's own refusal
  of a file that shrank came after the bytes were gone. Now every device step of a
  running microVM (`plug`, `unplug`, `grow`, a function's included) holds it
  (`devices::Steps`, a set of the microVMs one is under way in and a condition variable
  its end wakes the waiting with: no polling, no deadline) from its first read of what
  is plugged to its guest's last answer, as each step's reading depends on the last's
  answers (a slot's `devfn` taken back by an unplug and given to the next plug among
  them). So a disk's file is read and set by one growth at a time, only ever longer,
  ending at the largest asked; the VM is asked `GROW`, which takes its file's length as
  its capacity, only once the file has the length asked; and a size less than its file
  has, in whole 512-byte sectors (virtio 1.3 §5.2.4's unit), is refused typed
  (`NotGrown::Smaller`, asked and had), changing nothing, its VM and guest not asked.
  Steps of different microVMs do not wait for each other. No literal is added: the hold
  has no bound or timeout, its waits end as the step under way ends, and a step that
  fails or panics lets it go as it drops. Not covered: one file plugged writable into two
  microVMs at once, whose growths their two holds do not order (two kernels mounting
  one ext4 writable corrupt it before any growth does: ext4 is no cluster file system,
  and its multiple mount protection exists to refuse that mount, Linux
  Documentation/filesystems/ext4/mmp.rst); plug does not refuse that yet. Verified by
  `growths_of_one_disk_never_shorten_its_file` (the smaller growth paused between its
  read and its set, the larger asked meanwhile, its guest's write past 128 MiB kept) and
  `a_disk_grown_smaller_is_refused_and_keeps_its_bytes`, red with the hold removed (the
  file left at 128 MiB) and with the refusal removed (the file shortened, the VM asked).
- **Every run's microVM has four slots, and its template keeps them** (`SHARDS_PCI_SLOTS`,
  0 for none). Snapshot format 28 records a machine's slots (`MachineConfig::pci_slots`);
  an empty bus saves as nothing and a restore makes it again; a machine with a device
  plugged in saves none. On arm64 KVM a machine with slots has the GIC's ITS for its
  MSIs, so its snapshot now keeps the ITS, in arm-vgic-its.rst's sequences: the LPIs'
  pending state written to guest memory (KVM_DEV_ARM_VGIC_SAVE_PENDING_TABLES) and the
  ITS's tables (KVM_DEV_ARM_ITS_SAVE_TABLES) before the memory is saved, its registers
  read (GITS_IIDR, CBASER, BASER0 to 7, CREADR, CWRITER, CTLR); restored after the
  redistributors, reset, IIDR first, then the rest, its tables read back
  (KVM_DEV_ARM_ITS_RESTORE_TABLES), its CTLR last; each redistributor's PROPBASER,
  PENDBASER and then CTLR (EnableLPIs) with the GIC's state, as KVM takes the tables'
  places only while LPIs are off (vgic-mmio-v3.c).
- **Verified on real VMs** (`devices_are_plugged_into_a_running_microvm_and_its_disks_grow`,

- **A host's function plugged into a run for its workload** (`shards plug function
  MICROVM FUNCTION`, `shards unplug function MICROVM FUNCTION`; Linux): FUNCTION the host's
  name of it (`0000:01:00.0`), bound to vfio-pci, or its VFIO device node
  (`/dev/vfio/devices/vfioN`). The workload reaches it through its guest's VFIO, which
  gives a process a function only behind the guest's IOMMU (D154), and a guest's IOMMU
  core finds a function's IOMMU by its firmware's description as the function is added
  (the devicetree's `iommu-map`, Documentation/devicetree/bindings/pci/pci-iommu.txt;
  ACPI's VIOT, drivers/acpi/viot.c), which is its boot's. So:
  - **A run booted to take functions.** A run given VFIO's own nodes, its container
    (`--device /dev/vfio/vfio`) or iommufd (`/dev/iommu`), which name no function but are
    what a workload takes one through, as Docker's users give them beside a group's node
    (`run::takes_functions`), boots as a run given a group does (D154): the `kvm` kernel,
    which has VFIO and virtio-iommu, init's own sysfs, of no template; and its slots
    behind its IOMMU (`Config::pci_slots_iommu`, the VM process's `--pci-slots-iommu`).
    A run booted otherwise, whose guest's kernel has no VIRTIO_IOMMU, is refused one, its
    VM saying its slots are not behind its IOMMU: a firmware that put them behind one would
    have that kernel defer the probe of every disk plugged in (10 s where it has modules,
    driver_deferred_probe_check_state).
  - **Slots behind the IOMMU from boot, each an endpoint while plugged.** Each slot's
    requester ID is an endpoint of the IOMMU's that the firmware names from boot, beside
    the functions behind it; the IOMMU translates it only while something is plugged
    there (`Translation::plugged`, `unplugged`), and answers it as no endpoint
    (VIRTIO_IOMMU_S_NOENT) while vacant, PROBE and ATTACH alike. Unplugged, the endpoint
    leaves its domain, which goes with its last endpoint, and what followed it alone
    unmaps all it mapped, unpinning it (a group's other endpoints keep their follower,
    which shows one of theirs). A disk or a shared directory plugged into a slot behind it
    has its MSIs translated as a passed-through function's are (`iommu::Msis`): Linux maps
    an arm64 function's MSI doorbell in its domain (iommu.c, iommu_dma_prepare_msi)
    whether or not its driver's DMA goes through the IOMMU, which a virtio driver's does
    not without VIRTIO_F_ACCESS_PLATFORM; on x86_64 the MSI window is reserved and lands
    untranslated. The IOMMU offers no bypass there, as for functions passed through alone
    (D154): what a function reaches is what its guest maps for it.
  - **The daemon opens it, the VM plugs it.** The confined VM process opens no device
    (Landlock's rules are its start's, D30), so the daemon checks the function as a run's
    start does (bound to vfio-pci; a group of no IOMMU refused, whose DMA reaches all of
    the host's memory; a group already plugged into the run, through another of its
    functions, refused, as a microVM takes a group whole), opens VFIO's container and its
    group's node, or iommufd and its device node, and hands them over (`DEVICE`,
    `device::FUNCTION`). Landlock confines what a process opens, not descriptors it is
    given (security/landlock/fs.c, hook_file_alloc_security), as with plugged disks. The VM
    plugs it into a free slot behind the IOMMU (`Handle::plug_vfio_files`): a container,
    or an address space, of the function's own, which follows its endpoint as one it boots
    with behind the IOMMU does (D154), its MSIs routed where its domain maps their
    addresses (`vfio::Translated`); memory to plug and free page reporting stay, as a
    function behind the IOMMU pins only what its guest maps. From then on the VM process
    holds a host's device, so its run's client waits for it to be free (`HOST_DEVICES`).
  - **Its guest gives it to the workload.** Init's DEVICE built-in rescans the bus, gives
    the function to vfio-pci (driver_override, drivers_probe) through its own sysfs, and
    makes the node of it the workload opens, its guest group's (`/dev/vfio/G`) or its own
    VFIO device node, in the workload's `/dev`, with the VM's devtmpfs's numbers and mode
    (D44), and owned by the user and group the workload runs as (its effective IDs, as a
    plugged disk's empty top is, D38). devtmpfs makes both nodes root's and 0600 (the
    group's and the device's devnode callbacks, vfio_devnode and vfio_device_devnode, set
    no mode; drivers/base/devtmpfs.c's default), and a node of root's left so refused the
    workload of an image's own user: the first nested run of the E2E's run of `User: app`
    failed `open /dev/vfio/0: Permission denied` (EACCES, the mode's refusal; the device
    filter's is EPERM, kernel/bpf/cgroup.c's bpf_prog_run_array_cg). A run given a group
    at its start has it root's as Docker gives one (D154's runs use `--user root`); a
    function plugged in is for the run's workload, whose user cannot change once it runs,
    and the node its user's alone (0600 kept) gives nothing to another user of the
    microVM; the need is the one Kubernetes' `device_ownership_from_security_context`
    answers for a non-root workload's devices (Kubernetes blog, "Non-root Containers And
    Devices", 2021-11-09, https://kubernetes.io/blog/2021/11/09/non-root-containers-and-devices/). A function had by its device node is taken through iommufd too
    (vfio.rst, "Device cdev Example"), whose `/dev/iommu` is a misc device of a dynamic
    minor (10:M) and mode 0660, root's (drivers/iommu/iommufd/main.c, `iommu_misc_dev`):
    init gives the workload's its user and group as well while such a function is plugged,
    made with the VM's numbers and mode where its run was not given it, and answers what
    it was before (`made`, or its owner), which the daemon keeps from the first such
    function and has init restore as the last goes (taken out, or its owner again), so a
    run given `/dev/iommu` at its start has it as its host's node was given (D44) once
    nothing is plugged.
    That `/dev` is the run's own: a tmpfs init mounts at the run's root (`container_mounts`),
    which its command and execs share; each agent's domain mounts a `/dev` of its own, and
    each joiner (D119) makes its own in its mount namespace, so no other workload of the
    microVM is given it. The workload's device filter is
    then its run's rules and one `c MAJ:MIN rwm` for each function plugged in (and
    `/dev/iommu`'s, once, where its run's rules have it not already), given last,
    so that a run's given devices take precedence over the defaults (D44, `devices::allow`):
    done by init's own process, which keeps the run's rules and the program attached, and
    replaces it (BPF_F_REPLACE) each time with the whole list, so a function unplugged
    leaves it; a privileged run's has no filter. Anything else the step is asked to allow
    is refused: a character device's whole node alone.
  - **Unplugged once nothing holds it.** `unplug function` takes the node out of the
    filter first, so nothing opens it anew, then has init refuse, the filter put back,
    while any process in the microVM holds the node or the function's VFIO device open
    (its fdinfo's `vfio-device-syspath`, vfio_device_show_fdinfo, names which; a kernel
    that names none counts every VFIO device as the function's): its guest's remove would
    otherwise wait for the holder to close it (vfio_unregister_group_dev). Then init takes
    the node out of the workload's `/dev`, writes the function's `remove`, and the VM takes
    it off its bus, its container and its file in KVM let go of, the host's again.
  - **Verified:** unit tests of the slots' endpoints (vacant, plugged, followed, unplugged,
    a shared follower kept), of the slots' MSIs, of the firmware's endpoints, of a slot's
    endpoint across a plug that fails, of the filter's rules and their refusals (and
    `/dev/iommu`'s rule once, not again where given at the start), of the workload's IDs
    its node is given (hotplug.rs `the_workloads_user_is_its_effective_ids`), of
    `/dev/iommu` given back as it was (`iommu_is_given_back_as_it_was`), and of the
    daemon's reading of init's answers and keeping of what `/dev/iommu` was. Its E2E
    (`a_hosts_function_is_plugged_into_a_run_for_its_workload`, tests/plug.rs), nested as
    D214's VFIO test is (`SHARDS_L1_PCI_TESTS=01.0 SHARDS_L1_TESTS=plug:a_hosts_function`):
    a run of the image's user (`app`, 1000:1000) given `/dev/vfio/vfio`, the L1 guest's edu
    function plugged in by its name, its node the user's, its workload moving a page
    through it by DMA through its IOMMU, a second plug refused, unplugged and the node
    gone, twice; then, where the L1 kernel makes device nodes, plugged by its device node
    into that run (its `/dev/iommu` made the user's, gone after) and into one given
    `/dev/iommu` at its start (the user's while plugged, root's again after), its workload
    moving a page through iommufd each time; a run booted otherwise refused. Run nested
    first before the ownership fix, which failed as above; it passes nested now, at
    8928fbe4 on the M5 Max (Darwin 25.4.0), as the run's user, not root, both by the
    function's group and by its device node through iommufd; the CLI's steps of a
    function are not timed yet. Off Linux, `shards plug function` is refused by name with its host's own limit, as a run's start refuses one
    (`passthrough_refused`: on macOS, Hypervisor.framework's API assigns no device to a VM,
    PM M403), in tests/plug.rs's `devices_are_plugged_into_a_run_and_its_disk_grows`; the
    VMM's own refusal off Linux is `vm`'s `a_hosts_pci_function_is_refused_with_its_oss_own
    _limit`. The in-process test's steps' costs, n, p50, p90, p99 and max, as M430 gives a
    disk's, are `docs/research/measurements/pci-hotplug/vfio-nested.sh`'s (its
    `SHARDS_PLUG_ROUNDS` rounds, nested): 30 rounds at 8928fbe4 and at 89194593, its steps
    split, in PM M430, above.
- **Not yet:** tests/plug.rs and the in-process test's shared directory on jupiter, and
  their steps' numbers on WHP; a plugged share's DAX window; a plugged function's 64-bit BARs
  past the 32-bit window; a host's function plugged on bare-metal hardware (no host here
  has a spare one bound to vfio-pci: tested nested, on QEMU edu's model); the guest's
  remove's 29 ms on KVM x86_64, not yet split (PM M430).

**Its waits, on the kernel's word (audit of picked constants, 2026-11-09).** init waited
10 s for a plugged function, its driver, its disk, a share's tag and a function's VFIO node,
each looked at every millisecond, and as long for a grown disk's size: figures picked. The
kernel says when each comes, so init waits on that and on no clock:
- A rescan (`bus/pci/rescan`) adds what it finds before its write returns (drivers/pci/
  pci-sysfs.c `rescan_store`, `pci_rescan_bus`): a function not there after it is not
  plugged in, said at once (`hotplug::rescan`). Its driver is bound in the same write, its
  probe run before the driver is said bound (drivers/base/dd.c `really_probe`, then
  `driver_bound`), so a disk's block device and a share's virtio-fs tag are there as the
  driver is; none of virtio-pci, virtio-blk, virtio-fs and vfio-pci asks to be probed apart
  (no `PROBE_PREFER_ASYNCHRONOUS`, Linux 7.2). A share's tag is mounted once, after its
  driver binds: a refusal is the kernel's, said at once rather than after 10 s of retries.
- What comes later, a probe the kernel defers or runs apart, and a disk's new size (its
  driver reads it in a work item as the host's config change arrives, virtio_blk.c
  `virtblk_config_changed_work`), is waited for on the kernel's device events
  (`devices::Uevents`, NETLINK_KOBJECT_UEVENT's group 1, opened before the rescan, the bind
  or the look, so that no event between is missed): the device looked at again as each
  comes. A disk's size says so as it is set (block/genhd.c `set_capacity_and_notify`,
  KOBJ_CHANGE with `RESIZE=1`); a VFIO node is made before its device's KOBJ_ADD
  (drivers/base/core.c `device_add`: `devtmpfs_create_node` waits for it).
- A wait has no end of its own: the daemon's exec of the built-in ends it, and says so.

| Literal | Was | Now | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FOUND_WITHIN` (init hotplug.rs) | 10 s, looked at every 1 ms | none: the rescan's own return, then the kernel's device events | Linux 7.2 drivers/pci/pci-sysfs.c `rescan_store`; drivers/base/dd.c `__device_attach`, `really_probe`; lib/kobject_uevent.c; block/genhd.c `set_capacity_and_notify` |
| `FUNCTION_WITHIN` (init devices.rs) | 10 s, looked at every 1 ms | none: there at once, else the kernel's device events | drivers/base/core.c `device_add` (devtmpfs node before KOBJ_ADD) |

Owed: init's unit tests on a Linux host (they build for musl here, and run in a guest), and
hotplug's E2E (tests/hotplug.rs) on KVM, Hypervisor.framework and WHP.

**Amended 2026-11-14 (devices-11, ROOT's decision): a disk file has one writer.** Two
kernels that each mount one ext4 read-write corrupt it: each journals and allocates
without the other's knowledge, which ext4's multiple-mount protection exists to refuse
(Linux Documentation/filesystems/ext4/mmp.rst), and two runs' growths of it take
different holds of their microVMs' steps (devices-01). So `shards plug disk` claims the
file it opened, by what the file is, never its path: its device and inode on Unix (POSIX
`<sys/stat.h>`: `st_dev` and `st_ino` identify a file), on Windows its volume's serial
number and 128-bit file ID (`GetFileInformationByHandleEx(FileIdInfo)`, FILE_ID_INFO,
which ReFS's 128-bit IDs need where NTFS's 64-bit index would do). A hard link, a second
path or a symlink to the file is the same file. The claim is a reader-writer one:
- A writable plug is refused where any plug, of any run or this one at another path, has
  the file; a read-only plug where one has it writable. Read-only plugs share it.
- The refusal is typed (`DiskHeld::Writable`/`ReadOnly`, naming the holder's run and
  path), and said as `shards: cannot plug into NAME: FILE: microVM ID has its file
  plugged in writable at PATH`.
- A claim is taken as the file is opened, before its VM is asked, so two plugs at once
  cannot both pass; it is given back as the plug fails (as it drops), as it is unplugged,
  and as its run is found ended at the next claim (the claims of runs that no longer run
  are let go first, as `plugged` is). Where a failed plug's own unplug fails, other than
  as its VM saying the device is off its bus, its claim stays until its run ends: its
  VM may have the file still.
- A growth opens its disk's file by path again; it is refused where that is not the file
  plugged in, another put at its path since.
- The claims are the daemon's, of one `SHARDS_HOME`: another home's daemon, or another
  program, is not refused by them (an OS lock on the file would reach those; not built).
  A run's own disks at its start (its writable layer, its template) are the daemon's own
  files and are not plugged.
Unit tests and the guard's mutation: `a_disk_file_is_plugged_writable_into_one_run_at_a_time`,
`a_growth_refuses_a_file_put_in_its_disks_place` (docs/research/measurements/device-fixes/README.md).
Owed to ROOT: two running microVMs, `shards plug disk A FILE:/d`, then `shards plug disk B
FILE:/d` (and through a hard link) refused, `FILE:/d:ro` into B refused, then after
`shards unplug disk A /d`, `:ro` into A and B both plugged.


**Amended 2026-11-14 (devices-10): a device step's refusal keeps its cause on the wire.**
The VMM's plug, unplug and growth refused with text, and `DEVICED` carried a failure byte
and that text, so nothing past the VM process could tell a full bus from a driver still
bound or a host's VFIO failure but by its words (R04). They refuse by cause now,
`shards_ipc::device::Refusal`, each with what it names: no bus (`NoBus`), every slot taken
(`NoSlots { slots }`), nothing at a place (`NoDevice { devfn }`), a driver still driving it
(`StillDriven { devfn, reason }`), a file shorter than its guest was told (`Shrink { has,
asked }`) or not whole sectors (`Unaligned { bytes, sector }`), no microVM running
(`Inactive`), a malformed step (`InvalidRequest`), what the device cannot do
(`Unsupported`), the host's failure (`Host`), and, read on the asker's side, a VM that ended
before it answered (`ConnectionEnded`) or an answer that could not be read (`InvalidReply`).
Each says what its asker may do next (`Retry`): after a release (no slot, still driven),
after correcting the ask, after reconciling (the step may have been done), or unknown (the
host's). `DEVICED` after its number: `0` and the answer's text, or `1`, a cause byte, its
numbers big-endian and its text; anything else, cut short, past a field's range or with
text where its cause has none, reads as `InvalidReply`, never a success. The VM process and
its daemon are one build (D36), so no older encoding is read. Callers match causes: a disk
plug that fails after its VM took it keeps the file's claim unless the VM says it is off
its bus (`NoDevice`); an Engine plug (D235) tells a host's failure (`Host`) from the
microVM's; the CLI's and tests' words are made only to show one (the same words as before).
An allocation failure of the answer ends the VM's link, which its asker reads as
`ConnectionEnded`. Not typed by this: init's DEVICE built-in's answers, which come back as
an exec's status and its words (a run's host already tells `DEVICE_BUSY` from the rest).
Red/green: docs/research/measurements/device-fixes/README.md.

**Amended 2026-11-14 (devices-08, R03): what of a plug was a picked figure.**
- Its guest's steps (find, mount, unmount, grow, a function's release) had 30 s
  (`GUEST_TIMEOUT`), the one clock left after init's waits went to the kernel's word
  (above). They are waited for as the daemon's other built-ins are (`exec_answered`, D215's
  judge): while the microVM's process runs, before the built-in's first answer its liveness
  alone, then past the slowest seen ended where a whole one shows it ran no CPU, its host not
  the reason. Cold: the first plug of a daemon waits until its guest answers or its microVM
  ends. Its failure is the judge's typed cut (stalled, or its process unreadable). No figure
  of its own. Owed to ROOT: `cargo test -p shards --test plug` with a guest made slow, its
  plug done past 30 s.
- Owed, each with its derivation, not swapped for another figure:
  - the 4 KiB of a step's answer kept (`1 << 12`, shared with the daemon's other built-ins'
    reads): init's DEVICE answers a device name or a refusal naming a path (Linux `PATH_MAX`,
    4096, include/uapi/linux/limits.h), so its longest answer is init's longest refusal
    line, which init's own words bound; to be derived from them in init and the daemon
    together.
  - the run's 4 PCI slots (`pci_slots`): a bus has 32 device numbers (PCI Express Base 6.0
    §7.2.2); a slot is reserved as the microVM boots, into its template, so it cannot grow on
    demand. The derivation is every free device number less what a slot costs a boot (MSI
    routes, the window, an IOMMU endpoint): ROOT owes the boot latency and memory of a bus
    of 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and every free slot (`docs/research/measurements/build-ab/ab.py`,
    PM M430's method, each restoring one template, n, p50/p90/p99/max) before the default
    moves.
  - virtio-blk's, the GPU control ring's and virtio-iommu's queue sizes (256, 256, 64): the
    queue audit's Little's-law derivation above, owed its service and refill times.
  - `THROUGH_MAX` (1 MiB, a range's relay): the most one virtio-blk request carries is what
    the device advertises, `seg_max` × `size_max` (virtio 1.3 §5.2.4); it advertises
    `seg_max` alone today (254), so a request's length is the guest kernel's choice. With
    `VIRTIO_BLK_F_SIZE_MAX` advertised, one request is one round trip of at most their
    product; that changes the device's features, held in snapshots, and is owed with
    ROOT's run of `cargo test -p shards --test build` over a range (PM M442's case).

### D228. A client's paths are its own; the machine's are its owner's to grant (built)

**The need.** Through a context (D180) a laptop runs microVMs on a GPU or x86_64 machine.
Until now a command it sent ran as that machine's CLI, so `-v /home/me/src:/src` bound the
machine's `/home/me/src`, and every enrolled client could bind any of the machine's
directories (`-v /:/host`), plug in its files and PCI functions, take its GPUs, and make
its CLI read and write its files (`--env-file`, `--cidfile`, `save -o`, a build of a
directory there), all as the machine's user. That is Docker's model: its CLI sends a bind
as the path typed (docker/cli v29.8.1 cli/command/container/opts.go, `parse`: `Binds`
taken as given), its daemon resolves it on its own host (moby docker-v29.8.1
daemon/volume/mounts/linux_parser.go, `validateMountConfigImpl`: the source `os.Stat`ed
there; daemon/volume/mounts/mounts.go, `MountPoint.Setup`: a `-v` source made there,
createSource), and Docker's documentation says so: a bind mount is made on the daemon's
host, never the client's, so a client of a remote daemon cannot bind its own files
(docs.docker.com, "Bind mounts", Considerations and constraints). Whoever reaches a remote
dockerd reaches its host's whole file system: Docker's own documentation calls daemon
access root-equivalent (docs.docker.com, "Docker Engine security", Docker daemon attack
surface).

**Decided** (the user, 2026-11-07; shards is filesystem based, its memory's rule): a path
means the files where its user typed it, and nothing of a machine's own is reachable but by
its owner's grant, default deny, as shards' networks are.

- **A client's bind is its own directory, served from it.** The client reads its run's
  and create's `-v` and `--mount type=bind` as shards' parser reads them (`client_binds`,
  `here_binds`, by `flags::Parsed::positions`), relative paths from its working directory,
  a missing `-v` directory made there as `-v` makes its host's, a missing `--mount` source
  refused in the words docker/cli's daemon refuses one. Each crosses as a relay's token
  (`client_grants::Relayed`: `/.shards-client-bind/` then `d` or `f`, 128 random bits, its
  path as hex so that a Windows path's `:` splits no field), and the client serves it over a
  QUIC connection of its own (the bind step, `\0bind TOKEN`): the share server shards' share
  processes run (`fs::server::Server`, D38's confinement, its own budget), over the client's
  directory or a file's directory limited to it. The machine keeps one end of a socket pair
  for the token (`daemon/remote.rs`, `RELAYS`, by client and token, so that no client takes
  another's), the step's stream the other, and the run's start takes it (`take_relay`): its
  share process hands the VM that socket as the share's end as it is (share.rs), so the
  guest's FUSE requests reach the client's server byte for byte and its answers come back.
  On a Windows machine, whose shares' streams are pipes its daemon makes (D197), the relay
  is such a pair (`shards_ipc::byte_pair`): the step reads and writes its end through
  overlapped handles of its own (`platform::PipeStream`), and the run's request hands the
  VM the other in the share's place, the share process started for the machine's own
  shares alone, none where every share is a client's (`started_shares`, a pipe's handle
  told apart from a directory's by GetFileType). Nothing of the machine's is opened for it;
  a source of the prefix in an owner's run, or a client's bind of any other source, is
  refused (`refuse_bind`). A run joining another's microVM (`--network container:NAME`)
  takes none, its volumes its join share's (D119).
- **Plugged in as it runs** (`shards plug volume MICROVM DIR:PATH[:ro]`, D214): a directory
  of the client's is sent as its relay and served apart, as a detached run's binds are; the
  machine gives the VM the relay's end as the plugged share's stream, starting no share
  process, and the relay ends as the share is unplugged or its microVM ends. A named
  volume plugged in is the daemon's, judged by the client's grants where it binds a
  directory of the machine's.
- **What the relay gives.** The same server, so the same semantics as a bind of a local
  directory: no FUSE writeback cache is negotiated (server.rs `INIT` offers none), so a
  guest's write reaches the client's file before its `write(2)` returns; the guest's page
  cache is dropped at each open (no `FOPEN_KEEP_CACHE`), so data is close-to-open
  consistent with the client's other programs; names and attributes are trusted for a
  second (`VALID_S`), as a local share's are. Only the cost differs, each request a round
  trip to the client: over loopback on the GPU desktop an open, a 4 KiB read and a close
  took 251 µs at p50 and 399 at p99 against the machine's own bind's 136 and 206, a 64 MiB
  read 458 MiB/s against 468, a write 572 MiB/s against 2,157 (PM M511). No DAX window: a mapping maps a file of the host the
  guest is on, so the client's server tells its guest to map nothing (`serves_afar`: no
  `FUSE_HAS_INODE_DAX`, no `FUSE_ATTR_DAX`) and refuses a mapping's descriptor (EINVAL,
  `answer_afar`).
- **As long as its client serves it.** An attached run's binds are served by its command
  while it runs, and let go as it ends (`Relays`, hung up as it drops: a relay its run never
  took is kept there no longer). `run -d` and `create` serve theirs from a process of the
  client's own (`shards bind-server`, one of `cli::INTERNAL`, never a client's to send:
  `owners`), which says it is ready once each relay is kept, and ends as each relay does,
  as the run that took it ends. A relay serves one start: a container started again, or
  `--volumes-from` of a client's bind, is refused, said as its client's directory, which
  that client serves to that run alone.
- **The machine's directories and devices, by grant.** The owner grants a client by name
  (`shards grant client NAME --dir PATH[:ro] --device NAME --gpus`, `revoke client`,
  `inspect client`; or `invite client ... --dir ...`, kept for the client the invitation
  enrolls), kept in the home (`grants/NAME`, removed with the client). The machine's
  directory reaches a client's run only as a volume of it (`o=bind`, its `device`), the
  local driver's form Compose's `driver_opts` give, never as a bind's path, which is the
  client's. A client's `volume create`, a `--mount` volume's options, a volume one mounts
  (made by anyone), a `--volumes-from` of the machine's bind, and `plug disk|volume` are
  judged against its grants: by the path's real place before anything is looked at or made
  (`refuse_path`), and again by where the directory or file now open is, as the system names
  an open file (`refuse_opened`: `F_GETPATH`, `/proc/self/fd`, GetFinalPathNameByHandleW),
  which is what is shared: no rename or link between the look and the open reaches past a
  grant. The innermost grant decides whether it may be written. Devices: the machine's GPUs
  (`--gpus`, an Engine API create's device requests), CDI devices, VFIO's nodes, and `plug
  function` need a grant of each by its name; a `--device` of any other path is the
  microVM's own (D44), every run's.
- **What a client's command may not do in its own process.** A client's shards carries
  what is its own (D180's parts) and never sends words that would have the machine's CLI
  read or write the machine's files; a client that does is refused before the command
  starts (`refuse_words`): a kernel booted directly, a snapshot restored, a build or
  artifact build or signature of a directory there, `cp`, `buildx policy`, an import of a
  file there, `--env-file`, `--label-file`, `--iidfile`, `--metadata-file`, `-o` and `-i`
  but `-`, a `--cidfile` not told on its pipe, a seccomp profile's file.
- **Whom a request is for.** The listener names the client last in each command's
  environment (`SHARDS_CLIENT`, which no client can set: a request's variables are
  `frame::ENV`'s alone); the CLI sends it with each run and command (`Run::client`,
  `Command::client`), kept with a container's record, so that its start is judged by its
  client's grants however long after.
- **Docker's tools through a context's engine** (D180 part 4) are the client's too: the
  listener no longer connects a client's engine stream to `engine.sock` as any local
  client, but makes the connection itself and hands the API its other end with the client
  named (`take_engine_clients`, the listener woken), so that what its calls make is the
  client's (`engine_client`, the connection's thread's): a create's binds, which Docker's
  API carries as paths alone, are the client's paths, refused as shards' own CLI would have
  served them, and its devices and volumes judged by the client's grants.

Tested: unit tests of the grants' record, of what a client's devices and directories are
(a link inside a grant to a directory outside refused, by path and by what is open; a
directory not there judged where it would be made; read-only), of a relay's source (a
Windows path whole), of a run's binds rewritten (`client_binds`), of the share answering
afar; and `tests/context.rs`
(`a_clients_binds_are_its_own_files_and_the_machines_its_owners_to_grant`): the laptop's
directory and a file bound alone read in a microVM there, its writes landing on the laptop,
read-only refused, a detached run's write landing; nothing of the laptop's made on the
machine; a client's volume of the machine's directory refused, the owner's refused to the
client until granted read-only, then refused read-write, and refused again once revoked; a
named volume the client's; `--gpus` refused without a grant; and a directory of the
laptop's plugged into a running microVM there, read and written there, gone once unplugged. On
adacachy2 (Linux 7.3, KVM) and Fedora at 34408c9d, and with the plugged directory on
adacachy2 and on jupiter (Windows 11, WHP; the machine's side a Windows
daemon's, the relay its pipe pair). And
`a_contexts_engine_is_its_machines`: a create through the context's engine binding a
directory of the machine's refused.

**Not yet.** Docker's CLI through a context serves none of its client's directories, as its
API names a path alone. A context's relays measured across two machines (PM M511 has
loopback alone). A command whose run goes on without it that fails ends the process serving
its binds apart; one that succeeds but whose microVM is never started (`create`, then no
`start`) keeps it serving until its client ends it.

### D227. The guest kernel compiles BPF programs, and has no interpreter (pinned, PM M489)

**Why.** Every workload runs under a seccomp filter (D42) on each of its syscalls, and every
run's cgroup has a device filter (D44) on each device it opens or makes. Both are BPF
programs, and the guest kernel ran both interpreted: Firecracker's 6.18 configs, shards'
base, leave BPF_JIT unset (`# CONFIG_BPF_JIT is not set`, firecracker-x86_64-6.18.config
line 119, firecracker-aarch64-6.18.config line 100) beside `HAVE_EBPF_JIT=y` and
`ARCH_WANT_DEFAULT_BPF_JIT=y`, and none of shards' fragments (shards.config,
shards-aarch64.config, kvm.config, hyperv.config, gpu.config) set it. seccomp's action
cache (kernel/seccomp.c `seccomp_cache_check_allow`, Linux 5.11 and later, native ABI on
x86_64 and arm64) answers without the filter only a syscall the filter allows whatever its
arguments; one compared by its arguments (personality, clone's flags, socket's family) or
refused runs the program each call.

**Decided.** `CONFIG_BPF_JIT=y` and `CONFIG_BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON=y` in resources/kernel/
shards.config, so every architecture's kernel and every variant (kvm, hyperv, gpu,
hyperv+gpu) has them; one fragment, as scripts/build-kernel.sh refuses an option two
fragments name. Pinned: kernel-6.18.48-fa4edcc82303, built at 36e47536 (crates/shards/src/
kernel.rs, tests/common's `kvm` variant, README), after PM M489 measured it against
kernel-6.18.48-64a9427a8997, whose config differs in BPF_JIT, BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON and
BPF_JIT_DEFAULT_ON alone. shards.config's comments name this decision D215 and its
measurement PM M462, the numbers it was built under before both were renumbered for
decisions another branch took them for: the file is one of the kernel's inputs, hashed into
its release's name (.github/workflows/kernel.yml), so its words stay as they were built.

**What it gives** (PM M489, p50): a syscall the default profile's filter runs on costs
10.5 ns over no filter where it cost 30.6 (KVM x86_64), 20.9 where it cost 36.5
(Hypervisor.framework, M3 Ultra), 62.5 where it cost 262.5 (WHP, the hyperv variant), and
on KVM its p99 falls from 209 to 89 ns; the device filter, an eBPF program, costs an open
nothing measurable where it cost 11 ns (KVM), 2.6 where it cost 18.2 (HVF) and 25 where it
cost 200 (WHP); a run from a template answers 533 µs sooner on KVM's VM clock (the quietest
segment; 873 pooled) and 667 µs sooner on WHP's. And no workload's guest holds an
interpreter.

- kernel/bpf/Kconfig (v6.18): BPF_JIT "allows the kernel to generate native code when a
  program is loaded into the kernel. This will significantly speed-up processing of BPF
  programs." BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON "Enables BPF JIT and removes BPF interpreter to avoid
  speculative execution of BPF instructions by the interpreter", and pins
  /proc/sys/net/core/bpf_jit_enable to 1 (net/core/sysctl_net_core.c: its bounds both
  SYSCTL_ONE). It depends on BPF_SYSCALL, HAVE_EBPF_JIT and BPF_JIT, which the base and this
  change give both architectures. Commit 290af86629b2 (Linux 4.15) brought it in because the
  interpreter in a host's text was the gadget Project Zero's CVE-2017-5715 attack used from
  a guest: a guest kernel with no interpreter offers none to its workloads.
- Each architecture wants the JIT on by default: x86 and arm64 select
  ARCH_WANT_DEFAULT_BPF_JIT, and `bpf_jit_enable` starts at BPF_JIT_DEFAULT_ON
  (kernel/bpf/core.c), `def_bool ARCH_WANT_DEFAULT_BPF_JIT || BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON`.
- `net.core.bpf_jit_harden` keeps its default, 0, no constant blinding
  (Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/net.rst: "0 - disable JIT hardening (default value)").
- What shards loads needs no interpreter. Classic seccomp programs (init's workload, exec
  and build-step filters, crates/init run.rs, build.rs, domains.rs; crates/syscall-filter;
  the in-VM server's, crates/server) are turned into eBPF as they load
  (net/core/filter.c `bpf_migrate_filter`) and compiled by the architecture's eBPF JIT;
  init's device filter is a BPF_PROG_TYPE_CGROUP_DEVICE program (crates/init devices.rs),
  which both JITs compile. Programs with kfunc calls or deep stacks need the JIT anyway
  (`bpf_prog_select_runtime`).

**Its costs and risks** (PM M489: docs/research/measurements/bpf-jit/ab.py, fleet.py and
latency.sh, the kernel pinned before against this one, interleaved):

- **A load the JIT cannot compile fails.** With ALWAYS_ON, `bpf_prog_select_runtime` returns
  -ENOTSUPP where the JIT does not produce code; without it, the program ran interpreted.
  The JIT fails where its executable memory cannot be had (execmem, under memory
  pressure), or where a task without CAP_BPF or CAP_SYS_ADMIN would take the JIT's memory
  past `bpf_jit_limit` (`bpf_jit_charge_modmem`: half the module area on x86_64, half the
  vmalloc area on arm64, `bpf_jit_alloc_exec_limit`), which a workload's own filters would
  have to fill. A workload's start then fails as a profile that cannot load fails it (D42:
  exit 125, the reason in State.Error), closed, never without its filter.
- **Memory: a pack per template, not per VM.** The JIT's first program takes a 2 MiB pack
  of executable memory (kernel/bpf/core.c at v6.18, `BPF_PROG_PACK_SIZE`, `SZ_2M *
  num_possible_nodes()`), filled whole with trapping instructions (`alloc_new_pack`,
  `bpf_fill_ill_insns`); later programs take 64-byte chunks of it, and it goes with its
  last program. It is lazy already (no program, no pack); a lazier fill would leave unused
  chunks without the traps the fill is for. Init's device filter is the first, at boot
  (D44), so the booted VM holds 2.2 to 3.6 MiB more (KVM anonymous; 2.4 MiB footprint on
  HVF) and its template 1.5 to 3.1 MiB more on disk; every VM restored from the template
  maps the pack from its file, and the pool's warm VMs hold what they held interpreted on
  both hosts. A VM that starts a workload compiles its filter after the restore: on HVF
  that run holds 432 KiB more footprint (1.9 % of 22.3 MiB); on KVM, nothing measurable
  (its p50 592 KiB lower).
- **arm64's Spectre-BHB sequence.** arm64's JIT ends a classic program loaded by a task
  without CAP_SYS_ADMIN with a branch-history sequence (arch/arm64/net/bpf_jit_comp.c
  `build_bhb_mitigation`: CLRBHB, a loop of k branches and DSB ISB, or a firmware call),
  where the guest thinks its CPU affected. A run with `no-new-privileges` loads its filter
  so (D42). shards' VMM answers SMCCC_ARCH_FEATURES for ARCH_WORKAROUND_3 NOT_SUPPORTED on
  Hypervisor.framework (arch/aarch64/psci.rs), so no guest there calls its firmware from a
  filter; on the M3 Ultra a filter loaded with no_new_privs costs a call what one loaded
  with CAP_SYS_ADMIN does (M489, `nnp/*`).
- **Each start compiles its filter.** A seccomp(2) load takes 59.5 µs where it took 40.0
  (KVM), 42.0 where it took 30.8 (HVF), 65.8 where it took 46.3 (WHP). On HVF a run from
  a template answers 206 µs later on the VM's clock (1,197 to 1,404 µs), every template's
  interval above 0; on KVM and WHP sooner (533 and 667 µs). The HVF run's restored guest
  writes 45 more 16 KiB host pages than the interpreter's, 29 of them memory its template
  held free, one the pack's (M489, written.py): what a compile allocates, placed at random
  by the guest's allocators (SHUFFLE_PAGE_ALLOCATOR, SLAB_FREELIST_RANDOM), not the pack.
- **The JIT warmed in every template** (built; measurement owed, M489). Before a
  template's snapshot, init compiles one classic program of a run's filter's size (512
  instructions, past the default profile's 252 on arm64 and 397 on x86_64) in a child
  that sets no_new_privs, loads it and ends (crates/init/src/jit.rs, `warm`), so that
  what a compile allocates is in the template, freed, for every restored run's compiles
  to take again: the work moved before the snapshot, as D44 moved the device filter's
  load. The guest's code, for every host: KVM's and WHP's runs paid nothing measurable
  for their compiles (M489), and take the same template step, one compile, once a
  template; a failed warm-up is said on init's stderr and the template is saved without
  it, as one is without a JIT.
- **Code made for the boot CPU.** The JIT chooses instructions by the CPU the guest booted
  on, as the kernel's alternatives choose its own; a microVM moved to another machine is
  checked for the CPU features its guest may use already (D176, PM M460).

Open: the warm-up's measurement on HVF (written.py, fleet.py, latency.sh against the
interpreter: done when a restored run's footprint and latency are within the
interpreter's spread), and on KVM and WHP that it costs their runs nothing; whether
unprivileged loads should be blinded (`bpf_jit_harden=1`, which blinds the
constants of a program a task without CAP_BPF loads, a seccomp filter's among them) is not
decided.

### D219. A restart's waits come from what restarts cost on the host it runs on (built; measured on Fedora, macOS owed)

**Found.** The audit of what was taken from Docker (docs/audit/2026-10-16_docker-framing.md):
a restart policy's wait was dockerd's restart manager's figures (moby docker-v29.8.1
daemon/internal/restartmanager: 100 ms first, doubled to a minute at most, from scratch
after a run of 10 s). They say nothing of what a microVM's restart costs. On Fedora a run
of `false` costs its host 82 to 142 ms of CPU from its end to its next's start, and a
microVM whose command sleeps 2.4 to 16 ms a second (PM M484); a Mac's are other numbers,
and a loaded host's others again. A figure measured here, frozen into a constant, would be
as arbitrary on another machine as dockerd's.

**Decided** (`daemon/restart.rs`):
- **Kept, as scripts read them:** what each policy restarts, a stop or kill by its stop
  signal or SIGKILL cancelling the next, `shards start` starting the count and the waits
  over, `RestartCount`, `restarting` in `ps` and inspect while it waits, and each wait twice
  the last (binary exponential backoff: Metcalfe and Boggs, CACM 19(7), 1976; a loop's
  restarts from its first failure to any time `t` number at most log2(t / first) + 1, and
  the one after its cause is gone comes within as long again as the loop had failed).
- **A restart's cost is learned as each run ends:** its VM process's CPU time
  (`shards_vmm::platform::process_usage`: /proc on Linux, proc_pidinfo on macOS,
  GetProcessTimes on Windows), its restore and its run, without the time it idled in a
  pool. Where that cannot be read: the host's last, smoothed as pools' refill times are
  (RFC 6298 §2, α 1/8); where none was read, the run's own time.
- **An idle microVM's cost is learned from warm VMs:** each one's CPU from ready to
  claimed, against how long it waited, fitted by least squares. The slope is the idle rate.
  What a VM still does as it becomes ready falls in the intercept: the CPU over the time
  read 23.8 ms a second on Fedora, where a sleeping microVM costs 6.4, as a crash loop's
  short waits count that settling over and over (PM M484).
- **The first wait** is the restart's cost at the share of a CPU the run's limits give it
  (`resources::cpu_allowance_micros`). A crash loop's restarts then take no more of its
  host than its limits let its command take: a few milliseconds where it may use every
  CPU, 1.6 s for 80 ms of CPU at `--cpus 0.05`.
- **The longest** is the restart's cost at the idle rate: past it, a microVM failing for
  good costs its host what one idling would. A run that lasts as long has paid for its
  restart as an idle microVM would, and its waits start over.
- **Cold start.** What a host learned is kept in its home (`restart-costs`: the smoothed
  cost and the fit's sums) for the next daemon. Before any warm VM of the home's has idled
  and been claimed, the waits are not capped: they double on, and start over after a run
  as long as the last wait. A pooled run's first restart claims a warm VM, so the second
  decision has a rate.

**Deliberate differences from dockerd, each a script-visible one:** the first restart of
an unlimited microVM comes within milliseconds, not 100 ms; a microVM with a small CPU
share waits longer at first than dockerd's 100 ms; the longest wait is the host's figure,
seconds on Fedora's numbers where dockerd's is a minute; the start-over run is the
longest wait, not 10 s. No script reads more than restarts coming, counting and waiting
longer each time, which all hold.

**Tested.** Unit tests (`daemon::restart::tests`): what each policy restarts; the waits
from a cost, a share and an idle rate (first, doubling, longest, start over, a small
share, the log2 bound); a cold host doubling on; what a host learns from ready, claimed
and ended VMs, kept and read back from the home, a garbled file read as nothing; the slope
against the CPU over the time; this host's own process's CPU read
(`a_processs_cpu_is_read_on_this_host`, on every platform's CI). On Fedora, 9 of 9.
`resources::tests::a_runs_cpu_allowance_is_its_limits_share`. Measured: PM M484.
**Not yet:** the harness on macOS; the harness again on Fedora with the slope fit, to set
what the daemon learned beside its process tree's and cgroup's figures; the E2E restart
test (`tests/containers.rs` `restart_policies_start_microvms_again`, cold boots, so the
cold-start rule) and a pooled one, on real VMs on each platform.

### D208. A GPU on every Linux host: musl's GPU VM process, and Intel's GPUs (built)

The roadmap's item 6b, after D201: Venus on Linux hosts was built for glibc's and tested on
NVIDIA's and AMD's GPUs. shards runs on Linux with glibc and with musl (CLAUDE.md), and a
musl build carried no GPU's VM process: a run asking for a GPU was told this shards was
built without one. What every Linux host has now:

- **musl's GPU's VM process links musl dynamically.** A host's GPU driver is a library of
  its C library (D201): on a musl host, Alpine's, Mesa and the Vulkan loader are musl's,
  which a static program cannot dlopen(3). So musl's GPU's VM process is built on a musl
  host, against its musl, with musl's static default turned off for it alone (Rust's
  `-C target-feature=-crt-static`, "Static and dynamic C runtimes" in the rustc book) and
  linked by the host's C compiler (build.rs, `compile_gpu_helper`); `shards` itself and
  every other helper stay static (PM M281). CI's musl release job and the release's musl
  builds make the renderer in their Alpine container (scripts/musl-ci, given
  SHARDS_GPU_LIBS: bash, pkgconf, Python and Linux's headers added for scripts/gpu-libs,
  whose meson and ninja and PyYAML come as PyPI's musllinux wheels, pinned by hash beside
  the manylinux ones). The process's interpreter is musl's loader,
  `/lib/ld-musl-<arch>.so.1`: a musl build on a host of glibc's, which has none, refuses a
  GPU in words naming the glibc build (`helpers::vm_gpu`), where exec(2) would say only
  that a file it has is not there. It needs musl's libc and libgcc_s alone, which a musl
  host's Mesa drivers, C++, need too. Landlock lets it read musl's loader's search path
  (`/etc/ld-musl-<arch>.path`, musl's ldso/dynlink.c), where a host names one.
- **What else the GPU's VM process is allowed** (PM M425), found as tests/gpu.rs ran on
  Intel's UHD Graphics (Raptor Lake-S) under Mesa's Intel driver, glibc's and musl's, each
  refusal ending the VM process before its guest was ready or as its `vulkaninfo` ran:
  `sysinfo`, by which glibc's and musl's `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` says the host's memory
  to the driver, which sizes an integrated GPU's heap by it; udmabuf's UDMABUF_CREATE
  alone, by which Venus makes a dma-buf of the renderer's memory files where a driver
  exports no host memory it can map (virglrenderer's vkr_device_memory.c), /dev/udmabuf
  being Landlock's already (D201); a dma-buf's sync-file export and import
  (DMA_BUF_IOCTL_EXPORT_SYNC_FILE and _IMPORT_SYNC_FILE, linux/dma-buf.h), the implicit
  sync Mesa 26.1's Intel driver keeps; a thread's priority and policy refused with EPERM,
  as its CPUs are (D201), which Venus's ring thread sets as its guest asks (vkr_ring.c,
  setpriority) and Mesa's sets for the queues it starts at their least (u_queue.c,
  SCHED_BATCH and nice 19), both going on past the refusal, the VM process's threads'
  scheduling being shards'; and, for musl's build alone, membarrier's private expedited
  command and its registration, which musl makes as a process starts its first thread and
  as its loader installs a library's thread-local storage in every thread (musl's
  src/linux/membarrier.c, ldso/dynlink.c), and pwritev2 with RWF_NOAPPEND alone, musl
  1.2.6's pwrite(3) (src/unistd/pwrite.c), as a GPU's template is saved. Each is matched
  exactly, by request or command: the filter compares an argument's low 32 bits, as
  musl's `ioctl` passes its `int` request sign-extended.
- **The renderer's objects are position-independent wherever built** (scripts/gpu-libs,
  meson's `b_pie`): Fedora's gcc 16.2.1 makes none by default (built without
  `--enable-default-pie`), and the render server's objects' absolute relocations failed
  the GPU's VM process's link there, a position-independent executable.
- **Tested** (tests/gpu.rs on fedora: Core i9-14900HX, its UHD Graphics and an RTX 4070

### D209. microVMs on arm64 Windows hosts: WHP's arm64 backend (boot measured, E2E pending)

**Why.** The platform parity plan's step 10 (docs/audit/2026-10-27_platform-parity.md): WHP
has a released arm64 API from Windows 11 24H2's build 26100.3915 (QEMU's
docs/system/whpx.rst), which says so by WinHvPlatformDefs.h's `Arm64Support` feature, as
QEMU's whpx_accel_init and shards' `check_host` ask; shards' VMM drives it as it drives
x86_64's (D140). `hv::whp_arm64`, `hv = "whp"` on arm64 Windows.

- **Its types are the header's own.** windows-sys carries none of WHP's arm64 types (its
  metadata is x64's), so the backend declares them from the Windows SDK 10.0.26100's
  WinHvPlatformDefs.h, each size held to its C_ASSERT; its functions bound as first called,
  as x86_64's are (PM M113).
- **The platform's GICv3, at QEMU virt's places** (arch/aarch64's layout): its distributor
  and ITS frame given as the partition is set up (WHvPartitionPropertyCodeArm64IcParameters,
  as QEMU's whpx_accel_init gives them), each vCPU's redistributor by its GICR base register
  as it is made, the virtual timer's PPI 27 and the PMU's 23. SPIs asked of it
  (WHvRequestInterrupt); a PCI bus's MSIs through a GICv2m frame the VMM keeps, each an edge
  on the SPI it names, as the platform's GIC takes no ITS here (QEMU: "ITS not supported on
  WHPX").
- **PSCI is the hypervisor's.** A vCPU past the first is held in StartupSuspend until the
  guest's CPU_ON starts it, and SYSTEM_OFF and SYSTEM_RESET come back as an Arm64Reset exit,
  as QEMU's target/arm/whpx has them; the guest's devicetree names HVC, the guest having no
  EL2 (QEMU's `virt` too, without EL2).
- **MMIO completed from the exit's syndrome**, as KVM completes it (`kvm_handle_mmio_return`):
  the access's register, size and sign extension, PC past it.
- **Snapshots** keep each vCPU's registers by their encodings, as HVF's backend keeps them
  (arch/aarch64/state.rs): the general, SIMD and floating-point registers, the EL1 system
  registers QEMU's accelerator syncs, the pointer authentication keys and the breakpoint and
  watchpoint registers its ID registers say the guest has, its OS lock, and its power as
  StartupSuspend holds it; the GIC's state in the platform's own layouts
  (WHvGetVirtualProcessorState: the partition's global interrupt state, distributor and
  SPIs, and each vCPU's interrupt controller state, redistributor and CPU interface, in
  page-aligned buffers, as their types are page frames'); and the CPU's identity, MIDR
  from its vCPU and 15 global ID registers Linux takes its features by, read with
  WHV_ANY_VP. A guest given SVE or SME, whose vector state none of these keeps, and a
  vCPU stopped with an event pending take no snapshot. The guest's counter is set through
  CNTVCT_EL0. Partition time is suspended before the restored vCPUs are made; each counter
  is set before its timer registers, and the first run resumes time for them together.
  Per-thread host-counter samples at release caused a backward clock step in the busy
  snapshot E2E (M414). Working sets use WHP's Populate advice and the host's mapped pages,
  as on x86_64 (D196).
- **What the integration's backends do since, as x86_64's WHP does them** (built, not yet
  run here): a live move's watch of its guest's writes (D176 part 7), each writable range
  the partition maps kept, mapped again with tracking as the watch begins and its bitmap
  read each round (`WHvQueryGpaRangeDirtyBitmap`, its API x64's and Arm64's alike), a
  share's DAX window untracked as x86_64's; a guest restored on another CPU told the
  snapshot's (D176 part 6), MIDR_EL1 set on its vCPU and the feature ID registers on the
  partition (`WHV_ANY_VP`), each read back, a CPU that keeps any otherwise refused by
  name. A host's PCI function is given the VM's kernel where its hypervisor assigns
  devices, by x86_64's code (D154: `hv::whp`'s vpci.rs, included by path, as Microsoft
  Learn gives every virtual PCI function x64 and Arm64 alike, and the SDK's headers declare
  them and their types outside their architectures' branches), its partition allowed
  device assignment before setup, and each MSI the SPI the GICv2m frame the VMM keeps
  names, at VP 0, as WHP aims an MSI at one vCPU on Arm64; refused with the hypervisor's
  own answer where it assigns none.
- **Measured boot; feature E2E pending.** Its host is Windows 11 Pro arm64 26300.9457
  from Microsoft's ISO, nested under QEMU on this Mac (the user's decision, 2026-10-30).
  M414 records the failed HVF boots and the working TCG host, with TF-A at EL3, pointer
  authentication off and ACPI describing TF-A's PSCI handler. Windows reports its
  hypervisor started; the probe ran its real WHP guest, took an SPI, started its secondary
  through PSCI, and set back the GIC states. CNTVCT_EL0 is set per vCPU. Shards booted its
  pinned Linux kernel as a standard user through the confined VM process. Core snapshot
  restores and the busy-machine test at two and eight vCPUs passed. The full snapshot
  and feature E2E suite must still pass before step 10 is closed. CI's native
  windows-11-arm image has no WHP (M172); its VM tests saying SKIP remain no VM evidence.
- **A start is waited for while it runs** (M424, every host). Its full suite's failures
  were nearly all microVMs given up on as they booted, each running its start the whole
  wait: their least 10 s of it, 3.3 s of CPU. The deadline was a wall clock's, a minute
  held to by CI's runners, where a cold boot takes 1.6 to 2.2 s (M357), which this host's
  speed sets past it. Now the daemon follows a starting microVM's process by D215's judge
  (`ready`, ROOT's (3) slice 2, 2026-11-13; it was each `READY_STALL`'s 10 s, judged by an
  idle microVM's CPU, 63 ms in 10 s, `IDLE_VM_CPU`, given up on after `READY_TIMEOUT`'s
  minute): before this daemon's first READY, its liveness alone; then past W*, the slowest
  start it has seen (`Answers::ready`, which each READY teaches), looked at each W* and given
  up on where a whole W* shows it ran no CPU, its host not the reason. Every other wait on a
  starting microVM is judged so, each by a record of its own kind kept beside `ready`'s
  (#77's ready-judged slice, 2026-11-13, R03: "we do not tolerate arbitrary constants");
  each refusal still says what the VM was doing and for how long:
  - *A claim* (`claim`) waits while a VM of its pool starts, its watcher waking it as that
    VM is ready or given up, with no deadline of its own; with none starting and none
    planned (its template collected, its root filesystem unrecorded or replaced), none
    comes, and it is refused at once: "no warm VM of … was ready in …: none is starting for
    it". It was `READY_TIMEOUT`'s minute, which it waited out for nothing
    (`a_claim_none_can_start_for_is_refused_at_once`).
  - *A visit's VM holding its files* (`visit::await_holding`, its STARTED after RUN, timed from
    its RUN, its VM process read only past W*: D222, amended 2026-11-17) is
    judged on `Answers::held`: "its VM ran nothing of its start for …, past the slowest hold
    seen (…), … after it began". It was `READY_STALL`'s 10 s looks and `READY_TIMEOUT`'s
    60 s (`a_visits_vm_is_waited_for_while_it_starts_and_refused_once_still_past_the_slowest_hold`:
    a busy stand-in holding 1.5 s on is taken; a stopped one past it is refused).
  - *A VM's requests for access* (macOS, `grant`) after its first are judged each on
    `Answers::grants`, taught by each request that came after a wait, never by the link's
    end; a VM first quiet past W* between two is sampled once (sample(1)). Its spawn to its
    first request is its launch (`launch`), the host's to admit (PM M166: amfid, syspolicyd
    and secinitd's work, which its threads wait on asleep, so no look at its process tells
    it from a stall): followed by its liveness alone, its link's end, each launch learned
    into `Answers::launches`, and one past the slowest seen said once, to the log and to a
    waiting run's client on a terminal (piped, Docker's text), as macOS launch services' (ROOT's batch 26: a launch refused 16 ms
    still on a loaded host, M166's decision of 2026-11-14). The tests' judge takes a VM
    process still in its launch (`platform::in_launch`: no thread named as its own code
    names its main one, `platform::launch_over`) for its host's hold. It was `GRANT_STALL`'s
    10 s and a 60 s read timeout of `READY_TIMEOUT`'s.
  - *A builder's dial* (`builder::dialed`) is judged on its own `BOOTED`, as its `NEEDED`
    and `ENDED` are. It was `BOOT_PATIENCE`'s 30 s, judged each `READY_STALL`.
  Each is cold before its kind's first answer: the VM's liveness alone, its connection's
  end or its process's exit, typed as D215's `Seen::Cold`. Not caught: a guest that spins before it is ready (a panic
  resets it, `panic=-1`, which ends its VM). A READY there as its wait begins teaches
  nothing, as it was waited for not at all (D222's wait of nothing, read as D185's
  `Asked::waited` is): on macOS the wait begins once the VM has its grants, which a quick
  restore can end with its READY said, and its W* of next to nothing would have each later
  start looked at each millisecond (`a_ready_said_before_its_wait_teaches_nothing`). The log
  says once, as a start first outlasts W*, how far into it it is, to the µs; it said so at
  each look, a cadence, in whole seconds: "not ready in 0ns" of one under a second (HVF, at
  5ec3f86cc). A test's client past its deadline is waited on while its daemon says
  something (`common::Said`): a start past W* is said once, a cold one not at all, the cold
  start's gap (D215). `a_starting_vm_progresses_by_more_cpu_than_an_idle_one_takes` holds the
  basis to M357, and `a_sleeping_process_runs_nothing_a_boot_does_and_a_busy_one_runs`
  to the host's own process times.
- **A workload is waited for while it runs** (M424, every host). Five of the suite's cases
  failed after their boots, their guests' work run past a test's deadline at TCG's speed
  (a 64-vCPU storm, a 3 GiB build step, a 2.4 GiB allocation, two 1 GiB execs), where the
  daemon said nothing while a workload ran, so that no test could tell slow from stuck.
  Now its listener looks at each microVM a client waits on, an attached run's own client
  until its run ends or an exec's (none detached) until it ends (`EXEC_ENDED`), and logs its CPU time and page faults and what each grew by where it ran
  more than an idle microVM takes in as long (`shards_vmm::platform::progressed`, the
  basis `ready` judges a start by, moved beside `process_usage`, which counts each
  process's page faults now on every host). An idle or stalled microVM is said nothing
  of: a test's client past its deadline (`common::Said`) is waited on while its microVM
  runs, and given up on a minute after it last ran, as before. Where a microVM is the
  client's own, no daemon's (`shards run vm --kernel`, `shards restore vm`, `shards build image`'s
  builders), the test judges the VM processes under its client itself, by the same basis
  and slice (`common::Ran`, until W6's slice 2b part 2), while they start. Detached runs are not looked at:
  a busy server run with `-d` logs nothing. Not caught, as of a start: a guest that spins
  for ever, which its CI job's limit ends. Its looks were each `READY_STALL`'s 10 s; they
  are paced by `Answers::ready` now (#77's ready-judged slice): the first W*, the slowest
  start seen, after the client began to wait, each next twice as long after the one before,
  so that what one wait says grows with the logarithm of its length however small W* is
  (RFC 6298 §5.5's doubling of a retransmission timer), and none before the daemon's first
  READY, as a heartbeat is a diagnostic: a client's own wait reads the microVM's process.
  `a_microvm_is_followed_while_a_client_waits_on_it` holds who is looked at and the pace, and
  `a_busy_process_is_seen_running_with_its_cpu_and_faults` the look on the host's own
  process times.
- **Amended (2026-11-13, ROOT's R03 rulings): a microVM's heartbeat counts by what it did,
  as D215's judge judges a wait.** Superseded by W6's slice 2b part 2 (#77, below): `Floor`
  used R*, a refusal's diagnosis, as a bound on progress, and is gone with `Said::lately` and
  `Ran`; a heartbeat is a daemon line like any other. What it said: A nesting test whose runc hung waited on its microVM's
  heartbeat to Linux CI's 56-minute limit (8a50a9742, run 43391975331), and HVF's past its
  own bound (fafe35efc): the daemon says it each `READY_STALL` while that microVM's CPU runs
  past an idle one's (`progressed`), and a hung runtime's guest's timers run that much
  (63-110 ms in 10 s on HVF). First ruling (c06854111): past a wait's bound, `common::Said`
  takes each whole line its home's daemon says but that heartbeat (`common::HEARTBEAT`) for
  progress, a start said slowly among them, as liveness governs a cold start. Second ruling,
  which replaces "never counts": a heartbeat counts by its deltas. `common::Floor` learns, for
  each microVM the test process follows (by its home, its run's container and VM process; or
  by its VM process), the least CPU rate at which its run still answered (a
  `shards_api::Record`'s R*, taught by each window its run answered within: its client's
  output, which `run_command` tells `Said` and `Ran` as it comes, or a daemon line naming its
  container). During its cold start, before its run has answered, a slice counts by liveness
  alone; past it, only where its rate is not below that floor (`Rate::below`,
  cross-multiplication): an idle microVM's timer ticks are no progress, and a workload's CPU
  past what its run answered at is. `common::Ran` judges each VM process's slice the same way,
  so a build step that prints nothing for a while but works stays waited on. On HVF's nesting
  microVM the floor its first heartbeat taught once its run had answered was 110 ms in 10 s,
  and every idle heartbeat after it fell below. Held by tests/harness.rs's stand-ins:
  `a_cold_heartbeat_and_a_daemons_other_lines_are_progress`,
  `a_wait_on_idle_heartbeats_ends_at_its_bound_and_one_on_work_goes_on` (HVF's heartbeats as
  its runc hung) and `a_vm_processes_slices_count_past_its_cold_start_only_above_its_floor`,
  red before the judge and red again with it removed. What would falsify it: a wait held past
  its bound by a microVM idling below its floor, or one refused while its microVM works at or
  above it. Not caught: a run that never answers keeps its cold start, and its heartbeats count
  by liveness, as a wait begun before its kind's first answer does; and a workload that, silent,
  works below every rate its run answered at is taken for idle.
- **A command's wait has no bound of its caller's** (2026-11-13, goal 71's slice W6; the
  person's ruling of that day, as D180's values and D215 record it: "No record seeds. The
  cold start, and every wait after a run-out, follows the party's liveness and progress.
  After that the bound is the slowest answer seen. No ×2."). Found on WHP (jupiter): chain A
  at 0a3dde0db cut daemon.rs' six stop tests at their first run's 60 s (its pull done,
  "Status: Downloaded newer image" said, its microVM `Created`, a template-saving cold boot
  six at once, the daemon saying nothing), and chain B at 8cc1f6673 cut api_image's and
  build.rs' builds at their 120 s while they worked, both as kiln's headroom guard suspended
  the runner's processes to pace them (its `paced` record listing them, kiln's writes cut to
  6 MB/s). `common::run_command`, and with it every wrapper (`run_shards`, `run_shards_env`,
  `run_shards_env_in`, `run_shards_in`, `vm_run` and the helpers that only passed a timeout
  on: `home_with`, `restarts_cross_at`, `hub`, `hubless`, `hub_bases`, containers.rs'
  `shards_in` and `run_in`, which their `_within` twins fold into), takes no timeout:
  - *Its kind* is its call site (`#[track_caller]` through the wrappers), whose record,
    D215's (`shards_api::Record`: W*, the slowest answer, from the wait's start to its
    client's own end; R* and C*, a bound on a party past W* that ticks but never answers, D215), the test process keeps in
    memory and under `target/judge-records/<os>-<arch>-<logical CPUs>/<call site>`, read
    back by the next run on the host (ROOT: a record learned on the host is data, not a
    seed; every runner of one CI image shares its key, and CI keeps the records from run to
    run by its runner's image: D261, *CI's judge learns across runs*).
    Each answer is taught in, merged with what another process kept, and written whole and
    renamed into place, by a name of its own (its process's and its keep's), the read, merge
    and rename one transaction under the record's lock (`.<record>.lock`, std's
    `File::lock`: flock(2), LockFileEx), let go of before its file closes (M244): without
    it two processes' keeps each read the record before the other renamed, and the last
    to rename, the faster answer's, shrank W* (review waits-11, PM M576; red
    `harness.rs::concurrent_keeps_never_shrink_a_kept_record`). A keep that fails is the
    next answer's to make.
  - *Its key is its whole command line, what a run mints of its own made generic* (#77,
    ROOT's ruling (a) of 2026-11-13). Words alone left build.rs' two call sites one kind
    each: `build --push CTX`, refused, and `build --push -t localhost:PORT/team/built:1 CTX`
    both `shards build`; every `buildx policy eval` `shards buildx policy`. So a command's
    kind is `WaitKind::of(site, words, keyed_line(cmd))`, kept as
    `<call site>-<words>-<the line's SHA-256, its first 16 hex digits>`. The line is its
    program's file stem and every argument, each value the run minted said as the
    placeholder its minting helper registered (`common::minted`), longest first: a
    `TempDir` (its path and its canonical path) as `{dir NAME}`, the directory every one of
    the run's is under as `{testdir}`, each port a helper was handed (`fixed_port`, the
    registries, fake S3, Azure Blob and GitHub Actions, `serve_file`, and the tests' own
    listeners through `minted_port`) as `{port}`, and the process's ID, which the slices,
    builders and pipes the tests name are made of, as `{pid}`; a number is replaced only
    where no digit is beside it. A helper that mints a new kind of value registers its own
    placeholder; a value no helper registers stays as it is, its kind cold each run. Held by
    harness.rs' `a_call_sites_commands_are_keyed_by_their_whole_line` (red at 802f21ba4: one
    record for the refused and the real line; two after, and still two after two rounds
    with new directories and ports) and `the_triaged_call_sites_key_their_refused_command_apart`.
  - *Its words name its command in its key and its account* (#77, the CI
    triage at d24ef4cfd: build.rs' `policy_eval_answers` closure and
    `builds_push_what_they_build` ran many commands from one call site, and a W* of 13.4 ms
    and 3.49 ms, learned from quick refused commands, judged a real build and a push).
    `run_command`'s and `client_output`'s kind is `WaitKind::of(site, command_words(cmd))`,
    kept as `<call site>-<words>`. The words are the program's file stem, then its
    subcommand's: each a plain word (ASCII lowercase letters and `-`, no flag) up to the
    first that is not; its first argument; its second only where shards-cmdline's catalog
    names no command of the first that takes arguments itself (`run`, `push`, `build`, whose
    next word is an image, a name or a path), or shards' grammar reads the two as ACTION
    THING (`grammar::form`: `run vm`, `stop daemon`). So `shards run --rm alpine` is `shards
    run`, `docker push localhost:5000/x` is `docker push`, `docker compose up -d` is `docker
    compose up`, and no run's own name, path, tag or digest is ever a word: each run of a
    call site keys the same kinds. A wait on no command (`Patience`, `judged`, a guest's)
    keeps its call site's key alone (`WaitKind::at`), its kept record read as before; a
    command's key with no record is a cold start. The helpers that wrapped a wait without
    `#[track_caller]` (64 of them across the tests: containers.rs' `shards_in`, `home_with`,
    `hub`, the terminals' `exit`, the managed tests' `command`s, `quit`) carry it now; a wait
    made inside a closure, a `Drop` or a `Read` impl keeps that body's site, its commands
    told apart by their words. Held by harness.rs'
    `one_call_sites_commands_are_judged_apart` (a stand-in that exits, then one that works a
    moment three times between 200 ms of nothing, from one call site: red at f9bdaeda5,
    refused in its first quiet window) and `a_commands_words_are_its_subcommands`.
  - *Only a served answer teaches a command's kind* (2026-11-14, ROOT's batch 22 at
    f385b8dac, lane judgecli). Words and line keep apart a call site's commands that say
    different things, but one line can be refused or served by its home's state alone:
    containers.rs' `a_logs_history_is_what_its_user_set` runs `shards run --rm --pull never
    IMAGE exit 0` twice from its `shards` closure (call site 8499:34), first refused in
    5.4 ms for a settings file its user broke by hand (`disk:2:`), then, the file reset,
    served by a microVM's boot. On KVM (adacachy2, linux-x86_64-32) the refusal taught the
    cold line's record `5435520 0 5435520` (kept at 12:03:03.143, every record of that call
    site this run's own), and the served run, `Created` in its home 300 ms in, was refused
    at a look that found a 6.06 ms gap ("its last progress process 2352022 ran 13.8 ms ago;
    its record W* 5.43552ms, R* 0ns"), a host shared with another lane's harness units. A
    refusal stops at a check before or along its words' work, so its time says nothing of
    that work's gaps; a status of 0 is the one outcome that says the work was done, and a
    nonzero status from served work (a run whose command exited so) teaches nothing either:
    its kind stays cold, judged by its party's liveness, which is safe. So `run_command`'s
    and `client_output`'s waits call `Wait::unserved` at a client's end of any other status
    or a signal, which ends the wait unjudged from there and keeps nothing. A command's
    kept record begins with the word `served`; one without it, kept before this rule, may
    hold a refusal's answer and is read as none, its kind cold until its next served answer
    rewrites it (`common::SERVED`): no number changed (R03). Its R* of 0 ns is no reader's:

    follows every process this test's process started and what descends from them: the run

    account. On it: `booted` (`boot_stoppable` given `Duration::MAX`, a `BootStop` its stop)

- **Part 4: the last test constants, and what a judge cannot refuse** (#77, W6, part A:
  warm.rs, budget.rs, daemon.rs, containers.rs; 2026-11-13, ROOT's ruling on claims that a
  thing does not happen within a time). A judged wait cannot refuse "it does not happen
  within T" while its party idles, since an idle microVM's CPU is progress. So each such
  claim is an ordering against an observable later event of the test's, or, where no later
  event exists, a measurement taken out of pass or fail (`common::measured`: n, p50, p90,
  p99 and max by nearest rank, with the host's name and class and the revision, on the
  test's output as `MEASURED`). No constant is added.
  - *warm.rs.* The daemon link's and the client connection's reads at `TIMEOUT` are `told`,
    a `judged` recv on this test's own VM processes, the warm VM killed (its job's end on
    Windows) where refused, which ends the read; after the VM's exit its link is read to its
    end with nothing to wait on, its peer gone. Its stdout's end "within a second": after
    the exit status, with the VM frozen (SIGSTOP; on Windows already gone), a look that waits
    for nothing, as nothing can change while it is frozen. After the client hangs up, the
    VM's let-go has no later event of its own (its client's relay ends there): the end is a
    `Patience` wait, the VM found still running past it shows the end was the let-go and not
    the VM's exit, and the let-go's time is told.
  - *budget.rs* (Linux). The slice's statistics catching up with its counter is a
    `Patience`. The least room's search set a budget, waited 3 s for the daemon's word and
    set it again, all within `TIMEOUT`: now a `Patience`, a budget set again once the daemon
    has answered the one before (a budget set anew is always said, daemon/budget.rs) or once
    the slice has moved so that the budget it leaves is another.
  - *daemon.rs.* Waits bounded by `TIMEOUT`, 5 s, 10 s, 30 s, 60 s or 600 s are judged: a
    client starting its daemon, its end on its signal and its daemon's look at the lock
    (`Wait` on the client, then on the daemon its log names), the background client's stop,
    a slot taken by hand (`silent_slot`, a `Patience` over `try_slot`'s single look), the
    events stream's head (`judged`, the daemon killed where refused), the cost measurement's
    rounds, a restored home's daemon's end and a killed daemon's runs' ends (`Wait` on each
    process, its home or daemon gone, its threads said where refused), the followers' ends.
    Sleeps that stood for an event are that event: "past its idle time" (1.5 s past a 1 s
    idle) is another daemon of this build with that idle time, started after this one's idle
