    daemon's stop returns, within their most until their keep-alive empties them (`sleep(KEEP)`
    before that wait goes). The starved daemon's "collected while out" is the daemon's log
    order: its "offering slots again" before its collection's word. Upper bounds on elapsed
    time with no later event to order are measurements: the stop with its own stop timeout

- **Part 5: a machine's stages, and the host's work its guest waits on** (#77, 2026-11-14;
  ROOT's KVM run c33 on adacachy2, Linux x86_64, at 5ded5b857, every kept judge record
  cleared first). hotplug.rs:127 was refused: `the guest did not say "SHARDS-PLUG WAIT 2":
  its guest's progress made no progress for 1.090575ms, past the slowest answer of its kind
  seen on this host (1.056001ms), 4.185884ms into its wait ... (a machine of this test's
  process) ... its record W* 1.056001ms, R* 0ns of CPU in 1.056001ms`, its guest having said
  WAIT 0, `grow vda 4096`'s `GREW vda 37` and WAIT 1. Two defects, each enough for it:
  - *One call site's stages were one kind.* `ask`'s wait for `WAIT n+1` keyed its kind by its
    call site alone, so a grow (a size read again) taught the W* that judged a rescan, a
    disk's probe and its first 1 MiB read and write. A wait for a guest's line is now keyed
    by its call site and what it awaits (`Heard::console(awaited)`,
    `WaitKind::of(site, PROGRESS, guest_text(awaited))`, kept as a command's line is, by its
    SHA-256's first 16 hex digits): `common::guest_text` says what the run minted as its
    placeholders (`generic`, as a command's line) and every run of digits as `{n}`, so a step's
    number, PCI address, size and salt say no other work, and a run of more rounds
    (`SHARDS_PLUG_ROUNDS`) keys its stages as one of fewer did. hotplug.rs' `ask` keys each
    step by what it asked and the line it awaits (`until_asked`: `disk {n}:{n}.{n} {n} =>
    SHARDS-PLUG WAIT {n}`, apart from `grow vda {n} => ...`). Each new kind starts cold, its
    liveness alone, as every kind does (D215). The other guest-line waits (`Vm::wait_for*`)
    keep their call site's key (ROOT kept this slice to hotplug.rs:127's).
  - *Its party read no CPU at all.* `Members::Machine` was its console's words alone, so a
    guest that worked silently on the host's side (its rescan's config-space exits on its
    vCPU threads, its disk served by the VMM's threads) showed nothing. A machine's party
    now follows this process's threads beside its waiter (`common::Beside`): each look reads
    the looking thread's CPU counter, this process's, and the looking thread's again; the
    waiter ran at most what its counter grew from before the look before's process reading to
    after this one's, so what the process's counter grew past that, and past the two
    counters' resolutions as their OS says them, is the other threads': their vCPUs, devices
    and any test thread doing the host's part of a step. Unix reads the process through D215's
    `shards_api::Watch` (Linux's CPU clock, 1 ns; macOS' proc_pid_rusage, one Mach unit,
    42 ns) and the thread by CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID (clock_getres: 1 ns Linux, 42 ns macOS);
    Windows by QueryProcessCycleTime and QueryThreadCycleTime, exact cycle counts, no
    resolution to allow, and no CPU time said for them (R* is diagnosis). A look by another
    thread than the look before is based. Nothing here is a chosen number (R03): the
    uncertainty is the clocks' own resolution, cold start is D215's (no record, liveness
    alone; a first look based). Measured before choosing (macOS 26 arm64, this harness's
    method in Python, `docs/research/measurements/judge-machine/beside.py 200000 0` and
    `3000 0.001`, `CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID` at its 1 µs and the thread clock at 42 ns):
    a lone thread's bracketed lower bound passed zero in 9,430 of 200,000 back-to-back looks
    (worst 584 ns), never past the two resolutions' sum; with 1 ms sleeps, 0 of 3,000. So
    the resolutions are subtracted, never only zero. What it can hide: a binary whose tests
    run two machines at once counts each one's CPU as the other's progress, a stall seen once
    the other ends (hotplug.rs' second test runs only beside a host's edu function;
    guest_time.rs has one); and, like a VM process's (D215), a guest spinning on nothing.
  - Red with each guard removed, green with both, on adas-mac-studio-3.local (macOS arm64,
    kiln r1950, eb05eaeaa): harness.rs `one_call_sites_guest_stages_are_judged_apart` (a
    stand-in: a grow's stage answered at once, then a disk's after 50 ms of nothing; keyed by
    the call site alone, refused 18.2 ms in at W* 146 µs), `a_machines_host_work_is_its_progress`
    (a thread of the test spinning 200 ms as the host's work; with no `Beside`, refused
    11.8 ms in at W* 255 µs, "R* 0ns of CPU"), `a_machines_waiter_alone_is_no_progress` (a
    stand-in whose waiter spins on its looks, nothing else running: refused; with the
    waiter's own run not taken off, never refused in 10 s at W* 146 µs), and
    `a_guest_waits_text_is_keyed_without_its_numbers`.
  - Owed (ROOT): hotplug.rs and guest_time.rs on KVM, HVF and WHP, their records cleared;
    the harness's Windows run of `a_machines_waiter_alone_is_no_progress`, which holds the
    cycle counters' accounting of a running thread (unverified here).
  - *Linux's process clock lags its other running threads* (CI run 43575280954, aarch64
    glibc: `a_machines_host_work_is_its_progress` refused 181 ms into its thread's 200 ms
    spin at W* 239 µs, the process's clock last grown beside its waiter 2.6 ms before).
    `thread_group_cputime` (kernel/sched/cputime.c) brings only the reading thread's run up
    to date; a thread running on another CPU is in the process's clock as of that CPU's last
    tick or scheduler event, so between ticks it grows by the waiter's own run alone.
    A thread's own clock (`CPUCLOCK_SCHED` per thread, `task_sched_runtime` in
    kernel/sched/core.c) brings a running thread up to date as it is read. On Linux `Beside`
    now also reads each other thread of `/proc/self/task` by its own clock (`(~tid << 3) | 6`,
    include/linux/posix-timers.h `make_thread_cpuclock`, as glibc's and musl's

    bracketed clock or the threads' own clocks grew (the process's still counts a thread
    that ran and exited between looks). No new number (R03): the ID's encoding is the
    kernel's ABI; a thread found anew began since the look before, so all it ran is since;
    a first look stays based. Measured on adacachy2 (Linux 7.3.3 CachyOS x86_64,

    clocks 0 / 3 / 0 at 100 / 239 / 500 µs paces; with them removed (process clock alone)
    28 / 17 / 17. What it can still hide: a thread its host holds runnable but not running
    is no progress and no hold here (`Beside` reads no schedstat), so a host that holds a
    machine's threads past W* can still see it refused.
  - *A read's test began its clock after its stand-in's* (CI run 43575280954, Alpine:
    `a_judged_read_goes_on_while_its_party_works` "it answered 999.714051ms in", its read
    never refused): the stand-in's second of work starts as its connect returns, which can be

**The storm's watch, by the host's word (audit of picked constants, 2026-11-09).** The test
guest's storm said its main thread stood still after 15 s and took its host's stream for
stopped after 60 s, a copy of the host's `DAEMON_QUIET`. The host now tells it that quiet on
its command line (`shards_quiet_ms`, tests/snapshot.rs), which bounds the stream and gives
the kernel's account; and a stall is said once the main thread has stood still for more of
its watchers' looks than it ever had before (its own pace on the host that runs it), once a
beat.

| Literal | Was | Now | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| `STOOD_STILL` (testguest linux.rs) | 15 s | the longest the main thread stood still before | its watchers' looks |
| `STREAM_QUIET` (testguest linux.rs) | 60 s, a copy | the host's `DAEMON_QUIET`, told; since #77 none: no guest bound on the stream, and the account at both paces past | `stall::Watch`'s looks |
| `AWAIT_MOST` (testdir shards-testhelper.rs) | 300 s | none: waits while its test's directory is | `TempDir`, removed as its test ends, failed or killed |

Owed: the storm suites (tests/snapshot.rs) on KVM, Hypervisor.framework and the nested arm64
Windows host, and the remote and build tests that run the helper's `await`.

**The storm's quiet, learned in the guest (#77, 2026-11-13).** The told quiet was still the
host's fixed minute, copied into the guest (R03). It decided three things, now each from
the run itself, and the guest is told no quiet (`shards_quiet_ms` and `host_quiet` are gone):

- **The stream after a snapshot and the host's word at the end** wait with no bound of the
  guest's own (`waiting`, then a blocking `vsock_accept`), as the storm's other waits
  already did. The host is the one judge of a stream that stops: its reads are a judged
  wait (`common::Following`), and it waits on its guest while it says something new or
  carries bytes (`Heard::streaming`), and ends the microVM when it gives up. The guest says the bytes
  echoed since the snapshot as it waits, a line that changes only as they do, so a stopped
  stream gives the host no new line.
- **The kernel's account of a stalled main thread** (`stall::Watch`, testguest's library,
  one per watcher) is given once the main thread has stood still for more of a watcher's
  looks than it ever did before it moved on, and the echo has carried nothing for more
  looks than it ever went without while it carried: D215's rule, past its own bound a wait
  goes on while progress shows (the stream's bytes) and fails only after a whole window
  without any (the stream's own longest gap). M427's 26 and 56 s stand-stills at a clock
  check, with the stream carrying, are no stall; the account at the copied minute could
  have held CPU 0 as M427's at 15 s did.
- **Cold start, typed** (`Count::longest`): the main thread's pace starts at no
  stand-still, so each stand past it is said, one cheap line a beat (`Verdict::PastItsPace`);
  the echo's starts unlearned (`None`), so until it has carried a byte since the watch began
  (a restore whose host has not streamed again yet) no stall is found and the host's own
  reads say where its stream stopped. Counts saturate; the look is a second, the watchers'
  sampling, which sets the rule's grain and no bound.

Held by `stall.rs`' unit tests (red at daa598a12, the told minute; green with the learned
rule): `a_slow_main_thread_while_the_stream_carries_is_no_stall` (M427's shape),
`a_stall_is_both_past_their_pace` and `a_stream_not_yet_carried_makes_no_stall`. The gap: a
main thread stuck for good while the stream goes on carrying gets its `PastItsPace` line and
no account (the copied minute gave one), and the host, its stream carrying, waits on it
(`Heard::of`) to its job's limit. Owed (ROOT): the storm suites (tests/snapshot.rs) on KVM,
Hypervisor.framework and the nested arm64 Windows host.

**Part 6: a run's stop grace is its daemon's own deadline** (#77, 2026-11-14; ROOT's brief:
fix the judge's reading, not the bound). HVF at 0ce6cdc66 (adas-mac-studio.local, macOS
arm64, kiln r2081, `managed_output metrics::task_refusals_export_the_actual_kernel_event_counter`
alone, daemon.log timestamped by a watcher beside it): `stop daemon` (managed_output.rs:347)
was refused 259 ms into its wait, "no progress for 45.3 ms" past a W* of 36.0 ms, its last
progress "process 98449 ran". The daemon said "stepping aside" at 2.612 s, its run's end
("managed output closed", `Exited (137)`) at 12.632 s: 10.02 s, the default stop grace
(`STOP_GRACE`, Docker's 10 s) of a `/bin/testguest sleep` main that, its PID namespace's
init with no handler, ignores SIGTERM from outside its namespace (kernel/signal.c
`sig_task_ignored`, SIGNAL_UNKILLABLE), until its SIGKILL. Through the grace the daemon's
stop thread waits on its timer and the guest sleeps: nothing of the party runs, and nothing
is stalled. The party was whole: the client, the daemon and its tree by parent (spawner,
VM and network processes) are all members on Unix; it was not missing the spawner's
children, the first reading of the failure.
- *The rule.* A run's stop grace is a deadline its daemon holds, set by the run (`stop -t`,
  `--stop-timeout`) or the daemon's default. From the signal the daemon sends a run's
  command (its own stop, `stop_each`; a stop of named runs, `end_all`) until
  that command's SIGKILL or its end, the daemon keeps `stop.grace` in the run's directory
  (`shards_ipc::GRACE`: the SIGKILL's time, nanoseconds since the Unix epoch, written whole,
  removed by its guard's drop at the SIGKILL, the run's end or the stop's own end). A
  look (`Party::look`) that finds a process of its party live and nothing else (`Still`)
  while a run of its home is within its grace finds it `Held`: the daemon's own deadline.
  Past the grace it is judged as before, a whole W* without progress refused. Part 10 keeps
  a run's log's next try so too (`ship.retry`), for a wait on that log's delivery alone.
- *R03.* No literal: the grace is the run's own or the daemon's default, the deadline the
  daemon itself acts at. The clock is the system clock, the one std reads alike in two
  processes on every OS; a step of it moves the hold by the step. A grace that cannot be
  kept (past the clock's reach, a write that fails) is said in the daemon's log and keeps
  no hold: that wait is judged as before. A negative stop timeout (no SIGKILL at all) keeps
  none either: its wait follows the judge as before (the gap).
- *Held by* tests/harness.rs `a_runs_stop_grace_is_its_daemons_and_not_refused` (a
  sleeping stand-in daemon, a run of its home in its grace for 20 W*, a sleeping client),
  on adas-mac-studio-3.local (macOS arm64, kiln r2083, at 58ddf5b9d): red with the look's
  grace arm removed, refused 148.2 ms into a grace of 1.454 s (W* 72.7 ms); green with it,
  held through the grace and refused once past; harness.rs 27 passed, 3 ignored; clippy of
  shards and shards-ipc clean. The daemon's side (the file kept and removed) has no unit
  test: the real-VM run is its evidence. Owed (ROOT): `cargo test -p shards --profile
  test-release --test managed_output -- --test-threads=1` on HVF and KVM.

**Part 7: a restored guest's first answer is a kind of its own** (#77, 2026-11-14; ROOT's
brief: fix the judge's reading, not the bound). HVF (adas-mac-studio.local, main 6f3cd4428)
and KVM (c35 at 8fdd66512, c36 at 3f2705f8d): moved.rs
`a_moved_microvms_published_port_answers_there` was refused at :631, "a guest's stream made
no progress for 34.870583ms, past the slowest answer of its kind seen on this host
(17.694042ms), 70.9335ms into its wait ... (this test's own VM processes, its CPU its
liveness alone, daemon 47690 of …/ports-t-12) ... its last progress its daemon said
something 70.516834ms ago; its host not holding it; its record W* 17.694042ms, R* 0ns of
CPU in 17.694042ms".
- *The cause.* The test read its published port through one closure, `ask`, before the move
  (a running guest) and after it (the guest its restore on the other home had just
  started). `Following`'s kind is its call site and `STREAM` (`WaitKind::awaiting`), and a
  closure cannot be `#[track_caller]` on stable Rust, so both reads were moved.rs:629:9, one
  kind: the warm read's 17.7 ms answer was the W* that judged the restored guest's first
  answer. That answer waits on the restored guest's own work (its memory faulted back from
  its snapshot, its first accept) and carries no byte until it comes. A `Following`'s
  party's CPU is its liveness alone (`Cpu::Liveness`), so no reading of its processes would
  have shown that work as progress: the kind, not the party, was wrong.
- *Not the party.* The party was whole: no VM process is the test's own here, and the
  restored VM process descends from the other home's daemon (its spawner's child), which
  `Party::members` follows by parent. "R* 0ns of CPU" is the record's, not this wait's: the
  rate of the one answer that taught it, whose looks read no CPU between a first look (based)
  and its answer. The harness test below shows the same "R* 0ns of CPU in W*" with no party
  at all.
- *The fix.* moved.rs' two published-port tests read through nested `#[track_caller]`
  functions, so each read's kind is its caller's site: the read before the move and the
  restored guest's first are two kinds, each cold on a host until its own first answer
  (D215), each learning from its own answers alone. No literal and no bound changed (R03).
- *Held by* tests/harness.rs `a_moved_guests_first_answer_is_a_kind_of_its_own`
  (a stream answered 5 ms in, then one answered after four times the W* that taught, from
  two call sites of one `#[track_caller]` helper), on adas-mac-studio-3.local (macOS arm64,
  kiln r60/r64, dac3eafa3's tests): green 3 of 3; red with both read through one closure
  (moved.rs' shape), 2 of 2, "refused 81.1845ms into its peer's quiet: a guest's stream made
  no progress for 20.296125ms, past the slowest answer of its kind seen on this host
  (20.296125ms) ... its record W* 20.296125ms, R* 0ns of CPU in 20.296125ms". The whole
  harness binary (r42, the test's first form): its 27 others passed, 3 ignored; clippy of shards (`--all-targets -D warnings`) clean.
  Owed (ROOT): `cargo test -p shards --profile test-release --test moved --
  --test-threads=1` on HVF and KVM.
- *The old kind's record.* The closure's kind (moved.rs:629:9's `STREAM` record under
  `target/judge-records`) is read by no wait now: no code reads a kept record of an old
  kind, and each new site starts cold. The file is inert test-target data; it may be
  deleted, and no migration is needed.
- *Not reproduced: a build's refusal in nesting.rs* (HVF, adas-mac-studio.local, main
  f8f303ae7, `--test-threads=1`, beside other work on that Mac):
  `a_deadline_given_through_shards_api_is_met_or_said_passed` panicked at nesting.rs:147:14 (`Home::build`'s
  `shards build image -q -t nesting:1 …`), "made no progress for 731.985502ms, past the
  slowest answer of its kind seen on this host (389.415459ms), 790.740459ms into its
  wait". Its account (party, last progress, hold) was not kept. Run again at f8f303ae7
  with the same warm target, `cargo test -p shards --profile test-release --test nesting
  -- --test-threads=1`, 20 times beside a cold `cargo build -p shards --profile
  test-release --tests` of a separate clone (kiln r106, every run's output kept in
  adas-mac-studio.local:~/g121-tmp/moved-judge-diag/runs): 20 of 20 green, no refusal; and
  twice unfiltered, side by side: green. The judge is unchanged for it (R09). Two
  candidates, unconfirmed:
  - *A party gap in code.* `common::served()`'s registry is threads of the test process
    (`registry_serving_at`), and a judged command's party is its client, its home's daemon
    and their descendants by parent, never the test process: a build or pull from it
    waits on work no party counts. Each request also clones the whole image (manifest and
    every blob) under one `Mutex` (`image.lock().unwrap().clone()`), so a request waits
    on others' clones. This gap is real whether or not it caused this refusal.
  - *Disk I/O with no CPU.* A daemon blocked in an APFS write or fsync runs no CPU, and
    D215's look does not find it `Held` (runnable on no CPU, or stalled on memory).
  Owed (ROOT): that command looped on HVF until a refusal, its whole account kept (the
  "--- its wait" block, stdout/stderr and its process dump).

**Part 8: this process's servers are every party's; a waiter's own polls are no hold**
(#77 follow-ups, 2026-11-14; ROOT's brief from Part 7's two candidates and a load-sensitive
harness test).
- *A party gap: the test registry's threads.* `common::served()`'s registry
  (`registry_serving_at`) answers on threads of the test process. A judged command's party
  is its client, its home's daemon and their descendants by parent, never the test process,
  so a pull or build from that registry waited on work no party counted: a registry thread
  working for a request, its client and daemon blocked on the socket, was a still party.
  - *The fix.* Each connection's thread is followed as a server (`common::Server`, made by
    the thread itself, dropped as it ends), and every party's look counts what the
    process's servers ran since the look before as its progress, and one runnable that ran
    nothing as its host's hold (`Party::look`, under `Cpu::Progress` alone, as `Beside`
    counts a machine's threads). Each server is read where it runs, by its own counter, as
    its OS keeps one for another thread to read: Linux its CPU clock
    (`make_thread_cpuclock`, as `Beside`'s other threads) and its `/proc/self/task/<tid>/stat`
    state `R`; macOS `thread_info(THREAD_BASIC_INFO)` of its Mach port
    (pthread_mach_thread_np(3)), user plus system time and `TH_STATE_RUNNING` (running or
    waiting for a CPU, mach/thread_info.h); Windows QueryThreadCycleTime of a handle it opens
    for itself (cycles, exact; no state read, so no hold seen there). A server's last
    reading is kept as it ends, so the total never falls. No literal: any growth of a
    counter is a run, as D215's look counts any CPU at all.
  - *Its limit.* The servers are the process's, not one party's: a binary whose tests pull
    from registries at once has each pull's serving the other waits' progress, a stall
    shown only once the serving ends, as `Beside` says of two machines.
  - *The registry's own cost.* Each request cloned the whole image (manifest and every
    blob) under one `Mutex` and hashed every blob to find the one asked for, so a request
    waited on the others' clones and on CPU proportional to the image. The image is now an
    `Arc` taken under its lock and let go of at once (`common::Served`, `set` to replace it),
    each blob's digest computed once as it is set, and a body written from the shared bytes,
    its head first with `TCP_NODELAY` so the head is not held for the client's delayed ACK
    (RFC 896, RFC 1122 4.2.3.2). Its cost before and after is unmeasured (R14, ROOT's).
  - *Held by* tests/harness.rs `a_wait_on_this_processs_server_goes_on_while_it_serves` (in
    a stand-in, whose process nothing else runs in: a kind taught W* by a quick stand-in's
    end, then a stand-in that asks a `Server` thread of its process, which works 3 W* of CPU
    before it answers), on adas-mac-studio-3.local (macOS arm64, kiln r224, the tree of
    commit 37ecff8e1, test-release): green; red with the servers left uncounted (`Party::
    look` reading none), "refused 95.909834ms into its server's 114.523251ms of work: a
    stand-in asking this process made no progress for 57.591376ms, past the slowest answer
    of its kind seen on this host (38.174417ms), 78.591334ms into its wait".
- *A waiter's own polls taken for its host's hold.* harness.rs
  `a_wait_is_refused_though_its_own_polls_keep_its_daemon_busy` failed 3 of 4 on
  adas-mac-studio-3.local while it was busy (2 of 14 cores idle), "not refused 177-197 ms in
  (W* 59.554375ms)", and passed 6 of 6 quieter.
  - *The cause, from its looks' times.* The test's waiter polls `ps -a -q` between looks,
    synchronously. Its looks' times, kept on that host under load (a busy `yes` per core
    and per core twice and six times beside it, a diagnostic print of each poll's span
    and the wait's account, not committed; logs in
    adas-mac-studio-3.local:~/g121-tmp/judge-party/runs, `base-*`, `red*`, `diag-*`): its base look about 25-33 ms, each
    poll 35-50 ms, each look about 25-30 ms (each reads the process table through `ps -A`).
    The judge counts the time a look runs late, past its due or the look before's end, as
    its host's hold of the judge (ROOT's ruling, 2026-11-13), and takes it out of the
    party's window. A look here is late because its waiter was polling, not because its
    host held it: with polls and looks as long as W*, nearly every look is late, its
    window keeps only the looks' own durations and the on-time remainder of each W*, and
    the refusal comes only once those add up to a whole W*. With W* taught on a quiet
    host (59.6 ms) and polls and looks slower under load, that was past the test's 2 W*.
    Under the loads above the test passed (alone 6 of 6, 4 of 4 and 6 of 6; with the whole
    binary 4 of 4 and 3 of 3): each run teaches its kind its own poll as it begins, and the record keeps
    the slowest, so W* rose with the load (58, 80, 95 ms); the red needs polls slower than
    the W* taught, as the busy host's were.
  - *The fix: the waiter's own work is no hold* (`shards_api::Span::own`). Each `Wait` a
    thread makes on a command of its own (`Wait::begin`, run_command's) keeps its span as
    it ends (`common::OWN`, let go of as the thread's last wait ends); a look of another of
    its waits passes the judge the time those spans cover within its lateness, from
    `Judge::late_from` (its due, or the look before's end) to its beginning, and the judge
    takes only the rest for its host's hold. A look late for any other reason (its thread
    held, a frozen process) is held as before. shards-api's own `Follow` makes no polls
    between looks: its `own` is zero. No literal.
  - *Held by* crates/api judge.rs `a_look_its_caller_made_late_by_its_own_work_is_not_held`
    (the busy host's look replayed on an injected clock: base 0-33 ms, a poll 33-93 ms, a
    look 93-123 ms; its lateness its host's, 26 ms seen of a W* and it goes on; its
    caller's own, 60 ms, refused) and harness.rs
    `a_wait_is_refused_though_its_own_polls_outlast_w_star` (a daemon that runs no microVM;
    a kind taught W* by a state found at its first look; then a state that never comes,
    polled between looks by a stand-in of the test's own busy a whole W*: refused at the
    look after the first poll). On adas-mac-studio-3.local (kiln r224, 37ecff8e1's tree):
    green; red with `own` not subtracted, judge.rs's test failed and harness.rs's "not
    refused at its look past its first poll ... 115.439625ms in ... its record W*
    27.602875ms". Under a busy `yes` per core: the whole harness binary 3 of 3 (30 passed,
    3 ignored each), the three tests above 6 of 6.
- *A test's own VM processes leaked to every party.* At the merge of main ff437eddd, harness.rs
  `a_tests_own_vm_processes_are_known_by_their_ids` (5ee39c0ab) registered a busy stand-in
  as one of the test process's own VM processes (`common::OwnVm`), which every
  `Party::own` in the binary follows: run beside it, the two poll tests above were not
  refused, "its last progress process 89935 ran", that stand-in, 3 of 3 runs of the whole
  binary on adas-mac-studio-3.local. It now runs in a stand-in of its own, as `serving` and
  `spinner` do: the whole binary 3 of 3 green, and 3 of 3 under a busy `yes` per core (32
  passed, 3 ignored each); clippy of shards and shards-api (`--all-targets -D warnings`)
  clean there, and of 37ecff8e1's tree on adacachy2 (Linux x86_64, `SHARDS_HELPERS=skip`).
  Owed (ROOT): Windows (the servers' QueryThreadCycleTime reading) is unbuilt here; CI's
  matrix builds it.
- *Not reproduced: two moved.rs refusals* (ROOT, HVF, adas-mac-studio.local, main
  8d1c89a05, one run of `--test moved -- --test-threads=1`, 14 of 16):
  - moved.rs:62:19 `a_cpu_baseline_is_all_its_guest_finds_and_goes_with_it`: "shards run
    daemon --detached --listen 127.0.0.1:0 made no progress for 258.80546ms, past the
    slowest answer of its kind seen on this host (139.745917ms), 287.551833ms into its
    wait".
  - moved.rs:410:15 `a_microvm_moved_saved_keeps_its_cpu_image_files_and_connections`:
    "shards run -d --init --pull never --name mover 127.0.0.1:64972/test/image:v1 counter
    20 made no progress for 149.459707ms, past the slowest answer of its kind seen on this
    host (88.809208ms), 269.855625ms into its wait".
  Their accounts were not kept. From the code: `run daemon --detached` spawns the daemon as
  its client's own child (daemon.rs `detach`, one posix_spawn with setsid) and waits on its
  ready pipe, so while the client lives the daemon is of its party by parent; and :410's
  run is `--pull never`, pulling nothing from the test registry. Run again at main
  b4a018090 on the same host, `SHARDS_REQUIRE_VMS=1 cargo test -p shards --profile
  test-release --test moved -- --test-threads=1`, 10 times (kiln r151, outputs in
  adas-mac-studio.local:~/g121-tmp/jp-runs): 9 of 10 green, neither refusal; run 2 failed

  restored guest's first answer, Part 7's own kind): "a guest's stream made no progress for
  21.490209ms, past the slowest answer of its kind seen on this host (20.331ms),
  71.553208ms into its wait ... (this test's own VM processes, its CPU its liveness alone,
  daemon 60782 of …/ports-t-12) ... its last progress its daemon said something
  64.252916ms ago; its host not holding it; its record W* 20.331ms, R* 0ns of CPU in
  20.331ms". That kind's party is its words alone (`Cpu::Liveness`), so a restored guest's
  first answer slower than the slowest seen of it is refused while its VM process faults its
  memory back: open, ROOT's.

**Part 9: a run that never ends, and what a hang leaves** (the gitssh lane, 2026-11-14; ROOT's
batch 26 brief)
- *The hang.* HVF batch 24 (main 1f71dea19, Adas-Mac-Studio-3, `--test build --
  --test-threads=1`) held build.rs `add_fetches_git_over_ssh` for over an hour, and ROOT ended
  it. It was not the ssh fetch. The build and the first `run -u root sshed:1 stat …` had
  passed, and the three sshd listeners sat at "0 of 10-100 startups" because their fetches
  were long done. The wait was build.rs:5947, the image's next run, `shards run --rm sshed:1
  stat /s1/noise.bin` (client 59937, daemon 59933), "3722.43s in: its last progress process
  59939 ran 751.541µs ago; its host not holding it; its record W* 117.29ms, R* 148.60ms of CPU
  in 117.29ms".
  - A run's VM and network processes are its daemon's spawner's children, the network first
    (launch.rs `launch_with`). The client starts none (only a build's builder is the client's
    child, builder.rs `launch::builder`). So 59939, the client's pid plus 2, was most likely
    the run's shards-vm. The ps was lost with its home.
  - An idle guest's VM process ticks (D215: 10 to 30 ms per 10 s at 14 vCPUs), so the
    judge's "any CPU" saw progress at every look. That was a false negative of D215's look,
    not a livelock: a spin runs a core. It is closed by D215's rate rule (R*, C*, rated
    answers), whose harness test is this hang's shape.
  - Nothing in production bounds a run's command once its VM has said TAKEN, by design (a
    command may run for ever; cli/client.rs `ran_on`), so the test's judge is its only end.
- *What a hang leaves* (ROOT's ruling). A wait ended by SIGINT or SIGTERM (`dump_live_waits`)
  now says, beside each live wait's account, what its home wrote (`show_why`: its runs'
  stderr, its daemon's samples, its daemon log's last lines), which go with the home as the
  process ends. Each account's members (judgecli's member states, ed09f0570) now name each
  process and its parent from the look's own listing (`Party::kin`, no second reader), so
  "process 59939" reads as its name and parent: a VM process (`shards-vm`, the spawner's
  child), the network process, the daemon or the client.
- *Open: the wedge itself, not reproduced.* The guest asleep on the second `run --rm` of a
  built image (its first run, `-u root`, had answered). It was not reproduced in 64 runs on
  Adas-Mac-Studio-3 at ff69e4736: 15 and 40 runs of the test alone, about 4 s each, and 9 of
  build.rs from its start through this test at `--test-threads=1` with
  `SHARDS_REQUIRE_VMS=1`. Logs are in adas-mac-studio.local:~/g121-tmp/gitssh/logs, removed
  at the lane's end. The next one ends refused, its account naming the asleep process and
  its daemon's log. Its cause is what that says.
- *A wait whose own polls outlast W* was not refused* (harness.rs
  `a_wait_is_refused_though_its_own_polls_outlast_w_star`, ROOT's HVF runs; 2 of 20 on bare
  main 14e037fb0 and 8 of 20 at f749bf9fb on adas-mac-studio-3.local). Its account's judge
  figures (new: "still X of its W window, H of its looks' lateness out") said "still 10.2 to
  27.7 ms of its 10 ms window" against a W* of 1.2 to 1.4 ms. The window was the floor, the
  macOS CPU counter's 10 ms tick (`Judge::floor`, b26), over which alone the judge refuses.
  The test's polls were W* and 1 ms, so a look found a whole window only where a poll's
  process start happened to outlast the tick. The judge was right. The test's premise is
  fixed: each poll outlasts the window its judge's looks say (`Patience::window`). The one
  other miss in 40 ("its last progress its daemon ran") was its daemon finishing what the
  test's own `ps` gave it. An idle daemon runs nothing: 0.01 s of CPU before and after 10 s,
  none of its threads' CPU moving over another 10 s, each thread parked in poll(2) or a
  condition wait (`sample`, adas-mac-studio-3.local, f749bf9fb's build). So no housekeeping
  of the daemon's is counted as a wait's progress.

**Part 10: a log's next try is its daemon's own deadline for that log's delivery** (#77,
2026-11-16; goal fb3528f9, the syslog-wait lane, on the shards-green lane's root cause;
scoped the same day by ROOT's ruling, the syslog-scope lane). HVF at 6f5755ae1
(adas-mac-studio.local-2, macOS 26.4 arm64): containers.rs
`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_syslog_as_its_options_say` failed 2 of 2, once with `--nocapture`, at
its step "a server that comes up only after the run". Its wait for the server's first
connection (`accept_within`, a `Patience` on the run's home) was refused: "a state its party
comes to made no progress for 399 ms, past the slowest answer of its kind seen on this host
(241 ms), 763 ms into its wait".
- *The cause.* The run ends before its server listens, so its shipper's first send is
  refused, and `until_done` (daemon/ship.rs) sleeps `RETRY_FIRST`, a second, before it tries
  again (D163's retries). That pause is a deadline of the daemon's own, as a stop grace is:
  nothing of the party need run before it. The E2E judge was told only of stop graces (Part
  6). The daemon's registry of its threads' timed waits (`Waiting`, ecc4810a9) exists under
  `cfg(test)` alone, for its unit tests' in-process waits, and reaches no E2E wait.
- *The rule.* Through each pause before its next try, a shipper keeps `ship.retry` in its
  run's directory (`shards_ipc::RETRY`): the try's time, written and removed as
  `stop.grace` is (nanoseconds since the Unix epoch, written whole, removed by its guard's
  drop as the pause ends or as the daemon stops), and on the line after it the destination
  the pause holds up (`logging::destination`): the run's option that addresses its
  receiver, `KEY=VALUE` as given (`syslog-address=tcp://127.0.0.1:514`), else its driver's
  name. The run is the directory's. It reuses Part 6's mechanism (R12): one guard keeps both
  files (daemon.rs `Deadline`, which was `Grace`, writing a destination where it is given
  one and `stop.grace` none), and one writer and one reader serve both
  (`shards_ipc::deadline_text` and `deadline_in`, which were `grace_text` and
  `grace_until`). Each deadline has a file of its own: a run in its stop grace may have a
  shipper paused too, and one guard's drop must not end the other's hold.
- *Its scope* (ROOT's ruling, 2026-11-16). A pause holds up the delivery of its run's log
  to its destination and nothing else, so it holds only a wait on that delivery: a test
  waiting for its log line to arrive at a log server. Such a wait names the delivery it
  reads (`Wait::delivery_to`, `Patience::delivery_to`: the destination as the run's options
  name it), as containers.rs' `accept_within` does for each log server's first connection
  (syslog over TCP and TLS, the server up only after its run, the restarted daemon's; gelf
  and fluentd over TCP). The judge's look (`Party::look`, through `Party::graced`) holds
  such a wait while a run of its home keeps a `ship.retry` naming that destination, compared
  whole, and its account says so ("its daemon in run …'s log's pause before its next try to
  syslog-address=…, … more"). Every other wait on that daemon is judged on its own
  evidence, as before 03c0b8603, which held them all: a stall elsewhere in a daemon whose
  shipper retries is refused. A run's stop grace (Part 6) is unchanged: a deadline of the
  whole stop, it holds every wait on the daemon. Past a deadline a wait is judged as before.
  Its last `Held` look restarts the window, so a whole W* without progress past the
  deadline is refused; the shipper wakes at the deadline and connects.
- *R03.* No literal: the deadline is the pause the shipper takes (`RETRY_FIRST`, growing by
  half to `RETRY_MOST`, D163's sources), read on the system clock as Part 6's is. The
  destination is the run's own option; the keys it is read from are moby's drivers' own
  address options (`syslog-address`, `gelf-address`, `fluentd-address`, `splunk-url`,
  `awslogs-endpoint`, `gcp-endpoint`, each in its module's `OPTIONS`). A deadline that
  cannot be kept (its run's directory gone, a write that fails) is said in the daemon's log
  and keeps no hold: that wait is judged as before. A daemon killed in a pause leaves its
  file, which holds a wait on its delivery only until the deadline it names (`RETRY_MOST` at
  most), as a stop grace's file does. A `ship.retry` that names no destination (a daemon of
  03c0b8603's build) holds no wait. Its cost, a write, a rename and a remove a pause, is
  unmeasured (R14, ROOT's).
- *What it leaves.* A wait on a delivery its shipper never makes (its server up, yet
  unreachable to the shipper) is held through every pause, each try between them its
  progress, as its test's server is the receiver the retries are for: such a wait ends with
  its test, not its judge. Waits that read a delivery without naming it are judged as before
  03c0b8603: a log server's reads after its first connection (`Following::of_home`) and a
  UDP server's datagrams (`received`). None was seen refused in a pause, and none is changed
  (R09). The drivers' own pauses within a send are deadlines of their own too, and are not
  kept: fluentd's `fluentd-retry-wait`, gelf's reconnect delay, and a stream's wait for its
  receiver's delivery window (stream.rs `await_delivery`). None was seen refused, and none
  is changed (R09). On Windows the shipper's `Wait::pause` does not go through `timed`, so
  the in-process registry misses it in the daemon's own unit tests. That was read in the
  code alone, not reproduced, and is not changed.
- *Held by* (written, not run: the person's rule of 2026-11-16 leaves every test to ROOT):
  daemon/ship.rs `a_shippers_pause_before_its_next_try_is_its_daemons_deadline`, a send to a
  destination always refused, tried as a shipper tries it. Its run's directory keeps the
  pause's end and that destination: a first pause or more past the first refusal, and no
  more than the tries' pause past its read. None is kept once the daemon stops. Its reds,
  expected and unrun: the guard removed (no deadline through two pauses), its drop (the
  deadline kept past the wait), or its destination left out ("not the destination it holds
  up"). logging.rs `a_runs_log_goes_where_its_address_option_says`: the destination as
  given, the last of its key's, else the driver's name. tests/harness.rs
  `a_logs_next_try_holds_a_wait_on_its_delivery`, Part 6's test with its deadline
  `ship.retry` naming a server, 20 W* away, and its wait that server's delivery: held until
  the deadline, refused once past it (its red, expected and unrun: `graced`'s `RETRY` arm
  removed, or its destination compared to another's, refused before the deadline); and
  `a_logs_next_try_holds_no_other_wait_on_its_daemon`, the same deadline as far away as a
  refusal past one is waited for, and a wait on no delivery, then one on another server's:
  each refused before it (its red, expected and unrun: `graced` holding every wait by
  `RETRY`, as at 03c0b8603, or a wait on any delivery whatever its destination).
  Owed (ROOT): `SHARDS_HELPERS=skip cargo test -p shards --profile test-release --bin shards
  -- daemon::ship::tests::a_shippers_pause_before_its_next_try_is_its_daemons_deadline
  logging::tests::a_runs_log_goes_where_its_address_option_says` and `cargo test -p shards
  --profile test-release --test harness -- a_logs_next_try_holds
  a_runs_stop_grace_is_its_daemons_and_not_refused`, each red as said; and `cargo test -p
  shards --profile test-release --test containers -- --exact

**Part 11: a drain is judged by its requests' ends** (goal 1453357d, the own-38-released lane,
2026-11-17; ROOT's brief from CI 44007524337 at 0c3213356)
- *The hang.* ci.yml's `firecracker comparison (x86_64)` job ran to its 30-minute limit in 11
  of main's CI runs from 2026-11-15 to 2026-11-17, each in its Arrival step
  (benches/arrival.rs), which passed in 18, in 76 to 185 s (p50 100 s, p90 141 s). Each cut
  job ended 5 minutes past its limit with no step after Arrival run and no log kept: the
  runner never finished cancelling the step, for a cause no log shows. The daemon's stdio is
  not it (daemon.rs `detach`: a session of its own, its stdio its log, none of the step's
  pipes). Ten cut runs waited for each rate's requests with no judge, the eleventh with
  b713e66b2's. Method and records: `docs/research/measurements/arrival-drain/`.
- *The cause, read from code* (R09's live run is owed, below). A rate's requests were one
  wait on a state (`Patience::clients`): one kind for every rate, its party the clients,
  what descends from them and the home's daemon, its CPU progress. Cold (CI kept no record
  for benches, D261), it follows liveness alone, and the daemon lives through the bench. Once
  rate 2's pass taught W*, any CPU of the daemon or its pools' warm microVMs is progress, and
  they spend it whether or not a request ends. So whatever kept a request from ending, the
  bench waited to the job's limit, and said nothing: it reported only after its last rate.
- *The rule.* A drain waits for each next end (`common::requests_end`), as `guest_says` waits
  for each next line (D261): each end begins a wait for the next.
  - One kind at its call site (`NEXT_END`), whichever rate it drains, so that a rate's first
    drain is judged by what the rates before it showed. Kinds per rate, the interrupted
    lane's draft, left each rate's first drain cold in a fresh run, and with it a stall at a
    rate's onset, as its pools grow to a new demand.
  - Its party: the requests still outstanding by their clients (each end takes its own out),
    what descends from them, and the home's daemon, their CPU their liveness alone
    (`Cpu::Liveness`). The daemon's words are still progress, among them its heartbeat of a
    microVM a client waits on that runs (daemon.rs `log_progress`), whose gap doubles. Its
    host's holds hold it as they hold every wait: a member runnable on no CPU, stopped, or in
    its run's stop grace (Part 6).
  - Its W*: the slowest stretch this host has shown with requests outstanding and none ending,

    liveness alone. The setup's runs are answers in every run of the bench, so its drains are
    judged from its first rate on.

### D207. A Windows host's bind sources: its drives' paths (built)

**Why.** The daemon read `-v` as moby's parser for Linux reads it (linux_parser.go), splitting
it at every colon, and held a bind's source to start with `/`: on Windows `-v C:\src:/dst`
was "invalid mode: /dst", `-v C:\src:/dst:ro` an invalid specification, and a `--mount` of
`C:\src` (Compose's binds, its secrets and configs) not absolute. A Linux microVM on a
Windows host is the case moby's parser for Linux containers on Windows reads (lcow_parser.go,
beside windows_parser.go, moby docker-v29.8.1): its sources the host's, Windows', and its
destinations the guest's, Linux's.

**Decided** (`volumes.rs`, `Sources`):

- **A source of the host's is a drive's absolute path**: `C:\src`, `C:/src` or `\\?\C:\src`
  (lcow's rxHostDir), whose drive's colon ends no part of a `-v`. One from no drive's root
  (`/src`, `\src`, `C:src`) is refused, saying what a host path is there; anything else is a
  volume's name, as on Linux. A source of one letter before a destination (`c:/dst`) is a
  volume's name, as lcow's expression matches it, and no volume's name is one letter
  (`Store::valid`).
- **A microVM's own paths are Linux's on every host**: the binds a microVM's own engine
  makes (D181) name its files, not the host's.
- **What lcow drops, kept**: case, of the source and the destination (lcow lowercases a whole
  `-v`, windows_parser.go splitRawSpec, where a Linux destination tells case and so may an
  NTFS directory, FILE_CS_FLAG_CASE_SENSITIVE_DIR); Linux's modes, `z`, `Z`, propagation,
  `nocopy` and a consistency (lcow's rxMode takes `ro` and `rw` alone, and its validator
  refuses any propagation); and a file bound alone (windows_parser.go: "source path must be
  a directory"), shared through its directory as on Unix.
- **A source cleaned as Go's filepath.Clean cleans one on Windows**, `\` between its names,
  `.` dropped and `..` taken back to its drive's root at most, where lcow turns `/` into `\`
  and drops one trailing `\`. The CLI makes a relative `-v` source absolute against its
  working directory, as Go's filepath.Abs does on its host (`.\data` from `C:\work` is
  `C:\work\data`), where it had cleaned it as a path of slashes.
- **Not served, as lcow serves neither**: a network share's path (`\\server\share`; lcow's
  rxHostDir takes drives alone) and a named pipe ("Linux containers on Windows do not
  support named pipe mounts").

`volumes.rs`'s `a_windows_drives_paths_are_read` holds the reading on every host and
`a_windows_hosts_binds_are_its_drives` the binds on Windows; containers.rs, compose.rs and
engine.rs bind host directories on jupiter and CI's Windows runners (D197's slice 3).

### D202. A GPU on Windows: Venus in the GPU's VM process, its driver reached from a desktop of its own (built)

The parity plan's step 11, after D201: a run on an x86_64 Windows host is given its host's
GPU as a Mac's and a Linux host's are (`--gpus`, a CDI device of the render node, a build
step's `RUN --device`), Vulkan in its guest through Venus, rendered by the host's own
driver. What D144 and D201 built stands: the device, the window after RAM, `--gpus`'s
reading, the render node's mode, templates of their own (D150), and the `hyperv+gpu`
kernel. What a Windows host makes otherwise:

- **The renderer is the krunkit fork**, as on macOS, its Venus in the GPU's VM process:
  virglrenderer 1.3.0's contexts are served by its render server, over Unix sockets it
  forks or threads behind, which its Windows build does not have. scripts/gpu-libs builds
  the fork with clang-cl and shards' patch (resources/gpu/venus-windows.patch): the POSIX
  names its sources use are given the UCRT's, its ISO names where the UCRT deprecates the
  POSIX ones; Vulkan's loader is opened from System32 at its first call, not linked, so
  that a host without one is told so as a run asks for a GPU; and a blob is mapped by its
  pointer, as on macOS.
- **A blob's pages are the renderer's** (PM M383). WHP maps a driver's mapping of its
  host-visible memory into a partition, AMD's twelve host-visible types every one; but the
  driver frees that memory as the guest frees it, its blob or not, and the stage 2 follows
  the host's view (M341), so a guest mapping a blob freed could reach what took its place.
  Every allocation a guest may map is made of pages the renderer allocates and its device
  imports (VK_EXT_external_memory_host), held by the memory and by its blob and freed by
  the last of them; the device-local types, which no device imports host memory into
  (M383: the host-visible types not device-local import, 0xaaaa), are shown the guest as
  device-local alone, and the window is as long as the heaps of the types it may map. A
  blob is mapped whole, its pages the renderer's committed, writable memory, and one said
  to be larger than they are is refused.
- **The window is the partition's own**: each blob mapped at its place by WHvMapGpaRange,
  readable and writable, never executable, and unmapped as the guest lets it go, as
  Hypervisor.framework's stage 2 maps macOS's; a map's p50 34.0 to 37.6 µs (M383).
- **Confined as every VM process is, but for Win32k** (PM M385). The GPU's VM process
  keeps its AppContainer of its own, its Job and every other mitigation (D141). A Windows
  GPU driver is reached through Win32k: the Vulkan loader finds its drivers through gdi32's
  D3DKMT calls and DXGI, and gdi32 and user32 initialize in no process whose Win32k calls
  are disabled, nor in an AppContainer not granted the window station and desktop it runs
  on, with or without the mitigation (a process connects to its window station and
  desktop as it first calls user32 or gdi32: Microsoft's "Process Connection to a Window
  Station"). So Win32k's calls are allowed it, and it is made on a window station and a
  desktop of its own (`shards_ipc::Spawn::graphics`), granted to its AppContainer alone
  besides their maker, where gdi32 and user32 initialize. There it sends no window message
  to its user's desktop ("Window messages can be sent only between processes that are on
  the same desktop", Microsoft's "Desktops"), as Chromium's sandbox puts its targets on a
  desktop of their own for (chromium/src docs/design/sandbox.md, "The alternate desktop"),
  and its clipboard and atom table are its window station's, not its user's ("A window
  station contains a clipboard, an atom table, and one or more desktop objects",
  Microsoft's "Window Stations"). Only a process that makes one loads user32, which makes
  them; making them costs a GPU VM's start about 0.4 ms (p50; p99 1.1 ms, M385).
- **Tested** (tests/gpu.rs on jupiter: AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 and its Radeon 8060S, AMD's
  driver 25.20.32.06, Windows 11 10.0.26200): passes, 3 runs of 3 on the Windows daemon's
  branch with this merged, 48 to 52 s each. A run given `--gpus all` finds
  `Virtio-GPU Venus (AMD Radeon(TM) 8060S Graphics)`; a build's steps given the render
  node by a CDI device find it as root and as user 1000, as do a run given it by CDI name
  and a run of user 1000; and the GPU's runs restore templates of their own (D150). The
  renderer's own test passes there. The GPU's VM process is spawned so by the Windows
  daemon's spawner (`shards_ipc`, the parity plan's step 2), and lands with it: tested on
  step 2's branch with this one merged; and again on gpu-windows at e39a9218, with the
  Windows daemon, its pools and working sets as they landed (196.6 s, the test built by
  windows-binaries.yml at jupiter's paths, as kiln's guard there holds builds). CI's
  Windows runners, which have no GPU, build, lint and test the renderer, and skip what
  needs one.
- **Vulkan programs** (PM M386): llama.cpp's matrix multiplications in a guest on
  jupiter's Radeon 8060S get its CPU's results case for case, but for the 18 shapes of
  llama.cpp's integer dot product path that RADV gives NaN on Linux too (M384), which with
  it off match as well; TinyLlama's pp512 at 1,529 tokens/s (p50).
- **Not yet:** an arm64 Windows host (WHP's arm64 backend is the parity plan's step 10),
  Windows hosts of NVIDIA's and Intel's GPUs, none being here, and a GPU's VM process
  started from a user's interactive session, measured in session 0 alone (M385).

### D201. A GPU on Linux: Venus over its host's own Vulkan driver, in the GPU's VM process (built)

The parity plan's step 11 (docs/audit/2026-10-27_platform-parity.md, row 6), after D144: a
run on a Linux host is given its host's GPUs as a Mac's is given its own (`--gpus`, a CDI
device of the render node, a build step's `RUN --device`), Vulkan in its guest through
Venus, rendered by the host's own driver, NVIDIA's or Mesa's. What D144 built stands: the
device (`devices::virtio::gpu`), the window after RAM, `--gpus`'s reading, the render
node's mode, templates of their own (D150). What a Linux host makes otherwise:

- **The renderer is virglrenderer 1.3.0** (scripts/gpu-libs, pinned by digest), not the
  krunkit fork macOS renders with: its Venus is the upstream one guests' Mesa is written
  against. Its Venus contexts are served by its render server alone (meson.build,
  `with_render_server = with_venus`); the GPU's VM process runs the server as a thread of
  its own, given one end of a socket pair as its client's connection, the renderer the
  other (`get_server_fd`), and each context the server makes is a thread of it
  (`render-server-worker=thread`): nothing is forked or exec'd, and what the server logs is
  the VM process's (gpu/render_log.c, in syslog's place). Each context's fences are waited
  for on a thread of its own and said from there (VIRGL_RENDERER_THREAD_SYNC and
  ASYNC_FENCE_CB), as macOS's are.
- **Vulkan is the host's**, its loader opened by its soname (libvulkan.so.1) as the
  renderer starts: nothing of it is linked, a host without one is told so as a run asks for
  a GPU, and the window's length is every GPU's host-visible heaps as Vulkan says them (on
  the GPU desktop, NVIDIA's 100 GiB and RADV's besides).
- **The GPU's VM process links glibc, dynamically**, where every other helper is static
  musl (PM M281): a host's GPU driver is a library of its C library, which a static program
  cannot load. build.rs builds it for the `-linux-gnu` targets where SHARDS_GPU_LIBS names
  the renderer's libraries (`gpu_target`), and CI and releases build them there, as on
  Apple silicon. A musl build's links musl dynamically, built on Alpine (D208).
- **A blob is held by its descriptor** (PM M381). Venus exports host-visible memory as a
  dma-buf where the driver can, as both NVIDIA's and Mesa's can, and the renderer exports
  each mappable blob as it is made and keeps the descriptor: a dma-buf maps at any address
  the process chooses, is the driver's memory, and keeps its pages once the driver frees it
  while the descriptor or a mapping lives, what D144 held on macOS by remapping. A blob
  exported as an opaque descriptor, which no mmap takes, is refused, as is one said to be
  larger than its memory's pages.
- **The window on KVM is one memslot**, over a range the VM process reserves for it
  (gpu/window.rs), as a share's DAX window is (D189): a blob is mapped into it at the place
  its guest chose by mmap(MAP_FIXED) of its descriptor, and unmapped by reserving its range
  again; KVM's stage 2 follows the host's mapping through its MMU notifiers, a dma-buf's
  PFN-mapped pages (NVIDIA's, M381) among it. No memslot is made or removed for a blob, and
  a blob's place and length are whole host pages (`blob_alignment`).
- **Confined to what its driver needs** (PM M382), as NVIDIA's and Mesa's were measured to
  reach: Landlock lets the GPU's VM process read the loader's manifests and the libraries
  they name, the system's libraries and the drivers' data, sysfs, /proc/driver and four of
  /proc's files, and read, write and control the GPUs' device nodes (render nodes,
  NVIDIA's control, GPU, modesetting and unified memory nodes, udmabuf); its seccomp filter
  allows the GPU drivers' ioctls by their types (NVIDIA's 'F' and 'm', DRM's 'd'), which a
  rule matches by the request's bits 8 to 15 (`Rule::masked`), seven syscalls more, two
  fcntl commands, fallocate's mode 0 and getsockopt's SO_TYPE (and what Intel's GPUs and
  musl's loader make besides, D208), and fails symlink as its
  host does (NVIDIA's /dev/char links) and sched_setaffinity with EPERM (RADV's, which
  renders on, M384). Its drivers' shader caches stay off: it writes nothing of its host's.
- **Vulkan programs** (PM M384): llama.cpp's matrix multiplications in a guest get its
  CPU's results case for case, on NVIDIA's GPU and on RADV's, but for 18 of 1,684 shapes on
  RADV that are NaN in llama.cpp's integer dot product path alone (with it off, every case
  matches), as on Windows' AMD driver (M386).
- **The kernels:** the `gpu` variant for x86_64 guests as for arm64's, and `hyperv+gpu`,
  a Windows host's guest given a GPU, of kernel-6.18.48-64a9427a8997, whose release built
  every kernel before it byte for byte again and the x86_64 `gpu` kernel byte for byte as
  the GPU desktop's pinned builder did; scripts/build-kernel.sh takes variants joined by
  `+`.
- **Tested** (tests/gpu.rs, on the GPU desktop's NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti and Radeon
  610M, NVIDIA 615.78.08, CachyOS on Linux 7.2.9): passes, 5 runs of 5 of the build that
  adds D202, 19 to 71 s each, the host busy with other work (load average up to 119).
  A run given `--gpus all` finds `Virtio-GPU Venus (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti)` and
  `Virtio-GPU Venus (AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 16-Core Processor (RADV RAPHAEL_MENDOCINO))`
  through Debian trixie's Mesa 25.0.7, a build's steps given the render node by a CDI
  device find it as root and as user 1000, so do a run given it by CDI name and a run of
  user 1000, and the GPU's runs restore templates of their own (D150). It skips where a
  host has no GPU's device node, as CI's Linux runners, which build, lint and test the
  renderer.
- **Not yet:** an arm64 Linux host with a GPU is built and linted for and untested, none
  being here; and arm64 KVM maps a PFN-mapped page as device memory unless its mapping
  allows it otherwise (VM_ALLOW_ANY_UNCACHED), which a discrete GPU's dma-buf does not say.

### D199. A run's log sent to macOS's own log: `oslog`, and syslog's local default there (built)

`--log-driver oslog` is served on macOS, the journal's counterpart there (D166, D198): a
run's lines go to macOS's unified log, which `log show` and Console read. Docker has no
driver of macOS's, whose engine runs in a Linux VM there. Sent as every driver's are, from
shards' store, by the daemon's shipper (D163).

- **Through os_log, in the daemon.** macOS keeps nothing sent to syslogd's socket,
  `/var/run/syslog`, at any level, while its syslog(3) and os_log reach the unified log
  (PM M374). So a line is an entry the daemon writes with os_log_with_type, through a shim
  of its macros that only a C compiler expands (daemon/ship/oslog.c, libSystem's, no launch
  cost). Its message is public: what a run wrote is no secret of shards' to redact.
- **Found as journald's are.** Its subsystem is `shards` and its category the run's tag
  (its short ID unless `tag` says), as journald's SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER is: `log show
  --predicate 'subsystem == "shards" AND category == "web"'`. stdout's lines are of the
  default type and stderr's of the error type, as journald's priorities 6 and 3.
- **Whole lines, in parts os_log keeps.** os_log keeps a line whole up to 1,015 bytes, and
  of a longer one its first 1,015 bytes and `<…>` (M374). A longer line goes in parts of at
  most 1,015 bytes, each cut at a character's boundary, none of it lost. Bytes that are no
  UTF-8, and a NUL, are U+FFFD.
- **syslog's local default, there.** `--log-driver syslog` with no `syslog-address` sends
  to the host's own syslog, which on macOS is its unified log: there it is sent as oslog's,
  the run's tag its category. Sent to syslogd's socket, as before, every line went nowhere.
- **Its options** are every driver's (tag, labels, env, mode, the local copy's).
- **macOS's.** Elsewhere it is refused as its run is made, in shards' words: the unified
  log is macOS's own.

Tested on real microVMs on macOS (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_macos_own_log_as_its_options_say`):
`log show` has a run's line on each stream with its type, a 3,000-byte line in parts of
1,015, 1,015 and 970 bytes, and syslog's local default's lines alike. Elsewhere it tests the
refusal. A unit test holds the parts to os_log's bound and to characters' boundaries.

### D198. A run's log sent to Event Tracing for Windows: `etwlogs` (built)

`--log-driver etwlogs` is served on Windows, the journal's counterpart there (D166): a run's
lines go to the host's own event tracing, as Docker's Windows driver sends them. Sent as
every driver's are, from shards' store, by the daemon's shipper (D163).

- **Docker's provider and words.** Each line, and each part of a longer one (D163), is an
  event of moby's provider, `{a3693192-9ed6-46d2-a981-f8226c8363bd}`, written by
  EventWriteString at level 0 and keyword 0, its string moby's createLogMessage's:
  `container_name: NAME, image_name: IMAGE, container_id: ID, image_id: IMAGE_ID, source:
  STREAM, log: LINE` (daemon/logger/etwlogs/etwlogs_windows.go). A session listening for
  the provider has each, `logman start -ets NAME -p {a3693192-...}` and tracerpt among
  them, as for Docker's.
- **Registered once.** The daemon registers the provider with the first run that asks for
  it and keeps it for its life: a registration costs a call to the system, and a provider
  registered once is every run's; one that fails is asked for again by the next run.
- **Delivered as written.** An event is ETW's once written: a session that listens has it,
  and none that does not, for every sender alike. Its options are every driver's (tag,
  labels, env, mode, the local copy's); moby's reads none of its own.
- **Where Docker is wrong, shards is not.** A line holding a NUL fails Go's
  UTF16FromString, and moby's driver loses it; shards writes it, the NUL U+FFFD, as its bytes
  that are no UTF-8 are.
- **Windows'.** Elsewhere it is refused as its run is made, in shards' words: Event
  Tracing for Windows is Windows' own.

Tested on real microVMs on Windows (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_etw_as_its_options_say`): a
real-time ETW session of the test's own, its provider enabled, has a run's line on each
stream, word for word, and `logs` reads the run's own copy; an ETW session is an
administrator's or Performance Log Users', and a host whose user is neither says SKIP.
Elsewhere it tests the refusal. A unit test holds each event's words to moby's.

### D197. Host directories on Windows: a FUSE server over NTFS that keeps a Linux guest's files as WSL does (built)

**Why.** Every feature on every host (the user, 2026-10-27; the platform parity plan's step 6,
docs/audit/2026-10-27_platform-parity.md's host directories on Windows): a microVM's volumes
and binds reach it as virtio-fs shares (D38), whose device, FUSE wire and WHP DAX window
(D189, `fs/window_whp.rs`) Windows builds, but whose server (`fs/server.rs`), share process
and budgets are Unix's, so a run with `-v` or `--mount` is refused there.

**What a Linux guest's files need of NTFS, measured (PM M362, CI's windows-2022 and
windows-2025, as the runner's account and as a standard user, unelevated): every call below
did as asked.**

- **One server, its host behind a layer.** `fs/server.rs` answers FUSE requests in Linux's
  terms on every host; each call it makes of its host's file system is a function of its
  own (`host::Stat`, the `*_at` calls), Unix's the libc calls it makes now, Windows' the
  NT calls below. Its tests run on both.
- **Nothing past the share.** Each operation is relative to a handle of the shared tree, its
  name one component: NtCreateFile with that directory as its RootDirectory and
  FILE_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT, so a final reparse point is never followed, as `O_NOFOLLOW`
  holds Unix's server.
- **Owners, modes and device numbers** in WSL's extended attributes, `$LXUID`, `$LXGID`,
  `$LXMOD` and `$LXDEV` ("File Permissions for WSL", Microsoft Learn), set and read
  unelevated (M362), where Unix's server keeps them in the
  `com.docker.grpcfuse.ownership` xattr (D38): a file WSL made reads as WSL made it, and
  a file with none is root's, as Unix's.
- **Every other kind as WSL makes it.** Regular files and directories are NTFS's; a
  symlink, a FIFO, a character or block device and a Unix socket are reparse points of the
  LX tags, a symlink's buffer as MS-FSCC 2.1.2.7 lays it out, never an NTFS symlink, which
  "Developer Mode must first be enabled on the machine" to make unelevated
  (CreateSymbolicLinkW, Microsoft Learn).
- **Removal and rename as Linux's**: an open file's name gone at once
  (FILE_DISPOSITION_FLAG_POSIX_SEMANTICS), a rename over a file held open
  (FILE_RENAME_FLAG_POSIX_SEMANTICS), the holder reading what it held.
- **Names**: a directory the guest makes is case-sensitive (FileCaseSensitiveInformation),
  as WSL makes its own; a host directory keeps the flag its user gave it.
- **Inodes**: a file's ID (FileIdInfo), whose upper 8 bytes NTFS left unused (M362).
- **Its stream to the VM** a duplex named pipe, as a served share's on Windows (D38,
  `--slates-fs-handle`, PM M340).

**Built (slice 2): the server on Windows, `fs/server_windows.rs` over `fs/ntfs.rs`, held to
Unix's by the server's own tests, which run on every host** (66 on jupiter and Fedora, 65
on macOS, each Unix step given a Windows twin of its property: a junction where a symlink is
planted, the read-only attribute where a mode is taken away, WSL's device files where
/dev's are), and mutation-checked on jupiter (25 mutants of the Windows layer, each one
line, all caught but one equivalent). What the tests found, decided:

- **NT checks a handle's access, Unix its file's**: a Unix descriptor opened to read changes
  its file's attributes; an NT handle changes nothing it was not opened to. Each change
  goes through a handle that may make it (`able`: the one given, else another of its
  file's, a relative open of no name, as ReOpenFile makes one).
- **A guest's other attributes** are EAs named `SH.` and their name's bytes in hexadecimal
  (an EA's name is upper-case ASCII of 255 bytes at most, a guest's any bytes of either
  case), each value after a byte of 0: NTFS keeps no EA of no value, where Linux keeps an
  attribute of one (overlayfs's `metacopy`; `an_attribute_of_no_value_is_kept`).
- **A node Unix's server keeps as an empty file beside its kind** (a device an
  unprivileged host cannot make, RENAME_WHITEOUT's whiteout) is on NTFS the device it is,
  WSL's; a device's metadata is read and written as any file's, its reparse point reaching
  no driver (`DEVICE_OPENS_DRIVER`), and no descriptor is kept against a mode
  (`MODES_REFUSE_OPENS`), which refuses no NT open.
- **NTFS renames no directory a handle beneath is open in**, POSIX semantics or not, nor does
  MoveFileEx (EACCES; ntfs.rs `a_directory_a_handle_beneath_is_open_in_is_renamed_by_none`):
  before a guest's rename of a directory the server lets go of the descriptors it holds
  beneath it, a cache each opened again along its path (audit V09), so that the guest's
  rename is Linux's. The host's own rename of such a directory is refused as NTFS refuses
  it beside any program holding a file there; once the server has let go, it is made, and
  the guest's nodes there are stale, as Unix's.
- **Nothing is resolved beneath a reparse point opened as itself**: NT answers
  STATUS_REPARSE_POINT_NOT_RESOLVED (0xC0000280, measured on jupiter), which the server
  hears as ELOOP, a path through a planted junction stale (ESTALE), as Unix's through a
  symlink.
- **A host's junctions and NTFS symlinks are symlinks to the guest**, as a host's symlinks
  are on Unix, where they were empty directories: a relative symlink's target as it is, an
  absolute one's or a junction's on the link's own volume the path to it from the link's
  directory (MS-FSCC 2.1.2.4, 2.1.2.5), so that pnpm's node_modules, junctions within a
  project, lead in the guest where they lead on the host.
- **A handle opened to append writes at its file's end as the host has it**, whatever offset
  the guest's kernel names, on every host: WriteFile's end-of-file offset on Windows, and
  write(2) through the O_APPEND descriptor on Unix, where macOS's pwrite(2) writes at the
  offset named and clobbered what the host appended (`Zbc` for Linux's `abcZ`, measured
  2026-10-29; Linux's pwrite(2) appends, its BUGS section);
  `an_appending_handle_writes_at_its_files_end_as_the_host_has_it`.
- O_SYNC and O_DSYNC open to write through (FILE_WRITE_THROUGH); O_RDONLY with O_TRUNC
  truncates, as Linux's open(2); SEEK_DATA and SEEK_HOLE take a file to be all data, as
  POSIX lets an implementation.

**Built (slice 3): the share process and the daemon's shares on Windows**, a run's `-v` and
`--mount` reading and writing host directories there: containers.rs, compose.rs, engine.rs
and saved.rs on jupiter and CI's Windows runners, none skipped for this step but those of
shards' own shares' DAX windows (slice 4). What it took, decided:

- **The share process starts in its microVM's group's job with none of a confined child's
  mitigations** (`shards_ipc::spawn_in_job`): under `Spawn`'s no-Win32k and no-FSCTL
  policies the shards binary failed its DLL initialisation (STATUS_DLL_INIT_FAILED,
  0xC0000142, on jupiter), and its server sets reparse points, which are FSCTLs.
- **Each share's stream is a byte-mode duplex pipe the daemon makes**
  (`shards_ipc::byte_pair`): its server end given to the share process by number, its
  client end sent to the VM after the run's request, `MAX_FDS` a message (`SHARE_ENDS`),
  as Unix's share process hands its own: a stream given to a process on Windows hands no
  handle on, its holder having no handle of the process it would send one to. A run of
  five shares sent in its request alone had been refused, past `MAX_FDS`.
- **A microVM's share processes end with its removal**, each ended and waited for as
  the removal completes, its runs over (`end_shares`): NTFS renames no directory a handle
  beneath is open in, and a volume removed just after the last microVM that mounted it
  had been refused (HTTP 500), a `run --rm`'s anonymous volume left behind.
- **RENAME_EXCHANGE**, which overlayfs asks of a volume to remove a directory
  (ovl_cleanup_and_whiteout exchanges it with a whiteout), and of which NTFS has none:
  three renames, each over nothing, the first to a name of the server's own beside the
  first file, undone where one fails, the directories beneath both let go first
  (`an_exchange_swaps_two_names`). The server answers its guest one request at a time, so
  its guest sees none of it half done; another program of the host's may, as it may any
  rename on Windows not made at once.
- **A file with no mode of WSL's is 0755 to the guest, 0555 read-only**: Windows has no
  bit to say a file is not executable. WSL shows such a file with its Windows user's
  effective rights, "the same value for user, group, and other" ("File Permissions for
  WSL", Microsoft Learn); Docker Desktop "sets permissions on shared volumes to a default
  value of 0777 ... not configurable" (Docker Desktop's troubleshooting topics); BuildKit's
  fsutil sends a Windows file to a build as 0755 (shards-build's `host.rs`). shards takes
  the build's: a Linux program or script in a project runs from its bind, and its files
  stay their owner's to write, root's in the guest, as a Unix host's are.
- **A host's bind sources are its drives' paths** (D207).

**Built (slice 4): shards' own shares' DAX windows on Windows**, a volume's large files
mapped from the host's page cache as on Unix (D189), held to every host's DAX tests
(containers.rs's five and saved.rs's restore) on jupiter and CI's Windows runners. What it
took, decided (PM M412):

- **The share process gives the VM the file, not a section** (`fs/mod.rs`
  `descriptor_for`). The ask names the VM process and its end of the stream there. The share
  process duplicates that handle and holds it to be a client's end of its own pipe (one
  name, FileNameInfo; its own end the server's, GetNamedPipeInfo), refusing the ask
  otherwise (EPERM), then duplicates into the VM the node's file, opened as Unix's server
  opens a mapping's. A section of a file reaches no further than the file, which grows
  under the guest; with the file, the window makes its sections itself, each as long as the
  file then, and reads its size, as the Unix window keeps a mapping's descriptor.
- **A range the file ends within** is its placeholder split at the page after the file's
  bytes there: a view as long as those bytes (a view asked a page past its section's bytes
  is refused, M412), committed zeros after it, the two coalesced again as it is freed. The
  guest reads the file's bytes, and zeros past its end, as on Unix.
- **Followed as the Unix window follows a file**: before the guest hears a size,
  `reconcile` makes each range what the file is then, a grown file's new bytes the guest's.
- **Never zeros in place of a file's bytes** (memory-01, PM M573). A section to write is made
  only of a handle "created with the GENERIC_READ and GENERIC_WRITE access rights", one to
  read of one with GENERIC_READ (Microsoft's CreateFileMappingW, PAGE_READWRITE and
  PAGE_READONLY), and a share's server opens a mapping to be read alone to read
  (`SHARED_NEEDS_WRITE`). The window kept a node's first handle: a file mapped to be read
  and then, elsewhere in the window, to be written grew, no section to write could be made
  of the handle kept, and `reconcile`, having freed the written range's views, placed
  writable zeros over its file's bytes, the guest's stores reaching no file. So:
  - a node keeps the handle given for a mapping to be written over one given to read
    alone, as the Unix window's node keeps a descriptor opened to write (window.rs
    `Table::insert`);
  - a mapping's new section is made before anything of it is let go of, and where none can
    be made, or its file's size cannot be read, it is left as it was;
  - where a view cannot be placed once its old ones are freed ("BaseAddress and ViewSize
    must exactly match those of the placeholder", Microsoft's MapViewOfFile3, so a view
    replaces only a freed placeholder), its ranges stay placeholders (`Held::LetGo`), as a
    range let go of for a cut is, a vCPU that reaches one waiting until it is made again or
    unmapped;
  - each is refused, typed (`fs::Unfollowed`: its size, its section, a view), and the reply
    that would tell the guest the file's size is refused it (EIO): the guest never hears a
    size whose bytes its window does not hold. The request itself was the server's, done.
    Before replacing its success with EIO, the device retires only the unpublished reply's
    acquisitions (memory-18, found by the Windows P0 lane): RELEASE/RELEASEDIR for its new
    open handle, then one FORGET per entry, including READDIRPLUS's nonzero entries.
    Earlier accepted references and handles remain. The same cleanup follows a reply
    that cannot be written whole into guest memory. Completed creates/writes stay done;
    cleanup removes no files and undoes no mutation. These are ordinary framed FUSE
    requests, understood by the existing share servers. A cleanup failure is typed
    (`Unreleased`): a transport or malformed one disconnects the slot rather than reuse a
    partial exchange, and remaining resources then depend on connection/session teardown;
    a RELEASE the server refuses (`Refused`, an errno) is a whole exchange, so the slot
    stays and the entry is still forgotten, as Linux's `fuse_create_open` releases and
    forgets regardless and `fuse_file_put` ends a synchronous RELEASE with
    `fuse_release_end(args, 0)` (fs/fuse/file.c, dir.c).
    The frame bounds are `fuse_in_header` (40 bytes), `fuse_entry_out` (128),
    `fuse_release_in` (8 + 4 + 4 + 8), and `fuse_out_header` (16), from Linux v6.18's UAPI;
    FORGET's one reference is the count each entry acquires, not a policy value. No
    estimator/cold-start threshold is needed. Sources, alternatives, red/green, and
    unrun failure/platform cases: PM M574, `docs/research/measurements/memory-fixes-v1/memory-18.md`.
  Held by `a_range_mapped_to_be_written_after_one_to_be_read_stays_its_files` and
  `a_range_no_view_of_its_file_can_be_made_for_is_refused_never_zeros` (red before,
  mutation-checked); a view refused after its section was made is unit-unreachable, and
  unverified.
- **No cut under a mapping.** NTFS refuses to cut a file short while any section of it is
  held, a view or a handle (ERROR_USER_MAPPED_FILE, M412). So the window keeps views alone,
  each section's handle closed once its views are placed. A guest's own cut (a SETATTR of
  the file's size, an OPEN that truncates it) finds the file's views let go of first
  (`evict`), each range its placeholder until the reply; then `reconcile` makes them what
  the file is, cut or not. A vCPU that reaches one meanwhile waits, and runs its access
  again once it is made. A host program's cut of a file a microVM maps is refused, as NTFS
  refuses any program's cut of a mapped file; a hole punched, a rename and a removal are
  not (M412), and containers.rs holds the host's cuts to that refusal on Windows.
- **A window's head committed as its guest touches it.** A window's head, its guest's page
  structures for it, is a 64th of its length and more (D189), memory of the VM's own,
  which Windows committed whole as it reserved it: a window as long as the host's memory
  took that at its VM's start, past a group's 1 GiB budget (PM M413). Where the host
  charges memory as it is reserved (`platform::CHARGED_AS_RESERVED`), a window's head is
  reserved alone and each of its 2 MiB blocks committed as its guest first touches one:
  WHP takes a stage-2 map over memory only reserved, its guest's access exiting until the
  block is committed (M413), and the control device answers that exit
  (`WindowHeads::memory_fault`). So a head costs the page structures of the ranges its
  guest maps, as on Unix. A save reads its committed blocks alone, a restore commits the
  blocks it reads back, and a map-back gives a zero block back uncommitted. A writable
  layer's head (D190) stays committed whole, its VM writing it first.

**Slices.** 1 (built): the server's host calls behind functions of their own, `mod calls`,
Unix's in `fs/server_unix.rs`. 2 (built): Windows' calls and the server's own tests on
Windows. 3 (built): the share process and the daemon's shares on Windows, and the volume
and bind tests on its CI runners. 4 (built): shards' own shares' DAX windows on Windows.

### D196. Snapshots of WHP microVMs: a partition saved and restored (built)

**2026-11-14, platform-09 fixed** (6057451cf, 2f88e39b6; red 9c1632a7f; PM M578). A name's
versions (`write_in`, `newest_in`, `remove_in`) are the entries its directory takes for
`name.~N`: ignoring case (CompareStringOrdinal, Windows' ordinal file-name comparison),
unless the directory is case-sensitive (FILE_CASE_SENSITIVE_INFO,
FILE_CS_FLAG_CASE_SENSITIVE_DIR); a file system or Windows that keeps no per-directory
sensitivity (FAT; before Windows 10 1803) refuses the question and tells no names apart by
case. And `land` moves its next version past each one a rename found taken
(`next_version`), so a write ends at the first free name even where the file system takes
for the name an entry the comparison does not (a volume's own $UpCase table, older than the
system's). No literal. Owed to ROOT (R14): the cost of the directory's sensitivity query
each read adds to a restore's `newest_in`, on jupiter, `benches/restore.rs` before and after,
n=100 interleaved.

**Why.** Every feature on every host (the user, 2026-10-27; docs/audit/2026-10-27_platform-parity.md
row 2a): a microVM on Windows took no snapshot (D140), so `run --kernel --snapshot-dir`, `shards
restore` and everything built on them, templates (D25) and warm pools (D26), were Unix's alone.
What WHP keeps of a partition, and what a restore may set back, measured first (PM M345, a
probe on jupiter: a guest saved from one partition, restored into another, its memory a view of
