  frame asked for as a constant) and, on Windows, `pipe::tests::a_pipes_quota_is_its_callers_window_as_made`
  (a Stream pair's quota holds its longest message, a 16-byte frame's does not, the system's
  is CreatePipe's). Linted for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc; their Windows run is owed to ROOT:
  `cargo test -p shards-ipc --lib pipe` and `cargo test -p shards-ipc --lib slots` on
  windows-2025 (CI) and jupiter, then daemon.rs' `a_request_past_a_sockets_buffer_is_served`
  and `a_stopping_daemon_waits_for_no_client_that_reads_nothing` (a 123 KiB answer past the
  system's quota), and PM M340's throughput run (`docs/research/measurements/windows-pipe`, `cargo run --release` there on jupiter) at each new quota beside 1 MiB and 64 KiB.

The user's plan, item 3 (2026-10-18): a run's `--cpus` as elastic as its memory (D148),
every microVM given the host's CPUs, init bringing the run's online and `update --cpus`
more or fewer. Bringing a CPU online as a run starts costs what no start has: 13 ms a CPU
on HVF and 45 on KVM where the microVM has the host's (PM M265: 31 brought online in 1.40
s), and taking one offline stops every other (kernel/cpu.c, `stop_machine`). So every CPU
stays online, in the template and in every run, and a run is held to what it is given
inside its microVM, as a Linux host holds a container's processes (decided 2026-10-20, and
the user told).

- **Its microVM: every CPU of the host's** (`resources::microvm_vcpus`), whatever its
  limits, as D125 gave a run without one. Every run of an image restores one template,
  as every `-m` does (D148), where each count had its own, booted and saved by its first
  run.
- **Its workload: the CPUs its limits give it**, its cgroup's `cpuset.cpus`
  (`resources::cgroup`): `--cpuset-cpus`'s; else its microVM's first N, N `--cpu-count`'s,
  else as many as `--cpus`, the quota or `--cpu-percent` needs (`resources::run_cpus`,
  D155), every one with none; `cpu.max` as before. Its processes see what a microVM of
  those CPUs alone showed them, `nproc` (sched_getaffinity) N; its guest's online CPUs are
  the host's, as a container's are.
- **The host holds its vCPUs to the same CPUs** (slice 2, `vm::hold`). Its workload is
  held inside its microVM; but a workload root of its own guest may leave its cgroup —
  with `--privileged --cgroupns host` it writes itself into the microVM's cgroup root,
  out of the run's cpuset, onto every CPU (PM M289). So the VM process holds its vCPU
  threads together to as many of the host's CPUs as the run's limits let its workload use
  at once (`resources::held_cpus`: the fewest of `--cpu-count`'s, the quota's rounded up,
  and the cpuset's; none where that is every CPU). A governor thread reads each vCPU
  thread's CPU time (`platform::ThreadClock`: Linux its CPU-time clock, which counts its
  time in the guest; macOS thread_info, PM M288; Windows GetThreadTimes), and once a 100
  ms period's share is spent holds every vCPU out of its guest, by the same kick a
  snapshot uses, until the period ends; what a period overran comes off the next. The
  governor runs as it wakes, however busy its vCPUs keep the CPUs they may use: on macOS
  at the vCPUs' real-time policy (M8, M10), on Linux at their 100 µs slice (below), on
  Windows at THREAD_PRIORITY_TIME_CRITICAL, above them, where at their priority three
  spinning threads of a process held to two CPUs kept it from running and used up to 1.58
  s in a second held to one (PM M294). This bounds the whole guest — kernel threads, interrupts, and any escaped workload — to what
  a microVM of those CPUs alone could use, where the cpuset alone bounds only a workload
  that stays in its cgroup. It comes with the run (the `RUN` head's `cpus`), before the
  guest hears of the run, and `update` moves it (below).
- **A pause is the same hold, whole** (`Handle::pause`, the daemon's `PAUSE`, 2026-10-28):
  every vCPU kicked out of its guest and held there, whatever its share, until the microVM
  goes on; the daemon answers `pause` once its VM says each is held. It replaced a stop of
  the VM process (SIGSTOP), which Windows has no documented call for (NtSuspendProcess is
  ntdll's, undocumented), where WHP's kick is WHvCancelRunVirtualProcessor, documented,
  and holds for a run that has not begun (M198): one pause on every host. The VM process
  goes on answering its daemon and serving its devices as its guest is frozen, and a
  frozen microVM's VM process takes next to no CPU time, as
  `pause_freezes_a_microvm_until_unpause_or_stop` reads it from the host. A save of a
  paused microVM lets it go on for its guest to go quiet, as the stop's continue did.
- **`update` moves them, both ways.** A running run's `--cpus`, quota, `--cpu-count` or
  `--cpuset-cpus` changed writes its cpuset and quota at once (`builtin::CGROUP`, D40), a
  raise giving it CPUs it had not; before, a raise past its microVM's vCPUs bound at them.
  Where the CPUs its workload may use at once change, its VM is told the new hold first
  (`kind::CPUS`), on the link the cgroup write comes on after, as `update -m` tells it the
  new memory (D148).
- **Measured (PM M288; macOS on an Apple M5 Max, Linux on M258's i9-14900HX).** A count's
  first run 13.5 ms on macOS and 16.7 on Linux, where it booted and saved a template in
  216 and 694; one warm pool for every limit, three VM processes held where five and seven,
  22 MiB less footprint (macOS) and 63 MiB less Pss (Linux) in all; after `update --cpus 4`
  of a `--cpus 1` run, 4.01 and 4.04 CPUs used where 1.00 and 1.02. A run with a limit pays
  what one without pays: 5 MiB more of its VM process's footprint at `--cpus 1` (Linux 8.4
  of Pss), and its start, 2.5 ms more at p50 paced on macOS (12.73 against 10.23 ms), 2.6
  back to back on Linux; on a contended host 22 ms more (PM M292: 17.9 against 39.7 ms at
  p50, a `--cpus 1` run on 4 CPUs that 4 busy loops hold), slice 1's own, until its vCPUs
  woke at the shortest slice (below, PM M440). The host's hold
  (PM M289, n 10 a side): an escaped workload of a `--cpus 1` run uses 1.02 CPUs held, 3.99
  where only its microVM's cgroups hold it; on an idle host it costs a run nothing
  measurable.
- **Tested.** resources' `workload_limits_are_written` (a cpuset for every run: none given
  its microVM's every CPU, a quota's first N, `--cpu-count`'s); on real microVMs,
  `a_microvm_takes_its_cpus_real_time_isolation_and_annotations` (`--cpu-count 2` CPUs 0-1,
  every CPU of the host's online; `--cpu-percent 50` its share on half of them),
  `run_limits_a_microvms_resources` (`--cpus 1.5 --cpuset-cpus 0`: CPU 0, every CPU
  online) and `update_changes_limits_of_running_microvms` (`--cpus 1.5`, then the host's
  count: CPUs 0-1, then every one, and their quota). The host hold: resources'
  `microvms_are_held_to_their_runs_cpus` (the fewest of each limit's CPUs, none for every
  one); `vm::hold`'s own tests (threads held to one CPU use about the time passing, not
  every CPU's; a hold of every CPU holds nothing; the end lets a held vCPU go); on a real
  microVM `a_workload_past_its_cgroup_is_held_to_its_cpus_by_its_host` (a privileged
  guest-root workload that writes itself to the cgroup root, out of a `--cpus 1` cpuset,
  uses no more than one CPU's time, where without a limit four threads run free), and
  `platform`'s `a_threads_clock_counts_what_it_runs`. Mutation-checked: a run naming no
  cpuset given none fails resources' test, the CPUs test and the update test; a microVM of
  its run's CPUs alone fails the limits test and the CPUs test; the host hold removed, the
  escaped workload's four threads use four CPUs' time (11.41 s of CPU in 3.03 s, PM M289).
- **Its vCPUs wake as they are woken** (Linux, 2026-11-03). A start on a contended host
  was slice 1's regression (PM M292: 22 ms more at p50 on 4 busy CPUs, 2 to 3 idle,
  M288), in the guest's own start of the run, at each hand-off from one vCPU to another:
  a woken vCPU thread waited for the busy thread on its host CPU to run its slice out,
  2.8 ms on a host of 8 CPUs or more (EEVDF's RUN_TO_PARITY, `base_slice_ns`), where a
  microVM of one vCPU hands nothing off. So on Linux every vCPU thread, device worker and
  hold governor asks for the fair scheduler's shortest slice, 100 µs, as it starts
  (sched_setattr(2), SCHED_OTHER with `sched_runtime`, Linux 6.12 on;
  `platform::run_promptly` through `prioritize_vcpu_thread`), its nice value kept: woken,
  it preempts a thread of a longer slice at once (PREEMPT_SHORT), its share of the CPU
  its weight's as before. It needs no privilege, and the VM process's seccomp filter
  allows sched_getattr(2) and sched_setattr(2) of the calling thread alone; a thread at a
  policy its user chose is left at it. On macOS the vCPUs' real-time policy (M8, M10) has
  them preempt timeshare threads already. Measured (PM M440, 4 CPUs that 4 busy loops
  hold, n 100 a side): the guest's part of a `--cpus 1` start 9.24 ms at p50 where 20.82
  (p90 15.05 where 45.16), the wall 37.66 where 46.64; on 16 CPUs and 16 loops 7.90 where
  24.71; idle, alike (3.18 both, n 200). Against the build before slice 1 (1468f07d), a
  start is now 8.3 ms sooner contended and 4.7 sooner idle, where de2b1cf5's was 7.0 ms
  later contended and 5.8 sooner idle: contention costs slice 1's start no more than
  idleness does. Tested: platform's `a_prompt_thread_has_the_shortest_slice_at_its_own_weight`,
  and on real microVMs `a_microvms_vcpus_and_governor_wake_at_the_shortest_slice`.
  The tests establish or read their launcher's policy rather than assume SCHED_OTHER:
  an SSH session on adacachy inherited SCHED_IDLE, and both tests wrongly expected it
  to become SCHED_OTHER (2026-11-09). The unit fixture checks its inherited policy's
  slice and also checks that SCHED_BATCH and SCHED_IDLE are preserved, without needing
  privilege to leave an inherited idle policy;
  the microVM check compares against its launcher's policy, nice value and slice.
  `run_promptly`'s policy-preserving behavior is unchanged.
- **A held vCPU goes on as its period ends, by itself** (2026-11-03). The hold's cost to a
  memory-heavy run on a contended host (PM M292: fills 9 and 16% longer, n 8) did not
  repeat (PM M441: n 16, the held arm the quicker in 9 rounds of 16, the host's drift
  larger than either): there the host gives the vCPUs less than the run's share, and the
  hold holds in one run in four or five, for a few milliseconds. Its cost was its end: a
  held vCPU waited for the governor to wake at the period's end and let it go, and on a
  host overloaded (its load near 1,000) a governor 57.4 s late held one fill 333 s of the
  625 it took. Now the governor holds them until the period's end (`Hold::set_held`), and
  each held vCPU waits no longer than that (`Hold::wait`), however late the governor
  wakes; what they ran meanwhile is the governor's to count, as before, and comes off the
  next period. With the governor at the vCPUs' slice too, held vCPUs went on at most 3.2
  ms past their period on 4 busy CPUs (PM M441). Tested: hold's
  `a_held_vcpu_goes_on_at_its_periods_end_without_its_governor`, its other tests as
  before.
- **Windows: its vCPUs a step above normal priority** (2026-11-04, measured and kept
  2026-11-08, PM M495). Whether WHP's vCPU threads waited on a contended host as Linux's did
  was unmeasured (jupiter's runs were then held to a few thousandths of a core by its
  headroom guard). On a Windows client the hypervisor
  leaves guests' virtual processors to the root's NT scheduler (the root scheduler, clients'
  only one since Windows 10 1803; Microsoft, Manage Hyper-V hypervisor scheduler types), so
  a vCPU runs as the thread that runs it: threads of one priority take time slices in turn,
  and one of a higher priority that becomes ready stops a lower one "without allowing it to
  finish using its time slice" (Scheduling Priorities). A vCPU another wakes, at its host's
  busy threads' priority, may so wait for one's slice to end, unless the boost a thread gets
  as its wait is satisfied (Priority Boosts) lifts it past them already. The candidate
  (`platform::windows_thread`, through `prioritize_vcpu_thread`, where Linux's slice is
  given; device workers too): each vCPU thread and device worker at
  THREAD_PRIORITY_ABOVE_NORMAL, base priority 9 in a NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS process against
  the host's threads' 8, the least step above them, in any user's rights and below the 11
  past which a thread "interferes with the normal operation of the operating system"
  (SetThreadPriority). A priority is strict where Linux's slice kept a thread's share, and
  Microsoft lowers processor-intensive threads (Scheduling Priorities), so a governor reads
  each raised thread's CPU time every 100 ms (GetThreadTimes, as the hold does, PM M294):
  each look credits it half of the time since and charges it what it used, its credit kept
  to half a period and none; one out of credit goes back to THREAD_PRIORITY_NORMAL, and is
  raised again once a look finds it some: a raised thread takes half a CPU from the host's
  threads over a long stretch, and a period more at most, what a fair scheduler gives one
  thread beside one busy one. The credit carries a thread that waits across its clock's
  steps: GetThreadTimes charges whole 15.625 ms ticks to the thread running as each ticks
  (PM M294), 6.4 a period, and judged by each period alone a thread running 1 ms of every 6
  was charged 4 (62.5 ms) of one and put back to normal for a period
  (`a_thread_that_waits_between_its_runs_stays_raised`, CI's windows-2025, 2026-11-06;
  GetThreadPriority reads the base priority, which only the governor's SetThreadPriority
  changes: neither MMCSS, which shards does not use, nor Windows' boosts and their decay,
  which move the dynamic priority alone, Priority Boosts). A thread its program set at
  another priority is left at it. Not MMCSS
  (AvSetMmThreadCharacteristics), which moves a thread into the real-time range, 16 to 26
  (Multimedia Class Scheduler Service), nor power throttling off (SetThreadInformation,
  ThreadPowerThrottling), which chooses the cores and clock a thread runs at, "while
  scheduling priority remains the main metric by which the system determines which thread
  to schedule next" (Quality of Service); the harness tries it beside the priority, and
  HIGHEST (10). Tested: platform's `a_thread_run_long_goes_back_to_normal_and_is_raised_again_as_it_waits`,
  `a_thread_that_waits_between_its_runs_stays_raised`,
  `credit_carries_a_thread_that_waits_across_its_clocks_steps` and
  `a_thread_set_otherwise_is_left_as_it_is`. Measured as PM M440 was (PM M495, n 100 a side,
  interleaved, `cpu-elastic/phases.py` against `winnone.patch`, which leaves the threads as
  they start): on windows-2025's 4 CPUs that 4 busy loops held, the guest's part of a
  `--cpus 1` start took 217 and 337 ms at p50 with the vCPUs at their starting priority and
  8.2 and 10.1 at ABOVE_NORMAL (p99 454 and 681 where 45 and 79), the vCPUs raised from
  outside alike (`winslice.py`, 352 where 8.7), idle 49.9 where 22.0: Windows' wake boost
  does not give a woken vCPU its CPU, the priority does, and it stays. On jupiter neither
  moved a start past its spread, quiet or with its kernel busy, its starts held by something
  the priority does not reach (not found). Measuring it found a held daemon's microVMs
  given every CPU of the host: `available_parallelism` reads no affinity mask on Windows,
  so 32 vCPUs ran on 4 CPUs; `resources::host_cpus` counts the process's mask there
  (GetProcessAffinityMask), as Linux's reads sched_getaffinity(2) (D125, e2820ce9;
  `a_microvm_has_the_cpus_its_daemon_may_run_on`).

### D190. A run's writable layer on its host's disk: ext4 with DAX over pmem (slices 1 to 8 built)

**Review memory-16 (2026-11-13):** saving a head compares a nonzero block with
every distinct block already retained. The bound is the input's block count;
there is no selected limit on how many kinds can share. Cold saves start with
no retained kinds, and existing file errors propagate. This preserves the
documented “each kept block once” contract after the sixty-fourth kind too.
Worst-case comparisons are quadratic in input blocks; their cost is unmeasured
and owed to ROOT. Red/green and scope:
`docs/research/measurements/memory-fixes-v1/README.md`.

A run's writable layer, the upper directory of its root's overlay, was a tmpfs in its
microVM's memory (D16, D156): what it wrote was memory, held to its memory limit, and gone
with its microVM unless packed as it stopped (D37). A test suite's build there ran its 8
GiB microVM out of memory every round of the sustained-I/O benchmark (PM M266). Now it is an
ext4 file system in a file of the run's own on its host's disk, on a virtio-pmem device of
its own, mounted with DAX: the guest's CPUs read and write its files as the host's page
cache of that file, which the host writes back and takes back as it would any file's, and
the guest keeps their metadata alone.

- **The device.** A head, then the file system, the run's file mapped shared and
  writable (vmm `pmem::Layer`). The head holds an NVDIMM pfn info block at 4 KiB
  (drivers/nvdimm/pfn.h, `nd_pfn_sb`, PFN_MODE_PMEM), which the host writes and the
  guest's libnvdimm finds as it probes the device: so its kernel keeps the device's page
  structures, which DAX needs, a 64th of the device, in the head itself (a vmem_altmap)
  rather than in its memory: a 64 GiB layer took none of an x86_64 guest's, where M264's
  page structures took a 64th of the device (PM M277). Each of the device's 128 MiB
  sections takes a 2 MiB block of them, at a 2 MiB boundary past the info block's 8 KiB
  (mm/sparse-vmemmap.c), so the head
  is two blocks more than a block a section, and the device starts at a section
  (`layer_head`). Init finds it by the address the control page gives (`control::LAYER`)
  and mounts its ext4 `dax=always,noinit_itable,no_prefetch_block_bitmaps` where it
  mounted the tmpfs. A machine without one, a joiner's root among them (D119), keeps its
  tmpfs. `no_prefetch_block_bitmaps`: ext4lazyinit reads every group's block bitmap and
  builds its buddy cache in the background after a mount (fs/ext4/super.c,
  `ext4_run_li_request`), so that a first allocation does not wait on a disk, where a DAX
  device's bitmap is memory; and as a template mounts its layer before its snapshot,
  every restored guest did that work again, which in a nested arm64 guest under load
  held a CPU 22 to 27 s (soft lockups in the logs of each of 5 failing rounds before, of
  none of 6 after; PM M346). What it saves a warm VM's memory is unmeasured.
- **Mounted in the template.** A mount took 0.4 to 0.65 ms at p50 and an overlay over it
  0.2 to 0.32 ms more on a guest that had mounted it before, 1 to 80 ms the first time (PM
  M277), where a run's whole start is 0.73 ms at p50 (M230): so the template mounts it
  as it boots, before its snapshot, and the snapshot keeps it, and every run restored
  from the template resumes with it mounted. A restore is given, in the home's `layers`,
  the file system its snapshot kept as a copy-on-write clone of it, where the home's file
  system clones files (APFS's fclonefileat(2), Btrfs's and XFS's FICLONE: slice 3), its
  blocks the snapshot's until its run writes them, so that nothing is copied as it
  restores and, on macOS, nothing written back (PM M278); else an empty file, which it
  fills with a copy. Either is the very generation's it resumes: the daemon names the
  generation it cloned (`--layer-cloned`), and a clone of another, a template saved again
  meanwhile, is filled as an empty file is (`copies_layer`), so that no run is paired with
  another generation's layer. Before any vCPU runs; off the request's path, as warm VMs
  are restored ahead of their runs (D26), but for a run's own snapshot (D176), whose
  `restore vm` it is on: one that holds 512 MiB restores in 34.7 ms at p50 from a clone,
  where from a copy it took 206.0 (Fedora's Btrfs; on the Mac's APFS 106.6 against
  350.6), a clone costing a restore the same whatever its layer holds, and nothing after
  it pays for one (PM M282).
- **Made by the host.** `shards-ext4` makes the file system a boot is given: what mke2fs
  1.47.0 makes for ext4 by default, less what a layer has no use for (no blocks kept to
  grow it, for root, or for an orphan file), its inode tables zeros as the sparse file
  reads, which neither mke2fs's lazy init nor the kernel's then writes. Held to e2fsck
  1.47.0, which finds nothing to fix in any of seven sizes from 8 MiB to 64 GiB
  (`scripts/ext4/generate`, `e2fsck_finds_nothing_to_fix`), and to mke2fs's own
  checksums of each structure (`checksums_agree_with_mke2fss`); every guest of M277's
  mounted one with DAX.
- **Its size.** It holds 10 GiB unless the run asks for another (`--storage-opt size`),
  Docker's device-mapper driver's default for a container's base device, a block
  device's writable layer as this is (dockerd's `dm.basesize`): what the file system's
  own metadata, its journal and the blocks the kernel keeps back (2% or 4096 clusters)
  take is added (`shards_ext4::size_for`). A size is a template of its own (its key holds
  it). One whose page structures, a 64th of it, would take more memory as its microVM
  boots than its host has is refused, as one past what ext4 counts the inodes of is
  (`MOST_BLOCKS`, below).
- **Snapshots** (format 24) keep the layer's length in MiB, its head and its file system
  beside the memory: the head's 2 MiB blocks each once, after an index of them, since all
  but a few describe sections none of whose pages is in use, alike to the byte (a 10 GiB
  layer's head of 85 blocks kept in 5: 12 MiB where 170 MiB whole); a restore maps each
  block privately where the head had it. A save of a running microVM (D176) keeps both
  as a template's snapshot does (`prepare` makes a run's five files).
- **A template's head mapped back** (slice 4). A booted microVM's head is memory of its
  own, written whole as its guest's kernel probes the device, and the template's microVM
  goes on as its image's first run, which held it for its life: with a 10 GiB layer 282.3
  MiB of physical footprint on the Mac and 257.1 MiB resident on Fedora, where a warm
  microVM restored from the template holds 13.9 and 37.3 (PM M277, M284). Once the
  template's snapshot is written, with every vCPU still parked, the VM maps its head back
  from the snapshot's copy as a restore maps one (`Layer::remap_head`): each block
  privately from the copy, the blocks alike one block's pages in the host's page cache,
  as the template's restores' are, and the blocks of zeros fresh memory. HVF's stage 2
  holds the pages it maps (PM M193), so the head is taken from the guest meanwhile and
  given back after, through the stage 2 the layer is given as it is mapped
  (`Layer::placed`); KVM's follows the host's mapping as it changes
  (KVM_SET_USER_MEMORY_REGION, Documentation/virt/kvm/api.rst). The first run then holds
  112.0 MiB (Mac) and 89.7 MiB (Fedora), 170 and 167 less; the mapping takes 4.97 and 1.65
  ms at p50, while the run's start waits for its template anyway, and a program the run
  then runs from its layer, whose page structures its guest writes, ran as quickly within
  the runs' spread (PM M284). One that fails partway leaves each block the copy's or the guest's own memory,
  which hold the same, and is said; one whose guest cannot be given its head back leaves
  the layer lost (`Layer::lost`), and the machine stops.
- **A save's copy asks what the file holds with nothing mapping it** (slice 5). A save
  copies the ranges of the layer's file that hold data, as lseek(2) SEEK_DATA and
  SEEK_HOLE say, but APFS says that a file mapped shared and writable, by the VM process
  or by its guest through Hypervisor.framework, holds data throughout, untouched or
  written, flushed or not, until neither mapping is left (PM M285): a template's copy of a
  10 GiB layer read all of it, 3 to 12 s of its image's first run as the host's load went
  (PM M284, M285). Where a mapping
  hides a file's holes (`platform::MAPPED_HIDES_HOLES`, macOS; a test holds it to what
  the host's file system does), the save takes the file system from the guest's stage 2
  and withholds the VM's own mapping while it asks, then maps both back
  (`Shared::data_ranges`); a run's swap is saved the same way. A template's writing then
  took 127 ms at p50 where it took 4,178, and the image's
  first run 707 ms where it took 5,152; a run's save that leaves
  it running 356 ms where it took 3,313 (PM M285).
  Linux's Btrfs and tmpfs answer as they would unmapped, and nothing is taken away there.
  One whose guest will not give its mapping up, or whose own cannot be withheld, copies
  the file whole, as before; one that cannot be put back leaves the layer lost, and the
  machine stops.
- **A guest's fsync is the host's** (slice 6). A guest's flush of the layer
  (VIRTIO_PMEM_REQ_TYPE_FLUSH), which its fsync waits for (drivers/nvdimm/nd_virtio.c,
  `virtio_pmem_flush`), was answered at once, and the run's root overlay was mounted
  `volatile`, which omits every sync of its upper (Documentation/filesystems/overlayfs.rst):
  a microVM's fsync made nothing durable on its host, where Docker's overlay2 passes it to
  the host's file system. The root is now `volatile` only over a tmpfs, which nothing
  outlives, and the device makes the layer durable before it answers (`Layer::flush`,
  `platform::sync_mapped`), outside guest memory's access, which other devices go on taking:
  fdatasync on Linux, which writes back what the guest wrote through the mapping; on macOS
  F_FULLFSYNC, the one call there whose data is persisted when it returns (fsync(2):
  without it a drive may lose or reorder what fsync gave it, "not a theoretical edge case"),
  and which writes back pages written through a mapping, which fsync leaves dirty (PM M286).
  As Firecracker's flush msyncs its device's file (docs/pmem.md) and QEMU's fsyncs it. ext4
  commits with two flushes, a pre-flush then its commit block's FUA (`journal_async_commit`,
  one, it refuses with `data=ordered`), so a guest's fsync costs two: 3.64 ms at p50 on
  Fedora's Btrfs and 26.6 on the Mac, F_FULLFSYNC 3 to 16 ms as the host's load went, where
  before it cost 0.68 ms and nothing it wrote was the host's to keep (PM M286). A run's
  swap and an image hold nothing past their run: their flushes are done at once.
- **Its file is its run's, then its stopped microVM's.** A layer's file stays in the home's
  `layers` while its microVM serves its run, the daemon holding it with the microVM; what
  a daemon before left there is no run's by the next, which removes it as it starts. A
  run that stays keeps it once the microVM has gone (slice 2), in its directory as
  `layer.ext4`, in place of the layer it had; every other run's goes with its microVM.
- **Kept as it stops, not packed** (slice 2). As a run ends, its host asks the guest to
  keep its layer (`kind::KEEP`) where it asked it to pack one (`kind::SAVE`, D37): init says
  what the layer uses, writes beside its overlay's directories which directories its pack
  leaves out (`shards-made-only`: those holding nothing but init's own `/etc` files, as the
  image has them), syncs every file system (sync(2), its volumes' too), and writes the
  layer's journal in place (syncfs, then EXT4_IOC_CHECKPOINT, fs/ext4/ioctl.c, Linux 5.13:
  jbd2_journal_flush, every transaction written where its blocks are and the log emptied,
  `s_start` 0), so that its host reads it as it stands, with nothing to replay. A guest
  kernel without the ioctl leaves its journal committed, which its host replays (below).
  Then the VM process stops the machine, the guest having nothing left to write, rather
  than wait for its power-off (2 to 37 ms on the Mac), and says the layer is kept
  (`LAYER_KEPT`) only once nothing of the machine can write it: once no vCPU runs and the
  device workers are quiet, and on macOS once it has let go of the file too
  (`Running::wait_then`): there, whoever lets go of a file last after writing it through a
  shared mapping writes it back before the call returns, and whoever reads the file
  meanwhile waits (`platform::LET_GO_WRITES_BACK`). Until it says so the daemon reads
  nothing of the file: as the VM's link ended, its guest could still be powering off. A
  restore on macOS has its copy of its template's layer written back on a thread of its
  own as it restores (`platform::write_back_ahead`), so that what its VM lets go of at its
  end is its run's own writes. The guest's part took 0.50 ms (Mac) and 0.90 ms (Fedora) at
  p50, 1.9 at most, where a freeze (FIFREEZE: the same writes, and the file system then
  marked as needing no recovery, fs/ext4/super.c ext4_freeze) took 16 and 32 ms the first
  time in each microVM, 63 at most, and a read-only remount 3.6 and 7.3 (PM M278). A
  microVM whose run has runs joined to its network (D119) packs its layer as before:
  they go on in it, and its file with them.
- **Read on the host.** `shards-ext4`'s reader reads a kept layer as Linux 6.18 reads one
  (super.c, inode.c, extents.c, dir.c, namei.c, xattr.c, acl.c): its guest's bytes, which
  the host trusts no more than an image's, every structure that carries a checksum checked
  against it (metadata_csum), every number against the file system, a damaged one or one
  of a feature it does not read refused; held to e2fsprogs' own reader, debugfs, over a
  tree of every kind of file mke2fs -d copies into one, its directories indexed by e2fsck -D
  (`scripts/ext4/generate`, `a_volume_reads_as_debugfs_reads_it`), and read without panic
  however its bytes are changed. shards-archive packs it through `Files` as it packs the
  host's own files (`pack_from`), as go-archive packs a Linux host's, whatever the host:
  `commit` of a stopped microVM takes that pack, and its next run (`start`) and a visit
  to its files (`cp`, `diff`, `export`, D37) put it back as they put back a packed layer,
  the same bytes as its guest's pack of it (init's made-only rule now compares with the
  image's directory, where it compared with the root's own, which shows the copy: always
  alike).
- **Replayed where its microVM died.** A file system mounted is marked as needing recovery
  until its kernel unmounts or freezes it; one whose journal's log is empty, as a
  checkpoint leaves it, holds nothing to replay (jbd2_journal_recover: "No recovery
  required") and is read as it stands, the host writing nothing to it. A microVM killed
  before its guest wrote its journal in place leaves what its guest committed in its log,
  not yet in place. The run keeps it all the same where its command had started (a
  run that never started leaves the layer it had), and its journal is replayed on the host
  before it is read (`shards_ext4::journal`), as jbd2 replays one as it mounts it
  (fs/jbd2/recovery.c, its three passes: the log's whole transactions found, its revoke
  records taken, each block it logged written in place but those a later transaction
  revoked, each checked against its tag's checksum first), then, once what it wrote is in
  the file (as jbd2 syncs its device first), the journal marked empty and the file system
  as needing none: a host stopped partway finds it to replay again, or replayed. Held
  block for block to debugfs's own replay
  (`journal_run`) of transactions debugfs wrote (`journal_write`: blocks, one escaped for
  jbd2's magic, a revoke, a later block over an earlier), but for two fields of debugfs's
  own (`s_lastcheck`, `s_kbytes_written`); a transaction whose commit block does not hold
  is not replayed; and replayed without panic however its log's bytes are changed.
- **Measured against packing** (PM M278, n = 20 a side, interleaved). A stop costs the
  same. `diff` of a stopped microVM is 25 to 84% quicker at 4 and 64 MiB written on both
  hosts and at 0 on the Mac (6.75 ms against 32.56), and on Fedora at 0 0.41 ms slower at
  p50; `start` quicker on the Mac at every size (64 MiB: 275 ms against 397) and on Fedora
  the same at 0 and 4 MiB and 4% quicker at 64; `commit` the same or quicker. Open: the
  Mac's `run` right after the same daemon's `rm -f` and `rmi`, its p90 at 0 B 24.76 ms
  against 6.68.
- **Tests.** `shards-ext4`'s, including the oracles'; `pmem`'s for the head's size, its
  info block's checksum, a layer saved and restored, a head's alike blocks kept once, a
  booted head mapped back from its saved copy, its own memory given back, taken from its
  guest meanwhile, a save that asks where the layer's file holds data with its mappings
  away, and a flush answered once what the guest wrote is its file's; `platform`'s that a
  mapping hides a file's holes where `MAPPED_HIDES_HOLES` says;
  the snapshot's for a run's five files; `layers`' for the files the daemon makes and
  removes; on real microVMs, `a_microvm_takes_its_ipc_hostname_cgroups_umask_and_writable_layer`:
  sizes held to, refusals, and 256 MiB written under `--memory 64m`; and
  `a_stopped_microvms_layer_stays_in_its_file`: a stopped microVM's `layer.ext4`, its
  journal written in place, holding its file and its whiteout, put back as it starts
  again; a microVM killed after its guest committed a file, its layer kept with its
  journal to replay, replayed as `diff` visits it, and the file found;
  `a_stopped_microvms_next_run_goes_on_over_its_kept_file` (booted) and daemon.rs's
  `a_restored_microvm_goes_on_over_a_stopped_containers_kept_file` (restored from its
  template): each restart over the run's own kept file, the same file (its inode), what
  the run before made found, no microVM's own layer left, and 32 MiB written and removed
  each run given back, and a microVM whose layer holds little packed and put back
  (another file); `layers`' `what_a_layer_holds_is_its_blocks_past_an_empty_ones` and
  `a_restart_goes_over_from_where_packing_costs_more`. shards-ext4's `free_blocks_are_what_the_bitmaps_and_counts_say`
  (its free runs the groups' own counts, as mke2fs and e2fsck keep them, in `format`'s file
  system and in scripts/ext4/generate's tree, no block of a file among them) and
  `a_damaged_block_bitmap_is_refused`; `layers`' `a_kept_layers_freed_blocks_go_back_to_its_disk`;
  `pmem`'s `a_readied_file_goes_under_a_layers_device_in_place_of_its_own`; `platform`'s
  `what_is_given_back_reads_as_zeros_and_takes_no_disk`.

- **Read at random until its command runs** (PM M297). A run's first write into its root
  landed in a hole of its layer's file, a clone made for its warm microVM of whose pages its
  host held none, and the host read 4 MiB around it (Btrfs's readahead): 2.4 ms of a 5 ms
  start, every run. The layer's mapping is advised MADV_RANDOM as it is made
  (`platform::reads_at_random`), and to read ahead again as its command runs
  (`Layer::read_ahead`, as the guest says STARTED; a resumed microVM's at once): a
  sequential read of what the layer holds, cold, reads 5,089 MiB/s with readahead and 86
  without. A start on Fedora, its host busy, takes 2.6 to 3.5 ms at p50 where it took 8.1
  to 9.4, and on 4 contended CPUs 18.9 where it took 31.9; on the Mac, where no write paid
  it, a start stays about 1.2 ms. Held by vmm's
  `a_layer_reads_ahead_once_its_command_runs` (its mapping's VmFlags; mutation-checked both
  ways).

- **Its linear map in blocks on arm64** (PM M300, shards' kernel patch 0010). arm64 Linux
  mapped the device memory it added 4 KiB at a time under `rodata=full`, its default
  (arch_add_memory, force_pte_mapping), so that a page's permissions could change alone,
  which a DAX device's linear alias never does: a 512th of the layer in page tables, 133
  MiB of a guest's memory for a 64 GiB layer (M277). 0010 maps a file system DAX device's
  memory in blocks, but where debug_pagealloc or a realm needs base pages: a layer of 4 to
  64 GiB takes none of its guest's memory (-0.7 to 0.3 MiB at p50), and its probe is done
  11 ms (16 GiB) to 41 ms (64 GiB) sooner. The pinned kernel carries it (since
  kernel-6.18.48-8df0015cca35).

- **A restart goes on over the kept file itself** (slice 7, PM M443). A stopped
  microVM's `start` put its files back: the host packed its kept layer, and its warm
  microVM's guest unpacked the archive into the layer its template mounted, a copy as long
  as the layer's changes. Now the file goes under the microVM's layer device as it is.
  The daemon gives the VM the kept file where it is as long as the run's layer
  (`--storage-opt size`, which its template is made for; its journal replayed first where
  its microVM was killed), with `RunHead::layer_over`; the VM readies it
  (`Layer::stage`) before its guest hears of the run and tells the guest to go on over it
  (`run::kind::OVER`) where it sent the archive. The root, the image under the template's
  layer, is every process's and holds that layer's file system, so init (`over.rs`):
  makes a tmpfs every process's root (pivot_root(2), which moves each process of the
  namespace rooted at the old root, the memory's grower among them), the old root's
  mounts moved onto it and the old root detached, the template's standby ended (its own
  mount namespace's copy holds the layer too) and the layer's own mount detached and its
  descriptors let go of; opens the device exclusively, which a mounted file system's
  claim refuses (block/bdev.c, bd_prepare_to_claim), so that nothing of the template's
  layer is mounted under the file; asks the VMM to put the readied file under the device
  (`control::LAYER_SWAP`), which maps it where the template's was (`Layer::swap_staged`:
  `mmap(MAP_FIXED)` over the same host range, so that KVM's memslot, which follows the
  host's mapping, is unchanged; taken from HVF's stage 2 and given back around it, as a
  save's data ranges are, PM M285; on Windows a view in place of a view, below), and reads
  back that it did; then mounts the device's
  file system, the run's, the image under it, the mounts moved onto that, makes it
  every process's root, the tmpfs detached, and forks a standby again. A copy of a
  descriptor of the layer a process forked before held the layer's file system mounted:
  the grower closes its copies as it starts (`close_layer_fds`). The file stays the
  run's, where it is, through the run (`LayerFile::in_place`): its stop keeps it in
  place, the microVM's own layer, the template's clone, goes as the run is registered, and
  a daemon or microVM killed meanwhile leaves the run its layer as its guest
  committed it, replayed as it is next read. Before it lets go of the template's layer,
  init shuts that file system down unwritten (EXT4_IOC_SHUTDOWN, NOLOGFLUSH), and the VMM
  answers the flushes of a layer whose file is about to be replaced at once: its unmount's
  writes, each the host's fdatasync, took a restart 21 to 38 ms (PM M443). The new
  standby moves itself into the workload's cgroup as the template's did before its
  snapshot, which waited for an RCU grace period, 10 to 40 ms on a 32-vCPU guest, until
  cgroup2 was mounted `favordynmods` (Linux 6.0; a kernel without it mounts as before),
  0.3 to 0.9 so. And the file's new mapping reads at random until the command runs, as the
  one before (M297). The guest's part took 13.5 ms at p50 (18.3 at most, n = 41), its
  kept file system's mount, with its one host flush, 4.1 of it. Going over always,
  against packing (n = 20 a side, interleaved, Fedora's Btrfs, a loaded host), `start` of a
  microVM that wrote 0 B was 17.6 ms slower at p50 (79.33 against 61.77) and 15% quicker
  at 64 MiB (464.71 against 546.43): its cost is the go-over's, about the same whatever
  the layer holds, where packing's grows with it. So each restart chooses from what its
  layer holds (`layers::held`): its blocks in use, as its groups' descriptors count them
  with its bitmaps (`Volume::free_blocks`), less what an empty layer of its size holds of
  metadata (`Made::free_blocks`, a format made once a size in memory, nothing written).
  Linux's measured restarts cross at 5 MiB: at 0, 1, 2 and 4 MiB written
  packing was 5.0 to 14.1 ms quicker at p50, at 8, 16 and 32 MiB going over 13.6, 70.1 and
  110.3 ms quicker, the lines between 4 and 8 MiB meeting at 5.08 MiB. Chosen at a 5 MiB
  constant then, against packing always (894c2c67 against de2b1cf5, n = 20 a side,
  interleaved), `start` at p50 / p99: 0 B 55.66 / 64.28 against 53.63 / 67.19 ms (both
  packed: within the spread, p90 63.04 against 59.42), 4 MiB 95.98 / 126.78 against
  97.37 / 121.45, 64 MiB 482.05 / 503.19 against 576.05 / 899.66; `diff` alike at 0 and
  4 MiB and 28% quicker at 64 MiB; `run` and `commit` the same (PM M443).
  Visits (`cp`, `diff` and `export` of a stopped microVM) and joiners' runs (D119) put
  their layer back as before. On macOS the swap and the give-back are held by unit tests
  (`pmem`'s, `platform`'s), and both E2E tests pass on its real microVMs
  (`a_stopped_microvms_next_run_goes_on_over_its_kept_file`,
  `a_restored_microvm_goes_on_over_a_stopped_containers_kept_file`, on an M3 Ultra with
  macOS 26.4, at 8a13e492 3 of 3 and 4 of 4, 2026-11-07; at 5ae6a197, going over from 7 MiB, 3 of 3 each, 2026-11-08). macOS's and Windows' restarts
  cross later than Linux's (PM M496): going over costs a restart more there whatever the
  layer holds (an empty layer's 7.5 to 8.7 ms more than its packing at p50 on macOS, 233 on
  Windows), packing growing with what it holds as on Linux, the lines meeting at 6.8 to 7.9
  MiB on macOS (three runs, n 20 and 40; a fourth at load 19 to 23, its p90s overlapping
  at every size to 12 MiB, at 5.3) and 7.95 and 7.73 on Windows (jupiter, n 20, two runs).
  So the crossing is each host's own, its disk's, file system's and load's: no constant
  measured here is another machine's. **Learned on the host** (2026-11-08): each restart
  that may go either way (its kept file of the run's layer's length, what it holds counted)
  records the bytes its layer held and the time from the choice to its command executing
  (`STARTED`), per way, in the home's `restarts` (`layers::Restarts`): each way's
  least-squares line of time against bytes, kept online as its count, means and
  co-moments (Welford's updates), packing's cost growing with what the layer holds and
  going over's less so. The next restart estimates both at what its layer holds, each with
  its estimate's variance (the residuals' over the line's degrees of freedom, as a
  regression's mean at a point has it), and takes the quicker only where the two differ by
  more than their difference's spread, the square of the difference past the sum of the
  variances; where they do not (no records, fewer than three a way, layers of one size
  asked of another, or near the crossing, where either costs about the same), it takes
  the way recorded fewer times, packing on a tie: a new home's restarts take each way in
  turn until their records tell them apart. No literal is chosen: the one spread is the
  records' own, the three records the least that give a line a residual. PM M443's and
  M496's tables, given as records, hold it (`a_restart_goes_the_way_this_hosts_restarts_say_is_quicker`):
  wherever it decides, it takes the way measured quicker there (Linux, macOS, Windows'
  two runs); it is sure of packing an empty layer and of going over the largest; where it
  is not sure, 2 to 4 MiB on Linux and 6 to 8 on macOS, the two were within a few ms of
  each other. The two E2E tests give their home records that cross at 4 MiB
  (`common::restarts_cross_at`), their 8 MiB layers past it, their small one below.
- **Records that age** (2026-11-08). A host whose disk or load changes kept its first
  restarts' records beside its last, and its lines described a machine that no longer
  existed. Now each way keeps, beside its line, the records since its last that fell
  outside it, held out of it (`layers::Way`), and three in a row restart its learning
  from them: the line becomes theirs, every record before gone. A record is outside by
  the line's own spread: its distance from the line over `s·√(1 + 1/n + (x − x̄)²/Sxx)`, the
  spread a new record has about a least-squares line (its residuals' variance and the
  estimate's together), is Student's t with the line's degrees of freedom while nothing
  changes (Brown, Durbin and Evans 1975, "Techniques for testing the constancy of
  regression relationships over time", JRSS B 37(2): the recursive residual, their test of
  a regression's constancy as records arrive), and it is outside where t's two-sided tail
  past it is below `1/(n + 1)`. That level is the records' own count: of the line's `n`
  records and this one, alike while nothing changes, the newest is the farthest out with
  that chance, so a record past it is farther than the farthest of `n + 1` is expected to
  be once (the rank argument of conformal prediction, Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer 2005,
  *Algorithmic Learning in a Random World*, ch. 2). Three in a row are the least records
  that make a line with a residual, the line learning restarts from; while nothing
  changes they come with a chance of about `(n + 1)^-3` (about: the three are tested
  against one line, whose `s` they share), whose sum over a line's whole life is finite,
  so that a host whose restarts stay alike restarts its learning finitely often, and
  almost all of that while its line holds a few records. A record within the spread puts
  those held out back into the line with itself (their counts, means and co-moments
  merged: Chan, Golub and LeVeque 1979), as the line's own tail; dropping them instead
  narrows the line until noise alone restarts it. t's tail is the regularized incomplete
  beta function, `I_x(ν/2, 1/2)` at `x = ν/(ν + t²)` (Numerical Recipes, 2nd ed., eq.
  6.4.9), by its continued fraction (DLMF 8.17.22) and Lentz's method (Numerical Recipes
  §5.2, §6.4), its log-gamma musl's (the `libm` crate). The home keeps the held-out
  records as lines of their own in `restarts` (`packed-outside`, `over-outside`), which a
  daemon before passes over, and reads a home written before as nothing held out
  (`records_held_out_are_kept_and_merge_back`). The log says each restart of learning.
  Unit tests hold it with seeded records about Linux's packing (PM M443: 52 ms and 10.6 a
  MiB, its noise Linux's p50 to p90 at 0 B as a normal's, sizes the tables' at random):
  noise alone, normal, restarts no learning once a line holds 30 records in 32 lives of
  2,000; a log-normal tail, its p99 several times its p50's distance, which the normal
  test underrates, in 2 of them, three slow restarts in a row being a burst of load that
  the line follows and comes back from (`a_line_keeps_its_records_through_noise_alone`);
  60 ms more at every size restarts learning within 10 records in all 32 lives, and
  packing's cost a byte doubled within 100 in 30 of the 32, after which the line says what
  restarts take now (`a_line_follows_its_host_when_its_level_or_slope_moves`; Fedora,
  647f162e).
  A slope's change is the slower to find: records at the sizes it moves least stay
  within the spread and break the runs, and those a broken run puts back widen the line.
  A change smaller than the line's spread is no change to it: the line takes it in, as
  least squares does. PM M443's and M496's tables, given in size order, restart a line of
  their first three, which says little of their largest, where the costs curve: their
  test holds the lines alone.

  | Literal | Where | From |
  |---|---|---|
  | `1/(n + 1)` | the level a record is outside at | the line's `n` records and this one: the chance that the newest of `n + 1` alike is the farthest (Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer 2005) |
  | `s²(1 + 1/n + (x − x̄)²/Sxx)` | a new record's variance about the line | least squares' prediction variance; Brown, Durbin and Evans 1975's recursive residual |
  | `n − 2` (`n − 1` at one size) | t's degrees of freedom | the residual's: two estimated for intercept and slope (one, a mean, where every layer held one size) |
  | 3 (`RESTART_FROM`) | outside records in a row that restart learning | the least that make a line with a residual: two for its intercept and slope, one for the residual (as D190's lines need to answer) |
  | `I_x(ν/2, 1/2)`, `x = ν/(ν + t²)` | t's two-sided tail | Numerical Recipes, 2nd ed., eq. 6.4.9 |
  | `(a + 1)/(a + b + 2)` | where the continued fraction is taken of `x`, else of `1 − x` | Numerical Recipes §6.4: where it converges quickly |
  | `f64::EPSILON` | when the continued fraction has converged | a term that changes it by less than an `f64` tells apart |
  | `f64::MIN_POSITIVE` | a denominator kept off zero | Lentz's method (Numerical Recipes §5.2), the least normal `f64` |
  | `max(a, b) + 1` | the continued fraction's terms at most | past the `O(√max(a, b))` it needs (Numerical Recipes §6.4): a count read from a damaged file ends |
- **On Windows, a view in place of a view** (row 18 of the parity audit). Windows maps no
  file over a mapping as `mmap(MAP_FIXED)` does: a view is made at an address that is free
  (MapViewOfFile3), and a range unmapped then mapped again is free between the two calls,
  for any thread's allocation to take. A placeholder holds it instead: a layer's file
  system, a run's swap and a group's budget are each a view that replaced a placeholder of
  its length (VirtualAlloc2, `MEM_RESERVE | MEM_RESERVE_PLACEHOLDER`; MapViewOfFile3,
  `MEM_REPLACE_PLACEHOLDER`, whose address and size must be the placeholder's exactly), and
  the swap unmaps the template's view back to its placeholder (UnmapViewOfFile2,
  `MEM_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER`, "unmaps a mapped view back to a placeholder") and places the
  kept file's view in it (`platform::map_file_shared_at`), the address the same and
  the range never free (Microsoft's VirtualAlloc2, MapViewOfFile3 and UnmapViewOfFile2
  references). WHP's stage 2 maps a range of host addresses (WHvMapGpaRange): the layer's
  file system is unmapped from the partition (WHvUnmapGpaRange) before the views change and
  mapped again after, through the stage 2 the layer was given (`Layer::placed`), as HVF's
  is. A view that cannot be placed leaves the placeholder, where its own file's view is
  placed back; one that cannot be placed back loses the layer, and the machine stops, as on
  Unix. A view unmapped without `MEM_PRESERVE_PLACEHOLDER` frees its range, as VirtualAlloc2's
  own example frees its views, and a placeholder left alone is freed whole
  (`unmap_file_shared`). The daemon gives a Windows run its own kept file as it gives
  a Unix one, and the freed blocks go back there as everywhere (FSCTL_SET_ZERO_DATA on the
  sparse file, slice 8). Held by `platform`'s `a_view_goes_in_place_of_another_at_its_address`
  (the range a view, then a placeholder, then freed, as VirtualQuery says, and what each view
  holds its own file's) and `pmem`'s `a_readied_file_goes_under_a_layers_device_in_place_of_its_own`,
  both on Windows now, and `layers`' `a_kept_layers_freed_blocks_go_back_to_its_disk` on every
  host; `a_stopped_microvms_next_run_goes_on_over_its_kept_file` and
  `a_restored_microvm_goes_on_over_a_stopped_containers_kept_file` run on Windows too, the
  file's identity its volume's serial and file index (GetFileInformationByHandle). Both
  pass on WHP, on CI's windows-2025 and windows-2022, with every VM test required to run
  there (CI 42070454222 at 90de623f, 42134267973 at b8270370), and on jupiter. Against
  packing (PM M496, n 20 a side, interleaved), `start` at p50: 0 B 321.55 ms gone over
  against 88.66 packed, 4 MiB 652.89 against 494.89, 8 MiB 822.56 against 824.35, 16 MiB
  1,344.67 against 1,612.55, 32 MiB 2,205.23 against 3,126.39: Windows' restarts cross at
  7.95 MiB (7.73 run again, its tails kept); a Windows host's restarts learn their own.
- **What the guest freed goes back to the host** (slice 8, PM M443). pmem takes no
  discard (drivers/nvdimm/pmem.c), so a layer's file only grew while its microVM lived,
  whatever its guest deleted. As a stopped microVM's layer is kept, its microVM gone,
  the daemon reads its block bitmaps (`Volume::free_runs`: each group's whose bitmap was
  written, each checked against its descriptor's checksum, a `BLOCK_UNINIT` group's never
  allocated past its own metadata) and deallocates the free blocks its file holds data in
  (`platform::deallocate`: fallocate(FALLOC_FL_PUNCH_HOLE) on Linux, F_PUNCHHOLE on macOS,
  FSCTL_SET_ZERO_DATA on a sparse NTFS file), which read as zeros after, a free block's
  bytes never read. A layer whose journal is still to replay (its microVM killed) gives
  nothing back until it is kept again: its bitmaps may not say yet what its journal
  allocated. A microVM that wrote 64 MiB or 1 GiB and removed it kept a file of 64.35 and
  1,024.5 MiB on the disk, and now of 0.36 and 0.56 (n = 20 each, alike to the hundredth); the
  give-back took 11.1 and 160.2 ms at p50 (15.3 and 303.8 at most) on Fedora's Btrfs, as
  the daemon keeps the layer, after its run's client is told it ended and before a command
  that reads the layer goes on (PM M443).
- **Its bounds are ext4's and mke2fs's** (audit of picked constants, 2026-11-09). The most
  a layer may be was 2^32 blocks (16 TiB), said to be what 32-bit block numbers hold; with
  `64bit` they are 48 bits, and the count that binds is `s_inodes_count`'s 32 bits, which
  must be the groups times their inodes (ext4_check_geometry): at one inode to 16 KiB, as
  many whole groups as it counts (524287), 64 TiB less a group's 128 MiB. A host whose
  file system holds no file that long refuses it as the layer's file is sized (EFBIG), an
  error and not a panic. Held by `the_most_blocks_are_as_many_groups_as_the_inode_count_holds`;
  containers.rs's `--storage-opt size=70t` is the refusal's E2E (owed a run).

  | Literal | Was | Now | Source |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `MOST_BLOCKS` (lib.rs) | 2^32 | `(u32::MAX / (GROUP * BLOCK / INODE_RATIO)) * GROUP` = 2^34 - 2^15 | Linux v6.18.48 fs/ext4/ext4.h:1327 (`__le32 s_inodes_count`), super.c:4828 and 4840-4846 (ext4_check_geometry) |
  | `LEAST_BLOCKS` (lib.rs) | 2048 | kept | e2fsprogs v1.47.0 lib/ext2fs/mkjournal.c:359 (no journal below 2048 blocks) |
  | `MAX_LEN` (lib.rs), `INIT_MAX_LEN` (read.rs) | 32768 | kept | Linux v6.18.48 fs/ext4/ext4_extents.h:149 (`EXT_INIT_MAX_LEN`) |
  | `MAX_DEPTH` (read.rs) | 5 | kept | ext4_extents.h:87 (`EXT4_MAX_EXTENT_DEPTH`) |

**Next** (the slices after these).
- Visits and joiners' runs over the kept file too.
- A changed host's restarts, timed: the ageing's records and its restarts of learning
  read from a home whose disk or load is changed under it (the unit tests' records are
  seeded).
- Going over's fixed cost below packing's, so that a layer holding little goes
  over too: the mount of the kept file system and its one host flush, and the root's
  two moves (PM M443); on Windows its 233 ms, unmeasured step by step (PM M496).
- Joiners' layers (D119) on the microVM's own, rather than tmpfs.
- The head's boot: a 2 MiB block a section for the guest to write as it probes, on KVM
  1.9 ms a GiB when the host has huge pages free and up to 19 ms a GiB when it compacts
  for them (M277): a 10 GiB layer's template boot is 19 to 190 ms longer.
- Hosts whose runs restore no template yet (Windows, whose daemon is yet to come: D195,
  D196) boot every run, so each run pays the head's probe and the layer's first mount: not
  measured there yet.
- APFS fills a hole shorter than 16 MiB between written blocks of a sparse file (PM
  M277): a layer's file, as a swap file and a template's memory, takes more of a Mac's disk
  than it was written.

### D179. Other CPUs' images, emulated in their microVM (parts 1 to 3 built; one platform wherever a command names it)

**Container facts and copy ownership** (runs-06, 2026-11-13). A container's
`image_manifest` is its selection, even when its index's preferred platform changes.
Inspect reads that descriptor and its config through the store's existing digest/size
checks and OCI document/config bounds; ownership-mode copy uses those same facts.
A record with no selected manifest (made before shards kept it, 2026-11-03) has no
image facts, as one whose recorded selection cannot be read: neither falls back to the
reference's preference, another platform's facts where it changed (legacy-audit,
2026-11-14: the preference read for such a record before it): inspect has no image facts,
and copy refuses with the missing container/config identity. An available config with
no User keeps OCI's root default; an explicit run user remains authoritative.
A record with no image ID is refused by `cp -a` too (`CopyUserRefusal::NoImage`, "its
record names no image, so its user is unknown"), where it was copied as root, an empty
user (legacy3, 2026-11-14). That was a security-relevant fallback: an ownership-mode
copy into a microVM whose image runs as a non-root user would have left root-owned files
its user could not change, and a user nobody recorded was taken for the most privileged
one. No release made such a record: `image_id` came in 993756c9e (2026-10-02), before
v0.3.0, the first release, and in every release (`git grep 'image_id: ' TAG` for v0.3.0 to v0.7.0)
the daemon's one record maker writes `Some(prepared.image_id)`, the `None`s in test
modules alone. So there is nothing to migrate.
The image ID is required (legacy4, 2026-11-14): `Container.image_id` is a `String` with no
`serde(default)`, and a record without it, or with it null (how the `Option` wrote none), is
refused as the store reads it, typed (`containers::Unread::NoImage`, "its record names no
image ID, which every record shards makes names"), its microVM never seen and its
directory left as it is and noted, as an unreadable record's is. Every branch for none is
gone with the `Option`: `cp -a`'s `CopyUserRefusal::NoImage` (no record it reads can lack
one), `ps --filter ancestor`'s, `images`' counts and `prune`'s users, `inspect`'s image facts
and size, the Engine API's `ImageID` and the listing's `image_id` (an empty string for
none), a move's plan (the same), and a live move's look for its image by reference
instead (`unwrap_or_else(|| c.image.clone())`). Not one release could need them: the one
maker writes the image the run resolved (`git grep 'image_id: ' v0.3.0..v0.7.0`: the
daemon's `Some(prepared.image_id.clone())`, the `None`s in test modules alone), and no
release assigns the field after (`git grep '.image_id = '` names none in v0.7.0 or now).
A moved record (D176 part 6) is held to the same, refused as its stream's record is read.
Red/green: containers.rs `a_record_with_no_image_id_is_refused` (absent and null; both
read with no image before), and commands.rs `a_copy_as_the_user_of_a_record_gone_is_refused`
for the refusal that remains.
The two-platform store regression changes the preference both ways, checks each selected
User/Env/descriptor and a missing manifest. Real guest/inspect/copy agreement remains
ROOT's live check in the [runs fix record](../research/measurements/runs-fixes/README.md).

Images built on an arm64 Mac usually ship to x86_64 hosts, and the other way round, and a
build for both (`--platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64`, D87) runs each platform's RUN steps.
shards refused a step for a platform its microVMs do not run: "shards runs steps for
linux/arm64 only, the platform its microVMs run, not linux/amd64". Docker runs one under
qemu-user, which its binfmt tool registers with the host kernel's binfmt_misc
(`docker run --privileged tonistiigi/binfmt --install all`: every architecture the host
does not run, for every process on the host, until it reboots), and BuildKit runs the
step under whatever the kernel finds for its programs; Docker Desktop's VM registers its
own, Rosetta's for x86_64 on a Mac where it is on (M241: 4.66.1's VM has both, and
Rosetta runs x86_64).

A microVM has a kernel of its own, so the emulator is its kernel's to register: a builder
registers the emulators of the platforms its build's steps run, and nothing outside it
changes. That beats Docker in isolation and in what a build depends on: no privileged
container, no host-wide state that every process inherits and a reboot loses, no step of
one build reaching another's emulators (binfmt_misc is the kernel's: a privileged step
there changes the host's); the emulator is one pinned by digest, the same on every host,
where Docker's is whatever the host has installed, or Docker Desktop's own. It does not
beat Docker Desktop's speed on a Mac:

- **Measured (PM M241).** Docker's builds of qemu-user (`tonistiigi/binfmt`, BuildKit's,
  pinned) registered in a microVM as its tool registers them run another CPU's programs.
  From the host's side, an emulated run costs 4.6 and 5.5 times the cycles of a native one
  for sha256 and gzip at p50, and each program started about 5.5 ms more (15.5 times the
  cycles); a guest has no steal clock (the VMM answers SMCCC's PV_TIME_FEATURES with not
  supported), so its own CPU times count the time its vCPU waited for the host, and the
  host's figures are what a run cost. Docker Desktop on the same Mac runs x86_64 through
  Rosetta at 1.3 to 1.4 times native for compute and 12 to 13 for starts: compute 3.3 to
  7.6 times faster than qemu in a microVM, starts at much the same cost.
- **Rosetta is not shards' to use.** Apple gives Rosetta to a Linux VM through
  Virtualization.framework's `VZLinuxRosettaDirectoryShare`; shared into a shards microVM
  and registered as Apple documents it, its binary refuses to run: "Rosetta is only
  intended to run on Apple Silicon with a macOS host using Virtualization.framework with
  Rosetta mode enabled" (M241). shards drives Hypervisor.framework itself (D1), and does
  not get round Apple's check. Rosetta would mean a second kind of microVM on Macs,
  Virtualization.framework's, for other CPUs' work: the user's decision, open.

So emulation is for steps that cannot be cross-compiled, at qemu's cost; a native host of
the platform builds faster, reached as a context (the next item).

- **The emulators.** `tonistiigi/binfmt@sha256:400a4873…` (binfmt e29e7d7, QEMU 10.2.3),
  this host's platform's image of it, fetched as a base the first time a build needs it
  and kept as the build cache keeps what it made, until `builder prune`; never in the
  shards binary (QEMU is GPL-2.0). Its root is one more of the builder's pmem devices,
  which init mounts where no step reaches it, and registers each emulator the build needs
  (`shards_abi::emulate`: the binfmt tool's table, QEMU's magic and masks, flags
  CFP: the program's credentials, the emulator opened as it is registered so that every
  root and mount namespace reaches it, argv[0] kept, which the image's builds expect).
  Measured: written through printf's format, a register line's `\x` escapes are printf's
  to read, its mask comes out matching every ELF, the emulator's own included, and every
  program fails with ELOOP; init writes the line as it is.
- **What runs natively.** A platform a builder runs itself needs no emulator: its own, and
  linux/386 on an x86_64 host (the guest kernel's `IA32_EMULATION`; BuildKit's util/archutil
  probes a host kernel for the same). Apple's CPUs run no 32-bit Arm, so linux/arm is
  emulated on arm64 hosts. A platform without an emulator is refused at its step's turn.
- **A build's steps** (part 1, built): each RUN step for another platform runs in the
  builder as any step does, its programs under their CPU's emulator: the builder boots with
  the emulator image's root as one more pmem device, and before any step is asked
  (`EMULATE`) for the architectures the build's steps need, which init registers, or
  says why not (`EMULATED`). `tests/build.rs`
  `a_step_for_another_cpu_runs_under_its_emulator` builds `uname -m` for the other
  64-bit CPU, for linux/386 and linux/arm/v7, and for both 64-bit platforms at once, each
  step seeing its own CPU; with the registration left out, the step fails with the
  kernel's "exec format error".
- **A run of another platform's image** (part 2, built): a run of an image no guest runs,
  asked for by `--platform` or named by its lone manifest or by an image here, runs under
  its CPU's emulator. The daemon gives its microVM the emulator image's root after its
  other devices, and names it on the kernel's command line (`shards_emulate=DEVICE:ARCH`);
  init registers it in the initramfs before the image's root moves over it, which then
  keeps the emulator's mounts out of every process's reach (the workload's mount table
  starts at its own root). Its template, saved with the device, keeps it registered in
  every restore, the daemon's record of it naming the device it gives a restore. A run
  that names no platform is warned of, in dockerd's words (PM M250), exactly when it runs emulated:
  when no guest runs its image's platform itself (the host's platform, as the warning
  names it, arm64's `v8` or an amd64 host's level as go-archvariant v1.0.0 reads the
  CPU). dockerd's matcher counts 32-bit Arm as an arm64 host's own, for a CPU that runs
  it; no guest of shards' does (PM M250), so its runs, emulated, were not warned of, and
  now are. And a pull or a run that names no platform takes a lone manifest whatever its
  platform, and runs it under its CPU's emulator, where shards refused it (measured: Docker
  29.3.1 pulled `alpine@sha256:3e9b4b68…`, amd64's, on arm64, warned of it, and ran it). Of
  an index, a pull or run that names no platform takes, after the guests' own platforms,
  those a guest runs emulated, as it runs a lone manifest of them: the other 64-bit CPU's,
  then 32-bit Arm's v8 to v5 (on arm64: arm64, amd64, 32-bit Arm's; on x86_64: amd64 and
  386, arm64, 32-bit Arm's). containerd's order put 32-bit Arm first on arm64, for a CPU
  that runs it itself; a microVM's here does not (PM M250: its guest refuses an armv7
  program's exec), and emulated the two cost alike (M250: 32-bit Arm 11% less for sha256,
  amd64 6% less for gzip and starts). What decides is what a run can use: a 32-bit process
  addresses 4 GiB at most, where a microVM's memory can be the host's (D148). An index of
  the other CPU's alone, which shards refused, runs emulated and warned of, as its lone
  manifest did. Tested: `crates/image`
  `a_pull_of_no_platform_takes_the_other_64_bit_cpus_before_32_bit_arms`. A commit of
  another CPU's image is that CPU's, its base's variant kept (moby NewChildImage).
  `tests/images.rs` `a_run_of_another_cpus_image_runs_under_its_emulator` boots one,
  restores its template (without the emulator's device in the restore, it boots instead),
  and runs with no platform a lone manifest, an index of the other CPU's alone
  (`amd64/alpine:3.22`'s on arm64, `arm64v8/alpine:3.22`'s on x86_64) and one of 32-bit
  Arm's (`arm32v7/alpine:3.22`), each emulated and warned of.
- **An image's platforms** (part 2, built): an image keeps each platform pulled of its
  index (dockerd's keeps them too, PM M243), where shards' kept one, the last pulled: a run of
  another platform made a plain run of the image take that one, emulated and warned of.
  Its name names this host's best of its platforms here, which a run that asks no
  platform takes, and a pull of another platform leaves it so; the collector keeps each
  platform here unpacked. A name a load gives an index none of whose platforms is this
  host's names the index itself; a run of it takes its platforms here, where shards refused
  it ("its record names an index"), and one with none of them here is refused, with the
  words a `docker` script reads ("… does not provide any platform"). A run of a platform not
  here pulls it ("Unable to find image", then "Image is up to date", its name resolving to
  the index it did), and pull and run
  say whether it is up to date, the name resolved here to what it resolves to now, a
  digest's by a name of its repository (moby image_pull.go, resolveImage, answers a script
  the same). A run that may not pull refuses it, with the words a `docker` script reads
  ("image with reference … was found but
  does not provide the specified platform (…)"), as does a run for another platform of a
  lone manifest, which a pull takes whatever its platform. Deliberately unlike Docker:
  - a platform is here when all of it is, its config and layers with its manifest, where
    dockerd takes one whose manifest alone is, which a pull cut short leaves: shards pulls
    it whole again rather than fail the run;
  - an image named by its ID, for a platform not here, is refused, naming the image, where
    Docker's CLI reads a short ID as a repository's name and pulls that ("pull access
    denied for 11a3eb1597e8", M243).

  A build's base, for its guests' platform, is pulled for it where another platform's alone
  is here. `crates/registry`
  `an_image_keeps_each_platform_pulled_and_names_this_hosts` (mutation-checked: the name
  naming what was pulled last, a lookup taking its name's platform alone, a platform taken
  without its layers, a collection keeping its name's platform's root filesystem alone) and `a_lone_manifest_is_pulled_for_any_platform_and_found_for_its_own`;
  `tests/images.rs` as above, with this host's pulled first, then each refusal and status
  (mutation-checked: a lone manifest run for another platform than its own, an ID pulled
  as a repository's name, a digest's status by its own name's record alone).
- **A build on another CPU's base** (part 3, built): a build takes a base's lone manifest
  whatever its platform (containerd v2.2.1 core/images/image.go, `Manifest`, checks a
  platform of an index's manifests alone), where shards refused it, its steps run under the
  base's CPU's emulator (build.rs `a_step_for_another_cpu_runs_under_its_emulator`), and warns of it in BuildKit's check's words (InvalidBaseImagePlatform:
  "Base image … was pulled with platform "linux/amd64", expected "linux/arm64" for current
  build"). Asked for no platform, the image is its base's platform, as Dockerfile2LLB
  leaves an implicit target's; its stage keeps the build's platform, as dockerui gives
  the frontend the worker's first platform alone to detect a stage's by (v0.28.1
  dockerui/config.go), so no emulated platform is ever detected (measured: Docker
  29.3.1's BuildKit v0.28.1 on linux/arm64, its worker listing seven platforms, warned,
  ran the step emulated and made an amd64 image). BuildKit's step runs the base's programs
  under whatever emulators the host's kernel has, whatever the step's platform says: a
  builder registers, beside each step's platform's emulator, the one of the CPU of the
  base its root comes from, down the step's first inputs to its stage's FROM, so that a
  base of another CPU only copied from fetches no emulator. What a policy reads of a base
  (D101) is the manifest the build takes, its root filesystem left unbuilt. The planner's
  oracle gains a build that asks no platform (`scripts/agentfile/generate`,
  `implicit_target`), and `corpus/plan/base-platform.Dockerfile` and
  `base-platform-implicit.Dockerfile` hold the warning, the stage's platform and the
  image's to BuildKit's, asked for and not; `tests/build.rs`
  `a_step_for_another_cpu_runs_under_its_emulator` builds on the other CPU's lone alpine
  manifest asking no platform: the step runs emulated, the warning is BuildKit's, the
  image the other CPU's (mutation-checked: without the base's CPU's emulator the step
  fails with the kernel's "exec format error"; a lone
  manifest refused by a build's lookup, or by a policy's; the oracle planning every build
  with a platform asked).

**An emulated command is never PID 1 (2026-10-18).** A run of another CPU's image runs
its command under shards' reaper (`--init`'s), and a build step for another CPU runs its
command as its namespace's first process's child (`shards_abi::build::Step::emulated`, set
from the step's platform or its base's), where each was PID 1 of its PID namespace. The
emulator ends a program that dies of a signal by sending that signal to itself, its
default action restored, and waiting for it; a PID namespace's init is sent only the
signals it has a handler for (pid_namespaces(7)), so the wait never ended: every emulated
run or step whose program crashed, aborted or met an instruction the emulator lacks hung
for ever (PM M251), where a native one's fault ends it, the kernel's own signal reaching
init too. Now it ends as the native one does, 128 and the signal's number. What differs
from a native PID 1: a signal the command sends itself takes its default action, where a
native PID 1 is not sent it. Tested: `tests/images.rs`
`a_run_of_another_cpus_image_runs_under_its_emulator` (a program meeting an undefined
instruction, emulated: 132) and `tests/build.rs` `a_step_for_another_cpu_runs_under_its_emulator`
(an emulated exec-form step's crash fails its step, `exit code: 132`). Mutation-checked,
each caught: an emulated run's command left PID 1; no step marked emulated; the guest
ignoring the mark; the reaper ending 0 for a signal's end.

**amd64's levels (2026-10-18).** A guest runs its host's x86-64 level: KVM's supported
CPUID and a WHP partition keep the host's feature bits (vmm `cpuid.rs` rewrites only
topology), which `tests/images.rs` `a_guest_runs_its_hosts_x86_64_level` pins on every
x86_64 host CI boots guests on (the guest kernel's own flags reach the host's level). So an
x86_64 host's guests take amd64's levelled builds, `v2` up to the CPU's, as their own, the
highest first, then the level-less amd64 and 386; where shards ran every levelled build
emulated (no guest listed one), and an index of levelled builds alone not at all. The
emulator runs amd64's v2 and v3 and none of v4's AVX-512 (PM M251): an arm64 host's pull
takes amd64's v2 and v3 builds after its level-less one, and a run of a v4 image on a host
whose CPU lacks it is refused, saying why, where it would end at its first such
instruction. A pull that names no platform and finds none says the guest's level-less
platform (`linux/amd64`), as a script reading the refusal expects. Tested: `crates/image`
`a_guest_runs_its_cpus_x86_64_levels_best_first`,
`a_pull_of_no_platform_takes_the_other_64_bit_cpus_before_32_bit_arms` (v3 before 32-bit
Arm on arm64, the level-less first, v4 never) and
`the_emulator_runs_amd64_up_to_its_own_level`. Mutation-checked, each caught: arm64's pull
without amd64's levels; the emulator taken to run v4.

**The platform a user prefers (2026-10-16).** Docker's CLI takes `--platform`'s default
from `DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM` for `pull`, `import`, `run`, `create` and the classic
builder (docker/cli v29.8.1 cli/command/image/pull.go:61, import.go:53, build.go:159,
container/create.go:84, run.go:73), and buildx for `build` (v0.37.1 commands/build.go,
platformsDefault); shards took it, `SHARDS_DEFAULT_PLATFORM` first (D157), for `run`,
`create` and `import`, and not for `pull` or `build`, so `DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM=linux/amd64
shards pull alpine` stored this host's where Docker stores amd64's. Both take it now: a
pull as the flag said first, so that one named after it is the one kept, as pflag keeps
the last given; a build where the flag is not given, as pflag's first value given
replaces a string array's default whole (a build that names `--platform` builds that alone,
not an index of it and the default). Tests no longer inherit a default the host's user
prefers (`common::command`). Tested: `a_pulls_platform_defaults_to_the_default_platforms`
and `a_builds_platform_defaults_to_the_default_platforms` (an index of two platforms: the
default's stored and built, shards' variable before Docker's, a named platform over both).
Mutation-checked: pull's default not taken, Docker's variable read first, build's default
not taken, build's default kept with a platform named.

**One platform's microVM of an image, wherever a command names it (2026-11-03).** The
microVM need: an image here keeps each platform pulled (part 2), and each platform is a
microVM of its own, this host's run natively and another CPU's under its emulator. Someone
who builds on an arm64 Mac for amd64 hosts keeps both, runs the amd64 one emulated to test
it, and then has to look at that one (its config is what its microVM boots with, its layers
what its disk is made of), carry it alone to the host that runs it natively, publish it
alone, or free the disk the emulated one takes once done: its root filesystem, its layers,
the templates of its microVMs. Until now only a pull, a run, a create and an import took a
platform; every other command saw the platform the image's name names, this host's best,
and refused `--platform` as unserved. Now each of them takes one (`--platform`, which
Docker's CLI sends too), read as a pull reads it (`os[/arch[/variant]]`, normalized), and
chooses that platform's manifest of the image, here whole (manifest, config, layers), or
refuses in the words a script reads where the image has none ("image with reference … was
found but does not provide the specified platform (…)"; the Engine API's 404):

- **Inspection** (`image inspect`, `GET /images/{name}/json?platform=`) shows that
  platform's microVM: its config, architecture, size and layers, and as its descriptor its
  manifest, labelled with its platform; its ID the image's.
- **History** (`history`, `GET /images/{name}/history?platform=`) is that platform's
  config's steps, each layer's size from its manifest. The Engine API refused both.
- **A save** of some platforms (`save --platform`, `GET /images/get?platform=`) holds theirs
  alone, each one's manifest, config, layers and attestations. Of one, the archive is that
  platform's microVM alone: `index.json` names its manifest, labelled with its platform,
  and holds no index, so a load on any host takes it as the one image it is (a lone
  manifest runs whatever its platform, part 2); of several, the index, its other platforms
  not here, as a pull of some of them leaves it.
- **A load** of some platforms (`load --platform`, `POST /images/load?platform=`) keeps
  theirs alone of an archive's images: each must be in the archive, or nothing is named;
  the archive's other platforms leave the store at once, but what an image here held before
  the archive came, which a load never takes away.
- **A push** of one platform (`push --platform`) pushes that platform's manifest alone
  under the tag, with its config and layers, as an image of one platform; the image's other
  platforms, its index and attestations stay here.
- **A removal** of some platforms (`rmi --platform`, `DELETE /images/{name}?platforms=`)
  takes those platforms' microVMs alone, and their attestations: their manifests leave the
  store, and what they alone held (config, layers, root filesystem, and the templates made
  of it) goes with the next collection. The image stays with its names, and a name that
  named a platform taken comes to name the best left for this host's microVMs, or, with
  none left, the index itself, which a run pulls again; each platform's manifest is said
  deleted (`Deleted: sha256:…`, the line scripts and the Engine API's answer read). An image
  of one platform named with its platform is removed whole, as `rmi` removes it.
  Refused, the image left as it was: a platform another image is made of too (content is
  shared by digest; taking it would take it from that image), and one a microVM made of it
  holds, a running one whatever `-f` says, a stopped one unless forced. So a microVM keeps
  the platform it was made from: its record now names the manifest it was made of
  (`image_manifest`), and one from before names none, so is taken as made of the
  platform the image's name names. The microVMs of its other platforms hold only theirs:
  the emulated platform goes while this host's microVMs run.
