Tested: `crates/image` `one_platform_of_an_image_is_found_read_and_taken_away_alone` (found
where whole, read with its own config, held by another image of it, taken with its
attestation, the record naming the platform left, then the index; the collection taking
what it alone held), `daemon::rmi` `a_platform_goes_unless_a_microvm_of_it_holds_it`, and
`tests/images.rs`
`one_platforms_microvm_of_an_image_is_chosen_wherever_a_command_names_it`, on real
microVMs, from a loopback registry that takes pushes, no Docker Hub image but the
emulator: an index of the test guest for this host and a program of the other 64-bit CPU
for the other, with an attestation of the other's, pulled for both; each command names each
platform and one the image has not; the other's run emulated and this host's natively,
before and after its platform's removal; a removal refused while a microVM made of it
stays; a load of the other alone from an archive of both, run emulated.

### D178. A microVM's I/O limits, kept outside it

Review devices-04 (2026-11-14): a block device's stop cancels its own limiter wait under the limiter mutex before joining its worker. This neither pauses other devices nor erases debt; reset cannot lift the shared limit. Its owned token is cleared for a new worker only after the old worker joined. Malformed descriptor work is checked before charging bytes. Source/test evidence: `docs/research/measurements/device-fixes/README.md`; no fixed production timeout is introduced.


`--io-maxbandwidth BYTES` and `--io-maxiops N`, on `shards run vm` and `create` and in the
Engine API's `HostConfig.IOMaximumBandwidth` and `IOMaximumIOps`, are the most bytes and
requests a second of a microVM's I/O to the host's storage: its volumes (virtio-fs) and its
disks (virtio-blk). Docker takes them for its Windows containers' system drive alone:
dockerd on Linux refuses them (`Invalid QoS settings: linux does not support Maximum IO
Bandwidth or Maximum IO IOps`, moby 464cd50c daemon/daemon_unix.go), and docker/cli hides
them from a Linux daemon (their `ostype` annotation, cli/command/container/opts.go). A
microVM's limits per device (`--device-read-bps` and the rest, D44) are written in its
guest's cgroup, which the guest keeps; these the VMM keeps, outside the guest, where no
process in the microVM, its root among them, can lift them. A microVM's image (read through
memory, DAX) and its swap window (D159) are memory to it, not device I/O, and are not
limited.

Every request its devices serve is charged before it is served (devices/virtio/limit.rs):
a volume's READ by the bytes it asks for and its WRITE by those it gives, every request as
one request (the high-priority queue's FORGETs and INTERRUPTs, no I/O, not at all), a
disk's read or write by its data. Each measure keeps its theoretical arrival time (ITU-T
I.371's generic cell rate algorithm): when what it charged so far would have been done at
its rate. A request waits for that, then moves it on by its own cost: a microVM left idle
is served at once, a busy one is paced at the limit, and no window of time holds more than
its rate's worth and one request; one larger than a second's worth is served whole, and
the next waits it out. Two things a busy host does would cost the rate, and do not (PM
M240, where each was found by counting the device's requests and the limiter's waits): a
request that costs a measure nothing neither waits on it nor moves it, so that the zero-
byte GETXATTR the kernel asks with each write takes its time within the write's wait; and
a wait that runs past its deadline, as a loaded host's timers leave it, lets the next
request that measure charges keep its place in the schedule, which it would otherwise start
over, never going before it.

One budget a microVM, its VM process's, which each of its devices charges, one VM a
process; its rates come with its run's request, so that a warm VM restored ahead of its run
takes the run's. A wait is on a device's worker thread, never a vCPU's. While a snapshot
pauses the devices (D176), none waits: the request a worker has in hand is served at once,
its cost kept, so that a save waits for no limit. A run joining a microVM (D119)
does its I/O through that microVM's devices and takes no limits of its own: refused,
saying so. `inspect` reports them in its HostConfig.

Measured (PM M240, M5 Max, release build): the limit is a ceiling, kept: 16 MiB under 4
MiB a second achieved 0.844 of it at p50 and 0.894 at most quiet, 0.841 and 0.931 loaded,
never over it; where the host's storage answers within a write's place in the schedule
the rate is the limit's to 0.4% (4.001 s where its time is 3.98), and where it stalls past
that the writer gets the less it can take, catching nothing up, which would take a burst
past the limit. A limit that holds nothing back costs nothing measurable: 64 MiB with none
and with one of 1 GiB a second agree at p50 within 4%, either faster. Held by
`requests_are_paced_at_their_rates`, `a_late_request_keeps_its_place` and
`a_pause_lets_a_waiting_request_go` (limit.rs), and on real microVMs by
`a_microvms_io_is_paced_at_its_limits` (tests/containers.rs: 3 MiB under 1 MiB a second
takes two seconds and more, thirty synced writes under 20 requests a second three; the
limits in `inspect`; a joiner's refused; mutation-checked); the CLI's flags by docker/cli's
oracle (`MICROVM_FLAGS`), the API's by its create bodies.

### D177. `build --squash`: a build's layers as one

`shards build image --squash`, and the Engine API's `POST /build?squash=1` (docker-py's
`build(squash=True)`, the docker CLI's legacy builder's `--squash`), make the layers a
build adds past its base's one layer: the base's layers as they were, then one that makes
the build's tree of the base's. What a later step removed is in no layer, so it is neither
pushed, pulled nor kept; a file of the base's that the build removed is a whiteout. Its
history is moby's squash's (moby 464cd50c `daemon/images/image_squash.go`): the entries as
the unsquashed image has them, times and all, each past those of the base's layers an
empty layer's, then the merge's, `merge sha256:<unsquashed> to sha256:<base>`, at the
image's creation (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH where given, which moby's does not take); built FROM
scratch, every layer is the one, `create new from sha256:<unsquashed>`. moby keeps the
base's entries by index, which leaves the merge's layer without an entry of its own
wherever the base's history names fewer layers than it has (the test image's names none):
`docker history`, which pairs entries with layers in order (`daemon/images/image_history.go`),
then gives the merge's entry a layer of the base's. shards keeps, for
each of the base's layers, the entry the image pairs with it, so every layer has one and
the merge's is the merge's (`squash_makes_a_builds_layers_one`, mutation-checked against
moby's rule).

What it does not change is a microVM: shards flattens every image's layers into one EROFS
filesystem (crates/image), so a squashed image runs as the unsquashed one does. It changes
what a registry and the store hold.

Docker's own: BuildKit has no squash, and buildx warns it removed (`experimental flag
squash is removed with BuildKit`) and builds unsquashed. dockerd squashes an experimental
daemon's builds once they are done (`daemon/builder/backend/backend.go`), and only in its
graph-driver image store: the containerd image store, "now the default for fresh installs"
(Docker Engine 29 release notes), answers `error squashing image: not implemented` after
the whole build has run (`daemon/containerd/image_squash.go`). shards squashes in its one
store, and leaves no unsquashed image behind, where moby's squash leaves it untagged.
Before this, shards accepted the flag and ignored it (buildx still does): a client of the API
that asked for a squashed image got an unsquashed one, which only a warning said.

A step's layer is what its own step stamped in the tree (`diff::write_layer`, BuildKit's
overlay differ); a squash spans every step, so its layer is continuity's doubleWalkDiff of
the two trees from the root (`diff::write_squash`), which reads a file's bytes only where
its metadata matches and its data is not the same node's: a file no step touched is the
base's own. The steps run and are cached as ever, a build without `--squash` reusing them;
`mode=max` provenance names the layers the image holds, which the steps' of a squashed
image are not. Held by `a_squash_writes_every_step_between_two_trees` (diff.rs), and on
real microVMs by `squash_makes_a_builds_layers_one` (tests/build.rs) and
`images_are_built_from_a_context_in_the_body` and
`the_docker_cli_runs_microvms_through_the_engine` (tests/engine.rs: the API's `squash=1`,
and the docker CLI's own legacy `build --squash`, which it offers an experimental engine).

### D176. A running microVM saved whole, and resumed, here or on another machine (in progress)

`shards save vm NAME`, and Docker's `checkpoint`, save a running microVM whole: its
memory, vCPUs and devices as they are, every process, pty, pipe, socket within it and file
in its writable layer with them; `shards restore vm NAME` resumes it from there. Docker's
checkpoint is experimental and Linux's alone (docker/cli: `experimental`, `ostype`
`linux`), and needs CRIU 2.0 or later (docs.docker.com, `docker checkpoint`), which dumps a
container's processes one by one and refuses what it cannot: a `docker run -t` terminal,
device files, files sent over Unix sockets, locks held unless told to, processes joined
to anything outside the set it dumps (criu.org, "What cannot be checkpointed"). A
microVM's state is its memory and its devices', which shards' VMM already saves and
restores for templates (D25): HVF and KVM, on x86_64 and arm64 (D154), and WHP (D196). What
lies outside the microVM goes as with CRIU by default, and is said: connections to the
world beyond it, exec sessions and attached clients.

Lifecycle quarantine retains a typed first cause, PopulationObservation or Capture,
with its actual errno. Capture reuses the same held cgroup/pidfd containment; it
cannot relabel its allocation failure as a failed population read. Ended proof and
prior shared-boundary faults remain terminal. [Consumer and composition evidence](../research/measurements/managed-lifecycle/quarantine-cause.md).

A known unready managed tenant refuses the guest cut through typed run kind46,
`QuiesceRefused`, correlated with the existing private restore tokens. The declared
member, lifecycle reason and errno are checked; tokens never enter display/logs.
Guest Open/Draining/Committing/Quiet states separate earlier bytes from the fixed
reply. Readiness is checked before the first successful QUIESCED byte; a refusal
returns Open without changing tokens or ending healthy tenants. A partial success
cannot become a refusal. Stop/reap/control continues, so post-commit quarantine
still needs full P11 freeze/revalidation against snapshot publication; this narrow
guard does not certify a consistent cut. Host Idle/Waiting/Quiet/Refused/Ended and
QuiesceError deliver a refusal before the VMM snapshot call, with presentation only
at the legacy String boundary. [Decision, literal derivations, exact light checks
and unresolved acceptance gates](../research/measurements/managed-lifecycle/quiesce-refusal.md).

Templates are saved before their guest has plugged any memory or swapped (D148, D159). A
running microVM has done both, so a save keeps them:

- **Memory plugged** (part 1). The memory file holds the RAM, then each run of the blocks
  a virtio-mem device plugged, in the order of their addresses, all-zero pages as holes;
  the state lists the runs (snapshot format 17), and virtio-mem keeps what it asks for and
  what is plugged. A restore remakes the region as boot made it, plugs the same runs
  again through the hypervisor's stage 2, as a plug does, and reads them back before any
  vCPU runs. Held by `memory_plugged_is_saved_and_plugged_back` and, on real microVMs,
  `a_snapshot_keeps_the_memory_its_guest_plugged`: a guest plugs 512 MiB, writes 448 MiB,
  more than it booted with, and only then asks for a snapshot; the VM that booted and two
  restores find all it wrote. Mutation-checked: without the plug again, the restored guest
  faults at the first address of the region it reads.
- **Swap** (part 2). A run's swap file is unlinked once its microVM maps it (D159), so the
  VM process copies it, the guest's writes flushed to it first (msync(2)), into the
  generation's `swap`: the ranges the file holds data in (lseek(2) SEEK_DATA, SEEK_HOLE),
  of them the 4 KiB blocks not all zeros, asked, on macOS, with the guest's mapping and
  the VM's taken away for the moment: APFS says a file mapped shared and writable holds
  data throughout (D190, PM M285). The swap window's state keeps the length, and a
  restore maps a copy of its own back at that length before any vCPU runs (snapshot format
  18). Held by
  `a_runs_swap_is_kept_by_a_save_and_mapped_back_by_its_restore`. ext4 and XFS count a
  page written through the mapping as data before it is written back, reserving its
  block as it is dirtied (`ext4_da_get_block_prep`, `xfs_buffered_write_iomap_begin`), as
  Btrfs and tmpfs do (PM M285); the flush is for a file system that gives a page its block
  only at write-back.

A save is the host's to ask for (part 2), where a template's is the guest's. The daemon
prepares a generation in the microVM's directory, `snapshots/NAME/`: its memory, state
and swap files, empty, created there, since the VM process opens no path of its own (D30).
It hands them to the VM process with `SAVE`. The VM process parks the vCPUs, quiets the
devices, fills the files and answers `SAVED`, then goes on or stops; the daemon commits
the generation, synced, renamed into place, its pointer moved, as the VMM commits a
template. One save at a time, and none while a template is still to save, whose
coordinator would take the request for its own. The machine is taken apart only once a
save has let go of it: the save holds the VM and its devices by weak references, which
`Running` alone owns. What a save cannot keep whole refuses it, and the microVM goes on as
it was, with nothing of the save left: a host's devices (VFIO), a GPU's contexts, a
run joined to it (D119), and files it holds open in its volumes after removing them
that hold more than a snapshot's state keeps (part 5).

Runs joined to a microVM (`--network container:NAME`, D119) run in it, each a run of its
own: a snapshot would keep their processes, and a restore bring them back without their
runs. So a
microVM is saved while none runs in it, which its VM process, which takes the daemon's
messages in order, knows as no other can: a JOIN before a SAVE counts its joiner as it is
taken, and the save refuses while one counts; a JOIN after it is refused until the save is
done, its joiner's start failing with why. Once they end it is saved, its join disk with
the ranges their images had, each let go (snapshot format 19): its restored guest knows the
disk's capacity, and a run that joins the restored microVM takes the next range, no
place given twice (D119). Before this, a microVM saved with joiners running kept them, and
one any run had ever joined was never saved again. Held by
`a_save_refused_leaves_the_microvm_running_and_nothing_behind` (refused while a joiner runs,
saved once it ends, restored and joined again) and `a_join_disk_reads_each_image_at_its_range`
(the ranges kept, mutation-checked).

Saved with `--leave-running`, the microVM goes on. Otherwise its save stops it, and it is
told as stopped, not ended: its attached client says it was saved and as which snapshot,
and exits 148, the status a shell gives a job it stopped (128 + SIGTSTP); its run records
that status. The save answers once its run's record says it has stopped, so that a
`restore vm` asked at once finds it stopped: answered at its VM's word alone, a restore
straight after found it running, 2 of 10 back to back on a Fedora host (none of 20
since). Docker takes a checkpoint's stop for an exit like any other (moby
daemon/monitor.go, handleContainerExit): a restart policy restarts it, and `--rm` removes
it with its checkpoints, what was saved lost. A saved microVM is
neither restarted nor removed: what it is saved as is there to resume. Held, on real
microVMs, by `a_running_microvm_is_saved_whole_left_running_or_stopped` and
`a_save_refused_leaves_the_microvm_running_and_nothing_behind` (tests/saved.rs).
Mutation-checked: removed with `--rm`, and saved with its volume mounted.

`shards restore vm NAME [SNAPSHOT]` resumes a stopped microVM from a snapshot of its own,
its newest unless named (part 3). It is a start of the microVM again, whose VM restores the
snapshot rather than a template: its run's
log, ports, events and end are a start's. Three things a start does not have make it whole:

- **A cut with nothing in flight.** What the guest's init wrote to the host and the host
  had not yet read when the vCPUs parked is in neither the host's log nor the guest's
  memory: lost from every copy restored, and, for a microVM its save stops, from the
  microVM. So the VM process first asks init to QUIESCE, on the run's connection: init
  sends all it holds, then QUIESCED, then nothing until RESUME, and the VM process saves
  once it has read QUIESCED, all before it in the log. What the host sends meanwhile, its
  stdin and signals, comes after the cut in a restored copy, where it is not, as anything
  sent after the cut is. Held by `a_microvm_saved_as_it_writes_loses_none_of_its_output`,
  a guest writing as fast as it can through its save: every count once, up to the save
  and on from it. Mutation-checked: saved without waiting for QUIESCED, a restored copy's
  log went from 56,812 to 57,686, the 873 counts between them lost.
- **Its connections, dialed again, and only by init.** A restore resets the streams the
  snapshot held (D12). The VM process's run and signal ports take one connection each, so
  that a workload dialing one finds it taken (AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §9.7); in a restored copy
  the workload runs already, and would find a fresh port first. So a restored VM process
  has no run or signal port: the daemon gives each save two tokens, which init holds from
  QUIESCE on and the generation keeps (`resume`), and a restored init, finding its
  connection reset and its lineage's generation past the relay's (control::GENERATION),
  dials the exec port twice, each HELLO one token, as an exec's connection is checked:
  compared whole, in constant time, by the exec port's one reader. The VM process waits
  for them before its vCPUs run, and only where the restored init speaks this build's
  protocol (control::ABI). An exec's connection is its client's, which went with the
  microVM saved: init lets go of each as it redials, ending the exec's stdin as its
  client's going does, and what the exec writes after has nowhere to go and is dropped as
  it is read, as anything whose connection is gone is.
  Waited on, a connection the restore reset as it held what init had not read stayed
  established, readable to its end and never writable, the reset taking its credit
  (Linux's vsock, `virtio_transport_space_update`): init, which reads an exec's connection
  no more once its stdin has ended, never wrote the exec's end, and the run outlived its
  stop until its VM was killed, a give-back the save cut short once in 608 CI runs. Held
  by `a_microvm_saved_as_an_execs_stdin_waits_ends_with_its_run_once_restored`, the
  connection full of an exec's unread stdin as the save is taken, mutation-checked: without
  the release, the stop took 40.03 s and the run ended with its VM (PM M330). It had read an exec's
  output only while less than BUFFERED of it waited, so an exec that wrote that much more
  was read no more: killed with the run, it was never seen to end, and its run outlived
  its stop's SIGTERM and SIGKILL until its VM was killed. Held by
  `a_microvm_saved_as_an_exec_writes_on_ends_with_its_run_once_restored`, an exec writing
  as fast as it can through the save, its run stopped once restored: ended by the stop's
  SIGTERM (143). Mutation-checked: without the drop, the stop took 40.0 s, its 30 s
  timeout and the 10 s past its SIGKILL, and the run ended with its VM (255) (PM M328).
- **Its interface, as its guest holds it.** Its MAC, and its address on a network of its
  own (D46), are kept with the snapshot, and asked for again as `--mac-address` and `--ip`
  ask: a member that took the address meanwhile keeps it, and the restore fails, naming
  the snapshot's address. Its swap, a copy of the one the save kept,
  as sparse, is mapped back before its vCPUs run. Held by
  `a_saved_microvm_on_a_network_is_restored_at_its_address`, its peers reaching it at its
  name and that address, mutation-checked (restored at the lowest address free), and by
  `a_saved_microvm_keeps_what_it_swapped`: 96 MiB of a pattern under a 64 MiB limit, read
  back whole after the restore.

A microVM restored resumes where it was saved, as often as its snapshot is restored: its
log goes on from the save, once for each restore. Measured (PM M239, a 256 MiB microVM on
the M5 Max): a save left running parks the guest's vCPUs for 17 ms at p50 and 46 ms at
most on a loaded host, its going quiet first under 0.2 ms at p90; its caller waits 92 ms
at p50 quiet, the commit's sync among it, and a restore 18 ms at p50. `shards list snapshots NAME` lists a
microVM's snapshots, newest first, when each was saved and the disk it takes; `shards
remove snapshot NAME SNAPSHOT...` removes them, and `shards remove vm` with the microVM. A run on
the host's network (D124) is not saved: its guest's sockets are the host's, which no
snapshot keeps.

**Volumes** (part 5). A volume is served to the guest by its run's share process (D38),
whose FUSE server holds what the guest's kernel holds of it: each node by an ID the server
drew, with its parent, its name and its count of lookups, and each open handle. A snapshot
keeps those tables. As the devices are paused, each share's device asks its server for
them by a control frame of the VM process's own, marked by its length word's top bit,
which no guest's request sets (a guest's frame is at most a write's data and headers), and
the save keeps them in the device's state (snapshot format 20). A restored run has a share
process of its own, as every run has, and the restored device gives its new server the
tables before it asks anything, before the guest's vCPUs run. The server opens each node
and handle along its path as the guest uses it, checked to be the same file by its device
and inode, as it opens one it let go of; the guest's open files, its working directory in
the volume and its cached names go on as they were. A directory whose device numbers
changed, as a host's boot may change them, is taken as of the new ones; one that is
another directory, its root not the saved root's inode, refuses the restore, as every file
the guest held of it would be stale. A file the guest holds open after removing its last
name no path reaches, and its server holds it by a descriptor alone: its bytes go with
the tables, as CRIU's images carry such a "ghost" file's (Documentation/criu.txt, up to
`--ghost-limit`, 1 MiB unless told otherwise), within what a snapshot's state holds, 64
MiB, which a save now checks it is under as a restore does. A restored server holds each
in a file of its own, made in the home's private directory (`tmp`, 0700), which the
daemon hands each share process, and removed from it at once; one a crash left there
before its removal, the next daemon's start removes. A directory or special file removed
while open, and a removed file the server had no descriptor left to keep (past its
budget), still refuse the save. Held by
`a_saved_share_is_served_again_by_a_restored_server` (fs/server.rs: an open handle read on,
a directory's node, another directory refused, the device renumbered, mutation-checked),
`a_shares_tables_go_to_the_server_its_restored_slot_is_given` (fs/mod.rs), and on real
microVMs by `a_saved_microvm_writes_on_through_its_volume`, a guest appending to a file it
holds open, from the volume's directory, through a save and a restore: each count once, in
order (mutation-checked: without the tables, the restored guest writes nothing more), and
its guest writing and reading on through a file it removed (mutation-checked: restored
without its bytes, the file's next write fails); and by
`a_save_refused_leaves_the_microvm_running_and_nothing_behind` for removed files past what a
snapshot keeps.

**Docker's command lines for it** (part 4). A `checkpoint create [--leave-running] CONTAINER
CHECKPOINT`, `checkpoint ls`, `checkpoint rm` or `start --checkpoint CHECKPOINT` command
line, a `docker` script's, is read as `save vm`, `list snapshots`, `remove snapshot` or
`restore vm`, on shards' command line and through the Engine API (`POST` and `GET /containers/{id}/checkpoints`, `DELETE
/containers/{id}/checkpoints/{name}`, `POST /containers/{id}/start?checkpoint=`). docker/cli
shows them only to a daemon that says it is experimental (docker/cli v29.8.1
`checkpoint/cmd.go`, `container/start.go`: the `experimental` annotation, read from
`/_ping`'s `Docker-Experimental`), so the engine says so, as `info` and `version` do. What
it means for Docker, a daemon started with `--experimental`, CRIU installed and Linux, a
microVM needs none of. Their answers are dockerd's (moby 464cd50c `daemon/checkpoint.go`,
`daemon/start.go`), in its order: a name that is not `[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+`, or ends
in `.`, refused before anything is looked up (`invalid checkpoint ID "../x", only … are
allowed`, quoted as Go's `%q` quotes it), then the microVM, its state, a name taken.
`start --checkpoint` prints nothing, which is what a `docker` script reads of it, and
restores one microVM at a time. A paused microVM is not started, by `start` with a
checkpoint or without, where shards had answered it as one running already: it is refused
(409, `cannot start a paused container, try unpause instead`, the words a `docker` script
reads, validateState), before the 304 for one running.

Better than dockerd, a checkpoint's name is taken as its directory is made (mkdir(2)'s
EEXIST), where dockerd looks for it and then makes it (getCheckpointDir: os.Stat, then
os.MkdirAll): two creates of one name at once both go on, into one directory, and one that
fails removes it (os.RemoveAll), the other's dump with it. In shards the second is refused,
and a save that fails removes only the directory it made. Before this, shards looked and
then made it too: a second save of the name passed, waited for the first's lock, and then
saved over it, or, finding the microVM stopped by the first, failed and removed the
snapshot the first had saved, the stopped microVM's only copy. What a daemon's end cuts
short, a save or a removal, leaves a snapshot with no generation in place, whose name the
claim would hold, and whose files `list snapshots` would not show: the next daemon's start
removes it before it serves (`a_start_removes_snapshots_cut_short`, and on a real daemon
restarted, `checkpoint_command_lines_save_list_and_restore_microvms`, mutation-checked), and
a removal takes the pointer first, so that one cut short is never a snapshot a restore
would take.

A checkpoint directory of the client's (`--checkpoint-dir`, the API's `CheckpointDir`) is
refused, saying why: dockerd writes and lists checkpoints wherever its caller names, but
restores from none of them (`custom checkpointdir is not supported`, 403, which shards'
start answers too), so that its checkpoints move between microVMs and hosts only by
being copied into the one's own directory by hand. A microVM's snapshot is its devices as
they were, its disks and its interface's identity among them, which another microVM can
resume only with the same devices: a snapshot restored in another microVM, or on another
host, is part 6, which checks them. Held, on real microVMs, by
`checkpoint_command_lines_save_list_and_restore_microvms` (tests/saved.rs) and
`the_docker_cli_checkpoints_and_restores_microvms` (tests/engine.rs, the docker CLI
itself), and by docker/cli's own answers to the command lines (oracle_test.go).

**Moved to another machine** (part 6, roadmap item 7a). `shards move vm NAME CONTEXT`
moves a microVM to the machine a context reaches (D180): saved whole here, as `save vm`
saves it, and resumed there where it was saved. The context is the fleet: each machine's
daemon serves the clients it enrolled, and the move is a client of both, asking each for
its steps as `shards copy vm` asks for its own (cli/moves.rs; daemon/moves.rs: `save`, `ready`,
`export`, `import`, through the context's `MOVE_STEP` as its copy steps go), its stream
from the one daemon to the other through no file. Nothing of the one machine is the
other's but what the move sends, and what the other takes by content:

- **Its image, by digest.** The other machine finds it by the digest its name resolved to
  as the microVM was made, or pulls it from its registry by that digest (`repo@sha256:…`),
  converted as a run converts one; one no registry it reaches holds goes with the move,
  saved here and loaded there, and is given there the name it has here where nothing there
  has that name; a name that cannot be given, or a step unanswered, fails the move, resumed
  here (cli/moves.rs `name_there`). Both answers let go, a moved image was left unnamed there
  and the move said it had moved (`a_moved_microvms_log_and_image_go_with_it` on KVM, ROOT's
  run at 084891178), which step failed unsaid; that run's one other failure there was a
  context's handshake given up within the slowest seen (D180). Its request names it there by
  that digest, which no tag there can move.
- **The files its snapshot restores against**, each named relative to the home (its root
  filesystem by its image's ChainID, D18), checked byte for byte by SHA-256 on both machines
  before anything moves: those the other machine has alike are its own; those it lacks or
  has otherwise go with the move, into the microVM's own directory there. Its snapshot is
  then made to restore against them (`snapshot::relocate`), each file's identity the one
  there now, as a snapshot's state names its files by absolute path and identity (D14).
- **Its directory**: its record and request, its log, the snapshot it moves as and none
  other, its writable layer in the snapshot's generation (D190), never the copy its
  microVM left beside its log as it stopped.
- **Its volumes.** A named volume moves with it, as sparse as it is, where the other
  machine has no volume of the name, each file as its guest sees it, whatever either host
  keeps that in: Unix the guest's owner, group and mode in the share server's owner
  attribute beside the host's mode, and a device node it cannot make as an empty file the
  attribute names the kind of (D38); Windows WSL's `$LX` metadata and reparse points
  (D197); each its extended attributes under names of its own (Linux's `trusted.` and
  `security.` under `user.shards.`, Windows' as EAs of hexadecimal names). The move reads
  and makes each through the share server's own calls (`server::guest`: `read`, `set`
  and its makers), its stream (version 3) holding each entry's kind and mode, its device
  number, its owner where one is recorded (none where the host made it, so that it stays
  its share's default owner's, D38), its attributes by the guest's names, and its name as
  the guest's, which a Windows host keeps escaped as WSL escapes it; a directory takes its
  mode once all it holds is in it. So a volume moved between any two hosts shows its guest
  there what it showed it here, macOS's and Linux's attribute names, which differ, among
  them; a socket, its listener's, is left out, as tar leaves one. A file on Windows with a
  mode of WSL's alone is its share's default owner's, as on Unix, where WSL's metadata
  read as root's. Its restored share server takes the copy by its
  paths (`Server::restores_moved`, the share process's `--moved`): each node the file at
  its path there, whatever device and inode it had here, its guest's open handles and
  working directory in it going on. A bind's host path is the other machine's to share
  at the same place, as a network file system shares it, checked there before the move.
- **Its regular-file hardlinks** (migrate-05, 2026-11-13). Version 3 adds an entry naming
  an earlier regular file in volume data. The source's opened file supplies the share
  server's device/file-id and link count; only multiply-linked volume files retain a
  first-name record, for one stream, with fallible map/name growth. Both destination
  names must be allowed volume-data paths. `Beneath::make_hardlink` walks both parents
  through held directories, rejects a missing or non-regular source (including a
  symlink), and uses the existing Unix/NT `link_at` seam, never replacing a destination.
  No metadata or bytes are replayed for an alias: the inode's contents and attributes
  stay shared. POSIX.1-2024 `linkat` specifies shared identity and flags 0's no-follow
  behavior; the share server's LINK handler already uses that seam. Readers accept
  version 3 alone, as both ends of a move are one build's (D36): version 2's stream, read
  before beside it, is refused like any other version before extraction (legacy-audit,
  2026-11-14: `a_volumes_files_move_as_its_guest_saw_them` refuses versions 1, 2 and 4). Version/tag
  numbers are assigned grammar, path sizes retain the existing PATH_MAX bound, and
  link count greater than one is the host's alias fact, not a tuning choice. The red
  test `a_volumes_hardlinks_keep_shared_contents_after_move` failed at `73af9fb62`
  against the landed migrate-01 extractor. [Decision, tests and remaining platform/VM
  checks](../research/measurements/migrate/fix-review-2026-11-13.md).
- **Nothing it sends reaches out of the move's directory** (migrate-01, 2026-11-13). The
  machine moved to puts the stream's entries in a directory of the move's own
  (`private/move-…`), and a name that passes `relative` (no `..`, no root, no empty
  component) is not yet one that stays there: a link the stream made earlier is a way out.
  Until this, the placer joined each name to that directory and made it by path
  (`create_dir_all`, `open`, the share server's makers from the parent's path), every
  component followed: `LINK volumes/data/_data/out -> /some/dir` and then `FILE
  volumes/data/_data/out/new-file` made `new-file` in `/some/dir`, as the daemon's user
  (`a_streams_symlinks_never_lead_out_of_its_directory`, red at 9efde7252). Now each entry
  is reached from the move's directory held open, a component at a time, never through a
  symlink (`server::guest::Beneath`: openat(2) with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW`, as the share
  server's own `open_beneath` walks, each component checked a directory once open; on
  Windows NtCreateFile relative to its parent's handle with FILE_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT, which
  opens a junction as itself, refused as no directory), made there by its name and never over
  anything there (`O_CREAT | O_EXCL`), and given its metadata there. A symlink is data, made
  as its guest made it and never followed; what a stream names below one, or below a file, is
  refused, by an absolute or a relative target. And a symlink is taken only where a guest
  makes one, in a volume's files (`volumes/V/_data/…`, `holds_links`): shards makes none in a
  microVM's own directory or at the files its snapshot restores against, and the move's later
  steps (`adopt`: its record, `key-replaced` and request written, the files sent moved into
  `backing/`, a live move's rounds laid under its last save) reach those by their paths, where
  a link the stream put there would be followed. Held by that test (moves.rs, absolute and
  relative links, a file, directory, node and link below each, the outside left empty, and a
  link refused in the microVM's directory, at `key-replaced`, at a file its snapshot restores
  against, at a volume's `_data` and beside it) and `beneath_goes_through_no_symlink`
  (`server::guest`, every target). Not an
  archive of go-archive's (crates/archive), whose oracle is untouched: the move's stream is
  its own format (version 3; readers also take version 2).
- **Nor does any name it gives** (migrate-11, 2026-11-13). Beside its stream's entries, a
  move gives names the machine moved to makes paths of its home of: its plan's ID
  (`containers/ID`), its snapshot's (`containers/ID/snapshots/S`, which a live move's rounds
  are laid under and `snapshot::relocate` rewrites), its volumes' (`volumes/V`, renamed into
  place), and the volume names its record's mounts carry, each of which becomes the host
  directory its guest is shared (`volumes/V/_data`); and the machine it ran on joins the
  snapshot `done` names to its directory before `snapshot::remove`. None was checked, and
  `Path::join` takes `..` as it is and an absolute name as the whole path: a record mounting
  `/etc` would have had its guest shared `/etc/_data`, an ID of `../x` its directory
  outside `containers/`. Each is now one name of its kind (`Named::takes`), every rule from
  its own source: an ID as `containers::new_id` makes one, `2 × MICROVM_ID_BYTES` (32,
  moby's `stringid`) bytes in lowercase hex; a snapshot's one file's name by
  `synced::name_alone`'s Windows rules (Microsoft's "Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces"),
  the stricter, on every host, so that what one host takes every host takes; a volume's the
  local driver's (`Store::valid`, moby's validateName) and one file's name too, as the
  driver's rule takes a trailing dot and Windows' device names. Each refuses a separator,
  `.`, `..`, a root and a drive's colon, so none is more than one component; none is a
  chosen number (R03). A name that is not is refused typed (`Refused::NotAName`: the
  microVM, the field, the value), which the mover matches as it matches `ready`'s: `ready`
  checks the plan before anything else, `import` right after it reads the plan and before
  any entry is placed, `adopt` takes every name it joins through the same check
  (`one_name`), and `done` its snapshot before it resolves the microVM. `server::guest::Beneath`
  is not the seam for these: it places under a held root but renames nothing, and `adopt`'s
  steps are renames and reads by path, each now of one checked component. Held by
  `daemon::moves::tests::a_moves_names_are_each_one_name_of_their_kind` (each rule's
  takes and refusals) and `daemon::tests::a_moves_names_that_are_no_one_name_are_refused_typed_and_reach_nothing`
  (`ready`, `import` with a stream cut past its plan, `import` of a whole record whose mount
  names `../../x`, and `done`: each refused typed, the home's tree unchanged and no staging
  left), with a mutation of each check red (docs/bugs/2026-11-13/migrate.md, migrate-11).
- **Its CPU.** A restore on another CPU than its snapshot's is no longer refused where that
  CPU has every feature its guest found: the guest is told the CPU it found, each of its
  vCPUs given its snapshot's ID registers (HVF, KVM on arm64) or CPUID (KVM on x86_64),
  and goes on with the features it chose as it booted. One short of any is refused, naming
  each field it lacks (arm64's ID scheme, signed and unsigned fields as Linux reads them,
  `arch::aarch64::cpu`; x86's feature leaves, `cpuid::covers`). Hypervisor.framework says,
  and lets a VMM set, every ID register a snapshot keeps but ID_AA64ISAR2_EL1 and those
  after it, which it neither says nor sets (PM M460): an M5 Max's ISAR2 has CSSC and HBC,
  an M4 Max's not, and a guest booted on the M5 may have used them. So the move checks the
  two machines' CPUs as their OSes name their features (`hw.optional.arm.FEAT_*` but SVE's,
  SME's and MTE's, which no guest is shown; /proc/cpuinfo's flags or Features), refusing
  one to a machine lacking any the other has, before anything moves, naming each
  (`a_cpu_lacking_what_its_guest_may_have_used_is_named`, moves.rs).
- **Its connections**, dialed again by its init there as a restore here redials them
  (part 3), and its address on its network asked for again.
- **Its published ports**, bound again there as its restore starts it, as a start binds
  them (`publish::bind`: the host address its binding names, else its network's, else every
  one). The plan carries them as its run asked for them (`Plan::published`, `-p`'s own words,
  with its network), and the machine moved to binds each before anything moves, letting it
  go at once: a port another program holds there, or a run of its own, refuses the move
  (`Refused::PortTaken`), which goes on here, where it was refused only at the restore, after
  the whole stream. A binding with no host port, or a range, takes any free port of it there,
  as a start does. Its restore's bind stays what holds them, and fails the move should
  another program take one between. Two homes of one machine share its host ports, so their
  test publishes on a port each home picks (`a_moved_microvms_published_port_answers_there`);
  a fixed one is the two-host test's.
- **Its key, made anew where it lands and never carried** (decided by ROOT, 2026-11-13).
  A run's own key (D238: made by its host's daemon as its managed scope begins, held by its
  agent-control endpoint alone, its SHA-256 the `vm` line of the run's managed metadata) is
  its host's, and no private key leaves the host that made it. A restore there is a new run
  identity: its run makes a key of its own after the restore, as after every restore, since
  a key made before a snapshot would be every run restored from it (D238, "A key per run,
  never a template's"; D25's templates restore many runs from one). Step 33 issues a run's
  leases to its key and relies on that key unchanged for the run's life (kiln plan
  01a1d2b88be57304b972761e2a5c6781, steps 4 and 5), so the move replaces it: the leases
  bound to the old key are revoked at the move and reissued to the new, by the broker, which
  alone says which key is current. What the move does: its plan names the run's key where it
  ran (`Plan::key`); the machine moved to keeps it as the key replaced (the run's
  `key-replaced`, a fingerprint alone: none where the plan names none, nor what an earlier
  move kept in the directory sent); `move step key NAME [ASKED]` answers the run's key
  there and the one replaced (`key`, `replaces`: 64 lowercase hex digits, or null) and,
  asked under the replaced key, refuses typed (`Refused::KeyReplaced { asked, current }`,
  whose fields step 33's lease refusal takes); and `shards move vm` prints the microVM's
  name, then, where
  either is known, `{"name", "context", "key", "replaces"}` on a line of its own, for its
  controller to pin the new key and its broker to reissue its leases. Today a run with a
  managed scope is refused before anything moves (below), as a restore does not take a
  managed scope; the key side runs once one does, its restore making a new key and writing
  `vm` anew (D238). Held by
  `a_lease_under_the_key_a_move_replaced_is_refused_and_the_run_names_its_own` (moves.rs)
  and `a_managed_runs_move_and_a_lease_under_its_replaced_key_are_refused_typed` (daemon.rs,
  the daemon's own `key` step).
- **Refused before anything moves, by what refuses it** (R04). The machine moved to answers
  `ready` with a `Refused` (daemon/moves.rs) as JSON on stdout, beside its words on
  stderr, as any step's failure says them; the mover reads it typed (cli/moves.rs
  `unready`). It is one of: another architecture; another hypervisor
  (`Plan::hypervisor`, `hv::BACKEND`), whose own a snapshot's vCPUs, interrupt controller
  and devices are (KVM's x86-64 state is not WHP's, nor Hypervisor.framework's arm64 state
  KVM's), which a snapshot's head, naming its architecture alone, does not tell apart;
  another snapshot format; the fields of its CPU baseline this machine's hypervisor shows
  less of, each by register, field and both levels (`arch::aarch64::cpu::Short`); another
  CPU than the one it was saved on, where this machine's hypervisor restores a snapshot only
  on that one (WHP on x86-64, `Plan::cpu_identity`, D245); the
  features its guest may have used that this CPU lacks, by name; its ID, its name or a
  volume of its name here already; a bind's host path absent; a port it publishes that this
  machine cannot bind. Where the microVM runs, before it is saved: a run with a managed
  scope (`Refused::Managed`), which a restore does not take yet: a cold move's save would
  leave it stopped here, its resume refused too. Every field of `Plan` is in every plan
  (no `serde` defaults): one that lacks any, or holds one of another kind, is another
  build's, refused typed (`moves::plan_of`): `Refused::OlderInit` where its init's contract
  is not this machine's or unsaid, else `Refused::OtherPlan { name, saved_by, why }`. Held by
  `a_plan_missing_any_field_is_refused_typed` (moves.rs, red while the fields an earlier
  build's plans lacked defaulted, legacy5), and by
  `a_microvm_of_another_hypervisor_is_refused_before_anything_moves` and
  `a_refusal_is_typed_on_the_wire_and_says_what_it_said` (moves.rs),
  `a_move_of_another_hypervisors_microvm_is_refused_typed` and
  `a_managed_runs_move_and_a_lease_under_its_replaced_key_are_refused_typed` (daemon.rs, the
  daemon's own steps) and `a_refusal_is_said_from_its_type_and_else_in_the_steps_words`
  (cli/moves.rs); mutation-checked: without the hypervisor's check, `ready` took such a
  plan and answered what this machine lacked of it
  (docs/research/measurements/migrate/README.md).

What fails before it runs there leaves it here as it was, resumed from the snapshot it
was saved as, and what was made of it there removed: a move the other machine refuses
(another microVM has its name there) goes on here, its every count once. Held, on real
microVMs of two homes on one machine (one a context's machine to the other, as another
machine's is), by `a_running_microvm_moves_to_another_machine_and_goes_on_there` (a counter
appending to a file it holds open in its volume, from the volume's directory: each count

holds, saved and loaded) and `a_move_refused_leaves_the_microvm_running_here`
(tests/moved.rs); between two machines (run to another home of the same machine, each
passing on HVF and KVM, PM M462, and across two KVM x86-64 machines, PM M497; each skips,
saying so, where `SHARDS_MOVE_INVITE` names no machine) by `a_microvm_moves_to_another_host_saved_and_live`
(tests/moved.rs, to the machine whose invitation `SHARDS_MOVE_INVITE` names: saved, with a
volume and its image and files going with it, and live, a guest stamping 16 MiB as it moves)

item it carries, across two hosts, by
`a_microvm_moved_to_another_host_keeps_its_cpu_image_files_and_connections` (told the two
machines' CPU baseline, its guest's CPUs the same there; its image by its digest; the
snapshot it moved as alone, and no more files sent than it has; an exec and a stop's
SIGTERM there; a run with no key answered its name alone),
`a_volume_shared_here_moves_to_another_host_with_one_and_the_other_goes_on_here`,
`a_moved_microvms_published_port_answers_on_another_host` (at the port the machine moved to
bound, at its address; on `SHARDS_MOVE_PORT` where given) and
`a_move_another_host_cannot_take_is_refused_before_anything_moves` (another architecture or

here), written, not yet run (7a's step 5); with
the unit tests of `server::guest`, `server`'s `a_guests_files_show_it_the_same_copied_as_they_move`
and moves.rs's `a_volumes_files_move_as_its_guest_saw_them`, and to be measured there by
`docs/research/measurements/migrate/two-hosts.sh` (PM M460 its method).
Each check the move makes holds between two homes too:
`a_microvm_moved_saved_keeps_its_cpu_image_files_and_connections` (its CPUs as its guest
sees them the same there; its image pulled there by its digest though its name there tags
another; the snapshot it moved as and none other; of the files that snapshot restores
against, those the other lacked kept in its directory there, and no others; an exec run in
it there and a stop's SIGTERM ending it, its connections dialed again) and
`a_volume_shared_here_moves_with_one_and_the_other_goes_on_here` (a volume two microVMs share

leaves it appending on here). On WHP all of tests/moved.rs between two homes passes on CI's
windows-2025, saved moves with `a_volumes_guest_owners_move_with_it` among them and the live
move held refused, with every VM test required to run there (CI 42070454222 at 90de623f,
42134267973 at b8270370; windows-2022, whose WHP restores nothing, says SKIP for those that
restore, PM M345), and `server::guest`'s unit tests on every target.

Tested on CI's runners by `.github/workflows/migrate-e2e.yml`, run when asked: two-hosts.sh
`local` (two homes, 30 moves of each mode, then all of tests/moved.rs, between two homes and
to the listening home) on an x86_64 KVM runner, and on a macOS arm64 runner where it offers
Hypervisor.framework, which GitHub's own (macos-15) do not (`kern.hv_support` absent): its
job says so and moves nothing; n, p50, p90, p99 and max of what each move took and of the
time each ran nowhere in each job's summary. Between two runners, which take no connection
from each other and whose contexts speak QUIC over UDP, which no TCP tunnel carries, it
moves over a tailnet, where the repository has a Tailscale OAuth client
(`TS_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `TS_OAUTH_SECRET`); without one, that pair does not run. Between two
machines on one network, two-hosts.sh's own steps, its header saying each machine's in
order: the one moved to `listen`s at its default route's address, held in the background,
and makes an invitation for each of the other's tests (`invite`); the one moved from
`move`s N of each mode to it and runs the tests of another machine (`e2e`); then `stop`.
Whatever the network, the move is the context's: QUIC under TLS 1.3, each side's key pinned
by the other and the invitation's secret bound to the session (D180), the listening daemon
serving only the clients it enrolled.

**Over a slow link.** The first moves between two machines ran 2026-11-07, two M4 Max Mac
Studios joined by 2.4 GHz 802.11n Wi-Fi (about 1.3 MB/s in all; raw TCP carried 0.8 MB/s
beside the move's QUIC at 0.55 MB/s), cold, n 20, alpine:3.20. 18 moved: saved at about
0.11 s, ready there at about 0.2 s, `sent` at 65 to 248 s (94 s at p50), resumed 0.1 s
after. 2 ended mid-send, one "the connection ... ended: timed out", the other "reset by
peer", each going on here as it should. What changed for them:

- **A connection lives while it is heard** (`shards_remote::tls::QUIET`, net.rs
  `Liveness`). Both ends were QUIC's idle timeout (RFC 9000 §10.1), 10 s, the bound a
  client waits for a daemon's handshake (`IDLE`), which also ended a connection carrying a
  move whose peer went unheard that long: "timed out" its expiry here, "reset by peer" the
  other daemon's stateless reset (§10.3) of a connection it had let go at its own. Every
  packet the peer sends restarts it, each acknowledgment of the stream's bytes among them, so
  only silence ends it, and on this link a TCP connection rode out what 10 s of silence
  ended. An established connection's bound is now 100 s, RFC 1122 §4.2.3.5's floor for TCP
  giving up on data it has heard nothing of (R2, "at least 100 seconds"; Linux waits 924.6 s,
  ip-sysctl `tcp_retries2`); its handshake is still held to 10 s, by the driver, so that a
  client of an address no daemon answers at is told as soon as before
  (`no_daemon_answering_is_told_at_the_handshakes_bound`, tests/loopback.rs), as is a
  stranger that has not joined (server.rs). The keep-alives stay at a quarter of 10 s, as
  §10.1.2 has a peer that awaits an answer send PINGs, more often than the 30 s it finds
  most middleboxes keep a UDP flow's state for (since replaced, D180's "Its values
  derived": no idle timeout, each connection's liveness checked at use against the slowest
  answer seen on its path, its death a whole window with no progress, and keep-alives only
  where a connection on the path was found dead after a silence, or within an idle timeout a
  peer of an earlier build negotiated). A send's death in a whole window with no progress
  may end a move whose link goes silent longer than any answer its path has shown, as 10 s of
  silence ended 2 of these 20: that move goes on here as these did, its path's record marked,
  and the next move's connection starts as after a run-out (owed: the two-host Wi-Fi run under
  this build, ROOT's). No other deadline is on the stream's
  path: the CLI's pipes and the daemons' reads and writes block as the link lets them
  (cli/moves.rs, daemon/moves.rs, daemon/remote.rs `copy_step`); asking whether a restore
  with no answer runs there (below) is after the stream, and leaves the microVM held here,
  saved, saying so, never in two places.
- **Whether it runs there, its restore unanswered** (cli/moves.rs `running_there`; R03,
  2026-11-13). A restore there whose answer never came may have run, so the move asks the
  other machine whether the microVM runs (`inspect`) until it says: running, the move goes
  on; not, and gone there once removed, it goes on here; else not known, held here, saved,
  saying how to settle it. It asked twelve times, 5 s apart, figures of no derivation. How
  long and how often it asks are now that machine's own, as this move heard it, with no
  figure of shards':
  - *How long*: while that machine shows it is there. An ask that heard it, though
    unanswered (a connection it closed, its daemon stopping), is followed by another, however
    many; one that heard nothing too, until that machine has gone unheard (`Seen::heard`,
    the latest of its connections') longer than the longest it went unheard in this move and
    was heard again (`Seen::longest_silence`, the most of any connection the move made there:
    `ready`, the image's `load`, the import, the restore, these asks): its slowest answer.
    Not known then. An ask's handshake waits on while that machine has gone unheard no longer
    than that (`Heard::silent`, given `context::exec_with` as whether it waits), as a daemon
    whose last wait ran out has no handshake deadline of its own (D180), nor one whose
    handshake ran out past the slowest seen from it. The first ask goes out whatever that
    machine's silence, the wait after the restore's run-out following liveness alone, each
    ask held to the link's own bounds (its handshake's, then its liveness at use). The cold
    start, a move that heard nothing of that machine (none reaches this step, `ready` and the
    import having answered), ends at its first ask that hears nothing.
  - *A refusal* (`Answer::Refused`, typed on the wire): not known at once. That machine heard
    the ask and declined it (a client it no longer enrolls, a command it could not start);
    asking again asks it to decline again, nothing learned of when it would not, and a
    machine heard at each ask would be asked for ever.
  - *How often*: each ask begins a round trip after the last began, at least: the link's, as
    the connection that last heard that machine estimated it (RFC 9002 §5), the least time an
    answer takes. An ask that heard nothing waited out that machine's silence already, and one
    heard a round trip, so only one that failed here, before the link, waits.
  - *Its values' edges*: never heard, the silence is unbounded; the comparisons saturate
    (`Instant::elapsed`, `saturating_sub`), with no arithmetic to overflow. They are that
    machine's own showing, through connections authenticated both ways (D180): it can make a
    move ask longer, only while it is heard and never past its slowest answer of silence, and never make
    it take for an answer what it did not answer; not known keeps the copy held here. How long
    the asking runs on the links measured above is not measured: none of their moves left a
    restore unanswered.

  Held by cli/moves.rs's `a_move_learns_the_other_machines_slowest_answer_from_every_connection`,
  `the_other_machines_first_answer_says`, `a_machine_unanswered_is_asked_again_until_it_answers`,
  `a_machine_silent_past_its_slowest_answer_is_not_known` and
  `the_wait_takes_its_figures_from_the_link_alone` (asks a round trip apart; no number in its
  source but an answer's exit status), and net.rs's `Liveness::last_heard` in
  `a_connection_lives_while_it_is_heard_and_its_handshake_alone_is_held_to_its_bound`. Every
  move between two machines takes in each connection's `Seen` so
  (`a_microvm_moves_to_another_host_saved_and_live`, tests/moved.rs); no test leaves a restore
  unanswered, a fault case owed.
- **A restore refused at that machine's gate never ran there** (cli/moves.rs `resumed`;
  2026-11-13). That machine's daemon refuses a command before it starts it
  (`Answer::Refused`, typed on the wire): a client it no longer enrolls, words it refuses, a
  command it could not start (daemon/remote.rs `Machine::start`, shards-remote server.rs).
  The step's `there` flattened that refusal into its error, as it does an unanswered
  restore's, so it went to `running_there`, whose asks that machine refused too. A move
  whose restore was refused before it ran thus ended "not known", its copy held here.
  - The restore's answer now stays typed (`Asked`). Refused there, by its own failure or at
    the gate, what was made there of it is removed and the move goes on here. Only a restore
    left unanswered is asked about.
  - Held by `a_restore_refused_at_the_other_daemons_gate_goes_on_here`, with a fake `there`:
    red at e0cc059c7 (`NotKnown(..)` where `Here(..)` was due), green since, nothing asked
    of whether it runs there. A restore that failed, one done and one unanswered go as
    before. Green on the merged tree (origin/main 5bc134861 with 005dce1da; adas-mac-studio.local,
    macOS 26.2 arm64): cli/moves.rs's tests 7 of 7, clippy clean; its real two-machine move,
    refused at the gate, is not run (ROOT's).
  - *Refused before it started, or cut after* (ROOT's ruling, 2026-11-13). The remote
    server's relay can fail once `Host::start` has started a command (a thread or a handle
    it could not make; server.rs `relay`, or no listener's sender), and a frame out of place
    or cut short ends a command that runs; each was told `Tag::Refused`, which a move took
    for a restore that never ran, though it may have. Now the wire tells the two apart: a
    stream whose command started (`Stream::started`, set as `Host::start` answers) ends a
    refusal as `Tag::Cut` (42), and `Refused` says nothing of it ran. The client takes a cut
    for no answer (`exit_of`: "…, after the command started: it may have run"), as it takes
    a connection lost then, so a move asks whether it runs there (`running_there`), never
    going on here unasked. A client of an earlier build fails on tag 42 as on any frame it
    does not know, which is no answer too; a server of an earlier build still says
    `Refused` after a start, so both machines need this build.
  - Held by shards-remote's tests/loopback.rs `a_command_refused_after_it_started_is_cut` (a
    raw client starts `cat`, then sends a daemon's frame: red at af15d4532, `Refused` for a
    started command; green, `Cut`, and a stream whose command never started still
    `Refused`) and client.rs `a_cut_command_is_unanswered_and_a_refused_one_refused`.
- **What a move sends**, cold: the move's stream (`Writer`), its plan, then its directory
  but its other snapshots and its kept layer, its snapshot's state, memory, layer and swap
  among it; its volumes; and the files its snapshot restores against that the other machine
  lacks (none here: "0 of its 1 files sent", the image's root filesystem found there by its
  ChainID). Each file goes as the runs of it that hold data (SEEK_DATA), and its memory file
  holds only the pages its guest touched that are not all zeros (`GuestMemory::save`), so no
  untouched RAM and no zero page of RAM crosses; a run's zero pages of a layer or swap did,
  and nothing was compressed. A live move's rounds: every page not all zeros first
  (`each_used`), then each page written since, whole.
- **The stream packed for the link** (`crate::packing`): cut into frames of 1 MiB, each sent
  as zstd where that is smaller, else as it is, through shards-zstd (klauspost's encoder,
  which layers are compressed with) and read back by ruzstd, both already in the workspace;
  frames of 1 MiB of real logs keep 0.07 to 0.10 points more of their size than the whole
  compressed at once (PM M231).
  Compression overlaps the link and its effort follows what the link and the processor
  leave room for, as AdOC's does (Jeannot, Knutsson and Björkman, "Adaptive Online Data
  Compression", HPDC 2002: the slower the network, the slower and better the compressor;
  compressing before sending loses on a fast link). Here the level follows who waits: a
  frame for which the packer finds the queue of two ahead of the link full, and waits for
  the link longer than the next level took more to compress a frame as it last did (or
  that level untried), sends the next a level up, to klauspost's best; one the reader
  waited for, compressing having taken the packer longer than reading it, a level down, to
  none, as on a link faster than the compressor, where it stays, no wait of the packer's
  there covering a level's cost. Nothing is measured but the stream's own waits and its
  compressing. Every move's stream is packed: the machine moved to says it unpacks it
  (`Needs::unpacks`, `zstd`, a field every answer has) and is then asked `import --packed
  zstd`, which `import` requires. An answer without it, or one that does not unpack zstd, is
  another build's daemon's, refused typed before anything moves (cli/moves.rs `needs_of`,
  `OtherDaemon`); the send-as-it-is fallback for an earlier daemon, and `import`'s
  unpacked stream, are deleted (legacy5, the no-legacy rule). Likewise the move's `key` step,
  which every daemon of this build answers: one that fails is said ("NAME runs on CONTEXT,
  and its key there could not be read"), never taken as no key. Held by
  `a_packed_stream_reads_back_as_it_was`, `the_level_follows_who_waits` (packing.rs) and
  `a_needs_missing_unpacks_is_refused_typed` (cli/moves.rs).
- **Each move says what it sent and what the link did**, where `SHARDS_MOVE_TIMES` is set
  (`move: stream R bytes, sent W bytes, P of F frames as zstd; link A bytes acknowledged in
  T us, X B/s, rtt, packets lost, longest silence S us`), a failed move's too; two-hosts.sh
  records the bytes sent, the rate and the longest silence of every move, and a live move's
  rounds, with n, p50, p90, p99 and max.

- **Measured with this build** between two homes of a Mac Studio (M3 Ultra, PM M462), n 20
  each, every count once there: a cold move ran nowhere 1.09 s at p50 and 1.37 s at p90, its
  stream of about 83 MB sent packed as 21 to 33 MB, 55 to 69 of its 80 frames as zstd (on
  loopback the packer stays at zstd's levels, its reader seldom waiting on it); a live one
  0.28 s at p50 and 0.42 s at most, its rounds 4 at p50, ending with little left (12) or
  as they stopped shrinking (8).
- **A fresh home's first move** paid for the pinned guest inside its restore: a restore
  prepares its run's request as a start does (`run::prepare`), which downloads the pinned
  kernel where the home records none, 17 to 46 s of that p99 (the kernel's file in the
  home's `guest/` written the second the restore answered, PM M462), which a live move's
  microVM would wait running nowhere. The plan says whether its run boots the stored guest
  (`Plan::guest`, from its request: no kernel given), and the machine moved to fetches it as
  it readies, before the stream; a run given its kernel fetches none.
- **Between two Macs of different OSes, refused.** From the M3 Ultra (macOS 26.4) to an M4
  Max Studio (macOS 26.2), 38 of 40 moves were refused at `ready`, "this machine's CPU
  lacks FEAT_SSBS", each going on where it was (two more failed to reach the daemon there,
  and went on where they were too): macOS 26.4 names FEAT_SSBS on the M3 Ultra, 26.2 not on
  either M4 Max, which name FEAT_FPACCOMBINE, FEAT_WFxT and SME's features the M3 Ultra does
  not, so neither way is taken, as the check is meant to (PM M460, M462).
- **A CPU baseline**, for machines neither of which has every feature of the other.
  `shards configure cpu --baseline CONTEXT[,CONTEXT...]` asks this machine's daemon and each
  context's for its CPU as its own hypervisor shows a guest (`move step cpu`, which runs
  `shards-vm cpu`: a vCPU of a VM of no memory read, as the daemon is not entitled to the
  hypervisor) and keeps their meet in the home's `cpu-baseline`, each 4-bit ID-register
  field the lowest of them (`arch::aarch64::cpu::baseline`, `meet`: Linux's own rule across a
  system's CPUs, the Arm ARM's ID scheme; a signed field's 0xF the lowest). A setting of the
  home, as `configure guest` and `configure disk` are, not a flag of `run`: a microVM moves
  among the machines its home is told of, and `run`'s flags are Docker's. Each vCPU of a
  microVM booted there is told the lower of its host's fields and the baseline's
  (`Config::cpu_baseline`, `setup_vcpu`), its templates keyed by it (`run::template`), so
  that a baseline changed starts none from another's; `--none` takes it away and `shards
  inspect cpu` says it. Masked as a CPU model masks: a guest's kernel and programs use a
  feature only where a field says so, and an instruction a program runs regardless is not
  stopped. The run keeps what it was told in its directory (`cpu-baseline`), which moves
  with it, and a plan carries it (`Plan::baseline`): the machine moved to checks each field
  against what its own hypervisor shows (`covers`), not the machine it ran on's whole set;
  and by name only the features no register of the baseline can hide, on
  Hypervisor.framework ID_AA64ISAR2_EL1's, which it neither says nor lets a VMM set (PM
  M460, `feature_register`): FEAT_CSSC and FEAT_HBC. Its FEAT_WFxT and FEAT_RPRES the
  framework shows no guest where macOS names them (an M4 Max's guest finds no `wfxt`, an M3
  Ultra's and an M4 Max's no `rpres`, PM M499), so no move checks them, and the baseline
  test holds it on each Mac it runs on. A guest is shown less than the features macOS
  names in registers the framework does say too (an M4 Max's finds no `i8mm`, ISAR1's),
  which a baseline's fields, the hypervisors' own views, take in. On KVM x86-64 too (D245):
  CPUID's feature leaves, one vendor's, each register the bits every machine's KVM offers
  (`arch::x86_64::cpuid::meet`), the VM's supported CPUID brought within it before its
  shape is written in (`cpuid::within`), and checked by those bits alone, none by name.
  Not on WHP x86-64, which restores a snapshot only on the CPU it was taken on: `configure
  cpu` says so there, and a move checks that CPU before anything moves (D245). Between the
  two Linux hosts measured (one CPU model, Linux 7.2 and 7.3)
  every move went through without one (PM M497).
- **A listener that outlives its runner's restarts** (two-hosts.sh, the harness of these
  measurements). A runner that restarts ends what its runs started, the listening daemon
  among them, and kiln's ends a launchd job a session starts within seconds (3 s on the M3
  Ultra, PM M499), so no process of a run outlives it there. What does is the listening
  home: `listen` run again on it listens as the same daemon, its key and the clients it
  enrolled kept, inviting none, and the mover's series waits for it (`WAIT_PEER`), moving
  again a move whose error says the daemon was gone (`PEER_GONE`), counted apart from the
  failures; a hold restarts a daemon that ends while it lives. `two-hosts.sh restart` holds
  it on one machine (PM M499).

Between two machines on a wired gigabit link (two AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 hosts, Linux 7.3.3
to 7.2.9, KVM), n 20 cold: a move took 0.95 s at p50, 1.16 at p90 and 9.99 at most, and
ran nowhere 0.91 s at p50, 1.12 at p90 and 9.89 at most, the most the fresh home's first,
its image fetched as it readied, moves 2 to 20 at 1.26 s at most; its stream of about 81
MB sent as 33 to 76 MB at up to 110 MB/s; and tests/moved.rs's two tests of another
machine passed across them (PM M497). Not yet measured: the Studios' slow Wi-Fi with this
build (193 kB/s on 2026-11-08, their kiln runners restarting within the hour, each ending
the listening daemon its run held, PM M462), the levels packing settles at there, and the
longest silence each connection lived through, which says whether 100 s is enough.

**Where part 6 stands** (roadmap item 7a, 2026-11-13). Built, as above, with each step's
unit tests and clippy run on one host as it landed; its record, and its account against
R01-R16, are docs/research/measurements/migrate/README.md. Run on real microVMs: between
two homes on KVM x86-64 (PM M497), on KVM arm64 in the nested L1 guest (the parity audit's
row 16), on Hypervisor.framework (PM M462, M497) and on WHP x86-64 (CI's windows-2025 and
jupiter, rows 14 and 16); between two machines, KVM x86-64 from adacachy2 to adacachy
(PM M497), and between two Macs the refusals of a CPU lacking a feature (PM M460, M462).
Owed, the record's run sheet: the tests of another machine for each item a move carries,
on KVM x86-64 both ways, between two Macs with a baseline, and WHP x86-64 to KVM refused;
`light-gate.sh`'s mutants M11-M15; the key made anew where a run lands and named in the
move's answer, once a restore takes a managed scope (D238); between two Linux arm64 KVM
hosts and from Windows arm64, no machines here.

**Moved live** (part 7, roadmap item 7b). `shards move vm --live NAME CONTEXT` moves it as
it runs, by pre-copy (Clark et al., "Live Migration of Virtual Machines", NSDI 2005): its
memory, writable layer and run's swap copied to the other machine as its guest runs on,
round after round, each round what its guest and its devices wrote since the last, until
pre-copy no longer pays (`live::Stop`); then it saved as a save saves it, held, its
vCPUs parked and devices quiet, what its guest wrote of those three since the last round
sent as the rounds' last, in their stream, which the other machine lays over the rounds
page by page as each came; resumed there; and stopped here once it runs there.

- **Host copies survive unplug** (review memory-02, 2026-11-13): a live RAM
  record is copied under GuestMemory::Access into owned bytes, no larger than the
  existing wire record limit or a hotplug block. The hold ends before stream
  output; unplug may then withdraw the mapping without invalidating output bytes.
  A returned page is also owned. Red/green and outstanding VM validation:
  `docs/research/measurements/memory-fixes-v1/README.md`.

- **Host-reader lifetime and lost mappings** (reviews memory-03/05): save and
  precopy own one typed reader guard; teardown waits until it is dropped, including
  errors. Mapped-file reads hold the same owner as release and APFS mapping
  withdrawal. A scan resumes only intact mappings; loss is a terminal VM error.
  Focused red tests and remaining live fault-injection gates are recorded in
  `docs/research/measurements/memory-fixes-v1/README.md`.

- **When the rounds stop**, never by the clock, whatever the link's rate. A round sends what
  was written as the round before it went, so its bytes over that round's time are the
  guest's rate of writing, and the round before's bytes over the same time the link's: the
  rounds stop at the first that sends no fewer bytes than the one before, the guest writing
  as fast as the link carries, where another round would leave the last save as much (Clark
  et al. §4.1: the hottest pages "will be dirtied at least as fast as we can transfer them,
  and hence must be transferred in the final stop-and-copy phase"; §6.5, a guest writing
  faster than the network carries, suspended once its rounds did not outpace it). Also at
  the first that sends no more than 8 MiB, little being left (§5.3 stops under 256 KB, Xen's
  xc_domain_save under 50 pages); once the rounds have sent three times the first, all its
  memory held (Xen's `DEF_MAX_FACTOR`, "never send more than 3x"); and at 30 rounds, Xen's
  own (`DEF_MAX_ITERS`, "limit us to 30 times round loop"). Rounds that each shrink end, as
  each is fewer bytes than the one before. Until 2026-11-07 they stopped at 8 MiB or 30
  rounds alone: the first live move between two Macs over 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi at 0.55 MB/s, its
  guest rewriting a 1 MiB file every 50 ms (two-hosts.sh), had not finished after 30 minutes,
  its rounds' bytes unsaid, as a move said them only once they ended (not measured). The
  move's log says each round (`move: round N: pages, bytes, us`) and then their count, their
  bytes and why they stopped (`move: rounds N, B bytes, ended: ...`), which two-hosts.sh
  records; held by `precopy_stops_once_its_rounds_no_longer_shrink` (live.rs), each rule
  and the guest of that move among its cases. A live move's stream is packed for its link as
  a cold one's is (part 6), its rounds' bytes counted before. Between two homes of a Mac
  Studio with this build, n 20, that guest's rounds numbered 4 at p50 and 6 at most, round 0
  about 60 MB and each later one 9 to 19 MB, 12 ending with little left and 8 as they
  stopped shrinking; it ran nowhere 0.28 s at p50, 0.37 at p90 and 0.42 at most, its last
  save 83 to 228 ms of it (PM M462). Between two wired machines (PM M497), n 20: it took
  0.71 s at p50 and 1.03 at most, and ran nowhere 0.21 s at p50, 0.28 at p90, 0.35 at p99
  and at most, in 2 or 3 rounds, each ending with little left, its last save 51 to 161 ms
  and its last stream 9 to 41 ms of it. Not yet measured: its rounds over a slow link and
  the time it runs nowhere there.
- **Its rounds told as they go** (`Precopying`, `kind::PRECOPYING`): the VM tells its
  daemon each round as it ends, and within a round each further 8 MiB (the bytes a last
  round may send, at least a record's 1 MiB) its stream's carrier has taken, counted as it
  takes them (`Carried`, held by `a_rounds_stream_tells_what_it_carried_as_it_goes`); the
  daemon says each in the move's answer and in its log (`move: round N: ...`, `move:
  carried B bytes of its rounds`), so that what waits on a move follows its progress, never
  a clock (D209): a test's client is waited on past its deadline while its home's daemon
  says something within a minute (tests/common `Said`). At the slowest link measured,
  0.55 MB/s, 8 MiB is 15 s of it. Until 2026-11-07 a move said its rounds only once they
  ended: on step 10's arm64 Windows host, nested under QEMU's TCG, the guest stamping 64 MiB
  as it moved (`a_microvm_writing_its_memory_moves_live_with_none_of_it_lost`, build
  b8c98e7f, its rounds then bound by 8 MiB and 30 rounds alone) was killed at 120 s, its
  daemon silent for the minute before, though the WHP Arm64 backend's dirty bitmaps
  (`WHvQueryGpaRangeDirtyBitmap`, 4 KiB pages, as x64's) feed the same loop and its rounds'
  bytes are counted as every backend's are.

- **The last round in the rounds' stream**, record by record, never in the last save's
  files, which keep none of their pages: which pages a file holds read from its holes is
  its file system's unit, not the page written. NTFS keeps a sparse file's data in
  compression units, 64 KiB for sparse files ([MS-FSA] Appendix A, note 4; the unit
  `deallocation_unit` gives back), so a page written into a hole makes its whole unit data,
  the rest zeros. Laid from the last save's files, each page its guest wrote last brought
  60 KiB of zeros over what the rounds sent: on CI's windows-2025, the first WHP run, the
  restored guest's pmem queue was found zeroed ("driver published 65535 new buffers on a
  queue of 64"), its guest hung, and the move's restore never answered. Linux's file
  systems and APFS keep 4 KiB blocks, a page each, so KVM and Hypervisor.framework moves
  never met it. The last save's spawner hands it the stream again with its files
  (`SAVE_DELTA`'s last descriptor); its VM writes the last round and the stream's end
  before it answers, and the move's files follow.

- **What its guest writes**, watched by the hypervisor as it runs, through one interface
  every backend gives the pre-copy loop (`Vm::watch_writes`, `written`, `unwatch_writes`;
  `vm/runtime.rs` `precopy`):
  - On KVM x86_64, its vCPUs' dirty rings (api.rst 8.29; `KVM_CAP_DIRTY_LOG_RING_ACQ_REL`,
    else `KVM_CAP_DIRTY_LOG_RING`), a page of the host's for each vCPU, each writable
    memory slot's writes logged while the move watches, each vCPU whose ring fills emptying
    it as it exits.
  - On KVM arm64, and on an x86_64 KVM that keeps no rings (before Linux 5.11), each
    writable slot's dirty bitmap (`KVM_MEM_LOG_DIRTY_PAGES`, read by `KVM_GET_DIRTY_LOG`
    each round, api.rst 4.8), which every KVM has: without
    `KVM_CAP_MANUAL_DIRTY_LOG_PROTECT2` enabled, KVM clears each bit it gives and takes its
    page away for writing again before it answers (virt/kvm/kvm_main.c,
    `kvm_get_dirty_log_protect`), so a write after the read is in the next. Not arm64's
    rings: its GIC's ITS writes its tables and its LPIs' pending state into guest memory as
    a save writes them, with no vCPU's ring to note them in, which a ring needs KVM's bitmap
    beside it for (`KVM_CAP_DIRTY_LOG_RING_WITH_BITMAP`, api.rst 8.40, Linux 6.3); a slot's
    bitmap takes every write, a vCPU's or KVM's own (`mark_page_dirty_in_slot`), the ITS's
    in the last save's among them, read after it. The manual protect (api.rst 7.18), which
    clears bits apart from reading them and spares the write protect of a whole slot as the
    watch begins, is a cost the move has not measured yet, not a need. A slot deleted as it
    is watched has its bitmap read first; one whose bitmap cannot be read counts whole as
    written. Each bit is a host page, given the loop as the 4 KiB units it sends.
  - On Hypervisor.framework, its writable memory taken away for writing at stage 2
    (`hv_vm_protect`) and each page given back whole as its guest writes it, noted, the
    working-set recorder's mechanism (D25), with which it shares the one stage 2: what a page
    of each region has until its guest faults on it is the two's together (`Watch::rest`),
    nothing while a working set is recorded, all but its writes while the move watches them,
    else all of it, put back as either starts or ends, under both locks (the recording's,
    then the watch's, as each fault takes them). Until 2026-11-13 a recording's end gave the
    guest all its memory back whatever watched it (migrate-02): a warm run's recording, ended
    by its timer (D25) as a live move's rounds ran, left every page writable unwatched, its
    writes in no round and not in the last save, the restored guest finding the bytes it had
    before; and a watch begun within a recording gave the guest reads of pages the recorder
    had taken away. Held on the framework by `vcpu_and_gic_state_round_trip_through_a_fresh_vcpu`
    (hv::hvf, the crate's one test with a VM): a guest's read within a recording the watch
    began in is recorded, and a page it writes after a recording ended, the watch begun
    within it or it within the watch, is `written` each time (red at 9efde7252: none was).
  - On WHP, its dirty page tracking (`WHvCapabilityCodeFeatures`' DirtyPageTracking): each
    writable range the partition maps mapped again in place with
    `WHvMapGpaRangeFlagTrackDirtyPages` as the watch begins, as WHvMapGpaRange "replaces
    any previous mappings for the specified GPA pages" (Microsoft Learn), so its guest never
