  | gelf | 128 chunks over UDP, compressed as asked | the protocol: GELF's "MUST NOT consist of more than 128 chunks" |
  | gelf over TCP | what the destination has taken, learned from its refusals | first Graylog's documented `max_message_size`, 2 MiB (GELF states none); then each connection its receiver ends on a message (Graylog's input, past its bound), that message sent again cut |
  | fluentd | what the destination has taken, learned from its refusals | first Fluent Bit's documented `buffer_max_size`, 6,144,000 bytes (the forward protocol states none); then an event acked on no connection (Fluentd's `chunk_size_limit`, Fluent Bit's bound), cut again by the shipper, or without acks a connection its receiver ends on an event, that event sent again cut |
  | journald | the host's journal's LineMax | its configuration as journald reads it, as shards runs; journald.conf(5)'s 48K where none sets it |
  | splunk | what the destination has taken of a post, learned from its refusals | first HEC's documented `max_content_length`, 838,860,800 bytes; then each post answered 413 (RFC 9110 15.5.14), posted again in smaller posts, an event alone cut in halves |
  | awslogs | 1,048,550 bytes as CloudWatch counts them | the API: PutLogEvents' 1 MB event |
  | gcplogs | 256 KiB of entry, as JSON | the API: Cloud Logging's LogEntry size |
  | oslog | what the host's log keeps whole, read back as the daemon runs | entries of its own written and read back from its process's log store (OSLogStore, current process), by halves below os/log.h's stated 1,024-byte cap, which a line goes in parts of where the store cannot be read |
  | etwlogs | the listening sessions' | their answers as shards runs (ERROR_MORE_DATA, ERROR_ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW): first ETW's stated 64 KB less an EVENT_HEADER, then narrowed between the longest all took and the shortest refused; a line no session took sent again in halves |

  A bound the measurements show (M492, M494) validates the method; none is kept as a
  number. What a destination has shown (the longest message it took, the shortest it
  refused) is kept in the home, a file a destination in `log-bounds/`
  (`daemon/ship/learned.rs`), so that a daemon started again starts from it; only a
  refusal narrows it, the next message's most halfway between the two, and the file,
  removed, starts it again.

  A receiver's end of a connection says nothing alone of what it took. Some end one on a
  message they will not take (Graylog's GELF input, Fluent Bit's forward input past its
  `buffer_max_size`), Fluentd's in_forward with `deny_keepalive` after every message it
  handles, taken or dropped ("conn.close", fluentd v1.19.0 in_forward.rb
  `handle_connection`; one past its `chunk_size_limit` is dropped and the connection closed
  alike), and a restart or a network's drop ends them whatever their messages. So the
  stream asks, by evidence, once a connection ends with messages held (stream.rs
  `Asking`), each answer a message alone on a connection of its own:
  - fluentd's first: a Forward-mode message of no events, `[tag, []]` (Forward Protocol
    Specification v1, Forward Mode), which no bound refuses, in_forward emits as a stream
    of nothing and Fluent Bit ingests as no entries. Its connection ended cleanly after it
    shows a receiver that ends one after every message: the oldest held, where it was the
    ended connection's first, it took, and from then on each message goes alone on a
    connection of its own, its clean end after it delivering it (a reset does not), until a
    connection is found open after one. Without acks nothing shows such a receiver refuse
    a message, and none is cut. Its connection open after it, the receiver ends none after
    every message;
  - then the oldest held, resent unchanged: had and not ended on, it is delivered and
    messages go together again; ended on twice, longer than any the destination took,
    while a shorter message (the message of nothing, or one delivered) was had and not
    ended on, it is refused, and cut. gelf and syslog have no message of nothing: there a
    shorter one delivered shows it, and where none has gone the two ends alone do;
  - with acks, fluentd's ack is the evidence: an event is refused only where it went first
    on two connections of its own and neither acked it, a missing ack on a connection its
    receiver may have ended after its last ack sending it again at once on one of its own.

  Messages wait to be written, one at a time, while it is asked, the sender waiting on the
  answer, so that none waits in memory past what its receiver has. The ends are a FIN, a
  reset, or over TLS its close_notify, read from the records as they
  come (RFC 8446 §6.1: its sender "will not send any more messages on this connection"),
  which comes before its FIN and which a peek at the TCP socket read as bytes sent; and
  over a unix socket as over TCP. A message the shipper has not yet given up is cut again
  by it (`ErrorKind::FileTooLarge`), its parts' places its own; one already written that a
  stream holds is cut again by its driver.

  A fluentd event cut so keeps its line's identity. The forward protocol names none of an
  event's: its one ID is `chunk`'s, "an ID of a set of events", and a server sent one
  "MUST respond `ack`" (Forward Protocol Specification v1, Option and Response), so
  without acks there is none. A line's parts are joined by their records' own fields,
  moby's `partial_id`, `partial_ordinal` and `partial_last`: fluent-plugin-concat gathers
  them by tag and `partial_id`, sorts them by `partial_ordinal` and joins them at the part
  whose `partial_last` is true (filter_concat.rb at b8583840). So the pieces of an event
  that was a line's part go under its line's `partial_id` in its place: the first takes
  its ordinal, each the next, every part of the line after it goes as many places later
  (those held written again so, the shipper's still to come numbered so), and the last
  piece is the last part where the event was. What the receiver had of the line stands,
  and the line it joins is the line, where the pieces under an ID of their own had left
  it a part short. A whole line cut so goes as a line of its own ID.

  moby's copier cuts every line past 16 KiB whatever its receiver takes (copier.go,
  defaultBufSize), a character in two among them: a syslog receiver that takes 8,192
  octets cuts its parts short, an ETW session of logman's default buffers loses each
  whole, and Fluent Bit's, journald's and CloudWatch's take lines whole that Docker cut.
  A receiver that joins Docker's parts by their fields joins shards'. Cutting costs the
  shipper (M494): a part that fits as its driver's part says is written once, as moby's
  are (a 1 MiB line in 3.5 ms over gelf's UDP, 0.85 ms in 16 KiB parts). One whose
  message as written is not in a fixed ratio to its line (gelf's UDP datagrams by gzip) is
  cut where the ratio of written bytes to the line's, the last a part showed and as far
  again as it last moved, says the bound is reached, and grown once by its own ratio where
  there is room: written once to three times a part, where finding the longest by halves
  wrote it some 18 times (0.48 s a MiB of random bytes, M494). A driver that says only
  whether a message fits is cut by halves.
- **Delivered, not written** (`daemon/ship/stream.rs`, PM M233). Over TCP, TLS or a unix
  stream socket, a message counts as sent only once its receiver has it and has not ended
  the connection on it.
  - Over TCP, its receiver has it once its TCP has acknowledged its last byte, as the
    kernel counts them: Linux's SIOCOUTQ, macOS's TCP_CONNECTION_INFO, Windows'
    SIO_TCP_INFO, whose BytesOut counts the bytes sent again too (PM M373): there the
    bytes written less `BytesOut − BytesRetrans − BytesInFlight`, BytesRetrans's 32 bits
    counted past their wraps, the FIN while FIN_WAIT_1, CLOSING or LAST_ACK. A unix
    socket's bytes are in its receiver's buffer as they are written; on Windows an AF_UNIX
    stream's (afunix), Windows having no AF_UNIX datagrams: a `unixgram` address is
    refused there as its run is made, in shards' words.
  - A receiver that ends a connection on a message it will not take has had its bytes,
    its TCP acknowledging them as it reads. So a message is let go of only once the
    connection is found open the kernel's RTO after its receiver was first seen to have it
    (RFC 6298: the time within which the kernel takes what it sent to have been answered),
    and a unix socket's RFC 6298's least, 1 s, a unix socket having no round trip of its
    own; an end found before is followed. Nothing gelf or forward without acks sends says
    more: neither answers a message, and their receivers end connections on those they
    refuse. With acks, fluentd's ack says its receiver has it (D165).
  - The shipper keeps its place only as far as what is delivered. So a daemon that stops
    or dies costs sending again what was not yet delivered, and loses no line.
  - What a connection had not delivered when it ended (a reset, a receiver that
    restarts, a timeout after a partition) is held, and written again, in order, on the
    next. srslog, go-gelf and fluent-logger-golang lose it.
  - An end that a write meets before the stream finds it is followed as one it finds
    (PM M527). A write after its receiver's end meets EPIPE, on a unix socket at once and
    over TCP once the reset its first write drew has come; one under way as its receiver
    ends meets EPIPE or a reset. The stream then does as it does finding a reset: what the
    connection held goes again in its place, the message being written among it once the
    connection carried messages (over TLS, its handshake done), and the end is asked of
    and said as any other (`ConnectionAborted`). Whether any of that message went is not
    asked: macOS's write(2) that put part of it on the connection and then met the end
    says the error alone, where Linux's says the part. A receiver that ends a connection
    once more than its bound has come ends it on a message still being written wherever
    the connection holds less than the message: Fluent Bit's forward input closes one as
    its buffer is full at `buffer_max_size` (fluent-bit f5a3cd20,
    plugins/in_forward/fw_conn.c, `fw_conn_event`), and a connection took 2,720,256 bytes
    over loopback TCP on Linux before its writer waited, 1,465,848 on macOS, 233,152 and
    12,288 over a unix socket. Such a message had been its caller's to give again, never
    held, so never shown refused nor cut, and its run's log stopped there; and the close
    said the write's own error, `Broken pipe`, which CI's unit tests met (runs
    43183804136, 43189239973, 43250570050). A write its timeout gave up stays its
    caller's: the stream's own wait, not its receiver's end.
  - A connection ends only once nothing is held: what is held is written on one where
    there is none and waited on until it is delivered, so that a receiver's end after the
    stream's is its answer to it, and one before it is followed as any other: the close
    says so (`ConnectionAborted`) and is tried again, the driver cutting what connections
    end on. So a run's last message, refused at close, is sent again cut before the
    shipper ends, where gelf's and fluentd's without acks were lost; the shipper's end
    waits on its receiver's TCP and its end, and on no time of its own. Then the
    connection ends once its receiver has all of it:
    - TLS's close_notify is sent;
    - its write side is shut;
    - what the receiver still sends is read and let go;
    - the socket closes once all is acknowledged and the receiver has ended its side, as
      Winsock's graceful shutdown closes ("Graceful Shutdown, Linger Options, and Socket
      Closure", Microsoft Learn: the peer's FD_CLOSE before closesocket).

    A socket closed with bytes unread resets its connection, and what is not yet sent
    goes with it. TLS 1.3's session tickets are such bytes: no sender that only writes
    reads them. D163's first CI lost a run's last line this way, held back by Nagle's
    algorithm behind the line before it, on every x86_64 Linux run; the probe loses it in
    200 of 200 rounds on Linux and 90 of 200 on macOS. Docker's drivers close their
    sockets this way. Acknowledged is not read: a receiver's TCP acknowledges what its
    program has yet to read, and a reset, which a close also sends where the receiver's
    bytes come after it, takes on Windows all its receiver had not read. CI 40900902805's
    windows-2025 lost a TLS stream's one line so, its receiver's session tickets come after
    the sender's last read; `a_stream_ends_once_its_receiver_has_ended_its_side`, whose
    receiver sends after the sender's end, read nothing 3 times of 3 on jupiter with the
    close once acknowledged, and all of it 3 of 3 with the close at its end.
  - A receiver's TCP having a message is as far as TCP can say. fluentd's acks (D165)
    say its receiver has it.
- **Messages as Docker's driver sends them** (logging/testdata/syslog.json). Its formats (srslog's Unix format, rfc3164, rfc5424,
  rfc5424micro), its facilities, info for stdout and err for stderr, the tag (the short ID
  unless given), its framing (newlines, octet counting over TLS for RFC 5424), and udp,
  tcp, tcp+tls, unix, unixgram and the host's own syslog. All are held byte for byte to
  Docker 29.3.1's (`scripts/logdrivers/generate`: 25 transport, format and facility
  cases, recorded in shards-dind, and which options Docker takes).
- **Where Docker is wrong, shards is not.** Each difference is recorded, in the oracle's
  test where it has one:
  - a message is stamped with when its output came; srslog stamps when it sends;
  - it names this host; srslog names its socket's local address and port, which no RFC
    5424 HOSTNAME is;
  - its tag fills its fields: RFC 5424's APP-NAME and MSGID are printable ASCII of at most
    48 and 32 characters, and a space would end either format's tag early;
  - a datagram socket's send buffer grows to each message, since macOS takes none longer
    than it (PM M232). A line whose datagram its receiver refuses for its size goes in
    halves, down to RFC 5426's 480 octets. moby drops it;
  - nothing is dropped: a send that fails is sent again, and what a connection had not
    delivered goes on the next;
  - `syslog-tls-skip-verify` is refused, its CA asked for instead: shards sends only to a
    server whose certificate it verifies;
  - `unix://host/path` is refused. Go's parser takes `host` for a host, and moby's driver
    drops it.
- **The local copy.** A driver that sends its log elsewhere keeps it in the store too, as
  Docker's dual logging does.
  - `cache-max-size`, `cache-max-file` and `cache-compress` bound it. Docker takes them and
    applies none: its cache is the local driver with its defaults
    (loggerutils/cache.WithLocalCache passes the options unchanged).
  - `cache-disabled=true` keeps it from `logs`, which says so. The segments wholly sent go.
  - Every driver takes the `cache-*` options, as Docker's do; D161 refused them.
- **`inspect`'s LogPath** is empty, as dockerd leaves its local driver's: shards' store is
  its own, no file a reader of Docker's json-file logs could read.
- **Segments filled.** A record fills the room its segment has, the rest going on in the
  next. D161's rule moved a record that did not fit whole into the next segment. On CI's
  x86_64 Linux, whose guest's records are 32 KiB, that left segments of 64,000 bytes half
  full and a log half its retention; D162's test caught it there.
- **Not yet.** awslogs, gcplogs and etwlogs, each refused with a word that says so; gelf,
  fluentd, journald and splunk came with D164 to D167.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_log_is_sent_to_syslog_as_its_options_say`):

- UDP in srslog's format;
- TCP in rfc5424micro and local0, its time `logs -t`'s to the microsecond and its host a
  name;
- TLS with a CA made for the test, octet-counted, its connection ended cleanly with
  close_notify;
- a unix datagram socket, a 40,000-byte line in 16,384 + 16,384 + 7,232;
- a server that comes up only after the run, and one up only after the daemon restarted;
- `cache-disabled`, `logs` refusing it;
- the refusals, and an empty LogPath.

Unit tests cover:

- every message of the oracle, byte for byte;
- the options, against what Docker takes;
- addresses, ports and tag fields;
- the copier's cuts;
- the shipper's place, kept only as far as its receiver has the messages before it, and a
  reader resumed from it showing every line once;
- a TLS stream closed at once after its last writes, its receiver's session tickets
  unread, delivering all of them and ending with close_notify (mutation-checked: closed
  at once, its receiver sees a reset);
- what a connection reset by its receiver had not delivered, written again on the next,
  in order, before what comes after (mutation-checked: what is held dropped fails it);
- the segments wholly sent going;
- over TLS, a receiver's close_notify found as its end as the stream settles, no write
  failing (mutation-checked: read as bytes sent, no end is found);
- over a unix socket, messages held until delivered and a receiver that ends connections
  on one pointed at, as over TCP (mutation-checked: an end never found);
- gelf over TCP, a run's last message its receiver ends connections on, sent again cut
  before the close ends (mutation-checked: the close taking that end for its answer
  loses it);
- fluentd without acks, over TCP, TLS and a unix socket, a line's middle part refused at
  close and one refused before its last part is sent: every part within the receiver's
  bound, the line rebuilt whole by its places under its one ID (mutation-checked: pieces
  under an ID of their own leave it a part short).
- fluentd over TCP, TLS and a unix socket without acks, and over TCP with them, to a
  receiver that ends a connection after every message it takes (in_forward's
  `deny_keepalive`, its ack written first): whole lines and a line's three parts, one of
  3,000 bytes, all received as sent, nothing cut and nothing learned refused, the
  receiver found to end one after each message (mutation-checked: without the message of
  nothing, the ends are never told from refusals and the close never ends).

### D162. A run's rotated log segments compressed, seekably; a log that never holds up its run

D162 serves two of Docker's log options that D161 refused, `compress` and
`mode=non-blocking`, and serves both better than Docker does.

- **`compress`: rotated segments, seekable.** The daemon's packer thread compresses each
  segment once it has rotated. That thread is off every run's path, and off the files'
  thread that makes the segments runs wait for (D161).
  - Each segment becomes zstd frames of 1 MiB of it, each compressed alone at
    klauspost's best level. Their seek table follows, as zstd's seekable format lays it
    out (facebook/zstd contrib/seekable_format, v0.1.0). The file is `log.N.zst`, beside
    the segment's index, which stays as written.
  - Real logs come to 7.63% of their size, against 9.20% for Docker's gzip of each whole
    rotated file (PM M231).
  - A reader (`logs`, and its `--tail`) reads any record by decompressing its frame
    alone, 1.7 ms at most, its checksum checked. Docker decompresses a whole rotated file
    into a temporary file to read any of it. `zstd -d` reads the file whole.
- **Whole on every path.**
  - The compressed file is made durable before the segment as written goes, so a reader
    finds one or the other whole. It looks for the one as written first.
  - Retention removes either. A segment removed as it is compressed leaves nothing, and
    a microVM being removed is left to its removal.
  - As a daemon starts, it compresses what one before it left as written, including a
    file a crash left half compressed. The run's record says which logs compress
    (`log_compress`).
- **Which logs.**
  - `shards`, shards' own driver, compresses by default: 13 times less disk, for at most
    184 ms of a thread a 20 MB segment (PM M231). So does `local`, as Docker's default
    does.
  - json-file compresses only when asked: uncompressed is what the name means to its users. Its `compress=true` without
    `max-size` is taken: Docker refuses it for want of a bound, and shards' store always
    has one.
  - One file (`max-file 1`) never rotates, so it is never compressed. Asking for that is
    refused in shards' words.
- **`mode=non-blocking`.** The run's output is queued in its VM for the log's own thread,
  so a log that falls behind never holds up the run's output.
  - The queue holds at most `max-buffer-size` bytes (go-units' RAMInBytes, binary units),
    or moby's 1,000,000 when none is given (open in docs/audit/2026-10-16_docker-framing.md).
    Output that comes while it is full is dropped: non-blocking mode is chosen to drop rather
    than hold its run (moby's ring logger drops so too). Output that would pass the size goes only
    into an empty queue.
  - Docker drops in silence. shards counts what it drops (`LOST`'s second count, the
    record's `log_dropped`), and `logs` says it on stderr: `N bytes of NAME's output were
    dropped, as they came while its log's queue was full (--log-opt mode=non-blocking)`.
    `logs` still exits 0, since dropping is what the run asked for.
  - All that is queued is kept before the run's end is told.
- **Not yet.** The drivers that send a log elsewhere (D161's list), of which D163 serves
  syslog.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_log_is_compressed_and_queued_as_its_options_say`):

- 30,000 lines through segments of 64,000 bytes, four kept: three compressed, `logs` the
  output's newest, and `--tail 12000` read from the middle of compressed segments.
- json-file: none compressed by default, three with `compress=true`.
- `max-buffer-size=0`: what was kept and what was dropped add up to the output exactly,
  with 36 to 51% dropped in three runs, and the drop said. 4 MiB: all of it kept, nothing
  said.
- The refusals.

Mutation-checked: drops left uncounted, and shards' own driver not compressing, each fail
it. Unit tests cover:

- the format, read back across frames and as one stream;
- damage refused, in the seek table and in a frame's checksum;
- a segment removed as it is compressed, and retention;
- what a daemon compresses as it starts;
- every read of a log in compressed segments, against the plain way;
- the queue's drops, and the options.

### D161. A run's log, as `--log-driver` and `--log-opt` keep it

`run` and `create` take `--log-driver` and `--log-opt` as docker/cli takes them (scripts/docker-cli/oracle_test.go; served,
held to the CLI by the docker-cli oracle; options with `none` refused as the CLI refuses
them). A run's log is shards' own store (D27's segments), which `shards`, the default,
`json-file` and `local` name; `none` keeps none. `inspect` says the driver given, shards'
own where none was, and the options as a map (`HostConfig.LogConfig`).

- **Its bound, its own.** `max-size` (go-units' FromHumanSize, decimal, as both of
  Docker's file drivers read it) is each segment's most bytes, `max-file` how many it
  keeps, the newest written; they go to the run's VM with its request, and the daemon
  rotates by the run's count. A record fills what room the segment written has, the rest
  going on in the next, each saying whether it ends a line, so no segment is longer than
  asked, each is as long as it may be, and a line so cut is read whole. Before, a segment
  took a whole frame past its size (12 KB a segment where 1 KB was asked); then, until
  D163, a record that did not fit went whole into the next segment, which left segments
  of 64,000 bytes half full of a Linux guest's 32 KiB records. json-file
  keeps one file where only `max-size` is given, what the option means to its users (D161); where neither is, every
  driver keeps the home's bound, its user's (`shards configure disk --log-history`, 1 GiB
  by default, D186), or the daemon's environment's (`SHARDS_LOG_MAX_SIZE`,
  `SHARDS_LOG_MAX_FILE`), where Docker's json-file keeps one file that grows without end.
- **None.** No `RUN_LOG`, no segments sent: a detached run's output goes nowhere, an
  attached one's to its client alone, and `logs` is refused (`NAME keeps no log: it was
  run with --log-driver none`).
- **Details.** `labels`, `labels-regex`, `env`, `env-regex` and `tag` (a Go template of the
  microVM: `{{.Name}}`, `{{.ID}}`, `{{.ImageName}}`, `{{.Command}}`, ...) are what `logs
  --details` shows before each line, in the form `docker logs --details` prints, which scripts read: sorted by name, each
  `NAME=VALUE` query-escaped, joined by commas (moby logger.Info.ExtraAttributes,
  loggerutils.ParseLogTag), from what `inspect` says of the microVM's environment,
  labels and command.
- **Refused, in shards' words.** An unknown driver or option; values that do not read
  (`max-size`, `max-file`, `compress`, `mode`, the regexes); `max-buffer-size` without
  non-blocking mode.
- **Not yet.** The drivers that send a log elsewhere (`syslog`, `journald`, `gelf`,
  `fluentd`, `awslogs`, `splunk`, `gcplogs`, `etwlogs`), each refused with a word that
  says so. `compress` and `mode=non-blocking` came with D162.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_runs_log_is_kept_as_its_driver_and_options_say`): 10,000
lines through `max-size=1k` and `max-file=2`, the log the output's newest lines, two
segments; `none`: its client's output, nothing written, `logs` refused; `--details` with a
label, a variable (escaped) and a tag; the refusals; `inspect`. Mutation-checked: a run
logged whatever its driver fails it. Unit tests: each option's reading and refusal, the
attributes and the tag.

### D160. The streams a run's client attaches (`-a`)

`run -a` and `create -a` take `stdin`, `stdout` and `stderr`, in any case, as docker/cli takes them (scripts/docker-cli/oracle_test.go)
reads them (validateAttach, its refusal held to the CLI by the docker-cli oracle). A
run's client shows the streams it attaches and passes `/dev/null` for the others; its
log keeps every stream, as every run's does, so `logs` shows what the client did not.
None given, stdout and stderr; stdin is the command's with `-i` alone (Docker's
`OpenStdin`, which its clients set). A run attached to stdin alone shows nothing and ends with its command's
status. `-a` with `-d` is refused: a detached run's streams go to its log alone.

`inspect`'s `Config.AttachStdin`, `AttachStdout`, `AttachStderr` and `StdinOnce` say what
the command line gave: a created microVM's as the CLI's create sends them, which clients read back (stdout
and stderr without `-a`), which shards showed as detached before, its kept request losing
that it was a create; `run -d`'s none.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_run_attaches_the_streams_it_asks_for`): stdout alone, stderr
alone, each run's log holding both; stdin alone, its status 3; `-d` refused; `create
-a stdout` and plain `create` as `inspect` says them. Mutation-checked: the client
attaching every stream; a create's request kept detached: each fails.

### D159. A run's swap, written to its host's memory at the guest's own speed

`-m` with `--memory-swap` (by default as much swap again as memory), `--memory-swappiness`
and `--oom-kill-disable` are the run's microVM's own. Docker's swap is its host's swap
device, which a host may not have; on a cgroup v2 host it discards swappiness and
`--oom-kill-disable` with a warning. A microVM is its own kernel, and its host's memory
and disk are its swap.

- **The swap window.** Every run's microVM has one: a virtio-pmem device as long as the
  host's memory, the most a run may have and so its default swap, past everything else
  the guest is given and within the addresses the host allows (a window cut short holds
  less, as a host's swap device smaller than a container's allowance does). A run with
  swap gets a sparse file of its own, made anew each run in its run's directory and
  unlinked there once its microVM holds it, off the run's path: what it swapped out is
  nowhere once the microVM has ended. Its VM writes the file's first 64 KiB through the
  file's own path, then maps it at the window's start, shared and writable; init writes
  the swap header there (past the page cache) and swaps on before the command starts. The
  guest's CPUs write swapped pages as memory, into the host's page cache of the file:
  pmem completes each write as reclaim makes it (BLK_FEAT_SYNCHRONOUS), so reclaim frees
  each page at once (mm/vmscan.c, shrink_folio_list) and never waits on a host thread.
  The first page is the host's to write: the guest's first write to a page of the sparse
  file, through the mapping, takes the host's fault path to make the page, 3.4 ms at
  p90 and 80 ms at worst for the header, where written first by the host it is 23 µs at
  p50 and 31 µs at p99 (PM M230). The rest stays sparse: reserving the file's disk
  (`F_PREALLOCATE`) cost 5.3 ms at p50 for 424 MiB on APFS, 29 ms for 4.4 GiB (M230).
- **Why not a block device.** Swap was first a writable range of the join disk (D119),
  through a loop device, buffered and then direct. A workload within its swap was killed:
  under `-m 64m`, allocating 96 MiB, one run in four ended 137. Reclaim under a cgroup v2
  limit passes over anonymous folios under writeback rather than wait for them (mm/vmscan.c,
  folio_check_dirty_writeback and shrink_folio_list's second case), and 16 rounds without
  progress call the OOM killer (mm/memcontrol.c, try_charge_memcg). The VMM's worker
  completing the writes, on its own host thread, was too late under load (PM M230).
- **Hidden as the kernel boots.** Probed then, libnvdimm would give the window page
  structures, a 64th of it (2 GiB of a 128 GiB window: drivers/nvdimm/pmem.c,
  pmem_should_map_pages); swap needs none. Its transport reads as no device (DeviceID 0,
  virtio 1.3 §4.2.3.1.1) until init shows it (the control page's `SWAP`), with
  libnvdimm's drivers kept from binding of themselves meanwhile, and has its namespace
  probed raw (`force_raw`): mapped, never described. Before the template's snapshot, so
  a restore pays nothing for it. Its head reads as zeros until a run's file is mapped
  over it, what the kernel's partition scan reads; a snapshot keeps the window and never
  a run's file.
- **Sizes.** The device is the allowance and 20 MiB a vCPU (the clusters each CPU keeps,
  PM M229), whole 2 MiB, which the run's cgroup holds to the allowance
  (`memory.swap.max`); unlimited (`-1`) is as much again as the memory: a device as large
  as the host's memory would cost the guest's kernel 0.8 KiB a MiB of it (M229). The
  kernel's bookkeeping is in the microVM's memory, beside the limit (`swap_kernel_bytes`).
  A run without `-m` has none: its microVM grows to the host's memory (D148).
- **Swappiness** is the microVM's (`vm.swappiness`): the run's kernel is its own.
  **`--oom-kill-disable`** makes the limit a throttle (`memory.high`): past it the
  workload is slowed under reclaim and never killed, as cgroup v1's OOM control held a
  container's tasks, which cgroup v2 has no control for. `inspect` says both as given.
- **Agents take none.** An Agentfile's agents and harnesses (D59) have the memory their
  Agentfile grants and no swap (`memory.swap.max` 0 over their domains' cgroups): given
  the run's microVM's swap, an agent past its limit swapped rather than ended
  (`agents_out_of_memory_end_whole_and_spare_the_run`, which holds it).
- **A kill says why.** Where the kernel ends a run's or a joiner's process for want of
  memory, its init sends with the `OOM` what the run's cgroup held and was allowed then
  (`memory.max`, `memory.peak`, `memory.swap.max`, `memory.swap.peak`, `memory.events`,
  `memory.swap.events`) and the kernel's report of it (its lines that say why, among them
  the cgroup's `memory: usage ... limit` and `swap: usage ... limit`, read with syslog(2)
  where the run's /dev has no kmsg), which the daemon writes to its log. A joiner's kill
  was said nowhere: init removed its cgroup as it reaped its process, before its end was
  said, and the VM process's reader of a joiner's frames took no `OOM`. Now it is read at
  the reap, and a joiner is `OOMKilled` as a run is (D119). Found chasing a joiner killed
  within its swap on x86_64 CI (job 117491995198, run 39245355471): the next such kill's
  log says what its cgroup held of its swap.
- **Members share.** A run joining another's microVM (D119) swaps to that microVM's swap:
  the first member with an allowance maps its file, and the rest share it, each held to
  its own allowance by its cgroup, as a host's containers share its swap. Joiners had
  none of their own limits before: the daemon set them where it named a run's guest,
  which a joiner skips, its names its provider's; every run's are now set apart.
- **Costs** (PM M230, n=100 a side, interleaved). A run's start: +170 µs [+148, +182] from
  request to answer (p50 731 µs without, 889 with), of which the guest's header write is
  23 µs and swapon 25 µs (p50; 31 and 44 at p99), the rest the file's first page and its
  mapping. A workload 32 MiB past `-m 64m`: +12.6 ms [+12.1, +13.1], its pages swapped
  out at memory's speed where the block device's took seconds, or killed it. A template's
  boot, its window shown and probed: +0.6 ms [+0.4, +1.0]. The guest's address space, 40
  bits with a 64 GiB window where 36 without: a page-strided walk, every step a
  translation's miss, −0.1 ns [−1.3, +2.2] in one pass and +2.3 [+0.1, +4.2] in another,
  of 98 to 124 ns a step: at most about 2% of such a load, on the hosts whose microVMs the
  window takes past 36 bits (on this one, every microVM has 40 without it).
- **Not yet.** `update --memory-swap` past the swap a run started with, which its device
  holds; a build's `--memory-swap` (D64), whose builder has no swap window; what a host
  whose disk is full does to a microVM writing a new page of its sparse swap file, which
  is not measured.

Tested on real microVMs (`a_microvm_swaps_and_throttles_as_its_limits_say`): under `-m
64m`, 96 MiB allocated, five runs in a row; no swap with `--memory-swap 64m` (137) or
without `-m`; `memory.swap.max` for each allowance; unlimited; swappiness 10;
`--oom-kill-disable` past the limit; the refusals; `inspect`; a joiner held to its own
`memory.max`, killed without swap and swapping to its provider's microVM, twice.
Mutation-checked: without swapon; with `--oom-kill-disable` a hard limit; a joiner's swap
not mapped; a joiner's limits not set: each fails.

### D158. What shards refuses, in its own words

A refusal says what shards does with its microVMs and how to get what was asked; it does
not repeat what dockerd's or the Docker CLI's code says. An error reads `shards: MESSAGE`,
as Unix tools name themselves; the Docker client's `Error response from daemon:` is gone
(on a terminal the panel showed the message alone already). What scripts match is kept in
each message: `No such container: NAME`, `No such image: NAME`, `is not running`,
`port is already allocated`, `address already in use`, `executable file not found`; exit
statuses are unchanged. Compose and the Docker CLI decide by the API's status codes, not
by these texts: Compose matches its own "no such service" (cmd/compose/run.go), the CLI
the API's own words where it tries kinds of object (cli/command/system/inspect.go).

- **Reworded.** The microVMs' lifecycle (exec, pause, unpause, rm, stop, restart, kill,
  rename, logs, top, update); a run's network checks (what a joiner takes of its
  provider, the host's and no network, addresses, link-local addresses, endpoint
  sysctls); the network commands (connect, disconnect, create, rm, inspect, and the subnet
  checks, which leaked Go's netip errors); port publishing (another run's port, or another
  program's); image tags and removals (which microVM uses an image, and whether `-f`
  would remove it); volumes; the time windows of logs and events; signals; flags given
  together; a run's limits (`resources::verify`, with D159) and what `update` refuses of
  them (the CPU time set one way, updated another; memory past the swap already set). An exec that does not start says `shards: cannot start the command: WHY`.
  Each names the flag, or the run as it was given, never a 64-digit ID.
- **Not yet.** The build's texts, which its oracles hold byte for byte to BuildKit's; the
  CLI's usage and help texts and its checks of flags' values (crates/cmdline), byte for
  byte docker/cli's when piped; filters' and
  `inspect`'s validation; the Go errors of an image config that does not read; the
  guest's network setup errors.

### D157. shards' own names first; Docker's and buildx's still read

What a user writes or sets for shards carries shards' own name, as its build file is an
Agentfile before a Dockerfile (D35). The name Docker's or buildx's tools read for the same
is read after it, so that what a user has keeps working.

- **Ignore files.** A build's context is sent without what `.agentignore` excludes, else
  `.dockerignore`; one beside the build file, `NAME.agentignore`, else `NAME.dockerignore`,
  takes the context's place, as an ignore file beside a Dockerfile does for BuildKit's users (frontend/dockerui).
  The progress and a copy's warning (`CopyIgnoredFile`) name the file read; a build's
  `mode=max` provenance lists the one beside the build file it read. Verified
  (`the_agentignore_is_read_before_the_dockerignore`, mutation-checked: Docker's name
  looked for first; the warning naming `.dockerignore` whichever was read). The frontend
  image, which runs in another builder and reads what that builder's client sends, asks
  for `.dockerignore`, the file docker/dockerfile reads; it takes `.agentignore` with its own work,
  which comes last.
- **Environment.** `SHARDS_DEFAULT_PLATFORM` before `DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM`,
  `SHARDS_BUILDER` before `BUILDX_BUILDER`, `SHARDS_DEFAULT_POLICY` before
  `BUILDX_DEFAULT_POLICY`, `SHARDS_NO_DEFAULT_ATTESTATIONS` before
  `BUILDX_NO_DEFAULT_ATTESTATIONS`, `SHARDS_AUTH_CONFIG` before `DOCKER_AUTH_CONFIG`, each
  where set and not empty; a value one of them gets wrong is said of it by its name.
  `DOCKER_HOST`, `DOCKER_CONFIG` and `DOCKER_CONTEXT` stay where shards finds the user's
  Docker engine to read images from it: they are that engine's settings.
- **The policies' builtin module** is `builtin/defaults.rego`; a policy written for buildx
  imports it as `data.builtin.buildx_defaults` and gets it too
  (`the_builtin_is_imported_by_either_name`).
- **Code.** The crate that reads Agentfiles and Dockerfiles is `crates/agentfile`, its
  recorder `scripts/agentfile`. Functions, tests and files say what shards does, never
  that it is another tool: what a recording holds shards to is named as a recording
  (`plans_match_their_recorded_answers`), the recordings named for what they record.

### D156. A run's IPC, hostname, cgroups, umask and writable layer, as its microVM has them

A run's flags for the namespaces it has, its umask and its writable layer are taken as
Docker's CLI takes them, and mean what they can for a microVM: a run shares no kernel
with its host, so "host" is the microVM's, and what one run shares with another it shares
inside the microVM the other runs in (D119).

- **IPC: a namespace and a /dev/shm of the run's own.** A run's standby enters an IPC
  namespace of its own and mounts its own /dev/shm before the template's snapshot, and its
  execs enter both. Before, a workload shared init's IPC namespace and /dev/shm. No restore
  time resolved, and memory per VM within one 16 KiB step of what two templates of one
  machine differ by (PM M228).
- **Every /dev/shm of a microVM is half the memory it may have.** A microVM's /dev/shm is
  its own kernel's tmpfs, bounded by the microVM's memory alone, and what agents run share
  memory through: a browser's renderers, a data loader's workers (Playwright's docs and
  PyTorch's README tell containers' users to raise Docker's 64 MiB, which a container takes
  of its host's). The microVM's own, each run's, each joiner's and a builder's steps' are
  all half the memory the microVM may have in all (`run::sizes`, D148: a run without a
  limit, the host's), as Linux sizes a tmpfs by default (Documentation/filesystems/
  tmpfs.rst). The daemon tells each run its bytes with the run (its `shm=` setup entry,
  `run::shm_bytes` of the most of the run whose microVM it is: its own, a joiner's
  provider's), as every limit's runs restore one template (D148), whose own is sized by
  half all its guest may plug; a builder's are on its kernel's command line (`shards_shm`).
  The entry comes before any of the run's mounts, so that what the run mounts at or under
  /dev/shm (a volume, `--tmpfs /dev/shm:size=8m`) goes over the /dev/shm it was given, as
  a container's mounts go over its default one, and is never resized itself: told after
  them (32df9efc), a run's 8 MiB tmpfs there was made the microVM's 64 GiB.
  `inspect`'s `ShmSize` says them, held to what the guest's statfs says. A run's
  memory limit still holds what it writes there, as memory. A run wrote 128 MiB there,
  where 64 MiB refused it (`a_microvm_takes_its_ipc_hostname_cgroups_umask_and_writable_layer`).
  Each of an image's agents (D139) has a /dev/shm of its own, mode 0700, as large as its
  run's (`domains::shm_of`, the run's `shm=` entry): it kept Docker's 64 MiB, which a
  browser an agent drives outgrows (`agents_run_in_their_domains`: past 64 MiB, which the
  64 MiB mount fails).
  - `--ipc private` (the default) and `shareable`: its own; another run may share a
    `shareable` run's alone, as Docker's daemon allows (moby
    daemon/container_operations_unix.go, getIPCContainer). `--shm-size` sizes its own.
  - `--ipc none`: its own namespace, and no /dev/shm at all.
  - `--ipc host`: the microVM's, init's namespace and /dev/shm, which no run has unless it
    asks, of the same size as its own.
  - `--ipc container:NAME`: NAME's namespace and /dev/shm, inside the microVM this run
    joins (`--network container:` of a run in NAME's microVM, D119), NAME `shareable` (or
    `host`, the microVM's); a run sharing a third's is followed to it. A joiner's own is
    shared as the workload's is: init copies the other run's /dev/shm mount from that
    run's mount namespace with open_tree(2) and attaches the copy with move_mount(2) (no
    bind reaches another namespace's mount; its copy, an anonymous namespace's root, moves
    into any: fs/namespace.c, may_copy_tree and do_move_mount). `--pid container:NAME`
    takes the same rule: any run of the microVM it joins.
  - A /dev/shm a run does not own is not its to size: `--shm-size` with `none`, `host` or
    `container:` is refused in shards' words, where Docker ignores it.
- **`--uts host`: its host's hostname.** The microVM's hostname is the host's, as a run on
  the host's network has it (D124), inspect's and the guest's the same (dockerd gives
  `--uts host` a configured hostname its processes do not have). A joiner with it shares
  its microVM's UTS namespace. `--hostname` with it is refused: each names the host.
- **`--userns`**: a run's users are its microVM's own, unmapped, either way; `host` and
  none are both taken and shown.
- **`--cgroupns host`: the microVM's cgroup tree**, read-only, where by default a run sees
  its own cgroup as the root. Beside an Agentfile's agents it is refused, by the daemon and
  again by init, in shards' words (`beside::cgroupns_host`): their cgroups are in that
  tree.
- **`--umask`**: its command's and its execs', as the workload's limits are (Docker's
  daemon keeps the container's for an exec too: moby daemon/exec_linux.go). At most 0777,
  the bits a umask clears.
- **`--storage-opt size=`: its writable layer's size.** A run's writable layer is an ext4
  file system on its host's disk (D190), made to hold the size asked: its microVM restores
  a template of that size. A joiner's is a tmpfs in its microVM's memory, made at it, and
  unsized it holds what the workload's tmpfs does, all the memory its microVM may have
  (D148): the kernel's default, half the memory at its mount, held a joiner of a microVM
  that plugs its memory as it needs it to half of what it booted with, and a 256 MiB file
  failed with ENOSPC (`a_joiners_layer_is_kept_whole_as_its_provider_ends` writes one).
  Docker serves `size` only on overlay over XFS with project quotas; every run here takes
  it.
  `size` is the one key; above 0; for a joiner no more than the memory its layer is held in
  (`--memory`, or the host's, which the microVM may grow to), and for a microVM's own no
  more than the memory its page structures take as it boots, a 64th of it, of all its host
  has, nor than ext4 holds: each refused in shards' words.
- **A joiner beside an Agentfile's agents.** A run joining a microVM was held to its own
  image's rules alone, and the microVM's agents' went unchecked: a joiner could run
  `--privileged` beside them. It is now held to that microVM's (D115), by the daemon and
  again by init, either alone enough (`a_run_reaches_none_of_its_images_agents`,
  mutation-checked: with neither, a privileged joiner ran).
- Each refusal in shards' words; `inspect` says each mode as given (`private` where none).
  Verified on real microVMs
  (`a_microvm_takes_its_ipc_hostname_cgroups_umask_and_writable_layer`, mutation-checked,
  each caught: execs outside the workload's IPC namespace; no /dev/shm of the run's own;
  `none` leaving the microVM's; umask not applied, or not to execs; the layer not sized;
  `--cgroupns host` not entered; a joiner not entering the workload's IPC namespace; a
  joiner's donor's /dev/shm not copied from its namespace; sharing without the donor's
  leave; `--uts host` not naming the run by its host; a joiner's writable layer not
  sized; a joiner not in the microVM's cgroup namespace with `--cgroupns host`).

**Amended 2026-11-14 (devices-07).** The /dev/shm of a run that joins another's microVM
is sized by the run whose microVM it is, followed through every link, IPC
(`--ipc container:`) then the microVM's owner (`--network container:`, or the engine that
made it, D181), with no chosen depth: each lookup keeps the IDs it has passed and refuses
a cycle, a missing owner's record or no memory for its set, typed (`ShmOwnerRefused`). The
walk had stopped after 64 links and sized the mount by the 64th run's allowance, half its
host's memory where that run had no limit of its own, instead of the limited microVM's.
A start and an `inspect` refuse a run whose owner cannot be found; a listing's summary,
which shows no ShmSize (moby container.Summary), sums it up still. Unit red/green and
mutation: `docs/research/measurements/device-fixes/README.md`; the chained mount itself
is owed to ROOT's real-VM run (there).

### D155. A run's CPUs, real-time time, isolation and runtime, as its microVM has them

Every run is a microVM: its own kernel, its vCPUs host threads the VMM schedules. A run's
flags are taken as Docker's CLI takes them (crates/cmdline/tests/docker-cli.json), and do what they mean for a microVM, not what
Docker on Linux does, which refuses several of them for want of a VM.

- **`--cpu-count N`: its vCPUs.** Docker defines it for its VM-isolated containers as the
  VM's processors (moby daemon/oci_windows.go, setResourcesInSpec), and its CLI refuses it
  against a Linux daemon (cmd/docker/docker.go, areFlagsSupported). From 1 to the host's
  CPUs, past which a vCPU gives no more time; `--cpuset-cpus` names CPUs it has.
- **`--cpu-percent P`: the share of the host's CPU time its workload may use.** P% of all
  the host's CPUs' time each period, as the workload's `cpu.max`, on vCPUs enough for it
  (rounded up). One cap of CPU time at most: with `--cpus` or `--cpu-quota`, refused.
- **Real-time time, which runs did not have.** The guest kernel (Firecracker's base
  config: `CONFIG_RT_GROUP_SCHED=y`) gave a workload's cgroup no real-time time, which
  cgroup v2 has no files to give (they are cgroup v1's: kernel/sched/core.c,
  cpu_rt_group_init), so `sched_setscheduler` refused SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR with EPERM
  even to root with CAP_SYS_NICE (kernel/sched/syscalls.c), where Docker on a typical host
  allows them. Runs and builders now boot with `rt_group_sched=0` (Linux 6.16; shards'
  kernels are 6.18): real-time time is the guest's own budget. `--cpu-rt-period` and
  `--cpu-rt-runtime` set it (`sched_rt_period_us`, `sched_rt_runtime_us`), the run's alone
  in its microVM, where Docker on a cgroup v2 host refuses them ("kernel does not support
  CPU real-time scheduler"). Checked as the kernel takes them, the runtime within the
  period where both are given; what the guest keeps of the other is its kernel's own
  (950000 of 1000000 µs on 6.18; Linux 7 gives all of it, c2e390197ad1), which init reads
  and checks as the run starts, refusing in shards' words. No runtime without a limit
  (-1): init and the run's agents share its CPUs. Verified on real microVMs
  (`a_microvm_takes_its_cpus_real_time_isolation_and_annotations`, mutation-checked:
  without `rt_group_sched=0` root with CAP_SYS_NICE is refused; without init's write the
  budget stays the kernel's): root with CAP_SYS_NICE and the image's user within
  `--ulimit rtprio` run SCHED_FIFO, the rest are refused (EPERM).
- **`--isolation`: its microVM's.** `default` and `hyperv` (a VM's) are what every run
  has, in any case; `process`, a kernel shared with the host, is refused in shards'
  words. Docker on Linux refuses all but `default`.
- **`--runtime`: its microVM.** `shards`, runc's names (the default runtime's) and Kata
  Containers' (whose runs are VMs too) ask for what it is; any other is refused in
  shards' words. `inspect` names it `shards`.
- **`--annotation`**: kept, shown as `HostConfig.Annotations` and matched by `ps --filter
  annotation`, each with a key.
- **`--io-maxbandwidth` and `--io-maxiops`: its microVM's (D178).** A run's root is its
  image read through memory (DAX) and its writes in its memory: no drive of its own to
  cap. Its I/O to the host's storage goes through its virtio-fs shares and virtio-blk
  disks, which the VMM paces at them, outside the guest.
- `--help` lists `--cpu-count` and `--cpu-percent` as the microVM's; the CLI's oracle
  (scripts/docker-cli, against a CLI that knows its daemon is Linux's) holds every other
  answer byte for byte, and its test names each difference (MICROVM_FLAGS).

### D154. KVM on arm64, and a host's PCI function passed through (VFIO)

**Review devices-02 (2026-11-13).** An IOMMU MAP has an inclusive end
(virtio 1.3 §5.13.6.6), including `u64::MAX`. Translation bounds the
remaining inclusive span by the nonempty request before adding the final
byte, so a full-space MMIO mapping cannot overflow to a zero-length part.
No timeout, cache, allocation limit or platform-specific path is added.
Red/green evidence: `docs/research/measurements/device-fixes/README.md`.

**Review devices-03 (2026-11-13).** The IOMMU validates every writable
response span before applying a request. Its total must fit the split ring's
u32 used length (virtio §2.7.8). Reply staging is fallibly reserved, at most
one page as queried from the running host, independent of guest capacity;
properties, zero padding and the request tail stream through it. A failed
span validation writes no reply and applies no domain operation. If scratch
reservation or page-size lookup fails, a stack buffer sized from PROBE
properties plus the protocol tail completes the response without heap staging. This
adds no cache or selected transfer-size constant. The evidence above distinguishes
its bounded red guard test from the original allocator-pressure scenario owed
to ROOT.



D13 planned KVM on arm64 Linux hosts, and none ran a VM: the KVM backend was x86_64's.
D153's test path for VFIO is a guest given the test function, passing it to a guest of
its own, on an arm64 Mac (D132): shards' VM process inside that guest is an arm64 Linux
one. So both, in that order.

- **One KVM backend for both architectures.** What is KVM's everywhere is shared (hv/kvm):
  /dev/kvm opened and checked once, guest memory's slots, the run loop, the kick. Each
  architecture's VM and vCPUs are its own module's, and so are its ioctls.
- **arm64's VM is the arm64 machine's** (vm/aarch64.rs), as Hypervisor.framework's is,
  with KVM's semantics behind the same names. Its GICv3 is KVM's
  (KVM_DEV_TYPE_ARM_VGIC_V3, Documentation/virt/kvm/devices/arm-vgic-v3.rst): the
  distributor and redistributors at the machine's places; 96 interrupts, 32 private and
  then the SPIs the machine's devices use, in KVM's steps of 32; initialized once every
  vCPU exists, before any runs (KVM_DEV_ARM_VGIC_CTRL_INIT), as the machine's `finish`
  now asks of every backend. PSCI is KVM's (KVM_ARM_VCPU_PSCI_0_2, api.rst 4.82): the boot
  vCPU enters at the kernel with X0 the devicetree, the others start powered off, CPU_ON
  and CPU_OFF are the kernel's, SYSTEM_OFF and SYSTEM_RESET come back as system events.
  Each vCPU's MPIDR, which KVM derives from its id, is checked against the devicetree's
  (`arch::aarch64::mpidr`). The address width is asked of KVM
  (KVM_CAP_ARM_VM_IPA_SIZE); pointer authentication is on where KVM gives both kinds, as
  the guest has it under Hypervisor.framework; EL2 where KVM gives it (KVM_CAP_ARM_EL2: a
  CPU with FEAT_NV2 and a host booted with kvm-arm.mode=nested, arch/arm64/kernel/
  cpufeature.c has_nested_virt_support), its maintenance interrupt the devicetree's,
  INTID 25, which KVM reads from the attribute's `addr` (arm64/kvm/vgic/
  vgic-kvm-device.c), where arm-vgic-v3.rst says its `attr`.
- **Confined as on x86_64** (D30): Landlock, and the seccomp filter, whose system calls
  are x86_64's but those the generic ABI has none of (open, stat, access, mkdir, rename,
  unlink, readlink, poll, dup2), whose `*at` forms musl and glibc make there instead.
- **VFIO** (`run --kernel … --vfio NAME`, Linux): VFIO's container, group and device
  (include/uapi/linux/vfio.h; Documentation/driver-api/vfio.rst). The function's group is
  found by its `iommu_group` before the VM process is confined, and the container and the
  group are the only devices Landlock then lets it reach (IOCTL_DEV); VFIO's requests are
  in the seccomp filter, of no use without them. A group with an IOMMU takes type 1 with
  all of guest RAM mapped for the function's DMA, pinned; a no-IOMMU group
  (vfio.enable_unsafe_noiommu_mode) maps none, for a function that makes no DMA. The
  configuration space is vfio-pci's, which keeps from a user what it must not touch, but
  for the BARs, the expansion ROM and the interrupt line and pin, which the VMM keeps
  (D153's header); the memory BARs are placed in the bus's window, each at the next
  multiple of its size, and each access goes to the device's region at its offset; an
  I/O BAR is left out, as the machine has no I/O window. Each group is added to KVM's
  VFIO device (Documentation/virt/kvm/devices/vfio.rst) before its device is opened, as
  drivers that need the VM to open one ask; through it KVM learns whether the function's
  DMA snoops the CPU's caches, and on x86 honours the guest's memory types where it does
  not (virt/kvm/vfio.c, kvm_vfio_update_coherency). The VM keeps that device as long as
  it lives: KVM forgets its groups as its descriptor closes (kvm_vfio_release). A machine
  given a function has no memory to plug, no balloon (its DMA mappings pinned; QEMU's
  `ram_block_discard_disable`) and no snapshot.
- **Each host's answer** (the parity plan's step 13: a host's function passed through where
  its OS allows one, or refused with the OS's own limit and its evidence; M356, M401, M402,
  M403).
  - **Linux passes one through**, by VFIO, as this decision says. Its E2E runs nested, on
    QEMU's edu function a guest is given: on an arm64 Mac with EL2 (M3 or later), boot.rs's
    `a_nested_guest_runs_vms_of_its_own` and `a_run_is_given_a_hosts_vfio_group` as they
    are, and plug.rs's and hotplug.rs's through the L1 harness
    (`SHARDS_L1_PCI_TESTS=01.0 SHARDS_L1_TESTS=plug:a_hosts_function,hotplug` on
    `snapshot_tests_pass_on_a_kvm_host_of_this_architecture`). CI's x86_64 runners give a
    guest no virtualization of its own and no function to spare, so x86_64 Linux's VFIO is
    built, linted and unit-tested, not yet run on hardware.
  - **macOS passes none: Apple's APIs assign no PCI function to a VM.** Hypervisor.framework
    (developer.apple.com/documentation/hypervisor) maps a process's memory into a VM and
    runs its vCPUs; none of its 162 functions in the macOS 26.4 SDK takes a device (M403,
    `docs/research/measurements/whp-passthrough/macos-api.txt`). Virtualization.framework's
    devices (developer.apple.com/documentation/virtualization, "Devices") are ones it
    emulates, and its one passthrough, `VZUSBPassthroughDeviceConfiguration`, captures a
    host's USB device for the VM's emulated XHCI controller (the
    `com.apple.vm.device-access` entitlement: "captures USB devices and uses them in the
    guest"), no PCI function. A run that names one is refused with "macOS's
    Hypervisor.framework assigns no device to a VM, whose every device its VMM emulates"
    (`vm::passthrough_refused`, `PassthroughRefusal::HypervisorFramework`).
  - **Windows passes one through where its hypervisor assigns devices** (Discrete Device
    Assignment), by WHP's virtual PCI devices (Microsoft Learn, "Windows Hypervisor Platform
    API Definitions", its Virtual PCI (VPCI) Devices and each function's page, 2026-06-08),
    as Microsoft's own VMM drives them (OpenVMM's vm/whp/src/lib.rs at 29ff7a10, and
    vmm_core/virt_whp/src/device.rs at 58d8ab84, `AssignedPciDevice`). The function, dismounted
    from the host by its administrator (Dismount-VMHostAssignableDevice), is named by the
    instance ID it has then (`run --kernel ... --vfio PCIP\...`, as
    Get-VMHostAssignableDevice lists it): allocated by it with no provider
    (WHvAllocateVpciResource, a WHV_SRIOV_RESOURCE_DESCRIPTOR's PnpInstanceId, as M401
    allocated jupiter's reader), and made a physically backed device of the VM's partition,
    which is set up allowed device assignment (WHvPartitionPropertyCodeAllowDeviceAssignment,
    before setup alone: after it, E_INVALIDARG, M401) (`hv::whp::vpci`). Each is a device of the
    partition before the machine's layout, whose 64-bit window its BARs' sizes then size
    (WHvVpciDevicePropertyCodeProbedBARs, sized as PCI 3.0 §6.2.5.1 asks:
    `devices::pci::passed::sized_bars`). On the guest's bus (`devices::pci::assigned`) it is
    a function of its own on a device of its own, its configuration space the device's
    (WHvRead/WriteVpciDeviceRegister) but for what the VMM keeps, as of a function VFIO
    passes through: its BARs, placed in the bus's windows; no expansion ROM; no INTx pin,
    as WHP maps a function's MSI and MSI-X alone; its MSI and MSI-X capabilities, each
    message the guest writes mapped to the vCPUs its destination names
    (WHvGetInterruptTargetVpSet; WHvMapVpciDeviceInterrupt, MSI as interrupt 0, MSI-X
    vector k as 1 + k) and the message WHP returns written to the device, as that
    function's page says to, each MSI-X vector masked at the device while the guest's is
    and while its message changes; and its power state, the control register's D0 to D3
    set through WHP (WHvSetVpciDevicePowerState), as OpenVMM routes a guest's power
    management. In D0 WHP maps its BARs into the VM process (WHvMapVpciDeviceMmioRanges);
    while the guest's memory decoding is on, their whole pages but MSI-X's table and pending
    bits are in the guest by the partition's own mappings (WHvMapGpaRange), the rest reached
    through those mappings or WHP's register calls; out of D0 or decoding nothing, they read
    all ones (PCI 3.0 §6.2.2). Its DMA the host's IOMMU remaps to the partition's
    guest-physical addresses as the device is made (WHvCreateVpciDevice's remarks): all of
    guest RAM, as a VFIO function outside the guest's IOMMU, so a machine given one has no
    memory to plug, no balloon and no snapshot. WHP gives the guest no I/O address space of
    its own, which a guest's VFIO needs to give a function to a process: so on Windows a
    workload's `--device`, `--vfio-iommu` and a function plugged into a running microVM are
    refused with that limit, and `run --kernel ... --vfio` gives it the guest's kernel. Held
    by `devices::pci::assigned`'s unit tests (configuration, MSI, MSI-X, BAR windows and
    power, against a device of their own), `devices::pci::passed`'s (BAR sizing, capability
    lists), vm/mod.rs's `a_hosts_pci_function_is_refused_with_its_oss_own_limit` (the names
    a host that assigns takes and refuses), and on such a host the E2E boot.rs's
    `a_hosts_pci_function_is_assigned_where_its_hypervisor_assigns_one` (the dismounted
    function named in SHARDS_ASSIGN_FUNCTION at 00:01.0 with its instance ID's vendor and
    device IDs, its first memory BAR reaching the device while it decodes and reading all
    ones while it does not; with SHARDS_ASSIGN_DRIVER, the guest kernel's driver of that
    name taking it). Not yet known, as no host here assigns one: whether the confined VM
    process (an AppContainer, D30) may allocate the resource, which the E2E's first run
    answers; and whether WHP keeps resident the guest RAM a function's DMA reaches, which
    Microsoft's pages do not say.
  - **On arm64 Windows by the same code.** Microsoft Learn gives every virtual PCI function
    "x64, Arm64" (each function's page, 2026-06-08: Windows 11 24H2 build 26100.3915 on
    Arm64), and the SDK declares them (WinHvPlatform.h) and defines their types
    (WinHvPlatformDefs.h, its "Virtual PCI type definitions") outside its `_AMD64_` and
    `_ARM64_` branches, as it does AllowDeviceAssignment and the features' VirtualPciDevice
    and IommuSupport bits; so WHP's arm64 backend includes x86_64's `hv::whp::vpci` by path,
    its types windows-sys's (held to the header's sizes), its partition allowed device
    assignment before setup as x86_64's, and the machine makes the VM before its layout
    where it is given a function, as x86_64's does, its BARs sizing the 64-bit window
    (`vm::assigned_functions`, which both share). An MSI's target differs: the header gives
    WHvGetInterruptTargetVpSet x64 alone, and on Arm64 WHvMapVpciDeviceInterrupt "returns
    E_INVALIDARG when Target->ProcessorCount is greater than 1 or when
    WHvVpciInterruptTargetFlagMulticast is set, because the hypervisor targets each MSI to
    a single virtual processor on Arm64". The arm64 guest's MSIs go to the GICv2m frame the
    VMM keeps (WHP's GIC is given no ITS, D209), its doorbell the address and the SPI's
    INTID the data (Linux's irq-gic-v2m.c, gicv2m_compose_msi_msg; `boot::v2m_spi`, which the
    frame the VMM emulates now shares): so the vector WHP is given is that INTID, as Hyper-V's
    own virtual PCI takes an SPI's INTID on arm64 (Linux's drivers/pci/controller/
    pci-hyperv.c at d4872371, hv_msi_get_int_vector, its SPIs from 64; OpenVMM's
    vmm_core/virt_whp/src/device.rs at ba105dd7 handing WHP the vector its guest's virtual
    PCI asks for, built for both architectures), aimed at VP 0, an SPI going where the GIC's
    distributor routes it (pci-hyperv.c's hv_arch_irq_unmask: "SPIs is managed via GICD
    registers which Hyper-V already supports"). Held by `boot`'s
    `a_gicv2m_msi_names_one_of_its_frames_spis_at_its_doorbell`, the arm64 ffi's sizes, the
    refusal test above and the same E2E, now built for Windows arm64 too. Not yet known, no
    arm64 host here known to assign one (CI's windows-11-arm runs no hypervisor, M402; the
    nested Windows 11 host's answer, Windows 11's, not yet recorded): whether WHP delivers
    the SPI where the guest's GICD_IROUTER routes it or at VP 0; and the stage-2 attributes
    WHP gives a BAR's pages mapped into the guest.
  - **No Windows host plugs a function into a running microVM** (D214's VMM path outside
    the guest's IOMMU; behind it WHP's limit above holds). A partition is allowed device
    assignment as it is made, before WHvSetupPartition alone (E_INVALIDARG after, M401);
    Microsoft documents Discrete Device Assignment for a VM given its device before it
    starts and giving it back once stopped (Microsoft Learn, "Deploy graphics devices by
    using Discrete Device Assignment", 2026-01-30: "After a device is successfully mounted
    in a VM, you're now able to start that VM", "you must stop the VM and issue this
    command"); and WHP's pages (WHvCreateVpciDevice and every virtual PCI function's,
    2026-06-08) say nothing of a device made in a partition that runs, nor does OpenVMM make
    one (ba105dd7: its `new_physical_device` has no caller). So `Handle::plug_vfio` off
    Linux refuses (`vm::plug_refused`): where the hypervisor assigns devices with
    `PassthroughRefusal::NoPlug`, naming those limits and how to give the function as the
    microVM starts;
    elsewhere with the host's own answer. Untested on such a host, as none here assigns one.
  - **Windows refuses where its hypervisor assigns none**, with the hypervisor's own answer,
    asked as a function is (`hv::device_assignment_refused`: WHP's VirtualPciDeviceSupport,
    then AllowDeviceAssignment set on a partition of its own, never set up and mapping
    nothing, so that a process's one mapped partition, M345, is not disturbed). Every
    Windows host here refuses. jupiter's Windows 11 Pro, with an IOMMU, dismounts its SD
    card reader and allocates it, but allows no partition device assignment
    (0x80070032, ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED), makes no physically backed device of it (the same),
    makes one not physically backed that reaches nothing of it, and refuses Hyper-V's own VM
    given it as it starts (0xC035001E, HV_STATUS_FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE), WHP saying it has no
    IOMMU support (M401); its approved two-reboot experiment with `hypervisoriommupolicy
    Enable` on 2026-11-03 changed neither WHP's IommuSupport 0 nor its refusal 0x80070032,
    the original loader and boot manager restored exactly, the temporary entry removed, and
    BitLocker and Secure Boot kept on. CI's Windows Server 2022 and 2025, the edition
    Microsoft supports Discrete Device Assignment on, given server-class hardware that
    grants Windows the PCIe fabric's control and Access Control Services at its root complex,
    which force a function's traffic through the IOMMU (Microsoft Learn, "Deploy devices by
    using Discrete Device Assignment"), refuse the property too (0x80070032), inside Azure's
    VMs, which give them neither, as Hyper-V says (IovSupport False), and no function but
    Azure's own VMBus adapters; windows-11-arm runs no hypervisor at all (M402). A run that
    names a host's function there, by VFIO's nodes or as DDA's cmdlets name one (its
    location path, its instance ID), is refused with those words, said as a device the
    host cannot give (D154), as is `--vfio NAME` (`vm::passthrough_refused`). Held by
    `a_hosts_pci_function_is_refused_with_its_oss_own_limit` (vm/mod.rs),
    `a_hosts_pci_function_is_refused_where_its_os_passes_none` (boot.rs) and
    `a_run_given_a_hosts_pci_function_is_refused_with_its_hosts_limit` (containers.rs).
  - **Each refusal is typed** (R04), its variant the OS's own limit
    (`vm::PassthroughRefusal`, crates/vmm/src/vm/passthrough.rs): macOS's
    `HypervisorFramework` (Apple's docs: "Hypervisor maps the physical memory in the guest
    to virtual memory of the host process", the VMM to "Emulate memory-mapped hardware by
    emulating the memory access on exit"; M403); Windows' `Hypervisor`, the hypervisor's own
    answer; where it assigns devices, `NoGuestIommu` and `NoPlug`; a host without a backend's
    `NoBackend`. Callers that decide match it (`Vfio::of`, `plug_refused`, the tests); those
    that say it render it, in their own words around it (dockerd's "error gathering device
    information", the VM process's exit, the daemon's answer to `shards plug`), and text is
    all that crosses those processes. The hypervisor's answer (`hv::assignment::Refused`,
    written once for both WHP backends) is `NoPlatform`, `Unasked` (its words), `NoVirtualPci`
    or `NotAllowed`: AllowDeviceAssignment refused, in its words, with WHP's IommuSupport bit
    and the Windows edition, which says whose limit the refusal is. Microsoft supports
    Discrete Device Assignment on Windows Server alone: "DDA and GPU-P aren't supported on
    desktop-class hardware or client operating systems such as Windows 10 or 11 Pro"
    (Microsoft Learn, "Troubleshooting guidance for Hyper-V GPU assignment, partitioning,
    and passthrough", 2026-02-12), its host "running Windows Server 2016 or later" ("Deploy
    graphics devices by using Discrete Device Assignment", 2026-01-30); and on Windows
    Server it needs "server class hardware that's capable of granting the operating system
    control over configuring the PCIe fabric (Native PCI Express Control)" and Access
    Control Services at the PCIe root complex ("Deploy devices by using Discrete Device
    Assignment", 2025-02-19). So a client edition's refusal names the first limit and a
    server's the second, neither the other's: jupiter's Windows 11 Pro (ProductType 1, M401)
    the edition's, CI's Server 2022 and 2025 (ProductType 3, M402) the hardware's. The
    edition is the kernel's word, RtlGetVersion's wProductType (winnt.h's
    VER_NT_WORKSTATION a client; VER_NT_SERVER and VER_NT_DOMAIN_CONTROLLER a server; any
    other said as itself), read on the refusal path alone (`platform::product_type`); not
    VerifyVersionInfoW, which IsWindowsServer wraps, whose page says it "has been
    deprecated for Windows 10". No number is chosen here: the edition and the HRESULT are
    the host's own answers. Held by `hv::assignment`'s tests (each product type's edition;
    each edition's limit and not the other's), `vm::passthrough`'s (each variant's words),
    and `a_hosts_pci_function_is_refused_with_its_oss_own_limit`, which matches the variant
    its host gives.
  - Step 13's last part waits on hardware: the Windows E2E passing on a Windows Server host
    that assigns devices, and x86_64 Linux's VFIO on a host with a function to spare.
- **BARs in the guest's memory.** Each BAR vfio-pci lets a user map
  (VFIO_REGION_INFO_FLAG_MMAP: a memory BAR of a page or more, vfio_pci_probe_mmaps) is
  mapped into the VM process, and its pages, but for those of the MSI-X table and pending
  bits, which the VMM keeps, are memory slots of the function's own, which the guest
  reaches without an exit. They are in the guest while it enables the function's memory
  space, and leave before it disables it: vfio-pci then takes its mappings away
  (vfio_basic_config_write) and a vCPU touching one would fail its run (EFAULT); out,
  the BAR is trapped again, and a read with memory space off is all ones, as an access
  no function claims (PCI 3.0 §6.2.2, §2.3.2), which the test function now does too. A
  BAR of less than a page stays trapped whole, as its page in the guest holds others.
- **An IOMMU for the functions the VMM emulates** (virtio-iommu, virtio 1.3 §5.13;
  include/uapi/linux/virtio_iommu.h): a machine with the test function has one, last of
  its virtio devices, which translates the test function's requester ID alone: the
  devicetree's `iommu-map` on the host bridge (Documentation/devicetree/bindings/pci/
  pci-iommu.txt) and, on x86_64, ACPI's VIOT (ACPICA's actbl3.h; Linux
  drivers/acpi/viot.c). A passed-through function stays out of it unless it is given
  behind it (`--vfio-iommu`, below): its DMA reaches guest RAM through the host's
  mappings of all of it. The guest's driver attaches each endpoint to a domain and maps I/O addresses
  in it to guest-physical ones, a domain going with its mappings once its last endpoint
  leaves it, as Linux's driver expects (virtio-iommu.c, viommu_attach_dev); MAP refuses
  what is not whole pages or overlaps a mapping, UNMAP what would split one. On x86_64,
  PROBE gives each endpoint the local APICs' window, 0xfee00000 to 0xfeefffff, as a
  reserved region of subtype MSI (virtio 1.3 §5.13.3), so that MSIs need no mapping. On
  arm64 it gives none: Linux's MSI parents, GICv2m's and the ITS's, have the IOMMU map
  their doorbell for the device's domain (iommu.c, iommu_dma_prepare_msi), which VFIO's
  type 1 can do only in the software MSI window Linux's driver adds where the device
  reports no MSI region, mapped as device memory (IOMMU_MMIO), which the driver maps only
  where the device offers VIRTIO_IOMMU_F_MMIO; with a bypassed region instead, VFIO's
  MSIs failed (ENOSPC, msi_handle_pci_fail). The test function's MSIs are writes to an
  I/O address there, translated as its DMA is; on x86_64 an MSI into the window lands
  untranslated, as Linux takes a reserved region of subtype MSI (IOMMU_RESV_MSI), where
  the test function's had been translated through its domain, which maps nothing there,
  and dropped (`Translation::msi_target`). An endpoint attached to no domain bypasses
  translation until the driver says otherwise (the configuration's `bypass`, 1 from the
  start, as QEMU's `boot-bypass`): a guest without the driver keeps DMA by guest-physical
  address. Where only functions passed through are behind it, it offers no bypass at all
  (no VIRTIO_IOMMU_F_BYPASS_CONFIG, so no bypass domains, and a bypass flag refused as one
  it does not recognize): they are blocked, and pin nothing of the host's, until the
  guest's driver attaches them, as a guest needs the driver to give them to a process
  anyway (virtio 1.3 §5.13.4.2: the device MAY initialize bypass to 1). A device reset
  leaves `bypass` as it was, as the same section asks, where it had been set to 1 again. Linux defers probing a
  function behind an IOMMU it has no driver for, ten seconds where it has modules
  (driver_deferred_probe_check_state), so the `kvm` kernel has the driver.
- **A passed-through function behind the guest's own IOMMU** (`run --kernel …
  --vfio-iommu NAME`): what a guest's own VFIO needs to give the function to a process
  of its, as a workload's `--device /dev/vfio/N` does. A type 1 container maps one set of
  I/O addresses for all its groups, so the function's group gets a container of its own,
  as Cloud Hypervisor gives each VFIO device attached to its virtio-iommu (vmm/src/
  device_manager.rs, add_vfio_device: "a limitation of the legacy VFIO interface using
  container/group"; iommufd's address spaces lift it, a later layer). The container maps
  what the function's endpoint sees ([`iommu::Follower`]): all of guest RAM while it
  bypasses translation, from reset or in a bypass domain, as virtio 1.3 §5.13 has a
  bypassing endpoint's DMA go untranslated (Cloud Hypervisor's maps nothing there, so its
  device cannot DMA); nothing while it is blocked; and its domain's mappings of guest RAM
  otherwise, replayed as it attaches, then each MAP and UNMAP as they come. A mapping of
  device memory, an MSI doorbell's, is not the container's: the function's MSIs are
  VFIO's interrupts, which the VMM routes, each to where the endpoint's domain maps its
  address for a write, or into the MSI window untranslated (`vfio::Translated`). A request
  the host cannot carry out (no memory to pin: S_NOMEM; a mapping of what is not RAM:
  S_RANGE) is refused and changes nothing; an UNMAP the host could not make keeps the
  mapping here too, as the device can still reach it. The guest's kernel needs the
  driver, VIRTIO_IOMMU, as the `kvm` kernel has. Offering no bypass there, the IOMMU
  never shows a function all of RAM, which memory plugged later would outgrow: so memory
  to plug and free page reporting (D148, D151) work beside it. The host's IOMMU keeps
  the pages it pinned, so guest memory keeps each range a function's DMA holds pinned
  (`GuestMemory::pin`) from being given back under it: a report of it free keeps it, and
  an unplug of a block it meets is refused (virtio-mem's BUSY, which the driver retries)
  until it is unpinned. A function outside the guest's IOMMU (`--vfio`) reaches all of
  RAM, pinned, which neither may take from under it, so a machine given one has neither.
- **A host IOMMU group's functions in one device** (`vm::vfio_places`): the functions of
  one host IOMMU group, which the host cannot keep from each other's DMA (that is what
  makes them one group: Linux iommu.c, pci_device_group; peer-to-peer through a switch
  without ACS), share a device on the guest's bus 0, eight at most, so that the guest
  takes them as one group too and its IOMMU core keeps them in one domain, as the host's
  container does; and a workload given `/dev/vfio/N` finds all of them in it. Where they
  are one host slot's with its function 0, each keeps its function number; else they are
  numbered from 0 in their addresses' order, as a guest scans a device's other functions
  only where it has function 0. Each function of such a device reads as a multi-function
  device's (the header type's bit 7, PCIe 6.0 §7.5.1.1.9), and one of a device of one
  function as a single function's, whatever its own device says: Linux groups a
  multi-function device's functions by each one's own bit (get_pci_function_alias_group).
  And a function of a device of several reads as having no ACS, its extended capability
  taken out of the list (its predecessor's next pointer past it, or a header of ID 0 in
  its place at 0x100, which a guest passes over, as QEMU's vfio-pci hides one): ACS
  controls the host set would have the guest take it for isolated from the others
  (pci_acs_enabled), which it is not. Placed by slot alone, as at first, the functions of
  a group of several slots would have been groups of the guest's, whose domains one host
  container could not keep apart; and two functions of one group behind the guest's IOMMU
  each opened the group in a container of its own, which VFIO refuses (a group opens
  once): so a GPU with its audio function, the commonest passthrough, failed.
- **A group's endpoints share their follower** (`iommu::Follows`): one container for each
  host group behind the guest's IOMMU, which a type 1 container maps one set of I/O
  addresses for (vfio.rst). It shows the view of the last of the group's endpoints
  attached or detached, as the guest's IOMMU core attaches a group's devices one after
  another (__iommu_group_set_domain), and each MAP and UNMAP of the domain it shows
  reaches it once. A guest that kept the endpoints in domains apart would have the last
  one's view for all of them: of its own RAM still, all a container is given.
- **A run given a host's VFIO group** (`shards run vm --device /dev/vfio/N`, Linux, as
  Docker's is given a VFIO group's node; `/dev/vfio` gives each group in it, as
  DevicesFromPath walks it). The daemon finds the group's functions the host gave
  vfio-pci or another of VFIO's PCI drivers (/sys/kernel/iommu_groups/N/devices; its PCI
  bridges, which VFIO gives no guest, and what no driver holds stay the host's), as the
  run starts, a group it cannot give failing the start rather than running without it
  (`run::vfio_groups`), and boots the run's microVM for it, of no template, as a host's
  device is no snapshot's: the functions behind the microVM's own IOMMU, so that its
  guest's VFIO can give them to a process, with the pinned kernel's `kvm` variant
  (`KERNEL_KVM`), which has VFIO and virtio-iommu, or the kernel given. Its guest's init
