**Relayed UDP flows (network-12, 2026-11-14).** The host network's relay (hostbind.rs)
kept a relayed UDP flow as Linux conntrack keeps one, 30 s until answered and streaming,
then 120 s; it now keeps each RFC 4787 REQ-5's two minutes past its last datagram, either
way (REQ-6), as the network process does (D46, `shards_abi::bounds::UDP_MAPPING_IDLE`).

- **Asked, and said each time.** `--network host` alone gives it; every start of such a
  run says on stderr what it gives (`shards_abi::run::NETWORK_HOST`): its servers' ports
  are the host's, reachable from every network the host is on, and it reaches the host's
  own services and every network the host reaches. Docker's words where dockerd has some
  (PM M177): `-p` discarded with its warning; `--ip`, `--network-alias` and a second network
  refused as dockerd and the CLI refuse them; a `net.*` sysctl refused with runc's words,
  without containerd's and runc's prefixes, as every start's error is. Beside an image's
  agents and harnesses it is refused (D115): it would reach theirs.
- **Names: the host's.** Its hostname, cut to Linux's 64 bytes; its hosts file, whole,
  which `--add-host` adds nothing to; its resolvers as they are, loopback ones too, which
  are the host's own there (`--dns`, `--dns-search` and `--dns-option` as on a network).
- **Its clients: the host's.** Its network process's policy for it (`Policy::Host`) lets
  every unicast address through, loopback and link-local too, and takes the gateway for
  the host's loopback. The guest's loopback is the host's: its TCP and UDP to 127/8 go out
  of eth0 by a routing table of their own, ahead of the local table, and the network
  process takes each to the host's loopback at the address it was sent to; eth0 takes
  their answers from 127/8 (route_localnet; net/ipv4/route.c refuses a loopback source
  arriving otherwise). ICMP to 127/8 stays the guest's.
- **Its servers: the host's ports.** Each bind(2) and listen(2) of the run's processes,
  its execs' too, is notified to a process of init's (seccomp's user notification, the
  filter `seccomp-binds=`, loaded before the run's own profile so that one refusing
  seccomp(2) cannot keep it out; init forks it as it forks its DNS relays, having no
  thread). A bind of a TCP or UDP socket of the run's network namespace to an address of
  a kind the host has (every address, the loopback's, or eth0's own, which is the host's
  every address) is asked of the host first, which binds the same port with the socket's
  options: a port the host holds fails the guest's bind with Linux's EADDRINUSE, as on
  the host (M177), and port 0 is one the host chose. The process then binds the socket
  itself with the address it read and answers: what a notification shows can change
  before the call runs (seccomp_unotify(2)), and what it bound is what the host bound. A
  TCP socket's listen(2): the guest's socket listens, then the host's, so that none of
  the host's connections finds it not yet listening; a UDP socket's datagrams come as it
  is bound. What comes to the host's port reaches the guest by its network process: at
  the socket's own port on eth0's IPv4 address where it takes that address; for a
  socket on the loopback alone, on IPv6 alone or at eth0's IPv6 address, at a relay of
  the process's on eth0's IPv4 address, at a port the host holds too, which passes each
  connection or datagram on from the guest's own loopback (or to eth0's IPv6 address),
  so that its server sees a loopback peer, as one on the host's loopback does.
- **A server's loopback port is its own.** Once a TCP socket listens, or a UDP socket is
  bound to a port it named or to the loopback, its port at its address stays the guest's
  on the loopback: what the guest's own processes send it there, and its answers, by
  routing rules ahead of the host's. A client's socket, bound to a port of the kernel's
  choosing (busybox `nc`'s, musl's resolver's), keeps no rule, so that what it sends the
  host's loopback reaches the host.
- **IPv6: the host's too.** eth0 has an IPv6 address: `::2` of the last /64 of the pool
  dockerd derives its networks' from (the home's engine ID's ULA /48, whose other /64s
  the user's networks are given), its gateway `::1`, and its default route through it.
  Its network process takes that gateway for the host's `::1`, as it takes IPv4's for
  127.0.0.1, and lets every unicast address through. `::1` cannot leave the guest as
  127/8 can: Linux drops a packet that arrives on any link but the loopback with `::1`
  in its header (net/ipv6/ip6_input.c, ip6_rcv_core; RFC 4291 §2.5.3). So what the
  guest sends `::1` over TCP and UDP is translated (nftables, table `ip6 shards`): to the
  gateway's address at the output hook, from eth0's address at postrouting, connection
  tracking translating the answers back. A port its own servers hold at `::1`, or at
  every IPv6 address, stays the guest's: an accept rule ahead of the translation, the
  chain made again whole as they change. The answers, back at `::1`, are routed by the
  link they came in on, as `::1`'s always are (net/ipv6/route.c, rt6_need_strict), and
  that is eth0: `::1` is local on eth0 too, at the metric `ip route` gives (1024), past
  lo's (0), which the guest's own traffic takes.
- **Let go.** As a socket goes, which the kernel tells sock_diag's listeners
  (SKNLGRP_*_DESTROY), the host lets its port go; where those messages overflowed, the
  guest's sockets, listed whole, stand in. A port closed and bound again at once is the
  guest's: the bind that finds the host's port still held for a socket the guest no
  longer has, or let go since it was asked, is asked again behind the letting go; the
  network process answers a port's letting go once it has closed its copy, which the
  daemon waits for before it binds the port again, and only then. What a relay holds is
  passed on before it goes: a server's last datagrams, sent before its socket closed;
  and, at the run's end, which spares the relays, what their connections hold of their
  servers', each until its own end (PM M556; `hostbind::drain`, `Pair::drain`, its ends
  typed, `Ended`): the server's end (its FIN, or its reset once what it held was read, as
  a killed server's socket with its client's bytes unread resets) and all it sent before
  passed on, sent (TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT of a byte, which says POLLOUT only once nothing is
  left unsent, Linux 3.12 and later; where a guest's kernel refuses it, once written) and
  its end told; or the client's end, its reset or a failure, which nothing more can pass
  to. What the client sends then reaches no one, read and dropped, so that none is left
  unread to make the relay's close a reset (Linux's tcp_close()), and no client that holds
  its connection open without a word holds the run's end. Each run's relay drains once, so
  a drain of its own could tell it nothing of how long another took, and in-process
  learning is always cold: the cold start, the relays' own peers' ends alone, with no
  clock. A bound would have to be the host's (its runs' slowest drain, given in the run's
  setup), and none is: a client that stops taking a dead server's last bytes holds its
  run's end while it lives, as a closed daemon's client does (D185, PM M549), and the run's
  kill ends it. It was a second, the network process's grace (`netproc::GRACE`, PM M546):
  a client slower than that lost what the relays still held, and a server's reset ended
  its relay at once, what it held lost. The VM puts what the guest sent in the
  network process's ring before the daemon's word to close a port, which that process
  takes first. As a microVM ends, before its end is told, its ports go (PM M181): the
  VM asks the daemon to let go of them (`HOST_RELEASE`), which closes its copies, waits
  for the network process to close its own, then answers; the host may bind them again
  once `run` has returned, as dockerd's may.
- **Joiners: on the host's network too** (D119, PM M181). A run joining one on the
  host's network is in its microVM's network namespace, which is the host's network, as
  dockerd's joiner is in the host's network namespace: its binds the host's by the same
  process of init's (the run's `seccomp-binds=` filter is the joiner's too, its listener
  given to that process), each socket of the host's its run's (`HostBind::owner`:
  0 the run's own, a joiner's exec id), so that each run's ports go as it ends
  and the rest stay. Its servers stay the host's past its provider's command, and one
  it starts then is the host's too: the daemon follows the provider's microVM while
  runs joined to it are running, since their network is the one it gives them.
  It is told so as it starts (`shards_abi::run::NETWORK_HOST_JOINED`), which dockerd's
  is not.
- **No boundary.** A run on the host's network reaches what the host reaches, as it was
  asked to (AGENTFILE_ARCH §9.9); default deny is the bridge's and an Agentfile's, which
  refuses this beside its members.
- **Cost** (M178): a bind is a round trip to the host. A TCP listener, two: p50 0.24 to
  0.26 ms, where the bridge's is 1 µs; a UDP bind, one: p50 0.15 to 0.17 ms.
- **Open.** A bind to one of the host's own addresses (its LAN address) is the guest's
  kernel's to refuse (EADDRNOTAVAIL), as Docker Desktop's container's is (PM M177). A
  program on the host's network that installs a seccomp filter with a listener of its
  own gets EBUSY: the kernel allows one listener in a process's filters
  (kernel/seccomp.c, has_duplicate_listener).
- **Tested**: `a_run_on_the_hosts_network_is_on_the_hosts_network` (the warnings; the
  host's name; the host's own TCP and UDP services at its loopback, by clients that bind
  first, at 127.0.0.1 and at `::1`; servers at every address, at 127.0.0.1 and at `::1`,
  each reached from the host's loopback at the port the host chose, with the peer each
  sees; a UDP server's
  answer, sent as the server ends, twelve times, by the relay and from the gateway; a
  port the host holds refused with EADDRINUSE; a port closed and bound again 50 times at
  once; a killed server's port the host's to bind once its run's client has ended, three
  times; dockerd's refusals in its words), run 25 times, passing each time, and 20 more
  with IPv6, and mutation-checked: without the relays spared and drained at the run's
  end, without a relay's flows passed on as its socket goes, without the VM's flush
  before a port is let go, without the bind asked again behind the letting go, without
  `::1` local on eth0, with IPv6's UDP checksum zero, without the accept rules for the
  guest's own `::1` ports, without the ports let go before the end is told, it fails;
  without the daemon's wait for the network process, the daemon's
  `a_guests_bind_is_the_hosts` fails. `a_joiner_of_a_container_on_the_hosts_network_is_on_it_too`
  (told so; its server and its provider's the host's ports; its server the host's past
  its provider's end, and one it starts then; the provider's port free once its end is
  told, the joiner's once its own is), run 10 times, passing each time, and
  mutation-checked: without the binds' filter, with every listener the run's own, it
  fails; without the daemon following the provider's microVM past its end, or with
  every port let go at the provider's end, the joiner's late bind is never answered.
  `a_runs_gateway_is_its_neighbor_from_its_start`
  (below) fails without the gateway's entry at boot, after a new MAC, on a network of
  the run's own, or for IPv6's gateway. Init's
  `a_bind_goes_where_its_address_says`, `a_gone_sockets_cookie_is_read_from_its_message`
  and `a_calls_arguments_are_read_as_the_kernel_takes_them`; its drain's (PM M556),
  `a_relay_drains_its_servers_bytes_however_long_its_client_takes` (4 MiB to a client that
  reads only after 1.5 s), `a_relays_drain_ends_once_its_servers_bytes_are_sent`,
  `a_reset_servers_bytes_are_drained_too` and `a_relays_drain_ends_with_its_server_or_its_client`,
  each red with its guard removed (the second back, the sent-wait gone, a reset ending the
  relay, no drain); the network process's
  `the_hosts_network_reaches_what_the_host_does` and
  `a_hosted_port_is_let_go_by_its_number`; seccomp's
  `the_hosts_networks_binds_are_notified_on_every_abi`; the ABI's
  `host_binds_are_read_as_written`; `resolv_conf_on_the_hosts_network_is_the_hosts`.
- **Found and closed: answers held for ARP's (PM M180).** The test lost a relayed UDP
  answer once in 10 runs. The guest held it, not its device: each run's first datagram
  to its gateway waited in the neighbor's queue for ARP's answer, and the port went
  first (relayed answers lost under load: 5 of 1,000 without the gateway's MAC, none of
  1,000 with it). init gives eth0 its gateway's MAC as a permanent neighbor
  (`shards_abi::gateway_mac`, which the network process answers ARP and neighbor
  solicitations with), IPv4's and IPv6's, so that no run's datagram waits on it; the
  published UDP flake's first answer had the same cause.
- **Found and closed: UDP's answers over IPv6** carried a zero checksum, which Linux
  drops (D99's note): the guest's UDP to the host's `::1` went unanswered until each
  answer carried its own.
- **Found and closed: ports held past a run's end (PM M181).** At a run's end the daemon
  closed its copies of the run's host sockets and told the network process nothing, whose
  copies stayed until it ended, 3 to 10 ms later: a port a killed server held was still
  held once `run` returned, in 96 of 100 runs under load, where dockerd's is free. The
  VM now has the daemon let go of a microVM's ports before it tells its end, and the
  daemon waits for the network process (none of 100, quiet and loaded). A joiner's are
  let go so too; without it, the daemon's own letting go at the joiner's end came first
  in each of 100 runs, which nothing but timing ordered.
- **Found and closed: a slot for every listener ever published (network-10,
  2026-11-13).** Each `NET_PUBLISHED` pushed a listener slot and each `NET_UNPUBLISHED`
  only emptied it, so a guest on the host's network that binds and closes one port grew
  the network process's listener vector by a slot a cycle until its run ended. Listeners
  now take slots a free list hands on, as the guest's TCP connections do, each slot's
  generation in its poll token, so the slots are the most ever published at once and a
  slot's earlier listener's events never reach the next one's. Red/green and two
  mutations (free list, generation) on macOS arm64;
  [evidence](../research/measurements/network-fixes-v1/README.md#network-10-listener-slots-reused-under-generation-safe-tokens).
  ROOT owes the real loop: a host-network guest binding and closing one port 10,000
  times, the network process's fds and RSS flat, on Linux, macOS and Windows.

### D123. A run's record of processes: from the kernel, every one, whole

AGENTFILE_ARCH §9.9 makes each process a run's members start a record, and an audit trail:
`shards read processes MICROVM` shows it, `shards watch processes MICROVM` follows it, in
shards' grammar (`ACTION THING`, the user's, 2026-10-11). Docker has none; `docker top`
is a moment's list, which `shards top` keeps for the scripts written for it.

**`read` and `watch` are the grammar's views** (2026-10-16): what a microVM or an image
holds, read once, or watched as it comes. `read processes`, `read ports` (D122), `read logs`,
`read changes` (what a microVM changed of its image's files), `read history` (how an image's
layers were made); `watch vms` (what microVMs take of the host), `watch processes`, `watch
logs`, `watch system` (what happens to microVMs and images). Docker's verbs for these
(`top`, `stats`, `events`, `logs`, `diff`, `history`, `port`; crates/cmdline/tests/docker-cli.json) answer as Docker's own
commands, for its scripts, and are no form of shards' grammar nor in its help, where they
had been: `shards --help` is the grammar, piped as on a terminal, and an action of shards'
own alone opens its page wherever it is asked.

**Each form's page is its own** (2026-10-16). A form that runs a command of Docker's
(`list vm`, `watch vms`, `copy vm`) answered `-h` with docker/cli's page: `Usage:  shards
stats [OPTIONS] [CONTAINER...]`, its aliases Docker's command names, `docker cp` in copy's
usage. Its page is now the form's, on a terminal and piped: each way it is said (each of
its rows' alternatives that takes the thing asked, `shards copy vm [OPTIONS] NAME:PATH
PATH` and its other way round), what it does in the grammar's words, and the options of
the command it runs, what each does said as shards says it (microVMs, not containers; and
where Docker's words would still misstate it, shards' own: `--device` gives the command one
of its microVM's devices, never the host's, D152; `--annotation` is kept with the microVM,
no OCI runtime given it; `--isolation`, `--runtime`, `--privileged` and `--oom-score-adj`
act within the microVM; grammar::option_ours); Docker's own commands keep docker/cli's pages, which `scripts/docker-cli/generate` holds
byte for byte. And `-h` is help on every form, anywhere among its words but as a flag's
value or after `--`, where the context, client, invitation, guest and daemon forms took
it for a name (`context "--help" does not exist`) or refused it. Tested
(`every_form_of_shards_grammar_answers_help_with_its_own_page`, every row of the grammar
with `-h` and `--help`: its page, named as said, no `docker ` command and no `container`;
`a_forms_page_says_each_way_it_is_said`; `help_is_asked_for_anywhere_but_as_a_value`; grammar.rs),
mutation-checked: the form not kept; its options in Docker's words; shards' own words for
an option not taken; a device said as docker/cli's help says it (crates/cmdline/tests/docker-cli.json); a context's, a
client's, the guest's and the daemon's help not asked; a flag's value taken as help; a
bare alternative given nothing after it; `container` no `vm`.

Each record is a fork and its parent, an
exec and its command line, or an end and its code or signal, with the time, the member
(`command`, `agent NAME`, `harness NAME`, `joiner ID`) and the process's PID in the
microVM. Kept as the log is: segments of `--log-opt max-size`, as many as `max-file`, in
the run's directory.

- **From the kernel's process events** (`drivers/connector/cn_proc.c`), which init, in
  the initial PID and user namespaces, listens to as the run starts. They name a process
  by its PIDs alone; read with /proc, a shell's loop of 201 short-lived processes lost 42
  to 53 of them, and 33 to 38 of the rest their command lines (PM M176): a process gone
  by then has no /proc.
- **Whose a process is: its parent's.** A process a member's forks is that member's, as
  the fork's event says, which /proc need not; members cannot move a process between
  cgroups (§9.9). Only the processes init starts for a member, its own children, are the
  member their cgroup names (`/workload`, `/domains/<kind>-<name>`, `/join-<id>`), and
  init reads the events waiting before it reaps a child, so that a child's /proc is there.
  A process init moves into its cgroup after its fork (an exec, a joiner, a server
  instance) is recorded from its exec.
- **Its command line: the kernel's.** Linux sends none with an exec's event. Tracing
  would (perf's sched_process_exec with the new user stack), and Firecracker's config,
  ours, has no FTRACE; the audit subsystem would, and puts every system call of every
  audited task on its slow path (kernel/auditsc.c); seccomp's user notification shows a
  call's memory, which can change before the call runs, and §9.9 refuses it. So shards'
  guest kernel carries a patch (resources/kernel/patches/0002, kernel-6.18.48-4b8900bdffdd):
  an exec's event carries the command line the exec laid out, before the program runs,
  as much as a page holds with its whole length. Every exec whole, at no cost resolved
  (M176). The record keeps 4 KiB of one and says how much more there was. A kernel
  without the patch leaves /proc, read as the event is: the process's name, in brackets
  as ps shows one without a command line, where it ended first, or that nothing could
  be read, each said as such.
- **Its end.** The kernel queues an exit's event after the parent is told
  (kernel/exit.c, exit_notify then proc_exit_connector), so a run's record ends once
  every process whose start it holds has its end in it: the end of a run kills the rest,
  and their ends are waited for as they come. A PID namespace's first process ends only
  after the rest of it (kernel/pid_namespace.c, zap_pid_ns_processes); a process outside
  the command's, as under `--pid host`, is waited for.
- **Lost, said.** Events past the listener's 4 MiB of queue are a `lost` record, and the
  record waits for no end after one; a run whose record could not be listened to says why
  (`unrecorded`).
- **Past the command's end.** Joiners going on past it (D119), the records of their
  processes come on the run's connection while its writable layer is saved and after.
  Read as the layer's own frames, they failed its saving, and the layer it had before
  was kept: `a_joiner_is_a_container_of_its_own` found the provider's files empty, on
  CI's x86_64 runners every time and here five times in six. The VM passes them on as
  the relay does, from one reader of the connection for its whole life (the relay's own
  had read past its end and lost what it held), and reads on until the guest closes it;
  saying first that it asks no more, which init, its joiners ended, waits for before it
  powers off, rather than for a layer the host may not have asked for yet. The daemon
  reads them too (2026-10-11, D124's joiners): it followed the run's connection only to
  its command's end, or its layer's, and the records its joiners' processes made past it
  went unread; it follows it now while runs joined to the microVM are running.
- **Tested**: `a_runs_processes_are_recorded_as_they_start_and_end` (a child's fork, exec
  and end in order; 200 children, each over at once and reaped by its parent, each
  recorded whole; a child the run's end kills outside the command's namespace, freeing
  256 MiB as it ends, its end awaited; an exec followed by `shards watch processes`),
  mutation-checked: without the kernel's command line, without the parent's member,
  with netlink's padding read as arguments, without the wait for the last ends, it
  fails, and on the pinned kernel before this one, as M176 measured; init's
  `a_members_processes_are_recorded_from_their_events` and
  `an_event_is_as_long_as_its_message_says`; the daemon's segments and rendering.

### D122. The members an `EXPOSE` is for: one receiver for each incoming port

**eth0's own address alone (D285, lane xnet-s5b, 2026-11-16, ROOT's decision).** A run on a
network shared by runs has eth0's second address there (D285 slice 5), and the chooser's chains
took a port whatever address it came to. A UDP flow from a peer to a contested port at that
address, which `shared-in` gives the member a grant in names, was put in the port's holder's
zone as it came in, where the member's answers, unless it held the port, are tracked in zone 0:
they met no flow, and went out untranslated or not at all. Matching what comes in to eth0's own
address alone would leave the other case: a holder's answers to a peer there, put in its zone,
would meet the flow kept in zone 0.
- *So the chooser chooses for eth0's own address alone*: `chosen-zone`'s rule for what comes in
  and `chosen`'s translation each match eth0's address (`links::program_chosen`'s `own`, read
  as the chooser starts, after the run's `address=`), after their ports, so that a datagram to
  no chosen port pays nothing more in a chain that sees every packet; and a holder's answers
  are put in its zone only where they go to none of the run's networks shared by runs (its
  `shared`, each subnet's `not_within`), the flows there kept in zone 0 both ways. The flows
  of eth0's own address come from its gateway (a published port's, D143) or its network's
  members (D46), whose subnet no shared network meets (`SHARED_OVERLAPS`); a client at an
  address of a shared network the guest routes to that network, from eth0's second address,
  whatever its zone, so no flow the chooser could answer is left out of one.
- *Told as the run joins and leaves*: init sends the chooser each such subnet (its control's
  `S` message: on or off, the subnet's address and prefix, beside `L` and `N`) before eth0
  takes the run's address there, and after eth0 gives it back, and waits for its answer (`S`
  and whether its chains are programmed so, `Chooser::share`), so that no answer of a member
  there is zoned while the run is on it. A chooser that could not program them, or has gone,
  fails the change (the built-in's exit 1, as its other failures), told again, done again
  whole.
- *Not* a raw chain of the shared networks' own, always on (ROOT): it would cost every packet
  that comes in; this costs a chosen port's packets one comparison more (a new flow's first, one
  more in `chosen`), and a holder's answers one for each shared network.
- *Tests* (written, not run): links `the_chooser_takes_eth0s_own_address_alone` (each rule of
  the chains, with and without a shared network), chooser
  `a_shared_networks_subnet_is_told_and_answered` (the message both ways; init's wait ended
  by the chooser's answer, programmed or not, or by its going). Owed (ROOT): `cargo test -p
  shards-init --profile test-release --target <arch>-unknown-linux-musl -- links:: chooser::`
  on Linux x86_64 and aarch64; this entry's real-VM tests again, every chosen flow now matched
  to eth0's address (`cargo test -p shards --profile test-release --test build --
  a_port_comes_in_to_the_member_listening_on_it a_udp_flow_goes_to_its_ports_next_holder
  each_agent_answers_the_port_its_expose_names`); and, with D285's slice 4 on main, a member
  granted in on a shared network on a UDP port its `EXPOSE` contests, answered there whether
  or not it holds the port, and a holder's answers to eth0's own clients still in its zone
  (slice 6's real VMs, no test yet).

**Each port its own holder (network-06, 2026-11-14).** A contest had one holder for
its whole range, chosen where it listened on any port of it: with web listening on
7000 alone and api on 7001 alone under one `EXPOSE 7000-7001`, api's 7001 went to web.
The chooser's `Choices` now keeps each contest's ports as runs, each its holder's: a
port stays with its holder while it listens there, else goes to the first candidate
listening on it, else to no one, and adjacent ports of one holder are one rule, at the
holder's own ports (a mapped port keeps its member's). sock_diag's dump names the ports
each candidate listens on (`listened`), once per candidate per round, where the old
choice could stop at its holder's. Ranges two domains share only in part (each clipped
to its own network's grants, netplan `ingress_of`) are contested where they meet
(`contested` cuts at every range's ends) and `pre` programs only each range's
uncontested rest (`uncontested`). Unit red/green and mutations (adacachy2, x86_64
Linux): `chooser::tests::{each_port_of_a_range_goes_to_the_member_listening_on_it,
a_choice_keeps_its_members_port_and_joins_adjacent_ports,
ranges_that_meet_in_part_are_contested_where_they_meet}`
([log](../research/measurements/network-fixes-v1/init0406-red-green.log)). Owed to
ROOT: the split-listener fixture on real microVMs, TCP and UDP, one listener closing
(`cargo test -p shards --test build a_port_comes_in_to_the_member_listening_on_it --
--exact --nocapture`, extended to one unmapped 7000-7001 `EXPOSE` with web on 7000 and
api on 7001), and M513's contested bind/listen latency again, as a round now dumps
every candidate's sockets.

**Review gap (network-07, 2026-11-13), owed to ROOT.** IPv6 wildcard acceptance has
not been validated against IPV6_V6ONLY in the pinned guest. IPv4 selection must parse the kernel's
`INET_DIAG_SKV6ONLY` attribute; an absent/malformed observation must not be guessed
dual-stack. The fixed message's IPv6 source alone cannot establish acceptance.
The proposed live fixtures and failure/ownership requirements are
[recorded here](../research/measurements/network-fixes-v1/README.md#network-05-07-guest-kernel-and-api-reproductions).

An `EXPOSE … FOR <network>` opened a port of the microVM for every member of the network.
On a network of one member that is a receiver; on a network of several, a connection
coming in had none, and shards refused it. Default deny asks that every grant name who, to
whom, on which ports and which way (CLAUDE.md), and an incoming TCP connection or UDP
datagram is delivered to one socket bound to its port, as Docker's `-p` delivers to the one
process a container listens with (https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/,
`--publish`). So (AGENTFILE_ARCH §4.1, the user's syntax, 2026-10-11):

- **`--agents=`, `--harnesses=`, `--mcps=`** name the members a port is for, each flag
  members of its own kind: an agent and a harness may share a name, and a name never
  resolves to the wrong kind (§4.10). A name of another kind, or of no member of a network
  the `EXPOSE` names, is a build error that says what the name is. Without them, the port
  is every member's, as before.
- **One receiver for an incoming port**, across the three flags and across `EXPOSE`s: two
  members claiming one port is a build error naming both, and so is an unnamed port of a
  network of several. Egress, the destination port of connections going out, names any
  number.
- **`<port>:<member_port>`**, ingress's alone, in `-p`'s order (outside, then inside), so
  two members that both listen on one port are each reached.
- **Shown**: `shards read ports <microvm>` lists each published port with its member and
  that member's kind, in shards' own grammar; `shards port` keeps Docker's output where it
  is piped. A published port no member claims reaches the run's own command: what `-p`
  meant before a run had members.

- **At run**, init gives each domain the ports named for it, as pairs of the microVM's
  range and the member's: the uplink's DNAT translates a mapped port (nft_nat's proto
  register, as nft's `dnat to ADDR:PORT` writes it), and its forward chain, the switch and
  the domain's gate match the member's port. The image's ExposedPorts keep the microVM's
  port, where BuildKit's own `EXPOSE 8081:80` keeps the second.
- **Tested**: `each_agent_answers_the_port_its_expose_names` (two agents both on 7100, web
  at the microVM's 7100 and api at its 7101; `shards read ports`; the unnamed case refused
  at build; mutation-checked, the DNAT without the port's translation reaching no one);
  `ingress_reaches_a_networks_one_member` and the parser's cases; init's
  `ingress_goes_to_the_member_its_expose_names`.

`--mcps=` waits on local MCP servers joining networks: today each caller runs its own
instance over stdio, in its own confinement (D60, §9.6).

**2026-11-08, the user's decision: `FOR` takes a list of targets, networks and members
mixed, and a port of several members goes to the one listening.** This replaces "one
receiver for an incoming port" above:

- **`EXPOSE <port>… [AS …] FOR <network_or_member>…`.** Each target is a network or an
  agent or harness the lineage declares; a name that is both is a build error, and so is
  `--agents`/`--harnesses` on a line whose targets are members alone. A member named is
  given the ports on each network it is on (`CONNECT ... ON`), as `EXPOSE --agents=<it>
  <ports> FOR <its networks>` says (`agentfile::resolve_targets`, which the build applies
  before it checks and keeps the normalized Agentfile so); a member on no network is a
  build error, as no flow reaches a member but on a network. Every target gets the
  exposure, and nothing a target does not name is opened: both boundaries still apply
  (the network's `--ingress`/`--expose` and the microVM's `EXPOSE`).
- **Named members alone, both ways.** An `EXPOSE` that names its members opens egress for
  them alone, as it opens ingress: before, egress named for one member was every member's
  of the network (default deny: a grant to one is no other's).
- **Several members on one port: the one listening takes each connection.** A port the
  `EXPOSE`s give several members (a network's every member where none is named, several
  named, or members of several networks) goes to the member that listens on it, the first
  to listen holding it while it listens and then the next that does in declaration order;
  no member listening, it goes nowhere past init, as a port no member claims. This is a
  host's rule for a port (RFC 9293 §3.10.7.2: a SYN is for the socket in LISTEN on its
  port; POSIX bind(2): EADDRINUSE keeps a second socket off a bound port), the microVM's
  port standing for one host's. Two members' claims that overlap without being the same
  ports are a build error, as which holds the rest no rule says. Init's chooser
  (crate::chooser) makes it so: each candidate runs under a seccomp filter that notifies of
  listen(2) and bind(2) (seccomp_unotify(2)); the chooser makes a TCP socket's listen
  itself, and a UDP socket's bind to a contested port, refused EACCES as the member's own
  kernel would refuse a privileged one, so that it knows the socket takes the port as it
  answers; sock_diag tells it each socket's end in each candidate's namespace
  (SKNLGRP_*_DESTROY), and it asks sock_diag who listens before it chooses. Each choice is
  the uplink's chain `chosen`, before `pre`, programmed again whole. No grant rests on the
  chooser: every candidate's gate and the switch let the port in to it, and the chooser
  only picks among them. `shards read ports` names every candidate ("the one listening of
  agent web; agent api").
- **Tested**: the parser's and the plan's cases (agentfile.rs
  `ingress_reaches_a_networks_one_member`: FOR's mixes, named and unnamed members, overlaps
  refused, a member on no network refused; netplan's
  `ingress_goes_to_the_member_its_expose_names`: every member a candidate, egress the named
  member's alone; the chooser's unit tests of its filter, its contests and sock_diag's
  messages) and on real microVMs, build.rs `a_port_comes_in_to_the_member_listening_on_it`:
  two networks, `FOR front ops` giving three members four ports, each port reaching the one
  member listening, every connection, and a member no `FOR` names not reached.
- **A UDP flow follows its port's holder.** Linux keeps a flow's NAT binding for the
  flow's life (nf_nat_core.c; 120 s past its last datagram once it streams,
  nf_conntrack_proto_udp.c), so a client sending all along would have stayed with a
  holder that had closed its socket. Each holder of a UDP port has a conntrack
  zone of its own (network-04 below) (`ct zone set`, raw prerouting, the datagrams coming in and the holder's
  answers): a flow admitted before is new in the new zone and is translated to the new
  holder, its old entry left to expire, as a guest kernel without ctnetlink (shards' has
  none) has no other way to end one; the old holder's answers past the change are new
  flows no grant opens. Tested on real microVMs (`a_udp_flow_goes_to_its_ports_next_holder`:
  one client socket answered by web, then, after web closes and api binds, by api).
  A notification names the calling thread, which pidfd_open(2) refuses where it leads no
  thread group: the chooser, and the host network's binds (D124), open its group's leader
  then, so that a server binding on a thread of its own is seen (found by that test).
- **A zone is one holder's for the run (network-04, 2026-11-14).** Each change of a
  UDP holder took the next zone of a u16 counter, which wrapped to 1 while a flow
  conntrack kept there could still be translated to the holder it was made for (no
  ctnetlink in shards' guest kernel to end it; no clock ties the wrap to its expiry):
  after 65,535 changes the same client tuple went to the old holder. Each UDP
  candidate of each contest now has a zone of its own, fixed as the chooser starts
  (`Choices::new`), so every entry conntrack keeps in a zone is translated to the one
  holder that zone is for: a flow admitted before a change is new in the next
  holder's zone, and one kept from an earlier turn of the same holder goes to that
  holder again. No zone is reused and none retired, so no timeout or retirement
  proof is needed. The bound is conntrack's: a zone is a u16 and zone 0 every other
  flow's (`NF_CT_DEFAULT_ZONE_ID`, include/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_zones.h), so
  more than 65,535 UDP candidates refuse the run as its chooser starts
  (`chooser::Refused::Zones(ZonesExhausted { needed })`), before any domain runs.
  Unit red/green and mutations (adacachy2): `a_udp_zone_names_one_holder_for_the_run`,
  `more_udp_candidates_than_zones_are_refused`. Owed to ROOT: `cargo test -p shards
  --test build a_udp_flow_goes_to_its_ports_next_holder -- --exact --nocapture`
  extended to hand the port back to the first holder and to the second again with one
  client socket, each datagram answered by the holder of the moment.
- **What the chooser reads, at the sizes it comes in (network-12, 2026-11-14).** Its
  sock_diag dumps were read into 16 KiB and its socket-end notices into 8 KiB, chosen,
  and a namespace not yet read, or whose `ip_unprivileged_port_start` could not be read,
  was taken to start at 1024. Each dump datagram is now read whole at its own length,
  peeked first (recv(2)'s MSG_PEEK | MSG_TRUNC, netlink's since Linux 2.6.22); each
  notice, never read, is taken with no buffer (MSG_TRUNC); and the unprivileged start is
  the namespace's own, a namespace whose value cannot be read or is no port refusing its
  member to the chooser with the error said, a bind before the namespace is read being
  the member's own kernel's (`every_listener_of_a_long_dump_is_found`,
  `the_unprivileged_start_is_the_namespaces_own_or_an_error`).
- **A choice costs a commit, not a grace period (PM M513).** M498 found a contested
  bind(2) and listen(2) each at 16 ms (p50) where an uncontested filtered one took 19 and
  14 µs: the chooser programmed each choice on a netfilter socket of its own and closed
  it, and a netfilter socket's close (NETLINK_URELEASE, nft_rcv_nl_event) flushes the
  pending transactions' destroy work, which waits in synchronize_rcu (nf_tables_api.c,
  Linux 6.18.48), with the commit mutex held, while the member's next call waited
  behind it. The chooser and the host network's binds (D124, IPv6's loopback) keep one
  socket for their life, so that the destroy work's grace period passes on a kernel
  worker; and the chooser answers every call a round of poll(2) finds before it
  programs, choosing once for them all. Measured before and after, interleaved (M513,
  adacachy, n 2,000): a contested bind 15.98 ms at p50 (32 ms p99) before, 20.6 to 21.7
  µs (68 to 71 µs p99) after, where a filtered, uncontested one takes 19 µs; listen
  likewise. The chains stay rebuilt whole: their commit leaves a contested call a few µs
  past an uncontested one's, which a map keyed by port could not buy back worth its code.
- **A run's start closes no netfilter socket (PM M513).** The commits a run makes before
  its command executes were each on a socket opened for them and closed after, a grace
  period each where its start makes them: its confinement (`confine_eth0`, an image whose
  agents reach past the microVM), the host's loopback (`net::host_loopback`, D124), the
  agents' way past the microVM in init's namespace (`outside`, `outside6`) and each
  domain's gate (`attach_ns`), and a member's gate as its engine changes it (`regate`).
  Init's own namespace's are made on one socket kept for its life (links.rs `INIT_NFT`),
  let go only where an exchange fails; each gate keeps its own with its namespace.
  Before and after: the start-path trace of a run of each kind, owed.
- **Not yet**: ports past the microVM are IPv4's alone (D99). Unmeasured: a build step's
  device cgroup (`docs/research/measurements/step-devices/run.py`, PM M498); the
  chooser's round trip on an arm64 Mac; and Fedora's tail after M513 (max 21 to 107 ms in
  three runs at load 18 to 26, not interleaved).

### D121. Docker's AppArmor mount rule, in guests that have no AppArmor

Where AppArmor is enforced, as on Ubuntu, Docker confines every container with its
docker-default profile (moby profiles/apparmor/template.go), whose `deny mount,` keeps even
a container given CAP_SYS_ADMIN from mounting anything; `--security-opt apparmor=unconfined`
and `--privileged` lift it, `seccomp=unconfined` does not. A shards guest has no AppArmor,
and its devices are its microVM's, reachable by name: a workload given SYS_ADMIN could
mount a virtio-fs tag of its own microVM, its provider's shares or the join share (D119),
and remount a read-only volume writable. So shards holds every workload to docker-default's
mount rule itself, on every guest kernel, with seccomp, which all have:

- **The rule as a filter of its own** (`shards_seccomp::MOUNTS`, `seccomp-mounts=`): mount,
  mount_setattr, the new mount API (fsopen, fsconfig, fsmount, fspick, move_mount,
  open_tree) and pivot_root, each EACCES, AppArmor's answer to mount(2) (PM M174); umount
  left to it, as docker-default allows it. Compiled as Docker's profile is, for the native
  and compat syscall tables (x86_64 with x86 and x32, arm64 with arm), so no `int 0x80`
  gets past it.
- **Past docker-default, by design.** docker-default refuses mount(2) and lets fsopen and
  open_tree's clone through to a container with the capability (PM M174). A detached
  mount needs no mount point: fsopen, fsconfig and fsmount make one, and its descriptor
  opens its files, as Docker's container with the capability made a tmpfs and a file in
  it while docker-default refused only move_mount (M174, measured on both GitHub
  runners), so the rule that refused mount(2) alone would leave a microVM's own
  virtio-fs shares, a provider's and the join share, to any workload given the
  capability. shards refuses the new mount API too; a program that mounts gets EACCES
  from its first step instead of from mount(2) or move_mount.
- **Only where it protects something**: for a workload with CAP_SYS_ADMIN, not
  privileged, not `apparmor=unconfined`. Without the capability the kernel refuses every
  mount, EPERM, and Docker's seccomp profile refuses first. Installed before Docker's
  profile, whose errno then wins where both refuse (seccomp_filter.rst: the most recent
  filter's).
- **Unlike Docker, by design, and why.** Under `seccomp=unconfined` without the capability,
  mount(2) is refused EPERM, by the kernel, where AppArmor answers EACCES: the kernel asks
  AppArmor before it checks the capability (Linux fs/namespace.c path_mount:
  security_sb_mount, then may_mount; PM M174). A filter would change that errno alone, and
  would put a seccomp filter on a workload that asked to have none (`Seccomp: 2` in
  /proc/PID/status, where Docker's shows 0). With the capability under
  `seccomp=unconfined`, the filter stays, and so does `Seccomp: 2`: there it is what keeps
  the microVM's shares.
- **For all a microVM runs**: the workload, its execs (the run's filters are theirs, as
  runc's exec takes the container's) and joiners.
- **Tested** (`a_container_given_sys_admin_mounts_nothing_as_apparmor_keeps_it`: a mount, a
  remount of a read-only file, fsopen, open_tree and its microVM's own share refused EACCES,
  in an exec and a joiner too; umount of its own tmpfs made; `apparmor=unconfined` and
  `--privileged` mounting; EPERM without the capability, under `seccomp=unconfined` too;
  mutation-checked: without the filter, the mount went through; `a_container_given_sys_admin_has_apparmors_mount_rule`:
  who is given it). Docker's own behaviour where AppArmor is enforced is probed on GitHub's
  Ubuntu runners (`docs/research/measurements/docker-apparmor-mount`, PM M174).
- **Not taken from docker-default**: its /proc and /sys write rules, which Docker's masked
  and read-only paths cover in every container already, and its ptrace and signal rules,
  which PID namespaces keep between containers.
- **What CAP_SYS_ADMIN still reaches, as with Docker.** Docker's own seccomp profile gives
  a container with the capability `bpf` and `perf_event_open`, whose tracing programs read
  the kernel's memory, and with it every workload's in the microVM, as on a Docker host
  every container's on the host: the capability is the kernel's, AppArmor or not. So the
  rule is held where Docker holds it, and no further: under `apparmor=unconfined` a
  workload may mount its microVM's shares, a joiner its provider's, as it may read them
  through the kernel. What a workload without the capability could reach of another's is
  closed: the join share's volumes by names and node IDs none can guess (D119), so
  CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH opens no other joiner's file by handle. Kernel lockdown
  (`lockdown=confidentiality`) in the guest would close the kernel to the capability too,
  past Docker; not built.

### D119. `--network container:NAME`: a run joins another's microVM

Docker's container network mode gives a container another's network namespace and
nothing else of it (moby docker-v29.3.1 daemon/oci_linux.go: the joiner's netns is
`/proc/<pid>/ns/net` of the other's process; its mount, PID, IPC, UTS and cgroup
namespaces are its own). It takes the other's hostname and domain name, and its
`/etc/hostname`, `/etc/hosts` and `/etc/resolv.conf`, the same files
(daemon/container_operations.go initializeNetworking, initializeNetworkingPaths). A
microVM's network namespace cannot be shared with another microVM, so the joiner runs in
the provider's: its guest init starts the joiner apart, as a run of its own (its image its
root, its own mount, PID, IPC and UTS namespaces and cgroup) in the network namespace the
provider's command runs in. The microVM's boundary still holds the host; between the two,
the boundary is a container's, which is what the mode asks for.

- **What dockerd checks, held to its words.** As the joiner is made
  (daemon/internal/runconfig/hostconfig.go validateNetContainerMode, in order): `container`
  with no name ("invalid network mode: invalid container format container:<name|id>"),
  then `--hostname`, `--link`, `--dns`, `--add-host`, `-p`/`-P`, `--expose`, each
  "conflicting options: ..." in dockerd's words (containers.rs `a_joiner_is_a_container_of_its_own`). As it starts (getNetworkedContainer): no
  such container ("joining network namespace of container: No such container: X"), itself
  ("cannot join own network namespace"), one not running ("cannot join network namespace
  of a non running container: container X is STATE"), one restarting. `network connect`
  of a joiner: "container sharing network namespace with another container or host cannot
  be connected to any other network". dockerd lets the provider be stopped or removed
  while joiners run (daemon/delete.go checks no dependents).
- **The joiner's image, on a join disk.** A microVM has no PCI and no hotplug (virtio-mmio
  alone, its devices in the device tree or ACPI), so every microVM carries a read-only
  virtio-blk join disk, empty until a run joins, as Firecracker attaches a drive's
  file after boot (its `PATCH /drives` rescan). The VM process appends the joiner's EROFS
  file as a range of the disk and raises its capacity; the guest's virtio_blk reads the
  new capacity on the config-change interrupt (Linux drivers/block/virtio_blk.c,
  virtblk_config_changed_work). Init maps the range with a loop device at its offset
  (`CONFIG_BLK_DEV_LOOP`, in the guest kernel's base config), which reads it past the disk's
  page cache (LOOP_SET_DIRECT_IO: a builder's cache layers' copies there were held in no
  cgroup a hold holds, PM M350), and mounts it as EROFS,
  under a tmpfs overlay as a run's root is. One disk serves every joiner a microVM has,
  each its own range: no count of slots to run out of.
- **Its cost to every microVM, measured first** (PM M168): a restore with empty
  file-backed disks paid about 40 to 70 µs for each, 16 at once resolved from zero
  (+642 µs [+226, +994], +1,122 [+790, +1,440]), one not (+95 µs [−304, +383], +15
  [−160, +299]); each reopens its file through the grants broker, which a join disk with
  no file does not. The join disk as built cost no restore anything resolved against none
  (−513 µs [−1,682, +120]; none less join +330 [−370, +883]), and no memory per VM
  resolved (`phys_footprint` +0 KiB [−32, +16], PM M170), the RSS it adds being the
  template's pages every microVM restored from it shares.
- **Its life.** The joiner is a run of its own: its record, log, exit code, `stop`,
  `kill`, `wait`, `rm`, `inspect` (its NetworkMode its provider's ID, as dockerd keeps it,
  PM M169; its provider's hostname), and
  in its own namespaces and cgroup `exec`, `attach` (its stdin and output, never its
  provider's), `top`, `cp`, `export`, `diff`, `commit`, its size, `stats` and `update`,
  which init's built-ins do in its context. `pause` freezes its cgroup in the guest (init's FREEZE: `cgroup.freeze`,
  then `cgroup.events` until its `frozen` key says so, on the kernel's poll(2) event,
  where runc's v2 freezer looks every 10 ms), its provider running on; a
  provider's `pause` stops its whole microVM, its joiners with it, where Docker freezes
  the provider's cgroup alone. The daemon gives the provider's VM process the
  joiner's own connection and image (`kind::JOIN`); on that connection the joiner's run
  goes as a warm VM's run goes (`RUN`, `TAKEN`, `STARTED`, its log, `DONE`), so the daemon
  follows it as any run, and no command of the joiner's ever ends, pauses or reads its
  provider's VM as its own. In the guest the joiner is an exec of init's, PID 1 of a PID
  namespace of its own, its root its image's range on a loop device under a tmpfs
  overlay, Docker's mounts, a cgroup of its own under Docker's device rules.
- **It outlives its provider's command**, its own command its own to end (D119). As the workload ends,
  init kills every process but its joiners' (their `join-N` cgroups), says the workload's
  end at once, saves its writable layer if asked, and goes on serving the joiners; the
  microVM ends with its last run. Pod semantics, the joiners killed with the
  provider, was built first and dropped: a joiner finishing as its provider's command
  ended was killed (137) where Docker's finishes. Unlike Docker, its network stays whole
  (Docker's joiner keeps a namespace whose interfaces went with the provider's sandbox,
  the loopback alone); the provider's published ports and network names go with its run.
- **Its sysctls in its own namespaces**, written from within them:
  a child of init's enters the joiner's IPC, UTS and network namespaces and writes them,
  where init's own writes would be the provider's; a `net.*` one sets the namespace the
  two share, which a joiner may set on Docker too (runc libcontainer/configs/validate allows it where
  the network namespace is another container's). Tested, mutation-checked
  (`a_joiners_sysctls_are_set_in_its_namespaces`: written in init's namespaces, the
  joiner read the default).
- **Its changes, from its layers' descriptors.** Its root's layers are unreachable by
  path once it has entered its root, in a mount namespace that ends with it, so its child
  keeps them as init keeps the workload's: `O_PATH` descriptors of its image's layer and
  its writable one, opened before its root moves over them and handed to init with its
  users over a socket pair (`SCM_RIGHTS`). `diff` walks its root from within its mount
  namespace, where its `/proc` is its PID namespace's and has no `/proc/self` for init's
  child (Linux fs/proc/self.c: ENOENT where the reader has no PID), so the walk reaches
  the layers by descriptor alone (the image's from where it stands, the writable one
  opened a directory at a time, `O_NOFOLLOW`, never through a link the joiner put
  there), and reads the root's mount table through init's `/proc`, opened before
  entering. The workload's `diff` walks the same way. Its size and `commit` read its
  writable layer as init sees it; `commit` freezes its cgroup alone while it packs, where
  the workload's stops every process as dockerd pauses a container (moby
  daemon/commit.go). Tested (`a_joiners_own_commands_reach_the_joiner`: none before it
  writes, then `C /etc`, `D /etc/group`, `A /etc/variant`, `A /made`, committed and run).
  `top` of a joiner reads its `/proc`, whose PIDs are its namespace's: init's child no
  longer leaves out the one numbered as its own PID in init's (getpid(2) answers in the
  caller's namespace).
- **Its files kept as it stops**, as any run's (D37). After the joiner's end on its
  own connection, its VM process asks there for its writable layer (`kind::SAVE`), as for
  a run's; init keeps the joiner's connection and layers until the host has asked or
  closed it, and packs the layer in a child of its own, which writes to the connection:
  init's loop, serving the provider and the other joiners, never waits on it. So too the
  workload's own, once joiners outlive it, where init's loop packed it before and its
  joiners waited meanwhile; what init has for the host meanwhile follows the layer
  (`a_joiner_is_a_container_of_its_own`: the provider's file, saved as it ended beside its
  joiner, read once their microVM has gone; mutation-checked). The child goes on as the
  provider's command ends, however init then ends the rest of the microVM's processes:
  init spared it only where joiners outlived the command, and killed with the rest it cut
  the layer short, its host waiting for the rest and init for the host to close, so the
  run never ended (a `--use-api-socket` run whose member had ended, 3 rounds of 30 on
  x86_64 Linux, PM M296). And a child that fails, perhaps amid a frame, or is killed
  otherwise takes init's end of the connection with it: its host hears the end and keeps
  no layer (`a_joiners_layer_is_kept_whole_as_its_provider_ends`: a provider killed as its
  joiner's 256 MiB layer is sent; mutation-checked: killed with the rest, the layer is
  lost; without the close as well, the provider's run ends only as the daemon ends its
  microVM, 10 s after the kill). The provider's end is said at once where any joiner
  outlives it, running or ended with its layer still to come, not after that layer: held
  till the layer was sent, its end came after `kill`'s 10 s, whose escalation killed the
  microVM, the end and the rest of the layer with it (PM M303: 5 runs of 5 on the Mac, the
  provider's status 255; said at once, `kill` took 11 to 123 ms). From then on its guest
  takes the provider's layer asked for as one sent (`SAVE`), or its host's end of asking,
  and drops a `KEEP` (D190's layer kept in its file); so its VM asks `SAVE` of any microVM a
  joiner ever joined (warm.rs `joined`, ci-leaks). It asked `KEEP` where its count of joiners
  running read none, which a joiner whose end its guest had just said had left already, and
  each then waited on the other for ever, past the run and past its daemon (CI 43968984258,
  x86_64 musl: containers.rs `a_container_joins_another_containers_network` and
  engine_ring.rs `a_give_back_lets_an_idle_slot_go`, each provider's VM 20 minutes past its
  daemon's end, its `workload` thread reading its run's connection and its guest's relay
  never ended). That test now waits for its microVM's end too, its daemon going on. Its cost,
  a provider whose joiners all ended well before it packing its layer where it could have
  kept it in place, is unmeasured. Put back
  as it starts again: the VM process appends the layer to the join disk beside its image
  (`join-layer=OFFSET,LEN`), and the joiner's child applies it over its root as ApplyLayer
  does, before it reads its users and before anything is mounted in its root, with its
  root as its own (chroot(2)) so that no path or link of the layer resolves past it; the
  disk's pages it read are let go of as it reads them (`POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED`). Stopped, its
  files are visited as any stopped microVM's. Started again, its names are its
  provider's, given again at every start, since its provider's may have changed
  (containers.rs `a_joiner_keeps_its_files_as_it_stops`), and the create-time checks are
  not made again, being checks of what its create asked: before, the hostname its first
  start stored failed them. A
  joiner's layers, now let go of as all of it is said, no longer outlive a start that
  failed. Tested (`a_joiner_keeps_its_files_as_it_stops`: a file written and one removed,
  one copied in while it was stopped, all there after `start`; mutation-checked: the
  layer's entry left out, the create-time checks made again).
- **Its provider's PID namespace, or the microVM's** (Docker 29.3.1, PM M169). dockerd
  keeps another container's namespaces by its ID as the container is made, so that they
  hold as that one is renamed (daemon/daemon_unix.go, adaptSharedNamespaceContainer):
  shards keeps both modes so, where it kept the name as given. `--pid container:NAME`
  beside `--network container:NAME` naming the same run gives the joiner its provider's
  PID namespace, its child born there as an exec is (`pid=workload`); `--pid host`, the
  microVM's own, init's. Its command is then no namespace's PID 1, whose end the kernel
  would make the end of the rest, so init kills what is left in its cgroup as it ends, as
  runc kills what a container sharing one leaves (libcontainer signalAllProcesses), and
  removes the cgroup once all of it is said. `top` lists a run's processes by its
  cgroup, so that each lists its own: the workload's leave out the joiners' in its
  namespace. `--init` there is kept and not given, as dockerd gives its init only to a PID
  namespace of the container's own (daemon/oci_linux.go). `--pid container:` of another
  joiner takes the namespace that joiner's run took, as dockerd takes
  `/proc/PID/ns/pid` of its process: its own, which init knows by the joiner's exec's id,
  told the daemon with its start (`STARTED`'s payload, `pid=joiner=ID`); its provider's,
  or the microVM's, followed through any joiner that took another's; one not yet started
  is "container ID is not running", dockerd's errNotRunning. As that joiner ends, its
  namespace ends with everything in it, the kernel's doing, as with Docker. Refused:
  `--pid container:NAME` without its network, NAME's PID namespace being in NAME's
  microVM, where a network of its own is not built (D115). Tested
  (`a_joiner_may_share_its_providers_pid_namespace`: its PID 1 its provider's command,
  `top` of each, `--init` kept, an exec of its killed as it ends, `--pid host`, the
  refusals; `a_joiner_may_share_another_joiners_pid_namespace`: another joiner's command
  its PID 1, a third joiner through it, a joiner in its provider's passing that one
  on, the namespace's end its own; mutation-checked; `a_joiner_is_a_container_of_its_own`:
  its provider by ID).
- **`--init` in a PID namespace of its own**: a reaper is its first process, as the
  workload's is (D115), in its cgroup. Its user is the command's, which the joiner's own
  image names, and that image's users are read by its standby, born in the reaper's
  namespace as it builds its root: so the reaper, born first, lets go of init's
  descriptors at once and waits for its IDs, which init sends once the standby has
  reported its users, and init waits for it to be ready before the command may start, as
  for the workload: no process of the joiner's finds it root or holding init's
  descriptors. Tested (`a_joiner_under_init_has_a_reaper_of_its_own`: the command the
  namespace's second process, the reaper the image's user, `stop`'s SIGTERM ending at once
  a command that does not handle it; mutation-checked: no reaper, a reaper as root).
- **Devices and `--privileged`**, as the workload takes them (D44): the microVM's
  devices, found and given as dockerd and runc give a host's, their nodes made in the
  joiner's own `/dev` by a child of init's that enters its mount namespace (the
  workload's are made in the `/dev` init shares with it); its cgroup's filter, Docker's
  default as it is made, replaced by its own rules (`BPF_F_REPLACE`, its descriptor kept
  by the joiner's id until its cgroup goes) or, privileged, taken away, every device the
  microVM has then its, the provider's among them, as a privileged Docker container has
  its host's. Its I/O limits on its own cgroup, where the workload's were written whatever
  cgroup was named. Tested (`a_joiner_takes_devices_as_a_container_does`: Docker's
  default rules, a device at another path read and not written, a cgroup rule,
  `--privileged` opening the microVM's own; mutation-checked: its filter left the
  default).
- **Its volumes, through the microVM's join share.** A microVM's shares are its own
  run's (D38), each a virtio-fs device that run's share process serves; a joiner's come
  after boot, and a microVM has no hotplug, so every microVM carries one more virtio-fs
  device, its join share, served by none until a joiner brings volumes (its cost, PM
  M170: no memory per VM resolved, `phys_footprint` +0 KiB [−32, +32]; no restore time
  resolved; every template keyed by it, so none saved without one is restored as one
  with it). The first joiner to bring any starts the microVM's join share process
  (`shards share --join`), whose server's root is an empty directory of the home's,
  nothing made in it and nothing of it listed, each volume found there by its name alone;
  the VM is given the connection to it in a message of its own (`kind::JOIN_SHARE`),
  before that joiner's `JOIN` and so before any guest mounts the share. Each joiner's
  volumes go to the process on a link of the joiner's own (`kind::JOIN_LINK`,
  `kind::JOIN_VOLUME`, each answered), named so that no other joiner can guess them
  (256 random bits, as a run's ID), and are served until the link closes: at the
  joiner's end, or as a start fails. In the guest the joiner's standby, its root built,
  mounts the share in its own mount namespace, binds each volume from it as a run's are
  mounted (a file alone where one is bound; the image's files copied into an empty
  named volume, populateVolume; read-only by a remount of the bind), then lets the
  share's mount go: the joiner's root holds its own volumes and no way to the others'.
  Its destinations resolve in its own root, as the workload's do in its. The share is
  never mounted read-only itself: every joiner's mount of it is of one file system, read-only
  for all from a first mount that were. The server keys each node by its volume as well
  as its device and inode (one directory given read-only to one joiner and writable to
  another is two nodes), refuses a read-only volume's writes itself, moves nothing between
  volumes (EXDEV, as between two binds), shows a volume of one name as that name alone,
  and lets go of every node, handle and descriptor at a session's end (DESTROY, or the
  next INIT): the guest's kernel forgets a share's nodes without FORGET as its last mount
  goes (Linux fs/fuse/inode.c, fuse_evict_inode, only while SB_ACTIVE), and a join share
  is mounted again by each joiner after the last has ended. Tested
  (`a_joiner_takes_volumes_as_a_container_does`: a host directory both ways, read-only, a
  file alone, a named volume filled from its image, an image's `VOLUME`, `cp` from a
  volume, none of them its provider's or another joiner's, given again as it starts
  again; mutation-checked: the bind's read-only remount left out; unit tests of the
  server's volumes, sessions and listings, and of a link's volumes going as it closes, each
  mutation-checked).
- **Its boundary is a container's, within the microVM.** A joiner given `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`
  mounts none of the microVM's shares: docker-default's mount rule holds it, as it holds
  every workload (D121); under `apparmor=unconfined` the join share's root shows nothing
  and its volumes are reached only by names it has learned. One given
  `CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH` may open what the guest's kernel holds of the join share by handle
  (open_by_handle_at, Docker's reason to withhold it); a privileged one has the whole
  microVM, as a privileged Docker container has its host.
- **Not yet, refused by name before anything starts:** an Agentfile's image.
- **No count of holders.** A VM process runs one VM, so its join disk is a `static` of
  that process's (`Join::new` is a `const fn`), its device given `&'static Join`; a
  joiner's attached clients are kept by its id in the guest, as the workload's are. The
  disk keeps the transport's interrupt only while the driver has the device, taken once
  at activation.

### D117. Templates no VM process can forge, and VM starts the host has not admitted

A template is saved by a VM process into the directory it is granted, and every later run
of its image restores it. Review 8.2 took the directory from the VM before the run's
command reaches the guest: a second Landlock layer on Linux, the rename into place on
macOS (M102). Audit Q asked what a VM taken over while it still held the directory could
leave there, and what reads it.
- **Measured (M165).** On macOS the rename seals it: after it, neither a descriptor of the
  directory opened before nor the bookmark resolved again makes or rewrites anything. A
  link planted before stays in the template, as Linux keeps what was made before its
  layer.
- **Found.** Three readers followed what such a VM leaves:
  - the daemon wrote its record of the template (`origin.json`, the root filesystem
    restores are given as `--backing`, D25) into the template, with `std::fs::write`,
    while the VM could still write there: a link planted at that name had the daemon
    write its JSON into a file of the user's (`a_templates_saver_leaves_nothing_the_daemon_writes_through`,
    on the code before); a record planted there named the file every restore of the
    template was given, once a daemon read it back (refill);
  - the daemon and the restoring VM read the pointer, state, memory and working set by
    path, following links and waiting on FIFOs;
  - the macOS grant broker opened whatever a restoring VM asked for, following links: a
    generation's memory planted as a link opened any file of the user's for every restore
    of the template, a FIFO held the broker (`a_restore_reaches_nothing_its_saver_left_in_its_template`).
- **Now.**
  - The daemon's record is beside the template (`templates/<name>.origin`), in the
    directory no VM process is granted, written whole under a name of its own and renamed
    into place, read through no link and as a regular file alone; the collector removes
    it with its template, and one whose template is gone.
  - A snapshot's files are opened beneath its directory, a component at a time, through
    no link, regular files alone, refused before they are opened and checked again after
    (vmm `open_beneath`): the pointer, state, memory and working set, by the daemon, the
    restoring VM and its broker; a working set is written into a generation opened so.
  - The broker knows a restore's template (the pool's directory; `--template` for
    `shards grants`): what is asked beneath it is opened so, and nothing of it is granted
    for writing.
- **Why a check of each name is enough.** A template is read only once it is given up
  (renamed out of the VM's grant, or behind Linux's second layer): what was left in it no
  longer changes, so each directory below it is checked with `lstat`, the file too, which
  must be regular (a FIFO is never opened), and the file is then opened `O_NOFOLLOW` and
  checked again. A restore's four files cost 12 µs more at p50 so (M165).
- **Tested.** The two E2E escape tests above, each written as a taken-over VM would act and
  each failing on the code before (c1c2525's record; the broker's rule off); unit tests
  of the walk, the broker and the record; mutation-checked.
- **Recorded difference.** A template saved before has its record inside it and none
  beside it: it is saved again, once.

**VM starts the host has not admitted (M166).** On macOS a launch runs nothing until the
system has assessed the executable (amfid; syspolicyd's Gatekeeper scan, with a network
lookup of its notarization and XProtect's analysis; secinitd's App Sandbox set-up), and
every launch waits behind the executables launched before it, assessed about one at a
time. The VM process launched before starts in 21 ms at p50 and 60 at p99 (10,000, 16 at
once, load 60); a new copy in 200 ms alone and 8.6 s at p50 behind 64 others; while those
are assessed, the established one's launches take 1.6 s at p90 and 2.9 s at p99. A
process waiting there has run nothing, no system call and no user time, and sample(1)
shows nothing of it.
- Such a VM asked for nothing, and the daemon counted its wait a failure of its template:
  three removed the template and booted instead, adding another launch to the same wait.
  Now a VM the host has not let run is told apart (`platform::launched`), logged as the
  host's at the stall check rather than sampled, and counts against no template; a
  builder that does not dial back in BOOT_PATIENCE says whether the host had started it.
  No budget changes.
- The "VM grant stall" (60 s) and "the builder did not start" (30 s) fit this at a
  backlog of a few hundred new executables, as parallel builds make on this host. Those
  incidents were not captured; the next one is attributed in daemon.log.

### D116. Signatures and SBOMs of agents, harnesses and MCP servers, as OCI 1.1 referrers

§8 Q1 gave OSI artifacts "signatures and SBOMs as its referrers". Now they have them,
from the registry layer up to the build's policies.

- **Referrers** as distribution-spec and image-spec v1.1.1 have them
  (`shards_registry::referrers`).
  - A referrer is pushed by digest, after what it names.
  - Where the registry did not answer `OCI-Subject` (spec.md:499) and lists none by the
    API, the subject's list under the tag schema is updated: `<alg>-<ref>`, the reference
    cut to 64 characters. The entry is added once, with the manifest's `artifactType`
    (else its config's type) and its annotations (spec.md:501-511, 722-731). A tag naming
    something other than an index fails, and nothing is put.
  - Listing reads every page of the API (`Link: rel="next"`), at most a manifest's size
    in all, else the tag schema's index. It filters by artifact type where the registry
    did not.
  - Deleting needs distribution's `delete` scope. It removes the entry from the list
    where there is no API (spec.md:695-699).
  - Measured (PM M135): distribution v3.1.2 has no referrers API; zot v2.1.22 has it.
- **Signatures, as cosign v3.1.3 makes them with a key** (`shards_sigstore::sign`,
  `cosignkey`, `secretbox`). `shards sign agent|harness|mcp NAME --key FILE` signs what
  NAME resolves to: the index of several platforms, else the manifest, as cosign signs
  the digest a name resolves to.
  - Format: cosign's `sign/v1` in-toto statement, in a DSSE envelope, in a bundle v0.3
    naming the key by its hint. The referrer manifest is the one cosign's
    `WriteReferrer` writes, byte for byte apart from the time.
  - Keys: cosign's own (generate-key-pair, import-key-pair). They are read as cosign's
    `LoadPrivateKey` reads them.
    - go-securesystemslib's JSON, read as Go reads it.
    - Its three scrypt parameter sets alone, as its `CheckParams` allows (encrypted.go:
      125-139). AWS-LC's scrypt is given exactly their memory.
    - NaCl's secretbox: XSalsa20, written here and held to x/crypto, and AWS-LC's
      Poly1305, the tag compared in constant time.
    - Each refusal is worded as cosign words it.
    - Signing follows sigstore's default for each key type: ECDSA P-256, P-384 and P-521,
      Ed25519ph (as cosign signs Ed25519 keys), and RSA PKCS #1 v1.5.
    - The password is `COSIGN_PASSWORD`'s, else asked on the terminal, not echoed.
  - The signature is kept with the name and pushed by `shards push image`.
  - A key's signature is uploaded to no transparency log, as cosign signs with a signing
    config naming none; cosign then verifies with `--insecure-ignore-tlog`, as M135
    measured. Keyless signing came with D126.
  - Held to cosign by:
    - `scripts/cosign/generate`: LoadPrivateKey's answers for 27 keys, and 14
      secretboxes x/crypto sealed;
    - what cosign wrote (`testdata/cosign/measured.json`, verified here);
    - cosign verifying shards' signatures on both registries (M135).
- **SBOMs.** `shards build agent --sbom[=…]`, read as buildx reads `--sbom` (crates/cmdline/tests/buildx.json), runs the
  scanner over the artifact's content. It is a build of that content alone (`FROM
  scratch`, `COPY --exclude=<config>`), scanned as D81 scans a result.
  - The result's SPDX document is the one layer of a referrer of type
    `application/spdx+json` (IANA-registered to the Linux Foundation). Its config is the
    empty one, per image-spec's guidelines for artifacts.
  - There is one for each platform's manifest, kept and pushed.
- **Pull, inspect, delete.**
  - `shards pull agent`, and a build's pull of an artifact, takes its referrers as the
    registry lists them, in place of those kept: one deleted there goes here too.
  - A tag schema list is written by anyone who may push. A referrer that refers to
    another object is left, and said.
  - `shards inspect agent` lists the referrers.
  - `shards rm agent NAME --referrer DIGEST` deletes one from the registry, and its list
    entry, and lets go of it here.
- **Policies** (D101–D107), the one trust mechanism, rather than a new one. An
  `osi-artifact://` source was refused by `--policy` ("unsupported source scheme"), and
  was checked only after it was fetched.
  - To a policy it is now `input.image`, an object of a registry as an image is. It has
    the digest its name resolves to and `artifactType`, which no image has; an image's
    input is buildx's, byte for byte, as before.
  - Its `signatures` are its keyless cosign signatures, verified as the policy helpers'
    `VerifyArtifact` verifies an artifact's (Fulcio, SCTs, a log entry), of cosign's
    signature predicate.
  - `verify_image_signature(input.image, "cosign.pub")` is shards' own function, on
    buildx's `verify_*` pattern. It holds an artifact to a key the policy names, as
    `cosign verify --key` does.
  - It is asked by name before it is taken, as a base is before its metadata, then
    pinned with the definition. A pin of one is refused in BuildKit's words (D116).
  - `shards buildx policy eval osi-artifact://NAME` asks the same of an artifact on its
    own, before or after `shards pull image`, its kind read from its manifest.
- **At run** (the standing rule's twin). The brief assumed the normalized Agentfile names
  each artifact by digest; it names it as written.
  - A run re-verifies nothing per start. Signatures need the registry and the build's
    policy, against a 5 ms start.
  - A run cannot compare an agent's content to its artifact: the agent's layer is that
    content under `/agents/<name>`, of another diff ID.
  - The image as built is what runs: its layers content-addressed, its Agentfile checked
    against its digest at every run (D109).
  - So the build now records each artifact it took in the image's provenance, by
    digest, as a package-url of the `oci` type (purl-spec types/oci-definition.json).
    A signed image vouches for that list; a policy over the image skips the material
    with a warning, as buildx does any it cannot read, so that a policy written for buildx
    decides alike (D116).
- **Recorded differences from cosign:**
  - The tag schema's list carries the manifest's annotations, which the spec asks for
    and cosign leaves out.
  - A pull replaces the referrers kept with those listed.
  - An artifact of several platforms has its SBOM per platform.
- **Tested.**
  - `signatures_are_referrers_pushed_pulled_and_deleted_as_cosigns_are` covers both
    kinds of registry and a stray referrer; what it pushed verifies as cosign verifies.
  - `an_index_is_what_a_signature_of_several_platforms_names`.
  - `policies_hold_an_agent_to_its_signature` covers:
    - unsigned refused, signed allowed, another key refused;
    - a build elsewhere taking the agent with its signature;
    - a pin refused;
    - `policy eval`;
    - the provenance's material.
  - `an_agents_sbom_is_a_scanned_referrer`, on microVMs.
  - Unit and oracle tests in shards-registry, shards-sigstore and shards-image.
  - 32 mutants killed.
- **Open:**
  - Keyless signing (Fulcio, Rekor) and timestamped signatures (a TSA): done, D126.
  - An SBOM signed as an attestation.
  - Conditional (`If-Match`) updates of the tag schema's list. The spec's MAY;
    distribution takes none; concurrent pushers can lose an entry (spec.md:733-735).

### D115. A run's command reaches none of its image's agents and harnesses

An Agentfile's image runs its agents and harnesses beside the run's own command (D59),
each a domain confined in namespaces, IDs, a cgroup, Landlock and seccomp of its own. But
the command itself — the workload the run's `docker run`-style request starts — ran in the
microVM's own namespaces: its PID namespace was init's, which holds every process of the
microVM. So the command saw each agent's processes in `/proc`, and Docker's default
capabilities include `CAP_KILL`, so a root command could signal them; with `--privileged`
or `--cap-add`, it could trace them, read their memory and environment, enter their network
namespaces and use their grants, or reach the kernel they share. The agents were confined
from each other and from the world; the command was not confined from them.

The user's standing rule (2026-10-09): every security property needs a build-time check
*and* a run-time check, because an image can be crafted and the CLI mutates a run
([[feedback-runtime-and-buildtime-checks]]). D109 did this for volumes; D115 does it for
the rest of a run's reach into its domains.

- **The command is PID 1 of a PID namespace of its own, as a container's is.** Every domain
  already has a PID namespace of its own (D59), but each is a child of init's, which the
  command shared; a parent namespace sees into its children, so the command saw every
  agent's processes. shards-init now forks the run's standby (before the template's
  snapshot, M27) as the first process of a new PID namespace, a sibling of the domains':
  siblings do not see into each other, so the command sees none of the microVM's other
  processes — no agent, no in-VM server, no init — and is that namespace's PID 1, as
  Docker makes a container's command (`docker run alpine sh -c 'echo $$'` prints 1; every
  case here measured against Docker 29.3.1, PM M145). It has PID 1's signals
  (pid_namespaces(7); kernel/signal.c, sig_task_ignored): from inside the namespace only
  those it handles (`kill -TERM 1` and `kill -KILL 1` go unheard); from outside SIGKILL
  and SIGSTOP always, any other only where it handles it, so `stop` of a command that does
  not handle SIGTERM waits out its timeout and kills it, 137, with a second `kill` event,
  the events a client waiting on a stop reads (D115). The kernel ends the namespace, and the execs in it, with it; the
  orphans there are its to reap, as a container's command's are (`--init` takes them);
  init still waits for it and signals it across the namespace boundary.
  An exec joins its namespace (its `$$` is not 1; `/proc/1` is the command); a restart is
  a new microVM and a new namespace, the command PID 1 again. init takes its own PID
