  - A `/dev` holding Docker's six nodes (moby `DefaultLinuxDevices` less the console),
    runc's `fd`/`stdin`/`stdout`/`stderr` links and a `shm` of its own, remounted
    read-only.
  - A scratch `/tmp` of its own, mode 700 and its uid's, lost when it ends.
- **Only a loopback**, brought up; network grants are part three.
- **Its stdio:** stdin is `/dev/null`; stdout and stderr are pipes of their own, which init
  captures whole for its owner (D240). Where the run names no owner of a member's output
  (`shards.output`), the daemon reads it itself, keeps it in the member's log
  (`members/<index>` in the run's directory, as the run's log is kept, its label beside it)
  and shows it to a client attached to the run on that client's **stderr**, each line
  prefixed `[agent main] ` and written whole; `shards read logs` shows the same lines after
  the run's own output, and follows them with `-f`. The run's own stdout, stderr and log stay
  its command's. No member waits on a reader: the daemon credits a channel again as soon as
  what came is kept, a detached run's and one whose client has gone alike (PM M543). As the
  run ends, all such a member wrote is kept and shown before the run's end is said: init
  reads its pipes to their ends, which the run's end brings as it ends the member, and the
  daemon tells the run's end once its capture has kept the last of it (PM M543, "Lost at the
  run's end"). Every descriptor past 2
  is closed before exec. Every descriptor init holds is close-on-exec today, which the
  mutation shows: without the close, nothing of init's reaches the agent. The close is
  there so that one descriptor not marked close-on-exec, such as the O_PATH descriptors
  of the image's layers that `diff` keeps, cannot become a way into another domain.
- **Its command:** as its config says. A relative program is its directory's, and a bare
  name is found on Docker's default `PATH` before the clone. After the clone the child
  only calls the kernel: no allocation, as it is the fork of a process that may run
  threads. A failed step writes `shards-init: <step>: errno N` on its output.

The workload's end ends the domains, as it ends every process of the microVM.

Tested: `agents_run_in_their_domains` boots a real microVM. Its agent comes from an OSI
artifact pushed to a registry; beside it is an agent of files alone. The agent reports:

- uid and gid 200000, no groups;
- PID 2 of its PID namespace, under init's sealed reaper (PID 1; D59's owned native domain
  lifetime above), the two alone in its `/proc`;
- its host name;
- all five capability sets empty, and `no_new_privs`;
- the other agent's directory and `/sys` unreadable (EACCES);
- its `/dev`, and its descriptors (stdio alone);
- its own directory and `/etc` read-only (EROFS), `/tmp` writable;
- only `lo`.

The run's stdout stays empty, and the agent of files alone runs nothing. Each of these
mutations fails the test: hiding no other domain, keeping the bounding set, leaving the
system writable.

**A member's root shows the image's directories as the image made them** (2026-11-12,
kiln plan 01a1cd8e862e7169a074db3d5fa33f3d, step 7). A domain's root is an overlay of the
image under a skeleton tmpfs. The skeleton holds what init mounts over and the image may
lack: `/etc` always, and every mount point of its sockets, its server and its volumes, each
with its parents. overlayfs shows a directory both layers hold with the upper one's owner
and mode (Documentation/filesystems/overlayfs.rst, "Directories"), and the skeleton made
every directory root's, 0755. So a volume at `/home/node/.cache` showed the image's
`/home/node` (1000:1000 0750) as 0:0 0755, and `/etc` and the root as the skeleton's too.
Reproduced live with init's system calls in its order, in a user and mount namespace with
subordinate IDs on Linux 7.2.9 x86_64 (`docs/research/measurements/s7-home-workdir`,
`repro.py`, `repro-adacachy.log`).

Now each directory the skeleton makes that the image has takes the image's owner and mode
(fchownat, then fchmodat: a chown clears set-ID bits), and the skeleton's tmpfs root takes
the image root's (its `mode`, `uid` and `gid` options). A directory the image lacks stays
root's, 0755, as a mount point's. `a_skeletons_directories_are_the_images_own` runs the
real `skeleton` and `image_root` in a user and mount namespace and compares the root,
`/home`, `/home/node`, `/etc` and `/tmp` with the image's, and their owners too where it
runs as root of IDs past its own (`unshare --map-auto --map-root-user`). It fails at the
base revision, and with either guard removed: the owner and mode copied, the root's options
(`mutate4.sh`, `mutate4-adacachy.log`). Where a domain has plug roots (D235), its root's
own writable layer is the uppermost for `/`, and D235's `image_root` gives that layer the
image root's owner and mode. **Owed (ROOT):** the same in a real microVM on KVM,
Hypervisor.framework and WHP.

**A member's environment: init's, the image's, its own, its run's** (2026-11-12, kiln plan
01a1cd8e862e7169a074db3d5fa33f3d, step 7). A member got init's `PATH` (its directory, its
`bin`, Docker's), `HOME=/tmp` and `SHARDS_DOMAIN`, then its config's `run.env` (997f4e47e),
then what D231 stages: none of the image's own `Env`. The sources on that order:
- OCI image-spec v1.1.0 config.md, `Env`: "These values act as defaults and are merged with
  any specified when creating a container."
- moby docker-v29.0.0 daemon/commit.go, `merge`: the run's `-e` kept, and each of the image's
  appended whose name it does not give; then `CreateDaemonEnvironment` lays that over Docker's
  own `PATH` and `HOSTNAME` (daemon/container/env.go, `ReplaceOrAppendEnvValues`).
- Kubernetes, "Define Environment Variables for a Container": "The environment variables set
  using the env or envFrom field override any environment variables specified in the container
  image."
- D231: what is staged goes "over its image's".

So a member's environment is, the last given of each name winning: init's own; over it, the
image's `Env`; over that, its config's `run.env`, its own, as a pod's container's `env` goes
over its image's, where the image's is every member's and the run's command's alike; over all,
what its run stages. Two names keep init's rules:
- **`PATH`**: init's is the member's directory and its `bin`, then the image's `PATH` where it
  gives one, else Docker's: the image's replaces Docker's default, as in a container, and a
  member's own program is still found before the system's (part one). Its program is found on
  the `PATH` it runs with, a staged one included, where it was found on `run.env`'s alone.
  Confine-04: init prepares candidate strings with ordinary exec's PATH composer,
  but the member's child searches only after its mounts, confinement and cwd are
  established. Empty components mean cwd; relative components remain relative to
  that cwd. No executable availability/access decision is made in init's view.
- **`HOME`**: never the image's. One value for every member is private to none, which a
  member's `HOME` must be (step 7's acceptance), and the system it would name is read-only to
  a domain. A member's `HOME` is its scratch unless its own `run.env`, or its run, names one.

`SHARDS_DOMAIN` in the image's `Env` is refused, as in `run.env` and in staging, at each end:
the build of an image with agents or harnesses (`agentfile::image_env`, `ImageEnvRefused`), the
daemon's and the run host's reading of the image (`run::prepare`, `agentfile::members_env`),
and init (`shards_abi::run::members::image_envs`), all in the build's words. The image's
`Env` reaches init as `image-env=` setup entries, beside the domains' filter. An image of
neither agents nor harnesses keeps its `ENV` as BuildKit writes it. Tests: the order, the two
rules and the refusals (`a_members_environment_is_inits_then_its_images_then_its_own`); the
program found on the `PATH` it runs with
(`a_members_program_is_found_on_the_path_it_runs_with`); the entries made and read
(`the_images_variables_are_checked_as_staged_ones`); the daemon's
(`the_images_environment_is_its_members_as_its_build_checks_it`); the build's
(`an_image_with_members_never_names_their_domain_in_its_env`). **Owed (ROOT):** a member's
`env` in a real microVM on KVM, Hypervisor.framework and WHP, of an image whose `ENV` sets
`PATH`, `HOME` and another name.

Part two, after `no_new_privs`, before its command:

- **Landlock** (Documentation/userspace-api/landlock.rst; ABI 6 at least, which Linux 6.12
  brought and the pinned 6.18 has). A domain refuses to start on a kernel without it,
  rather than run unconfined. The ruleset handles every filesystem right and gives back
  reads and execution everywhere, writes and device ioctls in `/dev`, and everything in
  its `/tmp` and `/dev/shm`. It handles TCP bind and connect and gives neither, as no
  network grant exists yet. Signals and abstract Unix sockets are scoped to the domain.
  It is a second layer under the mounts: it refuses what the mounts allow, such as
  writing its own `/proc/self/comm`, and TCP on its own loopback.
- **seccomp**, compiled by the host with the run's own compiler (D41, held to libseccomp)
  and sent to init in a setup entry (`domains-seccomp=`). The daemon sends it for an image
  carrying the Agentfile label, and init starts no domain without it. Its profile is
  Docker's default compiled for no capability, which leaves bpf and perf_event_open, there
  only on capabilities' lists, refused. Docker's own allow lists already lack io_uring,
  keyctl, add_key, request_key and userfaultfd (moby profiles v0.2.3 `default.json`). Its
  `socket` rules, which refuse only AF_ALG and AF_VSOCK, are replaced by `socket` for
  AF_UNIX, AF_INET and AF_INET6 and `socketpair` for AF_UNIX alone, so netlink, packet
  and every other family is refused (EPERM). Measured by the test: without the filter, a
  domain opens AF_VSOCK, the host's channel (§9.7), and netlink.
- **`kernel.io_uring_disabled`** is not set. The domain filter refuses io_uring already.
  The sysctl is the whole guest's, so all it would add is refusing io_uring to the run's
  own workload where its owner asked for `seccomp=unconfined`, against what they asked.

Tested: the same E2E test, the agent also reporting:

- writing `/proc/self/comm` refused (EACCES);
- TCP bind and connect on its loopback refused (EACCES);
- AF_VSOCK and AF_NETLINK sockets, `io_uring_setup`, `keyctl` and `userfaultfd` refused
  (EPERM);
- Unix and IPv6 sockets made.

Mutation-checked:

- no Landlock: the write and the bind go through, and the connect is refused only for
  want of a listener;
- no filter loaded: vsock and netlink sockets are made;
- the daemon sending none: the run fails, naming the missing filter;
- Docker's unmodified default sent: netlink is allowed.

**`--processes=none`** (§9.9) is a filter of its own, `domains-seccomp-none=`. Its
`pids.max` is left as the microVM's, because pids.max counts threads and such a domain may
start them. The filter refuses `fork` and `vfork`. It allows `clone` only with
`CLONE_THREAD` set and no namespace flag: Docker's own mask 0x7E020000 plus CLONE_THREAD's
bit, `SCMP_CMP_MASKED_EQ`. `clone3`, whose flags a filter cannot read, already fails with
ENOSYS for no capability under Docker's profile, and musl and glibc then fall back to
`clone`. `execve` stays: it starts no process. Tested by a third agent declared
`--processes=none` from the same artifact: its thread starts and its `fork` is refused
(EPERM), while the first agent forks. Mutation-checked: compiling the ordinary domain
filter for it lets the fork through. Every other way to start a process is tried too
(§9.10): `vfork` as the kernel makes it (x86_64's own call, arm64's `clone` with CLONE_VM
and CLONE_VFORK, issued so that the child touches no memory: libc's `vfork` is
deprecated for the stack its child corrupts), a `clone` that is no thread, `clone3`
(ENOSYS for every domain), a spawn as libc makes it, and so any program run: each refused
(EPERM), each made by the first agent. Mutation-checked: `clone` left (D59), as Docker's rule lets
musl's `fork`, itself a `clone`, through.

The same test plants the file escapes of §9.10: a symlink in its scratch to another
domain's file, followed (EACCES: the domain is hidden); a hard link to it (EACCES) and to
the system's (EXDEV, another filesystem); and a set-user-ID-root program of the system
(`COPY --chmod=4755`) run, which runs as the agent (uid and euid 200000). Two guards hold
that: the system is mounted `nosuid`, which the agent sees (`statvfs`), and
`no_new_privs` (`nnp=1`), which Landlock and seccomp need besides. Mutation-checked: the
system mounted without `nosuid` fails the `nosuid` line while `no_new_privs` keeps the
euid; `no_new_privs` cannot be dropped alone, as no domain then starts.

Part three, network grants between domains (AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §4.6, §4.7, §9.7):

- **The switch.** Init makes a network namespace of no process's, held by a descriptor
  for as long as the microVM runs. Its forwarding is on. Each domain with a grant gets
  one veth link: `eth0` in its namespace, `d<n>` in the switch's. Each link is made in
  init's namespace, with both ends placed by `IFLA_NET_NS_FD` and their interface indexes
  chosen in advance, so the rules can name links before the links exist. Neither the
  switch nor any link touches the microVM's own namespace, its `eth0` or its workload.
- **Policy by link, never by address** (§9.7), in nf_tables, which init programs over
  nfnetlink in one transaction:
  - an `input` chain that drops everything, so no domain reaches the switch itself;
  - a `forward` chain that drops by default, accepts conntrack's established and related
    traffic, and accepts new traffic from `iif d<x>` to `oif d<y>` for each allowed pair.

  Whatever the protocol, UDP included, nothing else crosses.
- **Who may reach whom** (`netplan`). A network's members are the domains its `CONNECT …
  ON` names. Members reach each other (§4.6), except that `CONNECT x TO y` lets `y` only
  answer `x` (§4.7), unless another directive grants `y` to `x` outright. A domain has one
  link, so a pair any shared network allows is allowed. D58's reach graph reads a shared
  network the same way.
- **Addresses.** A network's subnet is its first IPv4 `--subnet`, or else the first /24
  of 10.244.0.0/16 that overlaps neither eth0's subnet nor a declared one. Its gateway is
  its first `--gateway`, or else `.1`. Members take addresses from `.2` in domain order.
  A domain holds each address as a /32 and routes the subnet through the gateway on its
  link (`RTNH_F_ONLINK`). The switch holds each gateway on each link that uses it, and a
  /32 route to each domain's address.
- **Names.** Each domain's `/etc/hosts` is Docker's lines followed by each member of each
  network it joins. It is written in the domain's scratch and bind-mounted read-only over
  the system's.
- **Landlock follows the grants.** TCP connect is refused unless the domain opens
  connections to someone, and TCP bind unless someone may open connections to it.
- **Ordering.** Domains now start once the run's own files are written, not before: the
  run replaces `/etc/hosts`, and replacing a file that another mount namespace mounts
  over detaches that mount (fs/namespace.c, `__detach_mounts`). The test found this: a
  domain's names resolved, then stopped resolving once the run's file was written.

Tested: `agents_reach_only_what_connect_grants`, four agents on a real microVM:

- `CONNECT a TO b ON back`, `CONNECT d WITH d ON back`, `CONNECT c WITH c ON side`;
- `a` reaches `b` by name;
- `b` finds `a` listening, and its connection times out: the switch drops it, and Landlock
  allows it, since `b` may connect to `d`;
- `d` reaches both;
- `c`, alone on `side`, may neither bind nor connect;
- each agent's `/etc/hosts` holds its network's members alone, and `localhost` resolves.

Mutation-checked:

- a forward chain that accepts by default, and `TO` that restricts nothing: `b` reaches
  `a`;
- Landlock handling no TCP right: `c` binds;
- no `/etc/hosts` of its own: names fail.

The planner has unit tests for pairs, pool allocation clear of eth0, declared subnets and
gateways, and capacity.

Part four, egress past the microVM, by port (AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §4.1, §4.6):

- **What is granted.** Two boundaries, each its own grant, and a flow crossing both needs
  both (AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §12 answer 6). A domain may open flows past the microVM to a
  port where, of a network it joins that is not internal, both open it outward: the
  network's own grant (`--egress`, `--expose`) and the microVM's for that network
  (`EXPOSE … FOR` it, both ways or `AS egress`). Ranges meet where both cover them
  (`agentfile::boundary`, and the guest's planner alike). The first version of this part
  (368663d) took either grant alone as enough, which opened what the decided grammar keeps
  shut; the test now holds a port that only the network grants to the switch's drop. A
  domain's grants let it connect, as far as Landlock is concerned. The build records the union of all domains' grants in the
  image's label `vnd.osi.agentfile.egress` (`443,53/udp,8000-8010`), as it records the
  Agentfile's digest.
- **The host holds the microVM to the union.** A run of a labelled image hands its VM's
  network process `NET_POLICY` before the VM has the run (warm VMs start before their run
  is known). That makes the policy `Ports`: what `AllowAll` reaches, on those ports and
  protocols alone, and never the host itself, its loopback, link-local addresses,
  multicast or broadcast. Other ports are refused at once, a TCP reset or ICMP
  administratively prohibited, as the default deny refuses them. A VM whose network
  process does not take the policy goes, as one that does not take its ports.
- **The switch holds each domain to its own grants, by link.** A veth links the switch
  (`up0`) to init's namespace (`agents0`), on a link-local /30 of its own, and the
  switch's default route goes up it. Its forward chain admits `iif d<x> oif up0` only
  for x's protocol and a destination port within one of x's ranges (`meta l4proto`; the
  transport header's port, compared as network-order bytes). Every linked domain's
  default route goes through its first network's gateway, so a domain without grants is
  dropped by the switch, not left without a route.
- **Init's namespace forwards it out** (`ip_forward` on). Its forward chain drops all but
  answers and `agents0 → eth0`, which it marks; its postrouting chain gives what is
  marked eth0's address. That is the address the network process takes frames from, and
  it maps the flows to host sockets.
- **The run's own command reaches no more than it did.** The host now opens the agents'
  ports to the whole microVM, so init's `out` chain drops every new flow leaving eth0
  except to eth0's own subnet (the network's members, D46, and its resolver relay).

Tested: `agents_reach_past_the_microvm_what_their_networks_grant`. A real microVM and two
servers run on the host's address, one port granted to network `out`, one not:

- `a`, on `out`, reaches the granted port, and is dropped on the other;
- `b`, on an internal network that names the granted port too, is dropped, though
  Landlock lets it connect to its peer;
- the run's own command is dropped.

Mutation-checked, each failing the test:

- no port comparison in the switch: `a` reaches the other port, and the host refuses it
  (ECONNREFUSED), which shows its own policy holds;
- no `NET_POLICY` sent: the host's default deny refuses `a`;
- `out`'s drop made an accept: the run's command reaches the host;
- the planner ignoring `internal`: `b` reaches the host.

The host's `Ports` policy and its encoding, the build's union, and the planner's
per-domain grants have unit tests.

Part five, names past the microVM:

- **The host's resolvers answer them.** A VM's network process knows the host's resolvers:
  the daemon passes each `--resolver`, from `SHARDS_DNS` (`ADDR[:PORT]`, comma-separated,
  as `dockerd --dns` names them) or else the host's own IPv4 nameservers in
  `/etc/resolv.conf`. Under `Ports`, a query to the gateway's port 53 that the network's
  members do not answer goes to the first of them, (D59), as Docker's embedded DNS asks the
  host's for a name its network does not hold. It goes as a UDP flow keyed to the
  gateway, so the answer comes back from the gateway. The host asks, so a loopback
  resolver (a local cache, systemd-resolved's 127.0.0.53) serves as it is, where Docker
  must replace it for a container.
- **Only agents with egress ask.** Each such domain's `/etc/resolv.conf` names the
  microVM's gateway (`options ndots:0`), mounted read-only over the system's as its
  `/etc/hosts` is. The switch admits its UDP to the gateway's address, port 53, and
  nothing else of DNS; a domain without egress keeps the system's file, and its queries
  are dropped at the switch.

Tested: the egress test runs a resolver on the host (`SHARDS_DNS`). `a` reaches the
granted port by name; `b`, without egress, resolves nothing (EAI_AGAIN).
Mutation-checked: a network process that never forwards, and a switch with no rule for
DNS, each leave `a` unable to resolve.

Part six, ingress:

- **What is let in.** A port is let in past the microVM where both boundaries open it
  inward: the network's own grant (`--ingress`, `--expose`) and the microVM's for it
  (`EXPOSE … FOR` it, both ways or `AS ingress`). `shards run vm -p` publishes it as any
  port; `EXPOSE … AS egress` stays out of the image's exposed ports, so `-P` does not.
- **To whom.** To the network's member. Which of several members a connection is for, no
  directive says yet, so the build refuses a network with such ports and more than one
  member, naming them (`agentfile::ingress`), rather than guess, as D58 refuses a path
  that only an undesigned relay could allow.
- **How.** A published connection arrives at eth0 as any does. Init's namespace's `pre`
  chain (nat, prerouting, NF_IP_PRI_NAT_DST) gives it the agent's address, its `forward`
  chain accepts `eth0 → agents0` on those ports, and the switch accepts `up0 → d<x>` on
  them; answers return as established. The agent's Landlock lets it bind. A port the
  agent listens on that no grant lets in stays the run's own: published, it reaches the
  workload's namespace, not the agent.

Tested: `agents_answer_what_their_networks_let_in`, a detached run publishing 7100 and
7200. The agent listens on both; 7100, which `front` lets in, answers with its host name,
and 7200, which nothing lets in, does not reach it. The build's refusal of a network of
two members has a unit test. Mutation-checked: no DNAT, and no switch rule, each leave
7100 unanswered.

Open: ingress to a network of several members (which one a connection is for). DNS over
TCP is D79.

A port the Agentfile declares `EXPOSE … AS egress`, and nowhere both ways or for ingress,
is named in the image's label `vnd.osi.agentfile.egress-declared` (D59; ranges as Docker writes
them). A run that publishes one, by `-p` or `-P`, is refused before its microVM is made:
an egress port is where agents reach out to, not where they listen (answer 6). Tested by
the ingress test (`-p` of an egress-declared port refused, its words), mutation-checked;
the label's ports by a unit test. (`--ingress`, `EXPOSE … AS ingress`: a published port to a
domain); remote MCP servers, whose grant names one destination and not a port; IPv6
subnets; process events; §9.10's escape tests beyond these.

### Default deny, made exact (D59, part seven)

Raised 2026-10-06 by the user, and now a rule of the project (CLAUDE.md): networks in a
shards microVM are default deny, and every agent is airgapped unless configured
otherwise. Parts three to six had let implicit grants through, each now removed:

- **Membership granted flows.** Members of a network reached one another (my reading of
  §4.6's "may communicate with one another"), with `TO` only restricting a direction.
  Now membership grants nothing; a flow exists only where a `CONNECT` names it.
- **Pairs reached every port.** A `CONNECT` pair passed any port and protocol. Now
  `CONNECT --port=<port>[/tcp|/udp]` (repeatable, ranges, TCP by default) names what the
  receiver accepts, and the switch passes those alone (`iif d<x> oif d<y>`, `meta
  l4proto`, the destination port's range). A `CONNECT` between agents with no `--port`
  is a build error; one naming one agent alone attaches it and grants nothing.
- **The network was no boundary inside the microVM.** A `CONNECT` port must lie within
  what each of its networks lets in (`NETWORK --ingress` or `--expose`), checked at build
  (`agentfile::connections`), as answer 6's two boundaries apply inside as at the edge.
- **Names of peers out of reach.** Each agent's `/etc/hosts` listed every member. It now
  lists the agent and the peers it is granted a flow to.
- **DNS came with egress.** It is now its own grant: `NETWORK --dns` (any name, on a
  network that is not internal), or a remote `MCP` server's host name alone.

**The agents' resolver** (`agentdns`), a process of init's in the switch's namespace,
answers on every switch address, so each agent asks its own gateway. It knows who asks
by the link the question arrives on (`IP_PKTINFO`'s interface index), not by any address
an agent could claim, and answers from the address asked. It forwards a granted question
to the network process under an ID of its own, never holding one query behind another,
and answers the rest REFUSED at once. The network process forwards what its policy
allows: any name if the image's label says `--dns`, else the remote MCP servers' host
names, REFUSED otherwise. That is the union of the agents' grants, held per agent by the
relay; the test's case shows why both are needed: an agent with an MCP grant alone beside
one whose network grants `--dns` (so the host allows any name) still has its other
names refused.

**Remote MCP servers are grants of that server alone** (§4.4, §9.6). The build labels
each server's `host:port` (`vnd.osi.agentfile.mcp`). An agent its `FOR` names (every
agent, with no `FOR`; no harness) gets a link, a network of its own if it has none, the
server's port up the switch, and its host's name at the relay. The network process lets a
TCP flow to that port reach only the addresses its resolver answered for the name through
this process (it reads each forwarded answer's A records, RFC 1035 §4.1), or the address
the URL names. Before the name is resolved, no address of it is reachable.

**What an agent cannot tamper with.** Nothing that enforces this runs where an agent can
reach it: the switch's rules, the agents' resolver and the network process are outside its
namespaces; it holds no capability (no `CAP_NET_ADMIN` to change its address or routes,
no `CAP_NET_RAW` for a raw socket), seccomp refuses netlink and packet sockets, and its
`/etc/hosts` and `/etc/resolv.conf` are read-only mounts of its own namespace. Identity is
by link, never by address: the switch's rules match the arriving and leaving link, the
relay the arriving one, and the switch's namespace runs strict reverse-path filtering
(RFC 3704 §2.2, `rp_filter` 1) so that a packet on an agent's link from any address not
its own is dropped by the kernel, as a second layer under the capabilities that keep it
from being sent at all.

Found while testing: the switch's `input` chain, dropping by default, dropped the
answers to the relay's own questions upstream until it took conntrack's established
traffic; and an edit that set `IP_PKTINFO` had not landed, so the relay received
questions with no arrival and dropped them, which a probe of the control data showed.

Tested on real microVMs:

- `agents_reach_only_what_connect_grants`: `CONNECT --port=7000 a TO b` reaches b on
  7000 and not on 7001, where b listens too; b's way back to a is dropped; d, paired with
  b alone, reaches b and not a, a member of the same network; each agent's names are its
  own and its granted peers';
- `agents_reach_past_the_microvm_what_their_networks_grant`: names past the microVM with
  `--dns`, and none without;
- `a_remote_mcp_server_is_a_grant_of_that_server_alone`: the server's address is refused
  before its name is resolved and reached after; another port is dropped; an ungranted
  name is REFUSED by the relay though the host would allow it; the agent cannot rewrite
  its resolver file (EROFS), open a raw socket or leave its network namespace (EPERM); an
  agent not named reaches nothing.

The build's rules (`CONNECT --port` required and within its networks' ingress, `--dns`
not internal, reach edges only from granted pairs) and the planner's (pairs, names,
grants, MCP scope) have unit tests. Mutation-checked: the relay granting any name, the
network process passing a named port without a learned address, and the switch ignoring
a pair's ports, each fail their test.

Open: process events; ingress to a network of several members. DNS over TCP is D79.
IPv6 is D99's: agents' subnets (part two), past the microVM (parts three and four).

**Amended (D278, 2026-11-16).** The relay answers a name its asker is not granted NXDOMAIN,
at once, where it answered REFUSED, which musl's stub resolver drops, waiting out its
timeout (D278's amendment of that day); REFUSED stays for what is no query of one question
and for a question past its asker's share of those in flight.

### A domain sees the image as built (D59, part eight)

Found by probe, 2026-10-07: an agent with no grant connected to a pathname Unix socket the
run's own command made at `/work/escape.sock` with mode 0777. A domain saw the microVM's
live system, read-only; connecting to a socket needs write permission on its file
(unix(7), "Pathname socket ownership and permissions") and no write access to its
filesystem, so the read-only mount and Landlock's write rights did not stop it. Landlock
closes this only from ABI 9 (`LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_RESOLVE_UNIX`, Linux 7.1, ae97330d1bd6),
and the pinned kernel, 6.18.48, has ABI 7. The live system also let an agent read every
file the run wrote and every volume it mounted, grants no directive made.

Now a domain's root is the image as built, an overlay with no writable layer of the
image's EROFS layers (the descriptor `changes::keep` holds for `diff`) under a tmpfs that
adds only what a domain mounts over and the image may lack (`/proc`, `/dev`, `/sys`,
`/tmp`, `/etc/hosts`, `/etc/resolv.conf`). Its first process attaches it over `/proc`
(`move_mount`), makes it its root (`pivot_root(".", ".")`) and detaches the system under
it, before any other mount. Nothing the run makes reaches it: not its files, mounts or
sockets, pathname or abstract. Only long-standing primitives hold this (the new mount
API, Linux 5.2; overlayfs), so it holds on any guest kernel a domain runs on, and for any
image; a newer kernel's Landlock rights would be a layer under it, never the only one.
The rule is the user's: fixes are version-agnostic where they can be.

An agent's own sockets, in its own `/tmp`, still work among its own processes; one
another domain made is hidden with its directory, and one the run makes does not exist
for it. No directive yet grants a domain a socket of the run's.

Tested on real microVMs: `an_agent_reaches_no_socket_of_the_runs_own`, where the run binds
`/work/escape.sock` (0777) and an abstract `shards-escape`, and an agent with no grants
tries both: `ENOENT` and `ECONNREFUSED`, its last try after the run bound both (one
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`). Mutation-checked: without the new root the agent connects.

### What a failing agent may take (D59, part nine)

Raised 2026-10-07 by the user: how a malfunctioning or compromised agent might abuse the
microVM, mitigated without burdening the Agentfile. Two ways it could take down everything
in it, init (PID 1, whose end is the microVM's) and the run's own command included:

- **Its output.** init relays an agent's output a line at a time and held an unfinished
  line whole, so an agent writing no newline grew init's memory without bound. Now a line
  is written unfinished at 16 KiB, Docker's bound for a container's log lines (moby
  daemon/logger/copier.go, `defaultBufSize`), each piece a line of its own
  (`frames::LINE_MAX`; test `a_line_without_end_is_written_in_pieces`).
- **Its memory.** Domains had no memory cgroup, and each one's scratch tmpfs could grow to
  half the microVM's memory (Documentation/filesystems/tmpfs.rst, `size`). The OOM
  killer chooses by resident memory, page tables and swap (mm/oom_kill.c,
  `oom_badness`), not a tmpfs's pages, so an agent filling `/tmp` would have the kernel
  kill the run's command, again and again. Now:
  - the domains together are a cgroup whose `memory.high` is what the microVM has as they
    start (`MemAvailable`, Documentation/filesystems/proc.rst) less what the workload's
    `-m` still allows it (`memory.max` less `memory.current` of its cgroup); the root
    cgroup has no `memory.current` (Documentation/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.rst), so the
    kernel's own estimate is the measure. Their tmpfs pages are charged to them;
  - each domain has `memory.oom.group`, so that one out of memory ends whole: a filler
    killed alone would leave its scratch held by the rest of the domain;
  - an agent's OSI config may ask a lower limit of its own, `asks.memory` in bytes, beside
    `asks.processes`. The user chose this over a per-agent share or no default.

  - **init chooses, not the kernel.** Charged past a `memory.max`, a write invokes that
    cgroup's OOM killer (mm/memcontrol.c, `try_charge_memcg`, `mem_cgroup_oom`), whose
    victim is again chosen by resident memory: with the domains' cap first a `memory.max`,
    an agent filling its scratch had others ended before it (in the first version of the
    test, y and z both), and a killed domain's tmpfs is freed only as its mount namespace
    goes. So the cap is `memory.high`: past it the kernel throttles the domains, in the
    charge itself every 64 pages as well as on the way back to user space, and kills none
    (Documentation/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.rst: "Going over the high limit never invokes the
    OOM killer"; the file names the case, an external process that monitors the cgroup).
    init watches the domains' `memory.events`, which the kernel marks modified as it
    changes, and past the cap ends the domain whose `memory.current`, scratch included,
    is the most, with `cgroup.kill` (Linux 5.14), saying so on the run's stderr
    (`[agent y] shards-init: ended: the agents' memory, …`). systemd-oomd and oomd choose
    by cgroup usage in the same way. A domain the kernel's OOM killer ended, whole, init
    says too, once, from its `memory.events`: at its own limit where it counted an `oom`,
    which the kernel counts before it chooses and never for the microVM's memory as a
    whole, else for the microVM's (`[agent x] shards-init: ended: its memory reached its
    limit, …`). A domain ended still holds the most until it has left
    its cgroup, which a process does after its namespaces, and with them its scratch, are
    gone (kernel/exit.c, `do_exit`: `exit_nsproxy_namespaces`, `exit_task_work`, then
    `cgroup_task_exit`), so no other is ended for memory it still holds; a rule waiting for
    it, written first, changed no outcome under mutation, and is not kept.

- **The agents' resolver.** It holds each question in flight under an ID of its own, 65,535
  at most, and refused any beyond: one agent asking without end could take them all, and
  every other agent's names with them, for as long as its questions wait (5 s, `WAIT`).
  Now each asker, known by its link, may hold an equal share of the IDs, `u16::MAX` over
  the askers: no asker can take another's, and the share is the ID space's, not a chosen
  number (`agentdns::Flight`; test `no_asker_takes_anothers_share_of_the_ids`, run in a
  microVM as init's Linux tests are on this host, mutation-checked: with no share, one
  asker took every ID).

- **Flows through the switch, measured: no change needed. Wrong, corrected by D61:** the
  flood measured was of flows conntrack evicts; flows it may not, held, fill one table
  for every agent. As first recorded: Conntrack's table holds 2048
  entries in a 237 MB microVM (`nf_conntrack_max`, sized by the kernel from memory), a
  count kept per network namespace against that one limit (net/netfilter/
  nf_conntrack_core.c, `__nf_conntrack_alloc`), and an unanswered UDP flow stays 30 s: one
  agent with a UDP grant fills the switch's table at once. But a full table evicts an
  entry not yet assured (`early_drop`), which a flood's are. Measured
  (`an_agents_flood_of_flows_takes_no_others`, 5 runs, each 200 of 200, MacBook arm64, macOS 26.4; in the one printed, a sent
  860,478 datagrams in 10 s, each from a new socket, to b's granted UDP port, while c made
  200 of 200 TCP connections to b, in 16 ms. The test stays, so that a rule assuring such
  flows would be seen. The kernel lacks `nft_connlimit` (`CONFIG_NFT_CONNLIMIT`), which
  a per-agent bound would need; none is needed.

`/tmp` stays where an agent's scratch is: the run's own writable layer is a tmpfs as well
(`run.rs`, `mount_root`), so every writable directory in a microVM is its memory, and a
programs' default temporary directory (POSIX `TMPDIR`) is where they look.

Tested on real microVMs: `agents_out_of_memory_end_whole_and_spare_the_run`, the run's
command holding 64 MiB under `-m 128m`: x, asking 32 MiB, below the domains' cap on every
host measured (66.8 to 80.9 MiB; asking 64 MiB, it met the cap first on an M5 Max), ends
with 26 MiB written (its resident memory the rest), init saying the kernel ended it at its
limit; y, asking nothing, is ended by init at the domains' cap, and z,
holding 16 MiB resident and no scratch, more than y's resident memory, lives; the run's
command outlives them, and each domain ended lost its PID 1 with its filler. Each guard
mutation-checked: without x's limit it wrote 82 MiB; without the workload's share taken
from the cap, the kernel killed the run's command; with the cap a `memory.max`, the
kernel ended z; with init choosing the least, z was ended; without a cap, init ended
none; without `memory.oom.group`, a domain's PID 1 outlived its filler; without init saying
what the kernel ended, x's run fails. Found while testing: an agent can fill and end between
two looks at `/proc`, each a whole `shards top`, which under load come further apart than it
lives (a D127 gate's failure, reproduced with looks 3 s apart), so the host reads the run's
log, which keeps what init says; so does `an_agents_daemon_ends_with_it` for its daemon. A
look without the filler's processes counted as its end where it came before the filler had
forked, and before z had named itself (CI run 38264181419): the host waits for init's line
in the log, then for a look taken after it.

### Protocols a network carries, and Unix sockets granted (D59, part ten)

Raised 2026-10-07 by the user: a network should say which protocols it carries, TCP, UDP,
Unix or any of them, with TCP and UDP by default; and agents, harnesses, the skills they
call and anything they run must use no Unix socket not granted. The interface is the
user's choice of three put to them:

- `NETWORK --protocol=<tcp|udp|unix>` is a boundary like `--ingress`: every port on the
  network, and every `EXPOSE … FOR` it, must be of a protocol it carries, checked at build
  (`agentfile::connections`). The runtime grants only ports already, so TCP and UDP need
  nothing more there.
- A Unix socket is a port, `unix:<name>`: let in by `NETWORK --ingress` (or `--expose`;
  `--egress` refused, since one never leaves the microVM) and granted by `CONNECT
  --port=unix:<name>`, one way or both as the `CONNECT` says.

At run, each name granted on a network is a directory of the tmpfs the run's writable
layer lies in (`/rw`), which no path from the run's root reaches, and which is no shared
mount, so nothing made there after the run starts reaches the run's mount namespace. init
copies the directory's mount for each agent granted it (`open_tree`, `OPEN_TREE_CLONE`,
Linux 5.2: a copy of a mount of init's own; copying one already detached needs 6.15,
c5c12f871a30, so none is), read-only where it only connects (`mount_setattr`, 5.12), and
the agent attaches it at `/run/networks/<network>/<name>/` (`move_mount`), whose mount
point its own skeleton holds: no agent sees the name of a socket it is not granted. The
preview put the socket at `<name>.sock`; a socket cannot be a mount point before it
exists, and a directory shared by every name would grant each agent every name, so a
grant is a directory, the socket inside.

Two more things a socket needs, found in the kernel's source:

- Connecting needs write permission on the socket (unix(7)), and `bind` applies the
  binder's umask itself (net/unix/af_unix.c, `unix_bind_bsd`), so a default ACL on the
  directory would not help: an agent receiving a socket starts with umask 0, its sockets
  then let in exactly who can see the directory, those granted. The directory is sticky,
  so none removes another's.
- Landlock refuses making a socket outside an agent's scratch: an agent receiving one is
  given `MAKE_SOCK` and `REMOVE_FILE` beneath its directory alone.

Tested: `networks_carry_only_their_protocols` (the build's rules: TCP and UDP by default,
Unix where named, a protocol not carried refused wherever named, a name not let in, a Unix
socket as egress, what is no protocol and what is no port) and, on real microVMs,
`agents_reach_only_the_unix_sockets_granted`: b receives tools and secret and makes both;
a, granted tools, connects to it, cannot make one there (`EROFS`), and secret does not
exist for it; c, granted secret, likewise; d, a member granted none, sees neither.
Mutation-checked: a sender's directory writable, every grant mounted in every agent, the
umask kept, the Landlock rule taken away, and the default carrying Unix each fail a test.

### Nothing past an agent's grants (D59, part eleven)

§9.10's sweep, on a real microVM (`an_agent_reaches_nothing_past_its_grants`): the run's
own command answers TCP and UDP on 7100 at every address it has; d, granted TCP 7000 to b
alone, and e, granted nothing, try it at the microVM's address, both ends of the uplink
and the microVM's gateway, and d its own network's gateway (the switch's end of its link,
DNS among it). What came of each, measured: d has no default route, an agent without
egress having only its network's route (via the switch), so every address past its
network is `ENETUNREACH`, and its gateway drops all (timeouts); e has its loopback alone,
so UDP has no route and TCP is refused by Landlock before it leaves (`EACCES`). d still
reaches b on 7000. Mutation-checked: with the switch's `input` chain accepting, d's
connection to its gateway is refused by it (`ECONNREFUSED`), an answer. Since D61, d has
egress and ingress on a network of its own, so it has a route past its network, and
every probe times out; its gateway is its gate's.

§9.9's double fork, on a real microVM (`an_agents_daemon_ends_with_it`): an agent lets a
grandchild go as daemons are (fork, `setsid`, fork), waits until the run's command has
seen it, and its first process ends; the grandchild ends with it, the kernel ending a PID
namespace's every process with its first. Mutation-checked: without `CLONE_NEWPID` the
grandchild outlives the agent.

§9.8's kernel channels, on a real microVM (`no_kernel_channel_joins_two_agents`): a makes
a System V shared memory segment and message queue of one key, a POSIX message queue and
a file in `/dev/shm`, and opens each itself; b, given none, opens none (`ENOENT` each), and
its signal to every process it may signal (`kill(-1)`) reaches none of a's. Mutation-
checked: without `CLONE_NEWIPC`, b opens a's segment and both queues.

Found by it: an agent could make no POSIX message queue at all, even its own. `mq_open`
makes one in its IPC namespace's mqueue filesystem, which no path of the agent's reached,
so Landlock refused it (`EACCES`). A Docker container has `/dev/mqueue` (moby
daemon/pkg/oci/defaults.go), as the run's command here does; now each domain mounts its
own there, which is the filesystem `mq_open` uses (ipc/mqueue.c, `mqueue_get_tree` keys it
by the IPC namespace), with every Landlock right beneath it.

Found while writing the sweep: `getifaddrs` fails in an agent, musl's asking over netlink, which
an agent's seccomp filter refuses; the test reads `/proc/net/route` instead.

### `SKILL --from=<agent>` (D54, continued)

`SKILL --from=<agent> <skill> FOR <other>` copies, at build time, a skill the agent's
OSI config lists (`skills`) into the other's grants (AGENTFILE_ARCH.md §12 answer 12): a
declaration in the Agentfile of what the agent brings, not one agent reading another.
The skill comes from the agent's content, the state `COPY --from=<agent>` copies from
(D56), and is checked and laid out as any skill. A path its config does not list is
refused, naming what it lists; so is an agent with no config, one from a path, Git or
an http(s) URL, as only an OSI artifact carries one. As `COPY --from=<agent>` does, it
makes the agent's declaring stage a dependency, except where that stage is its own: a
directive of the same stage comes first in it, and the first version, which made it a
dependency of itself, failed as a circular one (found by the test, and the same held for
`COPY --from=<agent>` in its declaring stage).

Tested: `a_skill_an_agent_lists_is_taken_from_it` (an OSI agent's listed skill laid in
another's grants, nothing else of its content; an unlisted path and an agent with no
config refused in their words), the listing check mutation-checked.

### D215. shards-api: Linux guests booted through the `shards` binary, for other programs (built: the client, its simulator and conformance suite; conformance passes on HVF, KVM and WHP records pending)

**Why.** A program that runs its own PID 1 in a guest and reaches it over vsock (Hex's
guest node is the first) needs a guest booted, a stream to a port, and the guest's end,
with every refusal typed. It may not link the VMM: on macOS the process that calls
Hypervisor.framework must be shards' own signed, sandboxed VM process (D30), and shards is
one binary (D36). So `crates/api` is a client of the binary: `boot` starts `shards run
--kernel … --vsock <socket> --no-console` (D38's direct boot, `--share` for its shares) in
a 0700 directory of its own, and `connect` speaks Firecracker's hybrid vsock handshake to
that socket (`CONNECT <port>` / `OK <host port>`, firecracker `docs/vsock.md`, muxer.rs).

**What it is.**
- `Guests`/`Guest`/`Stream`, the real `Shards`, `sim::SimGuests` (a closure as PID 1 over
  in-process socket pairs, with the same refusals) and `conformance::run`, which holds both
  to one behaviour; crates/shards/tests/boot.rs runs it against this build's binary.
- Its bounds are facts or records: a spec is refused before boot where shards-vmm refuses
  it on every host (a vCPU at least, memory even and at least the least); the vCPUs a host
  runs are its hypervisor's, and shards' own refusal comes back as `Refusal::Bounds`. Its
  waits wait on facts: the VM process's exit (reaped by its watcher), its output read to an
  end mark written after that exit, `Duration::MAX` as no clock. A record of one host
  bounds no other's (R03): CI's x86_64 KVM went past twice fedora's slowest boot and
  refusal (PM M541; `shards_api_conforms_on_real_guests`, "no OK within 2.41364452s", and

  The last bounds of that kind, the suite's and the crate's unit tests', twice the slowest
  run recorded on the host class (`shards_api::record`: `conformance::PATIENCE`,
  `UNSERVED_PATIENCE`, an unserved port's `OVERSHOOT`; PM M463, M464, M515), went with the
  waits that follow the guest's VM process (below), which the suite now waits with. The one
  patience it still gives, an unserved port's, is this host's own: what one refused single
  attempt there took (`connect_once_before`), the refusal coming at it, never before. How
  late past it the refusal may come has no bound: a bound on it would be a multiple of some
  time of this host's, a number of ours. An attach of a guest whose first client reaps it as
  it is held is refused `Exited` (PM M541).
- On Windows a guest's process is the `shards` that booted its VM, which holds the VM in a
  Job that ends with it (D141); it outlives a client that crashes or loses its guest, so
  `attach` takes it back as on Unix (parity step 14): held by a handle of its own with query,
  synchronize and terminate rights, which keeps its pid its own while held, its start that
  handle's GetProcessTimes creation time, its end waited on and made through it
  (TerminateProcess), which ends its Job and so its VM. Where Windows refused this before, the
  refusal was no limit of its API.
- Waits that follow the guest's VM process (`Guest::connect_while_runs`,
  `Guest::wait_while_runs`; ROOT's decision of 2026-11-13; `crates/api/src/progress.rs`): a
  wait for a guest's answer goes on while its VM process runs, and is refused, typed, when it
  stalls. They are opt-in: `connect`, `connect_before`, `connect_once_before` and `wait_for`
  keep their meaning, so Hex's calls do too.
  - *Learned per kind, in the client's process.* `Awaited::Boot` (an `OK` from a guest none
    of whose connects was answered yet: its boot to its first listener), `Awaited::Connect`
    (an `OK` from a guest that has answered one) and `Awaited::End` (its end) are kept
    apart, in memory (`progress::RECORDS`), never in source:
    - W*, the slowest answer seen, from a wait's start to its answer;
    - R*, the least CPU rate at which a VM process still answered: its CPU over that wait's
      wall time, kept as the (cpu, wall) pair and compared by cross-multiplication in u128
      of nanoseconds saturated at u64's most (584 years), so no product overflows.
    - Only the guest's own answers teach: an `OK`, and an end that was not this client's
      stop. A refusal teaches nothing, and neither does a wait no nanosecond long, which has
      no rate.
    - Boot is kept apart from Connect because a boot works through gaps (its timers, its
      devices) longer than a listening guest takes to answer: a W* learned from connects to
      running guests (a client that attaches first) would judge a boot by theirs.
  - *The judge.* Past W* from its start, a wait looks at its VM process once each W*. A look
    that finds it ran no CPU at all over a whole W* since a look last found it progressed or
    held, the judge's own lateness not counted (below), refuses the wait,
    `Refusal::Stalled(Stall)`: how far into the wait, the time looked over, R* and W*, kept in
    nanoseconds (each past u64's, 584 years, its most). Five `Duration`s in the variant
    enlarged every `Result<_, Refusal>`: a test's tuple of two of them crossed clippy's
    `result_large_err` (crates/api/tests/sim.rs, this lane's second run).
    - A host under load slows a VM process, and may hold it from running for a while, but
      a VM process that ran nothing for as long as the slowest answer took, its host not
      the reason, is stopped, deadlocked or frozen. So a look that finds no CPU since the
      look before refuses only where the host was not the reason (`Found::Held` is no
      refusal; ROOT's ruling, 2026-11-13): none of its threads runnable (Linux `R`, macOS
      `TH_STATE_RUNNING`, Windows ready, running, standby or transition) or waiting on its
      host's memory (macOS `TH_STATE_UNINTERRUPTIBLE`, which macOS keeps no pressure record
      of; Windows' KWAIT_REASON FreePage, PageIn, PoolAllocation and their Wr forms); nor, on
      Linux, its threads' wait for a CPU grown since the look before (each thread's
      `/proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/schedstat` `run_delay`, summed, Documentation/scheduler/
      sched-stats.rst), nor its own cgroup's CPU or memory pressure (cpu.pressure's and
      memory.pressure's `some` totals, Documentation/accounting/psi.rst; a task held over
      `memory.high` is a memory stall, mm/memcontrol.c).
      - A hold counts only where it is the process's own (ROOT, 2026-11-13). A cgroup's
        pressure is read only where its `cgroup.procs` is this process alone, as a daemon's
        VM process in its slice (D209); a shared cgroup's, the root's (`/proc/pressure`, the
        host's) among them, is its neighbours' wait too. Main's judge had read any: in CI a
        followed process shares the test runner's cgroup, or a container's namespace root
        whose pressure is the host's, so a `/bin/sleep 60` beside busy tests was found
        `Held` at every look and waited on for ever (main's CI at 5af644eab, run
        43474661701: ends.rs's `an_end_goes_on_at_any_rate_and_not_asleep_or_stopped` on
        three Linux targets, and daemon waits that never ended on Alpine; red at 790320602,
        `a_sleeper_is_still_whatever_its_cgroups_others_wait_for`, two spinners pinned to
        one CPU beside the sleeper).
      - The kernel adds a thread's wait to `run_delay` as it reaches a CPU or leaves the
        queue (Linux 7.2 kernel/sched/stats.h `sched_info_arrive`, `sched_info_dequeue`), so
        a thread that waited the whole time between two looks shows by its `R` sample
        instead. A kernel built without CONFIG_SCHED_INFO keeps no schedstat, and one where
        `sched_info_on()` is false reads it as zeros (fs/proc/base.c): `Queued::Unread`, and
        its looks are judged by CPU and the `R` sample alone. No number is chosen: growth is
        any nanosecond.
      - So a sleeping (`S`) process with no wait of its own grown is still, whatever its
        neighbours do; one stopped or frozen is refused whatever else shows, the CPU its stop
        ran included (a stop signal wakes a sleeper to stop itself, kernel/signal.c
        `do_signal_stop`: ends.rs's stopped teardown went on at ba81cd9d2, red at b665a2e61,
        `a_process_stopped_since_the_look_before_is_still_though_its_stop_ran_it`): Linux's
        leader `T` or `t` or a frozen cgroup (`cgroup.events`), macOS's `SSTOP`, Windows'
        every thread suspended. Only an end under way outranks a stop. macOS and Windows read each thread of the followed process (or,
        on Windows, of its tree) alone, no group's, and are unchanged.
      Read where each OS keeps it, with no
      privilege: `/proc/<pid>/task/*/stat`, `/proc/<pid>/task/*/schedstat` and the process's
      cgroup v2 files; libproc's `PROC_PIDTBSDINFO`, `PROC_PIDLISTTHREADS` and
      `PROC_PIDTHREADINFO`, which need no task port (`task_threads` would, and `task_for_pid`
      is refused for a hardened process not built to allow it); NtQuerySystemInformation's
      SystemProcessInformation records, each thread's state and wait reason. What cannot be
      read shows nothing, and that look is judged by its CPU alone.
    - The judge's own lateness is its host's hold (ROOT's ruling, 2026-11-13, #77). Each look
      knows when it was meant (W* past the one before was meant, `Judge::meant`: its looks
      keep D215's schedule, each W* past the wait's start, however late each ran) and when it
      ran. The time it ran late, from when it was meant (or from the look before, where that
      ran later still, so no time counts twice) to when it ran, is time its host held its
      thread: the host held everyone, and that time counts toward no party's window. A
      party's window runs from the look that last found it progressed or held; a look that
      finds it still refuses only where that window, less the judge's lateness within it,
      is a whole W* (`Stall::over` is that free time). A judge held past several looks makes
      one, its next due at the next W* past the start. Main's judge scheduled each look W*
      past when the one before ran, which added each look's lateness to the next window:
      ROOT's HVF run at d513d0a0b (macOS arm64, 18 cores, load 30/31/27) refused a live start,
      containers.rs `a_runs_log_is_sent_to_gelf_as_its_options_say`, "it ran nothing for
      101.091209ms, past the slowest start seen (98.915708ms), 202.999ms after it began": its
      first look ran 101.908 ms in (2.99 ms late) and found progress, its second 202.999 ms
      in, of whose 101.09 ms 5.17 ms were past the second's meant time (197.83 ms), leaving
      95.92 ms free, less than W*. Red at 30cf4f42b,
      `a_look_its_host_held_late_counts_its_lateness_as_held`, the run's own times on an
      injected look clock (`Judge::found_at`);
      its twin `a_judge_on_time_refuses_a_stopped_party_at_its_first_look` holds before and
      after. Cold start: a judged wait's first window runs from its start, so a judge on time
      or late refuses a party still from its start at its first look, over exactly W* free.
      No number is chosen: lateness is any nanosecond past a meant time, read on the clock
      the looks run by; a host that holds the judge a whole W* at every look holds its waits
      to liveness alone, as a host hold counts as held.
    - *Stillness is judged over what the looks saw* (#77, ROOT's KVM run at c120c8a95). Two
      looks that found no change show none from the first's end to the second's beginning,
      and no more: each reads its counters somewhere within its own span (`Span`: its
      beginning, its end, and its counters' resolution). A party's window without progress
      so runs from the end of the look from which it has been still, never from a time no
      look read, to the beginning of the look that judges it; and it is refused only where
      that window, less the judge's lateness within it, is a whole W* or its counters'
      resolution, whichever is longer (`Judge::found_over`): a counter that changes once a
      tick (/proc's utime, USER_HZ, proc(5)) shows nothing of a stillness shorter than one,
      so a window shorter than its resolution is no evidence. Resolutions are the OS's own,
      none chosen: Linux's, clock_getres(2) of the process's CPU clock (1 ns for the
      scheduler's clock clock_getcpuclockid(3) names, kernel/time/posix-cpu-timers.c
      `posix_cpu_clock_getres`); macOS's, one Mach absolute-time unit rounded up to whole
      nanoseconds (mach_timebase_info(3); 42 ns on Apple silicon); Windows', none, as
      QueryProcessCycleTime counts every cycle. Cold start: a look with nothing before it to
      compare with, a party's first or one that first found a process of it, is based
      (`Found::Based`): it shows neither progress nor stillness, judges nothing whether it
      is due or not, and the evidence begins at its end. `Judge::begin` takes its caller's
      first look as made at its beginning (`Follow`, which reads its VM process there, says
      so with a based look as that read ends; the daemon's watchers read theirs as they
      begin); the tests' waits, whose first look at their party comes later, say theirs.
      Main's judge took every finding as evidence since the look before, and a wait's start
      as a look, so that the time before a party's first look counted as seen still. Two of
      ROOT's KVM refusals ("its last progress its start") were so: managed_lifecycle.rs:209's
      stream wait, W* 3.527 µs, refused 18.416 ms in by the look right after its first, which
      had taken those 18 ms to list and find its VM processes anew (its reads are not paced
      while a look is due), its looks having seen microseconds; common/mod.rs:2601's
      `shards top` wait, W* 13.996 ms, refused 31.067 ms in, its first look begun as the
      wait began and not judged (not yet due), its judged look 2 ms of sleep after the look
      before ended, so about 29 ms of the window before any look's end. Whether either party
      would have shown a whole W* of real stillness after its first look is ROOT's rerun's
      to show. Red/green: judge.rs's
      `a_first_look_longer_than_w_star_is_based_not_still`,
      `a_window_is_judged_from_its_baselines_end`,
      `a_counter_coarser_than_w_star_widens_the_window_to_its_resolution` and
      `a_based_look_starts_the_evidence_anew_before_its_due`, the runs' own times on an
      injected look clock. The 3.527 µs W* was mis-keyed: managed_lifecycle.rs'
      `challenge_healthy` is `#[track_caller]`, so its `published` state wait (`Patience`)

      before its wait began, taught the stream's kind 3.527 µs. A test's wait on a state,
      a guest's words or a stream is now kept apart by what it awaits
      (`WaitKind::awaiting`). The third refusal, hotplug.rs:127's (W* 1.054 ms, refused
      2.109 ms in), had evidence for its whole window: its party is a machine of the test's
      own process, read by its console's words alone (no CPU of its own is read), and its
      words' baseline was read as the wait began. The guest said nothing for longer than
      that call site's slowest answer, whose asks (`grow vda`, a plug, an unplug) share one
      kind: what its guest did is not observable to its wait at all. Fixed by D209's Part 5
      (#77, ROOT's KVM run c33's same refusal): each of its stages is a kind of its own
      (call site and awaited text, numbers generic), and a machine of the test's process
      progresses while its process's threads beside its waiter run.
    - *No window shorter than its looks resolve* (b26, ROOT's HVF batch at 1f71dea19, PM
      M592). The run socket's judged send (`RunSocket::send`, `Answers::run_send`) teaches its
      kind from every send, and one that found room at once taught a W* of about one look's
      cost: 9.583 µs. A later send that did wait was refused 16.584 µs past its first look,
      29.958 µs in ("its process ran no CPU in 16.584µs past the slowest answer seen
      (9.583µs)", moved.rs:645 and three more moved.rs tests, containers.rs:2257; KVM's
      plug.rs:177 said "its guest: " and nothing, the DEVICE exec's cut dropped). Over such a
      window a reading shows nothing of a run: XNU adds a thread's run to its task's times
      (proc_pid_rusage) as the thread leaves its CPU or enters the kernel, which its quantum
      timer makes one each tick, and Linux's process CPU clock, read from another process,
      holds a thread running on another CPU as of that CPU's last tick (kernel/sched/cputime.c
      `thread_group_cputime`; CI's aarch64 run 43575280954 saw 2.6 ms of a spinning thread
      unshown). Measured (PM M592): a spinning child's macOS times grew in steps of p50 12 µs,
      p90 182 µs, p99 3.7 ms, max 12.9 ms. So a reading's resolution (`Watch::resolution`) is
      its step, not its unit: the counter's unit or the kernel's tick, whichever is longer,
      each the OS's own statement where it runs, none chosen: macOS's tick is
      `kern.clockrate`'s `tick` (sysctl(3) KERN_CLOCKRATE; 10 ms, hz 100, on macOS 26), Linux's
      the resolution of CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE (clock_getres(2): one jiffy, `LOW_RES_NSEC`).
      Windows' reading, QueryProcessCycleTime, keeps its resolution of none: whether it
      shows a thread running on another CPU before its next interrupt is unmeasured (owed).
      The judge then looks, and refuses, on a window of W* or its floor, whichever is longer
      (`Judge::window`): the floor is the coarsest resolution of its looks' counters and the
      longest of its looks, each learned from the wait's own spans (`Span`), so a W* below
      what its looks resolve is looked at no more often than a look takes or a tick passes
      (main's looked each 9.583 µs) and refuses over no shorter a window. Cold start: before
      its first look a judge has no floor, and every judged wait's first look is its based
      one, taken as it begins (`Follow::begin`), which sets it before its first due. Failure:
      a tick that cannot be read refuses the follow typed (`ProcessFailure`, macOS's
      `ProcessOperation::ClockRate`), never taken for no progress. The daemon's other
      readers keep the same standard: a cgroup's emptying (`parents::emptied`) judges its
      looks over its readings' resolution, and an end's watcher (`ends::Followed::goes_on`)
      takes a look sooner than its reading's step after the look before as no evidence, its
      end going on, the look before kept. An exec the judge ended says so wherever its
      answer is read (`reclaim::said_of`: a DEVICE step, a resource update, a network's
      switch), where plug said "its guest: " with nothing after. Red/green: health.rs'
      `a_wait_is_never_refused_within_what_its_reading_resolves` (a 10 µs W*, an idle
      process: refused only once a whole tick, read apart from shards-api, has shown it
      still; red with the unit as the resolution, refused microseconds in) and judge.rs'
      `a_w_star_below_what_its_looks_resolve_is_judged_over_what_they_do` (the moved.rs run's
      own times). Whether the five HVF tests and plug.rs pass on real VMs is ROOT's run's.
    - *Only an answer waited for teaches* (#77; docs/bugs/2026-11-13/waits.md waits-03). A
      test's wait moves through explicit stages (common/mod.rs `Stage`): `Begun`, its
      answer not yet found missing; `Awaited`, found missing at least once, by a look
      (whose callers look only after a check found their answer not come) or said so
      (`Wait::absent`); `Answered`. Its answer teaches its kind only from `Awaited`: one
      there as its wait began waited on no party, as D185's answers already in a slot and
      D209's READY already said teach nothing. Waits that could find their answer there
      check first: `Following` reads its stream once without blocking until a read finds
      nothing there, its end read as there where it is (2026-11-17, kiln goal a8b1ce42, lane
      own-36-tag: on Windows, whose FIONREAD counts no end, a socket of no bytes is polled,
      WSAPoll, and read where it has ended, and a pipe whose writers have gone reads its end;
      an end read as absent taught `an_answer_already_there_teaches_nothing`'s stream a W* of
      one look, 8.86 ms at 0 ns of its party's CPU, on CI's arm64 Windows runner, run
      44007524337); engine.rs' `Patient` reads what its daemon has sent before it waits;

      ended member's channel through `judged_there`, judged should it stall but teaching
      nothing. Evidence: ROOT's KVM run at 18b2e0d60 (adacachy2), api_image.rs:2288's
      `an_h2_sign_in_gives_the_harness_placeholders_and_its_refresh_is_answered_outside`,
      refused 181 ms into a read of its member's stdout ("no progress for 27.488912ms, past
      ... (20.972496ms)") while its network process waited on auth.openai.com's round trip:
      its kind's record, W* 20.97 ms with R* 0 ns of CPU over those 20.97 ms, an answer over
      which no process of its party ran at all, is an ended member's output read from its
      pipe, not a wait on the party. Its party did hold the network process: the run host is
      this test's child (session.rs `start_host`, posix_spawn with a session of its own, no
      second fork) and starts its VM and network processes as its own children
      (launch.rs, `spawn_in_group` with no group, api-run having no spawner). The judge was
      right to find that party still; its W* was no answer.
    - *A wait answered goes on as a drain* (waits-10). A command's client's end is its
      answer; what its streams still carry (a process it left holding them) is read in
      `Stage::Answered`, judged by a judge begun at that answer over the record the answer
      left, never cold (the answer just taught it, or it was learned), and a look that finds
      its party gone finds it still, as no process of it that could write runs. Main kept
      the client's own judge, which a cold kind never judges, so that a silent holder's
      liveness held its test for ever. The drain teaches nothing. A command's wait finds
      its answer missing as it begins (`run_ending`'s `Wait::absent`), as its client
      started just then: an end its first check finds before any look (the client quicker
      than its waiter's thread's first turn) is an answer, never one already there
      (`Stage::Begun`), which taught nothing and left the drain's kind cold, judging nothing
      until its holder's end (2026-11-14: adacachy2 at f385b8dac, 7 of 30 whole-binary
      runs; `a_commands_end_found_before_its_first_look_teaches_its_kind`, whose client
      has ended as its spawn returns, red there). So does each harness.rs wait that
      teaches its kind by a quick stand-in's end (`Wait::absent`, `Heard::absent`):
      `a_runs_stop_grace_is_its_daemons_and_not_refused` ("its kind learned nothing of an
      answer") and `a_streaming_guests_cpu_is_its_liveness_and_its_stop_its_hosts_hold`

    - *A member is ended only for the stillness of the party its answer waits on* (ROOT's
      ruling, 2026-11-17, goal fb3528f9, refining ROOT's (3) of 2026-11-13, not reversing
      it). A health judgment, such as `health::Wait::WhileRuns` on init's builtins, may end a
      member only where that party made no progress and its host did not hold it. A
      microVM without CPU while its answer waits on another party is not stalled. That
      party may be the host's network process, the daemon, or a host-side reply on vsock,
      and its progress and holds are then the party's too.
      - *Read, for the case that brought it.* CI 43968984258's x86_64 musl job ended a
        running member's connect: engine.rs `a_running_member_is_connected_and_disconnected_at_once`,
        "srv: its microVM ran no CPU in 5.675836ms past the slowest answer seen (3.041764ms)".
        - Init's answer waits on no other party. `members.rs` `connect` gives the member
          its address through the switch (links.rs `member_address`: netlink in the switch's,
          the gate's and the member's namespaces), its routes, and its grants again
          (`regrant`: the nftables tables, each in one transaction). All of it is the
          provider guest's own kernel and init, so the provider's VM process is the whole
          party, as `WhileRuns` follows it.
        - Its W* was another verb's. One record per builtin byte (`Answers::builtins`) held
          every `NETWORK` verb, and the test's two `make`s, which only record a network in
          init's memory, taught 3.0 ms.
        - Cure: each verb of a network's switch is a kind of its own (`Answers::networks`,
          `health::NETWORK_VERBS`), cold until its first answer, as D215 keeps each kind apart.
          Held by daemon.rs `a_networks_verbs_are_judged_each_by_its_own_record` (red with
          the one record).
        - Unproven (R09): whether the guest idled those 5.7 ms in its own kernel or its
          nested host did not run it. The run that would tell is owed to ROOT.
    - *Steal, as a VM host's judge sees it* (2026-11-17, goal fb3528f9, ROOT's question: CI's
      runners are VMs; is the hypervisor's taking their CPUs read as the host's hold?).
      - *Already counted.* From inside a VM, the hypervisor taking all of its CPUs stops the
        judge's own looking thread too. Its look runs late by that time, which is the host's
        hold and counts toward no party's window (the lateness ruling above, `Judge::meant`).
      - *Also counted.* A party thread woken onto a CPU the hypervisor holds is runnable
        until it runs. A pending wakeup's `TASK_WAKING` reads as `R` (fs/proc/array.c,
        `__task_state_index`), and so does a thread kept from a CPU. Its run-queue wait
        (`run_delay`, Documentation/scheduler/sched-stats.rst) is read too (`Queued`).
      - *Not read.* `/proc/stat`'s `steal` column (proc(5): time spent in other operating
        systems when running in a virtualized environment, in clock ticks). It would matter
        only where a party thread sleeps on a timer of a CPU the hypervisor holds while the
        judge's CPU runs, which nothing has shown.
      - *Read against the case that asked.* CI 43968984258's x86_64 musl refusals of engine.rs'
        create (`files_go_in_and_out_of_a_microvm_by_copy`) and `/system/df`
        (`images_are_tagged_traced_removed_and_pruned`) had their looks' lateness out (3.46
        and 2.21 ms). They found 5.67 and 6.31 ms of stillness past it, every daemon thread
        `S`, none runnable: the judge ran through it, so it was no whole-VM steal.
      - *Then.* No cure; the next traced run decides. A refusal's account now says where each
        member's threads wait (`common::waits_in`: `/proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/wchan`, proc(5)),
        so the next one names what the daemon's threads slept on.
    - *A party is what was found of it until it ends* (waits-09, waits-10). A process once
      found is followed until it has gone or ended, wherever it is listed since: a daemon's
      microVMs as they end after it (a daemon stop's party), a client's children reparented
      as it exits. Its daemon is the process its `daemon.pid` names by its ID and its start
      (`shards_ipc::Named`, D185), checked again once its watch is read, never another
      process given its ID. A process found ended (exited and not reaped,
      `shards_api::Watch::ended`: on Unix its look's end under way, which a zombie's every
      look says, on Linux once no thread of it is left (D185, amended 2026-11-17: a zombie
      leader whose other threads still run is followed, their exit its CPU); on Windows every
      process of its tree exited, which their handles read
      still) is no live member, its end progress once, at the look that first finds it
      under way: a test's wait on a state reaps nothing, so an end under way for ever was
      progress for ever.

      `a_context_runs_commands_on_its_machine_whole` was refused at context.rs:1625, its
      `shards images` run from the laptop's home with `SHARDS_CONTEXT=gpu`: "made no progress
      for 186.462ms, past the slowest answer of its kind seen on this host (97.9837ms)", its
      party "client 3060, no daemon yet in …ctx-laptop-25", "0 of 3 threads runnable". The
      daemon that served it was the machine's, another home of the test's, which its party
      did not follow, so its client's wait on that daemon read as the client's own
      stillness. Now a command's party (tests/common `Party::serving`) follows, beside its
      client and its own home's daemon, the daemon of the home that serves its context:
      the context chosen as shards chooses it (context.rs `chosen`: `--context`, then
      `SHARDS_CONTEXT`, then `DOCKER_CONTEXT`, then the home's current one), its record's
      `address` the one a home beside it listens on (that home's `listening`, which its
      daemon writes once bound and removes as it stops), and that home's live daemon by its
      `daemon.pid` (`shards_ipc::Named`). A command run here, or whose context names no home
      of the test's, keeps the party it had. Red/green (harness.rs, stand-ins, no microVM):
      `a_contexts_command_is_served_by_the_home_that_listens_on_its_address`, red under
      `own-38b-context-unserved.patch` (no serving home found). Whether the refusal recurs
      under load with the machine's daemon followed is owed to a run (ROOT's on jupiter).
    - *A refusal as its test unwinds says itself* (#77 slice 2): `run_command` refused while
      its thread is panicking (a cleanup's `Drop`) writes its account to stderr and returns
      a run of no status; a panic while panicking aborts the test binary, all its tests
      with it, as one of context.rs' did.
    - *A refusal names what each thread of its party was doing* (ROOT's word, 2026-11-18).

      their party "0 of 3 threads runnable" and no more, so whether its threads waited on a
      peer, a disk or a lock could not be read from them. A wait's account now says, on

      (shards-api `threads_said`: `SYSTEM_THREAD_INFORMATION`'s ThreadState and WaitReason from
      the system's listing, named as WMI's `Win32_Thread` and the WDK's KWAIT_REASON name
      them, a reason it does not name by its number), read once per member as the account is
      written, never at a look; Linux and macOS say what they read already (each process's
      status, its runnable threads, Linux its threads' `wchan`). The same listing, read for
      named threads of a process (`threads_held`), classes each as a VM process's hold does
      (`wants_cpu`: ready, running or standby; `pages`): one rule for the product's Windows
      reading and the tests' parties', whose side lands on the move of the tests' party to
      its own crate (crates/testwait). Host saturation (GetSystemTimes' idle) is no hold
      (ROOT, 2026-11-18): the host's, not the party's own (the ruling of 2026-11-13).
    - *A refusal's account changes nothing of what it describes* (ROOT's ruling (b),
      2026-11-18; CI 44227612442's x86_64 musl job 134545100600).
      - Why. That job's accounts of two commands refused in homes with no daemon
        (`configure disk`, a `build agent`) asked those homes `ps -a` (`stacks_of`). Each
        started a daemon there (21259, 22143) on the host the refusal had found slow, and the
        second's `ps -q` was refused in turn. A client asked where no daemon serves starts one
        (cli/client.rs `ask_slot`), and a daemon as it starts restarts the home's microVMs
        whose policies say so (daemon/restart.rs `restart_at_start`).

        that lives, or whose stopping record names one ending its runs, and says "no daemon
        running in HOME: none asked". On Windows the debugger attaches to a home's daemon
        only where its record names one that lives.

        same, and its client starts the next.
      - Test: harness.rs `an_account_asks_no_home_no_daemon_serves`. Red:

        - A home whose living daemon is of another build (containers.rs' `Gated`, its

    - Red/green (harness.rs, stand-ins, no microVM): `a_first_look_past_w_star_judges_nothing`
      (waits-02), `an_answer_already_there_teaches_nothing` (waits-03),

      fails its test (the carrier's mutations). No literal is chosen: W* and the windows are
