    - macOS's scheduler counts each thread's time runnable, running or waiting for a CPU
      (proc_pid_rusage(2) RUSAGE_INFO_V4 `ri_runnable_time`, sys/resource.h, Mach
      absolute-time units; public, and like the rest no task port). Grown over a time the
      process ran no CPU, it is a wait for one, as Linux's `run_delay` is (`Queued::Waited`
      on both, #77): a thread its host held runnable between two looks, but not at either
      look's sample, reads as held. Measured on adas-macbook-pro-2 (macOS 26, 18 cores, load
      10 to 38), one second each: `yes`, 1125.1 ms CPU and 1147.9 ms runnable over 1149.2 ms
      wall; `sleep 5`, 0 and 0; a shell starting `sleep 0.01` in a loop, 5.8 ms CPU and
      6.2 ms runnable. A thread that is runnable as a look samples it already read as held
      (`TH_STATE_RUNNING` is running or waiting for a CPU, mach/thread_info.h).
    - R* was in the refusal for diagnosis only, never a bound: ROOT's first design refused a
      look below R*, which would refuse a boot merely slowed by its host's load, the very
      failure R03 ends (ROOT, 2026-11-13, at this lane's report).
    - *R* and C* bound a party that ticks but never answers* (ROOT's ruling, 2026-11-14, the
      gitssh lane). "Any CPU at all is progress" was a structural false negative: HVF batch 24
      at 1f71dea19 waited 3,722 s on build.rs's `shards run --rm sshed:1 stat /s1/noise.bin`,
      "its last progress process 59939 ran 751µs ago" at every 117 ms look, its guest asleep
      for good. An idle guest's VM process still ticks: `shards run --kernel … --cpus 14`
      of the test guest's `idle` mode on adas-mac-studio-3.local (macOS arm64, 14 cores,
      ff69e4736) ran 10 to 30 ms of CPU in each of three 10 s spans over 18 threads, so it runs
      within any W* of more than a few ms. A spinning one runs a core or more. The judge now
      also refuses a party that progressed (`Judge::found_over`, `Stall::rate`) where all of
      these hold:
      - it has been seen to run unheld a whole window or more. Its wall is only the windows
        between due looks that its caller vouched for (`Span::work`): none of its processes
        held from running, stopped, starved of a CPU (`Watch::starved`, read under either CPU
        reading), ending or found anew, no run of its home in its stop grace, no progress
        that was this process's servers'. The judge's own lateness is out too;
      - its work since its start over that wall is below R*;
      - that work is more than C*, the most work any answer of its kind took (new in
        `Seen::Learned`). Without C*, a kind whose answers wait on a peer (a registry, a git
        server), their work alike and their wall not, would be refused at its first answer
        slower than all before, its rate then below all before. With C*, a party is refused
        only once it has done more work than any answer needed while running slower than any
        answer ran. A boot slowed by its host does its usual work and is never refused; its
        held windows are out of its wall besides. From one answer, R* times W* is C*, so a
        party can be under R* and over C* only well past W*: b24's ticks would have passed
        its C* within about a minute.
    - *A party waiting in its kernel is held, not slow* (ROOT's ruling, 2026-11-14, its batch
      32 at 8d732fb2d, HVF, 2 of 14 cores idle). api_image.rs's `shards guest use`, its kind
      W* 55.1 ms, R* 11.87 ms of CPU in 55.1 ms and C* 12.58 ms, was refused 224.7 ms in for
      13.23 ms of CPU over 143.0 ms taken for unheld, its one thread not runnable. That time
      was its host's: guest.rs `record` flushes each file it keeps to its disk's media
      (F_FULLFSYNC), and on that loaded host it spent 52 to 172 ms of its 69 to 192 ms in
      `TH_STATE_UNINTERRUPTIBLE`, at 14.1 to 16.2 ms of CPU, past that C* in every run (PM
      M600). A look that found it so vouched for its window wherever it had also run a
      moment in it, as `Watch::vouched_by` read starvation, stops and ends alone. Now a look
      that finds a thread of its party waiting uninterruptibly in its kernel (macOS
      `TH_STATE_UNINTERRUPTIBLE`, Linux `D`: `Hold::uninterruptible`) vouches for no window
      (`progress::vouches`): its time leaves the rate's wall and its work stays in, a doubt
      that raises the rate. Stillness: a look that ran nothing found macOS's uninterruptible
      wait `Held` (2026-11-13) and Linux's `D` still; since 2026-11-16 it finds either `Held`
      only where its host's disks completed I/O meanwhile (*A wait in a kernel*, below). A ticker
      asleep on an event waits interruptibly (`TH_STATE_WAITING`, `S`) and is refused as
      before. Windows reads no wait reason of a flush here: unverified there. Held by
      progress.rs `a_party_waiting_on_its_hosts_disk_vouches_for_no_window_of_its_rate` (the
      batch's numbers through `Judge`: refused vouching, going on in its kernel or held
      between its looks) and `a_process_flushing_to_its_disk_is_seen_waiting_in_its_kernel`
      (a child flushing a file, seen so on macOS and, `D`, on Linux).
      - *A hold between looks* (ROOT's ruling, 2026-11-14). A sample at one instant misses a
        wait that ends before the look; a look made once each W* (`Follow::look`) missed
        most. Where an OS accumulates its host's work for a process, that count's growth
        since the look before is held time between looks (`Io`, `Hold::held_since`,
        `progress::vouches`): the window vouches for nothing, and a look that ran nothing is
        `Held`. What each OS keeps (PM M601):
        - Linux keeps waited time only as its tasks' block I/O delays (`/proc/<pid>/task/
          <tid>/stat` field 42), and only while `kernel.task_delayacct` is 1, off by default
          since 5.14 (Documentation/accounting/delay-accounting.rst; off on adacachy2); and as
          a cgroup's `io.pressure` `some` total, read where that cgroup holds the process
          alone, as a daemon's VM process its slice. Both are `Io::waited`. Its storage's
          work, read always: `majflt` (stat field 12) and `/proc/<pid>/io`'s `read_bytes` and
          `write_bytes`, the process's whole (`Io::done`). Of 391 waits in `D` of 1 ms or
          more by fdatasync loops on adacachy2's NVMe, those counts grew across 368, 95% of
          their time.
        - macOS keeps no waited time. Its storage's work: proc_pid_rusage(2) RUSAGE_INFO_V4's
          `ri_pageins`, `ri_diskio_bytesread`, `ri_diskio_byteswritten` and
          `ri_logical_writes`, the last alone moved by a directory's flush. Of 55
          uninterruptible waits of 1 ms or more by F_FULLFSYNC loops on
          adas-mac-studio.local-2, 54 grew them (1,912 of 1,915 ms).
        - Windows keeps no waited time, and a thread's wait reason cannot tell its host's
          disk from a peer: one in FlushFileBuffers waits `Executive`, as one in a pipe's read
          that no one answers does (PM M603), so that reason is no hold. Its I/O counts
          (GetProcessIoCounters: operations and bytes, its pipes' and sockets' with its
          files') grew across 79% of a flusher's reads and none of a pipe reader's or a
          sleeper's: `Io::done`, summed over the followed tree's processes. Its windows of any
          I/O vouch for nothing, so its rate is judged over its quiet ones alone.
        Where an OS keeps no waited time for a process (macOS; Linux with delay accounting
        off and its cgroup shared), a wait bound by its rate also looks between its due
        looks while its process is not runnable, each its judge's least window apart
        (`Judge::resolved`: its counters' tick, 10 ms on macOS, Linux's 1/HZ, or a look's own
        length where longer), the finest its window's evidence is read at, never a rate of
        ours. A look there that finds a thread in its kernel holds that window
        (`Follow::schedule`, `Follow::sampled`). A runnable process, and a wait bound by
        stillness, are looked at only when due; on Windows none is sampled, as no reason it
        reads shows its host's disk, and one read of the system's records took 13 ms on
        jupiter. Held by progress.rs `a_rate_wait_samples_a_blocked_process_between_its_looks`
        and, on Windows, `a_process_flushing_to_its_disk_shows_its_storages_work`.
      - *A wait in a kernel is its host's only while its disks complete I/O* (ROOT's ruling,
        2026-11-16, kiln goal 683bc085, the member-share stall). ROOT's red on adacachy2
        (KVM; its btrfs wholly allocated): two `stop daemon`s refused at one moment, 28.9 ms
        into their waits, past W* 8.96 ms (4124d8c70's message: 34.75 ms past 19.24 ms). The
        cause, read from code by lane linux-kvm (Linux 7.2-rc4): a stop's `finish()` waits for
        its `--rm` runs' removals (`await_removals`), each renamed to `.ID.removing`, then its
        directory fsynced (`Removal::sync`). On btrfs that fsync is a whole transaction's
        commit (fs/btrfs/tree-log.c: the rename records the directory's `last_unlink_trans`,
        `btrfs_record_unlink_dir`, and `btrfs_log_inode` then returns
        `BTRFS_LOG_FORCE_COMMIT`). Two daemons stopping share one commit, which one task runs
        while the other sleeps in `D` (transaction.c `wait_for_commit`), doing no I/O of its
        own and counted none of the committer's: Linux's look read it still, where macOS's
        would have held it whatever its disks did. Two changes:
        - *The rule* (`Hold::disks`, `Hold::held_since`). A look that ran nothing and finds a
          thread of its party in its kernel (Linux `D`, macOS `TH_STATE_UNINTERRUPTIBLE`) is
          `Held` only where its host's block devices completed I/O between the look before
          and this one. Linux: `/proc/diskstats`' reads, writes, discards (4.18) and flushes
          (5.5) completed, and each device's milliseconds doing I/O (amended 2026-11-18,
          below), every line summed (Documentation/admin-guide/iostats.rst, its fields 1, 5,
          12 and 16, and 10; `os::disks_worked`). macOS: each IOKit
          `IOBlockStorageDriver`'s `Statistics`, `Operations (Read)` and `Operations
          (Write)`, summed (IOKit/storage/IOBlockStorageDriver.h, what iostat(8) reads;
          `shards_apple::storage`, IOKit bound when first read, as shards-apple binds every
          framework, PM M113).
          ROOT named reads and writes; discards and flushes are their devices' completions
          too, and a window in which only a cache flush completes, an fsync's last step,
          shows in field 16 alone.
          - The window is the judge's own; no constant. The count is read only by a look that
            finds a thread in its kernel: a party that ran nothing over a window and waits in
            its kernel at its end waited there at its start too, as it runs to enter a wait,
            so its look before read the count. A look whose look before read none, cold
            start among them, holds nothing by it.
          - Host-wide by design: the waiter on a shared commit does no I/O of its own.
            Partitions count with their disks and mapped devices with theirs, as only growth
            is read; a sum that fell (a device gone, a 32-bit kernel's counter wrapped) is no
            growth, saturated sums the same.
          - What it refuses: a wait in a kernel that no device serves across a window, a dead
            NFS mount's, is still, and refused past W*. What it cannot: one stuck for good on
            a host whose disks are busy with others' I/O is held while they are, and refused
            at the first window in which none completes any. It gives a party no authority:
            its own I/O held it already (`Io`).
          - Rate windows unchanged: a look that finds a thread in its kernel vouches for no
            window, its host's disks idle or not (`progress::vouches`, `Follow::sampled`).
            Leaving a window out of the rate refuses nothing, and a party stuck so that runs
            nothing is refused by stillness.
          - *R-D, amended 2026-11-18* (ROOT's ruling; own-38e, with own-35b; CI 44227612442's
            x86_64 gnu job 134545100614). A thread in its kernel is held too where, since the
            look before, its host's CPU or memory `some` total grew (`Hold::stalls`).
            - These are Linux's /proc/pressure/cpu and /proc/pressure/memory. They are read
              only at a look that finds a thread in its kernel, as the devices' count is.
            - PSI's `some` is "the share of time in which at least some tasks are stalled on a
              given resource" (Documentation/accounting/psi.rst). v6.18
              kernel/sched/psi.c:243-262 counts CPU `some` while more tasks are runnable than
              run on a CPU, and memory `some` while any task stalls on memory.
            - Why: that run had ten refusals: seven build.rs builds, api_image.rs's build,
              moved.rs's create and containers.rs's commit.
              - Each found a thread in `D`, in `jbd2_log_wait_commit`,
                `folio_wait_bit_common` or `__wait_on_buffer` (the image store's fsyncs,
                crates/image/src/store.rs).
              - Their host's devices were idle between two looks a few ms apart. W* was 15 to
                50 ms, learned on unloaded runners.
              - A journal commit first waits for every open handle of its transaction
                (fs/jbd2/commit.c:454, transaction.c:816-844), and for its own thread's CPU.
                A folio's or buffer's lock waits on its holder (mm/filemap.c:1251,
                fs/buffer.c:121-124). That is kernel work no device shows, held up by the
                host's CPUs or memory.
              - Why a waiter in `D` sees idle devices (v6.18). A task's plugged block I/O
                reaches its device only when the task sleeps: `schedule` flushes the plug,
                through `sched_submit_work`, only for a task that is not running
                (kernel/sched/core.c:7024-7025, :6990). A task preempted, or yielding at
                `cond_resched` (:7455-7458, `__schedule(SM_PREEMPT)` at :7113), keeps its
                plug until it runs again.
              - A journal commit shadows each metadata buffer (fs/jbd2/journal.c:430) and
                submits its journal write under one plug (fs/jbd2/commit.c:550-788, the
                write at :726, a `cond_resched` at :729). The shadow clears only when that
                write ends (commit.c:42), and `do_get_write_access` waits for it
                uninterruptibly (fs/jbd2/transaction.c:1092).
              - Writeback throttling (wbt) counts a write from `rq_qos_throttle`
                (block/blk-mq.c:3042, :3089), before it is plugged (:3222). So a writer
                throttled in `rq_qos_wait` (block/blk-rq-qos.c:275-276, uninterruptible) can
                wait on writes still in another task's plug. A folio's lock or writeback
                is held over its reader's or writer's plugged I/O too (mm/readahead.c:160-176,
                fs/ext4/inode.c:2862-2986).
              - So while the submitter waits for a CPU, its waiters are in `D` and no device
                shows work. That wait for a CPU is what CPU `some` counts. CI 44227612442's
                x86_64 musl job (134545100600) refused three more such waits: a build's
                client in `rq_qos_wait`, 411 ms since it last ran; `configure disk`'s
                client in `folio_wait_bit_common`; and, in a refusal's own account, a
                daemon with two of its threads in `do_get_write_access`.
            - I/O `some` is not read: a folio's or buffer's waiter waits in `io_schedule`, its
              own I/O stall, and would hold itself.
            - The limit, accepted: on a host whose CPU or memory pressure grows at every look,
              a wait in a kernel on work that never comes (a dead mount's) is held rather than
              refused, until its job's own bound. So is a thrashing refault's waiter, which is
              its own memory stall (mm/filemap.c:1262-1265, `psi_memstall_enter`; own-35b).
              The tests have no network and no dead mounts, and a false refusal fails CI on
              every loaded runner.
            - Where the kernel keeps no pressure record (no CONFIG_PSI, or `psi=0`), the
              devices alone decide, as before. macOS and Windows keep none, and are unchanged.
            - Each look that finds a thread in its kernel says what it read since the look
              before (`Watch::kernel`): its devices' work and the CPU and memory `some`
              deltas, or that no pressure record is kept. A hold's words say it, and so does
              a refusal's account, beside each thread's `wchan`. Each later hold or refusal
              then names the reading that decided it: R-D's after-evidence (R10).
            - Also read, and unused by the rule: each CPU's idle and iowait (ROOT's ruling of
              2026-11-18 on own-35b's bound).
              - At each look that finds a thread in its kernel, /proc/stat's per-CPU idle and
                iowait are read, in USER_HZ ticks (fs/proc/stat.c). Their deltas since the look
                before go in the reading, beside the PSI deltas. A window shorter than one
                tick is said to be "under a tick", as no count could show it.
              - They are the data that settles own-35b's bound after the tag. That bound would
                hold a thread in its kernel only where no CPU was idle over the window. cpuidle
                residency cannot say it, as it is added only as a CPU leaves idle
                (drivers/cpuidle/cpuidle.c:306).
              - Any growth is kept until then. A journal commit waits for every open handle
                of its transaction (transaction.c:816-844), whose holder may be busy on a CPU,
                not starved. A saturation bound would refuse those waits on a busy runner
                whose CPUs are not all full, and a false refusal fails CI on every loaded
                runner.
            - Tests: `progress::tests::a_wait_in_its_kernel_is_held_by_its_hosts_cpu_and_memory_stalls`,
              and on Linux `a_readings_cpu_idle_is_said_per_cpu_and_under_a_tick_as_such`.
              Red: lanes/redgreen/own-38e-rd.patch. Owed first (R09): run 44243183339
              (budget-e2e, build.rs in full on 8 ubuntu-24.04 runners) shows the symptom.
          - Windows, amended 2026-11-17 (kiln goal b2124227, lane ci-storms-judge; ROOT's
            brief: count Windows' hold only while its host shows progress, as Linux's and
            macOS's now are). A flush still shows by no wait reason (`Executive`, a pipe
            reader's too, PM M606), only by its processes' own I/O counts (`Io::done`). But
            its waits on its host's paging had been its host's hold at every look, whatever
            its disks did: a thread waiting `FreePage`, `PageIn` or `PoolAllocation` (their
            `Wr` forms too) was read runnable, and so was one in transition, whose kernel
            stack is out of memory ("waiting for resources other than the processor", WMI's
            `Win32_Thread`). A party so waiting with its disks idle was never refused.
            - Now each of those is its wait in its kernel (`os::pages`, `Hold::uninterruptible`),
              under this rule: held only where its host's disks completed I/O since the look
              before, and its look vouches for no window of its rate. Its disks serve each: a
              page-in is their read, and a page is freed by writing it out.
            - Its disks: every physical disk's `BytesRead` and `BytesWritten`, summed
              (IOCTL_DISK_PERFORMANCE, winioctl.h's DISK_PERFORMANCE; `os::disks`). Each disk
              is found by its MS-DOS name `PhysicalDriveN` in QueryDosDeviceW's list of every
              name (fileapi.h), and opened for no access, as Win32's "Calling DeviceIoControl"
              opens `\\.\PhysicalDrive0`: the IOCTL asks FILE_ANY_ACCESS. Bytes, as its
              `ReadCount` and `WriteCount` are 32 bits wide and wrap, which would read as no
              I/O. Every call is kernel32's, which every process has loaded: no library joins a
              launch (shards-api adds windows-sys's `Win32_System_Ioctl` feature, and names
              `Win32_Security`, which its `CreateFileW` already took through shards-ipc).
            - Why its disks, not its process's counts: a page-in is the memory manager's

              that ran nothing faulted nothing. Its own I/O counts hold it where they grow, as
              before (`Io::done`).

              says no size it needs. Cold: a look whose look before read no disks holds
              nothing by them. A host whose disks this user cannot open holds no paging wait,
              which its other evidence then decides. A sum that fell (a disk gone) is no
              growth. Host-wide by design, as Linux's and macOS's: a page-in stuck on a host
              whose disks are busy with others' I/O is held while they are.

        - *A `--rm` run's removal is not synced* (`Removal::needs_sync`, `Removal::sync_all`;
          D27 amended). The sync before a removal's name goes keeps a power loss from bringing
          a microVM back beside one that took its name. A `--rm` one brought back goes as the
          next start opens its registry, before it sees any name (`Registry::open_on`'s
          `auto_remove` arm), whatever of its directory the power loss kept. So its removal
          needs no sync, its name goes once it is set aside, and a stop's `finish()` waits on
          no commit for its runs that ended with `--rm`, nor does any `--rm` run's end. Every
          other removal syncs as before, and so does a `--rm` one whose record may not say so:
          one taken out of its reservation, its record maybe unwritten, and one whose `--rm`
          was set after its record was written (D181: an engine's microVM going with its
          provider; `Registry::rm_unrecorded`, cleared once a record saying it is written).
          Crash semantics: a daemon's crash after set-aside brings nothing back, as before; a
          power loss may bring back a `--rm` run's directory, which the next start removes
          before any name is seen, as it removes every `--rm` record (dockerd's restore
          removes its AutoRemove containers too, moby daemon/daemon.go). Held by containers.rs
          `a_power_loss_after_an_unsynced_rm_removal_shares_no_name` (every state the
          power-loss model allows, the name taken by the next microVM: none shared, the `--rm`
          one never seen, nothing set aside left) and
          `a_rm_removal_needs_no_sync_unless_its_record_may_lack_its_rm`; and by daemon.rs
          `rm_runs_ending_together_take_no_sync` (the completer's batches of `--rm` runs whose
          records say so: no sync begun, on Windows for their deletions neither) and
          `removals_ending_together_take_one_sync`, whose batch is now of `--rm` runs that end
          before their records are written. Written for runs recorded as `--rm`, that test
          waited for a sync that no longer comes, refused by the judge 198.8 s into its wait
          (CI 43990298220 at f6ad71083, aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu).

    - *A test's wait counts its own test's party* (2026-11-17, kiln goal b2124227, lane
      ci-read-6; ROOT's r669). The daemon's unit tests share one process, and their judge
      (daemon.rs tests' `Wait`) took this process for its party: any thread's CPU but its
      waiters' was progress (`others`: CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID, QueryProcessCycleTime), and
      no look was judged before the latest deadline any daemon thread of the process waited
      until (`latest_deadline`). Other tests' threads, and what ended tests left, held a wait
      that had stalled: CI 43990298220's aarch64-apple-darwin job held
      `removals_ending_together_take_one_sync`'s wait, which could not end, for 21 minutes, to
      its step's limit, where ROOT's r669 (f6ad71083, macOS arm64, that test alone) refused it
      81 ms in; Linux's jobs refused it only 198 s (gnu) and 853 s (musl) in.
      - *The rule.* A test's party is its own thread and every thread made from one of its
        party's: the daemon's, made through `DaemonThread` (std's builder, whose thread under
        test is a member of its maker's party), and the test's helpers (`party::spawn_in`,
        `party::spawn_member`). `Test::on` opens it (`party::of_test`) before its daemon makes
        a thread. A wait (`Counted::here`) counts what its party's members ran, each read by
        its own clock (Unix: `platform::ThreadClock`, D191; Windows: QueryThreadCycleTime, in
        the cycles the tests' `cpu` counts there, as GetThreadTimes moves in 15.625 ms ticks,
        coarser than a W*), the totals of those that ended kept, less what a member ran
        while it waited judged; and it is judged from no earlier than the latest deadline a
        thread of its own party waits until (`Waiting`, registered with its thread's party).
      - *Of no party* (counted by no party's wait): a thread made by another crate, by std, or
        by a module outside the daemon's (netproc's dial servers, context, the build proxy);
        the cuts watcher (daemon/cuts.rs), which is this process's and serves every daemon in
        it. A test's own thread was of its party but no member, its waiter (now a member, its
        own waits counting none of its run: amended below). A wait on a thread of no party
        counts this process, as before.
      - *Production is unchanged.* Every judged wait of the daemon's and shards-api's follows
        another process by its ID and start (a VM process, its holder, a home's daemon), so no
        other home's work is in its party. `DaemonThread` is std's builder there; two daemon
        threads made by `Scope::spawn`, which panics where no thread is made (R01), now are
        made through it: an exec's output reader (health.rs, the exec killed and the error
        returned) and `stats`' asks (commands.rs, a sample not taken).
      - *Tested* (written, not run; ROOT's): daemon.rs
        `a_waits_party_is_its_own_tests_threads_alone`, two tests' parties in one process, W*
        20 ms: one party's member waits on nothing; the other's spins for 250 W*, then sleeps
        until this wait has ended, its deadline 500 W* from its start. Green: the waiting
        party's wait is refused within a few W*, while the other still spins. Red where
        `Counted::here` counts this process: the other's spin, then its deadline, hold the wait
        past the 5 s the other spun.
      - *Amended 2026-11-17 (#36; ROOT's ask, and its approval of the test's thread as a
        member): one judge for every crate's tests, the test's own thread a member.* The judge
        is two crates. shards-judge is D215's `Record`, `Judge` and their rule (judge.rs, which
        shards-api re-exports whole). shards-testwait is the tests' party, deadlines and judged
        waits, the daemon's moved whole, a dev-dependency of shards and of shards-remote, which
        shards-api depends on and so cannot share shards-api's. The daemon keeps no copy.
        - *A test's own thread is a member* of the party `party::of_test` makes for it: a
          member's wait on its test's next step (shards-remote's stand-in hosts wait on its
          steers) counts the test thread's run and its hold, as D215 counts a held host. Before,
          a test thread its host held off a CPU looked to that wait like a party gone still.
        - *A wait counts none of its asker's run.* Each member's CPU while it waits judged is
          its own (`waited`), and a wait reads every member's clock but its asking thread's
          (`ran`). Subtracting the measured waiting CPU from the sum of every member's left the
          asker's CPU between its measure and the party's read, read as progress at about half
          its looks. So the test thread's own waits are judged as before, and members' waits on
          it only gain patience.

          timer is not refused before it (bounded since: *A driver's progress*, below). Its control tests' stand-in controller runs the product
          controller's liveness (no idle timeout and no keep-alive, `managed::transport_of`,
          D180): hyper-quic's default 30 s idle timeout, negotiated with the endpoint, put
          keep-alives on both ends, which a judged wait reads as progress, so that a stuck
          lane's wait would never be given up on.
        - *The product's timeouts, audited (R03).* Every caller in this workspace of the lane
          API's waits of a caller's patience (`PendingExec`, `PendingMcp`, `PendingMember`,

          Red (lanes/redgreen/remote-slow-lane.patch): the first waited for within 5 W* of the

          wait's party waiting on a process outside it (its events no member's) is refused at

          `a_cold_wait_refuses_a_still_party`; red (lanes/redgreen/cold-wait.patch) where a
          cold wait is not judged, its own judged wait giving up, never a hang.

        - *crates/remote's other tests, judged* (2026-11-17, #36, ROOT's batch): control/unix.rs,

          input go pass as the control endpoint does (`Service::refusal`), its owner's

        - *A driver's progress* (2026-11-18, #36, ROOT: CI 44227612442 at 7ca9f467e2,
          aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, job 134545100447). Two of shards-remote's tests held their
          step to its limit: managed.rs `a_vanished_owners_place_goes_to_its_successor_as_it_dials`
          and managed/input.rs's successor (`subscribed`). Neither awaited event was missing,
          and no party was busy with the awaited work. Each settled on its party's stillness
          after a refusal (`waited(|| false)`), and the stillness never came. The endpoint's
          driver probed the vanished holder it had asked for an answer, its probe timeouts
          backed off (RFC 9002 §6.2.1) and never given up, as no idle timeout ends a connection
          of this crate's transports (D180). Each probe's turn was read as its party's run, and
          each next probe registered as its party's deadline, before which no wait is judged.
          - *Its progress.* A turn in which a driver takes something in (a peer's datagram, or a
            caller's command and its wake), or in which its handler's own time comes. A turn its
            wait woke for on its own timer alone is its own clock's, as a member's run while it
            waits judged is (`waited`): its retransmissions, probes and keep-alives are no run
            of its party's (shards-testwait `party::own_timer_since`).
          - *Its deadlines.* Its judgments: its handler's own time, an open connection's
            handshake window (`Liveness::due`) or its look at a send that waits
            (`Liveness::next`), and a closed connection's drain (RFC 9000 §10.2: three probe
            timeouts, set once as it closes). Its transport's own timers (`poll_timeout`) too,
            whose retransmissions may bring a live peer's answer after a datagram was lost, until
            `PERSISTENT_CONGESTION_THRESHOLD` (3) of its waits in a row woke for its own timer
            alone. A path silent through that many probe timeouts lost all it was sent (RFC 9002

            takes something in or its handler's own time comes, its judgments alone. Never its
            keep-alives, which judge nothing and, answered, would plan another for ever.

            next attempt past its holder's probe timeout from that refusal, bounded from the
            holder's life (`net::probe_timeout_within`: every RTT sample its endpoint took of
            the holder came within it), as net.rs's newcomers do (item 4). That attempt takes
            the place, and a refusal of it fails the test (D180).

            progressed since its waiter last woke on its timer alone, so that an absence check

            - A replayed handshake: from the first ask, its handshake's cold probe timeout,
              999 ms (was 20 s).
            - A handshake that answers and never advances: from its endpoint's accepting it,
              seven backed-off cold probe timeouts, 6.993 s (was 30 s). It must not connect
              sooner than that after the test began (`COLD_PTO` times `COLD_PROBE_TIMEOUTS`,
              was the literal 6.993 s).
            - The learned window: from its accepting, its endpoint's slowest completed
              handshake, at most the slow round as the test saw it (was 30 s, with "below
              6.5 s"). It must not connect sooner than the slow round's held answer, 3 s (was
              2.5 s). The case's premise, a slow round shorter than the cold window, is
              asserted.
          - *tests/loopback.rs's numbers, ruled* (2026-11-18, #36 item 3). Its waits are judged
            by its own `Patience`: its subjects' transports (`net::View`, the datagrams their
            drivers heard and the windows they were judged by) and what the tests see them do
            (`PROGRESS`). An integration test builds shards-remote without `cfg(test)`, so the
            product's threads join no shards-testwait party there.
            - Judged now:
              - the machine's wait on its command (was a 5 ms poll): its child looked at as D215
                paces looks (`shards_abi::pace::pause`), its hangup heard as it comes;
              - two stdin pipes and daemon rooms filling (was 300 ms each): `settled`, nothing
                moving for a whole window of the slowest answer the path has shown
                (`View::learned`), or, before any answer, of the window the path was judged by
                (cold: seven backed-off probe timeouts);
              - `until_there` (was a look each 10 ms at most): `until`, looking again after as
                long as it has waited;
              - a frozen process's trickle (was "300 ms in"): until its echo is under way and
                both its sides have learned a window;
              - a gone command's writes reaching its daemon's driver (was 300 ms): until its
                daemon lets go of it (`Seen::Released`);
              - the relay's hold before a run-out (was four times the run-out's time): until its
                client is told the run-out (`Stall::Unreached` with its path's window). A probe
                past the run-out's due with no run-out told gives the run up, so the test fails
                instead of hanging.
            - Derived now:
              - a holder's wait past its probe timeout (was 200 ms) and a gone connection's
                draining, three probe timeouts (RFC 9000 §10.2.2, was 500 ms): from
                `probe_timeout_within`, RFC 9002 §6.2.1 with every RTT sample within the
                connection's exchanges as the test saw them, plus RFC 9000 §18.2's 25 ms;
              - a caller's give-up after a run-out (was past twice the slowest handshake): at
                the first probe past the run-out's due, the path's probe timeout and its slowest
                handshake (328 ms here);
              - the whole-process freeze (was 200 ms): past every window both sides learned and
                past kiln's measured freezes (124 ms, a 2 ms sleep's p99 on adacachy2).
            - Kept as inputs the cases are built from: a command's late tell (50 ms, `Late`,
              which sets only how surely a server that sent the exit first shows it), a client
              sending on to a stream its daemon stopped (200 ms, which nothing waits on), a
              daemon slow to answer (300 ms, `Answers::stall`), a silent command's 2 s, a
              remembered path's 1 ms, 300 ms and 1 ms, and a trickle's 2 ms a chunk. Also kept:
              the slower handshake's hold, between the first handshake and its client's probe
              timeout as that run measured them.
        - *The workspace's tests, swept* (2026-11-18, #36, ROOT: CI green has to hold under load
          everywhere). The sweep read every sleep, bounded receive or wait, duration literal and
          deadline in crates/shards/tests and in the tests of vmm, api, ipc, init, image and
          registry: 804 lines. Each was classed as judged, a poll's interval, a value or virtual
          time, a case's input, a measurement window, an absence check (which load can only make
          pass), or a fixed patience that fails its test at expiry. The fixed patiences are
          ranked by how likely a loaded or nested runner fails them falsely. None of them failed
          in the 16 CI runs' logs read, whose timing failures were judged waits refusing.
          - *Batch 1, crates/api's session tests.* They now wait through shards-testwait (a
            dev-dependency of shards-api), judged on their own threads.
            - Its feeder's first read and its release (was 1 s each): judged, the feeder a
              member of its test's party.
            - A host's first words kept (was 10 s): judged, its keeping thread a member.
            - The run's end closing its host's channel (was 10 s), and an orchestrator's ledger
              (was within 120 s): judged with the whole process as their party. The session's
              reader and its lessor's calls are the session's own threads, of no test's party.
            - Readiness told to a waiter (was 120 s): judged.
            - Kept and ruled: `BOUND`, the 120 s patience a test gives the session's own waits
              (`Shared::wait`, the API's input), which a correct run answers at once.
    - *Rated answers alone teach R* and C*.* Many kept records held R* 0 ns: answers reaped
      before any look read their CPU (`run_ending`'s `try_wait` reaped a quick client between
      paced looks), a floor that refuses nothing. `Seen::Learned` is now `{ slowest, rated:
      Option<Rated> }`. `Record::teach(wall, work)` is for work read through the answer
      (shards-api's `Follow` and the daemon's waits read their VM process at it). A test's
      `Wait` reads its party once more at its answer, a command's client while it is a zombie
      (waitid(2) `WNOWAIT`, POSIX.1-2024) or, on Windows, through its watch's handle, and
      teaches R* and C* only where no process of it was lost before that read
      (`Wait::read_through`, else `Record::teach_unrated`: W* alone). A kept record is
      `served W* [rated R*cpu R*wall C*]`. One without a whole rating, the older three
      numbers among them, is read as none: its kind cold until its next answer rewrites it.
      *Amended 2026-11-17 (CI 44076016255, arm64 Windows):* an answer read through its end
      whose work read none teaches W* alone too (`Record::teach`). It says nothing of the least
      rate a working party answers at, and R* 0 ns holds no floor. Windows' process times
      move in its clock's ticks (GetProcessTimes, 15.625 ms; "C* 15.625ms" in the runner's
      accounts): one of harness.rs' three stand-ins busy 50 ms read as none on that busy
      runner, its kind R* 0 ns over 70.6 ms, and the sleeper ticking 1 ms in 11 was served
      22.9 s in. Held by judge.rs `an_answer_of_no_work_teaches_its_slowest_alone` (red with
      such an answer rated). A wait's account and the tests' rest checks read a process's
      runnable threads on Windows too (`shards_api::runnable_threads`, from the same system
      listing a `Followed`'s hold reads); before, Windows read none ("unread").
    - *Where it applies* (ROOT's ruling, 2026-11-14). A caller passes `Span::work`, read
      through one rule (`Watch::vouched_by`: the look ran or rested, and its process was
      neither starved, stopped nor ending). The tests' `Wait` passes it everywhere. A wait on
      a VM process names its bound, with no default (`shards_api::Bound`, `Follow::begin`):
      - `Rate`, replies of bounded work: the daemon's wait for a VM's READY (daemon.rs
        `ready`), for a VM's next request for access (daemon.rs `grant`), on its own asks of
        a microVM (daemon/health.rs `following`: RECLAIM, ROOM, METRICS, each builtin), on a
        held visit (daemon/visit.rs), and on the network process's start (netproc.rs
        `NetLink::follow`). A VM asleep on an event that never comes is refused there, once it
        passes C* below R*.
      - `Stillness`, ends that come when their work does: shards-api's waits on a guest
        (crates/api client.rs, `Awaited::Boot`, `Connect` and `End`, which hold the user's
        own start to its first listener and the user's command) and a builder's waits
        (build/builder.rs: a build waits on its sources as long as they take). A user's
        `sleep 3600` is a guest asleep by design, its caller's to end.
      - parents.rs' wait for a leaf to empty and the daemon's CHILDREN judge pass no work
        and judge by stillness alone.
      An answer whose VM process could not be read at it teaches W* alone
      (`Follow::answered`, `Follow::ended`). No literal: W*, R*, C* and every window are
      learned where they run, and a kind with no rated answer has no floor. One derived count
      stands beside them: `judge::SPREAD`, 2, the fewest answers whose least and most can be
      two answers' (below).
    - *Held by* crates/api judge.rs:
      - `a_wait_slower_than_any_answer_is_refused_though_it_progresses`: b24's shape, refused
        at the first look its work passes C* and not the look before;
      - `a_busy_wait_past_w_star_goes_on`;
      - `a_wait_on_a_peer_past_w_star_goes_on_within_its_kinds_work`;
      - `a_window_its_caller_cannot_vouch_for_is_out_of_the_rate`;
      - `an_unrated_answer_teaches_its_slowest_alone`;
      - `a_record_merged_in_keeps_each_bound_past_the_others`;
      - crates/api progress.rs `a_rate_bound_refuses_only_a_ticking_sleeper`, real processes
        against a kind of W* 200 ms, R* 1/2 and C* 100 ms. A ticker (10 ms of work in each
        100 ms) is refused under `Rate` and goes on under `Stillness`. A spinner goes on. One
        doing its kind's work over more time (60 ms over some 600 ms: a peer waited on, or a
        host that slows it) goes on to its end. 5 of 5 green on adas-mac-studio-3.local (about
        9.7 s each, over 1d9dd1f07); red with `Rate` taken for `Stillness`, "a ticking sleeper
        was not refused under its rate";
      - and harness.rs `a_command_asleep_but_ticking_is_refused_and_a_busy_one_goes_on`. Its
        kind starts from a kept unrated record of R* 0 ns, is taught by three stand-ins busy
        50 ms, and then refuses one that works 1 ms in each 11 ms. A busy 200 ms one past W* is
        served. Green on adas-mac-studio-3.local (macOS arm64, 14e037fb0 and this change,
        test-release, kiln r1003), with the focused harness tests 9 of 9 and shards-api 81 of
        81. Red there with the rule removed (judge.rs's b24 and vouch tests failed, and the
        sleeper was served at its own end 95.2 s in, its kind `served 95238910958 rated
        1999931084 95238910958 1999931084`), and red with the old unrated record read as rated
        (R* 0 ns kept: served 103.4 s in).
    - *R* and C* refuse once two answers have taught them* (ROOT's ruling of 2026-11-17, goal
      fb3528f9's cluster 1). A record counts the rated answers that taught its R* and C*
      (`Rated::answers`), and `Judge` refuses a party by its rate only from two
      (`judge::SPREAD`).
      - *Why.* Four live, progressing waits on CI's loaded x86_64 runners were refused by rate
        against kinds one answer had taught: each record's R* CPU was its C* and its R* wall
        its W*, to the nanosecond. On a single answer, a new answer's work is above it, and
        its rate below it, each with probability ½ where a kind's answers are exchangeable,
        so one answer's bounds refuse its kind's own answers about as often as a coin. A
        refused wait teaches nothing, so such a record never widened.
        | CI run, job (revision) | wait | its work | C* | its rate | R* | W* |
        |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
        | 44076016255 x86_64 musl (8fc54dcfb7) | engine.rs `exec prov … api POST /containers/web2/wait`, its answer already printed | 12.888561 ms over 26.602167 ms unheld, 55.3 ms in | 12.055769 ms | 0.55× R* | 12.055769 ms in 13.66951 ms | 13.66951 ms |
        | same job | engine_ring.rs `exec prov … api-bulk ping 200` | 124.251167 ms over 79.756791 ms, 135.6 ms in | 85.736684 ms | 0.82× R* | 85.736684 ms in 45.075451 ms | 45.075451 ms |
        | 43950458285 x86_64 musl (1793da7c22) | containers.rs `shards export -o … exported` | 84.490594 ms over 111.063723 ms, 252.3 ms in | 70.457552 ms | 0.67× R* | 70.457552 ms in 62.346488 ms | 62.346488 ms |
        | same job | containers.rs `run --pull never -d --name user … sleep` | 594.112474 ms over 1.193788288 s, 1.86 s in | 524.831958 ms | 0.29× R* | 524.831958 ms in 309.39505 ms | 309.39505 ms |
        The first job restored its records from 44031797055's musl job, the same host model
        (Intel Xeon 6975P-C).
      - *Two, derived.* One answer's least rate and most work are that one answer, so two is
        the fewest answers with any spread. No constant beside it; R*, C* and W* stay learned.
      - *Counted once.* An answer taught adds one (`Record::teach`); a record merged in
        (`Record::merge`, a kept record read back) counts the more of the two, never their sum,
        as the same kept record merged in again would count its answers twice. Two processes'
        answers may so count as one's: a count low refuses later, never sooner.
      - *Kept.* A test's kept record is `served W* [rated R*cpu R*wall C* answers]`. One kept
        before answers were counted, `rated` with three numbers, is read as one answer's, until
        its next rated answer counts it two (tests' `WaitKind::learn_kept`).
      - *b24 still caught.* Its sleeper is refused once a second answer has taught its kind,
        at the first due look past C*, as before.
      - *Held by* crates/api judge.rs `one_answers_rates_refuse_nothing` (the engine wait's
        own numbers: unrefused on one answer, refused at the same look once the same answer
        is taught again; red without the count) and `a_sleeper_is_refused_once_two_answers_taught_its_kind`
        (40 looks unrefused on one answer, refused at look 16 on two). The rate tests above,
        judge.rs' and progress.rs `a_rate_bound_refuses_only_a_ticking_sleeper`, now teach
        their kinds twice; harness.rs' teaches three. Written, not run (ROOT's runs owed).
    - A look at a process whose exit is under way (a zombie; on Windows, a process of its
      tree that exited since) judges nothing. Its end is the wait's answer, and wins over a
      refusal it races.
    - A stalled guest is not stopped: it stays its caller's.
  - *Cold start.* Before its kind's first answer (`Shards::seen(kind)` is `Seen::Cold`), a
    wait follows liveness alone, the VM process's end. So does a wait that began cold and
    finds the record learned meanwhile.
    - The gap: a guest whose VM runs but never answers its first call is ended only by its
      caller. `Guest::stop` from a thread of its own ends a connect as `Ended(Stopped)` and a
      wait as `End::Stopped`.
    - `Shards::seen` tells a caller when its first call needs a cancel of its own.
  - *Its contract, and its gap.* It is for a wait in which the VM works toward its answer (a
    boot to its listener, a workload to its end).
    - A guest that idles before it answers (on a timer, an input) runs nothing and is
      refused. Such a guest is asked with `connect` and `wait_for`.
    - A guest that spins without answering keeps its VM process running and is never judged
      stalled: the limit the daemon's `Wait::WhileRuns` has too.
  - *Its readers* link no VMM (this entry's falsifier is a client that has to).
    - Linux: the process's CPU clock (clock_getcpuclockid(3), clock_gettime(2)). It gives
      its threads' run time in nanoseconds as the scheduler keeps it
      (kernel/time/posix-cpu-timers.c, `cpu_clock_sample_group`). It is read between two
      reads of the process's start and state (`/proc/<pid>/stat` fields 22 and 3), so a pid
      another process got in between shows.
      - ROOT first named `/proc/<pid>/stat`'s utime and stime (fields 14 and 15). Those
        count clock ticks (USER_HZ, 100 a second), in which an answer within two ticks
        shows no CPU at all.
      - Its last CPU, read once its exit is told (waitid(2), a pidfd readable, its state
        `Z`), is what it had run by that notice, not by its last instruction: the kernel
        tells the exit (kernel/exit.c, `do_exit`'s `exit_notify`) before the task's last
        switch from its CPU (`do_task_dead`), which charges its clock with what ran
        between. A later read of the same zombie can be more, never less (PM M584: 14 in
        5,000 `true` children on adacachy2 grew 3 to 8 µs after waitid saw them; the
        test's two reads differed 46 µs once). The watcher reads it once, and
        `progress::tests::an_exited_process_is_read_until_it_is_reaped` holds a later read
        no less than an earlier, never equal.
    - macOS: proc_pid_rusage (RUSAGE_INFO_V0): its threads' user and system times in Mach
      absolute-time units, converted by mach_timebase_info(3).
      - The same call gives its start (a pid given to another process shows) and its exit
        time.
      - It reads a zombie too, so the watcher reads a VM process's last CPU before it reaps
        it.
      - XNU fills those times from `recount_task_times`, as it fills PROC_PIDTASKINFO's,
        which shards-vmm's `platform::process_usage` reads (`rusage_times_are_task_info_times`
        holds the two equal).
      - The reader duplicates shards-vmm's (R12) because the client links no VMM.
    - Unix, both: the child shards-api starts execs into the VM process, so its pid is the
      VM's; a guest taken back is read by its identity's pid and start.
    - Windows: the child is `shards`, and the VM process is its child in shards' own Job
      (D141), so the reader holds that `shards` and every descendant.
      - Descendants come from a Toolhelp32 snapshot (CreateToolhelp32Snapshot with
        TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS; Process32FirstW/NextW's `th32ParentProcessID`).
      - A process is kept only where it started no earlier than its listed parent
        (GetProcessTimes' creation time). This is PM M528's rule: a pid is reused once its
        process has gone.
      - Each is held by a handle of its own (OpenProcess with
        PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION and SYNCHRONIZE), which keeps its times readable
        after it exits. One gone since the snapshot (ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER) or not this
        user's (ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED) is no process of the tree.
      - GetProcessTimes' kernel and user times (FILETIME, 100 ns units, summed over its
        threads) feed the record.
      - QueryProcessCycleTime's count of the cycles its threads used tells whether they ran:
        GetProcessTimes documents no resolution for its times.
      - Not a nested Job, which ROOT approved first: a Job counts only processes created
        after the child joins it; std starts no child suspended, so none can join before it
        runs (`ChildExt::main_thread_handle`, which resuming one would need, is unstable);
        and a guest taken back is in no Job of ours.
    - A read that fails while the process lives is a typed refusal, never a silent "no
      progress". It is `Refusal::Process` with its operation (`CpuClock`, `ProcPidRusage`,
      `MachTimebase`, `Snapshot`, `ListProcesses`, `OpenProcess`, `GetProcessTimes`,
      `CycleTime`, `WaitForExit` or `DuplicateHandle`) and code. A process that has gone
      since is its end, which is the wait's.
  - *Other implementors*: the trait's defaults follow liveness alone, as a cold record does
    (`connect(port, Duration::MAX)`, `wait_for(Duration::MAX)`). So do the simulator, which
    has no VM process, and `ManagedGuest`, whose native owner holds its process.
  - *Shared, not copied* (R12, 2026-11-13). The judge's records, schedule and verdict are
    `crates/api/src/judge.rs` (`Record`, `Judge`, `Found`), apart from the CPU they judge.
    The readers also follow a process by its pid alone (`Followed::of_pid`: its start read
    with it, and on Windows the process and what descends from it). shards-api's `Follow`
    is the two together. The daemon's waits on its microVMs' own answers are judged by it
    (D188, `Wait::WhileRuns`), with records of their own. A wait judged from outside, whose
    party cannot be looked at (a writer blocked in its write, the daemon's `slots_hold`),
    asks `Record::stalled(since, now)`: none while its kind is cold or less than W* has
    passed since its last progress, else the stall.
  - Tested (light), host starvation and the outside judge: judge.rs's
    `a_party_its_host_holds_is_live_not_stalled`,
    `a_look_its_host_held_late_counts_its_lateness_as_held`,
    `a_judge_held_past_several_looks_looks_once_and_keeps_its_schedule` and
    `a_wait_judged_from_outside_is_stalled_a_whole_w_star_after_its_last_progress`;
    progress.rs's `a_process_its_host_holds_is_held_and_a_stopped_one_still` (the decision,
    each OS's evidence), `a_stopped_process_is_seen_stopped_and_refused` (a SIGSTOPped
    child, seen stopped and refused), `a_spinning_process_is_seen_runnable` (Unix) and
    `a_processs_runnable_time_is_read` (macOS). Red
    at 7d5118297 with the rule by CPU alone (the hold read and ignored, `Record::stalled` a
    stub; adas-mac-studio.local, macOS 26.2 arm64): `Still` where `Held` was due for the
    throttled stand-in, and no stall where one was due; the readers' own tests passed then
    too, macOS's libproc reading a child's threads with no task port.
  - *Its literals*: 10^9 nanoseconds a second, a timespec's bound (POSIX <time.h>); 100,
    FILETIME's nanoseconds (GetProcessTimes); a zero-time wait (WaitForSingleObject, 0),
    which is a look, not a wait. Nothing else: W*, R* and every time judged are this
    process's own.
- `stop` kills the VM's process at once: the VMM has no host-to-guest power-off
  (vm/runtime.rs), so the page cache a guest held is lost, and a clean stop is the
  client's (ask the guest to sync and power off, `wait_for` its `PowerOff`).
- A stream is non-blocking, each read and write waiting in poll(2) to its timeout; its
  `buffer_sizes` are the OS's SO_SNDBUF/SO_RCVBUF.

**What it holds to** (the requirement its tests cite as D215):
- *A spec* becomes `run --kernel`'s flags as vm_run.rs reads them, the kernel first; one
  that asks for a GPU adds `--gpu`, which `shards` runs in the GPU's VM process (D144), and
  one that names the host's GPUs adds `--gpu-device` for each, by its exact identity (D232). A
  disk's or a share's path that ends in `:ro`, which shards would read as a mode, is
  refused `Unsupported`. Past shards-vmm's bounds (no vCPU; memory odd or under the least)
  it is refused `Bounds` before anything boots, and the hypervisor's own refusal of its
  vCPUs comes back as `Bounds` too; a host without a backend (macOS x86_64) is refused
  `NoBackend`, by name. Windows on arm64 is WHP's, the VMM's `hv::whp_arm64` (D209): the
  API names the backend the VMM builds on each host, and a host whose hypervisor runs no
  guest says so as its VM process starts (`check_host`).
- *An envelope* (2026-11-13, for Hex's reservations, kiln plan step 14):
  `envelope(arch, vcpus, memory_mib)` is the least spec shards-vmm boots on a guest of
  `arch` that holds the ask: at least one vCPU, and its memory rounded up to the VMM's unit
  and to at least `min_memory_mib(arch)`. Where that memory's bytes pass what a u64 holds,
  it is refused `Bounds` (`memory_mib`). `check` takes a spec exactly where the spec is its
  own envelope: one rule from one source, so a caller rounds an ask without restating
  shards' numbers.
  - Its literals are shards-vmm's own, restated with their sources: the unit, 2 MiB
    (`ram_bytes` in `vm/aarch64.rs`, `ram_ranges` in `vm/x86_64.rs`, which boot an even
    number of MiB alone); the least, 64 MiB on arm64 and 128 on x86-64 (`MIN_MEMORY_MIB`
    there); and the most, 2^44 - 2 MiB, the last even MiB whose bytes fit the u64 those
    functions count a guest's memory in (`checked_mul(MIB)`).
  - The unit's derivation is D29's ("Its size"). On arm64 it comes from the boot protocol:
    the DTB at RAM's top lies in one 2 MiB block of RAM. On x86-64, which needs none of
    its own, it is kept as its large page (ROOT, 2026-11-13), and what an odd tail would
    cost is owed as a measurement. The least rests on its comment (a kernel, its bss and
    early allocations, and on arm64 its DTB window); its measurement is owed too (D29).
  - Tested (light): lib's `an_envelope_rounds_up_to_the_unit_and_the_least`,
    `an_envelope_past_what_a_u64_holds_is_refused` and
    `check_and_envelope_agree_on_every_case` (each architecture's rule, at every bound and
    one past it), beside `bounds_are_refused_by_name`. Owed (ROOT): five guard-removal
    mutants, each of which must fail its test: the unit, the least, the u64 bound, the one
    vCPU, and `check`'s comparison with the envelope.
- *A guest's socket directory* is the client's alone (0700), named apart from its pid,
  short enough to bind (else /tmp on Unix; refused by name on Windows), and removed with
  the guest.
- *A connect* dials `CONNECT <port>` until the guest answers `OK`, within its patience: a
  patience of zero is one dial, `Duration::MAX` no clock, and the pause between dials
  `sqrt(2 c w)` of a dial's own work and the wait so far. An answer past
  `OK 4294967295\n` is refused; a port off the allowlist is refused before any dial; a
  guest that has ended is refused at once, `Ended`, or `Boot` with shards' exit and last
  words where it ended before any `OK`.
- *An end*: shards' exit 0 is `PowerOff`, 3 `Reset`, a kill by `stop` `Stopped`, any other
  `Failed` with its words. Its last words are quoted whole, its longest report a reset's,
  and no child that holds its output holds them back; a binary that isn't there is
  `Boot`, by name; no guest's process is left a zombie, dropped or not.
- *A stream* carries bytes both ways and a half-close; a read or a write waits at most its
  timeout, kept to the nanosecond, whether its peer stops reading or a clone took the
  bytes, and the connection goes on after; a clone is the same connection; its
  `buffer_sizes` are the OS's; and a write to a peer that has gone fails `EPIPE`, never
  raising SIGPIPE.
- *A wait that follows its VM process* returns at the guest's answer or end, as the
  no-clock form does. It refuses `Stalled` where its VM process ran nothing for a whole W* of
  its kind, once that kind has an answer, and never judges before. It learns its kind from
  the guest's own answers alone, and refuses typed a read that fails while the process lives.
- *The simulator* meets every case of the same conformance suite.

**Evidence.** PM M515 (an unserved port's refusal past its patience), M463 (what the waits
cost), M464 (what a refused dial costs, the pacing's `c`); the conformance suite and E2E on
HVF; and the waits' own unit tests (`progress::tests`, client.rs's stand-in tests), with
their runs below.

    (`Io { phase: Dial }`), where each later step's deadline is typed `Expired` by the clock
    after the step. So an attempt whose dial outlasted its patience, the least wait the
    streams keep (`kept_wait`, WSAPoll's millisecond or more), was taken for its end rather
    than asked again with more. A dial its deadline passed in is `Expired { phase: Dial }`.
  - `physical::report::windows::tests::pending_private_read_keeps_cells_until_positive_cancel_completion`:
    its deadline, `Instant::now().checked_add(kept_wait())`, took its now before the
    measure, so it was past as `frame` began; and `frame` judged its deadline before it
    issued a read, so none was left pending. `frame` judges its deadline where a read waits
    (`await_read`), a read always under way by then, and the test's deadline is taken after
    the measure.
