  file up by, each trusted for the second the server gives it (`VALID_S`; fs/fuse/dir.c
  `fuse_dentry_revalidate`), and a rename or removal through one leaves the others. On
  adacachy's KVM (Linux, which tells case apart) the same steps agree.
- *Decided:* a name the host found by another case or Unicode form of it is trusted for no
  time (its entry's validity 0), so that each use of it asks the host again; the name the
  host keeps, for its second, as before (server.rs `name_valid`). The name kept is asked of
  the host: macOS's getattrlist(2) `ATTR_CMN_NAME`, as Libc's realpath(3) asks each
  component's case; Windows' FileNormalizedNameInfo, which also says an 8.3 short name's
  long one. A Linux host is asked nothing: its names are found as given, and a directory it
  folds the case of (`chattr +F` on ext4, f2fs or tmpfs) is not handled, its variants
  trusted for their second. The cost, a call more for each LOOKUP on macOS and Windows, is
  unmeasured (ROOT's, R14).
- *Green:* the same test on HVF at `6de3842ac`; its mutation (every name trusted its
  second again) fails as the reproduction did.
- *A rename of a name's case alone* (`mv foo Foo`) changes nothing, and says it is done: the
  Linux VFS takes a rename whose two names are one inode as done without asking any file
  system (fs/namei.c `vfs_rename`, `if (source == target) return 0;`, torvalds/linux master
  of 2026-11), and Linux's own case-insensitive file systems do the same (measured on
  adacachy, Linux 7.2.9, a tmpfs mounted `-o casefold` and a directory `+F`: `rename("foo",
  "Foo")` returns 0 and `ls` says `foo`; a directory's alike). Alternatives:
  - *An inode of its own for each case of a name*, as 9p's uncached modes give each lookup
    one (fs/9p/vfs_inode_dotl.c, `v9fs_get_new_inode_from_fid`), by which WSL2's `/mnt/c`
    renames a name's case: the rename would reach the host, at the cost of two inodes of
    one file in the guest whose page caches, locks and inotify watches are each their own.
    Not taken.
  - *Another case not found* (ENOENT): the rename's target would be new and reach the host,
    but `stat FOO`, `open FOO` and every program that names a file by another case would
    fail where the host finds it. Not taken.
  - Decided: the guest's rename is Linux's own, as its case-insensitive file systems' are;
    a name's case is changed by two renames through another name (`mv foo tmp && mv tmp
    Foo`), as on ext4's casefold. The test holds host and guest alike to Linux's rule
    (testguest case.rs `renamed`).

**Host edits wake the guest's inotify (notices).** Linux's virtio-fs driver negotiates no
feature and has no notification queue (fs/fuse/virtio_fs.c, its `feature_table` empty;
virtio 1.3 §5.11's `VIRTIO_FS_F_NOTIFICATION` unused), and what a FUSE server notifies
(`FUSE_NOTIFY_INVAL_*`) tells fsnotify nothing: a host's edit wakes no watch in the guest.
- *Alternatives.*
  - *Lima's `mountInotify`* (Lima 0.21 and later, experimental): its host agent watches,
    and its guest agent sets each file's times through the mount (pkg/guestagent
    guestagent_linux.go `HandleInotify`, `os.Chtimes`): a write of the host's files, of
    writable mounts alone, and nothing for a file the host removed (lima-vm.io/docs/config/
    mount, "Inotify events are not triggered when files are removed from host").
  - *Docker Desktop's osxfs*: FSEvents mapped to inotify within its own file system ("Move
    events trigger IN_DELETE on the source of the rename and IN_MODIFY on the destination
    ... Some events may be delivered multiple times", docs osxfs.md): its own guest kernel's.
  - *A notification queue in the guest's driver*: a kernel patch no stock kernel has, never
    the base of a fix (version-agnostic, the person's rule).
  - *The guest polling its shares*: a cost each period whatever changed (R05). Not taken.
- *Decided.* The host is watched by its share process, each host's own way
  (vmm `fs/notices.rs`):
  - *Linux:* an inotify watch of each directory the guest holds, made as the guest looks it
    up and let go of as it forgets it (server.rs `watch_dir`, `unwatch_dir`), all of the
    process's one instance (`platform::watch_named`; PM M257): what the guest never looked
    at is watched nothing of, and a watch is one of its user's (`max_user_watches`).
    Confine-08: a native watch admission error refuses the directory's LOOKUP with
    its native errno before any guest reference is published or counted. A later
    lookup retries admission; no failed directory is silently retained as watched.
    Memory-19: EACCES alone admits it unwatched, a directory the share process may not
    read (inotify(7): the caller needs read permission), which it may only walk through
    (D38, *Walked through where it may only be searched*); no unprivileged program on its
    host is told of its changes, and its guest sees them as its entries expire (1 s).
  - *macOS:* one FSEvents stream of its shares' roots (shards-apple `fsevents`, CoreServices
    bound when first used), file events, the changes the process itself makes for the guest
    left out (`IgnoreSelf`), told at once (latency 0, `NoDefer`).
  - *Windows:* ReadDirectoryChangesW of each root and all beneath it, 64 KiB a read, the
    most it takes over a network (its documentation's).
  - Where the whole tree is watched (macOS, Windows), a change is told only where the guest
    holds its directory (`Server::holds_dir`). Each path waits once however often it
    changes.
  - *Lost changes* (confine-06, confine-09, 2026-11-14; was: at most 16384 waiting, Linux's
    default `max_queued_events`, past which a path's nearest waiting directory or its share's
    root stood for it). A host's watcher can say only that changes beneath a place were not
    each said: inotify's `IN_Q_OVERFLOW` (inotify(7)), ReadDirectoryChangesW's empty answer
    (its buffer overflowed, MSDN), FSEvents' `MustScanSubDirs` (which it sets on events the
    kernel or the stream dropped, FSEvents.h). Each is typed (`notices::Change::Beneath`)
    and told, as its changes are taken, by every node the guest holds at that place or
    beneath it (`Server::held_beneath`). Touching a directory wakes no watch of a file in it
    (an inotify watch is of its inode, not recursive), so the root alone, which was all that
    was told, left a guest's watch of a nested file asleep. Every watch the guest has holds
    its inode (inotify_user.c `inotify_new_watch`), and a FUSE inode is its server's node
    until the guest forgets it, so telling every node held wakes every watch there.
  - *What waits is bounded by what the guest holds* (R03): a share's changes, each told by
    its path, are no more than the nodes its guest holds as each is told (`Server::held`,
    its node table's size, the root's always among them, so never below one). Past them,
    telling each path costs more than telling every node held, which wakes every watch the
    guest has, so the share's changes are told as lost beneath its root; a share's places
    lost are as bounded, past them its root standing for them. No number of the host's
    enters: a guest that holds a whole tree (a recursive watcher looks up each directory and
    file) waits for as many paths as it holds; one that holds its root alone, for one, and a
    loss then touches the root, all it can watch. Cold start: the share's root alone, one.
    Uncertainty: a name the guest holds no node of is told past the bound only by its
    directory's own change, as inotify's own overflow tells it nothing more; a watch of the
    directory is still woken. Failure: a share with no server (none for its place) is told
    nothing of what it lost, as none of its nodes is held.
  - *Told on a pipe straight to the guest:* records `TAG\0PATH\0` (`shards_abi::run::
    notice`), TAG the share's virtio-fs tag (`shards share --notices TAGS`), from the share
    process to the stdin of the guest's `NOTICE` built-in, which the daemon and `shards
    api-run` start as the run starts (`STARTED`) and for each plug once it is mounted. No
    thread of theirs reads it.
  - *The built-in* (init notice.rs) is init's root as filesystem group
    `shards_abi::NOTICE_ID`, the first ID past every in-VM server's (`SERVER_FIRST_ID` and
    `PID_MAX_LIMIT`). It mounts each tag a notice names, attached nowhere (fsopen(2),
    fsmount(2)): the same file system as the guest's own mounts of the tag (virtio_fs.c
    `virtio_fs_test_super`), whose inodes inotify watches whichever mount set them; let go
    of after each batch, so that none outlives its device's unplug. For each path it walks
    the directories, following no symlink, and touches the file: its modification time
    asked set to now, its access time left (utimensat(2) `UTIME_OMIT`, `UTIME_NOW`), which
    the kernel tells as `IN_MODIFY` to the file's watchers and its directory's
    (include/linux/fsnotify.h `fsnotify_change`: the modification time alone is
    `FS_MODIFY`). A file the host removed: its name looked up again (an exclusive create,
    which revalidates whatever the kernel trusts, `LOOKUP_EXCL`), then its directory
    touched (`IN_MODIFY|IN_ISDIR`).
  - *The server* takes a request of the guest's root as group `NOTICE_ID` for a notice: a
    SETATTR is answered with the node's attributes as the host has them, nothing set, a
    read-only share's too; what only looks is answered; anything else is refused (EACCES),
    so that a notice changes nothing on the host.
  - *Default deny:* a notice is told through its share's own tag, and only a workload or a
    member that has that share mounted holds its inodes and hears the touch; init's own
    mount is attached nowhere. A read-only plug into the workload is read-only by its mount
    alone, its file system writable as every other share's (setup.rs, domains.rs and a
    member's plug already were), so that the notice's mount can touch it.
- *Verified* (light tests, the change's own): unit, server.rs
  `a_notice_changes_nothing_on_the_host`, `a_name_found_by_another_case_is_trusted_for_no_time`,
  `a_directory_is_held_while_the_guest_knows_it`, `the_hosts_changes_where_the_guest_looks_are_noticed`
  (Linux), `lost_events_wake_a_file_the_guest_holds` (Linux); notices.rs `changes_are_told_once`,
  `lost_changes_are_told_by_every_node_the_guest_holds_beneath`,
  `the_hosts_changes_are_told_where_the_guest_looks` (each host's watcher, a change made by
  another process); shards-abi's records; init's `notices_are_told_whole_across_reads`;
  shards-apple's `a_change_beneath_is_told_by_its_path`; share.rs's flags. Real VMs, tests/plug.rs
  `a_host_edit_wakes_a_watch_in_the_guest` (a bind, a read-only bind and a plugged volume:
  the host's new file `IN_MODIFY f`, its removal `IN_MODIFY|IN_ISDIR` of the directory, the
  host's files as it left them): adacachy's KVM and the Mac Studio's HVF. Mutation: with no
  request taken for a notice, the removed file's revalidation, an exclusive create no longer
  refused, made the file again on the host (`/rw: [.../rw/f]`), and the test fails.
  docs/research/measurements/s8-notices.
- *Known limits.*
  - *What a watcher hears:* a host's new, written or changed file is `IN_MODIFY` of its
    name; a removal, `IN_MODIFY` of its directory; a move, the new name's and the old
    directory's. Never `IN_CREATE`, `IN_DELETE` or `IN_MOVED_*`, which the guest's kernel
    tells only of its own changes.
  - *Echoes:* on Linux and Windows the share process's own writes for the guest are watched
    too, each told back as one `IN_MODIFY` more (macOS's `IgnoreSelf` leaves them out), as
    Docker's osxfs delivers "some events multiple times".
  - *A DAX file's guest* (D189, PM M550): a touch's SETATTR reply tells the guest's kernel
    the file's size as the host has it, so a reader past a host's cut reads the file's end
    once the notice lands; the kernel dropped a DAX file's entries there unbroken
    (`fuse_do_setattr`) until shards' patch 0007 covered it (kernel-6.18.48-54fba99afaee,
    released and pinned); and a file the host is still writing, looked up by its notice
    before it is 1 MiB long, is no DAX file until its guest makes its inode again (owed:
    weighed with how a notice tells of a name the guest has not looked up).
  - *Linux's instances:* one inotify instance a share process (a run that shares any
    directory, and each plug), of the user's 128 by default, of which a desktop's programs
    held 101 (PM M257); a share process given none tells nothing, and says so in its log.
  - *Not told:* a join share's volumes (D119), a direct boot's shares (`run vm --kernel …
    --share`, whose PID 1 may be no shards-init), a client's relayed directory (D228), a
    share another server serves (`--slates-fs-fd`).
  - A guest process of the root user and group `NOTICE_ID` has its own requests of a share
    refused (EACCES) but SETATTR's, which change nothing.
  - Its latency, host edit to guest watcher, is ROOT's to measure
    (docs/research/measurements/s8-notices/run.sh, tests/plug.rs `notices_latency`).

### D236. A network's destinations: a member reaches the hosts its grants name, the host itself at one port (built; real-VM validation owed)

**Why.** Kiln plan 01a1cd8e862e7169a074db3d5fa33f3d, step 9, and the harness bring-up's
finding H2 (docs/research/measurements/harness-bringup-v1): an Agentfile's egress named
ports alone. `NETWORK --egress=443` with `EXPOSE 443 AS egress` let a harness open TCP 443 to
any address past its microVM, and `--dns` let it resolve any name, where Codex needed
`api.openai.com` and `chatgpt.com` alone. Nor could a member reach kiln's MCP, served over
HTTP at `/api/mcp` on kiln's `http_addr` (`0.0.0.0:7070` by default, kiln
`crates/kiln/src/config.rs`): the host itself is what `Policy::Ports` never reaches (its
gateway and loopback refused, rootless-security.md R4.16). Only a remote `MCP` server's grant
named a host (D59 part seven); a run's command had D192's.

**Alternatives.**
- *A directive of its own* (`EGRESS host:port FOR member`): a second grammar for what a
  network's boundary says already, where D192 put destinations on a network. Not taken
  (R13).
- *Names held by what a flow says* (TLS SNI, HTTP Host: Squid's ACLs, cloud firewalls'
  FQDN rules): a client chooses what it says (domain fronting; ECH hides SNI). Not taken: a
  flow reaches the addresses its resolver path answered, which is what D59 holds.
- *Learned addresses held per member in the guest* (Cilium's toFQDNs policy programs each
  endpoint's allowed addresses from the DNS answers its proxy relays; dnsmasq's `--nftset`):
  D192's "held apart by the address its flows come from". Not built here: what the union
  cannot hold is refused instead (below), which lifts once it is.
- *The host at an address of its own* outside eth0's subnet (Docker Desktop's
  192.168.65.254, Lima's 192.168.5.2): any such address can be one of a user's own
  networks. The gateway is never a destination (it is the network process), and D124 takes
  it for the host's loopback already.

**Decided.**
- *Grammar.* `NETWORK --egress=HOST:PORT`, beside ports: TCP; HOST a host's name (RFC 1035
  §2.3.1 and RFC 1123 §2.1 labels, the last not all digits, RFC 3696 §2, so that no port or
  mapping reads as one), an IPv4 address, or `host.docker.internal`, the host itself (Docker
  Desktop's name for it; `.internal` is the top-level domain ICANN reserved for private use,
  2024, so no name in the DNS is it). Refused, saying why: one on `--expose` or `--ingress`
  (a destination is reached, never let in), on a network carrying no TCP, a pattern, an IPv6
  address (as D192), UDP, and `localhost` (the asker's own, RFC 6761 §6.3). One parser,
  `shards_dns::destination`, reads D192's option and the Agentfile.
- *Who, to whom, which port, which way.* The network's members (`CONNECT … ON` it, within its
  `FOR`) for whom the microVM's boundary opens the port outward (`EXPOSE … AS egress`, or both
  ways, `FOR` it; D122's `--agents` and `--harnesses` naming them): the host named, at its
  port, out. Two boundaries, as a port's (§12 answer 6); an internal network's reach nothing.
- *Names.* A member asks the agents' resolver for its destinations' names alone, as a remote
  MCP server's (`--dns` neither needed nor implied). The host itself is in its hosts file at
  eth0's gateway and never asked of a resolver: the network process forwards no question for
  it. A remote MCP server's URL may name the host itself too (`MCP kiln FROM
  http://host.docker.internal:7070/api/mcp FOR codex`, kiln's MCP), which its grant then is.
- *Held.* The network process's policy names each destination beside the MCP servers'
  (`encode_policy`): a flow to its port reaches only an address its resolver answered for the
  name through it, or the address it is; the host itself is the gateway at that TCP port
  alone, which it takes to the host's IPv4 loopback there (`Config::host_side`). The guest
  lets the member out on that port (its gate, the switch, init's forward chain); the run's own
  processes (`confine_eth0`) and its engine's members (D181) reach the gateway by TCP at its
  resolver's port alone.
- *DNS lifetime* (network-03): D192's current answer and received-TTL rules apply to
  these destinations too. Historical answers grant no later connection; zero-TTL
  answers retain no cross-transaction authority. Neither expiry nor replacement
  tears down an already admitted TCP connection.
- *Refused where it cannot be held* (`agentfile::held`, at build and as the daemon reads the
  normalized Agentfile): the network process holds the whole microVM to the union of its
  members' names on a port, and a member's init lets it out on that port to any address. So
  on a TCP port that one member reaches by name (a destination, or a remote MCP server), every
  other member granted the port is granted the same names and none a port grant of it; else
  the image is refused, naming both members and what each reaches. Remote MCP servers beside
  another member's other grants on one port, which passed before, are refused alike. Every
  member granted the port to any address (the image's port grant alone, or beside a name) is
  alike there and passes: it reaches any address on the port, so every name on it too, and
  D246's hold of a narrowed run counts those names as its reach (inithex-02, 2026-11-13).
- *Orchestrators* keep or drop destinations (`Narrowing.destinations`, D231, channel version
  3), never add one, and may hold each member to its own of those kept (D246, version 12). The
  build labels them (`vnd.osi.agentfile.destinations`) for Docker and Kubernetes; the daemon
  holds a run to its own reading of the image (D109).

```dockerfile
HARNESS codex FROM ./codex
NETWORK --egress=api.openai.com:443 --egress=chatgpt.com:443 --egress=host.docker.internal:7070 provider FOR codex
EXPOSE --harnesses=codex 443 7070 AS egress FOR provider
CONNECT codex WITH codex ON provider
```

**Literals.** `host.docker.internal`, Docker Desktop's documented name; TCP port 53, DNS's
(RFC 1035 §4.2.2), the gateway's one service to the run's processes; 63, a label's most, and
253, a name's as text, its 255 octets on the wire less its first length and the root's (RFC
1035 §2.3.4), as D192 had them. No bound, wait or size of its own.

**Evidence.** The implementer's record, light tests on Linux x86_64 (adacachy) and the
supported targets' lint: docs/research/measurements/s9-grants-v1.

**Evidence owed** (ROOT). On real microVMs (KVM, HVF, WHP): a member granted provider names
reaches them and nothing else (another host on their port, another port, an address no answer
gave), and resolves them alone; one granted `host.docker.internal:PORT` reaches a listener on
the host's loopback at PORT and no other port of the host, while the run's own command and
another member reach neither; an image `held` refuses fails its build, and its run when
crafted. The bring-up's examples (docs/examples/harness-codex, harness-claude,
harness-codex-signed-in, harness-claude-signed-in) moved to destinations once run so: each
grants `--dns` and `--egress=443/tcp` today, any host on 443 (H2), and its hosts come from that
run's resolver answers, not the records' host mentions, which include help-text URLs.

**Review (plan step 2):** [harness-bringup-v2/review.md](../research/measurements/harness-bringup-v2/review.md) (F1–F9 fixed: the leak check's chosen numbers, the real-VM test's and bringup.sh's clocks and polls, `sleep 600`, H1's stale text, R10's no-tool check on the recorded turns, fetch.sh's signature verdict, cosign's pin and arm64's builds, settle's one-swap write-back, signed-in.sh on macOS and the probe's own modes on Windows (F9); the real-VM runs and fetch.sh's real fetch owed to ROOT).

**What would falsify it.** A provider whose clients reach it at addresses its names never
answer (then address ranges as grants); a member that must reach one port by name beside
another member's other names (then the per-member hold above, which lifts the refusal).

**Absolute DNS names in MCP URLs** (inithex-04). The build's `mcp_endpoint`
and init's paired reader omit a terminal root dot before lowercasing the grant's
host, as DNS `query_name` omits that root label on the wire (RFC1034 §3.1).
`https://MCP.example./mcp` therefore grants `mcp.example:443`, with the source URL
kept as written. No unrestricted DNS or extra port is added. Two wire-question
regressions reproduce the former spelling mismatch at build and in init's real
netplan reader. [Evidence and owed real-VM variant](../research/measurements/inithex-fixes/README.md).

### D237. A program that carries shards writes its VM and network processes out beside its own `shards`, signed as it signs its own (built; real-VM validation owed)

**Why.** Kiln plan 01a1cd8e862e7169a074db3d5fa33f3d, step 16: kiln is one binary, as shards is
(D36), and it runs every harness in a microVM of its own through Hex, whose node boots it
through shards-api, a client of the `shards` binary (D215, D231). So kiln carries a `shards`,
and the VM and network processes that `shards` starts. On macOS each of those runs in App
Sandbox under entitlements that are its binary's signature (D30, D31), and kiln signs every
binary it installs or starts on a Mac with an identity of its own (kiln's `kiln signing
setup`, `crates/kiln/src/os/macsign.rs`): macOS's local network privacy knows a program by its
signature, and on 2026-10-18 kiln measured an ad hoc signed upgrade cut off from the local
network until someone allowed it again. A `shards` that writes its own helpers out (D36) writes
the bytes its build signed, ad hoc, and only a build on a Mac signs them at all (kiln's
releases are cross-built on Linux, where codesign is not); no carrier can sign them again in
place, as a file signed again is another size, which `helpers::complete` takes for a copy cut
short and writes over.

**Alternatives.**
- *Each helper written out by `shards` itself, as D36 has it:* the carrier gives its own
  `shards` and nothing else. Its helpers are signed only where the carrier is built on a Mac,
  ad hoc, never with the carrier's identity, and are new programs to macOS with each build.
  Not taken.
- *The carrier links shards' command as a library and serves `api-run` itself:* `crates/shards`
  is one binary's crate (D36); as a library it would link all of shards' daemon, builder and
  registry into the carrier, and shards' command line into the carrier's (kiln's own `run` is
  another command). Not taken.
- *`SHARDS_VM_BINARY` for the VM process:* it names a VM process for VMM work and tests, not
  the network process, and shards-api's configured client clears every variable it does not
  name (D233). Not taken.
- *A `shards` built to be carried (taken):* `SHARDS_HELPERS=beside` builds one that carries no
  helpers, as `skip` does, and starts the VM and network processes (and a GPU's, where one is
  there) from the directory it was started from (`helpers::beside`): the carrier writes the
  three out together, signed as it signs its own, and owns that directory's life. Nothing in
  shards writes, holds or collects it. kiln writes it whole (beside its place, signed, marked
  ready, renamed into it), names it by what it carries and by who signed it, holds it from
  each process that uses it, and collects the others no process holds, as D182 does
  (`crates/kiln/src/shards.rs`).

**D36 kept.** To kiln's users kiln is the one file to install and run: its `shards`,
`shards-vm` and `shards-net` are carried inside it and written out by it the first time a build
of it needs them, as shards writes its own helpers, and none is shipped, installed or
documented beside it. The VM and network processes stay processes of their own binaries for
D36's two measured reasons (each VM maps only its own; App Sandbox's entitlements are the VM
process's signature alone). shards' own builds are unchanged: by default a `shards` carries
its helpers and writes them out itself.

**Literals.** None.

**Tested.** `helpers::tests::a_carried_shards_starts_the_helpers_beside_it`: both helpers there,
the directory found; one missing, refused naming it; nothing written. kiln's own: its carried
Shards written whole once, found after, a folder not ready written again, and other builds'
folders collected once no process holds them (`crate::shards`'s tests).

**Evidence owed** (ROOT). Real VMs started by kiln's carried `shards` from its kiln-signed
helpers on HVF, and from its helpers on KVM and WHP; kiln's build time and binary size with
Shards carried and without (kiln's `docs/research/s16-vendor/`).

**What would falsify it.** A carrier that cannot keep its helpers in the directory its
`shards` runs from; a macOS that refuses a carrier's own identity the entitlements it allows ad
hoc (then ad hoc, as shards signs them).

### D238. Agent control over hyper-transport (its transport, suite, lanes and identity decided; where its TLS ends decided at the host from HVF's and KVM's runs, plan step 10, WHP owed; its endpoint built, step 11: its connection, refusals, stdio lanes, their controller, the daemon's endpoint per run, exec lanes at the endpoint, the controller and the daemon, each end's word on its TLS, and members' own lanes (a member's state, its end, its signals and its own terminal's size, goal 58's steps 5 and 6) built, the daemon's runs' and an orchestrator's (api-run); an orchestrator's run's members' stdio lanes, by generation, built (D252); log lanes built, goal 58's step 7: the lane, its controller, the daemon's log host, and the keeper of every member's log within the run's one log cap; its real-VM runs and its measurement against arm g owed)

**Why.** Kiln plan 01a1cd8e862e7169a074db3d5fa33f3d runs every kiln harness in a microVM of
its own, booted for Hex under shards-init (D231). The person decided how such a harness is
driven (the plan's header, 2026-11-11): "we'll primarily be controlling agents via networking
… We have an entire custom quic protocol in hyper-quic we'll be using. Both Hex and Shards
should offer and use this", and "all such communications should be AESGCM256 bidirectional
encrypted". kiln drives a harness over its stdio (its adapters stay stdio state machines:
Claude Code's stream-json, Codex's app-server, ACP), runs its sign-in and shows its own screen
on a terminal, and execs into it, signals it and inspects it (plan step 18). Today each of
those passes through processes on the member's own host: D180's QUIC carries a member's
streams to the daemon's managed owner (step 5, D240), `shards api-run`'s stdin and stdout carry
an orchestrator's (D231), and vsock carries everything between a host and its guests (D12).

**Decided** (the plan, from its version 9):
- *Transport:* hyper-transport on hyper-quic, the QUIC shards' contexts already speak (D180,
  `crates/remote`). Hex offers and uses it as well (plan step 4, Hex's
  `docs/design/hex-quic.md`).
- *Suite:* `TLS13_AES_256_GCM_SHA384` alone, both ways, with the hybrid post-quantum groups,
  and a test asserting the suite each link negotiated (D239).
- *Lanes:* control (exec, signal, inspect); terminal (attach, a TTY and its size); one stream
  for each member's stdin, stdout and stderr (D240); logs.
- *Identity:* the VM's own key, made where its TLS ends and never moved. It is enrolled with
  its controller's CA by a CSR, as Hex's nodes enroll with kiln's (hex-quic.md Q6), or pinned
  as D180's raw keys are; step 11 pinned it ("The microVM's identity", below). That key, not
  the host process kiln sees, is the agent to kiln's git signing, credential helpers and MCP
  tokens (step 18), and the identity a run's credential leases are issued to (step 33).

**Where its TLS ends: at the host** (plan step 10). It was decided from ROOT's runs on HVF and
KVM (PM M540), and ROOT approved it to stand until WHP, KVM's memory at more rounds and a loaded
run are in. The two candidates, measured at fleet density (R02, R14):
- *In the guest* (arm g): each microVM is a QUIC peer with its own key, reached through its
  run's network process (shards-net) and virtio-net. The host carries only ciphertext.
- *At the host* (arm h): one endpoint (the managed owner endpoint over D180's QUIC, as today)
  carries each stream on to its microVM over vsock, which never leaves the machine.

The harness is [control-end](../research/measurements/control-end/README.md) (d9caccfe8 to
4bf2fe812). It measures each arm against its own baseline (g and g0 in the guest, h and h0 at
the host): per-VM idle memory, handshake CPU at density under the hybrid ML-KEM groups, the
round trip and stream throughput, as n, p50, p90, p99 and max. Its record says what each
vehicle allows:
- Only a daemon's run gets a network process and published ports (arm g).
- Only a direct boot gives the host a vsock socket to dial. Docker's default seccomp profile,
  which shards-init gives a run's command, refuses `socket(AF_VSOCK)` (crates/seccomp
  `oracle.rs`). So arm h's guest program stands in for init's relay, and its endpoint for the
  daemon's.

ROOT ran it at 66113379c, 32 microVMs and 5 rounds an arm, on HVF (adas-mac-studio.local, Apple
M4 Max, macOS 26.2) and on KVM (adacachy, AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, Linux 7.2.9). PM M540 has the
numbers, and the harness's `results/` keeps ROOT's summaries. The p50s the decision rests on:

| p50 | HVF g | HVF h | KVM g | KVM h |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory per microVM over its baseline, idle and connected | +1817 KiB | +302 KiB | −192.0 KiB | +2541.8 KiB |
| Host CPU per microVM, first handshake | 3231 µs | 1590 µs | 11829.4 µs | 1568.2 µs |
| Host CPU per microVM, reconnect | 1573 µs | 936 µs | 4712.1 µs | 1440.5 µs |
| Round trip, 64 B (its p99) | 435 µs (4572) | 1505 µs (8658) | 269.1 µs (2312.2) | 586.4 µs (3912.4) |
| Download and upload, one stream (MiB/s) | 300.6 and 320 | 326.6 and 273 | 91.4 and 163.7 | 372.2 and 347.6 |

*Decided: at the host (arm h), on what each microVM costs a host at fleet density*, the question
step 10 asks first. Wherever the two hosts resolve it, the host endpoint costs less:
- *CPU per handshake*, on both hosts: 2.0× less on HVF and 7.5× less on KVM for a microVM's
  first handshake, and 1.7× and 3.3× less for a reconnect. Every microVM of a host reconnects at
  once when its controller restarts. In the guest arm the VM process carries most of the cost:
  on KVM, 10961.8 of 11829.4 µs.
- *Memory per microVM* over its vehicle: 1515 KiB less on HVF. On KVM the arms' differences
  (−192.0 and +2541.8 KiB) lie inside their rounds' spread, 1516.0 to 4915.1 KiB from p50 to
  max, so KVM's memory is unresolved.
- *Inside every microVM*: arm h's relay is smaller than a TLS endpoint, by 342 and 378 KiB of
  Pss and 196 and 188 KiB of anonymous memory.
- *Throughput*: on KVM arm h moves 4.1× arm g's download and 2.1× its upload. On HVF the arms are
  within 17% of each other either way.

The round trip goes to arm g on both hosts, and is recorded beside the decision. It is 3.5×
shorter on HVF and 2.2× on KVM at p50, and 1.9× and 1.7× at p99. Arm h's number includes the
stand-in endpoint's thread handoffs: the driver to a vsock writer, and a vsock reader back to the
driver. The harness records them as that stand-in's cost, not necessarily the daemon endpoint's
(its README's Limits). Step 11's endpoint is to be measured with the same harness against arm g's
numbers here (owed, ROOT's).

*The directive's scope* (ROOT's ruling, 2026-11-13, so the person is not asked). The person
wrote (2026-11-11): "we'll primarily be controlling agents via networking … hyper-quic … all
such communications should be AESGCM256 bidirectional encrypted". That covers every network hop
of control. Under arm h the only network hop, the controller's to the endpoint, is
TLS13_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, held from both ends (D239). The endpoint's AF_UNIX and vsock leg to
its microVM never leaves the host, like every other host-local IPC shards has ("Control that
crosses no TLS", below).

*The trust boundary.* Under arm h, the host's endpoint, in its daemon, holds every microVM's
control in plaintext. The host is already trusted with each guest's memory, through its VMM.

*Identity.* The harness's endpoint used one key for every microVM. Production gives each
microVM its own identity, held by the endpoint. Step 33 issues a run's credential leases to the
run's identity, the SHA-256 of this key, and needs no more of it (step 33's plan, kiln plan
01a1d2b88be57304b972761e2a5c6781, steps 4 and 5). It relies on three things, which this entry
keeps:
- one key per run, made after the run's restore and never shared by runs restored from one
  template, since a lease keyed to a shared fingerprint would cross runs;
- the fingerprint, known to the orchestrator before the run's first lease ask on each host;
- the fingerprint, unchanged while the run stays on one host. A move makes a new key at its
  destination, and step 33's leases follow it, released at the source and asked anew under the
  new fingerprint ("A moved microVM's key", below).

So, for step 11:
- The endpoint runs in the daemon, on D180's QUIC beside the managed owner endpoint, under its
  own protocol (`shards-control/1`; `/2` since its report names its bridges, D254's amendment).
- It makes each run's key after the run's restore. The key is never in guest memory, so no
  template carries one.
- The key's SHA-256 reaches the controller and the orchestrator in the run's managed metadata,
  as the managed endpoints' `server` fingerprint does (the microVM's identity, point 2, below).
- Step 11 serves each microVM from an endpoint of its own, bound where its caller says ("The
  stdio lanes' service", below). A controller dials that microVM's endpoint and meets its key
  there. The daemon binds each on loopback ("Where the daemon binds it", below), as an
  orchestrator's run host does (D252).
- Each lane reaches its microVM over vsock, as a host reaches a guest's service in Firecracker:
  an AF_UNIX connection to the VMM, then `CONNECT PORT` (Firecracker edb60617, `docs/vsock.md`,
  "Host-Initiated Connections"). Inside the microVM, shards-init's relay carries it on. The
  harness's guest program stood in for that relay.

*What reopens it.* ROOT runs WHP (jupiter, with the harness README's command), KVM at more
rounds, and a loaded run (`--spin`) on each host: step 10 asks for its numbers under load, and
both runs added none. A result that flips the comparison reopens this decision:
- WHP measuring arm g at or below arm h in host CPU per handshake;
- WHP measuring arm h above arm g in memory per microVM over its baseline, outside its rounds'
  spread;
- KVM's memory resolving in arm g's favour;
- a loaded run reversing a comparison the unloaded ones resolved.

One thing is not a condition, and is unmeasured: why arm g's guest on KVM spends about 10× the
controller's CPU on the same handshake (5149 against 503 µs at p50). HVF's host CPU, 2.0× in
arm h's favour, points the same way.

**Building: the endpoint** (plan step 11, `shards_remote::control`). It serves the lanes above
to a peer holding the enrolled or pinned identity, and nothing to any other. The plan's other
callers of it:
- Hex's member operations, which Hex refuses typed until it exists (Hex's
  `docs/design/shards-image-class.md` §8: `MemberExec`, `MemberSignal`);
- step 38's nested runtime, whose channel to its host it is (D234);
- step 39's node of Hex, run under shards-init.

Until step 10 decided, only what both arms share was built (ROOT, 2026-11-12): the connection,
the microVM's identity, who is refused, and what a lane says. The control lane (exec, signal,
inspect) and the terminal lane (attach, TTY) waited on step 6's member exec, attach and TTY
(D243, D244). Step 10 has decided for the host (above). The endpoint runs in the daemon and
holds each microVM's own key, and the key's SHA-256 reaches the controller in the run's managed
metadata. Exec lanes, members' own lanes (signal, inspect, a terminal's size) and the log lane,
which also waited on step 10, are built now, below, an owned member's log lane among them, as
the daemon keeps every member's output (D240, "Every member's log").

*The connection.* QUIC over D180's driver and TLS (`net.rs`, `tls.rs`): TLS 1.3 alone, D239's
provider (TLS13_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 alone, the hybrid ML-KEM groups), early data off, on an
application protocol of its own, `shards-control/2` (RFC 7301; `/1` until D254's amendment), which a context's endpoint and
the managed output's refuse, as it refuses theirs. The endpoint is the server and the controller
its client in both arms, as the controller dials. Every lane is a bidirectional stream the
controller opens; the endpoint opens none.

*The wire: hyper-quic under D180's driver, not hyper-raft's hyper-transport crate.* The crate
(classes, exchanges and lanes over hyper-quic, which kiln's `crates/kiln/src/net.rs` and Hex's
`hex-quic` take) carries messages: its lanes are one-way streams that last as long as their
connection, and its exchanges need their bodies' lengths before they are sent (hyper-raft
233b7fce `lane.rs`; `Endpoint::open`'s `body: Option<u64>`). Hex built a connection protocol of
its own over them for byte streams of no known length, a program's stdout among them (Open,
Accept, End, Reset and Credit frames, and a Welcome, as a TLS 1.3 client counts itself
connected before its server has verified it, RFC 8446 §4.4.4: Hex's `docs/design/hex-quic.md`
Q3 at d84730ee). A member's stdin, stdout and stderr are such streams, and a QUIC stream is one
already: its end (FIN), its abort (RESET_STREAM, STOP_SENDING) and its own flow control (RFC
9000 §2, §3, §4.1), which D180's driver and step 5's endpoints use now, and which ROOT's
step-10 harness measures in both arms. Hex and kiln take Shards' crates (Hex vendors
shards-api; kiln vendors Shards, plan step 16), so a controller's side is Shards' code
(`control::controller`), not a second implementation of this wire.

*The microVM's identity: its own key, pinned (decided).* The plan left it open: "enrolled with
the controller's CA by CSR, or pinned as D180's raw keys are; the key never travels".
- Enrolled by CSR. kiln's agents: "Agents generate their key locally and send only a CSR; the
  server signs it after checking the enrollment token. Private keys never cross the network"
  (kiln d6ffa45d `crates/kiln/src/pki.rs`). Hex's nodes: a PKCS #10 request (RFC 2986) under
  ECDSA P-384, admitted with the grant kiln issued for that name, once (hex-quic.md Q6).
  Kubernetes' kubelets: a "limited usage token" authenticates a CSR, approved by the controller
  manager or a person, renewed "when it is close to expiry" (kubelet TLS bootstrapping,
  kubernetes.io).
- Pinned. D180's homes: an Ed25519 key (RFC 8032) presented as a raw public key (RFC 7250), each
  side pinning the other's SHA-256. WireGuard's peers "are identified strictly by their public
  key", which they "exchange … through some unspecified mechanism" (Donenfeld, NDSS 2017, §2
  and §1).

What decides it:
1. *What vouches for a key.* With no remote attestation, only the party that started a
   microVM can say a key is that microVM's. A CA signs a CSR because a grant came with it, and
   the grant reached the microVM from its launcher; a controller pins a key because the launcher
   reported it. RFC 7250 §6: "Without a secure binding between identifier and key, the protocol
   will be vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. This document assumes that such binding can
   be made out-of-band", and "Using pre-configured keys is another out-of-band method for
   authenticating raw public keys". The binding comes from one channel either way; a
   certificate restates it, signed, so that a party that did not start the microVM can check it
   without asking whoever did.
2. *What enters the microVM.* A CSR's grant is a secret inside it (step 33: no credential value
   anywhere in the VM) unless the request leaves through the host, and a path from the microVM
   to the CA is a grant default deny gives no one. A pin needs nothing inside: the key's SHA-256
   leaves through the host that started the microVM, as the managed endpoints' `server`
   fingerprint does now (the run's managed metadata, `daemon/managed.rs`).
3. *Lifetime and revocation.* A certificate has a validity window (RFC 5280 §4.1.2.5) that a
   run must outlive or renew mid-run. A pin lives as long as its holder keeps it and ends as it
   is removed, as a D180 client's enrollment ends (`shards remove client`). kiln refuses its own
   agents by their keys' SHA-256 in any case (`ServerBook::revoked_keys`, kiln d6ffa45d
   `net.rs`).
4. *Clocks.* A certificate's checks read the verifier's wall clock. A guest's is set from its
   host at boot and after each restore ("Wall clock", above), so either arm could check one; a
   pin has nothing to check.
5. *Code and bytes.* Pins are built and tested (`identity.rs`; `tls.rs` `Pinned`, `AnyClient`),
   and a handshake's Certificate message carries the key's 44-byte SubjectPublicKeyInfo (RFC
   8410 §4). A CSR needs its encoding (rcgen, which shards-server carries into the guest
   already), WebPKI's path validation (hyper-tls) and a chain in every handshake.
6. *The controllers.* kiln's and Hex's own QUIC links verify certificates under kiln's CA and
   take no raw key; both reach this endpoint through Shards' crates, whose verifiers pin.

So the microVM's identity is an Ed25519 key made where TLS ends (`Identity::generate`, the
operating system's random numbers through aws-lc-rs), held only there, its SHA-256 its name.
The controller pins it, and the endpoint takes only the controller's key, enrolled as the run
starts. That fingerprint is the identity that replaces kiln's peer-process one: every lane of a
connection it authenticated is that microVM's (step 18's git signing, credential helpers and MCP
tokens; step 33's leases). Two rules follow:
- *A key per run, never a template's.* A key made before a template is saved would be every run
  restored from it (D25), so the endpoint makes its key after its run's restore.
- *A moved microVM's key* (decided by ROOT, 2026-11-13). In arm g the key would be in guest
  memory, which a saved and moved microVM's memory carries (D176), and its pin would move with
  it. At the host, which step 10 chose, the key is the host endpoint's, and the key never
  travels (the plan). So a move makes a new key at the destination, after the restore there,
  as at any run's start. Its controller pins the new key, whose SHA-256 reaches it in the run's
  managed metadata, as at a run's start.
  - Step 33's leases follow the move: they are released at the source, as at any run's end
    there, and asked anew under the new fingerprint. Leases are asked just in time, so nothing
    is carried. The orchestrator must have the destination key's SHA-256 before the
    destination's first lease ask, as for a fresh run (step 33's owner agreed, 2026-11-13).
  - What kiln's other uses of the key (step 18) do at a move is step 18's.

Falsified by a party that did not start the microVM having to verify it without its launcher (a
fleet peer, a third service), or a controller that cannot take Shards' code. Then the
controller's CA certifies this same key from a CSR the endpoint signs where the key is (RFC 8410
makes Ed25519 an X.509 key): a certificate is added and the identity kept, the key's SHA-256
naming the microVM either way.

*Who reaches it.* Each side refuses any other key at the handshake with TLS's access_denied ("A
valid certificate or PSK was received, but when access control was applied, the sender decided
not to proceed with negotiation", RFC 8446 §6.2), which rustls raises for this crate's verifiers'
`ApplicationVerificationFailure` (hyper-tls `error.rs`). "A server MUST NOT process incoming
1-RTT protected packets before the TLS handshake is complete" (RFC 9001 §5.7): a controller of
another key opens no stream the endpoint reads, and the endpoint's handler is told of no
connection of it. How a connection ended is typed (`control::Ended`, read from QUIC's codes;
callers match it, never its words), with which side said so:

| `Ended` | QUIC's code | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| `NotEnrolled(by)` | CRYPTO_ERROR 0x131 | access_denied (49): a key not enrolled or not pinned |
| `Handshake(by)` | CRYPTO_ERROR 0x128 | handshake_failure (40): no suite, group or signature in common (D239) |
| `Protocol(by)` | CRYPTO_ERROR 0x178 | no_application_protocol (120): a peer of another protocol |
| `Closed(by, reason)` | an application close | one of `managed::Reason`'s codes |
| `Silent` | — | its peer unheard for its idle timeout (RFC 9000 §10.1) |
| `Local`, `Transport(by)` | — | closed here; any other code, a reset, a version |

*Its lanes.* A lane's first frame names it (`control::lane`), and the endpoint reads no more of
a lane before it knows what it is (`LANE_MOST`). A member's stdin, stdout and stderr lanes open
with step 5's own subscriptions, byte for byte (`managed::subscribe`,
`managed::input::subscribe`: the run, its generation, the member, the channel, the offset), and
carry step 5's frames after them, so the endpoint serves step 5's streams as they are: one
record in flight each way, cursors resumed, ends and aborts typed. A lane the endpoint will not
serve is refused alone, a `Refused` frame of `managed::Reason`'s code then the lane's end, and
the connection and its other lanes go on.

*The stdio lanes' service* (`control::Endpoint`). One endpoint per microVM, bound at the address
its caller gives, serves the member streams its caller names (`control::Streams`), each with the
admission its caller would give step 5's endpoint of one stream (`managed::Admitted`), and hands
back each stream's producer or relay and its control, as step 5's endpoints do, and a `Revoke`
that ends it. Step 5's services are the lanes' (`managed::Service`, `managed::input::Service`):
one implementation of each stream's protocol, its records, cursors, ends and aborts, whether an
endpoint serves one stream or many. States and rules:
- *A lane:* `Opening` while its first frame comes; then subscribed to its stream (step 5's
  states), or `Refusing` while its refusal frame goes. One lane holds a stream: a second is
  refused `Scope`, as step 5 refuses a second owner. A lane done (its output finished, its last
  record acknowledged; its input's end told) is finished, its controller's side stopped
  (STOP_SENDING, RFC 9000 §3.5) so that the stream closes and its credit returns (§4.6), and
  its stream waits for the next subscription, which a finished output answers at once.
- *Its ends:* its controller's FIN or reset ends the lane alone, its record kept for the next
  subscription to the same cursor; a stream revoked (`managed::Control::abort`) resets its lane
  alone, waking the endpoint rather than stopping its driver (`managed::Stop::Lane`); a frame
  the stream's protocol refuses closes the connection with the refusal's code, as step 5's
  endpoints close their owner's, except a frame that raced its input's end, which only stops
  the lane's reading (`control::after`).
- *Its connections:* the controller's newest is its own. A newer one's handshake closes the
  older (`Reason::Stale`), whose lanes leave their streams for the newer's, which go on at their
  cursors: a record sent and never acknowledged comes again.
- *Wakes:* a stream's producer, relay or control wakes the endpoint with one unit command, and
  a full handoff is a wake already queued, whose turn serves every stream; so a producer's
  record beside a queued wake keeps its place (`managed::Producer::submit`, which treated a full
  handoff as its driver gone).

The transport's every value is its streams' (R03; the person, 2026-11-13: "we do not tolerate
arbitrary constants"): each lane's windows as its endpoint of one stream bounds them, summed for
the connection, the largest per stream; what the endpoint sends unacknowledged, each stream's
admitted window and a refusal frame for each stream the controller may open; one stream each;
and its handshake and datagram buffers the most; its liveness judged at use, as D180's links
are, with no idle timeout or keep-alive (D180's `QUIET` and a quarter of it before).
D180's driver tells a handler when its peer allows more streams (`Handler::available`), so that
a controller opens a lane as the endpoint's limit allows.

*The controller's side* (`control::Controller`, `control/drive.rs`). kiln and Hex reach a
microVM's lanes through it rather than writing this wire again. `Controller::dial` takes the
controller's key, the microVM's pinned fingerprint and its endpoint's address, both from the run's
managed metadata, and the member streams it drives (`control::Subscriptions`): each stream with the
admission its endpoint announced, and the cursor its lane opens at. Lanes open once the handshake
has taken the pinned key, as many at once as the endpoint's stream limit allows; the rest wait for
`Handler::available`. Each lane's handle is step 5's client of its stream:
- *An output* (`control::Output`): `next_record` gives its records in order. Asking for the next
  acknowledges the one before, since step 5 acknowledges a record only once its owner has it
  whole. `Got::Finished` comes once the output has finished. The admission its endpoint
  announced (the run's metadata `capacity`) is where its records start, not their bound: the
  endpoint grows a stream's record as the daemon's learner asks (`managed::Producer::admit`,
  QUIC's window as it was), so a lane reads a record up to the managed wire's own bound, one
  frame's (`managed::RECORD_MOST`, `run::MAX_PAYLOAD` plus a log record's head, remote-08), its buffer
  reserved at the admitted record and grown, fallibly, to what comes; one past that bound
  breaks the protocol. A lane that held the first admission as its bound closed the connection
  `Protocol` once an owned output's record grew (ROOT's KVM run of `log_lanes`, 2026-11-13;
  `control::tests::lanes::a_record_grown_past_the_admitted_one_is_had_whole`). What an owned
  output's records carry is the guest's capture record whole (`run::managed::Record`), which
  its owner decodes.
- *A stdin* (`control::Input`): `write` sends one record within the endpoint's room and returns once
  it is taken. The driver checks each taken against the protocol: it falls where the record ends,
  or, the first after a subscription, at or past its cursor, which counts the bytes an earlier
  connection's record gave. `end` and `abort` wait for the member's init to tell how the stdin
  ended. An errno is a `NonZeroU16`, under Linux's MAX_ERRNO.

A lane's refusal, its reset (its stream revoked), a stdin's end and the connection's end are typed
(`control::Fault`). D180's driver now passes QUIC's own error to a handler just before the loss
(`Handler::cause`), so a key not enrolled reads `NotEnrolled`, not words. The controller retries
nothing: each handle's `cursor` is where a later dial opens, and the endpoint keeps an
unacknowledged record and a stdin's place for that dial. Its transport is the endpoint's
admissions, summed over its lanes as the endpoint sums its own:
- what the endpoint may send on a lane before it is read, the largest per lane and their sum: a
  record with its head, a stdin's taken or end, or a refusal;
- what the controller sends unacknowledged on each lane, summed: an output's subscription and one
  acknowledgment; a stdin's subscription, one record and its end;
- no stream the endpoint may open;
- one command slot per lane, since each handle has one ask in flight.

*Where the daemon binds it* (`daemon/managed.rs`, `bind_agent`). A run asks for its agent-control
endpoint with the annotation `shards.control=true`, as it names its stdin members with
`shards.stdin` (step 5). Docker keeps a key's last value, and any value but `true` or `false` is
refused by name. Such a run's managed scope binds one endpoint instead of step 5's endpoint per
stream:
- *Its key*: made for this run as its scope begins, and held by the endpoint alone. Managed
  scopes are neither restored nor joined ("managed output scopes cannot yet be restored or
  joined"), so the key is never a template's, and it is never in guest memory.
- *What it serves*: the run's streams, with the admissions step 5's endpoints take for them, its
  owner's key alone (the run's enrolled client, step 5's owner), bound on loopback as step 5's
  endpoints are.
- *What it feeds*: each stream's producer, relay and control go into the same credits, bridge and
  relays that step 5's endpoints feed. One driver thread runs the endpoint; as it ends, every
  stream of the run ends with it, as a stream's own endpoint ends its stream.
- *How it ends*: the run's scope ending revokes it (`Owner::abort`).
- *What a controller reads*: the run's managed metadata gains `control ADDRESS` and `vm
  SHA256-HEX` in place of a line per stream, and `shards port` lists `agent-control/udp`.

Other runs keep step 5's endpoints, so nothing landed changes until a run asks. The budget the
scope reserves charges each stream its own buffers, as step 5's do. Its one endpoint's handshake
and datagram buffers are charged once per connection it holds as it binds (`link_bytes`, D252's
amendment of 2026-11-16), not once per stream.

*Exec lanes* (`control::exec`; ROOT chose design (B), 2026-11-13). A command run in a member is a
lane of its own, and its stdout, stderr and stdin are step 5's streams on lanes of their own, as a
member's are, so one stdio protocol carries both. The pieces:
- *The ask*: the lane's first frame (`MemberExec`) names the run, its generation and the member,
  then carries step 6's member exec as the run protocol carries it, a `run::Spec` byte for byte
  (D243). Its length is bound by the run protocol's own `MAX_PAYLOAD`, which is as large as Linux
  execs. An endpoint that admits no exec, or an ask for another run, generation or member,
  refuses the lane alone, typed.
- *Its scope where it serves no member stream* (goal 58, for D252's run host and D254): the
  run and generation an ask names are fixed as the endpoint binds (`exec::Execs::run`): its
  member streams', or at an endpoint of none the zero run and generation 0, as its socket lanes
  name them (D251); the controller names the same (`drive.rs`, its outputs' run else the zero
  run), and gives `Execs` with no output subscribed. Such an endpoint leaves the member to its
  host, which knows its run's members and refuses one it has not, typed. Before, the run was
  read from the endpoint's first output: an endpoint of none refused every ask `Scope`, and
  once an exec's own streams had joined its outputs, would have read the exec's run for its own.
  Tested: `control::tests::lanes::an_endpoint_of_no_member_stream_takes_asks_in_the_zero_run`.
- *Its streams*: the endpoint numbers each exec. The exec's stdout, its stderr (none on a
  terminal) and its stdin (where it reads one) are step 5's streams under a run of their own: the
  run's identity and the exec's number hashed (SHA-256), so the controller's subscriptions name
  them as they name a member's. Their record sizes are what the endpoint's caller admits for
  execs (`Streams::execs`). Streams are looked up by run as well, so no exec's stream answers for a
  member's.
- *Its host*: the endpoint starts nothing itself. It hands its host the ask and its streams'
  handles (`exec::Start`). The host charges the run's budget for each exec and replies
  `Started`, `Unstarted` (`Capacity`, `Refused` by the member, or `Failed`) or `Exited(status)`.
  While the exec runs, the endpoint raises the connection's stream limit and windows by its lanes
  (RFC 9000 §4.1, §4.6, through `Io::limit`), and lowers them as the exec is let go.
- *Its steering*: after `Started`, the lane carries the controller's resizes and signals (D180's
  `Resize` and `Signal` frames, a signal `1..=NSIG`), one in flight to the host at a time, as
  step 5 has one record in flight.
- *Its end*: its exit is told only once its outputs have finished, every record consumed and
  their end (the FIN) told their controller's lane, so no tail is cut. An output that finished
  before its lane came (a log lane with nothing to read, which has no record to wait on) is kept
  until that lane is told its end: let go at its finish, the lane that came after found no
  output and was refused `Scope` (managed.rs `End`, ROOT's HVF run of log_lanes.rs at edca0b3f6).
  Its steering channel stays open until the endpoint lets the exec go. A host keeps
  each stream's control until then, because a control dropped revokes its stream.
- *Its connection*: an exec belongs to the connection that asked for it. That connection gone,
  or the lane stopped, hangs the exec up: its steering is dropped, its streams are let go.

*Exec framing correction (control-07).* Both writer and parser admit MemberExec up to
`exec::ASK_MOST`, the ABI spec payload plus its scope, rather than an ordinary frame's
4 MiB cap. Other tags retain their existing bound; an overlarge exec header is refused
before waiting for its bytes. Framed storage reserves fallibly. [Red/green record](../research/measurements/control-fixes-v1/README.md).

*The controller's execs* (`control::Execs`, `Exec`, `ExecControl`). A controller dialed with
`Subscriptions::execs` asks for one with `Execs::exec(member, spec)`, and its lane opens with the
ask. Once the endpoint says `Started`, the controller opens the exec's stdio lanes, from their
first bytes, at the exec's streams. It hands back step 2's `Output` and `Input` handles for them,
and an `ExecControl` that resizes, signals (a signal outside `1..=NSIG` is refused before it is
sent) and waits for the exit. An exec that did not start says why (`Fault::Unstarted`). The
controller's handles now ask its driver through one channel and a unit wake, not a command slot
per lane, so lanes open as execs come. A lane over is let go, its handle's later asks answered by
none. The connection's windows rise by an exec's lanes while it runs, from the same admissions.

*The daemon's exec host* (`daemon/managed/execs.rs`). A run that asks for agent control admits
execs on its endpoint: an exec's output record is what one of its guest's output frames carries
(`run::CHUNK`), and its stdin's is a member's stdin's. The host takes each exec the endpoint hands
it, on a thread of its own:
- *As whom.* An ask whose spec sets what a member's exec does not take (a user, a builtin, the
  run's own hostname, resolvers, hosts, domain, cgroup or setup) is refused `Refused` before
  anything is made. What runs is the run protocol's EXEC with `in-member=N` alone in its setup,
  as `shards exec --for` sends it (D243), and its member refuses again what it has not.
- *What it costs.* What it holds while it runs: each output's record and its pump's buffer of the
  same size; its stdin's record; the windows its lanes add to the connection
  (`control::exec::lane_bytes`, the endpoint's own sums); the kernel's queues of its connection to
  its VM process, both ends, measured as the run's capture socket is; and its pipes' (Linux's
  `F_GETPIPE_SZ`, Windows' GetNamedPipeInfo, and on macOS, which tells no pipe's, xnu's most,
  `BIG_PIPE_SIZE`). The run's budget has room for it or it is refused `Capacity`, and the charge
  is given back as it ends.
- *Its start, typed.* It is handed to the run's VM process as `EXEC_RUN` with a flag of its own,
  `EXEC_TOLD`, once the run has started and not while it is paused (`docker exec` refuses a
  paused container's). The VM process then tells it `STARTED` as its guest starts the command,
  or, for one that never started, `EXEC_UNSTARTED`: the run protocol's `exec_failed` class and the
  guest's words, before its `EXIT`. Its member's refusal or its daemon's is `Refused`; its
  runtime's (a program not found or not executable), or an exec its VM process could not ask its
  guest for, `Failed`. Without the flag a client could not tell a command that never started
  from one that exited 126.
- *Its stdio.* Pipes, as the daemon's own execs use (health.rs). Each output is read into a
  buffer of its pump's and taken into a record only for bytes there are: a record taken and never
  submitted would keep its stream from finishing. Its stdin is written a record at a time, each
  told taken once the pipe has it whole, and its end or abort is the pipe's close. A write the
  pipe refuses ends it `EPIPE` (its reader gone) or `EIO`; an exec that exits with its stdin open
  ends it `EPIPE` at the bytes taken.
- *Its steering.* Each resize and signal goes to the VM process on its connection as `RESIZE` and
  `SIGNAL`, as a client's do, and is told taken.
- *Its end.* `EXIT`'s status is told once its outputs have ended, every byte its VM process wrote
  taken, and finished. A connection that ends without its `EXIT` (its VM process gone) aborts its
  outputs. Its steering closed before its end (its controller's connection gone, or its lane
  stopped) hangs it up: SIGHUP, as a terminal's hangup tells its session (POSIX.1-2024, General
  Terminal Interface, "Modem Disconnect"), its output let go of and its stdin ended, so that
  nothing it does waits on a controller that has gone. Its streams' controls are held until its
  steering closes.

*Members' own lanes* (goal 58's steps 5 and 6; `control::exec::Kind::Member`). A member itself
is a lane of its own, carrying its state, its end and its steering as an exec's lane carries an
exec's, and making no stream: the member's own are step 5's already.
- *The ask*: the lane's first frame is `Member`, the scope alone. It is refused as an exec's ask
  is: by an endpoint that admits no exec, for another run (`Scope`) or generation (`Stale`), or
  for a member it serves no stream of (`Scope`). One host serves both kinds of lane: the endpoint
  hands it an `exec::MemberStart` on `Served::members`.
- *Its state*: once the run has started, the host says the member runs, and the lane is told
  `Running`, naming the member. A member that ended before the ask is told its `Exit` at once.
  A lane the host serves none of is told why (`Unstarted`: `Capacity` where the run's budget has
  no room for the lane, else `Failed`).
- *Its steering, each steer answered*: a signal (`1..=NSIG`) or a resize, D180's frames as an
  exec's are, one in flight. The endpoint reads the next once the last is answered (`Steered`:
  0, or a typed `Unsteered`: `Ended` where the member's command has ended, `Terminal` for a
  resize of a member with no terminal of its own, `Capacity`, `Failed`). An exec's steers are
  told taken; a member's are answered. OCI's kill of a container that does not run must fail
  (runtime-spec runtime.md, "kill"), and Hex's `signal` of a member maps onto that (Hex
  `docs/design/shards-image-class.md` §2, `Awaits(MemberSignal)`); init refuses such a signal
  typed, and the refusal reaches the controller.
- *Its end, as it comes*: `Exit`, with the member's exit status, or `Signaled`, with the signal
  that killed its command (below, *A member's end, typed*), once its init says its population
  has ended (D231's `MEMBER_ENDED`). It is told only after any steer its host was handed has
  been answered. The member's life is its run's: a lane let go (its exit told, or its
  connection gone) closes its host's steering and ends nothing.
- *A lane's frames, in order* (exec lanes too): each told frame is staged only once the one
  before it has gone whole, and the next one due is staged at once (a member's answer, then its
  exit, which nothing else would wake the endpoint for). Before this, an exec whose host said
  `Started` and then `Exited` within one of the endpoint's turns, its outputs finished with
  nothing written, had its `Started` overwritten by its `Exit`, which its controller took for a
  broken protocol. Reproduced red on main `845d7eb93` with the test alone
  (`an_exec_that_starts_and_exits_at_once_is_told_both_in_order`: `Exit(0)` where `Started(0)`
  was due, adas-mac-studio-3.local, macOS arm64), green after.

*The controller's members* (`Execs::member`, `Member`, `MemberControl`). `Execs::member` gives
`Member::Running(MemberControl { steering, end })`, or `Member::Ended(end)` for a member that
ended before its lane asked, or a fault, typed. Steering and end are separate handles, so that a
caller can wait for the end on one thread and steer from another.
`MemberSteering::signal` refuses a signal outside `1..=NSIG` before sending it; it and `resize`
each wait for the answer within their caller's patience (below), with `Fault::Unsteered` for a
refusal and `Unsteered::Ended` for every steer once the end has come. `MemberEnd::wait` gives
the member's end, `exec::End`.

*A lane's ask, waited for within its caller's patience* (Hex's decision 9, the Hex lead's ask
from Hex's member-signal work, 2026-11-14). Every controller call that waited for its
endpoint's answer (`Execs::member`, `exec`, `mcp` and `log`, `Sockets::connect`, and a member's
`signal` and `resize`) waited on its lane's channel until the endpoint answered or the
connection ended, with no bound and no timed form: an orchestrator that wanted its own bound
needed a thread per ask, and one whose endpoint never answered could not let it go. Now each
takes a `patience: Duration`, the convention of `ManagedGuest::rate(rate, patience)` and
`host_use(patience)`, with `Duration::MAX` (or a patience past what the clock holds) waiting as
before. A lane's ask cannot be asked twice (a second would open a second lane, or send a
second signal), so a wait that runs out answers `Ok(None)` with the ask still pending, as
`ImageGuest::wait_for(timeout)` and `ManagedGuest::wait_ended(timeout)` do, and a later wait
follows the same ask on.
- *Its shape.* An ask is sent at once and gives its pending handle: `Execs::member(member) ->
  PendingMember`, `exec(member, spec) -> PendingExec`, `mcp(member) -> PendingMcp`,
  `log(source, channels, cursor, follow) -> PendingLog`, `Sockets::connect(name) ->
  PendingSocket`, each refused at once only where nothing could be sent (a frame that does not
  encode, a socket name that is no file name: `Refused(Protocol)`). Each handle's
  `wait(&mut self, patience) -> Result<Option<_>, Fault>` gives `Member`, `Exec`,
  `McpConnection`, `Log` or `Socket` once; a fault, then the same fault again, as every other
  handle of the module tells its end (`Output::next_record`, `MemberEnd::wait`); and, after its
  answer was given, `Fault::Unawaited`. `MemberSteering::signal(signal, patience)` and
  `resize(size, patience)` send once and answer `Result<Option<()>, Fault>`;
  `MemberSteering::steered(patience)` follows the last one on. A steer asked while one awaits
  its answer is refused `Fault::Awaiting` and never sent (the endpoint reads one steer at a
  time, and the driver dropped a second one silently before); `steered` with none awaited is
  `Unawaited`. Both refusals leave the lane as it was.
- *Its states* (R04). A pending ask is `Awaited::{Awaiting, Answered, Over(Fault)}`, its
  steering `Steering::{Ready, Awaiting, Over(Fault)}` (which replaces an `Option<Fault>`).
- *An asker gone* (D251's cut). The driver tells a lane's handle its number as it takes the ask
  (`Heard::Asked`). A pending handle let go hands the driver its channel back
  (`Ask::Withdraw`); the driver, which alone tells that channel, finds there everything it told
  and the handle did not hear, so no answer that crossed the drop is lost, and closes the lane
  both ways, as a cut lane is closed (RESET_STREAM and STOP_SENDING), whatever its endpoint
  said or says: one waiting for the endpoint's room never opens; one the endpoint has not
  answered is let go there (its host's steering closes, which hangs an exec or a member's lane
  up, exec.rs's reset path); one answered meanwhile is closed with what its answer made (an
  exec's stdio lanes). The member's life is no lane's, as before: none ends it.
- *Literals.* None: each patience is its caller's (R03). The clock's own bound decides only
  that a patience past it waits as `Duration::MAX` does (`Instant::checked_add`, as std's
  `recv_timeout` reads it).
- *Callers.* No production caller in Shards or kiln waited on these (the daemon's and api-run's
  are the endpoint's side); their tests and Hex's acceptance read the answers with
  `Duration::MAX`, as they did, through the pending handles. The blocking forms are gone.
- *Tested* (unit, loopback): `control::tests::a_lane_ask_is_sent_once_and_waited_for_within_each_waits_patience`

  07d8f670f (no answer within the test's 10 s, FAILED); green with shards-remote's `control`
  66 and `loopback` 33, shards-api's `control_lanes`, and the shards binary's
  `daemon::managed::tests` and `api_run::` 71 (1 ignored), every caller moved to the pending

- *Owed* (ROOT): the real-VM callers moved here, compiled and linted but not run:
  `api_image`'s member signals and MCP connection, `nesting`'s socket lanes, `managed_output`'s
