### D259. An orchestrator's run saved whole for its owner: `ImageGuest::save`, D176's save made by its run's host, and plan step 33's leak scan over what it writes (built; its real-VM test passing on HVF and KVM x86-64, PM M605, and on WHP once the scan left Windows' holes unread, step 33.10; again on KVM x86-64 with that scan, on KVM arm64 through L1 with its save scanned on the outer host, and step 33's real sessions, owed)

**Why.** Plan step 33's acceptance (D242) is that no credential value is anywhere in a
harness's microVM: its memory, its disk, its environment. Checking its memory needs the guest's
memory whole, saved at a point of a session: after a tool turn and a token's refresh. Shards
saves a running microVM whole (D176, `shards save vm`). But an orchestrator's run (D231) has
no daemon, and its handle, `ImageGuest`, had no save (kiln research
01a1d2b88be57304bf6b081fe46832e0, f19). ROOT's conditions (2026-11-13), because a run's memory
on disk is the most sensitive thing a run has:
- the save is the run owner's alone, asked over its own session, and written only where the
  owner names, nothing anyone else can ask for;
- it is typed, and refused when the run is in no state to save;
- it has a D-entry of its own;
- it reuses the daemon's save, or D253's template save, rather than build a second.

**Alternatives.**
- *The daemon's `save vm` (D176), as it is.* It reaches the daemon's own runs alone. An
  orchestrator's run is hosted by its own `shards api-run` (D231, D248), and no daemon knows
  it. A run's credential grants (D242) are an orchestrator's alone, so the sessions step 33
  must scan are such runs. Its machinery is reused below, all of it.
- *D253's template save.* It is the guest's own, made at its boot before any member runs, so
  it can hold nothing a session holds later.
- *Any path the owner names, held to a walk of every directory above it.* On Unix, OpenSSH's
  `auth_secure_path` (auth.c) walks a path so: every directory owned by root or the user, none
  writable by group or other. On Windows a directory's ACL can let another user rename what its
  owner made beneath it. Authenticated Users' Modify, inherited beneath `C:\`, grants `DELETE`.
  So a path's privacy there needs every ACE of every directory above it read. Shards already
  keeps guest memory in the home, D25's templates and D176's saves, which is private on every OS
  (0700; on Windows the ACL `%LOCALAPPDATA%` gives it, `os::owner_only_dir`). The save takes the
  home's privacy instead (ROOT, 2026-11-13).
- *The guest's RAM read from the host without a snapshot.* Its VM process maps its RAM
  privately inside its sandbox (D30), and its own save writes it already.

**Decided and built.**
- *The ask* (shards-api).
  - `ImageGuest::save(to, patience)`, image channel version 23 (after step 3's placeholders at 22): `to_host::SAVE` (15) carries a
    `SaveAsk { id, to }`, answered by `to_client::SAVED` (33), a `SaveAnswer { id, result }`.
  - Refusals are typed, `SaveRefusal`: `Destination` 0, `State` 1, `Unsupported` 2, `Failed` 3.
    They reach the caller as `ImageRefusal::Save(SaveRefusal, String)`.
  - A path that is not UTF-8 is refused as `Spec`, as a plug's is.
  - It is awaited as a room's is: an answer to an ask whose patience ran out is dropped.
  - `ImagePools`' runs pass it through.
- *The owner's alone.*
  - Its frame is read only on the run's own channel, in the run host's asks (`judged`), after
    its request.
  - A frame that comes before the request refuses the run (`before_request`, `Cause::Request`).
    Until its run comes, a warm host's channel is its pool's (D253).
  - The agent-control endpoint (D252) has no save, and neither has the guest.
  - The VM's `SAVED` answers only a save its owner asked (`Saving::answered`).
- *Where* (`api_run::destination`, `made`).
  - `to` is absolute. Its parent is canonicalized, so no link is followed past here, and must be
    the run's home or beneath it.
  - `to` is not at, beneath or holding a directory a guest reaches: each share's host directory
    (canonical as the run starts), each plug's, and the home's volumes (`volumes::ROOT`, made or
    not).
  - The directory is made then, its user's alone (`os::owner_only_dir`), and refused where
    anything is already there.
  - Each refusal is `Destination`, saying why.
- *One at a time* (R04, `api_run::Saving`).
  - `Idle` becomes `Asked` as the owner asks.
  - `Asked` becomes `Idle` as its VM answers, or where the ask never reached it.
  - Either becomes `Gone` as the VM's link closes, and a save awaiting its answer hears that
    its microVM stopped.
  - A save asked while one is under way, or after the VM's end, is refused `State`, as the
    daemon refuses one per run (`Inbox::saving`).
  - A host whose backend takes no snapshots refuses `Unsupported` (`shards_vmm::vm::SNAPSHOTS`).
- *The save is the daemon's* (R12).
  - `shards_vmm::snapshot::prepare(dir, true)` stages a generation: memory, state, swap,
    layer-head, layer, window-heads.
  - Its files are handed to the VM with `SAVE`, whose payload `daemon::snapshots::save_ask` now
    makes for the daemon's `ask_save` and api-run alike. warm.rs's `save_request` reads it as
    before.
  - With `SAVE_LEAVE_RUNNING`, its VM parks its vCPUs, quiets its devices and its guest (D176's
    `QUIESCE`), fills the files and goes on.
  - The run host then commits the generation: synced, renamed, pointed at.
  - Its tokens, D176's two of `run::TOKEN`, which a restore of it would dial with, are fresh,
    wiped here and kept nowhere: no save of an orchestrator's run is restored.
  - For the same reason, a host that saves but cannot restore (Windows Server 2022's WHP, PM
    M345) still saves.
  - A save that fails leaves nothing: its directory is removed.
- *The leak scan* (docs/research/measurements/s33-leak-scan, its README). scan.py reuses the
  bring-up's check where it lives (harness-bringup-v2/credentials.py): a secret is every value
  under a token, key, secret or account_id name, and a leak is the whole value or a run of
  `RUN` bytes, looked up at every offset. It adds:
  - the scan of a save's files, a disk image and each member's environment as given, each file
    mapped, not read in, and walked in time linear in its size, with a heap that does not grow
    with it (#74 step 10: a run of a form's bytes walked a host page at a time, windows looked
    up through anchors; the old unbounded match ran out of memory on WHP);
  - a save's holes left unread (PM M561): only each file's data, as lseek(2)'s SEEK_DATA and
    SEEK_HOLE give it, and on Windows as FSCTL_QUERY_ALLOCATED_RANGES gives it, the call the
    VMM's `platform::allocated_ranges` makes (step 33.10: on WHP the check never ended, reading
    every byte of a save's sparse files, a 10 GiB layer among them); each range widened by the zeros a
    finding can take, those that meet joined, as the call does not say it gives touching ranges
    joined; a run cut short of a unit where a read ends keeping its last byte;
  - each value's UTF-16LE and base64 forms;
  - the run's placeholders, given as public, whose windows are no leak;
  - the bring-up's credential shapes, those no value explains listed by where they lie;
  - exit 3 for a leak and 4 for unexplained shapes alone, never printing a value.
- *Under L1, the outer host scans* (KVM arm64, step 33.10; ROOT's decision, 2026-11-16).
  - *Why.* No arm64 Linux host here has KVM, so KVM arm64's run is boot.rs's
    `snapshot_tests_pass_on_a_kvm_host_of_this_architecture`: the test binary runs in a nested
    guest (L1) on an M3 or later Mac (D154). L1's initramfs holds the test binaries and shards'
    own (`common::linux_tests`), no Python and no checkout, so the test could not start
    scan.py there (lane s33-scan-2, read from the code, not reproduced).
  - *The test* saves as on every host. Where its environment's `SHARDS_L1_OUT` names the
    outer host's share, it leaves there the save and what the scan is given (`given.json`,
    `never.json`, `env/`) and scans nothing itself (`common::leave_leak_scan`). The copy keeps
    only the ranges that hold data and are not all zeros: `platform::copy_used`, the copy a
    restore makes of a snapshot's swap (D176) and writable layer (D190). So the sparse
    layer takes no more of the outer host's disk than it holds. Each file is synced before
    the test goes on.
  - *The share* is the outer run's `--share` (D38), a directory of boot.rs's own. The test
    guest's e2e mode mounts it (`shards0`) where /e2e/env's `SHARDS_L1_OUT` says, `/e2e/out`,
    with the mount its `share` mode makes (`virtiofs`). The `kvm` kernel has virtio-fs
    (shards.config's `CONFIG_VIRTIO_FS`, under kvm.config).
  - *The judge.* Once the guest is gone, boot.rs judges what was left
    (`common::judge_left_leak_scan`) with the function the test judges with in place
    (`common::leak_scan_judged`): the same scan.py, the same assertions, the same bytes at
    the same offsets. Holes read as the zeros they replace, and scan.py widens each range by
    the zeros a finding can take (its README, "Holes not read"), so a finding in the save
    should be one in its copy. Unverified: ROOT's run (Owed) is the first to check it.
  - *Alternatives.*
    - L1's console, its only way out until now (`E2E:` lines, `SHARDS_L1_CONSOLE`). It
      carries lines, not a 536870912-byte memory and a sparse layer (WHP's save's sizes,
      step 33.10).
    - A static Python and the scan carried into L1's initramfs: an interpreter built and kept
      for one test. Refused by ROOT.
  - HVF, WHP and KVM x86_64 scan in place. There is one scanner (R05).
  - No literal: the names (`SHARDS_L1_OUT`, `/e2e/out`, `leak-scan`) are names.

**Literals** (R03).
- The channel's version 23, kinds 15 and 33, and refusal tags 0 to 3 are sequence numbers, each
  the next free.
- The save adds no number: D176's tokens and the snapshot's file names are reused.
- The scan:
  - `RUN = SHOWN + 1 = 9` is credentials.py's. OpenAI's refusal shows a key's first 8
    characters, in harness-bringup-v1's record. The bring-up's review (F1) replaced the chosen
    24-byte windows, 8-byte stride and 31-byte promise that research f18 still cites; ROOT
    confirmed it, 2026-11-13.
  - A shape's random part is at least `ceil(128 / 6) = 22` base64url characters: RFC 6749
    §10.10 bounds a token's guessing odds at 2^-128, and RFC 4648 §5's 64 symbols carry 6 bits.
  - #74 step 10. Its walk and its anchors add no chosen number:
    - The walk finds a run by its first `RUN` units, the window's own width, and takes it a host
      page (`mmap.PAGESIZE`, read where it runs) at a time.
    - An anchor is `width // 2 + 1` bytes, read every `width + 1 - anchor`. That is the
      pigeonhole's split of `width + 1`: a window holds an anchor at `stride` consecutive
      offsets. Any split finds the same windows; halving it keeps an anchor no shorter than
      its stride.
    - Measured in the scan's README: on 16 and 64 MiB images the heap is flat (710268 B on
      macOS, 281300 B on Linux), where the old scan's reached 2239349400 B; the time is less
      than half the old; the findings are the same, digest for digest.
  - Exit 3 is credentials.py's for a leak; 4 is the next.
  - Step 33.10 adds no chosen number. FSCTL_QUERY_ALLOCATED_RANGES (0x940CF) and

### D260. A managed microVM's use: its vCPUs' guest time and its VM process's own, told on its vsock socket (built; real-VM validation owed)

**Why.** Kiln plan 01a1cd8e862e7169a074db3d5fa33f3d steps 13/14, the Hex lead's ask (#71). Hex's
learner charges a microVM by its measured use: per-vCPU guest time plus the VMM's own CPU
(step 14, Hex `learned-charge.md`). An image run gives its orchestrator both in its stats
(D241's `microvm`). A managed microVM (D215, D233) gave its client nothing but its process: Hex
read its whole-process CPU and could not tell its vCPUs' guest time from its VMM's own. On
Windows the job's CPU rate stays the hard ceiling, which then binds before Hex's governor
(D255's rate) can. With both parts, Hex's governor takes the rate less the VMM's own CPU and
binds first.

**Decided.**
- *The word* (`shards_abi::rate`, D255's path). On a microVM booted `--host-managed`, a host
  client may write `USE\n` on its vsock socket in place of `CONNECT <port>`, as it writes
  `RATE`. The muxer reads it as a host ask (`read_ask`'s `Asked::Use`) and hands the connection
  to the VM process's `rates` thread with it (`VsockHost::rate`, one channel of typed asks).
- *The answer* (`rate::used`): `USED`; then the vCPUs' guest times as `GuestTimes::encode`
  writes them for the daemon's `GUEST_TIMED` (`departed NS`, `vcpu INDEX NS [unread CAUSE
  [CODE]]`), or `guest-unread <why>`; then `host CPU_NS RESIDENT FOOTPRINT`, the VM process's
  own `platform::process_usage`, or `host-unread <why>`. A line each, then the connection
  closes.
  - The guest's times are read first and the process's use after them, as D241 reads an image
    run's: the process's CPU time holds its vCPUs', so the later read is never the less, and
    `Microvm::vmm_ns`, the process's CPU less its vCPUs' guest time, is never less than none
    past the clocks' steps (saturating).
  - Each vCPU's time comes from the backend's own clock, which `GUEST_TIME` already reads
    (guest-cpu-time-v1): KVM, the vCPU thread's stat (`/proc/self/task/TID/stat`); HVF,
    `hv_vcpu_get_exec_time`; WHP, `WHvGetVirtualProcessorCounters`' run time. Nothing new is
    measured, and no platform has a path of its own.
  - A part not read is its words, never a number: `the microVM has not started`, or the
    process-usage call's error (`its VM process: …`), and each vCPU not read is typed
    (`shards_abi::guest_time::Unread`) with the most it read before.
- *The client.* `ManagedGuest::host_use(patience) -> Result<ManagedUse, Refusal>`, where
  `ManagedUse { microvm: image::Microvm, asked: Instant, answered: Instant }`. One dial, its
  ask, and its answer read until the VM process closes it, within its caller's patience. The
  sample was read after `asked` and before `answered`: two samples' window is known within
  their asks' spans, measured on the client's own clock.
  - It is the same `Microvm` that an image run's stats carry, so the learner Hex already has for
    image VMs reads managed ones unchanged. `Microvm::vmm_ns()` is the VMM's own CPU time, or
    none where either part was not read.
  - Refused, typed: `Refusal::HostUse(UseBroken)`, where the answer is none of the protocol's
    (`Long`, `Text` (cut short: the VM process ended as it answered), `Word`, `Guest`, `Host`).
    `Unsupported { what: "host use" }`, where the VM process closes the ask unanswered (not
    booted `--host-managed`, or a shards before this) or does not answer within the patience.
    `ManagedIo` where the socket fails, and `Ended` once the guest has ended.
  - `rate` and `host_use` share one exchange (`host_exchange`): the rate's answer is whole at
    its newline, the use's at the connection's close. Its buffer grows fallibly, and its words
    are allocated fallibly, as the managed path's are.
- *One form.* `GuestTimes`, `VcpuTime` and their text, and `HostUse`, are now
  `shards_abi::guest_time`'s. The VMM and shards-api's `image::wire` re-export them, where
  each had its own copy, so the VM process's `GUEST_TIMED`, an image run's stats and a managed
  guest's use are one type with one codec.
- *Why the vsock socket*: D255's reasons. It is the one path every managed microVM serves on all
  three OSes, which a recovered client (`attach_managed`) reaches by its identity. The client
  could read the VM process's use itself by its pid, but not its vCPUs' guest time, which only
  the VM process holds. Both read there in order give one consistent sample.

**Literals.**
- `USE`, `USED`, `guest-unread`, `host`, `host-unread`: the protocol's words; `departed`,
  `vcpu`, `unread`: `GUEST_TIMED`'s.
- The longest answer is D255's `ANSWER_MOST`, the run protocol's payload bound
  (`run::MAX_PAYLOAD`). A use answer of a machine's most vCPUs fits far within it: at most 4096,
  as `arch`'s tests hold both layouts to, each line at most 70 bytes (`vcpu 4294967295
  18446744073709551615 unread hvf-exec-time -2147483648`). A guest's words are cut to leave
  room for the longest `host` line (`HOST_MOST`: its key and three u64s), a host's to what is
  left.
- No other number. The window is the caller's two samples on its own clock.

**Cold start** (R03). Nothing here is learned. The first sample is a reading from boot, and a
window takes two. A vCPU that has not yet run its guest reads 0. A sample asked before the
machine starts carries `guest-unread the microVM has not started` beside its process's use, so
its caller charges nothing it cannot split (`vmm_ns` none) rather than charging the whole
process as guest.

**Tested** (light, macOS arm64):
- abi `guest_time`'s `encoded_times_decode_as_they_were` and
  `text_other_than_encoded_times_is_refused` (moved from the VMM with the codec); `rate`'s
  `an_ask_reads_back_as_its_rate_and_nothing_else_does` (`USE` now among them),
  `a_use_answer_reads_back_as_it_was_said` and `a_broken_use_answer_is_refused_by_what_breaks_it`.
- The muxer's `parses_connect_lines_and_nothing_else`,
  `handshake_lines_are_bounded_by_the_protocols_words` (`USE\n`, shorter than its first read,
  read whole), `a_rate_comes_from_a_dial_on_the_socket_alone` and
  `a_rates_dial_is_handed_out_able_to_block`.
- vm_run's `each_rate_handed_over_is_answered_on_its_connection` (a use beside a rate, its
  process's use read for real) and `a_uses_answer_reads_the_guest_then_its_process`.
- shards-api's `a_managed_guests_use_is_asked_on_its_socket_and_read_as_answered` and
  `a_managed_use_unanswered_or_of_an_ended_guest_is_refused` (red against a refusing stub,
  then green), with D255's three rate tests over the shared exchange.

**Owed** (ROOT).
- The real-VM run on HVF, KVM and WHP, in D255's test, which now asks `USE` too:
  `cargo test --profile test-release -p shards --test boot a_managed_guest_is_held_to_the_rate_its_client_asks_on_its_socket`.
  A guest booted `--host-managed`, spinning its one vCPU, its rate lifted, asked `USE` twice a
  window apart: every part is read, its one vCPU's guest time grows by no more than the time
  between the asks (and by at least a twentieth of it, as D255's floor), and its process's CPU
  holds its vCPU's time. A guest booted without `--host-managed` closes `USE` unanswered. The
  confined VM process reads its own use there: Landlock's `/proc/self` rule on Linux, App
  Sandbox's process-info of itself on macOS, AppContainer's `OpenProcess` of itself on Windows.
- Guard-removal mutants, each of which must fail its test: `use_answer`'s order (host before
  guest), `read_used`'s `host` word, the client's close-unanswered as `Unsupported`, and the
  muxer's `Asked::Use` arm.
- These light tests on Linux and Windows (CI), and `scripts/lint` on the 7 targets.
- Hex's adoption: its learner reading each managed microVM through `ManagedGuest::host_use` on
  every OS, its governor taking the rate less `vmm_ns` over the window.

**What would falsify it.** A guest that reaches the use from inside. A sample whose
process CPU is less than its vCPUs' guest time read before it. A vCPU's guest time that falls
between samples. A machine not booted `--host-managed` that answers a use.

**Amended (#77): the process's CPU holds its vCPUs' guest time on Linux by its sources.**
ROOT's KVM run of the real-VM test (adacachy2, Linux x86_64, c120c8a95) read `host` 3.85 s
after `vcpu` 3.87 s (boot.rs, its process-holds-guest assertion): both whole 10 ms steps.
- *Why.* Both counts were /proc's. The process's `utime` and `stime` are its runtime
  (`sum_exec_runtime`, ns) split by `cputime_adjust` and each cut down to a clock tick
  (fs/proc/array.c `do_task_stat`, `nsec_to_clock_t`): up to two ticks short. A vCPU thread's
  `gtime` is charged a whole scheduler tick as each lands in its guest (kernel/sched/cputime.c
  `account_guest_time`), which can hold more than the thread ran, and is never adjusted.
- *Process CPU* (`platform::process_usage`, Linux): the process's CPU-time clock,
  `clock_gettime` of the kernel's process clock of its pid (`thread_group_cputime`: every
  thread's runtime, those gone too, and a running one's time since its last update), in ns.
  The clock ID is the kernel's encoding (include/linux/posix-timers_types.h), as glibc's and
  musl's `clock_getcpuclockid` make it, without the `clock_getres` they check it with, which
  the VM process's seccomp filter does not allow (`clock_gettime` it does). Every
  `process_usage` caller (the daemon's stats and restart's watch, the progress reports) reads
  ns now, where it read ticks.
- *Guest time* (`platform::thread_guest_ns`, KVM): the stat's ticks, then the vCPU thread's own
  CPU-time clock (bit 2 of the encoding, a thread of this process), and the less of the two.
  A thread's time in its guest is part of its runtime, so this removes only what the whole-tick
  charge made up. The thread's clock commits its running time into its process's group
  counters (`task_sched_runtime` calls `update_curr`), so a process clock read later holds it,
  posix CPU timers armed or not; a departed vCPU's last value stays within the process's clock,
  which keeps a gone thread's runtime. So: process CPU ≥ Σ thread runtime ≥ Σ guest time, by
  the kernel's accounting, and `vmm_ns` saturates at none for no real sample.
- *macOS* already held it: `pti_total_user + pti_total_system` and `hv_vcpu_get_exec_time` are
  both Mach absolute time (41.67 ns), the vCPU's within its thread's. *Windows*: the WHP
  counter is 100 ns of the VP's run time, `GetProcessTimes` the process's kernel and user time;
  whether Windows charges those by clock interval, and so can say less than the VP's counter,
  is unreproduced (no WHP run of the test yet, R09): left as is, ROOT's WHP run tells.
- *Literals.* 2 and 4, the encoding's `CPUCLOCK_SCHED` and thread bit, and 8, its three low
  bits: the kernel's ABI, which both C libraries build in. 1 000 000 000, ns a second. No
  other number; no tolerance. The wire form is unchanged (no version).
- *Cold start.* None learned: a vCPU that has not run reads 0 of each. An ID the kernel does
  not let this process read is an error, typed as the stat's (`Unread::ThreadStat`).
- *Tested* (light, Linux x86_64 adacachy2): vmm `guest_time_is_never_more_than_its_thread_ran`
  (red before: 3.87 s of 3.85 s), `a_processs_cpu_time_is_its_clocks` (red before: /proc's
  ticks short of the clock read before them), `a_threads_cpu_time_is_read_by_its_id`, and the
  existing usage and stat tests.
- *Owed* (ROOT): the real-VM test on KVM, HVF and WHP, `cargo test --profile test-release -p
  shards --test boot a_managed_guest_is_held_to_the_rate_its_client_asks_on_its_socket`.

**Amended (final use): a run's end carries what its microVM used in all.** The Hex lead's ask
for kiln's charging: `stats` and `host_use` answer only while a run runs, so a command VM
whose command exited before kiln deleted it went uncharged (Hex answered `NotRunning`).
- *When it is read.* In the VM process, in `Running::wait_then`'s `free`: every vCPU thread
  joined, so past its guest's last instruction, and before the machine's memory and devices
  drop, which they do as `wait_then` returns. Its vCPUs' times first, then the process's own
  `platform::process_usage`, as `use_answer` reads a use (D241's order): the process's CPU
  holds its vCPUs', so `vmm_ns` is never less than none. A later read would see the memory
  gone; an earlier one, a guest still running.
- *Each vCPU by its index* (`GuestClocks::whole`, `Handle::whole_guest_times`). A vCPU that
  leaves reads its clock a last time as before, and now also keeps it under its index
  (`Clocks::left`, summed over the index's vCPUs, the last leave's `Unread` beside it), so
  that once all have left the reading is each one's, `departed_ns` 0, its total a sample's.
  `left` holds one entry an index the machine has had: as many as its vCPUs.
- *Told* (`shards_ipc` kind `FINAL_USE` = 106, VM → owner): the use's answer as
  `shards_abi::rate::used` writes it, D260's one form, sent on a handle of the link the VM
  process keeps for it (`warm::Link::try_clone`), as the process ends. The link closes as the
  process exits (its relay's handle holds it until then), so its owner reads it before the
  close. The daemon passes over the kind (its `_` arm); api-run keeps it (`Told::used`).
- *Only for a run taken.* `warm::receive` keeps the final use's link (`took`) as the VM sends
  TAKEN, and only then; `FINAL_USE` goes on that link alone. As first built the VM process
  kept it from its start and told it whatever became of its run, so a warm VM that ended
  without taking one (a request it refused, a macOS template left where it was granted)
  said kind 106 where its owner reads TAKEN or the VM's end: the daemon's `taken` made that
  `Untaken::Unknown` and kept the run on the ended VM instead of handing it to another, and
  api-run refused it as "the VM said message kind 106 for its run". A VM that took no run
  tells none, and its end alone tells its owner the run never started. Found on KVM
  (adacachy2, main cf13e49e6): `tests/warm.rs`, whose `Warm::ends` read no `FINAL_USE`,
  failed 1 of 6 on kind 106 after DONE; it now reads exactly one, whole (`read_used`), and
  `a_warm_vm_that_takes_no_run_tells_no_final_use` holds the untaken VM to its end alone
  (red at the test-only commit, green with the fix); the unit
  `a_request_with_the_wrong_descriptors_is_refused` holds `took` empty for a refused request
  (red with `took` set before the request is read). No number added.
- *A taken run's one end, and no order with `DONE`.* `FINAL_USE` is told from the VM
  process's main thread as its machine comes down; `DONE` from its workload's thread
  (`warm::finish`): no ordering joins them, and neither is "last". Every reader reads the link
  to its close and takes both wherever they fall (api-run's `Told`, the daemon's inbox,
  `tests/warm.rs`'s `Warm::ended`); none may depend on their order. As built, a run whose
  setup failed after TAKEN was told no `DONE`: the VM process chose to tell a run's end by
  whether its client had been kept, which happened only at the end of its setup, so a
  failure between TAKEN and there (in `warm::receive`: the share process's handshake, the
  client's stdio taken, a relay; in the VM process: a resumed run's tokens, its engine's or
  MCP port, its CPU hold, its group's CPU budget, its layer, its swap, its resumed
  connections or init's ABI) told its owner TAKEN, then `FINAL_USE`, then the link's end. No
  reader hung on it: the VM process stopped its machine and exited, its link closing. But each
  read a wrong end: the daemon "VM ended before its command started" (its reason in the
  daemon's log, or on the client's stderr once its stdio was taken), api-run "the VM ended
  without its run's end", the client its connection's end with no status (`UNANSWERED`'s
  "stopped before the command ended" through a slot). Now the run is the VM's from TAKEN:
  `warm::receive` records it then (`warm::Taken`: its client, its final use's link) and the
  VM process decides on that, not on its client; `Taken::end` tells it once, whichever of its
  workload's end and its serving's comes first, as `finish` tells a failure: `UNSERVED` with
  why, `DONE` of `NOT_RUN`, its client `EXIT` of `NOT_RUN` and why on its stderr; a setup that
  failed after TAKEN stops its machine, whose guest would otherwise wait for a command that
  never comes. Its readers then report that end: the daemon logs why and ends the container
  with that status; api-run `Failed("its VM could not serve its run: …")` with its final use;
  the client exits 125 with why. The joiner's path (`warm::joiner`) already told `DONE` for
  every failure after its TAKEN. Live red/green on KVM (adacachy2, main aedbbe154):
  `tests/warm.rs`'s `a_run_a_warm_vm_took_and_could_not_set_up_is_told_its_end` (an empty
  group budget, D183) failed at the test-only commit 9a8ff4ed2 on its client's exit status,
  its connection ending with none; green with the fix (b92e3a8a6), with all of `tests/warm.rs`
  (8 passed, 1 ignored). Unit: shards-vm-process's
  `a_run_taken_is_told_exactly_one_end_whatever_fails_after` (the VM's side in a process of
  its own, as `receive` takes its process's stdio) reads TAKEN, `UNSERVED`, one `DONE` and
  the link's end, its client one `EXIT`; green on Linux x86_64 (adacachy2), red with `Taken::end`
  telling every call (two `DONE`s) and with the run taken without its client (no `EXIT`, as
  the old rule, knowing the client only once set up, told none). No number added.
- *On the image channel* (VERSION 28): `ENDED` carries `wire::RunEnded { end: RunEnd,
  final_use: FinalUse }`; `FinalUse::Read(Microvm)`, each part its reading or its words, or
  `FinalUse::Unread(Unused)`: `NotStarted` (stopped or refused before its microVM started),
  `Killed` (its VM killed for its orchestrator's asks, `STOP` or their failure, before it told
  it), `Untold` (its VM, its link or its run host ended without it), `Broken(UseBroken)` (an
  answer none of the protocol's). Never a zero.
- *shards-api.* `ImageGuest::wait_for` answers `Option<RunEnded>`; `ImageRefusal::Ended`
  carries `RunEnded`, so every ask of a run that has ended, `stats` among them, is refused
  with its final use. `stop` keeps an end seen before it, its final use with it; one that saw
  none is `Stopped` with `Unused::Killed`. A caller that charges a run whose command has
  ended awaits its end (`wait_for`) before it stops it: the end comes as the VM's process
  exits, its final use told, and a stop before that kills it first.
- *Every end, every backend.* `Exited` and a VM's own `Failed` (`UNSERVED`, a command never
  started) carry it whenever the machine came down in its process; a VM that crashed tells
  none (`Untold`); `Stopped` is `Killed`. A run's own command killed by a signal ends
  `Exited(128 + N)` (init's status byte; `RunEnd` has no `Signaled`, only a member's end
  does). The read is the backend's own clocks already behind `GUEST_TIME` (KVM's thread stat
  and CPU clock, #77's amendment; HVF's `hv_vcpu_get_exec_time`; WHP's run-time counter), read
  on the vCPU's thread as it leaves: no path of a platform's own.
- *Literals.* 106, the next free `shards_ipc` kind; 28, the next channel version; the
  `FinalUse`/`Unused`/`UseBroken` wire tags 0 to 4. No other number.
- *Cold start.* Nothing learned. A machine that never started reads `guest-unread the
  microVM has not started` beside its process's use.
- *Managed microVMs* (`ManagedGuest`; the person's filesystem rule: shards' own interfaces
  are files). A managed VM process has no owner's link and its vsock socket goes with it, so its
  final use is a file: `<vsock>.used`, beside its vsock socket (`shards_api::final_use_file`), in
  the directory its launcher made for the guest, which goes with the run (shards-api's own
  `PrivateDir`, or its launcher's). Written whole, by rename (a temporary beside it, made
  durable, then renamed over it), before its VM process exits:
  - The VM process, confined (D30), writes no file: once its machine is down (`supervise`'s
    `wait_then` free, as the warm VM's) it tells its keeper the use's answer, after its length
    (a u32, big-endian), on a channel of its own (`--final-use`), which the CLI that becomes it
    adds where it is booted `--host-managed` with a `--vsock` (final_use.rs).
  - Unix: the keeper is `shards final-use PATH`, started beside it in its launcher's
    containment as a managed VM's console recorder is, on a socket pair. It writes the record,
    then answers one byte; the VM waits for the answer (or the keeper's end) before it goes
    on to exit. So the record is in place before the VM process, whose end its client
    watches, ends. Not bounded by a clock: the keeper's work is one local file's write.
  - Windows: the CLI that waits for its VM keeps it, reading the pipe as it comes (a pipe's
    buffer may not hold it whole), and joins that before it exits, its client watching the
    CLI's end.
  - A VM killed, or one that ended before its machine came down, tells nothing or less than
    it said it would: no record.
  - The client: `ManagedGuest::wait_ended(timeout) -> Option<ManagedEnded { end: End,
    final_use: FinalUse }>`; `host_use` answers `ManagedUsed::Running(ManagedUse)` while it
    runs and `ManagedUsed::Ended(ManagedEnded)` after, from the same record, read once and
    kept. No record: `Unused::Killed` where its stop came first, else `Untold`; a record none
    of the protocol's, `Broken(UseBroken)`, read no further than the longest answer and a
    byte.
  - *Literals*: `.used`, the record's name; 4, the length's bytes (a u32, which the longest
    answer fits); the answer byte 1. `ANSWER_MOST` bounds what is read.
- *Tested* (light, macOS arm64): vmm `a_machines_whole_guest_time_keeps_each_vcpu_by_its_index`;
  shards `a_final_use_reads_its_whole_guest_then_its_process` (vm_run),
  `a_final_use_reaches_its_owner_on_its_link_as_said` (warm),
  `a_runs_final_use_is_as_its_vm_told_it_or_typed_by_why_not` (api_run); shards-api
  `a_runs_end_reads_back_with_its_final_use` (wire) and
  `a_runs_final_use_comes_with_its_end_and_answers_every_ask_after` (session), with the
  existing end and lease tests over `RunEnded`.
  Managed: shards `final_use::tests::a_final_use_told_whole_is_recorded_and_nothing_else_is`
  and `a_managed_vms_record_is_beside_its_socket`; shards-api
  `a_managed_guests_final_use_is_its_record_once_it_has_ended` and the existing use tests over
  `ManagedUsed`.
- *Owed* (ROOT): the real-VM tests on KVM, HVF and WHP, `cargo test --profile test-release -p
  shards --test api_image -- an_images_own_command_ends_its_run_with_its_status
  stop_ends_the_run_at_once` (a command's `exit 3` ends `Exited(3)` with every vCPU's guest
  time by index, none departed, its process's CPU holding them, and `stats` after it refused
  with that end; a stop's end `Killed`); the managed one's, `cargo test --profile
  test-release -p shards --test boot -- a_managed_guest_records_its_final_use_as_it_ends
  a_managed_guest_is_held_to_the_rate_its_client_asks_on_its_socket` (a spinning managed guest
  that powers off records its one vCPU's guest time and its process's CPU holding it; one not
  managed, and one killed, record none; the confined VM process's write to its inherited
  channel on each OS); Hex's adoption.

### D261. The guest's console is virtio-console (hvc0); the 16550 UART is gone; a panic before it is told by pvpanic and read from the printk ring (built; real-VM runs owed)

**Asked.** The person, 2026-11-14, on the emulated NS16550A (`devices/serial.rs`): "serial
queues strike me as poor design, we can and should do better." Approved direction: virtio-console
over virtio-mmio replaces the 16550 everywhere; the early-boot answer is pvpanic plus a
post-mortem read of the printk ring through VMCOREINFO, not a debug port.

**Decision.**
- **The console is virtio-console** (VIRTIO 1.3 §5.3; `devices/virtio/console.rs`): one port,
  no MULTIPORT, receiveq 0 and transmitq 1, the first virtio device on both architectures, so
  KVM, HVF and WHP on x86-64 and arm64 share it (R12). Every command line says `console=hvc0`;
  `earlycon` went with the UART it named.
  - Output: a buffer per notification, written out on the device's worker, never on the
    vCPU's thread. A UART traps every byte: printk before a tty opens costs an LSR poll and
    a THR write per byte (Linux 8250_port.c `serial8250_console_write`, `wait_for_xmitr`).
  - Input: into the buffers the guest posts, waiting while it has posted none, so nothing
    is lost or held by the device. A paused console takes none.
  - A snapshot keeps its queues alone.
  - D12's report (`devices/said.rs`) moved over unchanged.
- **Deleted, no dual path:** `serial.rs`, COM1 (its port 0x3f8, GSI 4, ACPI `PNP0501` and the
  now-unused `aml::io`), arm64's UART node, `stdout-path` and `layout::UART`/`SPI_UART`, and
  `serial::INPUT_AT_ONCE`.
- **Snapshots.** Format 31 is the machine without the UART. A user's snapshot of format 30
  holds a guest whose 8250 driver is bound to the deleted COM1/UART, so it is refused, not
  migrated: `ResumeRefused::OlderMachine { format, saved_by }`, the same type and message as
  olderinit's causes (D176), naming the shards that saved it. Format 32 adds pvpanic, so 31
  is refused the same way. Templates are remade, keyed by the format (D25).
  - The person's ruling (via ROOT): a migration that leaves a guest polling a dead port is a
    hidden degraded state. Its cost would have been 2 frame times per byte, `wait_for_lsr`,
    about 2 ms at the 9600 baud of divisor 12.
- **pvpanic** (QEMU docs/specs/pvpanic.rst; `devices/pvpanic.rs`): one register taking
  PANICKED (include/uapi/misc/pvpanic.h), written by the kernel's first panic notifier
  (pvpanic.c, `.priority = INT_MAX`) before `panic=-1` resets.
  - x86-64: found by ACPI `QEMU0001`, in the first page past the virtio-mmio windows.
  - arm64: found by a `qemu,pvpanic-mmio` node (Documentation/devicetree/bindings/misc/
    pvpanic-mmio.txt), at `GIC_REDIST_MAX_END`.
  - It tells the console's port; `Handle::panicked`.
  - The guest kernel gains `CONFIG_PVPANIC=y` and `CONFIG_PVPANIC_MMIO=y` (resources/kernel/
    shards.config).
- **The printk ring after a stop** (`printk.rs`). hvc0 registers only as its driver probes
  (device_initcall), and then replays the ring (hvc_console.c `hvc_check_console`,
  CON_PRINTBUFFER). A kernel that stops earlier said why to its ring alone, so where the
  console carried nothing, `Handle::console_said` reads the ring's last lines from guest
  memory under D12's bound.
  - VMCOREINFO (CONFIG_VMCORE_INFO=y in both base configs) is a page filled at subsys_initcall
    (kernel/vmcore_info.c l. 140-253), before any virtio probe.
  - It names `prb`, every ring offset (printk.c `log_buf_vmcoreinfo_setup`, l. 980-1036) and
    the address translation: x86-64 `phys_base` and `pgtable_l5_enabled`; arm64
    `kimage_voffset`, `PHYS_OFFSET` and `VA_BITS`.
  - The page is found by its first line `OSRELEASE=` at a page start. No channel hands it
    over here; QEMU's is fw_cfg, which shards has none of.
  - The ring is walked as `prb_read_valid`/`get_data` walk it.
  - The refusal is typed: `printk::Unread`.
  - Covered: panics from subsys_initcall on, which includes everything before hvc0.
- **No KASLR in shards' boots**, checked for this:
  - x86-64 boots `vmlinux` uncompressed (arch/x86_64/boot.rs), its zero page's loadflags
    LOADED_HIGH alone (l. 287). `KASLR_FLAG` is set only by the bzImage decompressor (Linux
    arch/x86/boot/compressed/kaslr.c l. 875) and read by `kaslr_enabled()` (asm/setup.h
    l. 85-88), so the direct map is at its unrandomized base.
  - arm64's base config has RANDOMIZE_BASE unset.
  - So `printk_rb_static` is at its link address on both.

**Found after S2 (boot.rs on KVM and HVF), and fixed.**
- **Lost boot log.** With `console=hvc0` the console lost every line before virtio_console
  probed. `init_port_console` registered hvc0 through `hvc_alloc` (CON_PRINTBUFFER, the
  backlog flushed at once by register_console's own message) before the port was on the list
  `put_chars` finds it on. Every write returned -EPIPE and `hvc_console_print` discarded it.
  - It is an upstream bug since 38edf58d73c2 (2010).
  - Fixed by kernel patch 0015, which puts the port on the list first; its header carries the
    upstream commit text. Pinned in kernel-6.18.48-7f8c931141dd with PVPANIC.
  - Red at 4da2f78f4 on the old kernel: boots_the_hosts_maximum_vcpu_count,
    boots_to_root_mount_without_a_root_device and brings_up_every_vcpu.
- **The patch's first version hung guests of two or more vCPUs** (KVM at 549b2752f, boot.rs
  1/3; pinned kernel-6.18.48-7f8c931141dd, reverted to 54fba99afaee in cd3b0b1e6). With the
  flush now reaching the device, `out_intr` on another CPU ran in the window where the port
  was on `pdrvdata.consoles` but not yet on its device's ports list: `find_port_by_vq` found
  nothing, and `flush_bufs` freed the used buffer `__send_to_port` was spinning on with
  `outvq_lock` held. Patch 0015 now also puts the port on the ports list before its console
  is set up, as a multiport device's already is (virtio_console.c `out_intr`, `flush_bufs`,
  `add_port`).
- **Output served in the exit.** With the backlog replayed, the transmit worker's wake-up per
  16-byte printk chunk (hvc_console.c `N_OUTBUF`) let only 250 bytes out before a no-root
  panic 49 ms in. The panic's flush then deadlocked on the port lock held by the CPU stopped
  mid-send. The transmit queue is now served in the notifying vCPU's exit, as the 16550's
  register writes were; Linux spins with interrupts off until each buffer is used, so the
  guest waits for the device either way.
  - A unit test holds that a buffer is used before notify returns.
- **What a blocked host output holds.**
  - A write to a stdout that blocks (a terminal paused, a full pipe nobody reads) stalls the
    vCPU in its exit, holding this device's transport lock (`virtio::mmio`'s state, held
    across `notify`). Exactly as the 16550's write held its own lock in the PIO exit.
  - Another vCPU's access to the console device, and a pause or snapshot of it, wait for that
    write. Other devices and vCPUs do not.
  - Daemon, builder and managed runs write to a sink (`Console::Discard`), which never blocks.
    Only `run --kernel` with its console on a terminal can.
  - Since then, one output path for every console (the person: two mechanisms, and sink work
    in the vCPU's exit, were not to stay). The notifying exit only takes the guest's buffer into
    the writer's slot, uses it and returns. The device's writer thread delivers it to the
    output, whichever it is (stdout, a sink nobody reads), and to D12's ring, then takes the
    guest's next. The host holds at most that one buffer; the guest's next waits in its ring of
    one (`TRANSMIT_SIZE`), the guest spinning on it.
    - A blocked output holds no transport lock, so other exits and a pause or snapshot land.
    - `Port::said` waits for the writer to deliver what it holds, so a reset's last lines are
      quoted.
    - Unit tests: `a_buffer_sent_is_used_in_its_exit_and_delivered_by_the_writer` (used within
      its exit, written on no exit's thread; red when the hand-off is cut) and
      `a_blocked_stdout_holds_no_exit_and_no_pause` (blocks when output is written in the exit).
- **Kernels shards does not build** (`shards configure guest`, D28; `run --kernel`) keep upstream's
  lost backlog. Built since: at the first buffer a fresh activation's guest sends, the console's
  writer reads the printk ring through VMCOREINFO (`printk::backlog`). It delivers, before that
  buffer, every record older than the one the buffer begins, matched by its time to the
  microsecond and its text's start, as hvc prints them (a prefix a line, `\r\n`).
  - A kernel that replays (patch 0015) sends its first record first, so nothing is added.
  - Nothing is added when the buffer begins no record the ring holds (the boundary is never
    guessed), after a restore, or when the kernel was told a level (`quiet`, `loglevel=`):
    VMCOREINFO says no record's level, so the console's filter cannot be repeated.
  - Unit test `a_late_console_is_given_what_it_missed_and_a_replaying_one_nothing`, red when the
    match is removed.
  - KVM x86-64 at 83d6e8613: boot.rs's three tests with the unpatched kernel 54fba99afaee 3/3,
    where they failed 3/3 before; with the patched 836568f8ad2c 3/3. Manual boots of each at 1
    and 4 vCPUs start at "Linux version", with exactly one.
  - Unit tests against rings captured from those kernels' memory (crates/vmm testdata/printk,
    `capture-ring.py`, KVM boots to a snapshot): the unpatched kernel's console is given every
    record from "Linux version" to "console [hvc0] enabled"; the patched one's, none.
  - Owed: HVF and WHP runs.
- **The console's name, one constant, told to orchestrators** (2026-11-14, ROOT's ask after
  Hex's break: Hex's own command line said `console=ttyS0`, and its guests panicked once the
  UART was gone). `shards_abi::GUEST_CONSOLE` (`hvc0`) and `shards_abi::CONSOLE` (the whole
  kernel argument, `console=hvc0`, the shape Hex asked for), both `&'static str` made of one
  literal, are the one source: the VMM's default command line (`Config::new`, every `run vm
  --kernel` boot that gives no `--cmdline`) and the builder's begin with `CONSOLE`, and
  shards-api re-exports both (`shards_api::CONSOLE`, `shards_api::GUEST_CONSOLE`), so that an
  orchestrator's command line names the console shards' guests have, never one of its own.
  `vm_run.rs`'s `the_console_shards_api_exports_is_a_default_boots` (run in the VM process's
  crate, which compiles `vm_run.rs`) holds it to a default boot's first argument, which is what
  that boot's `/proc/cmdline` begins with (kernel options are added after it,
  `with_kernel_options`).
  Red with the default command line set back to a literal other console. Owed (ROOT): a real
  default boot's `/proc/cmdline` against it.
- **PID 1 with no console to open** (2026-11-16, kiln goal 1c4faeef, plan step P1.6). `run
  --kernel --init`'s initramfs (`initramfs::root`) held `/dev/console` alone in /dev. A command
  line naming a console the machine has none of registers none, so the kernel opens PID 1 no
  stdio (Linux v6.18 init/main.c `console_on_rootfs`: "Warning: unable to open an initial
  console."). Rust's runtime reopens a closed descriptor 0-2 on `/dev/null` before `main`
  and aborts where it cannot (rust-lang/rust 1.98.1, library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/mod.rs
  `sanitize_standard_fds`), and shards-init mounts devtmpfs only in `main`: PID 1 ended, the
  kernel panicked and `panic=-1` reset the VM, its console silent. Hex met it in its own
  initramfs (g121, 2026-11-15) and has carried `/dev/null` since Hex 414aa30d.
  - Fixed: the archive holds `/dev/null`, 1:3 (devices.txt) and 0666 (devtmpfs's mode,
    drivers/char/mem.c `devlist`), 120 bytes more. shards-init's devtmpfs mounts over it.
  - Red (R09), WHP x86-64 (jupiter), 6a4b27d13 with f8f95832f's initramfs (the node removed):
    `shards run --kernel <pinned hyperv vmlinux> --init shards-init --cmdline "<c> quiet
    panic=-1"`, three boots each: `console=hvc1` and `console=ttyAMA0` exit 3 ("the guest's
    kernel panicked", reset through ACPI, nothing on stdout, 185-335 ms in); `console=hvc0`, no
    console named, and `console=ttyS0` exit 0 (x86-64's 8250 has its legacy 0x3f8 port,
    asm/serial.h, UART or not). The test below fails there: `console=hvc1`, Some(3).
  - Green, HVF arm64 (a Mac Studio), 6a4b27d13: all five lines exit 0, three boots each; the
    test below, `runs_init_as_pid_1_and_powers_off`, `survives_back_to_back_boots` and both
    panic tests 5/5; vmm `initramfs` units 2/2.
  - Owed (ROOT): the red on arm64 (`console=ttyS0`, Hex's case), KVM x86-64 both ways, and
    WHP's green (lane phase1-v's RUNS-OWED rows).
  - Tests: boot.rs `runs_init_where_its_kernel_opened_no_console` (`console=hvc1`, a port this
    one-port console never has, and `console=ttyS0`, Hex's line); vmm
    `initramfs::tests::archive_roundtrips` names the node.
  - Rejected: an init that skips std's start-up (`#![no_main]`) in shards-init and testguest
    covers those two, not the other `--init` binaries `run --kernel` takes; refusing a line
    that names another console leaves a kernel without hvc's driver (`configure guest`, D28)
    dying the same way; `CONFIG_DEVTMPFS_MOUNT` "does not affect initramfs based booting"
    (drivers/base/Kconfig).
- **The x86-64 CI boot failures after S2** (2026-11-16, kiln goal b2124227, lane boot-x86;
  read from CI's logs, not reproduced, so R09 stays open).
  - Symptoms, in every x86-64 run on main from 43696971451 (ec7de3568) on, and in none up to
    43615849356 (d7ff8a094):
    - KVM: `vCPU N: VM entry failed (hardware reason 0x7)`. `boots_the_hosts_maximum_vcpu_count`
      failed so in 6 of the 8 Linux test jobs that reached it (N = 31, 13, 9, 0, 1, 48 in jobs
      132841793999, 133067614182, 133067614137, 133283300166, 133508844000, 133593634113).
      snapshot.rs' 255-vCPU storms failed so too (N = 0, 89, job 133593634113).
    - WHP: the same test never ends (job 133508843966: 3170 s, then the step's 122 minutes).
  - What 0x7 is.
    - KVM_RUN returned KVM_EXIT_FAIL_ENTRY, "the vcpu could not be run due to unknown
      reasons", its reason architecture-specific (Linux v7.0 Documentation/virt/kvm/api.rst
      l. 6664-6666).
    - VMX gives it in two cases (arch/x86/kvm/vmx/vmx.c l. 6853-6869). An entry that failed
      while loading the guest's state reports its exit reason, bit 31 set. A VMLAUNCH or
      VMRESUME that failed outright (`vmx->fail`) reports its VM-instruction error.
    - 7 is the second's "VM entry with invalid control field(s)": the Intel SDM Vol. 3C's
      table of VM-instruction error numbers, and its VMLAUNCH/VMRESUME, "VMfailValid(VM entry
      with invalid VMX-control field(s))", for a failure of the chapter "VM Entries"' checks
      on the VMX controls.
    - SVM reports a failed VMRUN by its exit code (svm.c l. 3625-3628; SVM_EXIT_ERR is -1),
      never 7. So only Intel runners show it, and neither of shards' x86-64 hosts can:
      adacachy and jupiter are AMD.
    - The refused controls are KVM's own. On a runner KVM runs nested, so its VMLAUNCH and
      VMRESUME are checked by Hyper-V, through Hyper-V's enlightened VMCS where Hyper-V
      recommends it (vmx.c l. 643-676).
  - What the logs show.
    - Each failure came 5-10 s after its boot.rs binary started, before the guest said
      anything: early in a bring-up that took about 60 s where the test passed.
    - It is the host's, not one guest's. Other guests failed the same way only at the moment
      a 255-vCPU guest failed:
      - `brings_up_every_vcpu`'s 2-vCPU guest: vCPU 1, 230 ms in, reported 0.06 s before the
        255-vCPU guest's failure (job 133067614182).
      - `a_snapshot_keeps_the_memory_its_guest_plugged`'s guest: vCPU 0, 1.04 s in, the same
        second (job 133508844000).
      - Both passed in every other job.
    - It is not the later "smp: Brought up". Where the test passed, it took about as long
      from its binary's start as it did on the UART: 61 and 65 s (jobs 132841794040,
      133283300062) against 71 and 57 s at d7ff8a094 (132510702288, 132510702350). The
      failures came 50 s before that. hvc0's
      replay does not keep a KVM guest up materially longer, so the leading hypothesis of
      lanes ci-read and ci-read-2 is refuted for KVM.
    - No code a KVM boot's vCPUs run changed in d7ff8a094..ec7de3568.
      - hv/kvm gained typed errors and `went_on` (KVM_KVMCLOCK_CTRL), which runs only after a
        hold or snapshot wait (vm/runtime.rs).
      - vm/x86_64 gained the console, pvpanic and the ACPI power device. Its CPUID, MSR, LAPIC
        and register setup did not change.
    - What changed is what the guest does while its APs come up.
      - Up to 35e2de91e its console was the 16550, so every byte the kernel printed was a trap
        (above). That included the BSP announcing each AP as it kicks it (Linux v6.18
        arch/x86/kernel/smpboot.c l. 842-866, `announce_cpu`).
      - Since then nothing reaches a console before hvc0, so the BSP kicks its 254 APs with
        no exit between them: a burst of first entries on 4 nested CPUs.
      - That is the leading hypothesis, not reproduced.
    - The Linux jobs log no CPU, so whether the passes up to d7ff8a094 ran on Intel is
      unknown. The Windows jobs ran on Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C and AMD EPYC 7763, 9V45 and
      9V74.
  - WHP's hang has a separate cause: what the test now waits through.
    - WHP's guests bring their APs up one at a time (`cpuhp.parallel=0`). Up to d7ff8a094 the
      test saw the 16550's "smp: Brought up" within about 60 s and stopped its guest.
    - Since 35e2de91e the line comes only at virtio_console's probe, so the test watches the
      rest of the boot. The test's own record put the rest of a 64-vCPU boot on such a host at
      40 s and more.
    - The 255-vCPU guest did not reach hvc0 in 3170 s. Its VM process ran throughout and its
      first line never came, so the cold wait followed its liveness alone (D209) until the
      step's limit.
    - On bare-metal WHP with 32 CPUs the same boot reached hvc0 in 11 s (r542). Whether a
      nested host of 4 CPUs is only that slow, or stalls, is unmeasured.
    - It is not the 0x7: the windows-2025 job that hung ran on an AMD EPYC 9V45.
  - Landed (boot-x86).
    - The Linux test jobs, glibc's and musl's, log the runner's CPU and KVM's parameters and
      set `kvm_intel.dump_invalid_vmcs` (scripts/ci/kvm-host). Their failure steps print
      KVM's kernel log, so the next 0x7 shows the VMCS that was refused (vmx.c `dump_vmcs`).
    - The test's comment says what it now waits through.
    - No VMM change and no change to the test's code: neither cause is reproduced (R09).
  - Owed (ROOT).
    1. The next ci.yml run on main, jobs x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and
       x86_64-unknown-linux-musl. Read their "Host virtualization" step (Vendor ID, Model
       name, `enlightened_vmcs`) and, where one fails, its failure step's `kvm_intel:` dump.
    2. On a runner whose `kvm-host` line says GenuineIntel, compare n=10 runs of `shards run
       --kernel <pinned> --cpus 255 --memory 1024 --cmdline "console=hvc0 panic=-1"` against
       n=10 with `cpuhp.parallel=0` added. If only the parallel runs fail, the burst is the
       trigger. The remedy is then this entry's to decide (R02).
    3. On a nested WHP of 4 CPUs (a windows-2022 or windows-2025 runner), the same boot with
       SHARDS_JUDGE_TRACE=1: whether hvc0's first line comes, and when. Then decide the
       test's readiness signal (R02). VMCOREINFO is filled at subsys_initcall, so the ring
       could show "smp: Brought up" before device_initcall, but that would need a reader of
       a running guest's ring, which this entry has not got.
- **The bring-up A/B on CI's own Intel runners, and WHP's boot said as it comes**
  (2026-11-17, kiln goal b2124227, lane boot-ab). Owed item 2 above, one pair of boots a job,
  and item 3's question (whether hvc0's first line comes, and when) are now part of
  `boots_the_hosts_maximum_vcpu_count`, so every ci.yml run on main reads them. No VMM change.
  - Where. A KVM host whose first `vendor_id` in /proc/cpuinfo is GenuineIntel, which
    `scripts/ci/kvm-host` logs as lscpu's "Vendor ID": only VMX fails an entry with a
    VM-instruction error (above). Every other host boots arm 1 alone, as before.
  - Arm 1, "parallel": the boot as it was. It runs first, at the moment it always ran in its
    binary, so that it meets the host the failures met.
  - Arm 2, "one at a time": the same boot with `cpuhp.parallel=0`, once arm 1's VM process has
    ended. Never beside it: the 0x7 struck every guest on its host at once.
    - The parameter: "Enable/disable parallel bringup of secondary CPUs ... Default is enabled
      if CONFIG_HOTPLUG_PARALLEL=y" (Linux v6.18 Documentation/admin-guide/kernel-parameters.txt
      l. 952-956). An `early_param` (kernel/cpu.c l. 1797-1804) since v6.5 (18415f33e2ac).
      Told 0, `bringup_nonboot_cpus` brings each AP up in turn, "Full per CPU serialized
      bringup" (l. 1881-1893).
    - Otherwise the pinned kernel brings its APs up in parallel. x86-64 selects
      HOTPLUG_PARALLEL (arch/x86/Kconfig l. 303); Firecracker's base config has it (l. 711)
      and shards' configs leave it. Only TDX and SEV-ES guests turn it off themselves
      (arch/x86/coco/tdx/tdx.c l. 1193, arch/x86/mm/mem_encrypt_amd.c l. 509).
    - KVM's machine adds no `cpuhp.parallel` (WHP's alone does, `ONE_AT_A_TIME_CMDLINE`), so
      the arm's is its kernel's only one.
  - Each arm's outcome is a line on stderr as it ends, which CI's log keeps whether the test
    passes or not: `D261 A/B arm <arm> (<command line>): <outcome>; <time> from its start`.
    The outcome is `brought up`; or the VM process's own line naming the failed entry, `vCPU N:
    VM entry failed (hardware reason 0x7)` for the 0x7; or `failed otherwise`, with its panic
    above it.
  - The test fails as arm 1 fails, so its red stays; else as arm 2 fails. Each arm's wait is
    a kind of its own (`Vm::sized`), so neither arm's answer judges the other's wait.
  - No arm in the snapshot storms. Their 255-vCPU cold boots bring their APs up in parallel
    too, so they share the trigger. But their two tests boot 255 vCPUs beside each other, so
    an arm of one would meet the other's burst, and their restores bring no CPU up. A 0x7 of
    theirs is one more witness of arm 1's. (Since 2026-11-17 only the restores' storm boots
    the most, D14's storm sizes; the resumed one takes one vCPU more than its host's CPUs.) `brings_up_every_vcpu` and
    `a_snapshot_keeps_the_memory_its_guest_plugged` failed only at the moment a 255-vCPU guest
    did: victims, given no arm.
  - What each outcome says, per x86_64 Linux job on GenuineIntel, read from its two
    `D261 A/B arm` lines and its failure step's `kvm_intel:` dump of each refused VMCS:

    | Arm 1, parallel | Arm 2, one at a time | Reading |
    |---|---|---|
    | 0x7 | brought up | The burst is the trigger. The remedy is this entry's R02 decision, read with the dump: serial bring-up where KVM is nested in Hyper-V, or what the refused control names. |
    | 0x7 | 0x7 | Not the burst alone. If arm 2's failing vCPU was the one coming up at that moment, new vCPUs' first entries fail however spaced; if it was up already, the host refuses entries of its own accord. The dump decides. |
    | brought up | brought up | The runner did not reproduce it: no reading. |
    | brought up | 0x7 | Arm 2 met what arm 1 did not: not the burst. Read whether other guests failed in that second. |

    An AMD runner says nothing: SVM never reports 7.
  - **Amended 2026-11-17: the A/B's verdict, the experiment, and ROOT's ruling (R02).**
    - The A/B (CI 44007524337, x86_64 gnu, Intel Xeon 6975P-C) read "0x7 | 0x7":
      - Arm "parallel" was refused at vCPU 17, 1.73 s in; arm "one at a time" at vCPU 2,
        19.27 s in. Serial bring-up is no remedy.
      - 22 VMCS dumps came in three clusters, each while a 255-vCPU guest ran: dmesg
        1835.9 s (arm 1, and a 7-vCPU guest beside it), 1855.2 s (arm 2), 3536.5 s (the
        storm, 14 in 60 ms).
      - All 22 had the same controls (PinBased 0xff, CPUBased 0xb5a06dfa, SecondaryExec
        0x061013fa, Entry 0x53ff, Exit 0xbefff). Each followed an external-interrupt exit:
        L1's timer 0xec (19) or a call-function IPI 0xfb (3).
    - The experiment (`.github/workflows/d261-intel.yml`, run 44030858462, at c44866d727): 8
      copies, 3 on Intel Xeon 6975P-C, each arm alone (summary.tsv per copy):

      | vCPUs | outcome (3 Intel copies) |
      |---|---|
      | 8, 16, 32 | brought up 3/3, under 1 s |
      | 64 | 0x7 3/3: vCPUs 13, 13, 3, at 44 s, 1172 s, 0.34 s |
      | 128 | 0x7 2/3 (vCPUs 57 at 952 s, 75 at 28.9 s); 1 brought up in 339 s |
      | 255 | 0x7 3/3: vCPUs 138, 29, 1 |
      | 255, kvm_intel `enable_apicv=0` | 0x7 3/3: vCPUs 0, 1, 3, within 0.75 s |

      - Its dumps refuse four distinct control sets: APICv on in x2APIC mode (SecondaryExec
        0x061013fa) and in xAPIC mode (0x061013eb), and APICv off (0x061010eb, 0x061010fa;
        PinBased 0x7f). No one control is the cause, and APICv is not.
      - Refused vCPUs include 0, 1 and 3: the refusal is not of vCPUs past 32.
      - The Intel copies ran on Amazon EC2: lscpu's hypervisor vendor KVM, `systemd-detect-virt:
        amazon`. The 5 AMD copies (EPYC 9V74, 7763, 9V45) ran on Azure's Hyper-V (vendor
        Microsoft), where 255 vCPUs are entered.
    - Not a fault of shards'.
      - CPUID gives each vCPU its APIC ID by its index (leaf 1 EBX[31:24], 0xB and 0x1F EDX) in
        one flat topology. The MADT holds 8-bit IDs to 254.
      - shards sets only the TSC and TSC-deadline MSRs, and no IA32_FEATURE_CONTROL.
      - VMX's control fields are L1 KVM's own, chosen from what L0 offers. VM-instruction error
        7 is L0's VMfailValid on L1's VMRESUME.
      - What varies with the refusal is how many L2 vCPUs L1 switches among on its 4 vCPUs:
        EC2's nested KVM refuses a machine of 64 or more.
    - **Ruled.** The host's real vCPU limit is stated from its own machines, with no number
      chosen anywhere (`vm::limits`).
      - *Typed.* A refused entry ends its machine `ExitReason::Refused(EntryRefused)`, from
        KVM's FAIL_ENTRY (`hv::Exit::Refused`). It is said as the host's, never a hang or a
        crash: `vCPU N: VM entry failed (hardware reason 0x7): the host's hypervisor (KVM under
        Amazon EC2) refused to enter it`.
      - *Kept per host model.* A host model is its CPU's model (CPUID's brand string) and what
        it runs under: on Linux its platform's vendor (`/sys/class/dmi/id/sys_vendor`), else
        CPUID 0x40000000's signature. For each count it keeps how many ran, how many were
        refused, and the vCPU the last refusal named (`Limits::record`).
      - *Refused at once* (`Limits::admit`): a count refused on its host model and never run
        there, and every larger count. Said as the host's with the evidence: "the host's
        hypervisor (KVM under Amazon EC2) refused to enter vCPU N; on this host model, counts
        ≥ M have only been refused". **Amended (ROOT's decision, below): the tests' sizing
        alone. The product tries every count.**
      - *Tried:* a count that has both run and been refused, and every other.
      - *Ceiling:* the hypervisor's own most stays it.
      - *Tests.* `boots_the_hosts_maximum_vcpu_count` proves the most on hosts that enter it.
        Where the host refuses, it asserts the refusal is typed, said as the host's and kept,
        then proves the host's known-good count: its largest never refused, or the refused
        count halved until a boot comes up, each kept.
      - The storms size their largest arm by that count (`common::vcpus_admitted`).
      - CI keeps the counts beside the judge's records (`target/judge-records/<class>/vcpus`).

          to find it: App Sandbox starts a VM process in its container (hence `--cwd`), and its
          environment is filtered (`netproc::child_env`).

          `platform::open_made`). On Linux the VM holds it open before Landlock
          (`Limits::hold`), which gives it no rule for the file. Its reads and writes go
          through `platform::open_input`, as its disks' do.
        - *Said with the refusal.* A refused entry is said as the host's with what the records

          (`control::ABI`, `Control::on_announced`), which shards-init does once its CPUs are
          online and before anything it runs. Refused: on the vCPU the host refused to enter,
          as its machine ends. Not at the VM process's end: the daemon ends many by SIGKILL
          (idle warm VMs, a budget's reclaim, a stop past its grace, daemon/budget.rs and
          commands.rs), and kept only at their end, a count whose machines are killed would
          never show it ran, so one flaky refusal would refuse it for good.

          write, which a thread of its own makes on a descriptor of its own. Nothing its guest
          runs past its init, a workload that took the process over included, can then write
          in them (review 8.2's reasoning for the snapshot a VM gives up).
        - *Written in place* under the file's own lock (flock; LockFileEx on Windows), padded
          with empty lines where shorter. A VM process may not rename another file over it,
          and App Sandbox may not let it cut the file short.

          one only refused ("A count that has both run and been refused is attempted").

          announcement's hook runs once); the E2E of every boot on HVF, KVM and WHP, whose VMs
          now ask for their records.

          own entry of the nested guest that its hardware refused (`__nested_vmx_vmexit`, "After

          a vCPU's state only before it first runs, so none of these was the VMM's.

          with the refusal's words, its evidence and its witness, only with VMX's error 7 (said
          on an x86-64 host), on a host that is itself a VM (`HostModel::under`), and a witness:
          - its guest had run (`Refusal::entered`): port or MMIO I/O, which only its guest's
            instructions make, on its vCPU, or, in a booted machine, on any of its vCPUs
            (`runtime::Entered`); a restored vCPU's state is the VMM's, so only its own counts;

            burst width. One witnessed only by machines refused before their guests ran is not
            taken: a VMM error that refuses every first entry refuses many machines at once.

          Every other refusal stays a failure, its line saying why the gate did not take it.
        - *What a VMM's own 0x7 looks like*, which the gate never takes: the same vCPU refused
          at its first entry, before its guest ran, on every run, alone on an idle host, no
          machine whose guest ran refused within the burst width of it, its controls never seen
          entering there.
        - *The burst width, learned* (`limits::keep_refusal`; no number in code). Each
          refusal's moment, VM process and whether its guest had run are kept beside the counts
          while a burst may join them (`refusal AT_US MACHINE ran|first`). A chain of refusals,
          each within the width of the one before, of two VM processes or more and one whose
          guest had run, is a burst; the largest gap between its consecutive refusals is kept
          (`gap GAP_US`), never its span (ROOT's ruling of 2026-11-17: a chain's span widened
          the width with each close refusal it took in, so that a long chain of them made the
          window as long as the chain, and a refusal anywhere in it found a witness). The width
          is the largest gap kept or measured (`limits/bursts.txt`, each burst with its run and
          its span, checked against its job's log by
          `docs/research/measurements/vcpus/bursts.py`): 1.122999 s, between 44077430171's
          musl job's VMCS dumps at 2382.272392 and 2383.395391, its burst's span 1.132342 s. A
          burst's refusals each come within the width of the one before, so no burst the
          records see widens it: only a burst measured wider does. Each measured burst's
          witnesses still came within it: CI 44076016255's gnu arm and its three first-entry
          refusals 0.532868 to 0.702252 s after it, runs_init 0.641131 s after the musl arm.
          The measured bursts came 15.4 s or more apart. Held by `limits`
          `a_long_chain_of_close_refusals_leaves_the_burst_width_unchanged` (a hundred refusals
          a tenth of the width apart: a span of nearly ten widths, the width unchanged) and
          `the_burst_width_starts_at_the_largest_gap_measured_and_no_burst_widens_it`. Written,

          --profile test-release -p shards-vmm --lib vm::limits::tests`.

          the tests that failed so: boot.rs `runs_init_as_pid_1_and_powers_off`,

          `runs_init_where_its_kernel_opened_no_console`, refused so on CI 44164945050's x86_64
          musl job (its `console=ttyS0` boot's vCPU 0, beside the `shards_api` tests' refusals).
        - *No witness yet:* a machine past its init's announcement keeps no refusal, as its
          records are let go of then; a restore keeps none either, since it is given no records.
          Their refusals are said, but witness nothing, and a restore's refusal before its guest
          ran stays a failure.
        - *Tests* (written, not run; ROOT's): vmm `vm::limits`, the gate: the observed shapes
          taken, the VMM's shape failed every run, the width measured and learned, and a
          refusal read back as said.
  - WHP's boot said as it comes. On Windows the test starts its VM process with
    `common::Vm::spawn_timed`: each line the process prints is also said on stderr as it
    comes, `D261 WHP boot <time from the spawn>: <line>`. CI's log keeps them whatever ends
    the test, its step's limit included. hvc0's first line brings the kernel's whole log, each
    record with the guest's own time (`[seconds.micros]`): its arrival dates hvc0, and the
    records date the guest's milestones (its bring-up, each initcall level).
  - No bound past which WHP's test fails. None can be derived from passes in CI, so none was
    added (R03).
    - D215's judge bounds a wait by W*, the slowest answer of its kind on its host. A CI job
      then kept no records (ci.yml cached no `target/judge-records` until *CI's judge learns
      across runs*, below), so every kind started cold and followed its party's liveness (the
      person's ruling of 2026-11-13: no record seeds).
    - Kept records would still need a pass on a nested WHP runner, and the one such run read
      since 35e2de91e did not pass (job 133508843966).
    - Smaller guests' passes bound nothing here. Sizes are kinds apart because a smaller
      storm's W* refused a larger one (HVF at ddb88cd47).
    - Before hvc0 the guest's only sign is its VM process's CPU, which a guest of more vCPUs
      than its host has CPUs shows for ever (`Cpu::Liveness`). A number of ours would be a
      seed.
    - So on a nested runner the step's 122 minutes stand until the test's readiness is
      decided (owed item 3, R02). The options:
      1. See the bring-up where it is said. The VM process tails its guest's printk ring
         while its console has said nothing, from subsys_initcall (VMCOREINFO) on.
         `Handle::console_said` already falls back to the ring, and the tests'
         `machine_ended` reads it from a running machine.
      2. On a nested Hyper-V, boot this guest as every init's guest is booted there
         (`vm::late_cpus_cmdline`, M379), and check its count from init.
      3. Keep waiting through device_initcall.
      Option 1 restores the test's scope and every boot's early log, which the UART gave.
- **The boot judged by its guest's own progress** (2026-11-17, kiln goal b2124227, lane
  whp-boot-judge). ROOT's decision of option 1 above: "judge the boot by the guest's own
  progress". The person's ruling stands: no fixed time limit (R03). No VMM change.
  - **Where the ring is read.** `boots_the_hosts_maximum_vcpu_count` boots its guest in the
    test's own process (`vm::start`), as `two_vcpus_boot_to_their_end_in_this_process` does.
    - `Handle::console_said` is the one channel shards has to a running guest's ring: it reads
      the ring while the console has carried nothing, and the tests' `machine_ended` already
      reads it so.
    - A VM process offers none. `run --kernel` quotes its ring only as its machine ends (a
      reset or an error, `vm_run.rs` `supervise`).
    - Tailing the ring in the VM process instead would be a production change with a polling
      period of its own to justify, for one test.
  - **What it sees.** The ring from subsys_initcall, when VMCOREINFO is published, until hvc0
    registers at device_initcall; the console after.
    - smp_init logs "smp: Brought up" before the first initcall level (Linux v6.18
      init/main.c `kernel_init_freeable`: `smp_init`, then `do_basic_setup`). So the ring's
      first read already holds it.
    - The test's scope is then the UART's again, plus the core, postcore and arch initcall
      levels. On nested WHP it ended at device_initcall, which the guest had not reached in
      3170 s.
  - **Its wait** (`common::guest_says`, D215's judge, tests' `Heard`). Each line the guest had
    not said before is its progress.
    - The party is this process's threads beside the waiter (`Party::machine`). For a guest of
      more vCPUs than its host has CPUs, as every host's most vCPUs are, their CPU is liveness
      alone (`Cpu::Liveness`), from the start. Before its first line too: otherwise a stall
      before any line could never be refused, even on a host that has learned this wait.
    - Its first line's wait is a kind of its own. Each line that comes begins a wait for the
      next, of a second kind, whose W* is the slowest gap between two lines seen on that host.
      Both are keyed by the call site and the arm's command-line addition.
    - Only a pass teaches them. Once the bring-up line is found, the time to the first line
      (where its wait found it missing first) and the slowest gap after it are taught and kept
      (`target/judge-records`). A wait that stalls, ends or is refused teaches nothing: gaps
      taught one by one in a host's first boot would let its early, quick gaps refuse a later,
      slower phase of the same boot.
    - Refused, its failure says each line the guest said, with when a read first found it,
      from the wait's start; each kernel line carries the guest's own `[seconds]` too.
    - The guest is read at Young's optimum of the read's own cost against the wait so far
      (`shards_api::pause`, D215's pace), and before each look the judge makes.
    - Its machine's end ends the wait, the guest's last lines read first. A guest that said
      the bring-up and then reset (its root-mount panic, `panic=-1`) has said it.
  - **The console's level.** The command line is `console=hvc0 panic=-1 loglevel=7`.
    - A machine whose console no one reads is told `quiet` unless its line names a level
      (`vm::kernel_cmdline`). `quiet` would keep the bring-up off hvc0, so a host whose ring is
      not read would never see it.
    - `loglevel=7` is CONFIG_CONSOLE_LOGLEVEL_DEFAULT in both pinned base configs
      (resources/kernel/firecracker-*-6.18.config), which shards' configs leave. It is the
      level `run --kernel` booted this guest at, its console on stdout.
    - The arms' `D261 A/B arm` lines name it in their command line.
  - **One machine a process.** Hypervisor.framework refuses a process's second VM
    (`hv_vm_create`, HV_EXISTS, hv/hvf/sys.rs). boot.rs's two in-process tests take turns
    (`MACHINE`), each holding its turn until its machine has ended: `machine_says` stops the
    machine and waits for its end before it returns.
  - **Replaced.** `common::Vm::spawn_timed` is removed. On Windows each line is said on stderr
    as the reads find it: `D261 WHP boot <time from the wait's start>: <line>`.
  - **What it cannot judge.** Before subsys_initcall the ring has no published place. Finding
    it earlier needs the kernel's symbols, which an arm64 Image does not carry.
    - A guest that never gets there says nothing, and its first line's wait follows its
      liveness until its kind has a pass on that host.
    - CI then kept no records, so every CI job's wait was cold, and on CI "fails fast" needed
      that cache. ROOT decided to keep them: *CI's judge learns across runs*, below.
  - **What the next ci.yml run's x86_64 Windows jobs should show** (grep `D261 WHP boot`):
    - Expected: a burst of lines at the ring's first read, from "Linux version" through "smp:
      Brought up 1 node, 240 CPUs" (WHP's 240 at most on GitHub's runners, NR_CPUS 255), each
      with the guest's `[seconds]`, then `boots_the_hosts_maximum_vcpu_count ... ok`. The
      `[seconds]` say how long the bring-up took and how long the core, postcore and arch
      levels took after it.
    - Or no such line, and the step's limit as before: the guest did not reach
      subsys_initcall in the time left (cold, its first line's wait follows liveness). That
      places the stall before subsys_initcall. The next decision is then D261's option 2 (late
      CPUs on nested Hyper-V) or the records' cache.
    - How long nested WHP takes to reach subsys_initcall with 240 vCPUs online is unmeasured.
      Each text patch there waits for every online CPU (PM M379).

    waited on is one with no host CPU: eight 4-vCPU guests booting at once on windows-2022's 4

    are none and every CPU comes up at boot, as the product's do. With no workload, init says

- **WHP on a nested Hyper-V: a microVM has at most the host's logical processors** (ROOT's
  ruling of 2026-11-17, R02, option 1, "scoped to what was measured").
  - **The experiment** (whp-maxvcpu.yml, run 44127161851 at 0c2eb048a: the product's boot, its
    kernel told `maxcpus=1 shards_online=1`, shards-init bringing the rest online one at a
    time; runners of 4 logical processors, nested in Azure):

    | vCPUs | runner | host CPU | init said it runs at (guest uptime) |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | 8 | windows-2025 | AMD EPYC 9V74 | 0.88 s |
    | 8 | windows-2022 | AMD EPYC 9V74 | 1.28 s |
    | 15 | windows-2025 | AMD EPYC 9V74 | 26.3 s |
    | 15 | windows-2022 | AMD EPYC 7763 | 4550 s (9,504 guest lines) |
    | 30 | windows-2025 | Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C | 2500 s (21,266 guest lines) |

    - No CPU failed to come online in these four (the record's stuck-vCPU column empty). They
      failed only their wait for the kernel's power-off line, cured by f455a80c97 (*The test
      boots as the product boots*, above).
    - Every arm from 60 vCPUs up on both images (60, 120, 240, 240 `cpuhp.parallel=0`, 240
      with the guest idle register), and 30 on windows-2022, were still running past 1.5
      hours, against their 122-minute bound.
    - Each CPU's online, by the guest's uptime at its `smpboot: Booting Node 0 Processor N`
      (the arms' records, `arm.log`). Every arm took its first 7 to 9 CPUs within 0.7 to
      2.4 s; after that each next CPU took longer than all before it:
      - 15 vCPUs, EPYC 9V74: CPU 12 at 3.4 s, 13 at 4.8 s, 14 at 14.7 s; init up at 26.3 s.
      - 15 vCPUs, EPYC 7763: CPU 10 at 9.5 s, 12 at 186 s, 14 at 1683 s; init up at 4550 s.
      - 30 vCPUs, Intel 8573C: CPU 13 at 4.0 s, 14 at 16 s, 17 at 334 s, 29 at 2259 s; init
        up at 2500 s.
    - What it waits on, plain in the records: soft lockups. 488 such lines in the EPYC 7763's
      15-vCPU guest and 1,306 in the 30-vCPU guest ("watchdog: BUG: soft lockup - CPU#N stuck
      for Ns! [migration/N]"), none in the 8-vCPU guests or the EPYC 9V74's 15. Every one of
      them sits in `multi_cpu_stop`, called from `stop_machine_from_inactive_cpu`.
      - That function has one caller, x86's `cache_ap_online` (arch/x86/kernel/cpu/
        cacheinfo.c). For each CPU coming online it holds a MTRR/PAT rendezvous in which
        every online CPU spins at once with its interrupts off. A boot skips it: smpboot.c's
        `set_cache_aps_delayed_init(true)` leaves one rendezvous after `smp_init`.
      - So each CPU brought online late needs every online vCPU running at the same time.
        On 4 logical processors it cannot, past 4, until the hosts above time-slice them
        through it. A cap at the host's logical processors is exactly where that ends.
    - So bringing CPUs online took about 0.1 s for 3 (M379), 1 s for 7, 26 s for 14 and
      41 minutes for 29: far faster growth than the count. M379's mechanism fits: each
      cross-CPU call (`smp_call_function_many_cond`, text patches' syncs, grace periods as the
      scheduler's domains are rebuilt for each CPU) waits for every online vCPU to run, and
      past 4 most of them have no host CPU. A halted vCPU costs no host thread meanwhile:
      WHP's emulated local APIC holds it in the hypervisor (hv/whp: no HLT exit).
  - **The rule.** Where WHP's x86_64 host is itself a Hyper-V nested within another Hyper-V's
